There's no doubt that this game is a classic, whether you like or not. But if it's actually held up all these years, that's a little more subjective.
Expect blocky character models and low resolution (but still quite good looking, IMO) static backgrounds, and all the spelling and grammar errors from the original PC release are still here. However, the music has been replaced, the original MIDI soundtrack is now the same music used in the Playstation release, and the game overall has been optimized to run on new systems. The actual game mechanics and combat system are solid, and the story is also still good.
If you've never played the game, don't come in expecting something that can stack up to a game released today in terms of graphical quality. If you can look past its age there's still a great game and plenty of time to be wasted in it, though. If you're looking for a nostalgia kick then it's definitely worth the price as well.
The only detractor from what's overall a good game is the extra layer of DRM, requiring a Square Enix account, but considering it can be activated with your Steam account and ignored once you set it up the first time, it's hardly a hassle.

Ah... Hotline Miami...
Let's start off by saying that Hotline Miami is a game set in 1989, you play as an un-named, silent protagonist who is commonly reffered to as "Jacket". Jacket commonly recieves phone calls which give him seemingly harmless tasks, these tasks end up being hit missions to take down the Russian Mob.
Now let's talk gameplay:
The game is from a top down perspective and relies on fast reflexes and a good eye to spot enemies. If you do not have these skills, don't worry, learning these skills isn't too difficult and you don't have to have the skills, it's just that it's easier to have them. You can use melee or ranged weapons, depending on what kind of player you are you'll use one more than the other. Before starting a level you get to choose a mask, these masks give you a different ability depending on who you choose. I'd also like to point out that you die in one hit, but so do most of your enemies (sometimes you have to finish them off).
Time for the visuals:
The game has a very retro visual style, as it is influenced by the 1980's, it's nothing too special but it's effective. I've read that the colours can disorientate players and honestly, I can agree with that. If you're not good with bright neon and a lot of camera moving, maybe this isn't for you.
Soundtrack (This is a good one):
The soundtrack is a phenomenal mix of '80's style synthwave, it's calming sometimes, but it can also be intense. You're not just playing the game, you're also listening to it! It's an excellent soundtrack, it really is!
Verdict:
The game is excellent, it's not without its flaws but if you can get by that, then I guarentee you'll have a blast playing this!

The multiplayer is pretty much dead (Unless you have friends), but you'll never get bored playing against the AI in Skirmish mode, with plenty of maps and modes to choose from.
And if that's not enough, the mods for this game are really, really good. There are plenty to choose from, including maps, factions, overhauls, customization options, and maybe more.
Just buy the game.

This was my first game bought online on steam... years ago. It's an an-and-off relationship, and recently I got back into it a little, and the old fever caught on again!
Pro:
- not much required in terms of specs (although it can blow the fan a lot in certain situations)
- UI has a great visual design
- soundtrack is fitting
- game mechanics depend on other players to work out one way or another: good online games are common
- interesting game modes, for example: diplomacy. Everyone sees everything at the beginning, being in one team. Who defects first? Lots of maneuvering and chit-chatting among parties and backstabbing! Oh the backstabbing! Boy did we have fun with that!
- can't strain this enough: the players are awesome and you need to communicate with others in larger games
- there are some mods out there
- this is a fun game that at the same time illustrated the madness of nuclear weapons in real life: you juggle multiple millions of lifes around with the press of a button! It's not about winning... it's about losing the least!
Meh:
- Units need to be selected individually, no C&C-style multi-selection. This makes it extremely fiddly when starting an all-out attack, and you definitely give away that something is going on when slowing down the game speed as is necessary
- the community is still active, albeit in small numbers: sometimes you need to wait a while to fill a server. once you find a suitable game, it's awesome.
- usually longer games. my longest was 6 hours real time!
Con:
- smaller bugs live forever: sometimes units' targets can't be switched in time, and the UI seems unresponsive. Maybe it's a feature but it comes across as a bug because this made me blow up my own stuff by accident more than once.
Verdict:
Get it. Get it now! 10 bucks are fair for this game. Sometimes it's on sale. GET IT! And then everybody dies...

To start off, I liked this game a lot, it had interesting gameplay and story.
Graphics 5/5
The graphics works really well with the environment that the story and characters were trying to portray. Each area looked beautiful with its paint style graphics. Also for the most part each area had something different to offer in the way of environment.
Story 4/5
I was extremely interested in the story. The story was pretty dynamic for how short it was. The main part of the story is Dust trying to figure out his mysterious past while he essentially helps people in need. Stories like this has definitely been done before, but for some reason Dust's story catched my interest a lot more then some others. With this said, the story left a lot of questions unanswered. For example, what was the background story for General Gaius? The story painted an interesting picture for General Gaius, but by the end, they just left General Gaius as the main Antagonist with very little explanation of why he did what he did. Also, the story could have gone two different ways. I think there could have been a possibility for two endings based off your choices. This could have made the story a little bit more interesting.
Gameplay 4.5/5
The gameplay was fun and rarely got boring. The game was a mix of 2d platform, rpg and action. You gain experience by defeating enemies and gain bonus experience depending on how high of a combo you can achieve. When you gain a level you are able to put one gem like stat point into one of the provided stats. Although levels were important it was mostly the abilities that you gained through the game that helped you the most in battle. The abilities you gained also looked extremely cool. At one point you were able to gain a fireball ability and if combined with Dust storm you were able to light most of the screen on fire torching your foes. With the right timing you were able to get a 1000 hit combo or more which was also very fun to watch and pull off. There were also many collectibles to keep you interested as well as challenge courses. I found the challenge courses difficult enough to get me angry after the 20th attempt which was fun but also a painful experience. The cameo characters were fun and sometimes difficult to find as well. These collectibles and challenges were not needed, but was a fun diversion from the main storyline. For the most part the gameplay was very well thought out but there were a few issues that I had with the gameplay. The combat was fun but did get repetitive at times. I feel like there needed to be more variety of skills to use, to keep the game from getting boring. The issue of repetitiveness was some what remedied by the shortness of the game, but I feel if the game went any longer I would have gotten very bored with the combat. Also near the end of the game I felt like I was overpowered. This may not be an issue with the game though considering I was probably overleveling while I was trying to get all the collectibles and finishing all the challenges.
Sound/Music   5/5
Nothing much to say here. The music and sound effects made sense for the environments and situations. The music sounded very good as well.
Replayability 2/5
Im trying to replay the game on a harder difficulty for the last few achievements but I find myself to lack the motivation to finish the game for the second time. There really isnt any thing different if you play it a second time besides the possibility to obtain some achievements and playing a more difficult setting. So a game plus option would have been nice or maybe a secret chapter where you can play as General Gaius and so on.
Overall this game was amazing and well worth the money.

I think after 460 hours of play I’m ready to give a review for Duck Game.
Duck Game is a gift from the universe, much like Beethoven’s 6th Symphony, or the strong bond of companionship between two lifelong friends. It is one of those secrets of the world that once you find you will cherish forever.
What makes Duck Game so great is that whether you’ve just begun your first hour or have been playing for nearly 20 days’ worth of time, it is FUN. Pure, boundless, FUN.
There is no other game I have EVER played where I have laughed EVERY SINGLE TIME I have played the game. I remember, about 20 hours in, talking to people in game saying how every time I had played so far I had laughed and that it was blowing my mind. This is still true to this day. Every single time I play this game, at some point, I will laugh, without fail. Can you name another game that has done this for you? And, what more can you really ask for from a game that’s only $13?
Well, Duck Game gives you more than just that. Duck Game is, in addition to a bundle of joy no matter how much time you sink in, DEEP in terms of mechanics and skill, if you’re looking for that too. There is so much to learn playing this game, that, despite being relatively good (at least, in terms of who’s actively on these days), I am still learning things about this game each and every day. And that learning is part of the fun itself.
The first day I was actually able to pull off angling, I was SO happy. The first few times I could incorporate that into my actual gameplay, I felt like a god. Now it's part of how I play. Vert-stance with a sword, pogoing, and gun-jumping come to mind as other mechanics you’ll develop that increase the speed of your game and change the way you fundamentally perceive it and interact with it. I only mention those for people who have played the game to empathize with where I’m coming from, as you don’t actually need to know what any of that means or how to use it to play the game; a lot of it just comes naturally with time and patience. You’ll go from focusing on yourself and being surprised that a box just crushed you (which is always hilarious) to simultaneously watching four players move their ducks as you engage in what becomes akin to a complex, beautiful dance. It shifts from a random mess of joy into a controlled chaos that, while a slightly different in terms of an overall experience, is still INCREDIBLY fun. You’ll find yourself developing from a bumbling duckling struggling to climb platforms into a hardened mallard gliding around the map with the grace of a renowned ballerina who also happens to be shooting AK47’s and rocket launchers.
And even though it does take time to develop such elegance, the journey is part of the fun. Although there is a lot to learn and it will take a while to soak it all in, you don’t have to be some duck-pro to have fun playing this game. A death in the most ridiculous manner will make you laugh whether you’re playing your first match or your five-hundredth.
I hope that all sounds dandy, but it’s not even the icing on the cake. In addition to being a basket of bliss with surprisingly deep skill to pick up over time, the final part of what makes Duck Game the absolute blast of an experience that it is, is the community. Of course there are people who can be salty just like in any community, but in my experience, for the most part, the people who play this game are good, fun people. If I had to guess, it might be because this game draws out happiness in you and almost forces you to enjoy the ride, and getting to do so with others multiplies that joy.
You will share laughs and moments with so many people if you play this game, and to me that in itself makes Duck Game more than just a video game. It becomes an experience. It will change you, or at the very least, I feel it has changed me. I feel like a better person having had the joy of experiencing this game. Perhaps that’s just a reflection of my own life, but when I compare who I was when I first got Duck Game to who I am today, it is a world of difference. Did Duck Game do that by itself? Of course not. But having a constant source of laughs and being able to share those with my fellow duckgamers certainly has had a positive impact on who I am today. I am a happier person having played this game, and I think you will be too if you give it a shot.

I'm a huge fan of Monkey Island, Myst, and Sam & Max, so I confess my guilt and confusion that Deponia flew entirely under my radar for a long time.
However, upon a friend's recommendation, once I sat down to play it, I didn't stop until I'd finished the entire trilogy.
The reasons why it absorbed me are easy to identify: Story, World, and Characters.
The Story is fairly standard at a glance. It's about a self-centered antihero who thinks he deserves a better lot in life who by the end begrudgingly helps to save the world he so desperately wants to get away from. But escalating complexities in each character's conflicting motivations leaves you never quite sure who to root for, or who even to trust. Ultimately, it's a story about how people learn to tolerate each other.
The World is perhaps even more compelling. On the surface, it appears to be a mix of steampunk, science fiction, post-apocalypse. The setting bounces between the garbage planet Deponia and the the floating utopia Elysium, and sets up a class struggle between them. But there's also a message about prejudice in the way it demonstrates the vibrancy and resilience of people who eke out a living among garbage, or the complacency that breeds in sterile environments.
The Characters, however, made this game entirely. I said that it was a story about how people learn to tolerate each other, and to clarify, it's a story about people, none of which are innocent of selfishness or short-sightedness. But most of all, it's about how we as the player can learn to tolerate our antihero protagonist. And conversely, antagonists who seemed to be cut-and-dry evil begin to show more nuance. Even the female lead and romantic interest, who seems to be the moral touchstone and voice of reason behaves in strange ways that contradict her character.
Ultimately its cartoon animation and colorful art belies its deeper adult themes, partly because the characters are wonderful and hilarious, and partly because you have to cope with all the things you've done to them.

Hotline Miami is certainly not the easiest game I've played, which is (in my opinion) one of its biggest draws. The game is not very forgiving, sending you back to the last stage you completed whenever you die. Because all enemies can very easily one-hit you, you'll be seeing a single stage
times. Although you will be dying a lot during your playthrough of Hotline Miami it will always be
fault and not the game's. Dying means you have the chance to re-think the way you attempted the stage you failed and improve off of it.
A decent portion of Hotline Miami's story is left up to the player's interpretation. Completing an in-game puzzle answers a lot of questions the game may leave you with but I personally felt as if the fifth chapter in the game explained more than enough. Because the game doesn't spoon-feed you answers this could easily be considered a negative for yourself.
I couldn't see the full game (minus collectibles and achievements) taking you over ten hours. If you do decide to 100% Hotline Miami, I'm sure you could definitely add an extra twenty hours to your count. This game is also very replayable in my opinion.

Picked this up in a sale in a sale a while back. Looked like a nice casual match-3 with a retro twist. Well, the second part is certainly true, but I'm no longer so sure about the casual part.
In 10,000,000 the player character is controlled by matching 3 or more of the same tiles as he runs through dungeons. The actions range from attacking encountered monsters to collecting resources to opening doors and chests. So far it sounds simple, and perhaps still qualifies as a casual game. Now add to the whole mix some serious time pressure -- the time limits for the dungeons are very tight, and the only way to add time is to keep matching large sets of tiles and scoring combos; on the other hand just about anything in the dungeon is hell-bent on reducing your remaining time! Enemy attacks drain your time, doors and chests block your way until opened, and all you have to rely on is a randomly-populated board of tiles. Yeah, not so casual anymore.
On top of the match-3 dungeon runs there are castle upgrades (well, rebuilding the prison you're in) which unlock upgrades and perks that help deal with whatever awaits in the dungeon. Trick? It all requires significant amounts of resources, which have to be collected during dungeon runs. This is the grindy part -- wood and stone require luck in actually getting the required tiles on the board, and even then provide small amounts; gold is given for completing quests (more later) and as a stipend after each run. You're not getting anywhere without hundreds of runs, that's for sure.
To help motivate the players during long and boring runs there are in-game quests that give rewards. At any time there are 3 active quests, and any completed ones are replaced at the start of the next run. However, quests have a more important role than just motivation and rewards -- completing certain numbers of quests allows the PC to advance to a higher rank and gain access to more upgrades, perks, and better dungeons. Higher level dungeons have more difficult monsters but carry a larger score multiplier (up to 120x for the last dungeon!) and this multiplier is pretty much the only way to reach (in a single run!) the required 10kk points needed to finish the game.
Overall 10,000,000 is quite an enjoyable game, if a bit grindy. The pace in each run is fast enough that it leaves no time to remember that this is in fact the 100th time you're running this dungeon. It's a bit more noticeable when you look at the upgrade prices and remember just how little you earn per run. But that's nothing bad enough to ruin the fun. I sank some 5 hours into it, and that somehow was enough to beat the game once (10589378 points). I've since replayed the game to grab remaining achievements.

Mysterious Stranger, the badass, appears pretty often, who gives caps, random amount, sometimes can be a pain to find on time, but still fun.
Maybe an Elder Scrolls game, like Fallout Shelter, would be fun? Who knows!
Overall, very fun game, definitely recommend.

I think after 460 hours of play I’m ready to give a review for Duck Game.
Duck Game is a gift from the universe, much like Beethoven’s 6th Symphony, or the strong bond of companionship between two lifelong friends. It is one of those secrets of the world that once you find you will cherish forever.
What makes Duck Game so great is that whether you’ve just begun your first hour or have been playing for nearly 20 days’ worth of time, it is FUN. Pure, boundless, FUN.
There is no other game I have EVER played where I have laughed EVERY SINGLE TIME I have played the game. I remember, about 20 hours in, talking to people in game saying how every time I had played so far I had laughed and that it was blowing my mind. This is still true to this day. Every single time I play this game, at some point, I will laugh, without fail. Can you name another game that has done this for you? And, what more can you really ask for from a game that’s only $13?
Well, Duck Game gives you more than just that. Duck Game is, in addition to a bundle of joy no matter how much time you sink in, DEEP in terms of mechanics and skill, if you’re looking for that too. There is so much to learn playing this game, that, despite being relatively good (at least, in terms of who’s actively on these days), I am still learning things about this game each and every day. And that learning is part of the fun itself.
The first day I was actually able to pull off angling, I was SO happy. The first few times I could incorporate that into my actual gameplay, I felt like a god. Now it's part of how I play. Vert-stance with a sword, pogoing, and gun-jumping come to mind as other mechanics you’ll develop that increase the speed of your game and change the way you fundamentally perceive it and interact with it. I only mention those for people who have played the game to empathize with where I’m coming from, as you don’t actually need to know what any of that means or how to use it to play the game; a lot of it just comes naturally with time and patience. You’ll go from focusing on yourself and being surprised that a box just crushed you (which is always hilarious) to simultaneously watching four players move their ducks as you engage in what becomes akin to a complex, beautiful dance. It shifts from a random mess of joy into a controlled chaos that, while a slightly different in terms of an overall experience, is still INCREDIBLY fun. You’ll find yourself developing from a bumbling duckling struggling to climb platforms into a hardened mallard gliding around the map with the grace of a renowned ballerina who also happens to be shooting AK47’s and rocket launchers.
And even though it does take time to develop such elegance, the journey is part of the fun. Although there is a lot to learn and it will take a while to soak it all in, you don’t have to be some duck-pro to have fun playing this game. A death in the most ridiculous manner will make you laugh whether you’re playing your first match or your five-hundredth.
I hope that all sounds dandy, but it’s not even the icing on the cake. In addition to being a basket of bliss with surprisingly deep skill to pick up over time, the final part of what makes Duck Game the absolute blast of an experience that it is, is the community. Of course there are people who can be salty just like in any community, but in my experience, for the most part, the people who play this game are good, fun people. If I had to guess, it might be because this game draws out happiness in you and almost forces you to enjoy the ride, and getting to do so with others multiplies that joy.
You will share laughs and moments with so many people if you play this game, and to me that in itself makes Duck Game more than just a video game. It becomes an experience. It will change you, or at the very least, I feel it has changed me. I feel like a better person having had the joy of experiencing this game. Perhaps that’s just a reflection of my own life, but when I compare who I was when I first got Duck Game to who I am today, it is a world of difference. Did Duck Game do that by itself? Of course not. But having a constant source of laughs and being able to share those with my fellow duckgamers certainly has had a positive impact on who I am today. I am a happier person having played this game, and I think you will be too if you give it a shot.

From what I have played so far, I can tell you that this game is a very unique experience.
The game is an early access, FPS shooter. There are currently three gamemodes, Strike, Anamoly, and Coop. The game is a test of speed and skill as you try to complete each level as fast as you can to earn higher medals. The levels aren't a walk in the park either, they are all very challenging, and if you don't have the patience to repeatedly play levels over and over to get the highest medal, don't buy this.
The graphics are very nice. They are above average for a game like this, and compliment it nicely. The game has many graphics options which affect the performance. On a mid-range machine on high settings, I get around 50-60 fps. No complaints there.
The level designs are very cool and are part of the reason the game is so challenging. The levels are a decent size, but usually very narrow, or make you go in a narrow path. The constrictive environment makes the game more difficult, and I personally really like this idea.
Strike involves levels with robotic-looking enemies with guns and turrets. You have to run through the level as quick as you can without dying. Pretty straightforward, but can be difficult.
Anamoly is my personal favorite, but unfortunately doesn't have nearly as many levels as Strike. You have to run through the constrictive environments as quick as you can while trying to fight through a horde of zombies. Difficult, but fun, and the zombies are very cool.
I have not been able to test Coop due to the lack of players. Will update when I try it.
The developers seem devoted to the game, and I have no problem giving them 15 bucks for this game, it's worth it. They are committed to making the game the best it can be, and appreciate feedback. Updates aren't too far apart from each other, and add a decent amount of content. This game has a lot of potential, and the developers know that.
Things that I think would be great for this game:
A co-op zombie mode, where you fight waves of zombies until your team dies. I would personally love to see this.
Steam Workshop to allow people can share levels.
Map editor, a tool to create and share custom levels via Steam Workshop.
Custom gamemodes, it'd be cool for this game to be able to have user-created gamemodes like Garry's Mod.
Campaign? Not sure if there are plans for this or not, but it would be cool to have a story driven campaign mode for this game.
Weapon customization, weapon and health pickups on maps, and explosive weapons (RPGs, grenades).
Overall this game is great, and if you want to support it in its alpha stage, then buy it.

Overall, The Witcher 2 is a geat game, with an immersive storyline that reacts to your actions, good gameplay, and fantastic graphics.
For newcomers, I would recommend buying the game for the reasons listed in the description. What you do actually changes how the game plays. The dynamic story system was enhanced from the first game, since this time the quests available in Chapter 2 depend on a Chapter 1 decision (the Witcher 1 story wasn't impacted as much, though still a great story). The combat system isn't simply frantically clicking the LMB: you can do fast or strong strikes, counter-attack, etc. The graphics are fantastic: framerate was smooth with medium specs on an nVidia Geforce GT 740M, and the game looked nice.
Still, I disliked some things. A lot of the story was devoted to Geralt dealing with politics and intrigue. While the books also involve politics, there were less opportunites than in the first game to go out into the wild and kill monsters (example: when night sets in Act I of Witcher 1 and the phantom hounds come out). The first game made you feel unique as a witcher, since you had a special role as a monster-hunter, but here you could almost (I say almost) be any warrior/hunter/mage. The story has more and more politics going from Chapter 1 to 2 to 3, and it felt that the settings got correspondingly less interesting. Chapter 1 is fantastic, since you arrive in a well-depicted gritty outpost surrounded by a gorgeous forest, but I lost some interest as the game went on. Unlike the first game, there's not as much humour or light-heartedness Also, playing on normal difficulty, I found that a lot of new gameplay elements were unnecessary, like daggers and mutagens.
Fans of the first game might not agree with my thoughts  above (and the Witcher 2 is still a great game in its own right), so I would still recommend that they try this game. Story-wise, I would say that I prefer the first game.

The Witcher 2 is a phenomenally beautiful piece of RPG-storytelling that should be experienced by any and all fans of the genre, as well as fans of branching narratives and book-based media (authored by Andrzej Sapkowski).
Continuing immediately from where The Witcher 1 left off, Assassins of Kings dives into a rich story environment that pushes the player instantly into the lives of the fantastically vivid protagonists, yet this is no turn off for anyone who has yet to play the first game... In fact, it wasn't until my second playthrough that I actually purchased The Witcher 1 (and though largely the lesser in terms of quality, it remains a game I very much recommend). The Witcher 2 is no mere linear story: it is a game that forces the player to make decisions from multi-faceted issues without black-and-white morality and without any dominant strategy, splitting one section of the game into two completely independent chapters (increasing the replay value) and creating eight different possible game endings. The decisions the player makes affect not only the short term of the protagonists' lives, but the long term consequences that can save or destroy whole peoples (or both). This intricacy of the narrative is in my personal opinion the greatest reason to play and explore the game the way CD Projekt RED wanted it to be known.
The RPG elements and mechanics of the game are solid and simple enough for beginners and complex enough for those seeking the Insane difficulty and RPG experience. I personally recommend a mod to increase the amount of talents that can be distributed per each Level Up (2 or 3), as one may find themselves only having explored little of the Witcher's skills with the sluggish, vanilla XP-based system that provides only one per Level Up. Aside from this system, the game requires players to strategize their consumables and equipment for most combat encounters, as the necessity of potions, sword oils, and magic eliminate the Nash Equilibrium problem that can detract from the challenge of combat. The player is equipped with a steel and a silver sword, for normal and for monster encounters, respectively. Though The Witcher 2 differs from its predecessor by changing swordplay from style-based (strong, swift, or group attacks) to simple fast/heavy attacks as one might see in a hack-n-slash. Though I feel this new system is unusual, the game's environment allows it to coexist appropriately enough with the rest of the combat mechanics.
Thus concludes the two most important components of gameplay I believe important to the game. From a critical standpoint, the only naysaying I may have to do is in regards to the gamepad functionality and various cutscene bugs within the game, two of the most notable problems in a list of mostly irrelevant and petty whinings. In regards to the gamepad, I use an Xbox 360 controller and though gameplay is smooth, some button pressing and joystick adjusting requires that I first let go of other buttons, which I feel should just be a problem that is only for keyboards. This is an issue that is not existent on the actual Xbox 360 version of the game, and though a nuisance I find it as such not troubling to any greater degree. The other problem is with cutscenes, in which when skipping snippets of dialogue one may see that they have skipped the line afterwards, too, which is a problem for those of us who can read subtitles faster than their voices can finish, especially in important cutscenes.
Again, these criticisms are grains of sand to a desert, and I must say that The Witcher 2: Assassins of Kings was one of the first RPGs I played that hooked me on the genre. It is an epic tale with exciting gameplay.

Now I'd like to talk about the NS2 community.  They aren't really that mean.  l'd consider myself to be a less than average player, but it's very "RARE" that someone will actually attack a new player. I wrote this review to try to counteract the nay sayers who believe the community was out to get them.
NS2 has a very high learning curve. But if you are human, you can learn.
This game could be considered a Rock Paper Scissors game, if you look at it generically.  Every tactic has a counter tactic, and if one team is supposedly winning, then the other team will supposedly lose. It's quite balanced in that sense. But I have seen some genius commanders that have pulled their team out from being down to their last base, and on the defensive, to winning the game. It's very rare, but it does happen from time to time. (Our team had full upgrades though; 'twas a very fun game :P)
Now lets talk about the marine and alien teams.
As a marine, new players will probably see it as a fairly standard first person shooter.  But I will not lie to you; this is one of the fastest first person shooters I have ever played, and team work needs to be extremely cohesive.  Moving together as a squad, and keeping your fellow marines covered at all times. Or as a lone ninja, attack enemy structures, or maybe through stealth secure a new phase gate point for your team to back you up. It's all dependant on the ebb and flow of the battle. As an alien; same kind of thing.  New players, as aliens, will find this game fairly difficult.  The aliens are melee based, yet they can move fast and need to rely on ambush tactics until endgame, where they have enough resources to all go onos and stomp everything in sight. Unless you are playing against an expert marine commander / team, then you will actually have to learn how to use all life forms, and coordinate accordingly.  Yet with all this speed at your disposal, you WILL get disorientated.
And trying to maintain focus is very VERY hard.  But as I've said before, you are human and you can learn.
I had about 600 hours up, running around on the ground before I started commanding. And I'm still not that good. I'm reasonable sometimes, but one mistake can destroy the team. If you choose to  command, most of the Vets will help you a lot. But you have to be fast enough, otherwise they will eject you from the commanders chair. If you arent familiar with commanding, try learning the command chair in single player with the bots, just to learn how to place and use structures.
I was in a server with a marine commander that had a bit over ten hours in the game and we let him command; just to see if he could win for us.  We lost of course, but he was at least listening to the veterans, and learnt a few things.  But that was in a noob friendly server. Do not try to command as a newbie in pro servers, or you will generally be kicked instantly.  Unless of course it's a seeding game, and no one cares.
The best way to learn command is to watch other great commanders.  Watch what they do from the ground. For many hours. Especially in the pro servers.
It's the only way to build skill in this game. Listen to your team mates, and listen to your commander. Learn the maps first. AND, if you do choose to command, use voice chat or learn to type 1000 words a minute :P
Voice chat is integral for letting your team mates know about the other teams movement on the map. If you see the enemy moving to a certain part of the map, or you see that they are setting up forward bases, let your team mates know about it.  Players aren't always pushing C to bring up the map to get an overview of the battlefield.  They may be locked in combat, and might have missed something that you have seen.  Not the veterans generally, but there are sometimes newer players on your side that may need a heads up to let them know they have enemy heading their way.
The Veterans in this game didn't get where they are through rage quitting. They've put in a lot of hard work to get where they are now. And they have gotten stomped too; many times.
I'm currently a bit over 1000 hours and I'm still getting stomped.  But I love this game, and I'm always learning new things from the Vets.
The shuffle system in NS2 will put veterans on your team based on hive skill. The teams will be relatively balanced at the start of a match. But if someone is having a bad day, and someone on the other team is having a good day. Then your team will lose.
Unfortunately, nobody as of yet has developed a precognitive shuffle system, which can detect who is going to have a good day or a bad day in this game.  And the Veterans who have thousands of hours up, are still getting stomped right alongside the new players on their team. In EVERY match that I have ever played.
Someone has to lose in this game.  It's NS2

Pros:
For the most part, excellent physics.  This includes mud, water, and truck handling.
Nice graphics.
Lots to do.
Good replayability.
Excellent sounds.
Cons:
No "behind-the-wheel" view.
Toxic developer-publisher relationship.
Note: this review is for single-player - I have not tried multiplayer.
Overall, I highly recommend this.  The point of the game is to deliver logs through rural Russia to sawmills out in the middle of nowhere.  Mostly you are on dirt roads, though some are paved.  Sometimes you'll need to forge out into the wilderness without a road.  Other places the roads are so muddy you're actually driving through standing water.  The game has very realistic looking creeks you can drive through as well.  The game comes with about a half dozen different and challenging maps.
When you get stuck in the mud, you can winch to a tree or another vehicle to try to get out.  The game also comes with several different vehicles.  Most of which you can switch to all wheel drive and lock the differential to help navigate through the tough spots.  You'll have to manage your fuel usage, though the game gives you options to refuel although this itself is sometimes a challenge.  Once you get to the logs, you get to operate a crane to load your logs, then drive them on to the mill.
Maps are also obscured and you have to unlock portions of them as you explore.
As to the cons, there is no behind the wheel view as of today (11 Sept. 2016) so you'll be viewing everything from 3rd person.  The camera controls are a little clunky, but with experience you get the hang of it.  There is a way you can lock the camera on top of the truck cab - this is as close to 1st person as you can get.  The developer and publisher don't seem to play nice together.  Once the game quit working for everyone - accusations of sabatoge started flying, dev claimed it was a bug.  This was resolved in a few days, but players remained a bit wary that something like this could happen again.  That was months ago, and nothing similar has happened since.

The Binding of Isaac is a fun and addictive flash game well worth the price you're paying for it.
I have already put more hours in this simple little flash of 5 euros full priced than in a ''Next-gen revolutionary'' game.
The gameplay is easy to learn and understand and the later levels are always challenging.
But all good things must have a bad side.
Once you get an fair amount of items the game starts dropping in framerate which can be a bit frustrating.
Also the game can get really easy or really difficult depending on certain item drops.
Such as the ''Mom's knife'' and ''Sacred Heart'' combo which basicly allows you to 1-shot almost all enemies in the game (Including bosses).
Otherwise it is possible to receive only activateable items which you can only carry 1 of at a time, resulting in getting no proper stats making the game near-impossible to complete.
All things set aside I think it's a great game which is fun to play or watch others play.
The price can drop below 2 euros during steam sales so if you need a fun game that's easy to pick up, look no further!

First off, I have to admit, I fell in love with the opening sequence. It's the perfect blend of music, plot, voice acting and a beat to get me hyped all the hell when I start it up. DROP DEAD!
The game is really enjoyable. It's a Roguelike, but it feels less dependent on luck, and more on skill and planning then most others. I don't generally feel like I was screwed too hard when I die; As far as I can see it, you should be able to clear the game without getting hit, or at least close, if you're god-like at pattern recognition.
Every enemy has it's own pattern, which, I can't believe the game didn't refer to as it's unique Dance. Maybe it's too corny. As Cadence (oh, there's the corniness. Works, though.) remarks, 'learn that, and they'll never harm you.' (something like that.)
I think the one negative I've had in dealing with the game is in using items and spells. It's not impossible, but it takes a good deal getting used to. You only have 4 keys, the 4 directions. To use items, you combine them. Ex, an apple is Up+Left, or whatnot. Keeping your combo going while using them very rarely works out for me in the heat of a battle.
But, even then, you can bind those combinations to other keys, if you like. Up+Left could be bound to Ctrl, or Shift, or Left trigger.
Yes, it works with gamepads. Personally, I bound XBAY and the Dpad to all directions applicable. If your one hand gets tired, switch to the other! Or, if you have a Left+Right item, it works well using both hands, I find, so it's Left+B instead.
Aaaaanyway. Graphics are fine. Gameplay is fun (first level's tempo is a liiitle slow for my taste), and the feeling on beating a boss is rewarding. King Conga and his Zombie Conga Lines (yes) confused the hell out of me the first time, but when you learn it, it's just plain fun.
In short, I love installing large screen televisions in doghouses, and Crypt of the NecroDancer is a good game.

I usually don't buy Early Access games. Reasons are plenty and some of you have probably exprerienced some of them yourself, so I'm not going to go deep into that.
This game however (I'm happy to admit), proved me wrong.
As always, for those who like their reviews short - TL;DR is at the bottom
BIOS is as simple as a brick yet very deep at the same time. It tries to be a 90's old school hardcore no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t shooter and it plays and feels like one. It's very easy to pick up and play but quite hard to really master.
There is no story to speak of, just you, Finish line, enemies in between and a timer. Based on your success, you'll be rewarded with one of the 4 possible medals be it bronze or platinum. Devs are talking about implementing some kind of narrative elements to it, so some kind of story could be available later. #storymodeconfirmed (ha ha)
There are 21 challenges and 3 anomalies spread across 8 different environments to run & gun through. Environments vary from industrial complex, training facility, subway tunnels, ports and parking spots. Maps are short in length but highly replayable, well made and balanced.
Enemy placement is great. You actually have to learn and memorize their placements and attacks to succeed, so when you die, it's usually your own fault and not some cheap enemy spawn behind your back.
To counter this, BIOS needs tight and responsible controls, and they are. Mouse controls felt weird to begin with, but some fiddling in settings helped. Keys are few, and completely rebindable to your preference.
Graphics are nothing groundbreaking but they do their job pretty well. Lighting and explosions looks great and some environments are destructible, even though I can honestly say that you'll probably be too busy to notice since game is so fast paced. I know I was. There is a lot of graphic settings you can fiddle with to make it work.
Sounds and music are superb. Guns sounds really great and punchy, while music is kickass and fits the setting and theme well in my opinion.
BIOS is also surprisingly very well optimized and runs smooth as butter on my relatively old PC. I have played it for a few hours and except for a few FPS drops on 1 anomaly map, haven't experienced any bugs or glitches.
There are only 3 guns (SCAR, M4 and AK with some variations) in this game and they feel completely the same (except SCAR have 20 round mag while M4/AK has 30). At least they did for me.
You also can't change your loadout since guns are tied to specific maps. Like this M4? Can't have it, since this map only spawn you with AK!
Animations are simple and feels a bit unfinished.
As said before, maps are small, short and can be completed in 2- max 10 min each, with heavy emphasis on replayability.
If you're not into that kind of thing, you'll run through it in 1 hour flat and be disappointed.
This game is also pretty challenging, as in you die really fast if you stay in one place for more than 2 seconds. To be honest, this game is built for mostly hardcore players, so it's not for everyone.
Yet I personally think that some enemies need few damage tweaks, since some places are extremely hard, because enemies melt you before you even can react to their presence.
BIOS is a very fun and addictive game, and I'm having a blast playing it.
It's fast, it's challenging and it runs extremely well for an Early Access title. It is at the moment a little bit low on features but, developers seem dedicated and more content is in the works, like progression system, guns, maps, coop etc.
Hopefully, full release will be even better, more action packed and even more enjoyable. I almost can't wait :)

Name describes it well: in
you have to draw pictures by dragging lines between dots of the same color. The number in each dot shows how long the line is. You can't drag over another line.
Level design is overall excellent. The game begins with some extremely easy puzzles that show off the game mechanics of dragging. The puzzles gradually get larger, more complex and more difficult.
But only up to a point. The limit is set at a distinct length of 12, and no puzzle is larger than 25x25. Small puzzles keep the difficulty relaxed and lead to short completion times that are fit for a casual coffee-break-style game.
And to feed thy urge for completion, every beaten level is generously (sometimes even gratuitously) awarded with a single shiny achievement.
Graphically,
is really neat: abstract, with clear buttons and easy to view interface. The pictures are obviously pixel-art, simple but rather beautiful.
There's absolutely no story but the pictures have some recurring themes, like dragons, dinosaurs, cats, dogs, other animals and the occasional cartoon character or abstract symbol.
Note that the visual background is milky white, and there is no way to change it, so it might hurt your eyes if played in a dark room.
Background theme music has a few tracks of fitting, sometimes invigorating and othertimes relaxing tunes. I found myself speeding through the puzzles with certain themes and slowing down with the rest, so I think they did their job well.
As of writing, there's over 200 (official) puzzles to complete, an option to try out totally random ones, and to play through huge mozaic-type puzzles, that are made out of several puzzles.
Level editor allows you draw your own puzzles or even to import your own
files to create them. The editor will then automatically generate a puzzle out of the image. Infinite levels, yey!
I've got to note that mozaic/jigsaw puzzles do suffer from the usual dullness of jigsaw puzzles, with huge monochromatically colored "empty" areas being rather dull and arduous (and also the most difficult) experiences.
In the end, I spent 13.5 hours beating the 229 puzzles that were present at the time of writing. Just a few days ago five more official puzzles were added. I wouldn't be surprised if the content grew even more in the upcoming weeks/months.
Yeah, I liked what I played, and would likely spent a few bored hours more to relax with more of
s. Recommended at full price ($5)!

FF7 is not the best game ever made. It's not even the best Final Fantasy game ever made. That doesn't mean it's not quite good, however.
I'll be relatively short and blunt here: FF7 did have some really annoying flaws. Grinding for levels for an hour or two in the middle of the plot just to continue past a boss, not knowing if certain characters may randomly disappear from your party without much warning, some rather annoying minigames and so on, that kinda thing.
However... these are relatively minor nitpicks. Overall, the game's pretty much good by any standard. It has mostly likable characters with a wide range of personalities to choose from for your party to fit your play style, it has all the OCD joy of maxing out your characters and getting all the best stuff, and the plot really wasn't bad at all, nor were the mechanics.
As a whole, FF7 is a classic because it did everything RIGHT. It does have minor flaws, but even in those they can be argued as being part of the genre at the time and what players were actually looking for in their JRPGs back then. There's no really huge glaring problems with FF7, and it shows: it's polished in almost every way possible... perhaps not to a SHINE, but it's distinctly obvious that it has at least some polish to it.
To that end, it's actually a very reasonable option, even to this day, to introduce new players to RPGs in general, as it did back when it was new. I can still go back and play through it every 2-3 years and actually enjoy myself quite thoroughly each time, even with knowing what happens.
Personally, I'm an FFT girl myself. Not FFTA, just FFT for the PSX. It had better writing, better plot, better characterization, better mechanics, more interesting combat, and was just generically better as a whole overall. But... FF7 is still really fun, even if it does have it's share of mildly frustrating points here and there.
Final Verdict:
FF7 really did do just about everything right. It didn't truly shine in any one area, but it didn't really have any particularly stand-out bad areas either. It's solid enough to stand the test of time and still be fun today. Some people who actively HATE JRPG's may want to avoid it, however, but if you like RPGs otherwise, it's still one of the best out there and is worth picking up just to understand references made to it to this day; it's a cultural thing like the Godfather, or Spaceballs are to movies. You just can't not play it, really.
Overall Score: About 80%. It's well worth the $11.99 normal price, even when not on sale, and if you've never tried a final fantasy game before, it's a good introduction to the series.

I would give this 5/10
It would have been a fine game. The jumping from shadow to shadow was nice, as were some other abilities. It does have quite a few problems that make it look unpolished at least.
For example, for a game where sneaking is your main way of moving, as all enemies kill you in one hit with quite a distance, you can't hug walls or look around corners better than with just the third person camera.
The twist in the story is painfully obvious and can be guessed just 20 minutes in. Skip this paragraph if you don't want this spoiler but believe me, it will be no surprise. Least the game could have done was "your" side being the light clan and the ones you fight against being the shadow one, so that the twist would have been a bit more of a surprise, though it would still have been obvious.
The level design is nice enough, but there's never any hidden path for you to follow to emerge behind enemies. In fact, there's no "behind" as at least 80% of he enemies constantly walk around.
The speakers seem to be japanese, which I don't understand, or a made up language for all I know, but there's no way the subtitles in any way fits what was said. Some times the subtitles are paragraphes and what was said are 3 words. It would have been better without any voice, really.
You can distract enemies, but only with bells you carry, since aparently, you can't even throw stones. You gotta be pretty near for them to hear the bells, so the best way to distract enemies is to just stand out in the open until they got suspicious and the teleport to a shadow, that works with larger distances.
The graphics are stylisch and look nice, but objectively, they're quite dated. A tree without leaves, for example, has as many polygons as it would have had in an AAA game 10 years or more ago. The graphics never distracted me, so that is good, but I thought I should mention it.
But all of that could have been forgiven, it wasn't a story dense game anyway and mainly fun to play, which is after all the main point of any game. A game can look the greatest ever and still be crap if it isn't fun to play, and a game can look like undertale and still be fun.. save for 4 mayor points that really transform the game from "fun but not great" to "frack this game". In order of severity:
1. No quick way to kill. You get two ways to kill enemies, a normal attack and a shadow attack which you have to unlock. both of these take about 2 seconds (with initiation of the shadow one being an additional second). There's no way at all to swoop in, kill an enemy, flee. In a game where the paths and vision cones of the enemies often interlock and you have to go in in the short time an enemy is free, that is a real flaw. In fact, killing takes so long, in case you alerted the enemies and they go searching you, and one wanders off from the rest.. The search party will probably have come in range again and spotted you by the time you finally killed him, meaning whenever they search you, you can do nothing but hide. The only quicker way is the aerial attack but that one's pretty bugged, see 2.
2. No other ways to kill and no way to dispose nonviolently. One enemy at a time, always the same way, two different animations every time. There's no way to kill two that stand right next to each other, there's no way to use the environment to do it. You can, in fact, drop on an enemy to kill him, but that function is so bugged that I often had to run around a ledge several times until I finally found a spot to do it. There's an unlockable ability to kill enemies on a ledge from below, but I had not yet had any chance to use this, as enemies below climbable ledges are really rare. I don't think I saw even one since I bought that ability.
Not a single way to dispose of an enemy without killing him. Even stealthy games that gave you the option to run and gun instead, like Deus Ex, had options to take an enemy out of the game without killing him. That means on a no-kill run, you have to run away all the time, making it really not much fun to play.
3. The bosses are absolutely unfair. The whole game you've trained yourself to hide in the shadow and sneak and plot your path. Both bosses before the end one have a sixth sense to know exactly where you are. Disappointing but still kinda fine with the first one, as he rather slowly just walks in your direction and does not attack until he actually saw you, so you can stay far away from him until you dispatched the other enemies in the area.
The second boss though is a sniper sitting in a tall tower that sees you as soon as you are in line of sight, no matter if in the shadows or not, and teleports to a different tower as soon as you get too near. This was OK at first, as you leaped from cover to cover up to the tower, but later, normal enemies were introduced. Because there's no way of quickly dispatching of an enemy (see 1), killing someone that is in line of sight of the sniper results in your death, and since you usually teleport to a shadow near the enemy, you often only know it was when it's already too late. A shadow patch looks ideal to kill the enemy so you teleport there? too bad the sniper can see you. If that wasn't enough, there is a thunderstorm going on, so even if you are in shadow and out of line of sight of the sniper, a lightning will reveal your position to every nearby normal enemy, and one happens every few seconds. This is means pretty much no place can be used to recharge your shadow ability without getting spottet.
The end boss is laughably easy in comparison, managed it the second time and only failed the first because I had no idea what to do, while ol' sniperboss needed something in the ballpark of 15 tries.
4. The saving system. All of the other points could have been really reduced in severity if this one wasn't there. The game has no quicksave. In fact, it has no manual save at all. All you have is an autosave, and the save points are really few and far between. Exit the game and start it later again? Back to the start of the level even if there were save points in between. Made your way through undetected, killed tens of enemies, and one of the last one sees and kills you? Though luck, you start again at the start of the level because there never was a save point, which may have been 20 mins or more ago.
This is particularly rage inducing in the case of an enemy like the second boss above. Sure, that one saves after you stormed the hill, before other enemies were introduced.. but then you go to the next tower, really slowly, killing everything in your wake, reach it, go towards the next tower, teleport behind an enemy that you're sure is still out of line of sight (you can't be sure as you can't see sniper yourself).. well tough luck, he wasn't, you are kill and you can start again at the place other enemies were introduced, before the first tower. And if you somehow managed to survive that, there's a third area full of normal enemies (as many as a normal level) in addition to a superbly positioned sniper boss.
This was so infuriating that I pretty much gave up any 'good' way to play this game and just pretty much ran past enemies, giving no sht if they spotted me or not.
Let me save whenever I want, if the game gets too easy then, well that's on me, isn't it? Or at least distribute the save points a bit more than uncle scrooge distributes free money.

Probably the most underrated CRPG out there. This game is a gemstone that stands as an example to traditional role playing game developing companies like Bethesda and Bioware. It's been developed by a Polish game company named CDProjekt with no desire to be a part of today's competitive capitalist game industry. A lot of time and effort was spent in creating this game as it's a well polished, very original rpg unlike many unripe games we see today.
It takes place in a fantasy world where three northern kingdoms, Temeria, Redenia, Kaedwen (and previously Aedirn) deal with internal turmoils as a mysterious assassin begins to collect crowned heads as in south, expantionist Nilfgaardian Empire stands ready. Also, a resistance guerilla force including non-humans called Scoi'tel emerges to fight for the oppressed and the protagonist, Geralt of Rivia finds himself in the middle of the conflict.
The atmosphere of the environments are truly amazing thanks to stunning visuals and beautiful background soundtrack. Instead of wandering through one vast geographical area like the one in Skyrim, The Witcher 2 takes place in 3 different regions and the player allowed and encouraged to explore each one in all three chapters, Temerian village of Flotsam next to a swamp-forest, Dwarven city of Vergen on top of the Blue Mountains and finally the ancient city of Loc Muinne, now in ruins.
The game's combat system is rather old-school and takes time to get used to it. Once getting familiar with it however, you will see how fun it is. You carry two swords, a steel one for humanoids and a silver one for monsters. Gerald posseses 5 magical abilites called 'Signs' allowing you to stun, ignite, trap, convert enemies along with providing protection. Alchemy system allows you to craft potions and swords oils giving you various advantages, but you need to use them "before" the battle, not during! As Geralt finishes quests, contracts and kills monsters he levels up, providing skill points to spend in TW2's vast skill tree. Since you cannot unlock all nodes in the skill tree, you need to customize your character in Magic, Melee and Alchemy.
To sum up, if you call yourself a rpg person, you should definetly play this game. The first game of the installement is said to be very problematic but no worries, you can start of the series directly with TW2 as i did. The lore and role playing elements are well thought and captivating, encouraging you to do more than one playthroughs. It's a very cheap game for its quality. Have fun and remember, you never trust sorceresses ;)

Don't be fooled by FPS looks, spawning and shooting enemies. This game is not just about killing enemies. It is about teamwork and strategy as well.
There are two teams - Marines and Aliens. Each team has a commander that coordinates the team from perspective view, ordering his team to build structures and secure parts of the map. And when I said teamwork, I really meant it. Commanders needs to actively comunicate with the team, coordinate them in attack waves, securing crucial parts of the map and defending structures.
Sure, there is a lot of killing too. Shooting and biting skills are important as well and can make a difference, but controlling the resources is often more important. Well organized team and assault groups are more dangerous than lonely sharpshooters wondering randomly across the map.
As this gameplay relies a lot on communication, microphone is somehow almost necessary. You can play without it, but often you need to communicate with the team and there is no time for typing or reading.

This is a standalone expansion of the Warhammer 40K Dawn of War game where you get to play as any one of the seven factions in a Huge Single Player Campaign. This gives it a better replayability than other titles in the series since every faction plays differently in the game. You start out in a world map which is divided in different provinces and each of the faction including you, occupy alteast three of them. From there every factions gets a turn in which they can either skip or attack other faction's province which starts a new game. Here you start out with a single base and you know the rest. Typical win conditions are set in these scenarios but to my surprise there were a few instances where wiping out your enemy's base will not give you victory, you will have to accomplish given ínteresting' objectives in order to win the scenario which may be achieved without wiping the whole army of the enemy. You also get a "hero"of your faction which you can upgrade with different items which you acquire as you conquer different provinces.
That said I will keep my review short and just point out what I liked and didn't like.
P R O S:
- Play the whole compaign with any one of the seven factions.
- All factions play differently
- Hero Upgrade system
- Perfect gameplay
- Variable objectives in different scenarios
- Good maps
- based on Warhammer 40K
- Sometime unit goes into 'Finish Him' animation while taking out enemy unit which plays out great
- Blood & Gore (mild)
C O N S:
- Very few cinematics compared to previous titles
- Story is almost non-existent
- A very short Units Cap with a further cap on few unit types. :(((((
PS: At the time of writing the review I have completed the single player campaign only once using Space Marines and it took me approx 24 hrs.

The gameplay itself seems fun enough, but the game itself is fundamentally flawed: The game utilizes an internal resolution similar to that used for the game's screenshots (on its Steam page), and stretches those graphics fourfold. While the game'd be playable at the size the screenshots present, or even twice that, by the time it is upscaled to its actual size, it's so grainy and distorted that not only is it aesthetically displeasing, but it's hard to easily pick between the tiles, and it easily triggers headaches.
Of course, if you could drag the window or adjust the resolution in the game menu- y'know, one of the two being a standard option in a game?- it wouldn't be an issue. But inexplicably, the game forces itself to a size it was never meant to be played on.
I imagine if you have a small enough monitor, or your visual perceptions are inclined toward being able to more easily distinguish between such things, then it may not be much of an aggravation; however, for those of us with visual perceptions issues, I highly recommend avoiding this game (as it will be unplayable for you, as it is for me).
And really, regardless of how regular or irregular the element causing problems with gamers may be, it's such a terrible design decision (just from a convenience perspective) that it's worth dedicated negative mention regardless. There's just really no justification for locking a game to a fixed resolution where there's not a legitimate cause for such, and especially not to a resolution it's not even meant to be utilized in.
In sum: This game appears to be a mobile port which was ported rather ineptly to PC, and the flaws with the port may make the game unplayable for some players, regardless of how enjoyable the gameplay itself may (or may not) be.

Im not sure how to review this game because of the fact that IT IS listed as Mafia 3, but should have just been called something else, because I know that throws off a lot of people, and I honestly feel thats why this game gets such negative reviews. I will start by saying if you are looking for a sequel to Mafia 2, this is not it. BUT.. Thats not a bad thing, not even a little bit.
So, forget the title and dive right in, because let me tell ya, the voice acting is pretty god damn amazing, and the story is really well thought out, with some twists and turns, laughs and tears, blood and sweat. People are saying, "after 3 hrs it sucks".. I have no clue where that comes from. 3hrs in is like the intro.. Its not even the main game. You break up the rackets, kill the two little bosses, and then the head dude, who actually runs the district becomes your target. You kill them and then assign who ever you want to control the district. Moving on, theres perks for each of your bosses, the more you give them of the city, and the more you help them, the more♥♥♥♥♥♥you unlock. Shutting off phones so you can jack a car, making cops look the other way while you unload on a caravan of gangsters in the street,  orhave some armed backup help you out when the mission gets too tough.. Driving is easy.. Shooting from the car is odd, but once you get the locking system, its pretty simple. There is no fast travel, and at some points, it does suck. But I just recommend earning the better cars for your garage, and then when you get bored, customize the one you like the most..

Although the story is interesting and the game overall is just a complete breath of fresh air, the combat in this game is lacking to say the least. The animations are stiff, they lack fluidity and there's often a long delay before one animation can follow another - you also can't interrupt animations either, which means you can often die if you swing your sword just one extra time instead of rolling away. Essentially, because of how counter-intuitive the game's combat is, the combat can be summed up with: attack, roll away, activate magic-shield-thing, attack, roll away, activate-magic-shield-thing... There's no dodge and the parry system shares the same resource used to cast your magic, which means you can either choose to parry twice in a row or cast two magic spells twice in a row before waiting for the resource to recover.
I'm sure I'm missing a few things but frankly the rest of the game is awesome; the dialogue, story and characters are all interesting and engaging.

FF7 is not the best game ever made. It's not even the best Final Fantasy game ever made. That doesn't mean it's not quite good, however.
I'll be relatively short and blunt here: FF7 did have some really annoying flaws. Grinding for levels for an hour or two in the middle of the plot just to continue past a boss, not knowing if certain characters may randomly disappear from your party without much warning, some rather annoying minigames and so on, that kinda thing.
However... these are relatively minor nitpicks. Overall, the game's pretty much good by any standard. It has mostly likable characters with a wide range of personalities to choose from for your party to fit your play style, it has all the OCD joy of maxing out your characters and getting all the best stuff, and the plot really wasn't bad at all, nor were the mechanics.
As a whole, FF7 is a classic because it did everything RIGHT. It does have minor flaws, but even in those they can be argued as being part of the genre at the time and what players were actually looking for in their JRPGs back then. There's no really huge glaring problems with FF7, and it shows: it's polished in almost every way possible... perhaps not to a SHINE, but it's distinctly obvious that it has at least some polish to it.
To that end, it's actually a very reasonable option, even to this day, to introduce new players to RPGs in general, as it did back when it was new. I can still go back and play through it every 2-3 years and actually enjoy myself quite thoroughly each time, even with knowing what happens.
Personally, I'm an FFT girl myself. Not FFTA, just FFT for the PSX. It had better writing, better plot, better characterization, better mechanics, more interesting combat, and was just generically better as a whole overall. But... FF7 is still really fun, even if it does have it's share of mildly frustrating points here and there.
Final Verdict:
FF7 really did do just about everything right. It didn't truly shine in any one area, but it didn't really have any particularly stand-out bad areas either. It's solid enough to stand the test of time and still be fun today. Some people who actively HATE JRPG's may want to avoid it, however, but if you like RPGs otherwise, it's still one of the best out there and is worth picking up just to understand references made to it to this day; it's a cultural thing like the Godfather, or Spaceballs are to movies. You just can't not play it, really.
Overall Score: About 80%. It's well worth the $11.99 normal price, even when not on sale, and if you've never tried a final fantasy game before, it's a good introduction to the series.

Aragami really wants to be Dishonored, but focused around the importance of shadow like the old Thief titles. The problem is that it does neither very well.
- Soundtrack, obviously Japanese-inspired, tends to repeat, but does the job more than well enough.
- Graphical level design, many small details, more varied than for example Styx's ever same-looking gray locales.
- Good options menu, allowing you to even adjust third-person FOV, which is a rarity, and allows you to rebind all keys, including alternative keys; Vsync, framerate cap (30, 60, unlimited), FXAA, motion blur, all the controversial settings are adjustable.
- The controls that ARE there are fine and at least to me didn't fail to perform actions the way I meant to.
- Unlike, say, Thief 4, the rewards for completing levels a certain way actually do make sense: Kill everybody/Kill nobody/don't get spotted/don't cause any alarms, etc. These bonuses are awarded seperately, so while killing somebody rules you out of the "Kill nobody"-reward (duh...!), it does not affect your inclusion into any of the other bonuses.
- Wonky animations. While most moves are servicable, some look like they were sloppily motion-capped in, but then not properly polished off with key-framing afterwards.
- Writing. While I somewhat liked the premise, the language used really feels a little amateurish, almost childish at times, and just not fitting to the characters nor setting provided. It is also tropy as hell, but that I can forgive.
- Communication. The game is not particularly good at communicating information, may it be critical tutorials like upgrading skills, may it be priorities of targets, leading you to wonder whether some marked targets are optional or essential, may it be the ability to know where you're supposed to be going, where you can or can't go, which ledge you can stand on and which ones you'll slide off of, etc.
- No manual saving. While this did not annoy me as much as others, since I played without killing anyone, and the checkpoints are usually close enough to one another that you never really lose too much time, this has to be included for the people that dislike it, and because I really don't see any reason as to why this feature could not be provided.
- Stealth games are fun because they reward studying the level and the AI, planning your actions, and minutely executing said actions. This gameplay loop hinges on the predictability of level design and AI. If they are too predictable, the game poses no challenge. If the game does not make all necessary information somehow accessable to the player, even the best calculations will fail due to an unknown variable.
The latter is the sin Aragami commits. The game teaches you at every possible moment that the shadows are your friend. There's plenty of shadows around in the levels, since they are crammed with guards, as well. A non-violent playthrough thus requires you to look at the level, spot (and possibly mark) the guards patrolling it, and then gracefully blink from shadow to shadow at the right moments. You can see the level, see the guards, plan, and still there's one critical number you'll never know, which is the
. After all, this is also possible in Dishonored, right? Yes, but Dishonored was not about hiding in the shadows as much as it was about breaking line of sight and staying outside of vision cones, which is why the game provided you with the information to determine those. Thief was about hiding in shadows, and therefore you could rely upon being absolutely invisible in complete darkness. Aragami tries to be both and succeeds in neither, resulting in situations that make no sense: One moment you crouch behind a shadow on top of a torii, in line of sight of a guard on the ground, about 5 meters away from you, not being spotted. The next moment you blink on top of a hill into another shadow, same height, same distance, line of sight, you get spotted. Restart from last checkpoint, take different route.
This inconsistency results in the best tactic being to plan ahead roughly, blink from shadow to shadow, and in the case of unforseeable emergency, blink behind or out of sight of the guard that's about to spot you, praying that the shadow you blink into is not within magical unpredictable alarm-distance of another guard. That is half stealth, half lottery, not so frustrating as to ruin your experience, but the realization that this sloppy implementation of distance-based recognition is still a thing was rather disappointing.
In conclusion: If I could, I would give this a middle rating, as there's a lot to enjoy here, but since I really dislike stealth games that try to "surprise" you out of nowhere, assuming this would add to the fun, I guess I'll have to go for not recommended.

Superficially speaking, Hotline Miami doesn't immediately whisper "noir" to you, opting instead to let you wade through a bog of corpses in blood-soaked tennies only to find out that its been screaming it at you in screeching peals the whole time, with a cartoonishly large handgun pointed directly at your balls. Certainly a thing to be filed under the "neo-noir" label, and owing much more in style and intent to Tony Scott rather than something like Jacques Tourneur, but the tropes are all here once your eyes adjust to the garish palette (which, for me, happened after the main character's penultimate chapter... you know, right before you meet The Other Guy.) It's easy to reject Hotline Miami's tropes as being "un-noirish" out of hand, check that most of the action takes place during the day while night scenes are reserved for idiosynchratic quells in the gale. But then the afternoon calls, and the phone rings: duty gives way to self-awareness; jingoism gives way to bloody, hyper-gory sabotage. The Jacket was seemingly never given a choice, content to be goaded and mocked into action by his own conflicting yet self-serving delusions, ending in a fatalistic conclusion but not for the autonomous, or the truly deserving. ♥♥♥♥ everyone else, right? They got what was coming.
But there was always a choice; hell, its implied by the end that there were many choices that could have made, but the Jacket couldnt make the right ones, over and over. Was it programming? Was it PTSD? Could have been simple-minded bloodlust? Or maybe Miami just sucks so bad that there was nothing better to do except be the bad guy.
Well, not *the* bad guy; just *a* bad guy.
Noir keys: criminal, nobody wins, urban setting, violence, questions, answers (both, there are literally chapters in this game titled both "questions" and "answers"), mobsters, political philosophizing, dreamland
