Originally, when I wrote this review, the game was still pretty early on and I had just bought it after hearing some positive feedback from let's players that I follow. As a hardcore FPS junkie, the idea really appealed to me - it's a racing FPS game. You move as fast as you can and shoot as precisely as you can to get the fastest time possible. The character design and general aesthetic of the game, although rudimentary in early development, looked and still looks excellent and is very unique (I LOVE the helmet/HUD and suit, like a jet pilot mixed with SWAT armor). Of course, I really enjoyed the game. I felt really proud getting all platinum times, and it was still fun even when I continously threw myself at the same level over and over only to get eaten alive by the deadly maze of lazers and bullets. Think of the experience like a US version of Lovely Planet.
However, I still didn't endorse it. This isn't to say I dont still enjoy this game, because I really do. It's a fine example of how movement is so important to FPS games and how movement alone can make a game incredibly fun. That's also all that I can say the game is good for - a proof of concept about FPS movement. Simply put, the game is no longer in development, and the state that it's in is not good enough to be a true gaming experience. It's simply a polished up rough draft of the idea "racing FPS". This certainly isnt to say that the product is bad, because everything in the game is great, it's just that what hurts BIOS are the things which are not in the game (such as optimization - this game WILL be a challenge for any computer).
If this game gets continous updates and PIXYUL comes back to life, I will be one of the first to keep up to date and fanboy over it all. However, as it stands right now, it's simply not in good enough shape to recommend, and it doesn't look like it'll get any better in the future.
TL;DR - The idea is super cool and everything in the game right now is great but it's dead, only 30% done and incredibly unpolished.

Oh my goodness. I finally beat this game and it was absolutely amazing! This is a must have game that everyone should play. This game is up on my top 5 favorite games and I'm considering it to be my number 1 game. Enough raving about this game, let's get down to the review!
Game play is amazing and very smooth. Controls very well with an Xbox controller. At times, it could be headache inducing frustration trying to get to all the treasures and finding all the secret areas on the maps. I had to keep switching out of the game to look up where to find a tresure that I was missing or how to get to a secret area on a map. Although, it is very possible to do so without the internet to help but for some of the secret areas and treasures, there's no way it could be done without looking it up.
The trials feel like nightmares the first time you go through them. There's one where it's all portals and if you don't jump through the right one, you're bound to miss some floating angel lights. Same with the plant bombs, they are likely to frustrate you to none other if they get hit with spikes or explode before they hit the yellowish glowing walls.
The graphics are beautiful for an indie game. Seriously, everything stands out in it's own way. A dark background with bright enemies or bright background with dark enemies makes it easier to see and defeat them. However, there are some parts where you are in a cave or a very dark area and need to be wearing light rings if you want to get through those dark parts.
Unless you want to play the game for the story or are completely new to platformer RPGs, I suggest playing this game on tough or even hardcore mode. I played through on normal and from the beginning, I was wishing I played on a tougher difficulty. There's only one side quest where you are required to kill yourself and there was one other time I happened to die because I wasn't paying attention to my health. However, I had a revival stone that brought me back to life. Twice I died in the 20 hours of game play I put into it on normal difficulty. First time being the side quest, second time was my own fault.
If you want to make quests a heck of a lot easier, make sure you have duplicates of items so you can easily sell them to the merchants and buy them after the shops restock. This way, you won't have to grind on enemies to get items for some quests and even for crafting items.
The characters in the game are memorable and were fun to interact with. Boss battles were thrilling even if they felt very easy to defeat at times. However, the last boss battle will not disappoint as there are three stages to defeating him and sometimes it felt like my blows were doing little to no damage.
It is possible to beat the game with over 100% completion by finding all the treasures, doing all the side quests, and exploring all the maps. From what I was reading about the completion percentage, it seems it is possible to get it to 117% complete. Unfortnately, I was only able to get my game to 114% complete. I believe it was because I didn't get 4 stars in all the trials.
Dispite what I said about the trials being a nightmare, it is possible to get 4 stars in all 6 trials. It just takes time and practice to smash all the lights, finish before the time runs out, and defeat any enemies in your way. Even if the timer runs out, you don't fail. You just won't get that time bonus for points at the end of the trail. Be careful though becuase if you get hit during the trial, you do lose points.
Overall, this game is fantasic and I do recommend getting this game and playing it all the way through.
You will not be disappointed with this game!

This game is simply lovely. The music is hauntingly catchy, the graphic style is  perfect for the genre, and the play control is solid.
The whole game takes some simple concepts and weaves them in to a hybrid game that offers hours of enjoyment.
You are descending a dungeon, collecting items and slaying monsters along the way. The catch is, you're doing this to the rhythm of the dungeon.  Learning how each monster moves and attacks is simple enough - however making the right movement choices while you're under the threat of missing a beat is not always so easy.  This keeps the game fast paced and engaging.
True to roguelike form, the game has tons of little things that keep it interesting, spells, items, secret shops etc. allowing for many viable strategies for your dungeon delve. Once you master the game, you can unlock more characters to play as, each one with a unique attribute that will change how you play the game. I'm sure I will continue to play this for well over 100 hours. Easily one of my best purchases on Steam, bang for buck.
The developer updates have been constant and excellent. So no fear of this getting abandoned anytime soon.

Name of the game? 10,000,000. Your goal? 10,000,000. Yep, it's interesting.
Even though we have a strangely-named (or numbered) game title, it does seem to fit within the main game itself as you simply need to score 10,000,000 points in order to win the game. How do you score that, you may ask? Well, the game is rather simple in a way that it mixes match-3, endless runner and RPG-like elements all in one game. You match tiles in order to either gain resources, build up your shield, unlock loot, or even just kill some monsters that'll simply attack you in order to push you to the left side of the screen, which will make you lose. As you gain resources such as XP, gold, wood and stone, you use them to improve your dungeon that'll bring in many status upgrades ranging from dealing more damage when matching swords and staffs to gaining certain buffs such as gaining time bonuses when matching wood and stone.
Throw in some objectives, ranks, and some score and resource multipliers, you'll be well on your way to reaching 10,000,000! It's a fun game for those who like match-3 RPGs.
This game is almost TOO much fun. Not to mention it has one of THE BEST soundtracks you'll get out of a video game this year!

This game is FUN! When i picked it up I was not really sure what type of RTS it would be. I can say after some initial confusion it exceeded my expectation.
I am a fan of C&C, WarCraft, StarCraft and AoE type RTS games. Ones with resource gathering and elaborate tech trees. So when I started playing Deacon I was NOT in familiar territory. In fact my first play session I was so confused on the most basic controls that I lost 95m people without landing a single nuke on my enemy. I thought the game was broken…
… but then I cam back and tried again. I learned more each subsequent match until i FINALLY won!
Once you figure out the ins and outs of the game it is very rewarding. All sides start with the exact same resources and do not get anymore. It is all about unit placement (and starting territory) and then how you move and deploy them.
My only complaint is that there is not a more robust skirmish mode that allowed the user to make more unique scenarios.
If you like chess, the movie war-games or planning a nuclear winter, this is the game for you!

Several characters to pick from, a few more when you beat the 'hardcore' mode (a straight run through all the levels, a feat I've yet to accomplish at time of writing). A very satisfying game to play, could not recommend it any more strongly.

It looks like it could do with an anti-cheat programme; but, as it's a free game, I doubt that the developers would be willing to pay for one (which is a shame, but I can understand it).
Without the hackers, it's a bit of good fun.
However, it does seem that the knife is overpowered, and it seems to kill from about 6 feet away.
No problem, just beware of people who are heading towards you with a knife in their hand (hint: they're not running towards you in anticipation of a nice plate of steak and chips).
Keep your distance from them (backpeddle furiously) and you should be ok.
So, all up, Warmode is worthwhile playing as a fun shooting game.

This is a marginally improved version of the original.  If you liked the original game on the Playstation console, then you'll likely feel very similarly about this one.  The graphics are just a little cleaned up, converted to a higher resolution, but the story and gameplay mechanics are the same.  This is a plus and a minus, as I would love to see the polygons on the characters reworked to look more like the video versions of the characters.  Videos are untouched, which is also a good and bad.  Remember how amazing the video was the first time you played this on Playstation?  Yes, that feeling is gone on your big screen 1080p.  To be fair, they likely don't have the original models to render new videos from, so you get what you got.  Bottom line, this will not recapture the magic of playing FF7 on that 27" CRT TV in the early 90's.  What it will do, is make the experience smoother and a little cleaner on the TV/monitor you have.  And you can run it from your Steam hardware instead of hooking up the original console.  Also you don't have to swap between the three CDs of the original game.
Many people regard this as one of if not THE best Final Fantasy.  At the time it was released, I expected a bit more than it delivered, but FF7 was a solid game in its own right, with some annoyances that by design don't go away, so they're ultimately not 'minor'.  Monsters level up with you, which is a phase Square went through that I have always hated.  When I'm level 80+, I don't want to fear death from minor hostile woodland creatures.  You nearly HAVE to use a walkthrough in order not to miss getting the best weapons in the game; once you miss the opportunity to get (whatever), you cannot go back and get the things you missed.  Roughly 1/3 of the way through the game, one of your major characters goes away permanently as part of the story, which angered a lot of people, and in particular I hated that I had invested time and effort into developing a character that I lose for good.
This is a nostalgia game, giving a small breath of life to a game that people have loved for years.  If you loved the original and fancy another play-through, this is worth getting because of the improvements, as it will look a little better than your Playstation will on the same screen.  The story is decent and it's worth a play-through if you missed out (maybe you were too busy with your N64, or weren't born yet).  If you're looking for something to compete with the graphics of the latest RPG offerings, you will likely be disappointed.  If you're trying to recapture the magic of what might be your first RPG experience, it's not updated enough to wow you again in the same way, but you'll be taken back to that place in your memories where you first met Cloud, Tifa, Barret, Aeris, Sephiroth and all the other old friends you helped save the world with.

When Aragami goes well it's an excellent game that's a lot of fun.  When it goes wrong it becomes repetitive and frustrating.
In Aragami you're playing an 'Aragami', a spirit of vengeance.  Your powers are based around shadows and stealth letting you create patches of shadow and teleport to shadows that you've made or already exist.  You can also later make bodies disappear, set traps that devour enemies, gain temporary invisibility as well as the expected tricks of a ninja like throwing kunai at enemies.  As you likely expect, you need to keep track of enemies and move quickly to break vision if they see you as you'll only have a few seconds at most to try and hide or to kill them before they attack.
The game looks good and makes the most of the art style, particularly in using the changing colour of your cloak in a really unique way of showing your energy, ability uses remaining and whether you're in shadow or light (sometimes the cloak wraps around itself but I only noticed it happening a couple of times).  The sound effects fit excellently and the gameplay really encourages stealth and sticking to the shadows (though the medals for each level encourage replaying with different approaches).  The story unfolds through the chapters without taking too long or overloading you at any point but I found the twists fairly predictable.  Most of the controls are rebindable on mouse on keyboard, except bizarrely for the skills menu (F1, in case you're continuing the game after a few days away as couldn't find it listed in the key bindings).
My two main issues with the game are each fairly minor but the frequency of them was starting to affect how I felt about the game by the time the credits rolled.  I play most games on a relatively low volume so it's balanced with anything else that's open but the death sound from light weapons hitting you seemed like it was always at the max volume and not whatever I'd set it to.  With the sound I also noticed that if the game went into slow motion from being detected or if I'd messed up again and died that the volume of anything else I had in the background dropped for a few seconds in the same way Skype tries to lower the volume of anything else if you haven't changed that setting (which shouldn't be an issue in this case).  The other was the checkpoint system the game uses as it's just too far apart for my liking.  Ideally I'd love to see a quicksave system or more checkpoints within levels as a death late into a level can lead to replaying a lot of a level.
If you're looking for an interesting stealth based game that can be difficult but rewarding, Aragami is a good choice.  Personally I'd recommend picking it up on sale based on my 7.5 hours of gameplay to finish it but if it's a style or game you particularly enjoy and plan to replay to get all the scrolls, medals and techniques you'll likely find good value even at full price.

A classic from the Playstation 1 era. This is one of the first RPG games I ever played and has always set the standard of what I expect from an RPG. It features turn based, but active combat, a fun and more-or-less easy to follow story, and decent characters and personalities though some border on the cliche. Finaly Fantasy 7 has a good amount of side quests and minigames that can eat up plenty of time. From snowboarding to breeding and racing chocobos the handful of side quests and metagames can keep you entertained for quite a while.
I found that, as with almost all RPGs I play, one of my favorite things to do is collect all the strongest magics and weapons. There are monsters you can encounter that are even stronger than the last boss at the end of the main story. On top of that there are magic abilities that, if you have the patience to level them up, can make the final boss a walk in the park. Getting these weapons and magics require a great deal of grinding though, which is someting I find to be rather offputting. Squeezing every last ounce of gameplay from this title will probably take you somewhere in the neighborhood of 70 hours if youre the occational gamer like me.
Since it's initial release the game has not really aged well. If youre looking for a top-notch Final Fantsy expierience I would point you to one of the newer titles. It's kind of hard to look at the old graphics in high resolution. To help this they have an "original graphics" mode for people like me. It keeps the display to 480x640, but without the inherit funnyness of a SDtv set you still see plenty of jaggies and protruding polygons. The graphics didnt stop me from playing through one of my old favorites though.
Another gripe I have about the age is the clunky controls when roaming about but it's nothing you cant get used to. The button layout can be a tad confusing on the keyboard. If you happen to have a gamepad it eases this considerably, but you're probably going to have to spend a moment remapping the default controls-- no biggie.
One of my favorite aspects about the steam version is the cloud saving. True: its usless if you dont have an internet connection where you want to play. But I like the ability to play on my PC, go wherever, and pick the game right back up on my laptop. Aside from that there is also a "character booster" if you get stuck...or want to be a badass. I have not used the feature mainly because I forgot my square-enix login stuff moments after i made it.
Its not particularly weak in any areas but isnt as deep in character skill devlopment as I would like sometimes. Rather than molding your character(s) into what you want them to be, you have to play to each character's strengths-- again, no biggie.
Theres no voiceover, which is a huge plus for me. The story is good, characters are likeable, the gameplay is solid, and its good on length. It's probably 20 hours on the game clock on a casual playthough if you ignore endgame badass equipment, skills, and sidequests. All-in-all its worth it if it's on sale, but if you just want a stroll down memory lane you might be better off digging out the old PS1.

I'm really surprised by this game. I was hesitant because of it being EA even with the sale price of $12, but I'm definitly glad I picked it up.
Pros
+ Solid Gunplay. In the way they handle, sound, and the shots feel like they've got a good amount of weight to them.
+ Graphics are really well done and I would say look to be fairly on par with most AAA shooters.
+ Music fits the frantic nature of the game style.
+ Quick reset when you complete a match or die is great when you're powering through trying to get the fastest time.
+ The levels are very well designed and thought out. Also, the variety of the level themes is very nice and makes each one very distinct and have its own feel.
Cons (with this being EA, most of these are suggestions that could be fixed before the actual release)
- The name... BIOS? More like, "hardest to Google game title EVER!" Searching for this online is near impossible and brings up almost entirely unrelated results. Obiviously they can't change it at this point, but geez, whose idea was this?
- The menu. I don't know, it just looks ugly to me. Having all of the options up at the top is something I've mostly only seen in F2P games. Needs to be rearranged and polished.
- No option to change the color of your crosshair. Seeing how it's white and all the enemies are white as well, it's a bit hard to keep track of sometimes.
- Your character sometimes slides when you're trying to stop or change direction, usually when strafing. I've noticed this only seems to happen in some levels, like the one with all the freight containers.
There are other things I could mention (would be nice to have a rewards/progression system, story, extra content, etc...)but from what I've heard they're working on it. Overall though, great job guys! I look forward to playing more and seeing what is in the future for this refreshing twist to a genre that really needed something new.

This game is simply lovely. The music is hauntingly catchy, the graphic style is  perfect for the genre, and the play control is solid.
The whole game takes some simple concepts and weaves them in to a hybrid game that offers hours of enjoyment.

Learning how each monster moves and attacks is simple enough - however making the right movement choices while you're under the threat of missing a beat is not always so easy. True to roguelike form, the game has tons of little things that keep it interesting, spells, items, secret shops etc. allowing for many viable strategies for your dungeon delve. Once you master the game, you can unlock more characters to play as, each one with a unique attribute that will change how you play the game. I'm sure I will continue to play this for well over 100 hours. Easily one of my best purchases on Steam, bang for buck.

I've heard about the issues the game had at launch so I decided not to buy it at that time.
5 months later, I saw it at 66% off so went ahead and bought it for cheap, hoping the game was patched enough.
It wasn't.
I'll start with the pros:
- The storyline concept is awesome.
- The soundtrack is excellent.
- Audio is also great, for example the radio signal becomes weak when you are underground, it changes quality right after your car slammed into something, etc.
- Filler characters (NPCs roaming the streets) feel livelier than in many other similar games.
Now the cons:
- Screen tearing is still a big issue. I have a GTX1080 with an i7 6800K, SSD, 32 GB DDR4@3000 Mhz, watercooled GPU+CPU, the whole shebang. The game runs at 125-150 FPS with everything maxed out except for motion blur which makes me dizzy. there's some tearing, of course, so I enabled V-Sync... and well, the tearing got worse. For some reason, the game runs at 57-58 FPS (verified independently through multiple tools) instead of 60, and so the tearing becomes worse.
- Missions quickly became repetitive and unchallenging. I first expected stealth missions to be "a la Thief", where muscling in wouldn't help. I also expected hiding bodies to be a thing. Turns out stealth is just the "slower option" and hiding bodies is completely unnecessary.
- The AI (both cops' and gangsters') is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. They would come at you one by one and get mowed down in the process,   and they will be unable to see you even if your cover isn't sufficient. Furthermore, if you interrogate one guy while others have their guns pointed at you, they will politely wait for you to finish before resuming shooting. How nice of them. if you interrogate an enemy underboss while regular gangsters are searching for you, they will walk right past you (and sometimes right through you) without the slightest sign they have seen you.
- Graphical glitches are all over the place. From character geometry messing up to floating bottles and cigarette butts, from incorrect lighing to NPCs drowning when pushed into water... the game has plenty laughable glitches to offer.
- One particularly serious bug, which you can replicate, is this: go to a race, start the race, run overe the NPC who gave the start, then restart the race. All cars will be stuck in their starting positions forever, including yours. The race never starts, you can't exit the car, can't abort the race, can't select another mission. You can only reload from last checkpoint.
- Occasionally you can get stuck in places. You can only load last checkpoint.
- Secondary missions are active (steal that truck, steal this boat) but the truck/boat are not there.
All in all, despite the valiant attempt from the developers' side to bring us a rich, open world Mafia game... I can't recommend it. Maybe if it's on sale for 5-10 bucks, you could buy it as a time sink. But full price? Heck no.

Let me preface this: I'm someone who played the old NS1 Beta incessantly and also played NS2 incessantly when it became playable for me.
For a while now, the developers left the game to community devs and they have hardly released any new content. Sure, they patch and whatnot, but there is an aversion coupled with a lack of ability to release any refreshing content that will 1) keep the remaining playerbase active; 2) bring back the masses of hardcore players such as myself that left the game and 3) Entice new players to stay in the game upon joining.
A large portion of the remaining playerbase, most of them hardcore players, have turned into those that abuse new players "REEEEEEEEEEEEEEE GET OUT OF COMM CHAIR REEEEEEEEEEE" that does nothing to encourage one to carry on playing the game. For a playerbase that praises its own individuality and the learning curve that exists, it actively ostricizes and lambasts those that want to learn by-proxy of participation; ergo it's no wonder that the playerbase is so tiny now. There are some in the community that are amiable and kind, but they are few and far between.
TL;DR The game itself has become monotonous due to the lack of fresh and revitalising content; large portion of remaining playerbase don't take too kindly to new players.
Back in its day I'd recommend, though certainly not now.
Save your money and spend it elsewhere. I'd recommend Squad - a tactical FPS that relies much moreso on teamplay with a mass of content greater than ns2, coupled with a fantastic playerbase that will help you along the much steeper learning curve. If not this, then money and time spent elsewhere is money and time elsewhere well spent.

I played 'The Witcher' back when it released and decided to buy this game when it was on sale: 30/06/14.
Since 'The Witcher' was such a great game, in mostly all aspects, I didn't even bother to read the reviews of the product. It's a shame that I didn't read them, because I wouldn't have paid for this if I had (even if it was on sale).
OS: Linux (Fedora 20 x86_64)
Hardware: Pretty damn good
It turns out that 'The Witcher 2' is not actually 'The Witcher 2'. It is a port from Windows to Linux. In essence, a console to PC port (PC being Windows in this case). To clarify, this is actually the Windows game 'wrapped' to work on Linux. So everything that the game does (rendering, etc.) gets executed in Windows code and then translated to Linux code. That's when you see it. If you've ever played a game written in Java, imagine that, but worse. Cut scenes have ~1fps. The main menu and esc menu have frame rates in the single digits. The game itself shells out a beautiful 10-15 frames on average on low settings. Low. LOW. 800x600 too.
I'm sure if I had Windows installed I would be able to play this game just fine; performance wise; ~90 fps.
I would love to recommend this game, because I know it will be good, but I just can't play it. So for now (and probably forever), I won't recommend this game to anyone.

I grew up playing point-and-click Adventure games, and this game felt like the rightful successor to the Lucas Arts franchises like the Monkey Island games, Day of the Tentacle, etc.  There were some welcome additions like the ability to highlight every interactable object or character on every screen (saving you from having to pixel hunt your way through every puzzle), and an in-game hint system that nudges you in the right direction without spoiling the feeling of solving things for yourself.
The game features a charming story with memorable characters and a solid soundtrack.  The story has some interesting and surprising twists and turns all the way up until the end, and it felt refreshingly un-formulaic.  Some people apparently didn't like that, but I was impressed by the direction the writers took the story in.
I would enthusiastically recommend the game to those looking for a modern twist on a classic genre.  I would also recommend not being put-off by the people whining about the conclusion or complaining about the game not being politically correct 100% of the time.

Conclusion: A solid game with issues here and there.
Pros:
Simple mechanics that are easy to pick up on.
Solid gameplay basics.
Cons:
Auto-save points seem a bit too sparse.
Rough around the edges.
Neutral observations:
I like the art style, but that's an opinion.
The level design does a nice job of progressing. Early levels lack verticality, but later levels have several levels to navigate at once.
Gameplay is both forgiving and harsh; Guards will not instantly sound the alarm or kill you if spotted, so you have a window to kill them. However, the save point distance makes screwing up take a lot more time to fix. Dying also resets the level entirely, guards behind you will have respawned. Not really an issue moving forward, but if you are trying for a "kill-them-all" medal, avoid dying.
Ending was alright. Not what I expected, but I think it could have been done better.

And while the patrolling guards always return to their patterns after leaving them, stationary guards sometimes just stay whereever they are when their suspicion drops. This can also be quite the hassle. When you factor in that the punishment for failure is swift and harsh, this often turns the game into a frustrating experience.
But when it does work as intended it is a fun and beautiful stealth game with pretty solid mechanics.
Good luck with the learning curve against players that have over 2,000 hours.  That's the only remaining player base.  Dead.

Welcome to the past!  Sexy, sexy polygons.
Final Fantasy VII plays through your emotions by telling an intricate story about life, love, loss, confusion, revenge, and death.  The simple (almost lego) character models provided a challenge that we don't really worry about these days: The characters had to express emotions using body language (no facial expressions).  [Slight spoiler incoming] You can literally see the rage coursing through Barrett as he watches his hometown get destroyed.  I find this form of expression refreshing compared to the perfectly rendered expressions in videogames these days.  It makes it a bit difficult to empathize sometimes. But do your best- it's worth it!
Also, the polygons and twisty winding maps leave a LOT to the imagination- which is a good thing.  Imagination is a form of thought that games have been slowly eliminating through our advances in detail.  That's not to say I wouldn't want this game to be remade in beautiful stunning detail- I'm all for it!  It would be like reading a book -then watching the movie and saying, "Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ they cast Ender PERFECTLY!!"  -rather than skipping the book, watching the movie and thinking it had some cool concepts~
The real beauty in the game is a combination of the writer's inspiration and what they had to work with.  The writers poured their hearts into making this game- they had no idea it would be such a hit.  All they had were crummy PS1 graphics to work with, but they did what they could hoping people would like it.  Nowadays, game devs have more than enough money and the writers are getting less and less passionate because of it.  The Final Fantasy franchise has been going pretty strong and can still give me a good cry sometimes.  But why was 7 such a hit?  I'm thinking it was sincerity.
Something else that comes to mind is how the mini games weave into the standard gameplay like they ARE the standard gameplay.  A player is expected to adapt on the fly~  One moment you're fighting in a turn based system, then suddenly you're on a motorcycle swatting baddies on either side!  Don't forget snowboarding, chocobo races, and other golden saucer attractions!
-----------------------
SPOILER ALERT - personal feelings
First time through (I'm talking 12 years old), I put all my time into Aeris.  Her limit ability heals your entire party, so naturally she was my 'white mage'!  I thought she'd be there forever- we dated and everything!  I cried so many tears of sadness because of it.  *sobs

If you made speedrunning into its own game, it would be BIOS.  The game is punishing, yet fair and has nearly flawless level design. The amount of content already available for such an early in development game is astonishing, and the music is fantastic.  The best way for me to describe this game is as if Super Meat Boy were an FPS.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a 2D Side Scrolling action RPG game, which has great voice acting, and a nice quest system that you can play through in a little less than a day.
WARNING: Make sure to save, and not trust the Autosave. The game autosaved over my original copy; I had thought that it was my own save that was updating… this was regrettably not the case. Good bye days worth. Please learn from my mistake.
Dust: An Elysian Tail starts off very confusing, the story just kind of drops you into the game and says “Hey, you’re the hero, here’s a talking sword and an annoying fairy thing, go save the word!” Now that I think about it, this isn’t really an uncommon trait in video games.
I won’t spoil the story, but I like how the main character looks, the game is very Asian-cultured,  you have your annoying side-kick who just makes your character look better, it has all it needs to have to be a good game… The only down side is that the game goes by really fast.
The game play starts out very fast paced, I knew before I left the starting zone that I was going to enjoy it. The game is based on gaining exp through “combo’s” which you obtain through getting hits on enemies. You’ll figure out neat ways to go about doing this while you play the game and unlock new abilities.
Fidget (The side-kick / flying wombat / fairy-thing) throws magic, Dust uses a Magic sword and you use those two in collaboration in the air or on the ground. That’s what the game comes down to. Knowing when to fight in the air, and how and when to fight on the ground.
The achievements on this game are fun. I started the game right away on Normal difficulty, got nearly everything then reset my game and descided to replay on tough to get the final few achievements I missed.
When I started the game on Normal I was very over confident and thought I could just zip through the game without needing to learn where my heal button is… That didn’t work out so great, so it’s not “easy” but it’s not “Super Meat Boy”. Most of the achievements can be obtained relatively easily once you’re familiar with the game.
Dust: An Elysian Tail at normal price is going for $14.99, I would say that the game is priced fairly for the quality you will get. I only put 22 hours into the game, but I did rush a bit and had to look up a guide for the “find all your friends” achievement… The price might still be a bit high for someone with a strained check book.
As I say on most of my reviews, you may want to wait for this game to go on sale before you buy it, but it is definitely worth buying. Additionally it is currently in the Humble Bundle for the next eleven days! You might want to jump at the chance to get it now with a few other indie games:

I enjoyed this game, I felt that I got my money’s worth out of it, the story was excellent, the quality was impressive, the game play was fun. I don’t know what else you could ask out of a game like Dust: An Elysian Tail. I say this is a “Must Have” for anyone who enjoys 2D Indie Games.

As a puzzle and strategy enthusiast, I've played my fair share of games and it's always a treat when a game brings something new to the table.  Deviating from the typical 'Match 3' formula, you may find snapshots of the game misleading--the tiled board looks just like any other matching game--but 10000000 has a surprise for you:  You're not going to move the tiles.  You're going to move the BOARD.
'Hah!', I hear you scoff.  'That doesn't seem like much of a difference.'  That's what I thought, too, until I played it.  Manipulating the board this way bends your brain in a completely different direction, as you cannot simply adjust one tile at a time.  Every move you make will affect the entire playing field in ways you may not be able to predict at first and it adds new complexity as you struggle to speed through each encounter, which brings me to the other half of the gameplay:
You will encounter various monsters with different resistances and weaknesses, locks to pick, chests to open, and all the while the clock is working against you to clear the precise tiles you need to beat each challenge in a matter of seconds.  It comes with an RPG element that rewards your accomplishments and encourages you even after a defeat and, on the whole, it makes for a very engaging experience.  As for flaws, the music can become a bit droning after awhile and it's likely to become stuck in your head very quickly, and a few cracks show in the few scattered misspellings (you're going to be 'poisioned' quite a bit), but on the whole, it's a good game.
I feel like the developers missed an opportunity by not including more for the player to do.  Sure, you can keep playing it as long as you like, trying to raise your high score, but since the game revolves around meeting certain score or endurance goals, once you have completed all of said goals and related achievements, it feels like there's no further challenge.  It's just about right for the price and should provide several hours of entertainment.

DEFCON, in simple terms, is a simulator/game where you can destroy entire countries and continents by using nuclear weapons to decimate populations and cities whilst watching them burn. You can choose to be either North America (Canada, USA), South America (All South American countries), Africa (All African countries), Asia (Most Asian countries and far east countries), Europe (All European countries) or just Russia (Just russia, duh). There is a DEFCON timer, in which it starts from DEFCON 5 all the way to DEFCON 1, signalling nuclear war. The DEFCON system is a US defence and readiness condition system in which state the military should be readied at, depending on the current condition, five to one. Slowly or very quickly depending on what speed you want it on, the DEFCON level will drop until it reaches DEFCON 1 and nuclear war will begin. The game is based on a film called Wargames (1983) and is about a hacker who gains control of NORAD's nuclear missiles and threatens nuclear war. The GUI and game is very similar to Wargames' control systems and computer simulations. In order to start the game you need to select one of the continents, you can place down radars, missile silos and airbases. Each one of these has a certain strategic importance. Radars can detect incoming nuclear missiles from nuclear submarines or land based silos and show their trajectories. Airbases have the ability to launch fighter and bombers to city targets or fleets of ships in the oceans, the bombers can also drop one nuke onto a city or military target. Silos obviously have the ability to fire up to 10 missiles anywhere at a target. Silos can also become air defence systems in which they will shoot down incoming missiles, fighters and bombers within their range. There is also the ability to place fleets of ships (nuclear missile equipped submarines, battleships and aircraft carriers). Submarines can attack ships on the surface of the sea and sink them and can also fire nukes at cities within a shorter range than silos but they are more stealthy. Battleships are an all-round ship, they can attack all kinds of ships including aircraft. Aircraft carriers can launch nuke bombers to cities or military targets and attack them and launch fighter jets to attack ships. It is also worth mentioning, you can't win. It is impossible to win. As the games motto/slogan says "Everybody Dies". The whole object is to loose the 'least' by having less casualties.  For each 1 million citizens killed, your continent gains 2 points, for every 1 million citizens killed on your continent, you loose 1 point. The game is easy to grasp but can be a bit challenging at times and difficult to use. It does take time to learn, but hey, its really cheap on sales and what isn't good about nuking the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of Africa?
TL;DR
11/10 would nuke Africa multiple times again.

I think it took the fact that I had some 200 odd keys to redeem (many, many duplicates dating back to 2013) to get me to play this game. I just decided to start from the top of the list and work my way down. My list was sorted alphabetically so 10,000,000 was the logical starting point.
At the onset, 10,000,000 seems like just another match-3 games. Add in RPG elements of upgrading your gear and abilities and you have the perfect puzzle game. I normally hate match-3 games. Beat a level only to unlock a new level just gets boring after a while. What sets 10,000,000 apart is that you are not actually beating levels. You play until you either die or run out of time. My wife happened to walk by while I was playing and so eloquently put it "it's one of those match games" and after I told her there was a time limit, "so, like tetris."


The first time I played through the game, I did so on my phone. On top of everything I mentioned, I think I enjoyed the quick games you can play. I then decided to play on Steam because, you know, achievements (such a dumb reason to play a game by the way - says the guy who got two platinum trophies for My Name is Mayo...). 10,000,000 is almost as enjoyable but I get the feeling that the game was designed for mobile. I usually do not sit at my computer to play a quick game that lasts anywhere from 20 seconds to a few minutes. I hate referring to a game I genuinely like as something to kill time but ultimately, it is one of the factors I look for in mobile games.
I highly recommend this for anyone looking for a different take on the match-3 game. From its pixelated graphics and retro-style soundtrack, this is a perfect game when you need a quick break. I recommend the mobile version and not only because it costs two bucks cheaper. I loved playing a few rounds and then taking a break. The game has the tendency of being a grind and I feel this is more likely to occur on the Steam version when you are sitting down and playing longer than 5-10 minutes. The game only takes about 3-4 hours to complete. Why not make it last? As more daughter would say, "one more time!" Hopefully, you feel that way too when trying to put the game down.

I played 'The Witcher' back when it released and decided to buy this game when it was on sale: 30/06/14.
Since 'The Witcher' was such a great game, in mostly all aspects, I didn't even bother to read the reviews of the product. It's a shame that I didn't read them, because I wouldn't have paid for this if I had (even if it was on sale).
OS: Linux (Fedora 20 x86_64)
Hardware: Pretty damn good
It turns out that 'The Witcher 2' is not actually 'The Witcher 2'. It is a port from Windows to Linux. In essence, a console to PC port (PC being Windows in this case). To clarify, this is actually the Windows game 'wrapped' to work on Linux. So everything that the game does (rendering, etc.) gets executed in Windows code and then translated to Linux code. That's when you see it. If you've ever played a game written in Java, imagine that, but worse. Cut scenes have ~1fps. The main menu and esc menu have frame rates in the single digits. The game itself shells out a beautiful 10-15 frames on average on low settings. Low. LOW. 800x600 too.
I'm sure if I had Windows installed I would be able to play this game just fine; performance wise; ~90 fps.
I would love to recommend this game, because I know it will be good, but I just can't play it. So for now (and probably forever), I won't recommend this game to anyone.

This game costs $5. +3 if you want the additional expansion DLC.
In total, this game has earned me up to 100+ hours of gameplay. Its high replayability is sure to keep you satisfied, with extra secrets to find in every corner.
So the gameplay of this is simple; and that's what's good about it. You walk around and you shoot your tears on your enemies; which is very simple, clean, and there's nothing else to it. The attack patterns of enemies differ based on the enemy, which keeps the game interesting and new (although you might find some of the same room layouts which can tend to get a little annoying). Memorizing attack patterns are a definite help to the game and the player's overall experience of it. That's how you get better. As you play through the game, the levels become harder, and as you play more sessions, you get better at the game.
Don't be fooled by the disturbing first looks of the game, because there are bound to be things that are WORSE than the basement horrors. Believe me, a good sense of humor is a good requirement of this game as well as a good stomach. Speaking of which, the graphics are simple, but violent and gory. Hell, take the fly for example. When you defeat it, it explodes in blood and it splatters all over the place. Yeah, you might need to be a bit on the older side to play this game, but this is the 21st century, so obviously that limitation is bypassed.
The game's story is something that can easily fool you at first. The only explanations to the story are the introduction and the epilogue. The rest is for you to figure out as you go. If you figure it out, it gets better and you get more comfortable with the game, thinking it's a connotative rather than a big bundle of sticks at first glance.
The biggest aspect of the game is its extremely high replayablity. Most BoI players have a lot of time spent on this game, and you can't blame them for that because this game is very fun to play and it rarely gets old. This game features tons and tons of items (around 200 or 300, i think?) and every game you play is randomly generated, with many features and hidden aspects that cannot be easily recognizable. That I reccomend you read the wiki on. Trust me, it will help a lot.
The big problem with this game is the massive amount of bugs in it. As one example, negative luck giving good luck, enemies getting stuck in a wall, impossible rooms that have met uncommon circumstance, etc. The game is great, but the bugs make your runs a lot more painful or it just ends it. The bugs are what's stopping this game from getting a perfect 10.
Another problem with this game is the synergizing of the items. I won't exactly count this as a bad thing because flash, but it's something to keep in mind. Most tear-changing items will not work well with others. Read the wiki to see which ones are compatiable and which ones are not.
Overall, this game is violent, scary, and a big blast. The random generation will either challenge you or an absolute blast. This game is extremely replayable, and it's earned many people tens and hundreds of hours on gameplay. So come on, have a go at this game, it's really good.
8/10 for graphics - it's simple, and there's not much else you could ask for at a simple game that goes deeper as you advance. I have no problem with the graphics.
8/10 for gameplay - it's simple, and, like graphics, fits the style of the simple gameplay, but with a deeper meaning as your progress. The concept of the gameplay fits the game.
8/10 for story - it's actually incredible once you have a thought about it, it's an alright story at first but it's a greater one at the end.
11/10 for replayability - i cannot just give this game a 10, because it sucks you right back in after every time you lose or say "ILL NEVER PLAY THIS DAMN GAME AGAIN" and run off crying because the random generation of several chapters is simply amazing.
4/10 for bugs - unfortunately it's something I don't want either, but this game is buggy as hell. Sorry, Edmund and Florian.
overall, 9/10 - the replayability pretty much increases the score by a lot and the game is definitely worth playing. some of the more expensive games i buy do not compare to the amount of hours i spend on this game. it's $5 for the full game, and $5+3 for the full, FULL game! and even if my hour counter for this game is about 100 hours, i've spent even more time on spidermod (a client used for exploring the game and messing around with, as if it were sandbox mode)

The Witcher 2 is just an all round very, very good game and one of the more underrated games going around. It has all the things you need to suck you in for hours. You don't need to be an avid RPG fan to enjoy this, as the RPG elements aren't the deepest you'll find but are solid nonetheless. What this allows however, is an emphasis on the Story. It's interesting, enough that you'll pay attention to what's going on. There are a number of side quests that have variety, some for example, like hunting different types of creatures are Monster Hunter-ish in nature. The questing along with the Fantasy based story will keep you thoroughly entertained.
Character's are well crafted and are interesting. Not two dimensional. As for the Combat, a heads up, it requires some thought and Patience. You can't run into groups of enemies and 'hack and slash' your way through. Preparation (Potions and Tactics) is required but once you get past that learning curve, you'll actually like it, trust me. The game LOOKS good as well. Well designed chararacters and towns, lucious and believable environments and the general game world will immerse you. Even on low settings it's not too shabby.
Sooooo, highly recommend this game, especially as it is cheap as chips (especially when it's on sale). You'll just have a great time with The Witcher 2. Come on. Do it!

Aragami is a stealth game, which is normally just a test of patience and praying that you won't be spotted, but it does things a little different. With Aragami's shadow techniques, you can manipulate and traverse your environments with deceptive finesse.

+Gorgeous art style
+Rewards the player for how you play as well as how good you play.
+Pasifist "Yami" and Bloodthirsty "Oni" Routes.
+The shadow abilities have no right to be as cool as they are.
CONS
-A little buggy. (Nothing gamebreaking, but still annoying. Patches are being developed as we speak)
-Lighting is a little inconsistant.
-Music is OK.
-Skills are gained from finding hidden objects.
FINAL SUMMARY
A stealth game that had more than a really good plot or fun bosses to keep me going, a wonderfully interesting mechanic that is fleshed out greatly and provides multiple ways of dealing with a situation, and giving the player insentives to replay levels to either kill or spare all guards. What more could you ask for?

Deponia: The NOT-SO-COMPLETE-ANYMORE journey contains three of the now four Deponia games. You play as Rufus. A stupid, selfish, arrogant, sexist, possibly racist tinkerer prick who's tired of living on his garbage homeworld called Deponia and would rather spend his life on Elysium, a paradise where the elite resides high above the clouds. Will he reach this destination? There's like three games and all of them are named after the junk planet he's trying to escape from so your guess is as good as mine. Rufus at first I thought was going to be a generic point 'n click main character. The selfish, anti-social a-hole who is hated by everyone and will do anything to accomplish his goals, but still has a heart of gold yadda yadda, but this isn't the case. While he definitely has an arc throughout the entire collection, I feel that Rufus is a more of a unique character than most protagonists. He's essentially the mondern Guybrush Threepwood, but he's actually a bad person who will never think things through and hurts loads of people regardless of whether they deserve it or not. Sure, he sometimes does good things or at least tries, but the only reason he even would go through with it is for selfish reasons and I kind of like that. The game bursts with character. Rufus could nod and it will get a chuckle out of me. If you miss the old funny lucasarts point and clicks then you should definitely get this game.

This game is ultraviolent and has a steep learning curve, but I'll be damned if it isn't the most satisfying game I've ever played. It's very aware of its hyperviolent content, and it's very critical of it - not framing it as a bad thing, necessarily, but rather addressing the player with the question, "do you like hurting other people?" I've never felt so personally attacked by a game in my entire life, and I loved it. Some people might miss that bit, some might think that the game is only addressing Jacket and not the person holding the controller, but I for one feel like this game has a social commentary to it that shouldn't be easily missed.
The art style is incredible. It's grimy, the people have faces that make your skin crawl, it's ugly. But it's ugly in a way that's compelling and perfect for the setting. It's the most appealing kind of ugly there is, and I bow to the art team for their skill.
The music is fast-paced when it needs to be, and calm when the situation calls for it. It keeps the player momentum going and gets you right into the zone without distracting you from your surroundings.
The level design is clearly very well thought out. I don't really have a lot to say about this, because I think playing the game would be the only way to really do it justice, but I will say that the designers definitely put a lot of thought and care into their level planning. There really are multiple ways to do each level, and you will be scored in accordance to how you handled it. There is no wrong way to beat a level - only more and less efficient ways.
The story is... I'm not even sure how to begin to describe it. I think "mind♥♥♥♥" is an accurate word for it. I've never had such a thorough mind♥♥♥♥ from a game, ever.
I recommend this game if you like fast-paced action, the 1980s neon aesthetic, and/or the movie Drive (2011).

Okay, guys, for the stuff everyone's going to want to know:
I'm playing the Linux release. Running Archlinux x64 on a Fjutisu T730 with an 8GB RAM upgrade.
And a 'rock candy' generic 360 controller. Performance on my stock i5 moble is reasonably good, we'll get to that.
This game is a platformer. So, it has all the usual fare to be found for that genre. Spikes, climbing walls, magical moving platforms, jets of air to ride on, ect. You gain new abilities as you go though the game, and it does add incentive to go back to areas previously visited to get extra loot. You don't start out with so much as a double jump, but by the eind, you can traverse the map like a bat out of hell, and slaughter everything that moves (and a few thigns that don't).
The controls are suprisingly tight for an indie game, but it still has it's rage-inducing mechanics (Wal climbing around spikes, anyone, or howabout doing that in the dark?) It took me only  a few hours to get the hang of thigns (I've actually only logged 10 hours or so on the game, left it on by accident),, The rest of the time was spent using Dust and Fidget's abilities in new and intresting ways. For one, if you want to cross a level quitckly, it's possible to combo the enemies as you dash about the map, and use them as a method to get up to places. Fidget (the little flying creature that follows you around) can spit projectiles, which combine with your attacks to increasing the level of hurt you can dish out.
The real gem of this game, though, is the presentation. The story is linear, but quite intresting, with at least a few sidequests to add some flavor into the game. The game doens't take itself too seriously all the time, and it's better for it (Spoilier: Forth wall jokes are slipped in here and there). The graphics are fantastic for the price point, and the music is better then some of the games I've paid $60 for.
It has it's shortcomings, but mostly their small nitpicky things. The big one is: The game is short. It doesn't take very long at all to get to level 30-something and blast though everything, at least on casual (which is where I'm at while I get used to using a controller again) The Story is good, but it doesn't have as much dialouge as someone might expect, given the quality of everything else in the game. It's also possible, at least on this setup (I've not tried it on my windows box, I'll make a point to do so) is overload. You start slaying monthers in huge droves and this gmae will start to studder from the weight of the flashing and explosions and loot flying all over the place.
My final thoughts? It's a great game, assuming they opt to make a second one, I'll be sure to keep an eye out, though I've yet to finish this one. going to go do that now.

First I cannot decide if I give this game thumbs up or down. To explain my point of view I will first tell the game mechanics.
It's a mulityplayer bloons tower defense. You build your towers (apes) and defend against ballons (bloons). The 2 biggest differences to earlier games of this series is 1. the multyplayer and 2. that you choose your towers.
Step by step:
You have ingame currency (medals), which is needed to uprgade towers and to play the arena mode. The towers have 4 tiers, you start with tier 1 and 2 on some towers. The other towers are unlocked when you proceed. Therfor the higher upgrades of the towers are bought by the ingame currency. If you play a battle you pay for the entry with that currency. For example, the first arena costs 5, the second 20 and it goes up to 25.000. If you lose the game, you lose the invested medals, if you win you gain the amount of both players, which means if you invested 5, you gain another 5 and the 5 you invested, 10 in total.
How to play:
Every wave consists of ballons you need to destroy. They fly over a strict path. Before the game starts the players choose 3 towers of their choice and thier inventar. Another tower is randomly given by the game and it has all 4 stages unlocked. The map is choosen by a generator and can be changed once by each player. Since the 2. wave the players can also send ballons to the opponent. Therfor they need to pay but increase the general income. Later ballons like the MOBA will decrease the income drasticly. Both players start with 150 lives. Every time a ballon reaches the end the player loses lives. The ballons are all different. The first ones (red) are destroyed by a single hit, some need more hits, some need hits from special towers (metal ballons are not destroyed by simple darts) and so on. The first player who has no more lives left loses the entire game.
In total are there 4 modes: the arena, the card battle, the assault mode and the defens mode.
All modes are pretty the same, you try to beat your opponent by making his lives go 0 and at the same time you try to stay alive. The card battle is played with cards. Those cards are towers and ballons at the same time and the player chooses which one too play, if you drag it to your side its a tower, to the enemys side its a ballon card.
The assault mode is the same as the arena mode but you dont spend medals, but energy, which regenerats over time. If you win, you gain medals therfor.
In the defense mode both players have to beat the same waves, there is no sending of ballons by or to your opponent.
After all this it sounds quite fair, now I want to explain my problem
The first arena, which costs 5 medals, should be for the beginners, but more often I have to play against players, who have 2000 medals and more. Once I already played against a player with 100.000 medals. It seems to be no great deal but remember, those players have unlocked more towers and more tiers on this towers. Some will say, that you can even beat a higher player with low level towers and yes, thats true if you have luck, the depicked the wrong towers and cannot destroy some ballons or they dont pay attention. Normally the higher tier towers are also much stronger.
Why do high players, who could play higher arenas, play in the lowest one?
There is a win/lose ratio
To increase this ratio you need to win so what do you do, you play against beginners with low level towers. The real problem about this is, that often you spend all your medals on upgrades so you only have a few left and then you battle to gain more and get ranked against an advanced player and you lose. What do you do, when you have no more medals to play the arena? Either you spend your energie to gain 5 medals in assault mode or you have to wait for the free spin, which grants you with medals or special tickets. Those tickets are for arena/assault mode with special modi, like higher speed for example.
I like the game, I really like that it needs some kind of tactic to build up your towers and some kind of knowlegde when to send which baloons but its frustrating if you play against another player who can build tier 4 towers you havent even unlocked.
I think it would make more fun, if the win/lose ratio woulndt be visible so the advanced players would play on the higher arenas and not the low ones.
After all I give this thumbs up, because it is fun to play and its not the games fault, that advanced players play low arenas to get a better ratio.

NEGATIVES:
- Many repetitive elements

The full $60 price-tag is still not worth it (in my opinion) due to the minor graphical glitches, minor crashes, aand getting stuck on loading screens. Just poor optimization in general. But, other that that yeah I would recommend this game fully when the price gets lowered or a sale is going on.

I got this game because of all the rave about it's maturity, it being a realistic, gritty RPG. I was like, how can it be both fantastic and realsitic? And it's all in the small details, from the amazing hand-crafted textures and fitting artstyle, to the dialogue and actions all the characters have. This game will absorb you, it is one of those games that will stall you because the scenery is so rich and beautiful, or halt you in suspense of chosing which morally grey choice will make Geralt's life easier. The story plays a big part in this linear RPG, abundant with political intrigue and murder, you'll wish you were in Geralt's shoes, but it is all the more interesting. I reiterate, it is a linear game, but a equlibrium is reached with the openness of the choices to make.

Aside from story and graphics, The Witcher 2 has a hack and slashy combat that's not overtop, as it's not suppose to be, but rather deadly and effective, fitting to Geralt's reknowned swordsman skills. The difficulity, however, is not consistent as I would like it to be, you are immediately placed in a harsh combat scenario that might frustrate some, but worry not, there is flow once you get use to it. Besides swordplay, there are small spells called "Signs" that mixes things up and aid in different combat situations. Sadly, there will end up to be a typical pattern for the combat to play out. In the end, I'd say the combat gameplay is somewhat mediocre, but at times rewarding.
Since, this is an RPG, there are bound to be skill trees and weapon and amours to collect and compare. The skill trees are not as in depth as an MMO's and does not change your gameplay as much as Deus Ex: HR, but are adequate and will be worth exploring. The weapons and armours have detailed stats like: incineration, poision, bleeding, sign damage, resistances, block chance, and has a lot of character in their designs; CD Projekt Red's design is seriously top notch! What The Witcher 2 introduces is an alchemy system, an interesting way to prepare for battle and a reason to explore your environment and monster carcasses for ingrediants. You will mix potions, construct traps, and craft bombs where different potions, traps, and bombs will be useful in different scenarios. Reflecting, I think you'll be on this ride more for the adventure than for how you go about it, but the RPG elements have the potential to play a bigger role in The Witcher 3.
After playing through this twice, which you will want to because there are 2 radically different branching paths, I highly recommend this big bang for you buck. The story and graphics will be enough to latch your eyes to the screen, while the gameplay will interest you enough to experiment and generate more fun. This game has gotten me so into this universe, akin to how DA: Origins has, that I even had to buy the actual Witcher books and play The Witcher 1 to keep the journey going and to get hype for THE WITCHER 3!!! If you have patience to follow the narrative, which is about 30 hours btw, and dissect the subtle details, and read the codex, I think it could have the same effect for you too. Honestly, the best word to describe this game and the series in general is INTERESTING. Now that it constantly goes on sale for dirt cheap, the power of Christ compels you to GIVE THIS GAME A TRY!!

Ah, Natural Selection. I haven't discovered another game like it. The first NS game was released in 2002 as a mod for the original Half-Life. The sequel stays true to its essence and doesn't attempt any huge changes from the original formula that made the game so fun.
The setting of the game is reminiscent of the Alien sci-fi franchise, as it pits a team of Marines (humans) vs. Aliens (otherwise known as Kharaa). Most players play from a first-person shooter perspective, though one player on each team volunteers as the Commander who views the game from a top-down perspective and issues orders to other players ala Command & Conquer or Starcraft. While the Marines team plays more traditionally, players on the Alien side are immersed into various foreign bodies with their own grotesque sound effects, abilities, and nuances.
Overall, the game is well balanced and matches are usually filled with intense battles where the Marines and Aliens are taking turns conquering various points on the map. The pacing of the matches feels similar to other RTS games and it does a good job of making one feel like a single soldier (or creature) in an ongoing battle.
Sadly, the player count for this game is dwindling. However, whenever I launch the game, there are typically a half dozen servers that are filled with players so it is easy to find a match. The community is often positive and supportive of noobs with its plethora of rookie-friendly servers. Furthermore, the devs are miraculously still supporting it and releasing updates to adjust balancing issues, squashing bugs, and adding new features. The game can often be found during sales for only a few bucks, so I give this one a strong thumbs-up.

This game costs $5. +3 if you want the additional expansion DLC.
In total, this game has earned me up to 100+ hours of gameplay. Its high replayability is sure to keep you satisfied, with extra secrets to find in every corner.
So the gameplay of this is simple; and that's what's good about it. You walk around and you shoot your tears on your enemies; which is very simple, clean, and there's nothing else to it. The attack patterns of enemies differ based on the enemy, which keeps the game interesting and new (although you might find some of the same room layouts which can tend to get a little annoying). Memorizing attack patterns are a definite help to the game and the player's overall experience of it. That's how you get better. As you play through the game, the levels become harder, and as you play more sessions, you get better at the game.
Don't be fooled by the disturbing first looks of the game, because there are bound to be things that are WORSE than the basement horrors. Believe me, a good sense of humor is a good requirement of this game as well as a good stomach. Speaking of which, the graphics are simple, but violent and gory. Hell, take the fly for example. When you defeat it, it explodes in blood and it splatters all over the place. Yeah, you might need to be a bit on the older side to play this game, but this is the 21st century, so obviously that limitation is bypassed.
The game's story is something that can easily fool you at first. The only explanations to the story are the introduction and the epilogue. The rest is for you to figure out as you go. If you figure it out, it gets better and you get more comfortable with the game, thinking it's a connotative rather than a big bundle of sticks at first glance.
The biggest aspect of the game is its extremely high replayablity. Most BoI players have a lot of time spent on this game, and you can't blame them for that because this game is very fun to play and it rarely gets old. This game features tons and tons of items (around 200 or 300, i think?) and every game you play is randomly generated, with many features and hidden aspects that cannot be easily recognizable. That I reccomend you read the wiki on. Trust me, it will help a lot.
The big problem with this game is the massive amount of bugs in it. As one example, negative luck giving good luck, enemies getting stuck in a wall, impossible rooms that have met uncommon circumstance, etc. The game is great, but the bugs make your runs a lot more painful or it just ends it. The bugs are what's stopping this game from getting a perfect 10.
Another problem with this game is the synergizing of the items. I won't exactly count this as a bad thing because flash, but it's something to keep in mind. Most tear-changing items will not work well with others. Read the wiki to see which ones are compatiable and which ones are not.
Overall, this game is violent, scary, and a big blast. The random generation will either challenge you or an absolute blast. This game is extremely replayable, and it's earned many people tens and hundreds of hours on gameplay. So come on, have a go at this game, it's really good.
8/10 for graphics - it's simple, and there's not much else you could ask for at a simple game that goes deeper as you advance. I have no problem with the graphics.
8/10 for gameplay - it's simple, and, like graphics, fits the style of the simple gameplay, but with a deeper meaning as your progress. The concept of the gameplay fits the game.
8/10 for story - it's actually incredible once you have a thought about it, it's an alright story at first but it's a greater one at the end.
11/10 for replayability - i cannot just give this game a 10, because it sucks you right back in after every time you lose or say "ILL NEVER PLAY THIS DAMN GAME AGAIN" and run off crying because the random generation of several chapters is simply amazing.
4/10 for bugs - unfortunately it's something I don't want either, but this game is buggy as hell. Sorry, Edmund and Florian.
overall, 9/10 - the replayability pretty much increases the score by a lot and the game is definitely worth playing. some of the more expensive games i buy do not compare to the amount of hours i spend on this game. it's $5 for the full game, and $5+3 for the full, FULL game! and even if my hour counter for this game is about 100 hours, i've spent even more time on spidermod (a client used for exploring the game and messing around with, as if it were sandbox mode)

This is probably one of the best point-and-click adventure games out there. It's actually three games together with a few bonus, but it's a cohesive trilogy. What makes the game interesting is it's humor, present through the whole game, and some very interesting characters. The story is good with some twists even if the ending is a bit disappointing. Still, it is well written. The art and animations are great and the voice acting well-done for the most part. The music is also good. The gameplay is what you'd expect from this genre: click everywhere, talk to everyone, collect, combine and use items. There's also some interesting minigames. This edition also includes an interesting Developer's Commentary implemented in-game and a neat questlog. Regarding puzzles, i must say that the game is a bit hard and sometimes the solutions aren't very logical. You'll need to experiment a lot. But it's worth it. If you're a fan of this genre, this is a must buy, except if you own the separate games. If you're new to the genre, maybe this a great way to experiment point-and-click adventures. It may be difficult at times, but that's also a trademark of this genre. Still, buy it on sale anyway.

This game is ultraviolent and has a steep learning curve, but I'll be damned if it isn't the most satisfying game I've ever played. It's very aware of its hyperviolent content, and it's very critical of it - not framing it as a bad thing, necessarily, but rather addressing the player with the question, "do you like hurting other people?" I've never felt so personally attacked by a game in my entire life, and I loved it. Some people might miss that bit, some might think that the game is only addressing Jacket and not the person holding the controller, but I for one feel like this game has a social commentary to it that shouldn't be easily missed.
The art style is incredible. It's grimy, the people have faces that make your skin crawl, it's ugly. But it's ugly in a way that's compelling and perfect for the setting. It's the most appealing kind of ugly there is, and I bow to the art team for their skill.
The music is fast-paced when it needs to be, and calm when the situation calls for it. It keeps the player momentum going and gets you right into the zone without distracting you from your surroundings.
The level design is clearly very well thought out. I don't really have a lot to say about this, because I think playing the game would be the only way to really do it justice, but I will say that the designers definitely put a lot of thought and care into their level planning. There really are multiple ways to do each level, and you will be scored in accordance to how you handled it. There is no wrong way to beat a level - only more and less efficient ways.
The story is... I'm not even sure how to begin to describe it. I think "mind♥♥♥♥" is an accurate word for it. I've never had such a thorough mind♥♥♥♥ from a game, ever.
I recommend this game if you like fast-paced action, the 1980s neon aesthetic, and/or the movie Drive (2011).

By far and wide, one of the finest Dawn of War series games thus far...
DoW was linear strait through, though still mind blowingly awesome when I first played through it (and re-played it a few more times).
DoW:Winter Assault was linear with a bit more choices in which forces you could use.  I enjoyed the ability to play one faction and beat the game, then turn around and beat the game with other faction (within Order or Chaos there were two paths to victory, one for each faction).
DoW: Dark Crusade, was the best, and I'll tell you why in a bit.
DoW: Soul Storm was a SOLID and very awesome finale to the first DoW series.  But really, other than adding two more races, was merely just Dark Crusade...
DoW II:  Lets go from RTS to squat tactical.  Okay, for 40K fans, its more like lets go from WH40K 3rd Edition or higher back to 2nd Edition rules (i.e. more skirmish than company+ sized units).  Pretty good games, addicting in their own skirmish manner, but lacking anything beyond a linear plot...
On to Dark Crusade and why I think it was the finest entry (other than being a Tau player on the table top since WH40K 4th ed.).
Here was the first Dawn of War where you alone were the commander and could pick you course of action through the campaign of planetary conquest.  Gone was a linear story that you forced down a very narrow course of action.  With Dark Crusade, you had your starting base and territory, and from there, free reign over how to go about beating the game.  Given the age of the game, you can forgive Relic for making most battles the base building, wipe out the enemy base, type RTS game.  It was 2006 when they made it.  Those of us spending the money on games back then grew up on that kind of RTS.  They did a fine job of breaking up that monotony with special missions in some territories.  My personal favorite being the Space Port where base building was a hinderence, your primary mission was collecting servitors (gee, Tau Stealth suits are awesome for that mission, along with Space Marine Scouts...).
For hard core 40K table top fans, some of the 'non-canon' or 'canon breaking' 'non-Codex' units were a sticking point.  Didn't bother much (though I wish Tau had some sort of turret to build other than upgraded listening posts...).  Don't expect this game to match the table top without modification.  Which is another reason why the orginal DoW games rock so much.  People are still actively modding them to match their favorite GW canon and table top game favorite units and factions.  Even after the much anticipated DoW:III, people still come back to this series (so, yeah, get Soulstorm for the maximum enjoyment of the mods).  Dark Crusade, for me, was the best of the orginal as a stand alone game, especially with some of the early mods that matched the table top 40K codex information!
