Early years
Ancestry
Hitler's father Alois Hitler, Sr. (1837–1903) was the illegitimate child of Maria Anna Schicklgruber.[2] The baptismal register did not show the name of his father, and Alois initially bore his mother's surname Schicklgruber. In 1842, Johann Georg Hiedler married Alois's mother Maria Anna. Alois was brought up in the family of Hiedler's brother, Johann Nepomuk Hiedler.[3] In 1876, Alois was legitimated and the baptismal register changed by a priest to register Johann Georg Hiedler as Alois's father (recorded as "Georg Hitler").[4][5] Alois then assumed the surname "Hitler",[5] also spelled as Hiedler, Hüttler, or Huettler. The Hitler surname is probably based on "one who lives in a hut" (German Hütte for "hut").[6]
Nazi official Hans Frank suggested that Alois's mother had been employed as a housekeeper for a Jewish family in Graz, and that the family's 19-year-old son Leopold Frankenberger had fathered Alois.[7] No Frankenberger was registered in Graz during that period, and no record has been produced of Leopold Frankenberger's existence,[8] so historians dismiss the claim that Alois's father was Jewish.[9][10]
Childhood and education
Adolf Hitler as an infant (c. 1889–90)
Adolf Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 in Braunau am Inn, a town in Austria-Hungary (in present-day Austria), close to the border with the German Empire.[11] He was one of six children born to Alois Hitler and Klara Pölzl (1860–1907). Three of Hitler's siblings—Gustav, Ida, and Otto—died in infancy.[12] When Hitler was three, the family moved to Passau, Germany.[13] There he acquired the distinctive lower Bavarian dialect, rather than Austrian German, which marked his speech throughout his life.[14][15][16] The family returned to Austria and settled in Leonding in 1894, and in June 1895 Alois retired to Hafeld, near Lambach, where he farmed and kept bees. Hitler attended Volksschule (a state-owned school) in nearby Fischlham.[17][18]
The move to Hafeld coincided with the onset of intense father-son conflicts caused by Hitler's refusal to conform to the strict discipline of his school.[19] Alois Hitler's farming efforts at Hafeld ended in failure, and in 1897 the family moved to Lambach. The eight-year-old Hitler took singing lessons, sang in the church choir, and even considered becoming a priest.[20] In 1898 the family returned permanently to Leonding. The death of his younger brother Edmund, who died from measles in 1900, deeply affected Hitler. He changed from a confident, outgoing, conscientious student to a morose, detached boy who constantly fought with his father and teachers.[21]
Hitler's mother, Klara
Hitler's father, Alois
Alois had made a successful career in the customs bureau and wanted his son to follow in his footsteps.[22] Hitler later dramatised an episode from this period when his father took him to visit a customs office, depicting it as an event that gave rise to an unforgiving antagonism between father and son, who were both strong-willed.[23][24][25] Ignoring his son's desire to attend a classical high school and become an artist, Alois sent Hitler to the Realschule in Linz in September 1900.[a][26] Hitler rebelled against this decision, and in Mein Kampf stated that he intentionally did poorly in school, hoping that once his father saw "what little progress I was making at the technical school he would let me devote myself to my dream".[27]
Like many Austrian Germans, Hitler began to develop German nationalist ideas from a young age.[28] He expressed loyalty only to Germany, despising the declining Habsburg Monarchy and its rule over an ethnically variegated empire.[29][30] Hitler and his friends used the greeting "Heil", and sang the "Deutschlandlied" instead of the Austrian Imperial anthem.[31]
After Alois's sudden death on 3 January 1903, Hitler's performance at school deteriorated and his mother allowed him to leave.[32] He enrolled at the Realschule in Steyr in September 1904, where his behaviour and performance improved.[33] In 1905, after passing a repeat of the final exam, Hitler left the school without any ambitions for further education or clear plans for a career.[34]
Early adulthood in Vienna and Munich
The house in Leonding in Austria where Hitler spent his early adolescence (photo taken c. 1984)
From 1905, Hitler lived a bohemian life in Vienna, financed by orphan's benefits and support from his mother. He worked as a casual labourer and eventually as a painter, selling watercolours of Vienna's sights. The Academy of Fine Arts Vienna rejected him in 1907 and again in 1908, citing "unfitness for painting".[35][36] The director recommended that Hitler study architecture, which was also an interest, but he lacked academic credentials as he had not finished secondary school.[37] On 21 December 1907, his mother died of breast cancer at the age of 47. Hitler ran out of money and was forced to live in homeless shelters and men's hostels.[38]
At the time Hitler lived there, Vienna was a hotbed of religious prejudice and racism.[39] Fears of being overrun by immigrants from the East were widespread, and the populist mayor Karl Lueger exploited the rhetoric of virulent anti-Semitism for political effect. German nationalism had a widespread following in the Mariahilf district, where Hitler lived.[40] German nationalist Georg Ritter von Schönerer, who advocated Pan-Germanism, anti-Semitism, anti-Slavism, and anti-Catholicism, was one influence on Hitler.[41] Hitler read local newspapers such as the Deutsches Volksblatt that fanned prejudice and played on Christian fears of being swamped by an influx of eastern Jews.[42] Hitler also read newspapers that published the main thoughts of philosophers and theoreticians such as Darwin, Nietzsche, Le Bon and Schopenhauer.[43] Hostile to what he saw as "Catholic Germanophobia", he developed an admiration for Martin Luther.[44]
The Alter Hof in Munich. Watercolour by Adolf Hitler, 1914
The origin and first expression of Hitler's anti-Semitism remain a matter of debate.[45] Hitler states in Mein Kampf that he first became an anti-Semite in Vienna.[46] His close friend, August Kubizek, claimed that Hitler was a "confirmed anti-Semite" before he left Linz.[47] Several sources provide strong evidence that Hitler had Jewish friends in his hostel and in other places in Vienna.[48][49] Historian Richard J. Evans states that "historians now generally agree that his notorious, murderous anti-Semitism emerged well after Germany's defeat [in World War I], as a product of the paranoid "stab-in-the-back" explanation for the catastrophe".[50]
Hitler received the final part of his father's estate in May 1913 and moved to Munich.[51] Historians believe he left Vienna to evade conscription into the Austro-Hungarian Army.[52] Hitler later claimed that he did not wish to serve Austria-Hungary because of the mixture of races in its armed forces.[51] After he was deemed unfit for service—he failed his physical exam in Salzburg on 5 February 1914—he returned to Munich.[53]
World War I
Main article: Military career of Adolf Hitler
Hitler (far right, seated) with his army comrades of the Bavarian Reserve Infantry Regiment 16 (c. 1914–18)
At the outbreak of World War I, Hitler was living in Munich and as an Austrian citizen volunteered to serve in the Bavarian Army.[54] According to a subsequent report by the Bavarian authorities in 1924, Hitler almost certainly served in the Bavarian Army by error.[54] Posted to the Bavarian Reserve Infantry Regiment 16 (1st Company of the List Regiment),[55][54] he served as a dispatch runner on the Western Front in France and Belgium,[56] spending nearly half his time at the regimental headquarters in Fournes-en-Weppes, well behind the front lines.[57][58] He was present at the First Battle of Ypres, the Battle of the Somme, the Battle of Arras, and the Battle of Passchendaele, and was wounded at the Somme.[59] He was decorated for bravery, receiving the

ORION: Prelude (formerly ORION: Dino Beatdown and more recently ORION: Dino Horde) is easily one of the most underrated games of the last 5 years. It's been torn apart constantly and consistently by the gaming press and given a right beatdown of its own. Since its release in May 2012 I've put a solid 100 hours into the games and I can say with great confidence that it deserves much more credit than it is given. Spiral Game Studios has come a long way with this title and ORION: Prelude is a fresh, fun, and exciting gaming experience.
If you've ever played Left 4 Dead, Killing Floor, Gears of War Horde Mode, or Halo's Firefight you know what to expect from ORION: Prelude. It's a co-operative FPS where up to 5 players work together to defend or capture objectives by fighting off wave after wave of dinosaurs. To vanquish said dinos there are three classes to choose from at the start of each match; Assault, Support, and Recon. Assault sports a jetpack, Recon a cloaking device, and Support a healing gun. Each kill earns a player cash depending on the damage they contribute which can be spent on upgrades between waves. Those upgrades range from bigger guns and bigger knives to Augmentations like a double jump or stronger melee attacks. There's enough to choose from that you'll be mixing and matching with the different classes to create unique builds each match. This really helps the game stay fresh.
On top of the class customization there are plenty of different modes available to chose from including a VS mode called "Duel" which is akin to elimination style modes in other games. There's Survival, King of the Hill, Free for All and many others including a mode where you are able to play as the dinosaurs themselves VS other human controlled characters. Controlling the dinosaurs is a bit difficult at first as they are large and stiff feeling, but after a round or two you'll be crushing human face like a true prehistoric behemoth and laughing the whole time.
When it was first released in May of 2012 as ORION: Dino Beatdown it was, admittedly, a mess. The word "glitchy" comes to mind with a hard lean towards broken and many of the game modes mentioned above weren't available. It was playable, but dinosaurs didn't behave intelligently. They would clip through the stage and animate like caffeine loaded squirrels with rigor mortis, guns wouldn't make noise and would even sometimes disappear altogether. Not to mention the announcer getting stuck repeating lines such as "threat eliminated!" and "threat down!"  over and over until the match ended. But, for what ORION: Dino Beatdown was at its core, a co-operative horde-mode FPS with dinosaurs, it was amazingly fun.
Yes the game had its moments, to put it lightly, but it wasn't so bad that it deserved the media meltdown that ensued after its release. Spiral was quick to respond to community feedback and within a few short weeks issued a number of patches that corrected graphical errors, class balance issues, optimization problems, all the while preparing large and free content packs that were released the following months. Eventually the game was re-branded and soft re-released twice to what it is known as today: ORION: Prelude.
If you were to compare the two games side by side it would be like night and day. Should Spiral have released Dino Beatdown as it was? No, probably not. But I'm glad they did. After playing the game day in and day out over the past few years my friends and I all realized that playing it together was the most fun we'd had since Super Smash Bros. Melee on our old GameCube. Time and time again we found ourselves laughing to tears and getting chomped. Much like Melee, L4D and Street Fighter did before it; ORION: Prelude has earned itself a spot on the shelf as one of our go-to party games for years to come.

First real review, because the game really impressed me with how fast the game became mundane.
Pro:
- Easy control of the board/Responds well to input.
- Some chiptune tracks are pretty good (but obviously not made for the game).
Cons:
- Time restriction on both gameplay segments (restriction on the amount of time you can play on a save is bad, it makes it necessary to complete the game multiple times to get the achievements).
- Completely random board (it's not in herently bad, but in the case of a game with specific goals to advance on a time restriction, it goes against fun).
- Seemingly random/blind upgrades (you often spend a huge portion of your gold to get 0.1% crit chance, which ultimately makes you feel like the game is working against you, other times, you spend less and you get +10 damage. It makes no sense.).
- Little to no variety. (there isn't much else other than what is shown in the tutorial with stats increases).
- Very lazy pixel art. (yes, I'm going there).
Overall, even though it isn't expensive, I do not recommend as the whole basis of the game is completely random and won't make you feel good for doing good and needs to complete an exponential amount of runs (multiple runs (overall game saves) of multiple runs (individual game runs for ressources)) to do the achievements, which seems to be the only real goal this game has other than it's utterly repetitive "get to 10,000,000 score to escape" that will need you to do the same thing for 10 hours with little to no variety. (upgrades aren't variety in this case, as they add no complexity to the actual runs' gameplay) It's a time waster you have to pay for, and an unsatisfying one at that.

Try thinking your moves before the next beat, and you're pretty much dead.
Sporting a simple interface (only the directional buttons are used, for moving and attacking, making this game
), sprite-based graphics, and catchy soundtrack, I'm really eager to see the game develop itself to its full potential. As it is, it's already a damn playable and fun game; I wonder what will come of this bizarre and cute creative gaming effort.

Another tale of Geralt of Rivia, The Whitewolf.
If you want to buy witcher 2 because of the sale, I suggest you buy the witcher 1 first.
This story of the witcher is the continuation of the 1st event of the witcher.
I'll start explaining the gameplay :
- The battle is improving from the 1st. Witcher 2 is starting to shape like an action RPG, where you must move fast or you'll die (starting from normal difficulty). Not like witcher 1 that you just have to click the enemy in a perfect time to do more damage.
In witcher 2, you have to use your wits to win the battle. There are traps, bombs, flying dagger, sign, guarding and dodge (oh yeah you can't do this in witcher 1 lol) at your command to defeat the enemy or enemies. I really love this version of gameplay than the 1st.
- The crafting system is improving too. I kind of remember that in witcher 1st I rarely doing it, i prefer find and ancient weapons or potion.
- The potion system!! (The ♥♥♥♥ing "make it hard" gameplay) In witcher 2, you must prepare yourself when you go and plungin your enemies. You have to drink potion 1st because you can't do that while in battle. The potion itself is like a buff for you, there isn't any potion that automatically heal your Health Point.
So if you play the game at least from normal difficulty, you have to prepare your potion. But the ♥♥♥♥ing point is, you don't know when the battle will start, so if you don't prepare yourself, get ready to load the game (LOL).
- The leveling up system. It's the same with the 1st.
- The story. Well like I said in introduction, it's the continuation event from witcher 1. So if you didn't play witcher 1 and read the story, you might get lost in what is Geralt talking about. And in witcher 2 there are 8 ending or so i heard, so your choice in the story progress is really important in what ending will you get (I just got 2 ending from twice game play).
- The medallion radar. I kinda forget about this in witcher 1, but in witcher 2 you can use the "radar" to know where are the hidden items and trails.
- Playtime. You can actually beat this game in 24hrs if you're playing in easy mode. I got around 43hrs is because I'm playing it in hard and have to reload dozens of times to kill the boss and get the story that I want.
The cons that I want to share is just this one :
- The savegame. The game will automatically making a new savegame in some point (Autosave). And if you save for yourself, it will make a new slot. Well it's good to make a lot of save slot especially in witcher 2.
But BEWARE, if you have to many save slot, it will effect your game (because the save slot is using many space, I got 500MB for 1 game play) and make it slow when  in loading screen. And often crashing your game when you want to load.
So I suggest you keep it minimal in 10 save slot and delete whatever save slot you don't need.
Overall, my rating for this game is 9/10.
I would recommend this game for every RPG or RPG-Action lover out there.

The best-looking mud in any video game ever. If you've ever hiked on real logging roads out in the woods, you'll have instant nostalgia. It even squishes and deforms in 3D, water pools up in your tire tracks, and the color and shininess varies with the wetness of the dirt. The only perfect 10/10 mud in any videogame, period.
Oh, and driving the trucks is pretty fun, too. You drive fairly slow, but the maps are very detailed with very pretty trees, rivers, rocks, barns, and other nice little rural buildings. It's kinda like hiking out in the woods, you get to enjoy some very nice scenery as the sun rises and sets.
Also, it's actually a quite challenging game. You have to drive carefully, and it takes quite a bit of strategy to plan out your route. It's also great to play with a friend, so you have someone to help winch you out of the mud, flip your truck back onto its wheels, or carry an extra trailer of fuel.
The online community is probably one of the most friendly communities I've encountered. It's all co-op, and people will often help you out if you're struggling, and won't hesitate to ask for help when they're in a tight spot.

OVERALL: Aesthetics: 8/10; Music/Audio: 8/10; Gameplay: 7:10; Difficulty: 8/10; Story: 9/10; Entertainment: 9/10.
TOTAL: 9/10 - A VERY ENGAGING AND `BEAUTIUL` GAME THAT IS DEFINITELY WORTH YOUR TIME IF YOU ENJOY GREAT STORYLINE OVER SUPER-FANCY GRAPHICS, AND ENJOY POINT-AND-CLICK ADVENTURE AND PUZZLES.
NB: I CRIED AT THE END - I FELT A DEEP CONNECTION TO THE MAIN CHARACTERS AND HAD A VESTED INTEREST IN THEIR OUTCOMES, EVEN IF SOMETIMES I WANTED TO SLAP SOME OF THEM.
---
Aesthetically appealing game with developed/adult humour that isn't crass, along with some very clever puzzles and a very engaging storyline. The music works very well. The voice acting is brilliant. The ease of interaction is lovely.
This is a game that will stretch your logic and creativity, whilst having a highly engaging storyline where you can empathise with the main characters throughout, and will not be bored and not often frustrated.
There are some puzzles that require you to be very observant and to really think laterally, but it is not annoying or frustrating, but does feel very rewarding to solve.
Make sure to pay attention to speech and animations, as they all give clues beyond what you might deduce otherwise.
Some puzzles really need some creativity beyond what you may have ever encountered in a point and click adventure! (I especially think of one involving requiring a special 'password' that your character struggles to remember because of a certain distraction.)
I love it! It gets really addicting and I love the way the different things you pick up can change your character's appearance, my friends and I used to compare characters when playing through :P
This game has endless replayability and I would highly recommend it to any game lover.

I got this game off the Humble Bundle expecting a quick, easy game with little to no expectations to enjoy it for more than a few hours. I was completly and utterly wrong. Dust: An Elysian Tail was developed, and made entirely by one person with the exception for audio (voices and music) which would normally mean a game that wouldn't even make it off greenlight, however the game is incredible. The enviroments are beutiful for a platformer, going from a lush forest to a murky cave to a eery graveyard and a active volcano. The controls are smooth, easy to learn and let you piles up complex combos easily without having to memorize attack combinations. The game runs smoothly, with an openworld aspect of multiple areas that if you feel like a completionist you have to revisit after learning new skills, yet doesn't ruin the linearity of the plot. There is no demand for completing side quests all of which can be done by mere exploration and running through an area one more time. The characters are well defined and Dust is a character I found myself immediately liking, especially with his comedy companion Fidget. Well worth getting even if you have to pay the full price.

10,000,000 was a game i found out about completely by accident, browsing through some new games to pickup I saw this interesting dungeon looking pixel/puzzle game and it looked interesting. With the low cost to buy in I took the plunge and I couldn't be happier with the decision.
The game is primarily match-3, matching the tiles allows you to send your nameless dungeon crawler hurdling through the stone corridor towards his inevitable defeat to some combination of the hands of a nearby monster or a clock depending on how well things go for you. The simplicity of the gameplay makes it very interesting to play and progress through as you become better at finding and making matches.
The game features RPG mechanics in the form of resource collection to boost the effectiveness of your matches. Matching swords and staves vs monsters will produce different results depending on what that monster is weak or resistant to as well as improving the overall power of each match. You can also unlock perks to be given to your hero permanently by spending earned experience, and temporarily through the use of the toggleable potions which change how some of the game mechanics work.
Overall, if you like puzzles, racing against the clock, and mashing monsters, you'll likely enjoy 10,000,000. The only thing I wish was that the name was a bit more memorable!
Highly addicting. The RPG-elements make you want to keep farming resources forever. While the game is very repetitive, and somewhat luck-based, getting higher combos feels very rewarding.

Sporting a simple interface (only the directional buttons are used, for moving and attacking, making this game

I bought Deponia a while ago when it was on sale, but just got around to playing it yesterday. I believe I just started the second part of the trilogy.
Deponia is a point-and-click adventure game with futuristic and steampunk elements. The protagonist, Rufus, is a lazy scum bag who is perfectly happy mooching off others. However, due to events he finds himself wrapped in (partially by his own doing), he gets wrapped up in events much larger than himself and becomes the unlikely hero that the story needs.
Seriously, I have almost nothing but good things to say about this game. The aesthetic is charming, cartoony, and with a soundtrack that captures the setting well. All of the characters are engaging and fun, especially Rufus, who does progress with the story. Voice work is good, and the characters have voices that suit them well.
My one complaint is in the puzzles. Sometimes, the puzzles are too easy, where other times, there is no indicator in-game on how to reach the solution. Most of the time, trial and error worked well to get over hurdles.
Overall, this game is great.

Deponia: The Complete Journey is a really good game and is highly recommended to anyone who enjoys adventure games. I'd give it a 7/10.
Pros:
+ Very lengthy and worth the price - ~30 hours
+ Hilarious most of the time
+ Excellent voice acting
+ Some very nice puzzles
+ Well thought out world
Cons
- Puzzles can be obtuse
- Mini-game puzzles are mainly terrible
- Main character can be too much of a jerk to be likable
- Unsatisfying ending to series
This is the closest to a Monkey Island game we have had in quite some time(well, other than Tales of Monkey Island). It's nice to see a company that continues to make adventure games, a genre that is still active, but less so than in the past.
Other than some incredibly obtuse and unsatisfying puzzles, the majority of the game is  a lot of fun. I laughed, thought hard, solved puzzles, and had a smile on my face most of the 30 hour playtime.
I paid $6 for this game it was worth every penny. It has its drawbacks, but its positives far outweigh the negatives.

Deponia: The Complete Journey is a very well made point & click game trilogy that follows the story of an antihero called Rufus. Unlike usual game protagonists, he is a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and his main motive is to gain something only for himself. The art is done very beautifully and clearly a lot of love was put into it, as well as the music. These together make all of the areas very unique and memorable.
As the story progressed, you learn that Rufus starts to slowly drift towards a more nicer character, even though he still does a few very selfish, mostly just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ deeds every now and then. However, all of this escalates to him having an immense change of character in the end, which didn't fit his character that well in my opinion. Since the game really doesn't offer any options in the story, forcing you to follow a single laid out path, I was hoping that a miracle would happen and reward Rufus for his actions, since luck seems to have been on his side most of the time, when he most needed it. But in the end, nothing happened. This really left me craving for a more satisfying end to his long and eventful journey. It made me feel like the whole game was for nothing, since the culmination never happened. Unfortunately, cause of this I can not fully recommend the game, since I felt like I lost more than I gained through the story.

I really like this game! The gameplay is fun and the dialogue is more fun!
Although there are a few actions that the main character Rufus takes that are questionable, I'd personally say that in context Rufus never does it out of malice. For example the scene with the baby dolphins. He puts up a hoop to train them how to jump through it, but they end up jumping into the kitchen! I wouldn't say Rufus did it on purpose, as in his objective sheet, it never says "kill dolphins". Or when he convinces this black character to work as a monkey. Not is it the only job available to her so that she can afford to go back with her boyfriend, but when Rufus takes the money from her boss instead of giving it to her, it's because he was OWED the money, as well as needing to to SAVE THE WORLD. Reminder that EVERYONE would've died if he didn't get that money.
So, yeah, some of it is dark humor, not for everybody, but I feel all of it is not due to sheer racism or malice; it's played off to either make Rufus deservedly look like an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or to make him look as ignorant or stupid as a child.

Whenever you think of difficult and challenging video games the words slow-paced rarely come into play with it if it's not a turn-based genre, huh ?  Well SpinTires puts a new "spin" on that assumption. Starting quite literally from the ground up with it's amazing terrain deformation engine that'll kick up mud,dig gouges and tear new tracks into wherever your big rig this game delivers an impressive experience. As you switch between trucks the size of jeeps to ones bigger than anything legal on an american road you'll find this game to be a tough track to handle as you scout out the land on each map,unlock garages to plan routes and finally fill up your rig with logs to make the long journies. Between the size of this game,difficult terrain and the real to life design of torque over speed in your vehicles this is a game that will not test your reflexes but will test your planning,and guts. Will you risk forging that river will a full load or play safe with a smaller haul ? Is your fuel going to last another round trip or will you end up having to bring another truck around for an emergency refuel ?  All of these decisions and the unique difficulty imposed by each of the 7 maps will have you pushing the limits of your trucks and your driving. So throw on a good podcast,turn up your favorite long play album or just enjoy the sounds of that engine giving mother nature hell. Whatever your choice a steady hand, a good controller or wheel and some patience are all you need to enjoy this very unique and well made game !

TL:DR - IF this game works well on your rig, and you can live with occasional graphical glitches - well worth it for hours of fun shooting, driving and stalking, with an excellent story told well in an immersive game world.
PROS:
- Great story, great atmosphere: you can feel very invested in the game events and era. In particular the cinematic documentary style is innovate and adds a lot of interest
- Varied gameplay approaches: once you realise the game mechanics, a lot of fun can be had by taking different approaches. Need to draw out a racket boss? You can sneak through picking up the cash, or destroying the goods, or go in guns blazing. Pick off random elements you have tailed, shoot up trucks of contraband etc.
- Guns blazing - shotgun in your face? machine gun? rifle from distance? Using the different weapon types is very satisfying. Sneak: use the whistle and wait? or sneak through pulling people down from behind at speed?
- Driving: Is excellent. Cars are heavy beasts, and you can switch to simulation driving for a great experience. Also can change the view to over the dashboard.
- Originality and new take on the series - you are taking down the Italian mafia using the black mob, the Irish mob, and also parts of the Italian mob
VARIATION:
One of the common complaints is the gameplay is repetitive.
There is a repetiive mechanism: in order to draw out a boss, you have to disrupt their rackets, and kill or recruit the racket bosses. The racket bosses will show up at an area which you would have already visited.
This is a constant mechanic.
On the other hand - you can approach destroying the rackets in diverse ways (getting informants to talk and give up locations, tailing elements to disrupt their cash flow, sneaking in and taking the money, killing everyone on site, eliminated the enforcers or leaving them for the battle with the racket lead)
Each actual boss on the kill list is taken down in a different way - you will have scenario in an amusement park, in a hotel, a car chase, a sniper shootout.
Once you win districts, you assign them to your own underbosses, which has gameplay and story implications
There are also random elements (being hunted down by Sal sending out goons, tailing targets of opportunity)
To give an idea of the variation - here is what you do driving:
1. Drive from location to location (standard stuff)
2. Tailing racket delivery boys etc.
3. Chasing other vehicles
4. Being pursued by the police
5. Using the drive to intimidate people in the car
6. Shootups from the car
7. Racing
And more is coming with the DLC
So there are limits to the events and activities, but you can avoid a lot of the repetitiveness by taking different approaches and avoiding the use of intel and whistling.
NEGATIVES:
- Some repetitive elements (see above)
- Graphical glitches/ minor bugs/ game not that well optimised (I don't have performance issues, but others have had, and everyone will notice some graphical glitches)
- You don't play as the Italian mafia (this is a negative for people who want to play as someone like Vito)
- No fast travel: this will bother you if you don't enjoy the driving
OVERALL:
My personal view, worth the price on sale, and with the DLC adding more driving elements game is likely to get better.

I tend to agree with Rock Paper Shotgun that this is a game that does what Spelunky does best. It puts you in situations where it's easy to understand the mechanics and behaviour of each individual element, and relies on your skills and mental model to make a plan based on that. Each enemy's pattern is rather simple, as is each trap, block, and floor tile. However, taking all of those together creates complicated situations if you're not careful, and putting it to a very strict turn timer, i.e., the beat of the music, is a mechanism that encourages familiarity with the game's systems and quick thinking.
The game features other characters in addition to Cadence, the 'normal' character. Of those released, the Monk changes the player's playstyle the most: each enemy drops gold, which the Monk cannot touch, but he gets one free item from each shop. Playing the Monk now means you need to be careful about where you kill each enemy, and try to avoid killing (and thus avoid spawning gold) if possible. Other characters that have been released are easier or more difficult versions of the main character.
The game is not a roguelike in the same sense that Nethack or ADOM are, instead, its design is more similar to The Binding of Isaac in that area. There is a shop on every level, you must defeat a mini-boss or boss every level to advance, loot is drawn from one big pool, and chests, bombs, shrines, and other items are scattered throughout the levels. The skill, though, lies more on the player's intuitive and instinctive understanding of the game's mechanics, in much the same way the Spelunky does.
Crypt of the Necrodancer was created by Ryan Clark, who is very transparent and talks to the community (having replied to more forum posts than he hasn't, I think). It updates frequently, bringing new content, where each new item or game element has completely different behaviour than others, and changes the way you play the game when you interact with it.
I thoroughly recommend this game, especially if you're a fan of either of the other games I mentioned.

I was almost instantly intrigued by Crypt of the NecroDancer. It’s a roguelike that’s played to the rhythm of whatever song is currently playing in the level. Being a fan of dungeon crawlers in general, this rather ingenious spin on the genre got me interested. On the bottom of the screen is a heart with animated bars getting closer and closer. It’s like a simpler Guitar Hero; jump to the beat of the heart to keep your coin multiplier from depleting. If you’re attacked, you’ll lost the multiplier. Aside from things trying to kill you, traps in the environment will also try to ruin this multiplier. If you fall in a puddle your multiplier will be lost. Spike traps will injure you, trapdoors will send you to different areas in the level, sometimes surrounded by monsters, other times you are greeted by a singing merchant who will sell you armor, food to heal, weapons, anything useful. You’ll earn money by killing monsters such as skeletons, bats, ghosts, even monkeys.
You start every playthrough with a dagger, shovel, and a bomb. Chests will drop larger blades, crossbows, armor, and more items once you’ve unlocked them with diamonds. Diamonds are scattered throughout the map, sometimes hidden in walls that can be dug up using a shovel. Items found in chests can also be purchased from the aforementioned singing merchant.
Levels are divided into four zones. At the end of every zone, there will be a mini-boss (often a dragon) that needs to be killed in order for the stairs to the next level to unlock. However, if you wait around in a level for too long, the song that’s playing will end and you’ll be dropped to the next level. This is similar to the ghost that is sent after you in Spelunky when you’ve spent a long time in one level. Or like the music that’s used to cut actors off during their acceptance speeches when they’re boring. Whatever floats your boat. I mean, the game allows you to use your own MP3 files, so you could totally kill monsters to the Oscars’ “get off the stage” music.
Characters can sometimes be found locked in cages. If you haven’t found the key in a chest prior, there’s a good chance the merchant will have one on sale. Once these characters are unlocked, a new room will unlock in the lobby. These rooms contain practice courses and shops. You can use the diamonds you collected in your last playthrough to purchase upgrades and new items that will show up in chests. Also in the lobby is where you’ll find the entrances to zones, different game modes like Hardcore or an easier mode with fewer enemies, local co-op, character select, and more. Unlockable characters carry different abilities, such as Bard, who can move freely and not to the rhythm of a song. He’s a great character to use to take a break from the rhythm-based combat of Cadence, the story’s frontliner. Though there isn’t much of a story; it’s all set up in the opening cutscene, featuring Cadence falling into a dungeon and being taken over by the NecroDancer. Which would explain why she’s tasked to move to the beat of a song.
The Verdict
There isn’t much I could dislike about this game. I would totally understand your feelings if you dislike dungeon crawlers; it’s a love it or hate it situation. Crypt of the NecroDancer is available now for $14.99 on Steam. It can be played with a controller, keyboard, and even a DDR pad. If you dislike the genre, it’s likely you’ll dislike this rhythmic take on it. If you’re like me and enjoy roguelikes that put your persistence to the test, chances are you’ll enjoy it, maybe even love it.

After spending several dark, lonely hours with my boy Isaac, I can honestly say I've never had so much fun watching babies cry.
The Binding of Isaasc is a retelling (in very broad strokes) of the parable of the Biblical story of Isaac. However, instead of a just and merciful God, Isaac's mother is (probably) a schizophrenic hearing the "voice of God" demanding her son's sacrifice. No last minute reprieves from the President are expected. Faced with a psychotic, knife-wielding mother, Isaac's only hope lies in braving the mysteries and horrors of the basement...
Thematically:  The game setting is dark, bordering on blatantly sacrilegious, and completely irreverant, which is mostly  right up my alley. Some of the between-level cutscenes show backstory (real or imagined) portraying either Isaac's history or his fears; you can't sure which are which, and the cutscenes do much to provide a more grounded feeling of anxiety or sympathy to his character than the prologue is able to do (especially since you aren ot given much time to bond with the child at the beginning). Mechanically: The game controls are easy to learn, but difficult to master, especially when you are under pressure (such as having multiple enemies gunning for your teeny-tiny throat). The idea of bending Isaac's tears to hit enemies while on the move is a challenge, but with repetition and practice, it is possible to become very good at hitting the "sweet spot" while maintaining your increasingly precious heart value. Gameplay: I found the gameplay to be quite challenging, and also one of the more frustrating parts of the BoI experience. As item drops and dungeon layout are randomly generated, it is entirely conceivable (nay, likely) to receive non-synergistic or just out-right useless items during your run. This can be very distracting, especially if it happens multiple runs in a row. That being said, I truly appreciate the wide breadth of items and the thought that went into their creation. This also plays into the game's Replayability: Being able to see new enemies and new items every run is entirely enjoyable! The wide range of strategies that can be employed with each of the 5 (6 with the Wrath of the Lamb expansion) characters is enjoyable to learn and employ, and finding item synergies that enable you to roll over your enemies is also rewarding.
Overall, I recommend this game if you have a dark sense of humor and are not bothered by sacrilegious themes. It's a quick, sick, and enjoyable way to spend an afternoon!

A downside of the game, for me, is the utter randomness of it. Sometimes you'll get lucky and have a super build, sometimes you'll just get crappy items over crappy items. I should warn you about it's difficulty, too. Some rooms are very hard and you need extra quick reaction time not to get hurt, and this is where Flash was a bad choice, making the game laggy when too many elements are on screen.
Overall, it's still an awesome game that I recommended to lots of my friends, and some of them are even more hooked than me.

"Dust - An Elysian Tail" is best described as an action-rpg-platformer i guess.

I really enjoyed it and would recommend you'd give it a try, if you like this sort of genre.This is definitely worth a playthrough unless you're one of those people that's had a terrible childhood where your parents abused you and you weren't allowed to watch awesome 90's cartoons like Bucky O'Hare and Ducktales, instead you grew up watching That's So Raven and other junk which make you go OMG FURRY this is! Anyway...
This game is a side scrolling fighting story-driven game that does a lot of things good and a few things merely ok. Everyone harps on it being 'furry' but I think that's just kneejerk reaction. It's just got animal characters in it. If this is furry, so is Ducktales. No one will be yiffing anything. The combat is fun, but does wear a little thin near the end thanks to not much variety. You have a sidekick who is a squeaky voiced flying mouse bat fox creature, but she actually ends up being not annoying (at least in my experience) because she's a bit sarcastic and tends to be overly genre-aware break the 4th wall to crack jokes. The story feels a little rushed in places, but not bad. From what I understand, the dev basically had to work 20 hour days for a couple months to crank the game out, and while I can see some rough patches overall it's a pretty fun experience.
The best way to describe it without spoilers is if you combined the fantastical art style and platforming of Earthworm Jim games with the gameplay and character advancement of modern 2D Castlevania games, plus a bit of Klonoa thrown in for character design and story. Dust takes all of those elements and makes a very satisfying experience out of them.
Also Dust has one killer Camel toe so there's that.
My score for Dust: An Elysian Tail is:
4.5 Dust Camel / 5 Toes

If you like the classic 90s puzzle genre, you should absolutely pick this up and love it.

A rather simple match-3 with simple Rogue "lite" elements and a simple plot, Notice the pattern yet?
You awake in a stone chamber with a bunch of doors, all but one is locked off, entering the big door causes the game to begin. The game follows a runner format type of game, up top is your dude running from left to right, he'll run until he hits a obstacle (Monster or a lock) and you match what you need from the bottom puzzle board.
Sword & staves do damage while the keys unlock locks, also in the board are armor tiles, item tiles and resource tiles. You keep this up until you lose by the screen catching up with you, which then causes you to awake back in the stone chamber.
You can spend the resources you find to open and upgrade the rooms which in turn boost your abillity to play the game,
rinse & repeat until you get 10,000,000 score and you win the game, simple.
There are milestones and challenges to complete that give you some resources and multipliers adding your end goal.
All in all it's a short but addicting match-3, nothing amazing but simply solid in its execution.

One of the best RPG's I have experienced to date. Obviously the most standout thing on the surface is the graphics. While typical RPG's settle for bland and boring the world of The Witcher is colorful and well detailed. What really sells the game is the complex story telling, which features many different plot twists, and your choices actually influence the main storyline. Its not like Mass Effect where your choices don't mean anything to the storyline. Now the gameplay is difficult as long as you select normal or harder. You dont play as an OP badass, you can die after about 4 to 5 hits from about anything unless its a way lower level then you. Combat is hard, and you will need to plan ahead by drink potions before battle and seting up traps because you can drink potions while in battle and there is no health regen. How I would describe the openess of this game is semi-open world. You can travel freely among the land, but after completing enough main story quests you will travel to a new land, unable to go back to where you came from to complete unfinished side quests or anything you left back there. The game does this often so the best way to get everything done is sidequests first. It is a bit annoying to not be able to travel back but The Witcher 3 fixes this problem and is going full open world. Either way this a must buy for RPG fans and suckers for a good story, its a hell of a ride and the game doesnt treat you like an idiot, you will be presented with challenges that will make you s**t a brick. Now all i have to do is wait for The Witcher 3 and my life will be complete.

There simply aren't enough games with dinosaurs & even fewer of these that are actually worth playing! For me, Orion: Prelude (O:P) is that rare exception. Although not much in way of a story in the game (no single player after all), there is quite a tale on how Orion came to be the game it is today...
The short version is, that O:P is an evolution of previous Orion titles, Dino Horde & Dino Beatdown originally dating back to a successful 2011 Kickstarter campaign. Although recieving early criticism (that would normally kill a game ..dead.. disappearing into obscurity), the game continued to evolve with constant updates (big & small) over the years from the developers. Spiral stuck with it! This dedication & gradual refinement of the game has resulted in an excellent first-person co-op experience, with a well rounded collection of modes, weapons, enviromental effects, vehicles & more to enjoy.
PvP isn't forgotten; it's also selectable. PvP feels more alike to a retro deathmatches, than a modern PvP (in a good way!), but I mainly enjoy the co-op modes. In co-op, you essentially have to defend your power core against waves of bloodthursty dinosaurs. Dinosaur kills will reward you credits, which you can use to buy perks & weapon upgrades, in-turn helping you survive the later, harder waves. Some waves also have you securing objectives. Co-op doesn't feel ultra competitive, most of the time you don't watch your credits/kills, rather finding yourself just having fun surviving & helping your teammates! I've found the community to generally be helpful & friendly in-game too.
One of the real stand-out features in O:P has to be the enviromental effects randomly cycling on the alien world. From the day/night cycles to the extreme variety of climates & types of weather. Adds so much to the atmosphere. Couple this with excellent lighting effects through what seems to be a thicker atmosphere and the results can sometimes be spectacular! Even overwhelming! You definitely get that feeling when your final wave gets a night cycle with heavy rain .. you know you are gonna see an epic close quarter battle!
Along with the awesome effects, there are 3 distinct classes to mix-up the gameplay. Each has unique strengths & each you can progress/level-up in online play to unlock starting weapons, power-ups & perks. Initial learning curve isn't steep, so once you get the hang of the basic flow it becomes very easy to sink multiple hours killing dinos! O:P rarely feels like a grind; even at lower levels (without a lot of perks) you competently kill dinos & gain good XP. Plenty of dinos to go around too :)
If you can't find a friend to play with, there is also bot-support added in O:P to fill the ranks. This can be helpful to get playing quickly if server populations are low (which regrettably does happen).
The trilogy of classes are well balanced (no need for any other classes), as is the gameplay in general. Difficulty is super scalable. Weapons are mainly shared between classes so quickly become familiar, and vehicles are easy to use & offer a good range of practical & destructive uses. Repetitive? Sure, to a degree, it is the same thing over & over and despite there being a lot of 'accessories' to the spice up the character classes & tactics, modes etc, there are not a huge number of maps for each mode. I expect this will change soon with Steam Workshop support being added.
The A.I. generally employed by the dinosaurs is a fairly basic 'rush' tactic, which can feel pretty predictable (there are a few surprises though), but I find the larger dino numbers to counteract this limitation to a degree anyway. There are also the occasional technical glitches like querky physics (flying Stegosaurus anyone?) or clipping inside a dinosaur. Nothing game-breaking that I have experienced, but sure does make for some funny moments! Just like my many failed attempts at some of the more creative 'Ride a Dino for 10secs' & 'Slap T-Rex 100 times' achievements :)
O:P reminds me a bit of those classic, simple shooters like a Serious Sam or Left 4 Dead, but with a bit of high-tech sci-fi flavor. This future-tech feel across the game contradicts the jurassic era dinosaurs & remote wilderness landscapes nicely! O:P is not as complex mechanically or technically when compared to a top end AAA FPS, but its simplicity is also its underlying strength. 10 Million is, simply put, a match 3 game. While it boasts "rpg elements," they are extremely minimal and 99% of the game is spent on the puzzle board. If that's your kind of game, then look no further. This title is best suited for casual gamers.
- Cozy pixel graphics
- Entirely mouse controlled, fast response
- "RPG lite" element that allows you to spend resources to upgrade damage, defense, and other perks
- Objectives, or in-game tasks, are used to gate progression, giving you a sense of achievement.
- The alchemy lab potions allow you to customize your gameplay further to help you reach your goals
- Short. Only a couple hours to clear
- Low replayability after game completion outside of achievements
- Watch out in using items. If you are racing through and click an item before the character stops in front of the enemy, the item is wasted. This was a source of much frustration in speed runs. This behavior isn't explained in game.
- The chiptunes were nice at first but grew old fast. There were only a few, and they became distracting on the harder levels.
- This is a personal gripe, and probably minor, but I didn't see the upgrade button above the rooms until late game. I wish it had been more visible, and not grey. (Don't make my mistake and wait for the end to upgrade!)
Achievement hunters: You must exit the game for the achievements to register. Hopefully this saves you extra runs thinking you didn't hit the score achievements. Also watch out for the last two that require you to hit 10 million on lower difficulties. Jose especially becomes somewhat luck based to spawn a "clear path" to goal, took me many resets.

This was the greatest incarnation of the Dawn of War family of titles.
The original game was a solid but old fashioned RTS with linear storytelling and generic factions. Subsequent expansions added fun races, but it was only in Dark Crusade that it all came together to make a replayable, challenging, well balanced, addictive and rewarding turn based RTS experience (how else do you put it? Like Rome: Total War, real time battles contained within a turn-based overview map)
So what is the deal with Dark Crusade?
You could get away with calling it a lightweight title; an extra release with a rather deeply reimagined campaign style which turned out to be the most effective version of the game. You begin overlooking a 2-dimensional playing map, you can't pan, you can't zoom, what you see is what you get and, maddeningly, half the zones to the edge of the map seem to fall off the static sides thereof.
The zones are divided into kinda equal spans of territory, each span controlled by one of the factions - Space Marines, Eldar, Tau, Chaos Marines, Orks and the badass Imperial Guard. The content of the game involves moving your squad around the map, picking which zones you attack based on what kind of rewards you might get from them, as well as how difficult they seem to be relative to your forces at that point.
Different zones offer different bonuses. The great advantage of starting a map with an extra squad or two can be earned with some gutsy combat. A drastic boost in the requisition points you can use to pre-build units and buildings before engaging in combat can be secured by controlling a zone with massive buried industrial complexes rumored to be lying beneath its surface. Another zone you can wrest from control of the Space Marines (if you dare) allows you to airdrop troops directly into any zone of the entire map.
Beyond advantages, the zones also come with voiced narrative introductions - lightweight, as is much of the game presentation wise, but firmly in line with the idiom of the WH40K universe - and storylines which more often than not directly influence the type of scenario that plays out. In the map to control the spaceport the object of the mission is not to defeat the enemy but rather to capture a total of seven automated servitors who only head towards your base once you have come into contact with them - though they be liable to turn around and head to your enemy at the slightest influence of passing opponenets.
One fantastic achievement of the game is the balance of the factions. Whilst Imperial Guard seem to struggle usually - in all these years I've not played them, and they always seem to lose key territory and ultimately perish if left to ai controls -  all of the other races offer relentless resourcefulness with regards to sustaining ongoing, give-and-take, ebb-and-flow style battles. My faction of choice, the Tau, can be upgraded to fire highly accurate, highly powerful long range blaster rifle shots and, later, be supported by extremely powerful tanks, but their relatively slow buildup speed and limited numbers can leave them vulnerable to early attacks by the Chaos Marines, for example, who come supported by a wide range of very tough elite troops despite suffering from pretty pathetic frontline troop squadrons. The Space Marines field the mightiest troops across virtually of the spectrums, but they are expensive and relatively slow, their weapons boasting only reduced range when compared with the Tau.
The Necrons are an interesting race. If you get on top of them they can be easy to overrun, but if you find yourself undergunned to deal with their heavily armoured, self-resurrecting support vehicles you could be in for a pretty harrowing experience. A disadvantage may exist in the Necron leader unit, which is invincible - eternally reassembling and lurching to its feet a few minutes after the temporary setback of running out of hit points. If said leader makes an early foray into your base - something they are wont to do - and you are able to destroy him, you can build up forces around him and pretty much pin him in place for a goodly span of time going forward.
The aforementioned observations are all gleaned from the single player campaign, I've so little interest in multiplayer I'm not sure if this game even offers it.
Time to stop writing my thoughts about the game and conclude this review. More attractive graphics, more varied landscapes, more fleshed out factions with more relatable identities and a fresh take on campaign gameplay lead to this title being the pick of a pretty decent bunch of original Dawn of War offerings. I grade it highly. It is not a favourite, other RTS games of a similar era - Rise of Legends comes to mind - appealed to me more powerfully, but it is nevertheless a game I am happy to buy years later, and a game which I indeed play yet, all those years later.

A charmingly addictive match-3 puzzle game. I really like these type of games and when done right amazing results  can be had, just think about Puzzle Quest.
Now, 10,000,000 certainly isn't as good, there is no story to speak about, the graphics and music are rudimentary. Yet it has it's core mechanisms perfected so that it turns into an addictive game. It adds some basic skills elements to the mix, where you can improve your character and increase your chance of long-time survival when running a dungeon.
When starting a game, your character is running a dungeon, the tiles you match have an effect on what the current dungeon obstacle is. It's in your benefit to match the tiles accordingly. Additionally to that, objectives are given which you must try to complete, for example - chain 3 matches. This prevents the game from turning into a mindless tile clicker and will require you to keep your mind and focus to it.
If you're into this kind of game and are not put off by 8 bit graphics and music, certainly give this a try.

A worthy sequel to the first game, changed in many ways - some good, some not so good. It takes about 30-35 hours to finish it with almost all side stories done, which is about half of the first game, but no worries, it's enough. The graphics is easily more beautiful in motion than many other games just announced at E3, and we are talking about a game that came out 3 years before. The world is unchanged, it's dirty, it's corrupt, it's cruel, and the beautiful looks hide a dark, more realist story where everyone starves for power, money, sex, and there is rarely to no justice to those who would deserve it, and we don't play "The" hero who delivers it. The world (even if it's broke up to 3 Acts) is incredibly immersive, the lore is rich, and the RPG elements are well balanced with the tactical, action packed monster (and people) slaying.
Still, there are many flaws. From technical side, it's a miracle to achieve such graphics (max out, in motion, it's truly jaw dropping, breath taking sometimes) with this hardware requirement, but it's poorly optiamlized in a weird way, having fps issues that shouldn't occur. You can meet some even after playing for 20 hours without any problems, and suddenly you have 3 to 5 fps and only restarting the game fixes it. Sometimes the ground textures raise to waist level (take a steam screenshot with the small floating in steam overlay picture turned on, it fixes it. NOTHING ELSE WILL. I'm serious, tried all cfgs, drivers etc.), or the game decides to get stuck in between two menus and you can only force close the program. Or talking animations are like early 2000s, everyone standing still and talking with barely any emotions on the faces. Unforgivible, knowing the game came out after not one, but two Mass Effect masterpiece games, and those were done with a licensed engine, while CDProject developed their own engine. All this still being present after a 10-16Gb Enchanted Edition patch is not something I can forgive - however I don't regret buying the game a second time on steam, after getting the original boxed retail version. I recommend grabbing that if you are really into extra stuff, the basic editions come with OST disc, how it's made disc, extra guide books and maps etc. just grab a cheap copy on steam if you prefer the digital way when it comes to playing. It's definitly a game everyone who is into complex stories, betrayal and RPGs in general - while storywise it's not required, but it is very strongly recommended to finish if the first game before starting this, otherwise you'll lose a LOT you don't even know is there - you won't know people, your friends, their and your own history alone or together. The technical difficulties can be a serious setback at first, but there are (sadly and luckily) way too many guides around the web, about how to fix what. Buy it on sale, you won't regret it. Buy it anytime if you like the genre, you won't regret it.

It doesn't quite feel fair to write a review on an incomplete game, but I like the direction this game is going and feel that it deserves some praise. Crypt of the NecroDancer is a unique roguelike dungeon crawler where the dungeons are prodedurally generated and all character movement and enemy movement are done to the beat of the music. In the lobby, you can select which dungeon you want to enter and you can spend the diamonds that you find in those dungeons to unlock items and spells that will then have a chance to appear in your future dungeon runs.
Like many indie games do, CotND sports an oldschool, 2D pixelated artstyle. There is a two-player mode as well, and if one player dies, they will be revived once the other player clears the current floor. From the lobby, you can choose which zone to play (currently 3 zones, each with 3 floors and a final boss) or you can play Hardcore mode, where you start from Zone 1 with none of your unlocked buffs and the game only ends when you either die or you clear the end of Zone 3.
Positives:
+ Pretty sick beats by Danny Baranowsky (also known for his work in Super Meat Boy and The Binding of Isaac)
+ Lots of unique enemies with unique attack patterns that will keep you on your toes
+ Vivid, colorful sprites to make enemy identification easy
+ Enemy attacks are telegraphed through their animations making them avoidable, but the game is still a challenge when there is a large variety of them at once, forcing the player to think and plan their next few moves within 120 beats per second (or, you know, whatever the tempo happens to be).
+ Upon death, the cause of death is displayed and a replay of your final moments is shown to you so that at least you know how and why you failed so horribly and can learn from the experience.
+ Though I haven't gotten it to work myself, there is a way to replace the in-game music with your own. But really, why would you want to do that anyway?
Negatives:
- Various bugs, of course.
- (Not so much a rag on this game specifically but roguelikes in general) You are completely at the mercy of RNGesus. Sometimes you'll have crap weapons. Sometimes you'll start a floor completely surrounded by enemies. Yes, it's part of the challenge, but please don't make me fight 6 goblins in Zone 3-2 with just a dagger.
Focus the f***ing Necrons first!

I've heard this game's name tossed around the internet so much and heard so much praise that I simply had to give it a shot. And I immediately saw what all the fuss is about - this game is pretty awesome!
First off, if you don't like challenging games, this is not for you. This game is literally built around "trying and dying", and the enemy AI doesn't follow the same pattern 100% once feces hit the fan, adding more to the crazy and unpredictable nature of the gameplay. The control scheme, while simple, takes a while to get ahold of, but is still intuitive enough to enable fluild and smooth movement and manipulation.
Levels include you bursting into a building and literally slaughtering everything in your path. The catch is that you are basically a squishy, one-shottable weakling, which means you really have to soar through the levels to survive. Rinse, repeat. This might seem repetitive but the way the enemies are positioned differently and given different weapons if you completely restart the chapter plus the ability to equip masks that have different bonuses (lethal fists and move faster being my all-time favourites) ensures that the levels don't get stale and boring after a few tries.
The story is pretty loopy, I won't give anything away.
The pixely, oldschool style and the outstanding soundtrack are also praiseworthy. I love it when games have all the pieces of the puzzle!
The only negative I could find is that sometimes it seems the game's rules on what does or does not count as a hit are a bit fussy; for example, I had a lot of point-blank shotgun blasts resulting in a miss, some thrown weapons going through enemies, which can be a bit frustrating. But then again, "can be a bit frustrating" is pretty much the motto of this game.
Definitely recommend, even at full price you get plenty of gameplay. A+!

This is second stand alone addon to great rts/tactic game Dawn of War in W40k universe. This time we have much more freedom. There is part of planet to conquer which is splitted to several provinces. We have more "races" to choose and fight against: Space Marines, Imperial Guard, Chaos Marines, Orks, Eldars, Necrons and Tau. Each of them have stonghold on the map. Now You have basic strategy game (buying units and buildings to defend provinces, moving main army beetwen our own provinces and attacking enemy provinces. Each province gives resources each turn (We have one move per turn) and gives also something special (honor guard unit to accompany our hero or special "global" ability). I think most important is to obtain three of them:
-extra 1k resources on beginning of each battle,
-space port to be able to move/attack almost any province (except strongholds),
-two moves per turn.
When You commence attack or defending province You switch to rts game like original Dawn of War. This time there is much more variety of missions:
- defending Your own province - easiest mission. You have almost every building avaliable which You built when You attack this province, but in most cases You will not have Your main hero and his honor guards to assist;
- attacking province which can give honor guard unit - We need to destroy all enemy bases;
- attacking province with special ability - We need to finish some task and in many cases We do not need to destroy Our opponent;
- attacking enemy stronghold - We need to complete couple of tasks, but sometimes We can sneak through the map and kill enemy hero. This missions are the hardest, but after that whole "race" is out from the main map.
Like I allready wrote this addon expands gameplay and really gives freshness to this franchise.
Graphics is better. You can use full HD resolutions now.
Music and sounds are still great and builds climate.

Natural Selection 2 is a great game with a unique RTS/FPS element to it. However, it's lacking a lot of polish when it comes to game balance and server performance. The game was released before it was ready and had major issues during that time. It took years to correct those issues and just made it to a semi-polished release worthy state this year.
Hit registration is wonky at best. The game only runs on 30 ticks and it often times takes well over 60ms to process packets and send them back to clients. To make matters worse, the game just assumes every target is 100ms away instead of trying to compensate for ping.
Game developers have their own agenda when it comes to releasing updates and running their game. They are very dismissive when it comes to community feedback. Quite a few of the changes they push in updates people don't want. Server operators have to deal with their controlling and exclusive attitude, where they restrict basic necessaries a server needs to be succesful; on the basis of wether or not it fits the type of society they want for their game.
Over the past year, the game has really went downhill in the wrong direction. I probably wouldn't recommend this game for the community or culture. It's a gaint melting pot with a really steep learning curve. Development is hindered by the utopian society Unknown Worlds Enterintainment has created. They destoryed the competitive and modding communties. Freedom of speech of  non-existent on the hub. Anything they don't like is locked or deleted.
As a Canadian, this is not the type of society I want to be a part of. I was going to launch a server for this game, but was banned and isolated by a developer due to a difference of views.

12/22/17 Update: The big update is disappointing. The pace feels a lot slower and there is still very little trap strategy unless you either a) grind for hours to unlock traps from a random chest drop or b) buy chests and hope the random number generator gives you the trap you want. You can get a better video game experience from OMD1 and OMD2.
Side note: There is a board game version by Sandy Peterson Games! This nicely captures the coop tower defense feel, with 4 players! Missing the Siege mode? Then go head to head in 1v1, 2v2, 3v3, and 4v4 in the Versus mode of the board game.
In its present state, I cannot recommend investing time with this game. When the open beta started in March 2016, the PvE mode, Survival, allowed up to 5 players to play together and defend against the orc waves. That feature was removed in July, making the maximum number of players for a normal Survival game be limited to 3 players. If you play coop games with your significant other, or with a large group of friends, this player cap severely limits  your fun with this game.
Now they are removing the PvP mode, Siege. I didn't play much against other humans, but I did thoroughly enjoy playing against the AI bots. That, and this was the only way to continue playing with a player party size larger than 3.
There is a lot of potential with this game, and I would like to see it succeed. Until the party size is increased again, though, anyone wanting the OMD nostalgia is better off playing 1 or 2 from the franchise. And it will be several updates before the player limit comes back, if ever.
Aside from the player limit cap, I also cannot recommend this game because of the severe amount of grind involved. It takes a long play time to build a sizable deck up to compete against level 30+ maps. The game also removed the trap experimentation found in the earlier franchises because you have to purchase/unlock a trap before you can use it. This tedious process of "unlocking" traps limits how many traps you actually get to play with and removes the OMD fun of discovering trap synergies. This trap frustration is exacerbated further by requiring you to upgrade your trap's strength tiers in order to compete with the monster difficulty that scales at a faster rate than you can.

Final Fantasy VII, whether you love it (as I did) or hate it (for how overrated you believe it to be), is a game that arguably changed the direction of game industry history in the mid-late 90s.
It is the single most important game in Sony's history, as it was a flagship title for the PlayStation One at a time when the world still wasn't quite sure if the Nintendo 64 or the PlayStation would triumph as the defacto console of the generation.
It is in my humble opinion, the game that won over skeptics to Sony's camp. I remember thinking how weird it was that a company that was making TVs was making a video game system and that Nintendo was the winner over SEGA this time for sure, but after seeing Final Fantasy VII in action at a friend's house, the PlayStation One was immediately on my Christmas wish list.
At that time, Final Fantasy VII's graphics alone were enough to warrant trailers for the game in movie theaters and on television. But the huge scope, the cinematic storytelling, the music, and the incredible animation were what really gave it a place in history.
Final Fantasy VII remains the single greatest game in history for me because it was the first game to move me to tears. It remains my favorite Final Fantasy not only for its gigantic leap forward in graphical fidelity when compared to Final Fantasy VI (my 2nd favorite Final Fantasy), but also for the amazing breadth of game mechanics within it. Not only do you get the standard fight monsters and level up fare, but a motorcycle chase mini-game, a snowboarding mini-game, a chocobo racing AND a chocobo raising mini-game, as well as a submarine mini-game, and countless other games within this massively ambitious title. Since then, no other Final Fantasy has come close. Sure there have been card games and underwater soccer, but no other Final Fantasy had anything akin to Gold Saucer.
You may think Cloud is "emo" or that Barret was a racist stereotype, or how, off course, the English translation was riddled with countless mistakes ;), but you cannot argue how important Final Fantasy VII was.
I recommend Final Fantasy VII to those who want to find out what the fuss was about, or to those who wish to see how ambitious a game can be and still succeed. I know that those born after a time when FInal Fantasy VII was released will find it harder to enjoy, due to its poor aging when looked at from a modern standpoint. Its blocky low-polygon characters pantomiming exaggerated animations and low resolution pre-rendered backgrounds are more than enough to push most gamers away...
However, if you can see past its wrinkles and compare it fairly to all the other games that were out back then, I promise you will be taken on a journey that will make you understand how wonderous it was for all of us when it arrived.

You wake in the forest, unaware of who you are or were. An overly energetic flying naive sidekick helps you, like a little sister, not Navi. As you stumble through the world you find villains. The villains are fueled by more than just an evil identity and all have a brief telling of their fall. After each battle the game makes you wonder if your hero is any better than them, fighting a war only seeing one side.
Game Play: 1/3
The game has a spectacle fighter style. You need to keep moving and keep fighting, there is no blocking or hiding. To make this style work, there is no depth to the combat. When you level up, you add points into one of the standard pools, strength, health, defense or magic. You are limited on how you level up and leveling up attack early allows you to blow through the game. The game’s equipment are linear upgrades, simply find the next, not debate the pros and cons.
Re-Playability: 0/1
With limited builds and no unique items the game relies on the story and dialog for your attention. Once you beat the game there is little left for you.

The premise is that I am playing all the DoW I games in a row, so i might be a bit "overfed" with them. That might help justifying the judgement on this one after the very positive ones i gave to the previous ones.
To start with, battle mechanics themselves are unchanged from the first 2 games. And they share the same plus and cons (I might have seen a better squad movement here, but I am not sure). Two new armies, very interesting, nice variety of new mechanics, super good as usual. Some new units as well for the existing armies, very good addition too.
Now we go to the campaign part, this is where it changed completely from the previous 2 games.
The campaign is no longer linear, and this is good. Main map mechanics very similar to the ones in EiR, very nice thing is bases persistence, nice having some special provinces as well.
But it falls flat. It becomes repetitive, long and sorta boring. The story feels flat, just faction-based generic cutscenes and no more characters based. Beside, being quite long, and not allowing you to use multiple factions as in WA, you end up playing it once, then maybe a couple of skirmishes with other factions and that's it.
A pity, cause technically it is old but gold, but the above mentioned issues make it feel much worse than it's predecessor (specially WA and its very nice campaign).Still very enjoyable, but a step back for me compared to the base version and the wonderful Winter Assault.

I've been wanting to play this game for quite awhile now. It was definitely worth the wait. I really enjoyed playing through this game from beginning to end.
The best parts were definitely the exploration and the interaction of Dust and Fidget. I wanted to explore the world. Figure out where the nooks and crannies were. Everytime Fidget and Dust would start talking about something I knew I was in for a treat. For those two reasons alone this game is worth picking up.
The gameplay is good. It isn't necessarily a stand out and it doesn't suck. It's just good. The combo system is pretty easy to pick up, though button mashing is a pretty good way to go half the time. Or just spamming Fidget's attack. One of the two. The flow of Dust's sword swings is what really makes the combat enjoyable. The animation for those is nice, and the speed of the attacks is quick enough to please.
There are some faults to the game though. The character designs are on the bland side of things. The way they're drawn isn't terribly impressive either. Which is sad since the drawings during the final credits are very nice. If more of the drawing in the actual game looked like that it would be more pleasing. The plot of the game is kind of forgettable. It serves it's purpose and manages to pull a heart string or two, it just isn't going to blow any minds. Really the only thing I would say is a huge knock against the game is that Dust runs so freaking slow! I found myself spamming the dodge button so that I could get through screens a little bit faster. I wish they would have sped up his running speed.
Really though this is a fun game and well worth the time and money to play it. I would recommend this to any friend that wants a fun game to pick up and play!

The name of the game is assymetric gameplay.
Yep, you have aliens on one side and marines on the other. Completely different factions.
For those that haven't read the description of the game, this is basically a combination of rts and fps. One player on each team players as the commander and takes care of RTS stuff. The goal of the game is to basically destroy the other team's base.
As i said, both factions play differently. What I mean is unit composition. Aliens mostly fight in close combat, can run on walls, fly, turn invisible. While marines get assault rifles, shotguns, jetpacks, exo suits, flamethrowers.
But what i love the most about this game is the pacing. The games can take long - 30/45/60 mins, and at first you start out as a basic grunt, only with your assault rifle or the basic alien. As the game progresses, the commander will be giving all sorts of goodies to the team - better weapons, more alien spicies, passive upgrades. All that gives this game a MOBA feel. That sense of getting stronger as the game progresses. How early, mid and late game are so different.
The game also has really cool atmosphere. Personally, i just love the Alien, and the developers have numerously referenced the alien franchise. The way marines look is pretty much a 100% copy of the aliens movies, and the aliens while not looking like xenomorphs, are still pretty damn good. Mostly importantly they play like predators. Like they are in control and can attack you at any moment.
Since this is part RTS, there is a resource war. Marines need to first turn on power in the sector to get the resources from that zone, while aliens don't. Being a marine in a sector that has no power is pretty scary. And as i said, aliens can become invisible far later into the game. That really adds to the tension, considering that they can jump on you even from the ceiling.
