Well, what a journey! I'm a big fan of games with storylines and this is one of the better ones out there. I just finished playing through the story and finished all three parts. Now I have to say that the end is not what I expected but it fits the complete journey well. The only downside is the feels after the end.
The artwork is amazing! Cartoonish and just fun. There is much going on in the scenes but it doesn’t distract you from your story. The story is very well designed. I could relate to some of the characters and parts of the story. Maybe that’s why it’s such a great game for me, but I’m sure that others could have the same experience.
The music and comedy are a big part of the whole experience. It wouldn’t be the same if it wasn’t there or if it would be different. It suits the story, which is a story about love and life. It’s also fun to see that the music is integrated into the world and that characters interact with it.
This game is mostly a point-and-click game but has also a lot of puzzles or mini-games in it. Which can sometimes be a nice change-up from the storyline. If you are a puzzle game fan, you will have a blast with Deponia. If you’re not really into puzzle games, just use the skip button or a guide. I had to use a guide for puzzles one or two times myself.
The game ending is, like I said, not expected. It had a twist which left me with some double feelings. But to know what I mean, you have to play the game from the start and go through the 30+ hours to hopefully get that experience. The end leaves also room for a follow-up, although I doubt that they will make a sequel to the Deponia trilogy.
I’m recommending this game to anyone who loves great storylines in games. No matter what kind of games you normally play. Try this one and play through all three parts. It’s a great game and you’ll love it.

First off, the game is a point-and-click adventure. This should inform your choices immediately.  It means that there's going to be stupid pixel-hunts and completely nonsensical puzzles. There aren't ways to /die/, really, so I'm able to apply the word 'forgiving' to it.  However, it is almost best played with the walkthrough at-hand, or else you're going to be reduced to the lowest form of inventory mix-and-match that plagues the genre.
The game has a certain dark humor to it that is really enjoyable, and the characters are well-voiced and fun. The controls have a 'reveal' system that alleviates the pixel-hunt parts, and most maps are well designed with speedy-travel links that allow you to complete good parts of your missions without having to wait for characters to walk across the screen for the hundreth time.
The 'director commentary' makes it clear that it comes from a zany bunch of people who love the art form.  That might actually be why these games are just 'good' and not 'great':  They are pure tributes to the Infocom greats, instead of modern re-imaginings of the genre like Telltale is producing. Still, the zany is the game's saving grace.  Tune in for the musical interludes, and if you miss it in-game, make sure you Youtube the "Nothing To See" easter egg song.
Fans of the genre should get this game as it is sure to be a classic. If you aren't a fan, though, I'd probably start with Telltale instead.

Stars bolt around the screen as if being gazed upon by some drunk in the middle of the night, only to fade to the image of a young woman holding a basket of flowers, strolling into a vast industrial city the only light being the faint flicker of houses and the green glow of the mako reactors, amongst the pitch black polluted sky above. "Final Fantasy VII" scrolls across the screen as a drum roll picks up, slowly zooming into a platform, with quick interruptions from a speeding train grinding to a spark spitting halt. A woman and three blokes jump out and take down several guards, "C'mon Newcomer" shouts the burly black guy in am armless shirt. A spiky headed blonde, purple jumpsuit sporting dude backflips of the train with a sword bigger than him. Battle commences and you are thrust straight into the fray, swinging said sword and conjuring lightning.
Cinematic gold within five minutes.
From start to finish, Final Fantasy VII is an intense roller-coaster ride in terms of everything you'd expect from a video game and more. As if seeing the copious amounts of five star reviews for this game wasn't enough, one quick search for FF7 provides commercial acclaim left and right. People hold this game close to their hearts, stick up for it vigilantly, often ignore its (minimal) shortcomings and its not difficult to understand why. Released in 1997, 2 years after the Playstation One's world wide release, VII boasted a brand new, groundbreaking experience. Not many games were spread across three discs.. but the length of the game pretty much demanded it. My first experience of this game was in 1998 whilst visiting a friend I witnessed something fascinating, simply hearing the music as I walked into the room was enough to peek my interest but actually seeing 3 mysterious characters using all sorts of magic and summoning gigantic beasts to aid them in battle was, for lack of a better word, breathtaking. A few months later the same friend turned up LATE for my 8th birthday party, suffice to say all was forgiven when I realised what he had given me. By far the best gift I have ever received, it put all other presents to forgotten shame, and that was the beginning.
The battle system in Final Fantasy has largely remained unchanged throughout the early games, utilising 3 varied characters, each with a different class or set of abilities and stats, to ultimately defeat an opposing enemy. Taking turns, making use of magic, physical attacks and abilities. Often offering a different experience each time. VII is no different but improves on its predecessors considerably with new additions such as the materia system. Materia, a large part of the game involved not just in combat but story as well, is essentially an item equipped to enable the use of the specific magic within it. Its a rather unique system as there are so many combinations and levels in materia alone that its worth exploring the entire world to find every last type. The world itself is a strong reason alone as to why this game is so vast, featuring several locations ranging from the massive powerhouse conglomerate city of Midgar to a small snowy village where the only pass time is snowboarding. VII's amusement park, Gold Saucer is a marvel to behold, abundant in mini games that make the stresses of the game fade slightly if only for a moment.
Surroundings alone aren't enough however, Square had to go one further and get veteran composer Nobuo Uematsu to come up with one of the most memorable and emotional soundtracks ever made. The music enhances not only the environment but also effects the mood during dialogue. A whopping 85 MIDI tracks have never sounded this good. Whether its a sense of urgency, romance, pure adrenaline fuelled action, the soundtrack comes up trumps every time. Stories are a dying aspect in recent video games, its all for graphics and gameplay alone, with no magic, no plot, no heart. VII in many ways is like a novel, with thousands of conversations and sub plots to get stuck into, you can't help but experience them all. I can understand how insane that must sound, comparing similarities between a video game and a novel, but that just shows how in depth the story really is and how high I regard it. Keep in mind that many gamers would avoid or completely disregard a video game dubbed to have similar qualities of a book.
In the beginning you are thrust into a job with a group of environmentalists/activists/terrorists known as AVALANCHE, trying to take down ShinRa Inc. the ones behind the reactors that suck the land dry of its life source, mako. As you skulk through Midgar with your group you get to know all of its members, finding main characters along the way, get sidetracked, separate and reunite after major battles only to finally discover there is a greater evil at work. Events take you all around the globe via boats, submarines, airships, buggies and or course chocobos. You'll witness more incredible scenes at caverns, beaches, glaciers, temples, mountain tops, marshes, the ocean floor, the sky and even outer space, all whilst taking on nightmarish enemies and gaining new powers. Limit Breaks spice up battles using unique individual abilities to deal major damage after taking enough yourself. Secret characters hide away and must be convinced to aid you in your quest to save the world from utter chaos and destruction. If all that wasn't enough, you can try your hand at taking on optional bosses that appear in the later stages of the game, some with over 1,000,000 Hit Points. Final Fantasy VII has endured so much success it has spawned several spin offs.
Advent Children, a film set 2 years after the events of VII
Dirge of Cerberus, a PS2 game revealing further insight to one of VII's most mysterious characters
Last Order, a short anime film remodelling one of the epic events of VII
Before Crisis, a mobile phone game about ShinRa's special branch, The Turks
Crisis Core, a PSP game shedding light on events before VII
With all that you could say Square-Enix have milked the franchise, but to be fair to them, they have gone about it with respect to the original and catered to the fans needs. Its no wonder that with all this success, the internet forums are a buzz with the hype of a remake. If all my ramblings of reminiscant nostalgia hasn't at least tempted you, my apologies, but it is my impression that you are missing out on an absolute gem and the best game ever made. 15 years later, its still going strong.

I don't want to go so far and say this is a bad game. I think the creators worked very hard but it is loaded with issues noticible by the first hour of play. Lets start with the first thing noticed; movement.
Movement is something i'm particularly picky about and this game really bothered me right from the start. Ascethically you are a shadow ninja, you would assume that would mean you are athletic and nimble but I didn't get that feeling for a second. You cannot jump in this game, which isnt inherintly a problem as you have the ability to teleport to shadows on a constant basis. If you play for pure stealth the entire game is essentially just using the dishonored blink ability to jump through the level. This is frustrating when you have to look directly at where you have to teleport. If for example you are on a cliff face with a small wall infront of you and you want to blink to the otherside you have to teleport first onto the wall then over. This is a problem because the walls are normally not cloaked in shadow and standing on them will get you spotted. Secondly the movement feels sluggish and the animations don't help with that. For a ninja you move slow and all the animations are slow, except for blinking so thats what you will be doing the entire game. also your character will occasionally move in ways you did not tell them to. Teleport into a shadow just big enough to hide you? Too bad your character decides he cant stand there and without you pressing anything walks out. Stealth games rely on player control so when they make a mistake they know it was them and not the game being unfair and anytime they do things like this it takes off points.
Okay now lets actually talk about stealth. The game functions by shadows being good and light being bad. All abilities use shadow and recharge in shadow while bright light drains them. its a good concept but the problem is that it is the only way the game recognizes stealth. Hiding behind a wall but not in shadows? Spotted. Directly above an enemy on a rafter but not in shadows? Spotted. Essentially if you are out of shadows and there is a guard anywhere nearby, spotted. So stick to the shadows I hear you say. this is where the second problem comes in. You can stand right next to a guard and as long as you are in the shadows its fine but only if you are crouching. Because for some reason a shadow ninja in a shadow is less likely to be detected even though the guard is facing the other direction if they are crouching. It just doesnt make any sense and when I found this out it threw me right out of the world.  Now any sort of movement that you perform in the game pretty much gives away your position. walking and running are not safe but you are able to crouch walk in shadows with only a small chance of being seen. so if moving will give you away the only real choice is to blink. And that is exactly what this game is. Just blink through the entire map (just hope that where you blink is big enough to hide in). Its the most effective strategy and the game prety much forces you to do it. Too bad it just isnt fun. Unlike in other stealth games you don't have a world to play with. Its not a sandbox with interesting AI, cool tactics or visceral animations. It's more like a puzzle game of where to point and Right Click. Now you can left click to create shadows too, which was cool the first time I did it. But all this means is more blinking. Left click, then right click... wait to recharge. that is the game.
This isnt to say its all bad. It has a cool asthetic and I like how everything looked even with me not being a huge fan of ninjas. The Character designs are all right and the world and story they were painting were intriguing me. I wanted to see more of the story but sadly the gameplay had such a disconnect that I have dropped it after about an hour. I love stealth games and I am picking. Maybe i will come back to it at some point, but for now i'd rather just go play Mark of the Ninja.
This game is not bad, it just has a lot of problems. If you are out of stealth games sure give this one a try but don't expect a lot. To everyone else looking for a Ninja stealth game. Get Mark of the Ninja. And if you want to be a teleporting assassin get Dishonored.

Greetings fellow Gamers!
Here we have the second expansion to a game I consider a classic that helped change the RTS genre.  Does this expansion hold up to the original?  Well…it’s complicated.  I love this series and will always be a series that I feel was ahead of its time, but it hasn’t kept up as much as I’d like.
I can’t move there’s a tank next to me:  Okay, pathing feels worse, not sure if it is but it feels worse than the previous expansion.  Tanks constantly stop squads of infantry from moving around corners and with the games desire for tight combat this is something that kills the pace.  I don’t remember it being this bad but the game is very old.
Still some assembly still required:  They did a good job at increasing screen resolution natively without a mod but the game still requires a zoom out mod to make the best of this, so I am happy with that.  I feel I have to say again, this is to be expected with a game this old but I don’t want to make excuses for the game.  The graphics are still passable in my opinion, not as good as any of the latest games (would like to see a DOW2 graphics version of this).
Story Exists…kind of:  Again we left with a story without the focus being the Blood Ravens.  To be fair at least the Space Marines are Blood Ravens but the game moves towards a campaign mode with light storytelling, there are intros and outros and good stuff for those of us who happen to devour any small bit of fiction tied to my beloved Chapter.  Overall the campaign is enjoyable however, with buffs and bonuses you can acquire by holding certain territories and equipment that can be gained through completing challenges.  Your commander feels neigh unstoppable in the end (especially the Necron one) and you get special units that are higher quality than their normal versions.  One particular annoyance is some of the Honor Guard is single infantry units; it would have been nice to give these the ability to attach or at least give them another infantry in the squad to allow more use as they devolve into holding objectives early and sitting in base in the end.
Overall, if you like DOW you should get this, if you like Warhammer 40k, still get this.  With that you should know if you want this, still an amazing game that maybe didn’t hold up as much as we’d like.  Enjoy!

There are time trials, 100 plane movements (ie: combined take off and landings) and an open ended best score unlimited time. A few different personalities to give you an extra crash or slower speed when you want to slow a plane down.
It's really a puzzle game trying to manage landings and take offs.  But having said that is highly addictive and I couldn't stop playing it for a whole day, trying to beat my top scores etc, so in that essence it is a lot of fun and well worth the $5 I bought it for. Not too accustomed to writing reviews, so forgive me if something seems shortsighted or off-kilter here.
That being said, I feel the need to give this game the recognition it deserves. It isn't often that a game comes along and leaves me with my mouth agape, shocked at the ratio of quality to manpower given to bring something to fruition. It was basically a one-man job, with a few exceptions to music, voice-acting and parts of the writing. This is not a game that makes you think that at all.
Beautiful, strong, crisp, varied, colorful aesthetic that leads to gorgeous graphics. Music that evokes that classic, childlike sense of wonder of exploring, excitement, and adventure. Every time I would just bring up the map screen to teleport to a different area, it's evoke a powerful sense of nostalgia from me.
Combatwise, everything is done with a blade and elemental ranged attacks, with ways to mix and match them all together. It's basically like a side-scrolling, platforming brawler with a nice degree of variation on enemy types and available tactics on taking them down.
The story starts off somewhat simple, and feels like it's treading familiar territory for a little while, but quickly becomes more complex as it goes on. I won't give any spoilers, but needless to say, I wasn't expecting the game to do what it did later on, close to the finish.
If I have any nitpicks, they are few. The lip-synching on the characters is a bit off, without much difference between the few mouth movements available. The voice-acting, while quite good overall, tends to give certain characters voices that don't quite fit, in addition to there being rather uneven sound quality amongst the performances. Still, these are both very minor issues, and I stopped noticing them after a while. It's just something I thought I should mention.
Honestly, I could go on with this, but I don't want to keep you waiting. Overall, Dust: An Elysian Tail is one of the best games I've played in quite a while. It was a stellar experience, and I think that anyone who is able to make a game like this almost by themselves definitely deserves support. I recommend it to just about anyone.

Overall: I adored this game. I knew it was good--I'd heard the hype and a friend had recommended it to me--but I don't think I was expecting to be as drawn into this game as I was. I was really surprised by the quality of the story and voice acting--it's not FANTASTIC but much better than I was expecting, for sure. As noted above sometimes the story can dip into being a little cheesy but usually when it did I found it enjoyable, and there were a lot of twists I didn't see coming, plus some genuinely funny moments (I laughed out loud at the conclusion of a quest involving a missing box) and even a few moments that tugged on my heartstrings a little.
But the real star here is the gameplay. It is a FUN game. The combat can be a little easy but it never stopped feeling satisfying for me, and the system that rewards great combos with bonus EXP motivated me to avoid mindless button mashing. The platforming is VERY satisfying--difficult enough for me to feel engaged but intuitive enough that I rarely felt frustrated by what the game was trying to get me to do. And I really enjoyed the exploration, which is unusual for me. I'm normally not much of a backtracker but I really enjoyed going to previous locations when I got new abilities to find hidden items and secrets.
This game seriously might make it on my list of favorite games, which I was NOT expecting. I'm already itching for another playthrough. Once I get through more of my backlog I'm probably going to replay on hard difficulty to see what it's like and maybe try for 100% completion. I DEFINITELY see this being a game I'll replay sometimes to relive some of my favorite moments or just to enjoy the combat and platforming.

10,000,000 is a very fun game where your objective is to get a score of 10,000,000. The game is basically a fusion of a bejeweled and item based rpg game, but slightly different mechanics than bejeweled as it moves the whole column instead of swapping the two.
This game is not easy by any means as it is more complex than it seems. The matching matters because there are melee and magic attacks based on your matches. There are also matches that give you wood and stone which you can use to upgrade your "home" outside. By upgrading your "home" you can get upgrades that help you in your next run. You also get experience points which you can buy certain upgrades for different things with. Lastly you get gold which you can upgrade your armor, weapons, and shield with. There are a lot of things to upgrade, but the game gets harder and harder. Basically if the left side of the screen catches up with you, you are forced to leave the run with whatever score you obtained. I really enjoyed the concept and especially the execution a lot. Furthermore, the music fit really well with the graphics and vice versa. This was just a rather complete game.
The only thing I would say isn't as good with this is the purple treasure matching thingies or whatever they are. They really didn't do too much help. Also the tutorial was rather short and I had to learn some things again the hard way later on.
But those are just minor compared to the positives. I would recommend this game to anybody who likes a roguelike genre, BeJeweled related matching (but different), or anyone who just wants to have some challenging fun.

10,000,000 is a match-three style adventure game with RPG elements. The gameplay is very simple and tactics are similarly uncomplicated. Your character runs along a dungeon hall and encounters various monsters, locked doors or locked chests. It's up to you to slide either columns or rows of symbols on a grid to match at least three of the same symbol to perform an action. The more symbols you match, the more effective the action. Where this differs from the classic match 3 experience is that you must defeat whatever obstacle is in your path with the appropriate matched items. You have to match keys to unlock locks and defeat monsters with swords or wands. Meanwhile you also try to manage your board, gather resources for improvements to equipment and ultimately hit the magic score.
All in all, gameplay is smooth, game is fun. Get it.
I have 10,000,000 on both PC and Android platforms and while I definitely can recommend picking it up either way, my prefered platform is actually Android.

First off, the game is a point-and-click adventure. This should inform your choices immediately.  It means that there's going to be stupid pixel-hunts and completely nonsensical puzzles. There aren't ways to /die/, really, so I'm able to apply the word 'forgiving' to it.  However, it is almost best played with the walkthrough at-hand, or else you're going to be reduced to the lowest form of inventory mix-and-match that plagues the genre.
The game has a certain dark humor to it that is really enjoyable, and the characters are well-voiced and fun. The controls have a 'reveal' system that alleviates the pixel-hunt parts, and most maps are well designed with speedy-travel links that allow you to complete good parts of your missions without having to wait for characters to walk across the screen for the hundreth time.
The 'director commentary' makes it clear that it comes from a zany bunch of people who love the art form.  That might actually be why these games are just 'good' and not 'great':  They are pure tributes to the Infocom greats, instead of modern re-imaginings of the genre like Telltale is producing. Still, the zany is the game's saving grace.  Tune in for the musical interludes, and if you miss it in-game, make sure you Youtube the "Nothing To See" easter egg song.
Fans of the genre should get this game as it is sure to be a classic. If you aren't a fan, though, I'd probably start with Telltale instead.

Overall positive perception.  Think of it like Monkey Island with a more crass spin.
The main character, Rufus, was rather annoying to me.  He constantly had an inflated opinion of himself and could not learn from his mistakes, and as an engineer who appreciates failure as a teaching option, this bugged me.  He sometimes found himself in bizarre situations, but unlike Guybrush Threepwood, who found himself in bizarre new situations caused by banjo duals or by wayward denizens of undead pirate lords, these situations were often of Rufus' own making, so he deserved it, and when he found a way out of them with a self-righteous attitude, it just wasn't very entertaining.  Think of someone you've met who, even in the face of overwhelming fact that he screwed up, will pass off the fault.
Puzzle crafting turned into a "keep guide open on the secondary monitor" routine.  If you want to solve it without a guide, you may be required to keep track of every single item that you can examine in the environment and a keep a record of a lot of conversations, and even then there are puzzles for which there is no hint in any of the "look at item in inventory" dialogue.  But if you keep a guide open, it isn't bad.
Everything else though is very good.  The art is very expressive, the narrative is very well crafted and quite entertaining at times.  A lot of work went into the dialogue, and the songs between sections are sometimes hilarious (keep subtitles on)!  And the music, oh yes the music + background noises flesh out every scene.
Overall, my impression is that this is a well-done game with an annoying lead character who drags it down.

Mafia III is one of the very best open world experiences so far!
yes, that is my honest opinion and not ironic in any way. if you want to know why, read on:
mafia 1 and 2 were great games, mainly because of their story, dialogues, setting and characters. they had a few weak points, of course, but that didn’t distract from the fun (at least for me).
Mafia III is set in the 1960s in a New Orleans-inspired city, which immediately strongly appealed to me when the game was announced. my only concern was the game being the next watered down casual, grindy, collectables ridden open world mess that we've seen recently. and the first reviews seemed to confirm that...
H/e i like the setting so much that i had to give it a try, not expecting to be great and hoping it won't be as bad as the majority claims.
installing and starting was all fine my end (not everybody has been that lucky!) and it ran smooth in full hd, all setting on high (except for the AA, which lowered to medium i liked better= less blurry image), no hick-up, lag or anything like that.
also very few of the infamous glitches and graphic oddities encountered by many players- luck here as well, i guess.
the first few hours are just great, but that is widely acknowledged anyway. and after that... well, it gets a bit repetitive, BUT not grindy or boring in any way (do you remember Far Cry 3 or AC: Black Flag? THAT was grindy and repetitive!!! so much so, that i couldn’t finish AC and don’t intend to- not many games have achieved that for me;))
the reason why it still feels ok to go to the same places and do the same things (not all the time, but a considerable amount of the time) is that the world you are acting in feels real: everything makes sense, everything is in its places, nothing really breaks the immersion; all collectables are very suitable for the time and are placed in very plausible places, AI is not that bad (suggest playing on hard and not use the x-ray ability of your character), sound and music is awesome!, city and surroundings are quite nice (didn’t have that lighting bug so far...) and everything just feels well placed (even the directions when driving are very unobtrusive, looking like road signs).
the little stories you can catch on the radio, in side missions or from people on the streets add to the overall impression that a lot of care and thought has been put to details...
so to sum it up: in my experience is has been a great, great open world game, with very well written dialogues, characters and overall story, nice graphics and sound, amazing music (if you like that period), a very immersive and coherent world, satisfying shooting and cover mechanics...
it may not have the most varied missions (although by far not as bad as suggested in reviews, once again, because the things you do make sense and are well embedded into the storyline...), not aaa+ graphics or any revolutionary mechanics, but it is far, far, far better than the reviews and ratings it is getting suggest. it feels like the stories abt racism and unrest, that are there, really matter and the developers had a very clear idea what they want to achieve with this game. in my view, they have succeeded.

APM4 has less taxying and more focus on getting everything to synch, sneaking a takeoff between 2 landing airplanes to keep the passengers happy (or pushing up the daisies untill you learn that trick). APM4 focuses on challenges more than just diversifying the airports, but there are some interesting ones like like Area 51 and a Carrier battle group.
To add some flavour to it all, a chopper can drop by to fill up on juice, and there can be a snowstorm, which turns the ground white which does not help with the white aircraft you are trying to guide. APM4 fortunately also have hotkeys for quickly assigning speeds to aircrafts instead of you having to click em, and you can simply drag airplanes to whatever runway you want it to land on.
Oh and emergencies and weather can be turned off and you can manually adjust how much trafic you want using a slider. Speaking of sliders - this game would be perfect if it had sliders to adjust the volume of sound/music/voice.

Airport Madness 4 is an arcade-like game about airplane management that is, at best, alright.
If your standards are early 2000s flash games.
You are put in the role of the airspace controlling whatever it is called(I can't really remember the name of the job) at an airport and you have to manage your aircraft to let them land and take off without making them wait too long or crash into eachother.
And that's about it.
You'll occasionally find yourself getting a helipad added to your entrusted airport, and in level 1 even an extra runway, but it doesn't change or become more complex in any way after you figure out the basics.
It's a simple concept with decent replayability, but it is incredibly repetitive and shallow as far as a full game goes.
It's just a slight bit more than what would be a succesfull flash game one would find on games sites, but not much more than that. It seems to be about the same size as one would expect from a flash game, and has about the same animation(Very poor explosions). A price of 10 euro is then very, very steep for what you get.
Coupled with the simple gameplay comes a few issues. The resolution is tiny(The steam preview pictures? That's almost full size, almost.), full screen mode will stretch everything if you're on a widescreen monitor, and your area of operations is tiny to the point where you can not even see the aircraft before they're starting their landing on some of the maps.
To say it's an amusing way to spend a few hours is correct if you're a fan of the game and have absolutely nothing better to do. But to call it a full game and worthy of 10 euro? Not even close. Mafia III is one of the very best open world experiences so far!
yes, that is my honest opinion and not ironic in any way. if you want to know why, read on:
mafia 1 and 2 were great games, mainly because of their story, dialogues, setting and characters. they had a few weak points, of course, but that didn’t distract from the fun (at least for me).
Mafia III is set in the 1960s in a New Orleans-inspired city, which immediately strongly appealed to me when the game was announced. my only concern was the game being the next watered down casual, grindy, collectables ridden open world mess that we've seen recently. and the first reviews seemed to confirm that...
H/e i like the setting so much that i had to give it a try, not expecting to be great and hoping it won't be as bad as the majority claims.
installing and starting was all fine my end (not everybody has been that lucky!) and it ran smooth in full hd, all setting on high (except for the AA, which lowered to medium i liked better= less blurry image), no hick-up, lag or anything like that.
also very few of the infamous glitches and graphic oddities encountered by many players- luck here as well, i guess.
the first few hours are just great, but that is widely acknowledged anyway. and after that... well, it gets a bit repetitive, BUT not grindy or boring in any way (do you remember Far Cry 3 or AC: Black Flag? THAT was grindy and repetitive!!! so much so, that i couldn’t finish AC and don’t intend to- not many games have achieved that for me;))
the reason why it still feels ok to go to the same places and do the same things (not all the time, but a considerable amount of the time) is that the world you are acting in feels real: everything makes sense, everything is in its places, nothing really breaks the immersion; all collectables are very suitable for the time and are placed in very plausible places, AI is not that bad (suggest playing on hard and not use the x-ray ability of your character), sound and music is awesome!, city and surroundings are quite nice (didn’t have that lighting bug so far...) and everything just feels well placed (even the directions when driving are very unobtrusive, looking like road signs).
the little stories you can catch on the radio, in side missions or from people on the streets add to the overall impression that a lot of care and thought has been put to details...
so to sum it up: in my experience is has been a great, great open world game, with very well written dialogues, characters and overall story, nice graphics and sound, amazing music (if you like that period), a very immersive and coherent world, satisfying shooting and cover mechanics...
it may not have the most varied missions (although by far not as bad as suggested in reviews, once again, because the things you do make sense and are well embedded into the storyline...), not aaa+ graphics or any revolutionary mechanics, but it is far, far, far better than the reviews and ratings it is getting suggest. it feels like the stories abt racism and unrest, that are there, really matter and the developers had a very clear idea what they want to achieve with this game. in my view, they have succeeded.

Dear God. This is a game that wants to be about big ethical choices and whether a person can really change, but is actually about feeding people toilet cakes and brewing ersatz coffee.

In the first game, you (the player) are forced to make the lead character act like a jerk and then watch him get berated for it. The second game entirely undermines the ending of the first by repeating exactly the same threat as the first game does. The third game explains why the main character can't change (this bit I actually liked) but then makes you sell a woman into slavery and watch her perform for her master.
The love interest in all this is stripped of agency at almost every turn, and even the kinda heroic ending (which I won't spoil), is entirely undermined by a humorous bit character. It is also a downer ending and raises more questions than it answers.
If you liked the Monkey Island series, by all means try this one, but don't expect to feel good playing it.

Duck Game is one of those Games that I can boot up whenever I feel like it - play it for a while - and actually leave with a smile. Not many Multiplayer games do that, since you are likely to get salty.
You could best describe it as a mix of Wario Ware and Smash Bros. - Every round, you are put in a new Arena which is either by default in the game, made by you, made by some scrub over at the steam workshop, or maybe even randomly generated - there players are spawned and left on their own - the objective of each Map is to be the last Duck alive - and this can be achieved in many different ways. Maybe you'll tactically wait for the Ducks to kill themselves, and leave the small fry for you to sweep off. Maybe you'll take advantage of the Map-Dynamics. When a round is done, the winning Duck gets a point, and off to the next Round - all of this happens in a rather rapid speed - like the game itself.
Expect Madness - and a hole lot to learn!
However, Duck Game manages to make deaths rather amusing  - and not only that, but most of the time, Deaths are your own fault.
The game offers something for both a Casual audience which just wants a fun party game to play with friends through Fun weapons, Maps and RNG to keep stuff lighthearted, while not leaving the competitive audience empty handed, through the insane skill ceiling available in both weapon-usage, movement, but also just general knowledge of mechanics.
But let's go over a quick Summary of pros and cons :
+ Good Soundtrack
+ Both Multiplayer(Available Online and locally) and Singleplayer-Challenge mode*
+ Level Editor
+ Fun and fast paced Gameplay
+ Lighthearted atmosphere keeps things amusing, rather than salty.
+ A giant variety of Weapons and different ways to kill enemies.
+ Upcoming Level-System will add a much needed layer of progression.
+ Dev is a cutie.
Neutral :
- Fast paced Gameplay may not be something for everyone - there is a lot of stuff going on, and some might be
overwhelmed, and thus can't keep up.
- Amount of Default Maps is rather limited, and finding good custom ones can be difficult since the entire Workshop is basically "Baby's first map"
- Price might be too high for some people.
- *The Singleplayer is NOT THE MAIN MEAT OF THE GAME - It's a challenge mode to get used to the mechanics and Unlock extra stuff.
Negative :
- Depending on where you live and your Region, MP can be dead on times since the Playerbase is not the largest - however, from my experience as a filthy germ, there are most of the times 5 active Servers of Players around in Europe - for more stats, check our Steamspy.
- Some Maps are not really fun, and there has yet to be a way to remove them.
- You are sometimes going to meet "the lagger" in a game, you know the one, someone who is trying to play Duck Game in Africa through WW2 Internet.
Overall, I recommend getting a group of friends to play this game with to get the maximum fun out of it, as playing with Randoms is, while still enjoyable, just a downgraded experience.
There is also an Update coming out soon™ adding lots of new Stuff which would just make this game more seducing for players.
Updated so the game gets a chance in the "I knew it before it was cool" Award space.

Aside from a few issues in multiplayer, DEFCON is everything I hoped for. A simple system of deployment of your missile silos, airbases, and fleets streamlines the flow of the rest of the game. While overall "strategy" in this game is kind of abstract and not very broad (kind of a choice between first-strike, hunker down, or a combination of both), the tactical decisions of how many nukes, which targets, when, etc... make playing this game a diverse experience. Visually, the "commanding radar" kind of view, where ships, missiles, and planes are blips on the screen, is quite enjoyable and the lack of detail actually enhances the whole nuclear warfare experience.
And there is nothing more satisfying than seeing your submarine pack unleash their nuclear arsenal on an unsuspecting, unprotected coast of the enemy.

Story: Aragami has a simple story that is easy to follow. Very lacking, but has enough elements for the player to keep playing, and see what will happen next. You the player, are this shadow ninja of vengeance. You continue to unravel mysterious and unanswered questions by the clues given to you.
Graphics: Made with the [Unity Engine] the graphics are cartoonish, but have great visual effects. In my childhood, I grew up playing Sly Cooper, and The Wind Waker, which in my opinion have a great resemblance to Aragami.

At first when I found footage from this game, I had no idea what I was looking at. Watching a couple of videos was all it took for me to make the purchase and I am very glad I did.
Crypt of the Necrodancer is a thoroughly enjoyable and ridiculous hybrid of a dungeon crawler and a rhythm game, where actions like moving, attacking, casting spells, and using items are all done to the beat of the music. The sprite animation style is incredibly charming, reminiscent of certain Super Nintendo titles with more fluid motion that make the game sing.
The game's soundtrack bears special mention. Since music is so important in CotN, the music is upbeat, powerful techno and dance tunes that will get your head bobbing and your fingers flying. When using custom music, a very cool feature, there can be some weird inconsistencies in the beat the computer records and the actual music, but nothing tremendously off-putting.
Currently there are three zones in the game and multiple characters (I only have access to two at the moment, counting the starting hero), which gives a good incentive to keep playing, acquiring items, and retrying dungeons with the new equipment trying to progress.
For an Early Access game, Crypt is an incredibly polished, enjoyable experience. Fans of old-school games, rhythm games, and anyone who enjoys a good soundtrack should definitely buy in.

What you should know before playing the game:
1: This is a BETA expect it to be a BETA, not a fully published game that has been refined.
2: If you are looking for something like OMD1/2 then you MIGHT find it here if you play survival.
3: This is a F2P game, it has a grind to it, most F2P games have a grind.
4: This is NOT P2W, if you think buying a chest that is RNG is P2W, and that consumables that are only survival (pve) can be bought is P2W then this isn't for you.
What you should know playing the game:
1: It currently has a small player base, so matches might take a bit to find.
2: do NOT jump into siege pvp, trust me on this, go co-op and learn the ropes, or survival for trap placement, even custom games where you set-up the lobby to at LEAST know the map, you can do 1v0.
3: While you are playing siege, the roles dictate what you do, not what buffs you get, a attacker attacks, a defender defends, and a pillager roams the map for minion portal exp.
4: While you are playing survival, listen for audio that signifies whether barricade killing minions spawn, or a boss/hero spawns.
5: The Minimap is your FRIEND USE IT, awareness to what is going on is one of the most powerful things you can have in this, the more you are aware of what is happening to your offense and your defense the better you are at the game.
6: If you are playing with someone that is high level / knows what they are doing, LISTEN to them, talk to them, they might seem frustrated but they just want to help you get better.
My Experience:
As you can see with my hours on record I have played this game A LOT, I play both siege and survival and have seen the devs make some AMAZING decisions and some terrible decisions. But through it all I still play, It is a refreshing take of a moba where you decide what you send and how you defend, it is more objectively based than other MOBAs and has great elements. Oh and did I mention verticality? There's verticality which can be fun to have a height advantage shooting down a melee character.
In survival early on you might feel heroes > Traps, Traps > Heroes later on, there is a good mix of how power-ful a hero is and how power-ful a trap is, if you don't upgrade your traps you won't be able to survive stronger waves, if you don't play and get to a high enough lvl (account lvl) your hero won't be strong enough.
I have played with friends and with-out, it is more enjoyable with friends, but duly note, a survival party is a max of 3, but siege can go up to 5, so if you are someone who plays with 1 or 2 friends the game is very fun to casually play in survival. if you are solo, it CAN be fun to find new friends in survival. If you are a competitive player you will like the siege game mode, it has LOTS of tactics and strategy and skill to master the game.
Overall Rating 8.8/10, Beta but good, shows that the devs care, they livestream at

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

Allow me to begin by saying this was a truly unforgettable experience. When I first heard about and saw Aragami, I was quite amazed by the gameplay mechanics. This game does what not a lot of stealth games do anymore.
There's two main options that you can take in every route. You can either go full stealth and stay hidden from your enemy as you progress through the story, or you also have the choice of murdering them in your wave of silence. Whichever you chose, you have to think carefully of your steps. A single mistake will force you to start all over. The enemy is not dumb either. They may even be more aware than you are. Guards are extremely serious about their job, and they will hunt you down fearlessly until they've disposed of you, or until you get away.
Gameplay wise, controls are smooth, responsive, and have no issues. It may take a while to get used to the layout, but it quickly becomes second nature once you really put to practice every single skill you learn as you progress further into the game.
Visuals are incredibly detailed and really throw you into the world. Trees, water, the grass, even the rain. The game's environment does an amazing job with the aesthetics. It's always night time to fit with the setting of the game, but I'm sure that even in daylight, the environment's beauty would surpass its own story.
There is one thing that I'm still a little fuzzy about, and that's the animations. It is understandable why they won't be top-notch. At times they seem a little rushed and camera angles tend to hide certain "goofs" like clipping. Facial expressions can seem vague and very basic, and the lip-synch is non-existent. Regardless, they still count as passable.
One last thing, is the multiplayer. It's a basic P2P connection, but it's enough for two people to enjoy the game. Timed kills or dodging the enemy becomes much more serious when you're sharing the moment with someone else.
Would I recommend Aragami? My answer is yes. The game delivers from level 1 and will continue to do so. Although the story may seem random at times, it slowly develops further to the point where it all clicks in your head and you're left wanting for more. This is the type of gaming experience that has slowly faded due to the high popularity of multiplayer games. Whether you play alone, or with someone else, Aragami is an exciting challenge of patience, timing, and precision. It is a great way to pass time, living through a story that you'd expect from a book.

DEFCON is a strategy game developed by Introversion Software and originally released in 2006. You play a superpower, and you will wage nuclear war against your enemies.
When playing the game for the first time, DEFCON doesn’t seem that complicated. You start by placing buildings and units that will defend your cities from nuclear attacks as well as launch nuclear missiles at your enemies. The selection of buildings and units are very limited and the gameplay looks simple enough.
The game has 5 levels of DEFCON. The game starts at DEFCON 5, but a timer is constantly running that will slowly reduce the DEFCON. The lower the DEFCON, the more you can do with your units and buildings. At DEFCON 1, nuclear missiles can be launched. As you can only place units and buildings at higher levels of DEFCON, it is important to have a gameplan and a plan already at the beginning.
And here is where DEFCON gets interesting. You need to plan waaay ahead and wait for opportune moments. The gamepace is slow and even though DEFCON is technically an RTS game, it has very few similarities with – for example – Starcraft. DEFCON makes me feel like i am playing a boardgame like Risk or an advanced version of chess.
If you like tactical games and planning ahead, you should give this game a try. There is also a free demo available, so if the game sounds interesting there is no reason at all not to try it.

To start with pros, Aragami has a great art style for the type of game it is. The games uses vibrant but dark colors to paint it's scene for the use of your shadow abilities that make up a huge part of the game.
The abilities you can obtain through the small but well thought out skill tree change how the game can be played. These abilities let you determine how your play style can be. Unlocking traits like invisibility and enemy spotting can lean towards a more sneaky and zero kill type of playstyle. While abilities like Kunai knives and body hiding can reveal a more offensive play style. The skill tree is made in a way to determine how you want to play and works very well.
The story, while not very deep or creative, offers depth to the game and slight meaning to your character and others in game. The story makes the game feel like it's not just a mindless slaughter and adds meaning to your actions.
The level design is perfect for this game and works wonders for your shadow warping and allows you to take different ways to your objective along with minor optional points of interest to increase and buy abilities.
Multiplayer works great, i have not had a single problem playing through with a friend and multiplayer brings new ways to cooperate and play.
CONS
Now for the cons, I have to talk about the many bugs present in this game. Being an indie game, players should expect bugs but the amount I have found is annoying. Combat can be wonky for example, when rushing towards an enemy and starting your kill animation, the hitbox of your enemies attack can still be present as you kill them resulting in you dying from their attack as the enemies death animation continues. This makes the enemy die but in a way that is unnatural as blood appears randomly and they recoil form nothing because your character inst their because of bad hitbox detection.
Enemy detection feels unfair at times when enemies are able to spot you when you are standing still behind them for no reason.
When enemies are aware of you and begin to blow a horn to alert other enemies, if the enemy has even barely started to blow the horn and you begin to kill him, the horn still activates and all enemies in the area are alerted.
At times after respawning, all enemies will be on full alert as you spawn for no apparent reason.
The game is optimization is very bad for how little tasking the game appears to be. On a GTX 970 and I5-6600K i have experienced frames as low as 40 on high graphics which is not acceptable for a game like this. Having played through with a friend on a 1080, the frames were nearly the same.
All in all, I am enjoying Aragami and believe the bugs are not too bad and easy to overlook. Be wary when buying as optimization is poor. Playing with a friend can greatly increase the fun and i strongly recommend it. With all this taken into consideration, I believe this game does deserve a thumbs up.

What you should know before playing the game:
1: This is a BETA expect it to be a BETA, not a fully published game that has been refined.
2: If you are looking for something like OMD1/2 then you MIGHT find it here if you play survival.
3: This is a F2P game, it has a grind to it, most F2P games have a grind.
4: This is NOT P2W, if you think buying a chest that is RNG is P2W, and that consumables that are only survival (pve) can be bought is P2W then this isn't for you.
What you should know playing the game:
1: It currently has a small player base, so matches might take a bit to find.
2: do NOT jump into siege pvp, trust me on this, go co-op and learn the ropes, or survival for trap placement, even custom games where you set-up the lobby to at LEAST know the map, you can do 1v0.
3: While you are playing siege, the roles dictate what you do, not what buffs you get, a attacker attacks, a defender defends, and a pillager roams the map for minion portal exp.
4: While you are playing survival, listen for audio that signifies whether barricade killing minions spawn, or a boss/hero spawns.
5: The Minimap is your FRIEND USE IT, awareness to what is going on is one of the most powerful things you can have in this, the more you are aware of what is happening to your offense and your defense the better you are at the game.
6: If you are playing with someone that is high level / knows what they are doing, LISTEN to them, talk to them, they might seem frustrated but they just want to help you get better.
My Experience:
As you can see with my hours on record I have played this game A LOT, I play both siege and survival and have seen the devs make some AMAZING decisions and some terrible decisions. But through it all I still play, It is a refreshing take of a moba where you decide what you send and how you defend, it is more objectively based than other MOBAs and has great elements. Oh and did I mention verticality? There's verticality which can be fun to have a height advantage shooting down a melee character.
In survival early on you might feel heroes > Traps, Traps > Heroes later on, there is a good mix of how power-ful a hero is and how power-ful a trap is, if you don't upgrade your traps you won't be able to survive stronger waves, if you don't play and get to a high enough lvl (account lvl) your hero won't be strong enough.
I have played with friends and with-out, it is more enjoyable with friends, but duly note, a survival party is a max of 3, but siege can go up to 5, so if you are someone who plays with 1 or 2 friends the game is very fun to casually play in survival. if you are solo, it CAN be fun to find new friends in survival. If you are a competitive player you will like the siege game mode, it has LOTS of tactics and strategy and skill to master the game.
Overall Rating 8.8/10, Beta but good, shows that the devs care, they livestream at
go ask them questions if you aren't too sure of downloading yet!

Personally I do enjoy this game and while this game certainly does have its ups and downs, I am not here to praise or criticize this game. I am here to offer a phenomenal 4 Cheese Ravioli recipe!
Here are the ingredients you will need!
Ravioli Dough: 2 cups all-purpose flour, 1 pinch salt, 1 teaspoon olive oil, 2 eggs, 1 1/2 tablespoons water.
Ravioli Filling: 1 (8 ounce) container ricotta cheese, 1 (4 ounce) package cream cheese, softened, 1/2 cup shredded mozzarella cheese, 1/2 cup provolone cheese, shredded, 1 egg, 1 1/2 teaspoons dried parsley.
Pesto-Alfredo Cream Sauce: 2 tablespoons olive oil, 2 cloves garlic, crushed, 3 tablespoons prepared basil pesto sauce, 2 cups heavy cream, 1/4 cup grated Parmesan cheese, 1 (24 ounce) jar marinara sauce.
1. Mound the flour and salt together on a work surface and form a well. Beat the teaspoon of olive oil, 2 eggs, and water in a bowl. Pour half the egg mixture into the well. Begin mixing the egg with the flour with one hand; use your other hand to keep the flour mound steady. Add the remaining egg mixture and knead to form a dough.
2. Knead the dough until smooth, 8 to 10 minutes; add more flour if the dough is too sticky. Form the dough into a ball and wrap tightly with plastic. Refrigerate for 1 hour.
3. While the dough is resting, prepare the ravioli filling. Combine the ricotta cheese, cream cheese, mozzarella cheese, provolone cheese, egg, and parsley and mix well. Set the filling aside.
4. Heat 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the crushed garlic and pesto sauce and cook for one minute. Pour in the heavy cream, raise the heat to high, and bring the sauce to a boil. Reduce the heat and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the Parmesan cheese and stir until the cheese melts. Remove the pan from the heat and keep warm.
5. Meanwhile, in a separate saucepan, warm the marinara sauce over medium-low heat.
6. Preheat an oven to 375 degrees F (190 degrees C). Beat the egg with the tablespoon of water to make the egg wash.
7. Roll out the pasta dough into thin sheets no thicker than a nickel. To assemble the ravioli, brush the egg wash over a sheet of pasta. Drop the filling mixture on the dough by teaspoonfuls about one inch apart. Cover the filling with the top sheet of pasta, pressing out the air from around each portion of filling. Press firmly around the filling to seal. Cut into individual ravioli with a knife or pizza cutter. Seal the edges.
8. Fill a large pot with lightly salted water and bring to a rolling boil over high heat. Stir in the ravioli, and return to a boil. Cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the ravioli float to the top and the filling is hot, 4 to 8 minutes. Drain well.
9. Grease a baking sheet. Place the cooked ravioli on the sheet pan and bake in the preheated oven until brown, about 4 minutes.
10. To serve the ravioli, divide them among four warmed serving bowls. Drizzle the marinara sauce over the ravioli and then top with the cream sauce.

Initially when I started this game I instantly thought "oh look another match 3 game, this will be fun like 10 minutes" but then I started to realize it was kinda fun. The challenges or "quests" for each level kept me playing beyond the first 10 minutes and as I went up through the first few levels it got harder and I started to get stuck till I realized the boarded doors were not different levels but upgrade stations which is where the RPG elements come into it. Progression is the big thing that will keep you playing the game, upgrading your sword, staff and armor helps you get through later levels as they get harder.
While it does play just like a matching game similar to games like candy crush the RPG elements set it apart enough to almost not resemble games of the same genre. In this game your goal is to get to 10,000,000 points but points are not achieved making matches but by moving forward in the dungeon. This is where different types of matches are important for facing different types of challenges like opening doors, chests or killing enemies. Standing still will push you back so preparing and understanding your board is important to success which means you can't just match everything in sight and do well.

I don't want to think about how much time I put into this series pre-Steam. If you like Warhammer, it's hard to do better than this. If you like RTS games, this is near the top of the list. If you like both, you'd be a dummy not to get it.
My only complaint is you need to buy all of them (the core game and all the expansions) if you want the full roster, so I'd wait until they're on sale and you can get a bundle for somewhere around 10$.
PROS:
+One of the most colorful rosters of factions to grace science fiction wargaming
+ Carnage. Way back in the day this game was considered a bloodbath, with loving detail put into all the little dudes on the screen mauling each other.
+Good map design, good base building mechanics for each different faction.
+Dark Crusade's campaign mode is basically a series of skirmishes tethered to a strategic world map consisting of territories that yield certain buffs, resources or units. Each game plays out a little different, and the strongholds are all fun, creative sequences. Definitely the best in the bunch.
+Mods.
CONS:
- Given how old this series is, it's obviously a bit...dated  looking, but the designs of the armies and worlds themselve still shine through this.
-Some of the features in vanilla mode like army painter are a bit lacking.
-Imperial Guard grenade spamming in the first 3 minutes of any match will ruin your life.
Final Verdict: I really like Dawn of War 2 for a different set of reasons, but if you're looking for only one Warhammer game to own (and really that's not an unfair expectation with so much of it being shovelware pumped out by cellphone game sweatshops) this is absolutely your go-to.

Ok I was wiff waffling on buying this becuase of some of the reviews about server latency and FPS drops and optimization and a toxic community thats fast paced and mean to new people. Gues what I experienced! NONE OF THAT STUFF! Ok lemme give you guys my system specs I know this an old game so just about anyone can run it but hey what the heck! I have a crappy FX4300 3.8ghz-4ghz turbo and a MSI RX470 OC Armor gaming with 4GB of DDR5 v-ram(this game only uses 2gb at the most so dont trip if thats what you got) and finally 8gb's system ram. I get a cpu bottleneck on newer next gen games obviously but on this I have v-sync on and set to double buffer and graphics all the way up and play in HD and I have never experienced a single frame rate drop below 59fps and thats like literally for a millisecond but other than that a SOLID 60FPS. As for server latency I had one instance at like 2AM when I was on a european server and it got unbearable and ping was too high other than that NOTHING! Now the other big complaint that I saw THE COMMUNITY! I havent experienced anyone being an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ yet, everyone is helpful and even when we are losing and are commander sucks♥♥♥♥♥or is new no one gets bent outta shape like in other games which is suprising to me. I also read in one review that the Mechs in the preview or the giant Rhino monsters never get used or rarely? Thats a lie, every match Ive played Ive been a mech or Oros(giant rhino). Idk why this game is getting so much beef lol Its WEIRD! It really is WEIRD to me!
GRAPHICS-Its an older game but it still looks great at ultra in HD and is really well optimized, Ive had a solid 60fps no matter what whether its me and 8 marines all shooting flame throwers and grenade launchers and firing mini guns at an alien hive a SOLID 60FPS.
GAMEPLAY-Its fast paced, interesting, and intense at times. The marines try to stick together and keep resources flowing and the power on while the aliens stealthily creep through the vents or latch to the ceiling just above a doorway and listen for the sound of your combat boots inching closer then POUNCE! CHOMP! CHOMP! One dead marine lol From the COMMANDER perspective the game plays like a good RTS with you being able to research upgrades for the other players on the team and enable weapons for them to purchase with their individual points their earn through combat and building and destroying enemy buildings. You can as the marine commander play turrets and extractors for resources and armories for refitting your fellow marines and even robot buidlers. The Alien side is a different experience with you only being able to build in areas infected with cysts which coat the surrounded area in this seething mass of organic material upon which you can build and you research evolutionary traits that your team mates can evolve to obtain by entering a sort of cacoon. Its diverse and very fun and when you get bored of the shooter side then be commander and BOOM! Its a totally different GAME!
COMMUNITY-I have never be griefed or trolled by any players besides one and he was on the enemy team and was like 16 so typical internet stuff nothing pervasive or out of the norm. Other than that the more experienced players have been laid back and helpful and dont seem to sweat losing or playing with noobs. Now the game isnt dead you can always find people playing at all times and when the match isnt full there are bots that can be your marines or even command(SOMETHING NONE OF THOSE REVIEWS MENTIONED) Ive played MUCH MORE TOXIC games than this and honestly idk what people are talking about in these reviews lol
IN CONCLUSION-I was almost not gonna buy this game becuase people said its dead, the communities evil and toxic, the game is unoptimized, and the servers are all crap. Well I bought it and NONE OF THAT is true and Im honestly perplexed by those reviews. Seriously idk what happened that made them so bitter sounding but damn son, the game is AWESOME! Its got a original concept with the RTS/FPS hybrid style that is saddly lacking in todays game creation and in my opinion one the most exciting and fun developements in game concepts since open world games started becoming a norm and craze. I know when I first started the game a message popped up about a new patch they did I didnt really read it but maybe they fixed all the things those people where upset about becuase none of the negatives in the thumbs down reviews that I read before getting this have I seen or even experienced. I recommend this game becuase its like 2 good games in one a good fast paced shooter and a good RTS and each faction has unique and interesting play styles and characters. Games alil old but looks great too! Im giving it a rock solid 8/10 now if they had a 3rd faction and 3v3 maps ooooh boy! 9/10 easy! So get it if your interested becuase its really suprised me just how good it is and how muddy its reputation has gotten with a few bitter reviews.

Natural Selection 2 is a great game. Not only is it a good team based FPS but it is also a good RTS and its that blend of genres that makes NS2 so great and unique in a genre populated by Pay to Play shooters, rushed shooters and the occasional good one. Its fast paced at times while also being strategic at others and theres nearly always a creepy vibe when you enter a new room and hear the scuttling of a skulk. The sound design is great but there are times when it could be a little better (it cuts out from time to time) but nearly always its good. The mechanics and how they work feels smooth and polished aswell. Exos and Onos are the biggest, slowest and strongest of the two sides that you can play and you really feel the power when being either of them. The building aspects are fun and strategic layout is key to a succesful base. The community is mature but can be a little rough sometimes. None of the maps feel bland and all of them have different feelings in them and are asthetically intreguing. Biodome has a more futuristic and polished look to it while Derelict looks wild and overgrown like it was abandoned.
I highly recommend Natural Selection 2 to anybody who likes Fast Sci-Fi shooters and strategy games because NS2 incorporates both of those genres into one polished game.
P.S: The pice is really good as well.

Ok, this game is unbelievable. You wouldn't think that a rhythm game/dungeon-crawler would make for an entertaining experience, but it is astoundingly addicting.
As of the writing of this review, the game is still in Early Access, but the game has enough content to warrant pulling the requisite $15 from your wallet.
The game is simplistic, but has great depth. The game is controlled with only four buttons; (but a d-pad won't work, as opposite directions need to be pressed at the same time) up, down, left, and right. These buttons will either move your character, or attack in the direction selected. Combinations of the four buttons are assigned to spells and items. This makes the game compatible with a USB dance pad if you so choose to play it that way. Though it lacks falling arrows, the mechanics become remarkably similar. Moving your character to the beat of the music comes suprisingly naturally, and plays out as more of an action-puzzler than anything else.
Of course, no rhythm game is complete without an awesome soundtrack, and this game absolutely delivers in the auditory stimulation department. The chiptune dance tracks go perfectly with the artstyle of each floor, but do not get old as most songs do on other dance-pad games. And, if they ever do get old for you, the game offers support for adding in your own jams. The beat detection is good, but for your own sanity, pick songs that don't vary much in tempo, or you will be losing your combos.
All in all, solid 10 from me. The only qualm I have with it is that the difficulty curve is fairly steep, and may be a little too much for those inexperienced with the falling arrow games arcade gamers grew up with. For those who are seeking a challenge, there is Aria mode, which is essentially a perfect-only mode.

But at its core, there is a clear love for kooky comedic puzzle solving, and I certainly hope the gang at Daedalic has a long and successful career to continue to express it.

For the Deponia and Chaos on Deponia - BRILLIANT. These series are really brilliant. A rare old-school point-and-clicker out there, with a good funny plot, completely worth to play.
For the Goodbye Deponia part: SCREWED. Finally and completely. Just after Rufus gets green chemical to do the culminating thing... it's all screwed up completely. If I could, I would recommend game authors to redo everything just after this moment. Gosh, it will even *sell* again with a different finale!
To clarify: it's not a *BAD* ending. It's *AWFULLY DONE* finale, not only ending, but climax/afterclimax as well. The climax, afterclimax and outcome are all complete, utter and total failures. It leaves you with a complete sense of disappointment, makes the  hours spent in game pointless, and overall tastes awful.
It looks like something's happened in someone's head when team was working on the game at that moment, and completely prevented them from doing anything decent. Game mood is completely ruined after then, and the game ending is quite nonsensical as well, dull and dummy. No ending at all, and no chances for continuation. Be prepared for this when you play the last part of it.
Nevertheless, I would recommend it. It'll give you a decent amount of giggling and laughter.
---
Now for the goodies: what do we have there:
+ Clever tasks and puzzles (almost all are logical, only few are at a point of being foul, and only one thing in Chaos part totally crosses the red line).
+ A lot of toilet humour and slapstick comedy
+ Excellent graphics, decent animation, excellent music
+ Fun, lots of fun
+ Friendly interface, too friendly up to the point it makes game a bit easy (plans and hints) after you're acquainted with it
+ Totally made with love (until the aforementioned third part moment where it's all screwed up).
+ A bit of romance. Although it leaves us to wish for a bit more.
+ Huge diversity of situations.
And for the bad side:
- - - - - - - COMPLETELY SCREWED UP after certain moment in Goodbye. Well, no more about that.
- Too linear a plot. You cannot deviate even a bit, few ways to solve one thing could give player feeling of freedom, and it could took more game time to find all the routes and achievements.
- Some bugs in task and hint tracking system, sometimes it dings when it should not.
- Not all puzzles are solved via logical steps. Beware of some. Although as I said before, anything except for one moment should be walk in the park.

Here is what I wrote on 9 Aug, 2016 @ 4:19pm :
I played and cleared Orcs Must Die 1 and 2.
Compared to those two, this game has a really different feel and experience.
- Most (virtually all) levels are not possible to be cleared alone
- Heroes are more powerful than traps (it used to be a complement for traps)
- Traps takes countless grinding to unlock and upgrade. To fully upgrade ONE trap you will need the equivalent of ~12 hrs of grinding
- Too many unneeded game resources. Trap unlocking, upgrading, gear unlocking, hero upgrades, hero unlocks each have their own separate resources to grind. They could have made skulls the single resource for the game to make things less complicated.
- If you dont have a party of 3, good luck getting players to play in survival mode. The matchmaking is totally broken, may have to do with the game forcing you to play specific maps depending on your account level instead of populating a map. Almost impossible to win alone (on higher levels enemies destroys barricades, only possible to defend one lane with one hero and maps normally have four spawn portals), barely winnable with two, and hard to complete with three if you have unupgraded traps.
- Too few maps. Difficulty only varied by number of monster waves and monster type.
- The "deck" system is totally ♥♥♥♥ed. It's a system of gear+traps+guardian+boss+minion selection setup for this game. Think of the mastery, rune, and summoner spell system in LoL, but all of them are put together instead of separately and you are not able to modify it during game lobby.
I loved OMD 1 and 2 but this game totally blows.

I had been browsing Steam for at least an hour, looking for something that might hold my interest for more than a few minutes. By the time this game turned up, I was not very hopeful. The gloomy title conjured up images of a tedious slog through yet another Tolkein knock-off world. The screenshots reminded me of a hundred junk titles that bill themselves as "retro" and "8-bit" to lure long-time gamers into parting with their money in a quest to recapture good memories from their childhood. The description, touting the unlikely fusion of roguelike and rhythm genres, left me almost certain that this was nothing more than a concept gimmick that would fail to meet even the lowest of expectations.
I could not have been more wrong.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is the most inspired, refreshing contribution to gaming that I have encountered in years. This game blends the simplest and most predictable mechanics with enough variety to be challenging and so much creativity that even casual players will have a whole lot of goofy fun. I've played countless times over the past few weeks, died in most of them, and found myself smiling anyway, because it was almost always my own fault rather than the result of an impossible situation or bad user interface, and because it's easy to jump right back in.
Each creature has a specific pattern of movement with consistent restrictions, and is easily identifiable on sight, so you can usually predict what it will do next. It will always move on the beat of the music. Press one of the four direction buttons, and you'll move, interact with an obstacle, or attack an enemy in that direction. Do it on the beat, or you'll be sorry. Use items from your inventory by pressing two buttons at once. Following these rules, you'll find yourself learning the patterns of movement (or dances) required to subdue each monster and make your way deeper into the dungeon.
On top of that solid foundation sits a cast of unique bosses, playable characters with different abilities, unlockable upgrades, training areas, cooperative mode, instant replays, a level editor, gamepad and dance mat support, cross-platform compatibility, a surprisingly good chiptune-style soundtrack, and the ability to import whatever music your dungeon-crawling heart desires.
And it's still only an alpha.
