I really, really wish I could give a neutral instead of a thumbs up or down.  I just beat the game and well...my opinion on it is decidedly mixed.  Probably not a good thing considering how much of a fan of point and click adventure games I am.  On the whole, I'm giving it a thumbs up, but probably because the game only cost me $5 and I got quite a few hours out of it.  Not sure I'd have felt the same if I had forked over a whole $40.
As far as the game goes, I've played worse in this genre.  The artwork is delightful, the voice acting is quite good (not earth shattering, but quite good), the universe of the world is facinating and creative, the dialog is genuinely funny at several times, and the plot twists are fun, prepousterous and in the vein of the story telling of Terry Pratchett and Douglass Adams.  At its best it stands next to classics in the genre, particularly the monkey island series.  As far as value goes "The Complete Journey" is long, so depending on your penchant for punishment you might be getting your money's worth here.  I'll say it succeded in captivating me, though frequently not for the best reasons, and with that...
...the game itself can get quite exasperating!  I consider myself a pretty seasoned point and click adventurer.  I'm not past needing to open the occaisonal walk through, but I've made it through my share of titles not having to do so.  I had to consult a walk through no less than 4 times in this title and possibly more (my memory's fuzzy in between the swearing).  Only once did the revealed solution actually impress on me that "I should have thought of that!"
The game's puzzles all suffer from over construction and frequently hinder game flow.  Just when you think you've made progress on a puzzle you come to realize the designers are just toying with you and you've now got 20 other steps to go through.  All puzzles paths are plagued with red herrings and "Oh, I need to examine that before using it and then it works?" BS.  It comes off as a slap in the face more than being entertaining, and I frequently suffered from puzzle fatigue and started spam clicking in the vain hope of progress.  The game would honestly have been more fun with *less* content, but maybe it wasn't so bad if you played each episode piecemeal as it came out as opposed to the binge play through I did.
My last complaint (WARNING SPOILERS) is an observation others besides myself have made--there's basically unignorable undertones of sexism, racism and maybe even a little trans-phobia within the plot.  I am seriously no SJW; on the contrary, I can laugh at the occaisonally well thought out racist or sexist joke, but none of these things struck me as particularly well thought or funny.  "Yeah, yeah, lighten up, it's a comedy, whatever."  But seriously I'm male, and I can't ignore that almost all the female characters are voluptous eye candy that suffer at the hands of the protagonist all for comedic relief.
The game starts in the protagonist's ex-girlfriend's house.  It becomes apparent quickly that Rufus is a leech, without a home of his own, living off her well after their relationship has soured and her life is made mostly miserable by it.
Then there's the major supporting female character, Goal, who ends up in the center of the plot only because Rufus, the protagonist, accidentally knocks her off the vessel she's journeying on, damaging her brain implant.  She then spends the first game mostly unconconcious and dragged about by Rufus like a rag doll (because I guess he's just smitten by her because "She's hot!"). In the second game her personality is split into three alter egos (by yet another thoughtless accident of our main character).  The game play of this episode consists of swapping her digitally stored personalities into and out of her cadaver with a remote control all the while attempting to win the heart of each side of her personality.  In the third game she's all but entirely absent having been killed and re-cloned as a baby (yet *again* the result of an accident by the protagonist).  Her character has zero development.  She's just there as a token damsel.  All her misfortunes are not her fault, yet she nobly stands by Rufus's side until the end because...well why wouldn't somebody love an accident prone ego maniac who hurts all his friends with his misdeeds?
In the third game there's an interracial couple at the heart of a "gag" puzzle, the solution of which has the white member killed by some alien parasite while the black member is sold to a circus performer to humiliate herself as a scantly clad dancing monkey in the sewers (I swear I'm not making that up nor embellishing).
There's a brutish trans-women with a 5 o'clock shadow whose voice fluctuates between falsetto and booming base.  And did I mention you have to steal her hormone pills to solve a puzzle in the third game?  There's a Gondola operator who fakes a terrible Italian accent and gets in your way.  There's a fortune teller that looks like a generic buddah statue, complete with thick Asian accent...
Even if the game developers hadn't intended these things to be social statements and "all in good fun, wink wink," it kind of piles up and gave me serious mis-givings.
On the whole though, for $5?  Eh, it was entertaining.  Your mileage may vary.

--- 10,000,000 ---
* Don't mind my time played here, I have logged 100+ hours of the iOS version because this game is perfect when on the move.
* I really don't recommend the Steam version of this game because of the awkward controls.
What is this....
10,000,000 is a match-3 endless runner with a twist. There is no story to speak of, the goal is to escape the dungeon/castle you find yourself locked into. You do this by getting a high-score of 10,000,000 or above. Sounds easy? It kind of is, the first times. This game get tough as nails when you try and beat it the forth time and beyond tho. This is something the game calls "ace levels" which basically is a NewGame+ mode that ramp up the difficulty progressively. The question is who is even going to want to play this game for that long with these awkward mouse controls? Anyway...
The games single biggest problem is it's useless control scheme. I understand that there really are no good alternatives for games like this. (SO DON'T ♥♥♥♥ING RELEASE THEM ON STEAM!) The Steam version of 10,000,000 is not nearly as good as it's iOS counterpart. 10,000,000 is a touch screen handheld device game - and should not be anything else. It's atrocious to play this with a mouse. It's like night and day. This is a game that relies on quick inputs and mild planning how to arrange the table, and with this clumsy mouse ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t that's just not satisfactory.
This is one of those games that are perfect in bite sized chunks - for when you are on the train or having a break at the job. If I play for more then 10-20mins in one go I quickly get bored. It's "one of those games".
The good music (2 songs...) is still awesome and the gameplay is smooth and dandy on this version. It's just that you cannot get around the deal-breaker here. This should be operated with touch controls. Nothing else. I have not tried, but if I would guess I'd say this game probably is as good as it can be on a iPad.
Mechanics....
Match 3 or more of the same symbol from the board and you "get" that symbol as a attack on your enemies. A sword for instance is a physical attack. A staff is magical etc. There are symbols you can match and collect too like wood, gold and experience which is used to buy new skills and upgrade your castle/dungeon to improve physical/magical/skill damage output. Oh, and all of this has to go fast because the more you earn the faster the game wants you dead by throwing even more monsters at you. It gets pretty frantic later on. There is more to it but this is the basics.
Final verdict....
The iOS version 8/10. The Steam version 3/10

Dawn of War: Dark Crusade is arguably the best expansion in the series. It abandoned linearity within the campaign that it's predecessors had and replaced it with a Risk-like game. You have your own region on Kronus and your objective is to build up your army and conquer the other factions on the planet. It was fun, challenging, and refreshing.
RTS games have never been good at conveying a story, so rather than waste time and money trying to create a story around characters that are emotionless superhumans built only for war, they went with a big map for you to have your own fun. This in my opinion was a smart decision and gave Relic more room to work with now that they don't have to create a narrative.
There are of course the commanders that go back and forth with each other bickering about whose side is better. And while that may sound annoying, they actually did a really great job. The commanders feel like they have more personality and are commited to their cause while not putting the attention entirely on them individually. In my opinion, this was a step in the right direction. Because now the rest of the focus is on the military aspect of 40k (which has always been it's selling point).
Kronus is an Imperium controlled world with a native population of Orks and a ever growing Tau civilization. This has caused many skirmishes throughout the planet's history and has awaken the long dorment Necron hordes. Eldar of Ulthwe come to intercept the Necrons and defeat them before they can fully reawake.
Meanwhile the forces of Chaos, the Word Bearers legion arrive to take the planet of Kronus for their own sadistic needs in the name of the Chaos gods.
The Orks, riled up more than ever now that there is a full planetary war want to sink their teeth on the battlefield. Led by the infamous Warboos Gorgutz, the Orks push into Tau and Imperium controlled regions to plunder the riches of the land and crush anything in their path.
The Tau have called in reinforcements to respond to all of this discord. Taking full advantage of this war distracting their enemies, they are more than willing to take the planet for the greater good.
And the Space Marines, mighty warriors of the God Emperor are locked in a conflict of interest with the Imperial Guard. The Guard, refusing to stand down and obey orders from the Space Marines have left the two factions of the Imperium fighting eachother in all out war.
Because I covered the base factions in my last Dawn of War review I'm just going to talk about the Tau and Necrons.
The Tau are a young race of aliens that have advanced in technology at an accelerating rate. Because of this they have access to mobile battle suits, advanced stealth technology, and raw fire power that can turn entire platoons of soldiers into nothing more but stains on the battlefield. I find them to be borderline over powered in Dark Crusade. They simply deal waaaay too much damage far too quickly. Have a decked out squad of Guardsmen? Not anymore!
Their only Achilles heel is melee. Units like Chaos Raptors or Assault Marines can make short work of Tau Fire Warriors. The problem is, not all factions have melee units with jetpacks... Now a lot of people on the forums would strongly disagree with me that on-foot melee units like Banshees can get in Tau ranged lines. But if you are fighting an intelligent player that knows his or her weaknesses as Tau, those Banshees will be knocked down to a quarter of their squad size by the time they reach the Fire Warriors. And since most Tau players build two to three squads of Fire Warriors, expect them to be shooting the remaining Banshees.
Other than just the insane amount of power they have, they're a decent faction. They lack defense turrets in their base, which means that if you attack a Tau base they have no other option but to send their forces back to support their base. This in my opinion is a reasonable weakness and doesn't make the Tau nigh unstoppable. Eldar can easily use this weakness to their advantage so it leaves some options.
The Necrons....I don't know what's worse, the fact that they are completely broken or that they are possibly the most boring faction to play as. They're ungodly slow, have no satisfaction to their gameplay whatsoever, and they are so hard to kill that it makes easter egg hunts for Eldar bases at the end of a game look fun. If you are new to Dawn of War DO NOT play Necrons first. They will suck all of the fun you could be having in the game out of you leaving you with a bitter taste in your mouth. Necrons are however fun to play against with friends in team games. But outside of being just a good bad guy to fight, they aren't worth playing. Unless of course you want to be a troll and ruin everyone's day with Pariah's.
It's a 9/10. The campaign was great, some of the balance changes for the other factions were decent, and the two new factions were a welcomed addition despite the questionable balance behind them. However because of the two additional factions and their balance issues I have to count it as a negative. It's like no one at Relic thought about it "oh yeah! Space terminators that can never die and are slow as ♥♥♥♥ to progress with will be fun!" The lack of mods is also unfortunate because that means you have to get Soulstorm for mods like Ultimate Apocolypse.
But overall Dark Crusade is a must buy if you are getting the base game of Dawn of War.

Aragami promises to be a stealth game, but it's only that in the loosest sense of the term. Much of the game revolves around killing enemies and the final level boils down to "kill, run, kill, run, etc."
PROS:
+ Decent, cell-shaded graphics.
+ Co-op gameplay, which is always a nice feature.
+ A fair amount of stealth gameplay (although this changes as the game progresses).
+ Free DLC.
+ Steam Cloud.
+ Level Editor.
NEUTRAL:
+/- Dialogue is voiced entirely in a made-up Japanese-like language with subtitles. I've added this because some people really dislike foreign language with subtitles in games, so it's something to consider if it's a pet peeve of yours.
CONS:
- Graphics and audio are mediocre at best; not terrible, but definitely not state-of-the-art.
- Co-op gameplay has unusually long synchronization issues at the start of every level.
- Checkpoint saves instead of the far superior "save anywhere" game mechanic utilized by manual saves and quicksaves.
- The game is terrible at providing information and instructions to the player, which results in a ton of trial-and-error gameplay. For instance, on the controls screen, the game fails to tell the player that the "B" button on the XBox controller brings up the power wheel or during the final battle at the end of the game, there's NO indication what you're supposed to do and how to do it.
- The last level disregards stealth entirely and instead forces you to fight an enemy who is invulnerable to ALL of your abilities and can track you wherever you attempt to hide. Sneaking and hiding was, up until this level, a key component of the game and suddenly, everything is thrown off-track and becomes an action game.
VERDICT: I wish Steam had a neutral rating, because while Aragami has MANY faults, it's not a terrible game.
Maybe Aragami would play better as a single player game. My wife and I played it together in co-op and stealth games can be quite difficult in when you have to take into account another person.
That said, because Aragami has been advertised as a stealth game, I'm going to judge it as one and as such, it fails.

TLDR: In Aragami you play as an adept assassin with the ability to manipulate shadows. Aragami is a linear yet open ended stealth game allowing you to tackle missions the way you desire, whether that be a murderous assassin or a sneaky ninja. You get to explore beautiful and stylish landscapes with a charming soundtrack to enjoy. Delve into an intriguing story involving the evil army of Light and help this mysterious girl who has summoned you to this world. Complete with customisation and collectibles, Aragami is a very decent stealth game.
Aragami is a stealth game where you play as a reincarnated spirit, summoned by an imprisoned girl who needs rescuing. It's a third person game, and has a unique game mechanic where you can create and teleport to shadows. You have a nice variety of unique unlockable abilities so you can complete missions in different exciting ways.
- Aragami features a simple yet aesthetically pleasing visual style. The environments are gorgeous which make it a joy to roam about within them. While detailed and beautiful, the balance of simplicity means there is no visual clutter and thereby enhances the feel of the gameplay. The animations are fluid and effortlessly blend together, making a concatenation of takedowns a blissful sight. Overall I would say that Aragami is a really visually stunning game. I have some pictures
- The music is nicely orchestrated oriental music. It fits the setting of the game perfectly and allows you to become immersed. In moments of action, the music ramps up to induce adrenaline. While the 'action' music does sound great, you will hear that same song every time which eventually leads to monotony. The sound effects are quite decent though they could be better. The sounds whenever your sword meets flesh is fine but feels too unvaried. Overall the audio of Aragami is really quite good.
- In Aragami you have to complete certain objectives within considerably large and open levels. You only need to reach certain areas and acquire certain items; killing optional. The antagonists, the Kaiho, have swords imbued with Light essence. They're a formidable foe that are able to instantly disintegrate you with a swing of their sword. The Kaiho do take effort and planning to take out, in order to avoid alerting nearby enemies. The game gives you decent variety of abilities to help you fight or evade them.
You primary ability is possessing the power to teleport between shadows. Doing this uses Shadow essence which only regenerates when you're within a shadow. Because of this you'll be constantly lurking in and scrounging for shadows as they are an essential component of the gameplay. Your other main ability is the power to create a temporary shadow, so that you may teleport to it. These 2 abilities are the only ones you need, and you'll be using them a lot. Other abilities, such as ranged attacks and going invisible, first require unlocking using skill points acquired from scrolls. Scrolls are hidden throughout each level, but there's an ability which shows you the location of all of them. Each of the special abilities only have 2 charges, but can be replenished by finding a shrine.
I'll also note that there's no health in this game, for enemies or yourself, so every attack will result in an instant kill. There's some special attacks you can accomplish, such as a drop assassination (dropping on an enemy and killing them) and a ledge kill ability (teleport up a ledge next to an enemy to kill them). The gameplay reminds me of Dishonored in a way, and I really enjoyed it.
- The game is about an 'Aragami,' a vengeful spirit summoned who has been summoned by Yamiko. She is being held captives by a clan of light adepts known as the Kaiho. The Kaiho had fought against Yamiko's people and killed nearly all of them, taking their land. This game nicely sets up the Kaiho as really evil and malicious people. In order to rescue Yamiko, you need to break the magic seal by finding all 6 talismans. Along the way you'll get the help from a raven which will help you find your objectives. The story also explores existential aspects; the Aragami is a reincarnated person, but what was its previous identity?
- You'll be pleased to here that this game does come with an FOV slider, which maxes at 90. The performance of this game is stellar, as even with max settings I never experienced any frame drops. Blood is also toggleable if that concerns you. I found this game to be mostly devoid of glitches however there were a few minor annoyances (AI gets stuck sometimes), but nothing gamebreaking.
- This game has no HUD which I really liked, so your level of Shadow essence and number Shadow Powers you can use are conveniently displayed on your back. I found the controls to be a bit difficult in this game however. Many actions, such as opening your skill powers menu, are not explained so you have to look through the key binding menu to see you need to press F1 (which is a strange choice; I rebinded it to tab). To exit menus you need to press spacebar, because pressing escape won't work. The actual menu interfaces are nice and easy to navigate though. Some powers have no explanation on how to even use them, not even in the key bindings. For example the Shadow Kill power, which tells "Summon a monstrous beast from the shadows to erase a target from the physical realm and recover one use of your equipped Shadow Technique." That sounds cool, but how do I use it? I was not very impressed with having to scour through the forums to find out how to use an ability which wasn't explained in game. Overall though, Aragami is easy to pick up and get into so it has a mostly good user experience.
- There's customisation in the form of different skins to choose from. You can choose from 4 default skins, and also unlock 9 more.
Longevity/replayability - The average time to beat the game is only 6 hours (
[
] ) but I've only completed 8 out of the 13 chapters and already have 6 hours clocked. Each mission has 3 medals to unlock (and it's impossible to get all 3 in one go) so if you want to 100% the game you'll certainly need to replay all the levels. The game is not very long but its length is fairly decent.
Modablity - This game comes with a level editor and workshop support, so once you've beaten the game there's still plenty to do. As of now there are 483 community made maps available to play.
Support - The developers are working really hard on improving their game. This is from the latest patch: "We are still hard at work to support and improve Aragami. This patch contains more than 100 minor bug fixes." They are also going to add more content in the future.
Is it worth the money? For $20, it really depends how much you like this type of game. I'd recommend to pick this up on sale of 30% off or more.

Let me tell you my little story about MorphVox.
It all started on release day, I saw it and thought "Neat, I want that." I wishlist it and go about my day on TF2. I come across someone selling it for 4 keys because they decided against it after buying it. I thought it was a steal, so I got it. I hopped off so I could download it. A short time later, I boot it up, configure it, and play with it. I had so much fun with it. Even programmed in a Dalek voice. The voice and effects packs came out, I got them to continue the fun. So much so, I just kept it as my default mic so I wouldn't have to fiddle with configurations when I wanted to change my voice. But that's when everything changed.
Soon, they released some other DLC that was far too expensive for what it was. I thought that since it didn't add any new features that I would use, I wouldn't get it. Around that time, I started using Mumble. I kept getting "Your mic is cutting off at the end." Since it never did that before, I chalked it up to Mumble. I'd restart Mumble, and it'd be fine. Thought nothing of it. One day, while playing TF2 I hear the dreadded "Your mic is cutting out." Now, I was angry. This never use to happen. What had changed? I can tell you what. I had made MorphVox my default mic. It was creating a delay. So when I'd let go of my PTT button, my full sentence wouldn't get through. So I come to Steam to see if anyone else has this issue and if they figured out how to fix it. Click the forums button... No forums. Click the group button... no group. I go to their site. I had to dig for a good 10 minutes before I got an email address. I send an email. Once I got an email back, they suggested I check a few things in the settings. I set them like they suggest. At first, it seems all good. I get in a few days of TF2 before I'm told I'm cutting out again.
I rage quit right there. Tried another mic, still cutting. Different VOIP software. Cutting.  They obviously had given up much hope for this program before they thought they could milk a few more dollars out with Steam. This program is an abandoned piece of garbage that doesn't work like it was promised. DO NOT BUY THIS! It will only make you want to pull your hair out.
EDIT: I have started using it for short bursts, no longer sessions. I'm going to see if it works fine with a much much better mic.
EDIT 2: After some usage in short bursts, it still delays eventually. It feels like there has been no progress made to fixing this issue.

I love this game. A lot. Now, take into account what most of the high-rated reviews say, because I agree with them. But what I'm going to touch on is something specific that I find most interesting and perhaps wholly unique about this game. Put simply, it reminds me of chess. In fact, one of the final boss room types is a chess set, which you can see briefly in the trailer, but that's beside the point. All enemies have set actions (or perhaps reactions), and will always make them according to the rhythm and how you move. For instance, the red dragon will move once every two beats toward you unless you are any distance directly to the left or right of him, in which case he will shoot a row of fire. The goblins will run away if you approach them, but pursue if you move away from them.
Now, normally, if you had all the time you needed, you could plan out a perfect attack and kill everything without taking damage, but in this game, you have to move with the beat. You have to think quickly if you want to work your way out of a tricky situation. When you die, you feel like it was your mistake and the game had not cheated you, which is generally the case (though there is a small chance of the game generating an absurdly difficult enemy encounter). Even so, due to the random generation, it is possible to find a good weapon or food early on, making giving you an advantage. I always hope for an awesome weapon, but sometimes find myself doing surprisingly well with just a standard dagger. It's action/strategy/cool music-y rhythm/rogue-like at its finest.

A very fun game, though not a particularly challenging one.
Combat is very responsive and flows nicely; almost too nicely since you'll very rarely get hit. I would recommend playing the game on Hardcore difficulty so its at least a little challenging at the start, though it quickly becomes a cake walk anyways once you level up a bit. Later on in the game, after you've torn through thousands of basic enemies, some more interesting enemies start showing up, such as one that can only be hurt by projectile attacks and one that can mimic your aerial dust storm ability. Unfortunately, by that point, you're so ludicrously overpowered, that it doesn't matter, even on hardcore difficulty.
But while it's a very easy game, its also a very fun one. You can impale enemies, launch then into the air, then turn into a tornado of slashing chaos and launch into the air before sending the poor creature back down to earth. And then you zap everyone on the screen with lightning.
So if you're looking for a challenging game to test your skill against, look somewhere else; but if you just want to pass the time with some fun hack'n'slash action against hordes of hapless opponents, you could certainly do a lot worse than this. And that's really the whole point of video games, isn't it: FUN.

Short Review:
A very good castlevania-like action rpg that despite that has a very interesting plot and a fluid combat, with the only downside of having a short length and the fact that, perhaps, the cartoony and furry-like creatures might turn off people.
Long Review:
Dust was probably a big surprise for me and for many people, with its extremely detailed animation, fast paced combat and a very intriguing plot that will really hook you in (despite it will often stop a lot for no real reason. No really, they'll tell you it's not time yet). What really fails in this gamem, IN MY OPINION (and I want to underline it, IN MY OPINION ONLY), are two things:
1)The game is rather short: I finished in 20 hours....BUT only because I went for the secrets and finished the game at 100%, including the challenges and the secrets, while without them might last about 8 or 10 hours, even less if you want to rush through the game, since it's not a very hard game either (unless you go on higher difficulties, of course).
2)The furry-like characters (keep on reading....): The characters are all depicted as animals basically, recalling a sort of Disney-like feel on them and...it is actually very good! Dust especially is a joy for the eyes to see, with his movements and skills moving so swiftly and so smoothly that I really enjoyed it...a bit less on the npc, that aren't as animated as him.
My problem with the furry-like creatures is that it's because of the plot, which is basically a story of racism...and as far as I noticed a lot of racism stories uses this mechanism to focus on the differences, which is a bit tiresome.
HOWEVER.
I cannot deny the fact that it does fit the style and I would be lying if I said the opposite: consider this just a nitpick from me.
But still the game has a lot of good things about it: the main character is extremely likeable but still is pretty cool and isn't actually a bothersome character, which is very hard to achieve nowadays, with either being extremely annoying or overly cheerful: he's a pretty good balance, in my opinion...a bit less for Fidget.
It's definitely worth a shot for this game, even if it's a bit short but if you will spend time on it, you won't be disappointed.

I don't normally do Steam reviews, but for this game I had to make an exception.
For quite a few years now, I've found that today's games often feel stale and have lost a part of what makes them fun. I can't quite put my finger on why, but I do know that whatever it is that's missing has been revived in Dust: An Elysian Tail. I haven't found quite as much enjoyment out of a game since Oblivion, and Dust may even replace it as the #1 game I've ever played, in my book.
I thoroughly enjoyed everything that the game has to offer. The gameplay is fun: racking up awesome combos while smashing through groups of enemies is quite satisfying, and I found the game is at times challenging but never too hard nor too easy (based on my playthrough on Tough difficulty). The RPG elements help balance things but aren't at all too prominent or overpowering. The art is stunning, full of colour and atmosphere. The voice-acting, in my opinion, is excellently performed and the story is unique and quite touching. The soundtrack is amazing and each track matches perfectly with it's respective environment (I immediately had to buy the official soundtrack afterwards). Overall, an incredible amount of attention to detail has gone into Dust, and a level of polish you don't often find in the industry these days.
After completing the main storyline, I went for 100% completion of the game (well, 116% or whatever it goes up to), not only for the obvious challenge, but also because it was simply fun to keep playing. I've got a lot of unfinished or half-arsed playthroughs sitting in my library because properly completing them just feels tedious and like a waste of time. This definitely isn't the case here and it took me back to those classic childhood games I could just keep playing for hours until I had explored every location and collected every item on offer.
In terms of negatives, the only ones I experienced are very minor. Occasionally an item may glitch into a wall with no way to get it out, but it rarely happened and was no big deal. Also, out of the 20 or so hours in the game it did crash twice – thankfully, though, the autosave system was there to minimise the amount of progress lost from those unfortunate times. None of these issues are at all game-breaking and don't really taint the game in any way, however. I personally don't think there are any major flaws at all with the game.
Considering everything, I'm blown away that the entire basis of Dust was designed and programmed by just one person. It's quite clear that he understands video games and what they're truly about. I definitely recommend this game to everyone – even at full-price it's totally worth it – and you should at the very least give it a try. Not doing so would be a disservice to yourself as a gamer.

Just a few points that keeps me from coming back to the game after playing a lot of hours during the early development and launch when the game felt like a different exprence. Things seemed pretty good at first with matches feeling like a proper match between two groups trying to fight it out for supremacy. This lead to some crazy moments with some teams turtling to draw out the matches, others doing blind rushes to reset another teams upgrades, and other such moments. Over time those moments faded away as the game was pushed more towards the esports scene. During that time you could feel the change in the game, but everything stayed pretty much the same with some games being a quick match with one team dominating while others were as I descirbed before. Now I come back to the game after a long pause due to a friend to find that the community is toxic and the matches have been sped up to crazy speeds. I've jumped in and out of a few matches because even back when they started making huge overhalls you would end up with some teams that just didn't mesh well with one another. All I could ever find is one team always dominating another. On top of that is the toxic community that I mentioned a few sentences back. You can look in the community and see the tip of what I mean with comments like this game not being friendly to noobs or just flat out saying that the vets in the game are aggressive to anyone new. I played a game just the other day with four vets that refused to join a team because of this new mechanic called hive score. I don't even know the details of it. The most that I get from the mechanic is that it is some way to try and rate a player much like the old gear scores that you would see in MMOs.
You can take this whole review as me just missing the old days back when there were a larger number of people to play with. It might have been a situation that with that larger number you had a higher chance of ending up with people that wanted to play just to have fun in the game. Now, it's turned into just another arena shooter that attaches a skinner box to give you a reason to play or in some cases as the match from before to not play a match. The game had it's time for new players before becoming what it is now.
For the price, the game offers many hours of enjoyment.

Aragami is a fun and atmospheric stealth-action game reminicent of classic titles such as Tenchu and Splinter Cell. You play as Aragami, a spirit of vengeance brought back to life by Yamiko in hopes of rescuing her from her captors. You must make use of the shadows to hide from your enemies, who can kill you in a single blow with their powers of light. Like Tenchu you can perform stealth kills when enemies come within your vicinity and you can also unlock various abilities to help you more easily navigate further levels. There are a total of 13 levels and they aren't terribly long. In one sitting you could probably complete Aragami in 6 to 8 hours. The cel-shading suits the style and ambience of the world and the story is very well written and presented and has a few twists along the way. Starting off, the difficulty is a little unforgiving, but once you begin to unlock Aragami's abilities, it becomes way too easy. At least, until you reach level 12, which is one of the most frustrating, unfair, and anger-inducing levels in video game history. Overall, Aragami is a lot of fun, and worth the $20 price for what you get. If you miss the classic PS1 and 2 days of stealth-action, and are still holding out for a new Tenchu (like me), it's definitely worth your time. I recommend playing with a controller as well for a smoother gameplay experience.

The Witcher 2 is an epic RPG that can easily stand next to games like Skyrim and Dragon Age.  The Witcher 2 tells a very interesting tale full of dwarves, elves, witches and war between nations.  Let me begin with what I found to be the good parts of this game:
-Interesting and fleshed out story
-the ability to make choices that will affect the outcome of the story
-gorgeous graphics
-visceral and satisfying action combat
-a good amount of loot to find, craft, buy and sell
Now, the game was certainly not perfect, however.  The following are a few of the things that I was not very fond of:
-no fast travel (prepare to backtrack a lot)
-a difficult to follow quest marker
-linear areas (no open-world exploration)
-a convoluted menu system that is difficult to controller with a gamepad
Overall, I found the game to be a great RPG.  I would certainly recommend it, and I look forward to part 3!

I love this game. A lot. Now, take into account what most of the high-rated reviews say, because I agree with them. But what I'm going to touch on is something specific that I find most interesting and perhaps wholly unique about this game. Put simply, it reminds me of chess. In fact, one of the final boss room types is a chess set, which you can see briefly in the trailer, but that's beside the point. All enemies have set actions (or perhaps reactions), and will always make them according to the rhythm and how you move. For instance, the red dragon will move once every two beats toward you unless you are any distance directly to the left or right of him, in which case he will shoot a row of fire. The goblins will run away if you approach them, but pursue if you move away from them.
Now, normally, if you had all the time you needed, you could plan out a perfect attack and kill everything without taking damage, but in this game, you have to move with the beat. You have to think quickly if you want to work your way out of a tricky situation. When you die, you feel like it was your mistake and the game had not cheated you, which is generally the case (though there is a small chance of the game generating an absurdly difficult enemy encounter). Even so, due to the random generation, it is possible to find a good weapon or food early on, making giving you an advantage. I always hope for an awesome weapon, but sometimes find myself doing surprisingly well with just a standard dagger. It's action/strategy/cool music-y rhythm/rogue-like at its finest.

Final fantasy VII is a classic, a game which deals with a lot of real world issues cleverly by mixing it into the fantasy world. It is a hybrid of fantasy and reality, with an industrialized/modern world meeting beasts and untamed lands. This game is however relatively dated (although some elements stand the test of time), but it is a must for any JRPG fan, as it offers traditional turn based combat, an intuitive magic (materia) system, lots of "sidequests", a strong narrative and an open world to explore. This game captivated me when it was first released, and even to this day continues to do so. Final fantasy VII also uses humor throughout the game, and gives you "options" with how to handle scenarios in the game, which impact the world, it is therefore a game you will find yourself playing again and again to revisit events and experience other paths (albeit all leads to same game ending). The cast of characters is colorful as well, and they have become iconic in their own rights. This game is designed with the "traditional" JRPG elements of the time, something not often seen today, as such it is worth exploring for both fans and the untested alike. Overall this game is a full recommendation, its style may not be for all, but it is a relatively accessible and enjoyable gaming experience and it is priced appropriately, giving you a substantial amount of game (30+ hours easily).

I don't normally do Steam reviews, but for this game I had to make an exception.
For quite a few years now, I've found that today's games often feel stale and have lost a part of what makes them fun. I can't quite put my finger on why, but I do know that whatever it is that's missing has been revived in Dust: An Elysian Tail. I haven't found quite as much enjoyment out of a game since Oblivion, and Dust may even replace it as the #1 game I've ever played, in my book.
I thoroughly enjoyed everything that the game has to offer. The gameplay is fun: racking up awesome combos while smashing through groups of enemies is quite satisfying, and I found the game is at times challenging but never too hard nor too easy (based on my playthrough on Tough difficulty). The RPG elements help balance things but aren't at all too prominent or overpowering. The art is stunning, full of colour and atmosphere. The voice-acting, in my opinion, is excellently performed and the story is unique and quite touching. The soundtrack is amazing and each track matches perfectly with it's respective environment (I immediately had to buy the official soundtrack afterwards). Overall, an incredible amount of attention to detail has gone into Dust, and a level of polish you don't often find in the industry these days.
After completing the main storyline, I went for 100% completion of the game (well, 116% or whatever it goes up to), not only for the obvious challenge, but also because it was simply fun to keep playing. I've got a lot of unfinished or half-arsed playthroughs sitting in my library because properly completing them just feels tedious and like a waste of time. This definitely isn't the case here and it took me back to those classic childhood games I could just keep playing for hours until I had explored every location and collected every item on offer.
In terms of negatives, the only ones I experienced are very minor. Occasionally an item may glitch into a wall with no way to get it out, but it rarely happened and was no big deal. Also, out of the 20 or so hours in the game it did crash twice – thankfully, though, the autosave system was there to minimise the amount of progress lost from those unfortunate times. None of these issues are at all game-breaking and don't really taint the game in any way, however. I personally don't think there are any major flaws at all with the game.
Considering everything, I'm blown away that the entire basis of Dust was designed and programmed by just one person. It's quite clear that he understands video games and what they're truly about. I definitely recommend this game to everyone – even at full-price it's totally worth it – and you should at the very least give it a try. Not doing so would be a disservice to yourself as a gamer.

As JRPGs go, there's something especially magical about this one. Many argue it's the last great Final Fantasy game -- created before the big company shake-up that changed everything.
The incredibly imaginative world, gripping story, legendary music, great combat system, and (of course) Japanese sense of humour are all here. It balances drama and silliness perfectly in a wonderfully creative package.
The best things of all is that this is quite simply the best version of FFVII there's ever been: The iconic videos that blew everyone away in 1997 are presented in a higher resolution than ever before, the script has finally had more of the typos and inconsistencies removed, and the 3D looks better than ever. Plus, for the first time ever, the PC version features the original PSX music!
On top of this you have Achievements, Cloud Saving and XBox Controller support right out of the box.
If you've never played FFVII, this is the version to go for: Works on all modern systems, too!

A few years I had a friend start playing Deponia. when i watched i didn't learn much about the story beyond. "This guy is trying to escape Deponia" which is told to you if you so much as glance at it. what I loved was the cartoonish style and the witty if occasionally offensive humor. A game made for the crass that doesn't tiptoe around potential issues so much as jump right in like a gleeful child in the mud. it had a kind of charm i hadn't seen in a game yet.
Dispite myself thinking I didn't like the character for his actions and personality in the story I was so very surprised to find that at the end I was very dissappointed. A let down so large I sat in my chair shocked verbally repeating to myself "No, that can't be the end. there must be something after the credits right?" So I sat, watched, and listened to the music until the title screen appeared. at which point I immediately opened up the bonus content and searched for something I missed.
But no, there was no alternate ending. No promise of another game in the future to explain or keep me going. and then I had to ask myself why the ending was such a lurch for me. And I had to admit to myself that yes. the character Rufus had grow on me at some level beyond my imagination.
I cannot say more lest I give away something integral to the plot. So in summarry or TLDR: If you want a game that gives you satisfaction for solving all of it's puzzles and the enjoyment of success. turn back now. because you won't find it here.

Little, but important, the menu allows a lot of customization. You can do everything from remap the buttons to resize and reposition your health bar display. It's such a small thing, but I'm amazed this sort of functionality isn't standard in every games options.

You'll need to save your money for a therapist to help you work out whatever issues you have that make you percieve things like Bugs Bunny and Mickey Mouse in only a sexual context. In progress review. The negative reviews don't need any help, so I'll try to explain if you should buy the game. I got it on a deep discount and wouldn't recommend paying more than $30. While reportedly much better than at launch, there's still numerous issues
It's a heavily story driven game, so if you're looking for action or fast gameplay it's not for you. Cutscenes look great with high fidelity graphics and characters, but in-game graphics are somewhat poor. Effects such as weather and water look bad and the whole game appears through a muddy filter IMO
Performance is good and stable for me at 1440p on a gtx 1070 and i5 6600k with 50+ frames at Max and 70+ with reflections and volumetric turned down. I haven't encountered any stuttering or frame drops and performance is very consistent. Perhaps the low graphical fidelity warrants better performance, but it runs great for me
Combat is frankly awful (playing on Hard). It's a lousy cover based shooter with imprecise shooting. No steadying aim (crouch etc) or precise aiming for headshots. Mêlée is simple and I haven't used the counter button once since mashing attack has never failed. Guns feel pretty good but very limited ammo capacity, often only two clips total. Since combat is a main part of the game, this is a turnoff to many
AI are a poor experience so far. They like to sit back and snipe with clip after clip of pistol and smg. The repetitive sound of clip reload clip reload is droning. I'd much prefer them suicidally charging on Hard to increase challenge as there's often no shortage of enemies. Stealth isn't good but I wasn't expecting better
I really like the driving, both on Normal and Simulated. Cars are very drifty and feel more realistic than GTAV. More comparable to GTA4 IMO but with more control
So again, you may like Mafia 3 if it's on a deep discount and play it solely for the good story and setting

I waited months for them to fix this game up, even just fixing the awful driving camera or improving the framerate just a little bit, but it seems like now they've moved on to just doing DLC so I decided to play through it anyways. I'm a long-time fan of the Mafia series. They were never hugely popular games, but they were unique, and weren't afraid to do an open world third person shooter without copying as much of GTA as they could. Mafia 3 unfortunately seems to be going for that larger audience, except they mangled almost every part of it.
Story-wise, Mafia 3 is pretty great. If you're expecting anything actually mafia-related you're in for a disappointment because this is more of a revenge story in which you never even join the Mafia than anything, and in fact you spend the entire game fighting against the mafia (or at least its less interesting underlings, with the actual Family being barely present at all for most of the game, but still) but it's a decent story in its own right with a neat presentation that switches between the current game time and clips of modern-day interviews with the characters or videos of court proceedings from after the game's story But the gameplay is such a weak link that even the tiniest cutscene feels like a welcome break from the tedium; almost the entire core of Mafia 3's gameplay revolves around taking out a hit list of bad guys, which you do every single time by running from one dot on the map to the next mowing down a few guys and then moving on, then once you've mowed down enough little guys you get to mow down the big guy of that district in a place you've probably already been to and shot up before, and the whole thing starts feeling like a grocery list routine after the first one. The main missions that you unlock in between these are good and the opening hour or two of the game is great, and there are some neat mechanics like negotiating territories between your three underlings, but they're so far and in between that it doesn't feel worth it.
Just about every aspect of the gameplay feels like a step down from Mafia 2; the cops no longer care if you drive like a maniac, only a small selection of cars allow you to customize them (the ones that can be called to you on-demand from a helper) and the customization is heavily stripped down, and in general there's just nothing to really do with your money. You can't buy clothes, most of your weapons are given to you for free, and most of the time the only thing I used it for was to refill my ammo and health shots, which is a service that you have to pay to even use because the only way to do any of that that I could find was to hire the gun van to come stock you up. The whole game is a big boring mess, and the only thing to do aside from the big boring mess is a bunch of races that I didn't care to do (because I'm "race-ist, haha, get it?").
Mafia 3 just feels like the developers finished a Mafia 2 style game with a short, more linear but much better campaign, and then got word from 2K that they needed to make it more like GTA to fit in with what the kids like these days and had to add dozens of hours of filler content that isn't fun to play at all. Mafia 3 has a great soundtrack selection, great cutscene direction and storytelling, some fantastic characters, and fun main story missions, but it's all for nothing because all that makes up about 1/4 of the game and the rest will put you to sleep. Big fans of the series will find little bits of great content here and there throughout the game that might make it worth trying, but otherwise I'd say just stay away.

Fallout Shelter is an interesting time sink. I've never played a clicker, but the word comes to mind as I manage what amounts to a game of clicking, waiting, and some planning. There is a fair amount of strategy involved in playing this game, not only as  the Overseer, but in combat, but don't go looking for a lot of depth.
For a free piece of promotional fun, Fallout Shelter really satisfies. As the unseen but all powerful Overseer, you are tasked with managing your inhabitants, or 'Dwellers', building your Vault, and issuing commands during combat. The concept starts out simply, and progresses rather well as your population grows and your vault becomes just a little deeper and more complex.
The rooms all provide something, most of it useful for developing your Dwellers or your Vault itself. There isn't much to do but place your dweller in said room and occasionally click a resource, a level up icon, and such. During a
all kinds of things can happen, and Disasters can come randomly or if you “Rush” a room for its given resource. In most cases these are manageable, but there is one type of disaster that is woefully imbalanced. More on that in a moment.
The game is not without issues. Controls can be pretty wonky, particularly with clicking. I didn’t remember having too much trouble when my vault was new, but with more rooms and Dwellers it seemed as though clicking on one of the Dwellers would instead click the room. Dragging a Dweller to a room to perform a task also has a lot of inconsistent results. A green silhouette indicates that a Dweller has been selected and when I drag them over a room they will often go to the next room above or below. The same goes with locating the Mysterious Stranger; a random encounter in the vault that if you locate will rearward you with free caps (the game's currency). I would find the stranger, and when I try clicking him, despite where my cursor is located, I will instead get the room and zoom in, but not get him. This can become very aggravating.
One of my other big complaints revolves around the aforementioned disasters, specifically, radscorpions. During a disaster, such as a fire, it will grow, maybe spread to adjacent rooms, and generally just be a minor but solvable problem. These disasters get harder as your population gets bigger. By 50 Dwellers you begin to get radscorpions. They are extremely powerful, and not only do they do great harm to Dwellers, they are tough to kill, drain power (one of the most precious resources in the game), poison your Dwellers with radiation making them harder to heal, and they move around to random rooms. They are incredibly destructive and tough to kill. I had to evict a lot of Dwellers to lower the population to 49 just to keep the menacing attacks away. There are training rooms, better weapons, and other ways to mitigate this problem, but that will take weeks of time sinks and grinding to get to that point. The game's developers could have balanced this much more fairly. As it stands it is a harsh and largely unpleasant difficulty spike.

I love this game. A lot. Now, take into account what most of the high-rated reviews say, because I agree with them. But what I'm going to touch on is something specific that I find most interesting and perhaps wholly unique about this game. Put simply, it reminds me of chess. In fact, one of the final boss room types is a chess set, which you can see briefly in the trailer, but that's beside the point. All enemies have set actions (or perhaps reactions), and will always make them according to the rhythm and how you move. For instance, the red dragon will move once every two beats toward you unless you are any distance directly to the left or right of him, in which case he will shoot a row of fire. The goblins will run away if you approach them, but pursue if you move away from them.
Now, normally, if you had all the time you needed, you could plan out a perfect attack and kill everything without taking damage, but in this game, you have to move with the beat. You have to think quickly if you want to work your way out of a tricky situation. When you die, you feel like it was your mistake and the game had not cheated you, which is generally the case (though there is a small chance of the game generating an absurdly difficult enemy encounter). Even so, due to the random generation, it is possible to find a good weapon or food early on, making giving you an advantage. I always hope for an awesome weapon, but sometimes find myself doing surprisingly well with just a standard dagger. It's action/strategy/cool music-y rhythm/rogue-like at its finest.

What began as a private corporation, grew to encompass the governership of the world's largest city, Midgar. You begin as Cloud, an ex-operative of SOLDIER, a special forces unit of the ShinRa military.  The game evolves one of the greatest storylines in RPG history.  Follow the journey as Cloud discovers the secrets of his past with ShinRa, his involvement with the rougue SOLDIER operative known as Sephiroth, and the inner workings of the practical capital of the world, the City of Midgar.  Leave to discover ShinRa's presence across the globe, and join the fight in a global resistance movement to stop ShinRa, and ultimately Sephiroth himself.  Spanning an epic tale, this game is a large reason why the Final Fantasy name became the houshold one which it did.

Dust: An Elysian Tail is a game where you play a humanoid rabbit in a turquoise outfit running around killing things with a talking meat cleaver and an orange companions who is essentially a slightly less annoying version of Navi from LoZ: OoT. It's called an Elysian "Tail" instead of "Tale" because it's a furry game. Now, details:
Dust's gameplay is similar to Vanillaware games like Dragon's Crown or Muramasa. You go through a 2d level hitting things until they die.
those games however, Dust's gameplay is incredibly simplistic. I wasn't kidding when I said all you do is hit things until they die. The "advanced move list" consists of 8 whopping combos. In addition to that there are 3 types of special attack that can use to endlessly stunlock most enemies. This ultimately doesn't even matter however, since after leveling your attack stat twice you will kill everything on the level in two standard attacks anyway, and I played on the hardest difficulty.
The game has a parry system in place which gives quite a lot of leeway and you will often find yourself parrying simply by spamming attack. There is a dodge ability that has good distance and will phase through enemies, all complete with i-frames. It's actually quite easy to avoid getting hit at all since most enemies will be interrupted and stunned momentarily by both standard and special attacks. The problem comes with a basic failure in design. All special effects and some environment setpieces are placed in front of enemies and the character, leaving you effectively blind. On the highest difficulty in a new area, you will most likely from one attack before leveling up. It's not uncommon to have an enemy attack you from behind an environment or special effect when you didn't even know it was there. When you dodge to either side and immediately attack, your character does a dash back about half the distance you originally dodged, often putting you right back in the face of the enemy you just dodged away from. Enemies are essentially just reskins of eachother. Some of the behave in a different way than others, but they are all countered in exactly the same way: hitting the attack button over and over.
On the other hand, boss fights are also made ludicrously easy. With the exception of the very last one, you will be only fighting one enemy. You can walk from side to side spamming homing special attacks and the boss will be stunlocked and unable to do anything. There is a limiting factor on special attacks, and that's the energy bar. Problem with this is that the energy bar is refilled by hitting enemies. If your special attacks are hitting enemies then it barely goes down fast enough to even justify its existence at all.
The story was clearly intended to be a large part of the game, but I couldn't get into it. The villain is made to look like a pretty caring, down to earth guy in every cutscene you see him in and not once do you even get to hear his motivation for his murdering thousands of people, only that he did it. It's incredibly poor characterization to have a supposedly evil and monstrous villain only to not have him even have any motivation or explanation for it at all. The characters are pretty generic and soulless and at the point in the game where the character makes a completely unironic "I am the sword of justice" speech I just had to laugh.
Overall the game is pretty average. I can understand this however. From what the credits seem to say basically all of the game was made by one person apart from the music. I can sympathize, but I can't recommend the game. Unless you're a furry, then I guess you might enjoy it more than I did.

I feel largely the same way about Mafia III as I do about Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, Homefront: Revolution, XCOM 2, and most of the sequels I played this year: it's not a bad game, but it could have been so much better.
Mafia II had some of the best writing I'd seen in games in years. I had problems with its ending, but the journey was a unique, enjoyable one. I was hoping for the same kind of experience here.
But unlike Vito, Lincoln doesn't really grow throughout the story. There's a significant change early on (and the sequence in question is easily the best in the entire game) but after that it's just revenge, plain and simple.
The underboss and territory system hurts the game more than it helps. Having to complete a bunch of small, repetitive tasks before you can move up to take on the leader of an area gets quite dull. And while each of the bosses has a different personality, working your way through the list feels like a chore. I desparately wished this had been some optional money-making mode instead of mandatory for advancement. Tying the perks and upgrades to it makes it that much worse.
There are also a ton of collectibles and things to do that are totally optional: they aren't even tied to achievements. It would've been so much more meaningful if they unlocked something, or were permanently available in the menu across playthroughs. As is, you can spend dozens of hours getting them all and then the instant you begin a new game they're gone. This is exacerbated by the single autosave file saving system, which might be my biggest gripe about the entire game. It's 2016 and you made a game without multiple saves? Shame on you.
And you
be playing through multiple times. While technically possible to 100% in two playthroughs, unless you're following a guide from the very beginning you'll have to get at least partially into a third playthrough. This is beyond annoying: the game simply isn't fun enough to warrant replaying large portions of it.
The gameplay mechanics and the graphics are a bit below par - the game is not as smooth in either regard as its predecessor. Again, they're not awful, but I expected more. The cinematics are quite good, but they often last way too long and break up the action too much.
Where the game does excel is in its music and atmosphere. They nailed the 60s and New Orleans. I just wish they had fit a better story and sytem into that setting.

A smart and challenging roguelike that keeps your toe tapping to the beat. There's very little bad about this game, the enemies are varied and interesting, the bosses are tough, the weapons are varied and interesting, the buffs are varied and interesting. Some of the hard-core challenges are insane. It is perfectly playable as-is but could benefit from a little polish going forward -- more gentile level transitions, and it is tough to play with a gamepad since items are triggered with the directional keys.
The game is tough as nails but the unlocks for upgrades / drops keep a sense of progression. The unlockable practice rooms are genius. And dying is never that big a deal since the music is so fun to play to.
If you like rhythm games and don't have much experience with roguelikes, you will find an excellent rhythm game that keeps you mentally engaged as you stay a few beats ahead of the action to position yourself to survive. (And it wouldn't hurt to read a minor spoiler or two to get a leg-up on the roguelike discoverability game mechanics.)
If you like roguelikes and don't have much experience with rhythm games, you will find a top-notch roguelike that requires attention to detail, offers plenty of discoverability, and has deep and challenging game mechanics -- all set to a fantastic beat.
If you like rhythm games and roguelikes there is absolutely zero reason to not pick this up immediately. And maybe also remember to send the developer a valentine next Feb. 14th.

This game is totally amazing. It Is great in pretty much every way. It's a a rogue-like which means when you die you have to start over. Unless of course you have a magic potion that gives you another life, but more on that later. It is a top down turn by turn grid based dungeon crawler.
The game has, as of right now, 3 zones, each with three levels then a random boss level. The levels are randomly generated dungeons where the creatures get more challenging each level, followed by a boss battle, The unique aspect of this game is that a turn happens on the beat of the music, and you get a gold multiplier bonus for moving each turn along with the beat and not getting hurt. Sort of a combo system that gets your more gold. It sounds slightly confusing, but it ends up being a completely unique and awesome gameplay mechanic that makes the game one of the best I have ever played.
This brings me to the first point, and that is the totally gnarly soundtrack that never gets old for me. You slay beasts left and right while collecting gnarly loot as you grind through level after level with death just one wrong move away, to a totally grooving soundtrack the whole time. Pure Awesomeness.
It is challenging, but if you learn your enemie's movements and attacks, you  can slay dragons, minataurs, and nightmare steads with a few slices of your glass rapier. If going zone by zone you unlock permanent perks through the dungeonmaster, merlin, and hepheastus at the starting area. You can also play hardcore mode which gives you only one attempt to beat all the zones in one run, with all itmes unlocked, but no upgrades from the lobby. THE TRUE TEST OF BEAT SHREDDING MONSTER SLAYING. It'as fantastic.
Your character has a bunch of different equipment slots. Head, torch, weapon, armour, legs, ring, and shovel. And each slot has tons of gnarly items that can go in them.
There are rings of regeneration, peace, war, protection, might, luck, and phasing just to name some. Each has a unique property that changes your gameplay syle.
Ton's of awesome weapons that each have their own unique playstyle. Daggers, broadswards, longswords, rapiers, spears, flails, whips, bows, crossbows, cat'o nine tails, a blunderbuss, so much awesomeness. Plus there are different types of weapons too, iron, gold, blood, glass, titanium, and obsidian, each with thier own perks.
Many types of armour so you can take more punishment. Leather, chainmail, plate, obsidion, glass, heavy plate, and more.
Your shovel allows you to dig up certain types of blocks where you can find rooms full of enemies, or a hidden chest, or even keys to special chests.
Different types of boots give you the ability to ignore certain types of traps, terrain, or other various things, each helping out in it's own way.
On your head you can equip a crown of teleportation, circlet of telekenises so you can see enemies and the contents of chests, or a helmet to increase your armour more.
Torches help you spot monsters in the darkness or secrets in the walls. Magical torches shed light on everything so even well hidden secrets become yours.
SOOOO many monsters!!! Each with unique movements and attack patterns, then on top of that different versions of each monster that get harder each level.
In the end, get this game, it's in alpha and it plays like it could be a standalone. I rarely run into glitches or problems and I play this game alot. If you like rogue-likes at all, this is one that will make the top of your list. Revolutionary in so many ways just like ToME and other new rogue-likes.

Take the role of Dust, an enigmatic warrior who wakes up in a glade one day with no recollection of who he is. Together with the sage Blade of Ahrah and its cute Nimbat guardian, Fidget, the trio set off to explore the magical land of Falana to try and get back Dust's memories.
Dust: An Elysian Tail has a lot of Metroid and Castlevania in its makeup. You'll be doing things like backtracking, and finding areas that you can't initially access. You'll have bosses to fight and goodies to find- it's that sort of game. Refreshingly old-school in many ways. The action is more akin to a brawler, however. Something like the Shank games, Odin Sphere or Muramasa: The Demon Blade.
Options-wise, the game supports an XBox 360 controller if you wish to play with that, but there are no inherent drawbacks to using the mouse and keyboard over the controller. You can rebind the keys for your convenience if you wish as well. It's like you could barely tell this was originally a console game!
One great plus is that colour-blind mode is present, which will give you a text indicator of what colour the gates in the game are (I don't think this is giving much away, but you will collect different coloured gems to open up corresponding coloured gates). It's not something that is a personal issue, but it is hard to see how this would be a bad thing.
Another great option is HUD scaling. You can alter the size and position of all the HUD's elements- the health bar etc. This can greatly increase gameplay comfort and pleasure.
This is probably the most crucial factor- the game runs smoothly, like warm butter on toast. You have different resolution options, but it ran on my laptop, 4GB RAM, Intel i5 dual core processor, without any slowdown or any performance hindrance that was noticeable. It did not crash once. I can only imagine how well it runs and how great it looks on more powerful machines.
It just seems incredibly well-optimised for computers. It's just excellent, in that respect.
*Ahem* gameplay. Dust's bread and butter is a chain system. You have a few different sword combos you can perform, as well as Fidget being able to shoot magic bolts. The higher the combo chain you can get without breaking it, the more experience you can gain. Get enough, and you'll level up, getting a skill gem to put into a stat you wish to improve (HP, damage etc). You can also parry and counterattack if you have a good sense of timing, in addition to being able to dodge your enemies' strikes. There's also a light economy and crafting system. You can get some equipment to enhance your stats, and you can also collect dropped items and make them into new equipment.
The mouse is incredibly responsive when it comes to attacking, and combat is generally satisfying. You can fairly easily go flying through the air like a whirlwind of destruction! The chain system is something that gives you more reward, more experience, the better you are at it, encouraging you to hone your skills.
Beauty is very much in the eye of the beholder, but the game looks gorgeous, in terms of both art and animation. There's a hand-drawn cartoon style to the characters, all of whom are anthropomorphic animals, making look like the best Don Bluth movie he never made. That's meant with the highest respect. Backgrounds have a nice painted style to them like something out of Rayman, and Dust has some idle animations, again, an old-school throwback. It's a world crafted with a lot of love, with lots of different environments and terrain to go through as well. Colourful, but dark when the environment calls for it.
The story is generally very compelling and well-written, with one or two twists and turns that you may have not seen coming. It's a script that also has a few game references, but doesn't relentlessly shove it in your face that it's trying to reference something. It's rather sensible and grown-up in that respect. The voice acting is generally well done, also. If you have a discerning ear, you can possibly pick out slight differences in audio quality, but it's nothing serious enough to wreck your experience. The soundtrack, by Hyperduck Soundworks, is particularly exceptional, with music that fits the mood of each area well.
Length-wise the game will clock in at approximately 8-10 hours, depending on your pace, but the length can easily double if you pursue all the collectibles and side-quests.
In terms of downsides or nit-picking, the game is arguably on the easy side, but you can remedy this if you play on Hard or Insane difficulties. It depends a bit on how well-seasoned with games you are.
Another limitation for some is that there is only the one weapon that you stick with throughout. You can't unlock or use different weapons, nor can you unlock different combo attacks. You can get, without giving too much away, new abilities, or variations on what you have, but you can't get a bona fide new weapon or any new combos. The upgrade system when you level up is rather linear- you can put points, as it were, into any skills, but you can't go too far into one stat compared to the others. It's strictly making you tougher, stronger and so on. No new attacks or anything special like that.
It's a game that's very much worth your time. You will not regret playing it, I have that much confidence in the title.

The Deponia trilogy dumps you right onto the surface of the eponymous junkyard planet - several times, usually badly charred and at terminal velocity - puts you into the shoes of our hero Rufus and then expects you to escape its gravity well using your awesome powers of kleptomania, sexism, egoism, general stupidity, the uncanny talent to befriend enemies and alienate friends, McGuyver skills, and an awesome scarf, on your quest to save the world. Just kidding, screw the world, the agenda is to get out of here and hopefully win the affection of some space ladies.
Gameplay-wise, if you have experience with point and click adventures, you have already played this game. The controls are the pinnacle of the genre and its final evolution (disregarding weird experiments like Broken Age's dragging items from the inventory instead of clicking them like a rational human being), complete with a dedicated button to highlight active zones on the screen if you don't feel like pixelhunting. Albeit your pixelhunting skills will prove useful as there are easter eggs that can be collected only by doing so.
The story is certainly interesting, and jumps from old-fashioned slapstick to serious themes, the resulting emotional rollercoaster never failing to give you whiplash. It's got plenty of filler, but the characters are memorable and plotholes few.
It is also a sort of a character study of Rufus, examining his motivations and constantly putting him into the dark to ask what he is. The answer to the question is always the same. What is the answer? You're going to have to find out.

If you haven’t bought the Deponia trilogy, the Complete Journey is the best option to experience this famous, not so child-friendly, but in the end quite enjoyable adventure game about a very egotistical protagonist and his struggles to save and/or leave his home planet.
Deponia: The Complete Journey adds very little to those who already played the trilogy as separate games– it is nothing but a merged version of them. But it is excellent for those who are new to the world of Deponia or want to play the whole story without interruptions (if we don’t count the tutorials, since they were left in there for all three parts).
On the surface, the story is about the struggles of the protagonist, Rufus, and his plans to escape the titular Deponia planet, so he can join the upper society of Elysium. But, looking closer, it is more of a tale of a very egotistical man who uses everyone to his advantage; not because he is evil, but because he honestly thinks he is doing the best for everybody by trying to do the best for himself. The result is not only some slapstick gold, but also excellent dialogues and character synergy between Rufus, his newfound love (Goal from Elysium), and all the others who help them or try to stand in their way.
The characters and the dialogue are the strong points of Deponia, even though the plot suffers from a few problems. It tends to get sidetracked all the time, and as the games progress, the number of plot holes and abandoned story threads increase drastically.
As a point ‘n’ click game, it shows an interesting difficulty curve: it starts off mild, then ramps it up to almost early 90s levels, only to end in some poorly designed or medium level puzzles. This creates a mixed bag for the Complete Edition, but a good bag nonetheless.

As a kid, I remember playing countless point and clicks, becoming enraptured by the open worlds of Myst and Riven, the clever script of the Monkey Island games, and the subtle charm of Grim Fandango. As I grew, I wrote the genre off as dead, thinking that no game could rival any of the previous with todays graphical capabilities and marking the audience as a small, esoteric, mostly gone group. I am pleased to find out how indeed wrong I was.
Deponia, sequel Chaos on Deponia, and the culminating Goodbye Deponia all deliver on several fronts. The puzzles are complex and daunting, the atmosphere alluring, the characters intriguing and unique, and the art breathtaking. It has a very big "Fallout 3" feel to it (in terms of aesthetic) and brings with it a very immersive and captivating story to boot.
Play as the loud-mouthed Rufus, a citizen on the junk-ridden planet of Deponia, and self-professed genius. Infamous around his home town as a harbinger of accidental explosions, he grows obsessed with the idea of leaving. His destination? The mystical cloud-city known as Elysium. When a wayward escape attempt brings him on board a sky-ship headed for Elysium, he finds an Elysian woman in trouble. Ever the hero, but quite the klutz, his rescue attempt brings them both crashing to the planet below. Now, he must get the Elysian woman, Goal, back to her home, and thwart the evil plots of the mysterious Orgenon.
That's the idea, anyway.
I really really enjoyed this game. I actually anticipated coming back to it after a long day at work, and spent hours avoiding tutorials to try and figure out the puzzles. Lots of inventory combinations, lots of seemingly convoluted puzzles (that seem obvious once you figure them out...), and a HUGE cast of characters from which to gather information, and items.
If I had any complaints, they would be few. The soundtrack, although absolutely wonderful, gets tiring at times, especially when you're looking at one screen for an hour trying to work out which way to move the lever to open the door. There is also an illusion of choice and a "moral" system in the game via conversation, but in reality, there are no other paths to the end result, and additional dialogue choices are either there just for comedic purposes, or to further showcase what an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the main character actually is. My final complaint will be spoiler free, but I absolutely despise the ending, although I understand why it ended how it did.
I'd shy away from grabbing just the individual copies of the game. It is absolutely a three-part game, with all three parts needed to complete the story. Hope you guys like it! :]
