I feel largely the same way about Mafia III as I do about Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, Homefront: Revolution, XCOM 2, and most of the sequels I played this year: it's not a bad game, but it could have been so much better.
Mafia II had some of the best writing I'd seen in games in years. I had problems with its ending, but the journey was a unique, enjoyable one. I was hoping for the same kind of experience here.
But unlike Vito, Lincoln doesn't really grow throughout the story. There's a significant change early on (and the sequence in question is easily the best in the entire game) but after that it's just revenge, plain and simple.
The underboss and territory system hurts the game more than it helps. Having to complete a bunch of small, repetitive tasks before you can move up to take on the leader of an area gets quite dull. And while each of the bosses has a different personality, working your way through the list feels like a chore. I desparately wished this had been some optional money-making mode instead of mandatory for advancement. Tying the perks and upgrades to it makes it that much worse.

It would've been so much more meaningful if they unlocked something, or were permanently available in the menu across playthroughs. As is, you can spend dozens of hours getting them all and then the instant you begin a new game they're gone. This is exacerbated by the single autosave file saving system, which might be my biggest gripe about the entire game. It's 2016 and you made a game without multiple saves? Shame on you.
And you
be playing through multiple times. While technically possible to 100% in two playthroughs, unless you're following a guide from the very beginning you'll have to get at least partially into a third playthrough. This is beyond annoying: the game simply isn't fun enough to warrant replaying large portions of it.
The gameplay mechanics and the graphics are a bit below par - the game is not as smooth in either regard as its predecessor. Again, they're not awful, but I expected more. The cinematics are quite good, but they often last way too long and break up the action too much.
Where the game does excel is in its music and atmosphere. They nailed the 60s and New Orleans. I just wish they had fit a better story and sytem into that setting.

If you like rhythm games and roguelikes there is absolutely zero reason to not pick this up immediately. And maybe also remember to send the developer a valentine next Feb. 14th.

This game is totally amazing. It Is great in pretty much every way. It's a a rogue-like which means when you die you have to start over. Unless of course you have a magic potion that gives you another life, but more on that later. It is a top down turn by turn grid based dungeon crawler.
The game has, as of right now, 3 zones, each with three levels then a random boss level. The levels are randomly generated dungeons where the creatures get more challenging each level, followed by a boss battle, The unique aspect of this game is that a turn happens on the beat of the music, and you get a gold multiplier bonus for moving each turn along with the beat and not getting hurt. Sort of a combo system that gets your more gold. It sounds slightly confusing, but it ends up being a completely unique and awesome gameplay mechanic that makes the game one of the best I have ever played.
This brings me to the first point, and that is the totally gnarly soundtrack that never gets old for me. You slay beasts left and right while collecting gnarly loot as you grind through level after level with death just one wrong move away, to a totally grooving soundtrack the whole time. Pure Awesomeness.
It is challenging, but if you learn your enemie's movements and attacks, you  can slay dragons, minataurs, and nightmare steads with a few slices of your glass rapier. If going zone by zone you unlock permanent perks through the dungeonmaster, merlin, and hepheastus at the starting area. You can also play hardcore mode which gives you only one attempt to beat all the zones in one run, with all itmes unlocked, but no upgrades from the lobby. THE TRUE TEST OF BEAT SHREDDING MONSTER SLAYING. It'as fantastic.
Your character has a bunch of different equipment slots. Head, torch, weapon, armour, legs, ring, and shovel. And each slot has tons of gnarly items that can go in them.
There are rings of regeneration, peace, war, protection, might, luck, and phasing just to name some. Each has a unique property that changes your gameplay syle.
Ton's of awesome weapons that each have their own unique playstyle. Daggers, broadswards, longswords, rapiers, spears, flails, whips, bows, crossbows, cat'o nine tails, a blunderbuss, so much awesomeness. Plus there are different types of weapons too, iron, gold, blood, glass, titanium, and obsidian, each with thier own perks.
Many types of armour so you can take more punishment. Leather, chainmail, plate, obsidion, glass, heavy plate, and more.
Your shovel allows you to dig up certain types of blocks where you can find rooms full of enemies, or a hidden chest, or even keys to special chests.
Different types of boots give you the ability to ignore certain types of traps, terrain, or other various things, each helping out in it's own way.
On your head you can equip a crown of teleportation, circlet of telekenises so you can see enemies and the contents of chests, or a helmet to increase your armour more.
Torches help you spot monsters in the darkness or secrets in the walls. Magical torches shed light on everything so even well hidden secrets become yours.
SOOOO many monsters!!! Each with unique movements and attack patterns, then on top of that different versions of each monster that get harder each level.
In the end, get this game, it's in alpha and it plays like it could be a standalone. I rarely run into glitches or problems and I play this game alot. If you like rogue-likes at all, this is one that will make the top of your list. Revolutionary in so many ways just like ToME and other new rogue-likes.

I love this game and wish I could recommend it.  It's got a great community and great devs.  The reason I can't recommend it is the apparent lack of balance.  It's a really cool setup of humans vs aliens.  I love the alien system of evolving into different creatures which act as classes (with Lerk being my favorite by far).  I play aliens whenever I can as I find marines to be exceptionally boring.  YMMV
So where's the issue?  Marines use guns as expected and aliens have to chomp with jaws of fury.  Well, once marines get shotguns, grenades, and grenade launchers it gets incredibly difficult to even get near them.  Don't even get me started on the mech suits that are extremely difficult to take down.
See, here's how I believe it's supposed to work, marines are supposed to have the range to take out aliens while aliens are elusive.  There are numerous tunnels and sneaky passsages you can use as aliens to get around and near to the marines.  3 of the 5 aliens are extremely squishy.  Skulks (the default alien when you respawn) dies in .5 seconds from a machine gun.  Lerks are a little less squishy.  What do they have to make up for it you ask?  They have passageways to get close and then they have speed.  They're meant to be elusive and to be up down infront behind all over humans.  What offsets their incredible squishiness is their speed.
The issue with speed however, is that it's made entirely useless by the extremely poor server performance.  This is why I cannot recommend this game.  It will ultimately lead to frustration and uninstallation.  It doesn't seem to matter what your ping is when playing on a server nor what your opponent's ping is.  It's like the server artificially treats everyone as though they had the ping of the player with the worst so if someone has 250ms ping, everyone does.  Don't know if this is how it actually is but it sure seems like it.  Far too many times I've run up and dashed around a marine or got surprised and ran away.  You're so fast, you're out of the room immediately, take a turn fly down that hallway, round another corner to safety... and then you die.  From what?? Well, the game heavily prioritizes the shooter so on his screen you were still in that first hallway slowly moving so he blasted you away and it doesn't matter that you're half way across the map on your screen, server takes his side and you die.
So basically the whole agility thing the aliens are *supposed* to have going for them is removed from the game because of poor server performance.  To top it off, there's no kill cam which makes it even more infurating when you get away only to die anyway and you can't even see how it was done.  When I fly to an empty room, latch onto the ceiling, turn invisible and can clearly see there's no one around me yet die anyway, it pushes the uninstall button for me.
I personally don't even have a bad ping.  My average ping while playing this game was 35ms.  Most people in the game have a pretty good ping but for some reason the game still behaves as though it were 350ms.
Every couple nights over the past 2 weeks I've been hopping on and playing this game after I found it in my library where I forgot about it ages ago.  I now remember why I'd uninstalled it back then.. 90% of the games I play, marines. If you're worried about buying this game because you see complaints of lower playerbase im here to try to alleviate some of that apprehension. This game may not have a large playerbase(around 3000 a day according to steam spy and ~500 concurrent at peak hours) but the base it does have seems very dedicated to this game. Its not uncommon for me to see people with 1000+hours on this game in servers i play.
If you live in central europe or North America and you have somewhat reliable internet there will likely always be a close to full game for you to hop into. i find peak EST hours lend at least a dozen populated games and even well into the late night i can always find a handful of very active servers.
On to the game itself, its complex and unlike anything ive ever played before. For most players the RTS elements seem nonexistant initially as they dont see beyond the scope of their role(non commander that is) but strategy is key here. To fully enjoy this game you should always be mindful of what you're doing, what your team is doing, where enemies are focusing and commander orders. This sounds like a lot to balance and at first it is but its something that you will start to do naturally.
The players who dedicate themselves on this game always in my experience seem helpful and will gladly give tips. But you have to ask, If have a question ask your com or teammates. They're incentivised to help because they want you to be effective so they can win.
Rookie servers are still alive and kicking, cut your teeth there and use the sarter missions.
Overall this is one of my favorate games on steam and id love to see the playerbase grow and for more to get their hands on this game.

I'm not gonna lie, this game was fantastic, and when it was I got about 50 hours of fun out of it making it well worth the purchase, but now one downside is basically killing it. Lack of public servers to play on and people to play with.
Back when this game started out, it was awesome, you could always find a server to play on that was populated with a bunch of people (I believe there were even some official servers, what ever happened to those?), back in those days anyone could enjoy this game for all it's worth.
Now, my server browser can hardly find any servers most of the time, I'm lucky if it finds 3 within my ping range (which I set to a generous 100ms, don't want much higher than that in a shooter do we?), and I need to be lucky twice because chances are these servers are either full or empty,
It happens that you find a good server to play on and you can play and play for hours with lots of people and have loads of fun, but you can't just pick up the game and play with the state of things being like this. I could always use the 'play now' featurewhich automatically finds a server for you but this would mean playing with♥♥♥♥♥♥latency and that dampens the fun quite a bit.
Besides this glaring issue, tha the game basically feels like it's dying... The game is actually amazing, it's one of the most fun shooters I've ever played. There are two teams, Aliens and (space)Marines one player on each team has to be the commander, for this player the game is an RTS game, their job is to build bases and oversee and direct the rest of the players on their team to victory, the rest of the players are either marines or aliens, playing as marines and playing as aliens is a very different experience (no matter if you're the commander or a regular player)
For the commander, the difference is of course the types of structures available and the pre-requisites for these structures to work. For marines a power generator needs to be built and kept online for structures in a room to operate, for Aliens cysts need to be built in the room to spread 'infestation' around it in order for you to be able to build in it.
An alien commander can build without the help of his teammates as long as his teammates secure locations and keep the enemies out (or just busy), meanwhile the Marine commander needs other players to build his structures for him and has to order them to build for him. He can later build bots to do this for him but they are slow moving and come at a price.
As for the infantry of both teams, the marines evolve by upgrading their weapons for example by buying shotguns or flamethrowers, later in the game their most elite technology is the exosuit, works kinda like the ones in the matrix.
Aliens have a much more complex progression, aliens evolve by actually evolving, they all start as a 'skulk' which is the basic footsoldier which runs around and bites people's heels, from there they can turn into a gorge (support unit that can help the commander build and heal other units), a lerk (a pterodactyl with ranged attacks), Fade which is a humanoid stealth assassination unit that can deal lots of damage but only from melee range, and finally Onos to compete with the exosuit (it's basically a Triceratops that runs around and bashes things real violently).
And that's about it, most of the game will be fought to control resource extraction points and base locations until one team manages to take over all the base locations exterminating all the opposing team's command centers/hives, both teams start with one command center/hive, they can build more in specific areas on the map and they have to contest each other for these areas. Once built, even if you lose your starting base you still haven't lost because you can run over to your alternate base and retake command from there.
This game seamlessly blends strategy and tactics in a unique way, and I really really wish I could give it a thumbs up because of how great the game itself is, but no matter how great the game is, it doesn't really matter much if I can't really play it unless I have a private server and about 20 friends to join me. When you're hosting a server, you're lucky to get players. When you're playing, you're lucky to find a server, it's a hellish loop that no one enjoys. But I do sincerely hope that the developers will not give up on this game, find a solution to this problem before you make Natural Selection 3, and I will definitely buy that one too. If they are indeed developing Natural Selection 3 anytime soon then I hope they will also make commanding easier to do, the micro-management needed to command well in this game is nuts.

Okay, I just finished the whole game and I have a couple of things to say to those who aren't sure about buying this game. I wasn't even sure myself when I bought it so I hope this will help someone. This is my first ever review so we'll see how it goes. I will also try to make this as spoiler free as possible.
I haven't played many point and click games so I wasn't surprised that I needed to look at a walkthrough every now and then. Some reviews say that the puzzles don't always make any sense and I agree. I would still be stuck somewhere if there wouldn't be any walkthroughs out there. But I didn't mind it that much most of the time. I have to admit, sometimes I thought "How was I supposed to get that??". Though when I did get something right it felt pretty good.
The humor of this game was okay. It didn't make me laugh at any point and some jokes were plain horrible, but it did keep me entertained for the 30 hours it took me to finish it. I knew what horrible things were waiting for me when I bought the game so I never really took it seriously. I think that's how it was supposed to be. I didn't always agree with the things the main character, Rufus, did or said but I didn't see the point of getting mad about it. It's just a game, made for entertainment.
What comes to Rufus, there isn't a nice way to describe him. He's egoistic and makes all the worst decisions. Everything he does backfires sooner or later. He's not the kind of person one would like to hang out with in real life. But on some weird level I liked him in the end. It could be that I really like his design or it could be that I just went through a long adventure with him. It could also be that the other characters, like some of the players, didn't really love him. Rufus wasn't treated like he was amazing or special which made it easier not to get mad at him. Whatever the reason is, I will miss him.
And now about the ending everyone seems to hate. I completely understand why people don't like it. It leaves questions unanswered and it leaves this empty feeling and a thought "This can't end here!". It wasn't the best ending but it was still an ending. Rufus did what he thought was best thing to do and I respect that. It was the final selfless deed.
Not to make this too long I will say these few things shorty; I loved the look and animation of the game, the soundtrack was good, I liked the characters and the plot and sometimes the game surprised me with being clever. That all said, I recommend playing Deponia: The Complete Journey. But maybe when it's on sale. And if you still aren't sure, I suggest playing the free demo of the first game. I did that and here we are.

Governor of Poker 3 is the best free multiplayer poker game with a great design. In this multi-player version of Governor of Poker you compete live with thousands of real poker players to proof you are the best and number 1 Texas Hold ’em poker star! I remember playing the first Governor of poke long ago on my bad desktop. I don’t remember how I found the game or why, but I do however remember wishing I could play with friends or real opponents. Thus, Governor of Poker 3 was born! There are lots that I love about the third instalment in the franchise including the fact that you play with real people. I also enjoy the variety the game offers, not only Poker “Texas Hold ’em” but games like Blackjack also are involved with money currency. The different Achievements want me to continue playing and all in all a fantastic game. I’m a pro by this point in my life and am already a “Shark” online! This ISN’T just a kid’s title; grown men play this too… I think this may very well be the best "free-to-play" game on Steam. That doesn't mean the game does not come with the usual quirks associated with micro-transaction (free) games. And maybe I am being a bit biased because I was already a fan of Governor of Poker 2. Both games are very similar to each other. The major difference being that in GoP 3 you can now play online against human opponents. The money isn't real, but that feeling of playing with real people is what makes the game priceless. GoP 2 was single-player only, but it had one advantage over this game. You could buy properties, organize tournaments, and play against boss-characters. I still recommend it if you don't mind playing alone.

Aragami is a third person stealth game that casts you as an undead assassin with the power to control the shadows. Teleport to any shadow, become invisible (for a few seconds), materialize weapons (one actually) or even summon a shadow dragon (snake more like it) to infiltrate the enemy ranks and dispose of your targets.
If you like stealth game and/or ninjas it does sound great, doesn't it. Well, Aragami does many things well and just a few things badly, but boy if it does something wrong it goes all out. You're playing as Aragami, which is some sort of shadow-spirit-ninja guy. You're killing and/or stealthing your way through the levels to rescue a kidnapped princess. A plot twist is involved, it's so very twisty you might notice it as late as 3rd chapter (there are 13). Anyway, the story is just some filler for you to have a reason for doing what you're doing.
Now, Aragami is a decent stealth game, with nice enough graphics. With various skills, that you won't use. I would put it on Styx level when it comes to nice stealth games, but the boss fights and the arcade segments. Oh boy, do they break the whole stealth game image. The boss fights are dreadful, you need to perform several stealthy things in a very slim time window as the bosses always know where you are and relentlessly go to your current location. Surprisingly the final boss is an exception and this fight is almost ok thanks to that. And there are arcade elements where you have to shadow jump from point to point, and here you fight against slim time windows and crazy angled camera, because these are mainly in enclosed spaces. There are not many of these fights and puzzles, but they are annoying.
I liked:
* stealth and possibility of fully stealth playthrough
* stealth killing is entertaining for a moment
* option to either kill or stealth your way through
I disliked:
* atrocious performance
* boss fights
* arcade segments
Get this if:
* you like stealth games and can live with boss fights
* you're ok with cellshaded graphics
Don't get this if:
* you cannot stomach arcade elements in a stealth game
* you play games for the story
All in all it's not a bad game and I would cautiously recommend it for anyone into stealth games for 11 or so hours of fun (more often than not).

I backed an Orcs Must Die product on Kickstarter for $150 and was given this game and some bonus content for free - Thus begins my tale of woe:
1) I have to register on a particular website to get access.
2) The site *forces* me to accept receiving their newsletters and marketing emails or I can't register?
3) No option in profile settings to turn their email advertisements off except terminating my account. Did I just get forced to sign up for a lifetime of spam?
4) Checking the site on Trustpilot. Score 1.4 out of 10?! That is literally the worst score I have ever seen. Multiple user reports of the company trying to scam them out of money and unencrypted handling of their sensitive information. The ♥♥♥♥ did I just have to sign up for to try this game?
5) The website bugs out. I apparently have 2 passwords for different sections of it, each with a different password policy and their password reset function is bugging up.
6) Password reset works on third try - time to get the client!
7) Installer sprints to 99% in 40 seconds... then gets stuck there forever.
8) After an hour, I reboot the installer and it shows completion. Now a different installer starts for all the patches. I thought the first one said it was already installing those?
9) I come back later and want to start the game. A third installer comes up for installing all the patches. Didn't I just do that twice?
10) Game starts!
11) Tutorial is pretty nice!
12) I have a big flashy red notice warning me that I only have 5 hours after installing the game to begin spending real money or I miss out on a special deal. That doesn't inspire a lot of confidence... you haven't even shown me a single game mode yet!
13) So... the game itself is free to begin with... I don't own a single hero (there's a rotation though)... my only other Kickstarter rewards are cosmetic skins... for heroes I don't own and can't play. Seems the Kickstarter reward was pure advertising and no content - they could at least have given the equivalent of a few hearthstone card packs to get started.
14) Tried 1v1 against a bot. Game seems to have a lot of potential.
15) Wait, I have no choice at all in my equips and tons of slots are empty. This looks very pay to win?
16) Tried PvP tutorial. Crashed. Worked fine on second try.
17) So... the game keeps telling me I am earning reduced rewards because I am not playing a hero I own. And I own no heroes because I have not yet earned the rewards to buy any...
18) Why does *everything* in this game require unlocking!? I have no choice at all. If I want to have one more choice of tier 1 minions, it seems to take 10 wins for a common (AKA non-interesting) card. New heroes seem to take about 40 wins. Daily quests give about the same as 1 win.
19) Looking at minions... there are 9 uncommons, 9 rares, 8 epics and ...2 commons to unlock. Will be more expensive than expected to unlock some new options.
20) 11 different crafting resources!? Why would you *EVER* use 11 different crafting resources? I can't decipher any reason they wouldn't just use a single resource that you spend for everything. This is not even counting the premium gold coins - and apparently there's some sort of chest system though I haven't seen any yet.
21) Oh god... there are 25 additional types of items listed under "materials". I dare to hope they are not truly crafting materials - they seem to be crafted from the first 11 types.
22) Played a couple of co-op games. Fun though not a challenge.
23) Verified that my starter content really does lack fundamental stuff. I cannot summon tier 4 minions, until I buy some of them to equip in my "deck", and there are about 8 other equipment slots that are also empty still. Some of them seem to offer flat stat boosts.
I have never had to jump through so many ridiculous hoops to play a game before, and most of the process felt rather exploitative. The menu navigation is obscure and the game appears to have infinite layers of needless complexity. That's speaking as a dedicated CCG'er and MOBA-player btw, and as a fan of the first 2 games. At least the game itself makes more sense than all the mess in the menus.
The gameplay was showing great potential and may be quite good, either already or by the time they exit beta. Some good ideas there for using the Orcs Must Die mechanics and theme to innovate the MOBA genre.
There seems to be a *lot* of long term progression to find. I personally gave up on the game before ever truly starting, when I invested a couple of hours and found that it would seemingly take the first 200+ hours just to not be gimped on stats - and 400+ hours to also actually have some interesting choices in what you do. It may turn out to be faster than that, but the game felt extremely aggressive about pushing me to spend real money if I didn't want to lose out on both power and interesting choices.
This game hurts my soul but I love it.

Double Dragon… I played this game at a friend of mine who owned a Nintendo in the late 80s. Double Dragon 4 was for sale for around 5 euro with the same look and feel as the old game. This was for me a no-brainer to buy this game.
In 1 word: crap. It is not so easy to get your keyboard settings done. It is not an intuitive system. Check very good what you are setting (keyboard or pad) and make sure you select the right input controller. The standard buttons are not common, so make sure to change it so you can play it your way.
I also didn’t find a normal way to exit the game. As far as I know, there is no exit button. So use Alt+F4 to exit the game. It is obviously a port from console, because on console there is no exit neither.
To finish the tower to level 100, I played with a friend. However, to connect and configure 2 controllers/keyboards didn’t work very well. Somehow via the gamepad my friend could press buttons that moved my character as well, while I was using keyboard. Of course you can play on 1 keyboard, but it is a bit cosy to play with 2 people on 1 keyboard for hours.
In the end we found a solution: Connect 2 keyboard, and select keyboard 1 and configure the keys, then select keyboard 2 to configure the keys, but make sure he uses for every key another key then player 1. Like this you can play both on your own keyboard and you only have to make sure not to press a button by accident that means a move for the other player.
The story mode is pretty awesome. Don’t buy the game for the story, but who does that with Double Dragon 4? The levels are challenging enough and the music makes good “retro” fun. Beating enemies up, throw knives at them, stones or fireballs, or use a flying kick or head butt, everything is possible. The length of the story mode is good: not too long, not too short. Depending on the character you play the game with, to finish the story can be either very easy, or very challenging.
I managed to get all 29. Some achievements are very easy to get, but to finish the story mode with characters like Soeno is difficult. Finishing the story mode with characters like MysteriousWarrior or Ashida you can do without dying once. I found out that it is not possible to save when you play with the extra playable characters. So in order to get the achievement, you have to finish the story mode in 1 playthrough.
Tower mode is pretty fun, but unforgiving when you make 1 mistake. Especially the bullets from the end boss costs you 1/3 of your life. I managed to get to level 70 on my own with MysteriousWarrior. With 2 people we managed to get to floor 116. As far as I have seen on youtube, no one got that far.
The same tricks that worked in 1989, works in this game. For example, on the bottom of the screen you are not touchable for enemies, except only sometimes for ninja’s sometimes, so be careful. At level 8 you can stand on the very edge of the bottom near a pit, and you will see that all 8 enemies will 1 by 1 fall down the cliff and die. This trick is possible on some other places as well.
Without this “can’t touch on the bottom” trick, I think to reach level 100 on tower is almost not possible.

For sure worth the money. Although a bit repetitive, there is enough fun and challenge to beat the story mode with all characters. Unfortunately the game misses online multiplayer, what would it make much more easy to find people to finish the campaign together.

Love this game, it's addicting!
First off what the game is about. It's a procedurally generated rogue-like, where you're this girl looking for her dad (according to the trailer anyways, but is not mentioned in the game). You navigate on a grid tile floor and all your moves can ONLY BE MADE TO THE BEAT OF THE MUSIC indicated by the moving bars at the bottom of the screen. And that's what makes the game. You play through "zones" which each are a different set of enemies, traps, and rewards. Each Zone has 3 floors and a boss floor. You can dig through weak enough walls and must kill monsters on the way to the stairs, use the earned gold to buy better equipment. Theoretically you can play through the whole game untouched from damage, as you can predict the movements of the enemies. However, the tempo of the game pressures you to keep moving with the beat and maintaining your timing which may cause you to make a wrong move. If you're off beat, or you prematurely try to move, you miss the beat and won't move. This also resets your gold multiplier, and the enemies will make their move anyways.
My favorite thing about this game is all this combined with kickass music. That's what makes it so addicting.
Definitely play with a controller tho. Playing with the keyboard made my wrist hurt real quick. I play with the WASD keys (who moves with arrow keys?) and the rhythmic repetition quickly hurts your wrist in a short time.
That aside, this is one of the most unique games I have ever played. The developers did a fantastic job with it so far. 99% positive reviews!
For good reasons.
If I had to criticize the game in ANY way, it would be the menu navigating. It's confusing until you realize (for some reason) left is to go back and right is to confirm selection, and the start button is not to resume the game but also a confirm selection button.
I highly recommend this game. A must have!

My recommendation comes with a reservation for those on the fence.
The artwork, story, music, gameplay, comedy and Deponia mythology are all top shelf. In fact it's so well-done I found myself occasionally feeling like the puzzles were a hindrance to the story. If puzzle solving is your primary interest then don't hesitate to buy these games, you should be very satisfied. If you ever feel like puzzles can be a nuisance then do NOT buy these games. If you're somewhere in the middle then buy the games and follow a guide whenever you feel like the pace has become stagnant.
Besides pace I have two more critiques: it doesn't mention in-game you can double click destination arrows to insta-travel. I played for nearly an hour before discovering this. Achievement hunters take note: for better or worse (it's worse) this package bundles all 105 achieves across the 3 games into one set. So you're committed to ~30 hours of gameplay to get to 100%, and that will be for 1 perfect game not three.
Overall I got more than a bargain for my $8 and would love more Deponia story/mythology, but perhaps in another format.

The stealthy mechanics we're really fun.  Darting between shadows felt a little like Dishonored's blink ability, with the added bonus of charging up your "mana" by staying in darkness.
The powers you unlock add variety to the way you choose your attack, and I appreciated the options of playing each level your own way.  (Kill em or avoid em)
Worthy of play if you enjoy the genre.  It does everything well, with the exception of its saving system.  The auto save only feature shouldn't be.  In a game that takes patience and missions that can take near 60 minutes, I want the ability to save any time I need to go,  Waiting to find the next checkpoint can be off putting.
All in all a great experience.

Gameplay: Metroidvania meets JRPG meets DMC. That's it in a numbshell.  You play Dust, at the start of the game you have limited abilites, except for slash and dash. Enter room kill waves of enemies, yet as you explore and unlock things you gain new abilites and unlock new areas to exlore in return. This is the best, most streamlined stealth game I've ever played.  Think Dishonored, or Mark of the Ninja, but with much of the complexity pared away to emphasize the pure quick stealth and nothing else.  The game captures this ideal ninja experience - one part careful, patient planning; one part lightning-fast, silent action.
And it IS lightning-fast: the game borrows the teleportation mechanic from Dishonored and matches it to the one-shot-one-kill gameplay of Mark of the Ninja, which means that you can easily jet around the large maps from shadow to shadow, killing or avoiding guards according to your preference.  Like many games, Aragami offers the best rewards to players who (undetected) either kill everyone, or kill nobody at all, but there's no morality attached to the decision (you don't get a "bad" ending for killing everyone), and one option doesn't have cooler abilities - ghosting through a crowded map feels just as good as systematically taking out everyone you meet with traps and stealth kills.
There are some hiccups - the detection system is occasionally touchy about letting you know when you are going to teleport onto solid ground (as opposed to a wall over an insta-kill body of water...oops), but these detection problems usually happen when you're getting a little too creative with your sneaky pathfinding.  There are also a couple parts of the game which make you do some fast-paced precision aiming to cross a chasm or ascend a tower that can be really frustrating if you're used to being more cautious and stealthy, but not enough that it's a dealbreaker.
The story is good (but not great), the world and art are pretty and decently-realized (but not too memorable), and the soundtrack has some solid moments (but mostly stays unnoticed in the background) - but it's hard for me to either complain or talk up those elements.  They just keep the excellent gameplay front-and-center.  Duration-wise, the game probably has a good six hours to the campaign, but this is the first stealth game I've ever played where I immediately wanted to go back and replay levels where I'd missed the ghost achievement or wanted to try a total kill run, even just after I'd beaten the game.  So, with even some basic replay value, you're likely to get nine hours (at least).  And that doesn't include the Multiplayer.  Yes, there's multiplayer in this game.  I haven't even touched it, but I'm really curious to see what it's like.
If you liked the stealth aspects in Dishonored, or Deus Ex, or Thief, or even one of the Bethesda RPGs, this is absolutely the perfected stealth gameplay those games have been working toward.

This game can best be described as Tetris-like.  Your object is to arrange the tiles in groups of three or more in order to eliminate the tiles, gain a bonus, and have more tiles drop into the field of play.
In my opinion, You Must Build A Boat (YMBAB) -- which is by the same developer -- is exactly like this game and is much better.  If I had bought this game before YMBAB I might have liked it more.  But, unfortunatley, it suffers from the fact that the two games are essentially alike.
I have read other reviews that describe this game (and its other incarnation) as adventures in grinding.  This is true.  To be honest, I had enough of grinding when I played WoW for seven years.  I'm tired of grinding.  It's pointless and those moments of my life are more valuable then to keep edging toward some arbitrary goal -- in this case, ten million points.
I always have a questionable amount of fun playing games that are laregly influenced by luck.  Perhaps I am not good at thinking visually in three dimensions and, therefore, I'm not able to plan and strategize well in this type of game.
Even YMBAB suffers from this influence of luck.  Ultimately, you can move tiles as quickly as you want or need to, but if you don't get the right tiles dropped into place then it you're eventually doomed.  Therefore, it really doesn't matter how well you make decisions, how fast you operate, or what your strategy is.  Eventually, you will succeed just because of the forces and fates of luck.
I did enjoy this game -- but to be clear I don't think you need to own both this and YMBAB and YMBAB offers more compelling interest.  There just wasn't enough positive happening here when I succeeded to compel me to continue.
Buy either this or YMBAB but not both.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

As an avid musician and part time gamer, Crypt of the NecroDancer was a "have to" buy for me. The idea of incorporating music as the mode for a metronomic gameplay system was intriguing. After finally getting this loaded up, I thought for sure that I had an advantage in this game given that I've honed my own internal metronome for nearly a quarter century and my gaming skills for nearly 3 decades but little did I know that this game puts a whole new meaning into the expression "beat down." To elaborate on that further frankly,
With NecroDancer, it takes more than just timing and gaming experience to survive, as this is a calculated, quick-witted, speed chess match and really is not a game you are going to get far in if you are distracted or not all in to it.
The sound track is great and is one of the biggest reasons (for me anyways) to play this game. Being that I am a musician, my rig is setup with an audio controller and studio monitors, so that I can pump out some decibels and at high volumes this game sounds even better! If you don't have a decent sound setup, a good pair of headphones is crucial. The sound track has a wide range musical styles from the trancey-technoish electronic, chillin mellow reggae-ish, flowing hip hop beats, beatnik jazzy swing, to the grinding heavy metal; all of which is synthesized and composed sequencing. This is understandable considering the game play is tempo driven, though from a musicians point of view, some music wasn't meant to be synthesized and even though musically it is written well, the metal doesn't feel right. A minor gripe. Regardless, every style has a lot of energy with a beat that really delivers the tempo when playing. My last gripe, though petty, I think a little more could be done with the sound effects during gameplay to incorporate them into the music a little cleaner, being that attacks and movement must be done on beat. It is still early access, so we'll see.
There are 2 things that bothered me about this game. One I can look past and most people do not mind the uncontemporized 8-bit graphics but I'm hoping there is a little bit more updating to set it aside from the rest (again, early access). My other issue I had was perplexing and that was the controls. After calibrating to compensate for the latencies, I went to the options to personalize my joystick controls. The devs offer a lot of options in this screen, which is nice, but they have controls labeled 'Combo: Up + Down', 'Combo: Left + Right', 'Combo: Up + left', etc... that you assign to a button. What? This was confusing at first. Well, turns out that these are for using items and using some menu functions. It gives the controls an additional method by using both the movement combinations as well as assigning it to a button. This gives a huge advantage for using a keyboard over a joystick. I also found that when using the keyboard, it was much easier to keep the timing, as though it felt more "instrumenty' than the joystick. My last gripe about the controls is that they are not actually "full controller supported" as stated on the store page. Stick 2 on my 360 controller could not be assigned controls during setup. Oh well, I like the keyboard more for this game anyways!
The gameplay is simple. Using the directionals, you move and attack on beat. The enemies will too, though they all do not move the same manner or count and as I mentioned earlier, this really makes it more of a speed chess match. If you are in the wrong square, miss a beat, or move incorrectly, it could mean game over. This adds a whole new dimension of difficult and for those of you that cannot keep a beat there are additional modes, like turn based, so even the musically challenged can enjoy this game. There are a lot of power ups and items available, though at the moment doesn't exactly feel "rouge-like" just yet but I'm sure that'll change. There are also a multitude of in game mutations that ramp the difficulty level up significantly. Even without them, this game is hard, which should appeal to anyone who likes a challenge in gaming.

Double Dragon II: The Revenge is easily in my top 10 NES games of all time.  It was perfection and is still fun to play.  Double Dragon IV is not total perfection, but still manages to be a lot of fun.  I played the two games back-to-back.  Here's the rundown:
Double Dragon IV pros (Double Dragon II cons):
- There are more special moves and they are easier to execute
- There's a dedicated kick button
- There aren't as many annoying platform sequences
- There are more "missions"
- They added characters from Street Fighter (not really, but ~Ibuki and ~E. Honda are in there)
- It's also a fighting game -- there's a versus mode where you can use the brothers or any enemy to fight your pals (local only)
- More enemies (every enemy from the previous game, plus new ones)
- You can unlock and play as any enemy in the game (!!!)
Double Dragon II pros (Double Dragon IV cons):
- Somehow runs smoother
- The enemies wait their turn to fight you instead of all piling on at once
- The music is better (even if you turn on Double Dragon IV retro music)
- You can attack behind you with 1 button
- The grapple moves are better (up kick!)

At first I was a little skeptical because some of the music didn't really sound chip-tuney enough to match the classic aesthetic of the game (and there are also these weird crates in story mode that look like they don't match the rest of the game,) but as I continued to play I gained an increasing appreciation for Double Dragon IV. A lot of the classic moves and combos from the original Double Dragon's have found their way into this one, and they are more fun and elaborate than ever before! A lot of classic tunes are also a treat, although some of the remade versions of songs aren't half as good as their original 8-bit counterparts. There are segments of levels that are clearly made in the memory of segments from the original games, and most of them bring authentic value to the playthrough experience. Some of them, however, do not feel genuine either because of nuances in the graphics, music, or gameplay. Overall, I feel that the true spirit of Double Dragon was captured in this game, which is a huge success. An even bigger success is that they were able to build new, yet authentic feeling game modes.
As a total package, one of the things that made this game shine the most for me was the surprise of Tower Mode. ***Spoiler Alert*** you earn this mode after beating the game, and it allows you to unlock A TON of playable character for all game modes. Each character has their own unique moves and combos, and there are some really surprising unlocks if you can get far enough.

*-Rating: 7.5/10  Good game for the price.  It only takes just over an hour to beat but it's fairly challenging at first and pretty enjoyable overall.  Very good music and similar gameplay to Double Dragon 2-*
First of all, I loved the old Double Dragons and have been keeping my eye on this game until it went on sale (even though it was already cheap).  Playing through Double Dragon 2 like crazy, I consider myself a pro as I could beat the game solo pretty quickly.
Let's start with the worst parts or what people seem to be moaning about.  Double Dragon 4 only took me just under an hour to 'almost' beat the first try.  I was in the final level so my assumption is it may have been 5-10 minutes longer than that (correction it was 15ish).  I guess you could say it's a short story; but I could beat Double Dragon 2 in an hour flat easily and that was $80 when it first came out.  A lot of the enemies are repetitive, but so were they in the second game.  I didn't have any freezes or any issues with my wireless Logitech controller.  You can full screen with Alt + Enter; apparently some people still don't know about this feature that's been around for decades.
Now with the good parts.  Double Dragon 4 offers co-op play and 5 extra credits (continues) which entail 3 lives each (for a total of 18 lives).  There is a duel game mode (which I haven't tried) and something in ??? I assume is unlocked when you beat the game.  The music is 8/10 in which one of the levels I found myself bopping my head to as I played.  You can switch bewteen retro and remastered music before you start playing.  This game can be pretty challenging in Single Player mode.  The game throws tons of enemies at you that seem to be on a timer, so if you kill enemies slow you're going to have a lot of trouble.
The game itself looks like Double Dragon 2.  We have the same super moves + several others.  You can find out how to do the new ones in the menu.  The controls feel a little off at first (it's no NES controller) and they don't feel precisely the same as the NES Double Dragons as some things are slightly off.  It's not a problem, though, as you can easily get the hang of them within a minute or two if you've ever played the original games (at least I didn't have a major issue with this).
In conclusion, if you really liked the Double Dragon games especially the second, i'd say go for it and buy it.  It's 9 bucks and if you hate it you will have beaten the game before the 2 hour refund limit anyways.  If you have any questions feel free to ask.  Good luck and happy purchasing!
*Edit/Semi-Spolier*: I beat the game on my third try.  The '???' marks unlock to a 'Tower mode' in which enemies are a lot weaker than in the 'Story mode'.  I made it to floor 25 and died.  This unlocked most of the characters/enemies you can play as in any mode including Story; which is a neat feature.
Also, there are a couple levels where you have to pick the right paths to go.  If you go the wrong way it loops back to the previous part you just did.  In one instance, you have to pick the right 'one of three' doorways or you end up fighting the same floors of enemies endlessly.  This was probably the biggest nuisance and in-game life killer of them all, but I figured out all the proper doorways by the third time through.  Just a heads up as the previous Double Dragons had nothing like this :).

The Binding of Isaac is a tough as nails, but oh so rewarding game. You start out weak, but find items that effect your character in a multitude of ways. You advance through the floors, not knowing what will come in the next room, and must use your best judgement and skill to get the best items for the dangers that you may face.
Due to it's completely random nature, you will not have the same run twice. The items you get will differ, the rooms and enemies that spawn will be different, and you will always have a different outcome each time you play. To show the value of this game, at the time of writing, I have sunk more than 100 hours into this game, and I have yet to see a huge amount of what the game has to offer. The difficulty curve may be somewhat harsh, but it is so rewarding once you perfect your play style. Couple this with the incredible Wrath of the Lamb DLC, which is so cheap but adds a huge amount to the already expansive game, you've got a game that has incredble replay value and is potentially the most fun you will ever have with a game.

This game is very simple, and it plays exactly how it appears; a fast-paced match-3 game. After each run that you don't score 10 million points, you're simply sent back to the main dungeon screen - the sanctuary, so to speak - to spend the resources you gained on your last attempt to upgrade your attack and defense, as well as various perks.
And I can safely say that scoring 10,000,000 is not an easy task even if you've fully upgraded everything; I had a fully upgraded arsenal complete with all the potions, and scoring 10 million still took me several tries.
After you beat the game, the game doesn't reset automatically; after the credits, you can continue playing to obtain a higher score (keeping your current stats/upgrades which you'll most likely have maxed out anyways), or you can delete your save data and start anew at any time.
The soundtrack consists of 3 songs - the "home" theme song, and 2 different dungeon themes - and I've found each of them to be fantastic; in all the time I've spent in-game, the songs never got old nor did they bore me. You can probably listen to the songs on youtube somewhere if you're curious.

As an avid musician and part time gamer, Crypt of the NecroDancer was a "have to" buy for me. The idea of incorporating music as the mode for a metronomic gameplay system was intriguing. After finally getting this loaded up, I thought for sure that I had an advantage in this game given that I've honed my own internal metronome for nearly a quarter century and my gaming skills for nearly 3 decades but little did I know that this game puts a whole new meaning into the expression "beat down." To elaborate on that further frankly,
With NecroDancer, it takes more than just timing and gaming experience to survive, as this is a calculated, quick-witted, speed chess match and really is not a game you are going to get far in if you are distracted or not all in to it.
The sound track is great and is one of the biggest reasons (for me anyways) to play this game. Being that I am a musician, my rig is setup with an audio controller and studio monitors, so that I can pump out some decibels and at high volumes this game sounds even better! If you don't have a decent sound setup, a good pair of headphones is crucial. The sound track has a wide range musical styles from the trancey-technoish electronic, chillin mellow reggae-ish, flowing hip hop beats, beatnik jazzy swing, to the grinding heavy metal; all of which is synthesized and composed sequencing. This is understandable considering the game play is tempo driven, though from a musicians point of view, some music wasn't meant to be synthesized and even though musically it is written well, the metal doesn't feel right. A minor gripe. Regardless, every style has a lot of energy with a beat that really delivers the tempo when playing. My last gripe, though petty, I think a little more could be done with the sound effects during gameplay to incorporate them into the music a little cleaner, being that attacks and movement must be done on beat. It is still early access, so we'll see.
There are 2 things that bothered me about this game. One I can look past and most people do not mind the uncontemporized 8-bit graphics but I'm hoping there is a little bit more updating to set it aside from the rest (again, early access). My other issue I had was perplexing and that was the controls. After calibrating to compensate for the latencies, I went to the options to personalize my joystick controls. The devs offer a lot of options in this screen, which is nice, but they have controls labeled 'Combo: Up + Down', 'Combo: Left + Right', 'Combo: Up + left', etc... that you assign to a button. What? This was confusing at first. Well, turns out that these are for using items and using some menu functions. It gives the controls an additional method by using both the movement combinations as well as assigning it to a button. This gives a huge advantage for using a keyboard over a joystick. I also found that when using the keyboard, it was much easier to keep the timing, as though it felt more "instrumenty' than the joystick. My last gripe about the controls is that they are not actually "full controller supported" as stated on the store page. Stick 2 on my 360 controller could not be assigned controls during setup. Oh well, I like the keyboard more for this game anyways!
The gameplay is simple. Using the directionals, you move and attack on beat. The enemies will too, though they all do not move the same manner or count and as I mentioned earlier, this really makes it more of a speed chess match. If you are in the wrong square, miss a beat, or move incorrectly, it could mean game over. This adds a whole new dimension of difficult and for those of you that cannot keep a beat there are additional modes, like turn based, so even the musically challenged can enjoy this game. There are a lot of power ups and items available, though at the moment doesn't exactly feel "rouge-like" just yet but I'm sure that'll change. There are also a multitude of in game mutations that ramp the difficulty level up significantly. Even without them, this game is hard, which should appeal to anyone who likes a challenge in gaming.

Over the last few years we have seen some excellent retro sequels with Mega Man 9 & 10 being ones that spring to mind but sadly upon booting up Double Dragon 4 you will see that nothing has really changed from the days of the NES and so compare it even to scrolling brawlers of the SNES era Double Dragon 4 seems unbelievably shallow and dated.
Obviously the point here like the aforementioned Mega Man games is t prey on our sense of nostalgia but there are already better sequels to Double Dragon and way more advanced games such as Final Fight and Turtles in Time and as such you feel like you are playing some lost levels to the old game but sadly the old game in 2017 rather than the way you remember it through Rose Tinted Glasses.
An even more unusual choice is the decision to base the game on the NES port rather than the arcade original. Again maybe something trying to play on nostalgia as this is the version most of us will remember but still, this is an odd design choice that really doesn’t pay off.
All of the memorable negatives are here. The unable to hit off-screen enemies, the cheap knockdowns and the vertical hit detection being so very precise. There are also some issues where enemies wait as you scale up and down ladders meaning that getting hit in some cases is nearly unavoidable.
As such you end up trying to knock enemies down into one pile and simply start spamming attack as they stand up. A trick that works nearly flawlessly every time if you can manage to line all the enemies up together.
There are a few graphical flourishes in the background to make the game look slightly more modern but in just this really does look like a game from the NES library.
Double Dragon 4 is a game I really wanted to like having fond memories of the original but sadly all it is a few more levels of the original rather than the retro-inspired brawler it should have been.

WARNING: If you don't like giant explosions, war, nuclear weapons, or even the thought of committing mass genocide, then stop reading and get another game, like Galacon 2. However, if you like the former, then keep reading.
Imagine being in an underground bunker, for say the United States, and there was a massive series of crisis that unfolded. Your clock ticks ever so slowly towards zero as Defcon 4 approaches. You start mobilizing your navy to try to defend your coasts against the inevitable assault against your country. You establish airfields and silos along the coastline and close to your cities, so you can protect them. It's Defcon 3 now, and the enemy started to mobilize their forces against each other. Only 5 minutes later a battle fleet has come into radar range of your fleet. Your fleets start to open fire, aircraft carriers launching bombers and fighters while your battleships launch cruise missiles and fire massive guns at your enemy. It's Defcon 2 now, and you are being attacked from the east and the west. Finally, it reaches DEFCON 1. You hear a woman crying in the background, knowing that she is disturbed greatly by the outcome of the events beforehand. You start opening your missile silos and launch multiple nukes at your nearest enemy: Europe. Luckily, you had an alliance with South America, who was helping you defend against the enemy assault. However, 10 minutes after you launch a salvo of nukes, your radar detects a nuke heading towards your country. That nuke becomes 2, then 3, then 6. Your radar detects even more nukes coming from Europe. You then detect a strategic missile sub off the East coast, but you destroy it with depth charges before it can fire. However, you then see a wave of nuke bombers coming from Europe. Your defenses are spread thin, and only 2 bombers were shot down before they fired. You then launch almost every nuke you have against Europe, only to realize that Russia has also fought against you. You launch your last nukes at Russia, only to watch 10 nukes land in Europe successfully, of the 25 you have launched. You then admit defeat as tens of nukes tear your country apart in a glorious storm of radiation and fire, killing almost every human left in your country.
This is what you will experience in DEFCON. What I didn't mention in this, is the atmosphere is EXTREMELY effective at what it does. The occasional woman crying in the background, and the ominous, and slightly creepy, soundtrack just makes you feel remorse, even dread, just for launching fake nukes at a fake country. Yeah, it's THAT powerful of an experience. Hell, the game even comes with a manual on how to survive a nuclear war.

With 41.8 hours on record, I just finished "Deponia:  The Complete Journey" with 100% Achievements.  I would have probably taken a tad longer, but I had played the first game in this compendium ("Deponia") stand-alone somewhat earlier (so you can probably add eight or nine hours to my expected play).  As with the stand-alone version, I'm recommending this version (which, along with "Deponia," includes "Chaos on Deponia" and "Goodby Deponia).  The game play across all three games is pretty consistent:  a pretty good point-and-click game with very good art work, tongue-in-cheek humor, and good voice-acting.  The puzzle difficulty does vary across the games just a bit (I'd say the second game is a bit easier than the first, and the third game harder than the first two).  I've got three gripes with the game.  First, the protagonist, Rufus is a jerk.  If there were more character growth in him as the game progressed, I'd have been happier.  But, it's just sort of irritating to have him constantly do really wrong things at every turn for three games (he actually gets worse from game to game). Superman is the most boring hero ever. Even though he has some weaknesses, the person itself is just too perfect to be very likable (in my opinion, that is). The reason I'm stating this, is that Deponia has gathered some critique that its main protagonist is too much an a**hole for players to really get into the story, something that is very important for adventure games. I disagree with that. Good adventure games do not have a perfect protagonist, lest they would be too short. Deponia's story of two people trying to overcome the impossibility of leaving a life full of trash would never be as enjoyable as it is now if most of the obstacles that lie in the way weren't created by the protagonist itself! Of course the player does not like the way Rufus is handling things, but this creates hilarious possibilities for puzzles that otherwise never would have happened. Deponias story is very strong because the player knows why he is in a certain situation. There isn't some kind of Deus Ex Machina that throws us back every time we make some progress in our mission, no, we do it ourselves. This creates, besides a lot of comical events, also a story that you really want to complete, since you know what you are fighting against.
Rufus may not be the most social being on the planet of Deponia, but at least his story is far from boring. Something a perfect protagonist never would have achieved.
If it's not your style, you won't like it. For a cheap game, it's worth a try; but I see it as more of a time waste than anything else.

The understated nature of this game, belies the tension and psychological sucker-punch it delivers. The simple graphics, so familiar to any child of the 80's raised on a diet of Cold War paranoia, apocalyptic films & TV series, and abject fear for the survival of the species, beautifully captures the ethos of the era. The countdown timer, coupled with the slower game speeds available, maintains steadily increasing tension which is only reinforced by the marvellously scored soundtrack and atmospheric sound suite. The level of investment in your populations when the fateful arcs of missile trajectories begin to slowly crawl across the map and your desperate efforts to minimise fatalities, is matched only by the abject horror as you realise that any successful strategy on your own part condemns millions of innocents to immolation in the fires of an unstoppable nuclear holocaust which will leave large swathes of the globe an uninhabitable, irradiated hell.
You'll enter into this game for the glorification of destruction, you'll leave it with a creeping sense of unease at your own capacity for atrocity on a scale unparalleled in all human history...

The definitive edition of Dawn of War, that still hasn't been surpassed, even by it's sequels.
One of the best RTS games in the past 10 years, and I've almost been playing it that long.
Pros:
+Great entry point for everyone looking to get into Warhammer 40,000.
+Seven races playable both in the Campaign and Skirmish modes...
+...that all feel different and unique to each other.
+Campaign features a "Wargear" system that lets you upgrade your Commander after certain achievements you get during the length of your campaign, adding an RPG feel to the game. (Ex: Conquer 3 territories, Have a 3:1 unit kill ratio...)
+Great voice acting, truly stellar.
+Inovative RTS mechanics, at least back when the game came out. Still, they stood and continue to stand the test of time.
+Excellent graphics that continue to impress to this day. Especially the unit models, which rival the tabletop game Dawn of War is based on.
+Like the Campaign, the Skirmish mode can offer a lot of variety, with good number of maps that can hold up to 8 players and the option to chose from multiple victory conditions (Ex: Destorying the enemy's HQ, Controlling certain points on the map for an amount of time, Assassinating the enemy commander...)
+Army painter; A tool you can use to create a unique look for your favorite race. You can even import custom pictures as your army's banner.
Cons:
-The Easy difficulty in the Campaign is too easy, making your units have five times the health of your opponent's...
-...while the other difficulties don't make the AI smarter, just decrease the difference in heatlh.
-The Skirmish  AI also leaves something to be desired, as it doesn't get smarter after the "Standard" difficulty and instead resorts to cheating.
-Despite the excellent models and detail, some of the textures can look a bit muddy.
-When moving in large groups, the unit pathing is horrible, with units moving backwards and vehicles getting stuck.
-Some balancing issues.
Overall rating: 8/10
Highly recommended to RTS players and Warhammer fans alike.

Whether you're a vicious button masher (like myself) or a combo-obsessive technician, you can get hours of entertainment out of this game as you wage your war against evil. I found that this game was easy to binge despite its simplicity.
So, we've got a visually pretty game with a fun little combat system, right? Well, in terms of criticism, I can only really levy any on a single element: the story. The story itself, where you play as the mysterious warrior protagonist Dust, is a pretty straightforward affair. You attempt, with the help of the mystical Blade of Ahrah and its dimunitive guardian Fidget, to recover Dust's identity while helping to defeat an evil that has plagued the land of Falana for years. The dialogue and banter between Dust and Fidget can be kind of fun at times, but the dialogue in general can be very wooden at times, especially during the game's climatic ending. The story is simple (To be fair, this was a game built for the XBox Live Arcade) but, while easy to follow, it definitely leaves you wanting a little more in a bad way. While the game touches on Christian and Taoist themes (Shout out to my friend Olse for pointing this out to me initially), it definitely comes off a little more ham-handed than one might expect. The voice acting is roughly above-average, as it shines in some areas (particularly some of the banter between Dust and Fidget), while sagging in others.
All in all, for spending $4, DAET was a fantastically fun Action-RPG romp with gorgeous visuals. Its standard price is a little steep in terms of game length and replayability, but not so much that I wont recommend it. This is a game that I really suggest you buy and try.
(As an additional note, I gather than Humble Hearts, the game's developer, is a one man operation. If you take my recommendation and purchase it, know that you might be enabling another game like this!)

Sometimes, you just want to watch the world burn. And sometimes this feeling comes at a time that you are fascinated by the whole concept of neon-glow. DEFCON is an atmospheric/minimalistic approach to the time honored wargame genre. It does not exault in the slaughter of millions as so many games do. All it provides are the bare statistics of all those you killed at the push of a button, and a rather haunting soundtrack to give you the full understanding of what you have just done. Some games push realism in wargames through more and more complex and life-like gore, but as we all know, society is a master of desensitizing itself in the face of horror. Thus DEFCON proves that thought-provoking and yet satisfying gameplay CAN and does exist in the surreal sub-genre.

Would be buyers be warned that this game's art style and content matter may offend and/or repulse.  However, if, like myself, you could care less about or even like the above then you'd be silly not to check this out.  This game has amazing replayability courtesy of it's myriad of unique items, cornucopia of secrets, and randomized level layouts.  The game plays by moving and shooting with the arrow and WASD keys respectively (these can be flipped for personal preference).  You advance by clearing increasingly difficult floors (levels) while collecting items that can help or hinder you.  Although you can beat the game in under an hour there's much incentive to play it through over and over such as: new characters to unlock and use, alternate endings, and endless item combinations.  For what you're getting you really can't go wrong with the price.  If you like/don't mind the art and want a challenging, highly replayable game, then this game is a must.  The DLC only makes everything better.  I do recommend playing the core game for a while first before downloading the DLC as it does add quite a bit more difficulty to the game.

There is a slight undercurrent which, when viewed from the right angle and without the context of the final game could be mistaken for riské irony. For example the female love interest and primary plot thread called "Goal". Oh yes ha, I see what you did there. Very good.
The second game suffers primarily from much poorer puzzles. A spattering of comedy accents which again, from an optimistic point of view, are treading the line but in good humour.
Then we get to part 3, which features a heavily implied paedophile trying to lure children into his caravan, and selling a black woman to be a monkey for an organ grinder. No, really. That one screen (They're both on the same one) puts the entire trilogy in a completely different light and will leave you very uncomfortable for the (far too long) remainder. If you can stomach continuing at all.

Let's start at the beginning, 'Deponia: The Complete Journey' is a click-and-point adventure with alot of minigames in between. The complete journey is a combined trilogy of 'Deponia', 'Chaos on Deponia' and 'Goodbye Deponia' in which you follow Rufus, our brave hero on his quest to save the world.
Even though this is a really great game for a wide ranged audience be aware of the insane difficulty (if you don't want to search hours for a missed clue or impossible to crack minigame, I recommend using a walkthrough from time to time).
Is it worth buying if you already have one or two of the deponia games? One word - YES! I already had the first part of the trilogy and there is one big difference between the individual games and The Complete Journey: Developers commentary. You might ask; Why would this make a big difference? Well first of all, the commentary is written by the creative director of Daedalic Entertainment Jan Müller-Michaelis better know as 'Poki'. Who gives the player not only a look behind the screens, but also hilarious facts and discussions between himself, other developers or characters of the game. Which all adds up quite a few hours to the playtime. Believe me after listening to him for a while, you would want to learn German to play the game in the original language.
Even though I could continue to ramble onwards about the positive sides of this game, let's switch to it's negative points. Let me first start with saying that during my Journey through Deponia, I encountered a fair amount of bugs. Most of them small and only ennoying, there was also one big game breaking bug. But don't be afraid future inhabitants of Deponia, most of the bugs have already been squashed by regular patches.
Conclusion: This is one of those games that after finishing it, you would want to forget everything about it, just so that you could play it again with the same anticipation as the first time. Definitely a recommendation!

One caveat before I begin my review: I got this game for roughly $4 through the Humble Store, so some of my opinion is emotionally affected by the price point. Now, onto the rest of the review!
I've played a lot of 2D side-scrolling action games with RPG elements at this point, but "Dust: An Elysian Tail" stands out at first because of the game's impressive artwork. The backgrounds are splendidly rendered, and the character design is neat and well done. In short, Dust is a very pretty game, and it rates well on eye-candy alone. However, what sucked me in the most about this game is its fun, simplistic combat system. Whether you're a vicious button masher (like myself) or a combo-obsessive technician, you can get hours of entertainment out of this game as you wage your war against evil. I found that this game was easy to binge despite its simplicity.
So, we've got a visually pretty game with a fun little combat system, right? Well, in terms of criticism, I can only really levy any on a single element: the story. The story itself, where you play as the mysterious warrior protagonist Dust, is a pretty straightforward affair. You attempt, with the help of the mystical Blade of Ahrah and its dimunitive guardian Fidget, to recover Dust's identity while helping to defeat an evil that has plagued the land of Falana for years. The dialogue and banter between Dust and Fidget can be kind of fun at times, but the dialogue in general can be very wooden at times, especially during the game's climatic ending. The story is simple (To be fair, this was a game built for the XBox Live Arcade) but, while easy to follow, it definitely leaves you wanting a little more in a bad way. While the game touches on Christian and Taoist themes (Shout out to my friend Olse for pointing this out to me initially), it definitely comes off a little more ham-handed than one might expect. The voice acting is roughly above-average, as it shines in some areas (particularly some of the banter between Dust and Fidget), while sagging in others.
All in all, for spending $4, DAET was a fantastically fun Action-RPG romp with gorgeous visuals. Its standard price is a little steep in terms of game length and replayability, but not so much that I wont recommend it. This is a game that I really suggest you buy and try.
(As an additional note, I gather than Humble Hearts, the game's developer, is a one man operation. If you take my recommendation and purchase it, know that you might be enabling another game like this!)

Although I recommend this game, it's not without it's flaws. Since playing Path Of Shadows I was eager to get into Aragami since the time it was released. It's nice to see that a lot of the elements of Path Of Shadows made their way into Aragami. Those are mostly the good things and are the main elements of the game - Leaping through shadows, distracting guards and being all-around stealthy. Unfortunately I feel like the design around those elements falls flat. The game starts off strong but starts using the artificial difficulty that designers tend to use when they are out of ideas. "Our player needs to stay in the shadows so this level will be 90% lit up!" "The player can get killed instantly by guards if spotted, so lets put a bunch of guards around all staring at each other!" That doesn't make a game challenging, that makes it tedious. Not that all of the levels are like that but there's a good amount of that stuff in there. Overall the game fills the void that has been lost by games like Tenchu (the obvious ninja/stealth choice) and I enjoyed it enough to get every achievement (which requires playing each stage AT LEAST twice - also a bit tedious) so don't think these complaints mean the game is bad. It's not.
