Summary: This game is amazing, beautiful, elegant; a definitive example of what a modern action platformer should aspire to. You'd have to be stupid not to buy this game
-----------
Dust has you predictably playing Dust, an amnesiac swordsman who struggles between his present and past personas. He embarks on his journey with a realist talking sword named Ahrah and an idealistic furry fairy, Fidget. The story is the standard hero arc, fighting mobs and defeating bosses to gain the power to defeat a large evil force. The plot is on rails, as a platformer should be. There is precisely one moral choice, between playing a prank on a pompous♥♥♥♥♥or not, and that's the extend of it. While sometimes predictable, the game manages to strike a few heart-strings, and the ending is very satisfying.
The action in Dust is flawless. Attacks and motion are very fluid and enjoyable. Enemies are varied archetypal fantasy mobs. Dust has attacks that will bodyslam enemies into the ground, shoot them into the air, and/or bring them back to earth. On easy or normal difficulties this boils down to button mashing, but you can turn it up to hardcore mode, where many enemies have attacks that take 1/2 or all of your health. At that point, you appreciate the skill based nature of combat. Mastering dodging and blocking are key. Gameplay is of the Metroid-vania type, but with not as much backtracking.
The art is the centerpiece of the game. It's simply amazingly well done, and no amount of praise can adequately express how beautiful the game is. Screenshots are an insult; you simply have to see the game in action. Everything is handled with care and precision, even backgrounds, mobs, and minor NPCs. Music and sound effects are similarly well done, even the voice acting. The only NPCs to not get a voice are the most minor of NPCs. Fidget's voice is of note as being particularly grating, however. Still, I can't say it doesn't fit the character, and I've certainly heard worse.
Oh, and 90% of the game was done by one guy. Like I said in the summary, you'd have to be stupid not to buy this game.

MUSIC: Ok, some decent original music as well as some Double Dragon 'classics'. Can switch between retro & modern style. The sound effects aren't perfect sometimes, seem to be pretty much the same as DD2.
GRAPHICS: Alright, like Double Dragon 2. (Maybe with some more colours here & there). Retro 8 bit style, nothing amazing.
PRESENTATION: Alright. There's a story with an intro, cutscenes & ending (though the story's not had much effort put into it), with 'nods' to past Double Dragon titles, which is nice to see. This game is obviously tailored to retro DD nostalgia fans, after all. The ending seems to end a little 'abruptly', though.
GAMEPLAY: Fine. The controls & hit detection seem fine. Some of the levels are kinda short, but there's a decent amount of levels. The levels seem to start easier & progressively get harder, as they should. There's no online play, which seems a shame. There is local 2 player. After you've beaten a level, you can then start the game from the last level you beat, with all your lives & continues replenished, which is a thoughtful touch. The moves at your disposal are the same as DD2, plus a couple more, which is good. It's good that air juggle combos are in this game, as that is something you can't do in any of the N.E.S. Double Dragons. Jumping is made easier as it's assigned to just 1 button, another plus. Special attacks from a crouched position are now easier to do-some may see that as a bad thing but I don't. (Especially when a lot of enemies are attacking you at the same time) The relative ease of which some enemies can knock you down combined with when you are being attacked by many enemies at once may seem 'cheap' to some, but the game isn't unbeatable.The game varies from being like a traditional scrolling beat 'em up where you can move up, down, left & right, to being 2D on a horizontally flat ground where you can walk just left & right, and there's also platforming sections dotted here & there to make fighting bad guys over & over less monotonous. A lot of people don't like the platforming sections in Double Dragon games & say they're very difficult, but in this game I think their difficulty is well balanced. When you beat story mode, it unlocks 'Tower Mode', a high score, level ascending challenge with wave after wave of bad guys. As you progress through the game, you can unlock a wide variety of characters to play as too, with varying move sets (some can run, some have a fast retreating dash, some have projectiles), which gives the game some replay value.
OVERALL: Although it seems that maybe this isn't a deadly serious legit chapter in the Double Dragon story, and it doesn't exactly push the envelope & revolutonise scrolling beat 'em ups (4 player, 2.5D, interspersing the play with mascot fighting or tournament fighting style gameplay are some possibilities), I can recommend this game to retro style beat 'em up fans, especially for the price I got it for (about £5.50), & I reckon it's better than Double Dragon 3.

Oh ♥♥♥♥ yes. You’d better believe I bought this game up as soon as I saw it on sale. I’m a longtime lover of stealth games like sly cooper and Dishonored. I don’t know how I missed seeing this, but, apparently, this game was released October 2016 and It never even once popped up on my radar. That’s quite unfortunate – and it’s about time to rectify this personal error.
Going in I wasn’t sure what to expect. Admittedly I was more than a little skeptical – and with good reason knowing the amount of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥we keep getting shoveled onto steam these days.
To start - there is a very stylized artistic feel present and it that feeds perfectly into the atmosphere. The somber shadow hugging gameplay gave me the feel that I truly was an elite spirit assassin- and had complete control over the shadows.
There is no traditional combat in this game- for say. Instead the entire game relies upon sneaking around and assassinating your foes. The way you do so ranges from stealthidly shadow stepping and slicing a neck to bumb rush stab or be stabbed action. One hit will kill – and If you’re as impatient as me you will die a lot! My impulsiveness  lead to some thrilling action sequences – but more often than not ended up with me getting discovered and murdered. This is a game of patience and timing.
The levels are generously laid out and provide a semi-linier way to get from point a to point b. I found myself impressed on more than one occasion at how beautiful and well thought out each map was – despite there being a very noticeable reuse of models. In fact this game reuses a lot of things… There’s not much enemy verity... there’s only two enemies you’ll be facing throughout the game – and I don’t only mean that there’s only two different types of enemies – I quite literally mean there’s only two different enemy models with about 3 different haircuts.
This game borrows a few concepts from Dishonored – one of which is that you can chose to either complete the obje7ctive passively or through blood soaking funtime. I of course went for the blood and enjoyed every drenching minute of it.
The killing animations are a tinyyyyy bit repetitive, but, along with some pretty entertaining abilities – it flows together quite well into a neat little dance of death. I had a blast seeing what kind of combinations I could string together whilst chopping my way through each level.
Ok, let’s talk abilities - Some of the more enjoyable ones you can use include, shadow kuni, shadow clone jitsu, black holes, and summoning a shadow beast to consume your foe – this is by far the coolest.
As usual in my reviews, I like to take a few seconds to share some of the in game soundtrack with you. Here you are:
Length wise the game is thirteen chapters long. I should point out though that a few of these chapters are strictly boss fights. With the lack of the traditional combat system the boss fights are remarkably well put together and can be pretty ♥♥♥♥ing challenging.
Surprisingly- there is a co-op mode available that allows you and a friend to hop into a map together. Unfortunately though, on pc there is a lack of active game lobbies – so you’d have to rely on hosting firsthand or attempt to seek out people elsewhere.
Looking at endgame there are a few things to do. You can play through the story again and find any skill points you missed or attempt to complete things in a different way. There’s skins to collect and end level rankings – so you 100% completion nuts would have plenty to reach for. Also, there’s a pretty solid map editor that gives you the complete control to build whatever you like.
Without giving away any spoilers - the story is one of the strongest parts to this game. You are a vengeful spirit, or aragami. And your entire purpose is to enact your wrath on the Kaiho – also known as the light.
I haven’t had an attachment to a story as strong as this in a long time. While you progress, you get bits and pieces of a fragmented story and by the end you’re fitting it all back like a puzzle that seamlessly comes together.
Time for my conclusion, thankfully this game is no steamy turd. It defiantly stands out and it DEFINATLY left a lasting impression on me. If nothing else I’d seriously recommend you at least check out a let’s play and experience the story.
Finally - If I was to rate this games overall playtime for an average person I’d say you could get about a solid 12 hours. That’s counting two play throughs, some time messing around in co-op, and the map editor.

Bejewel meets, Indiana Jones meets, RPG in this odd mix. Fight your way through hordes of monsters, while using your puzzle skill to kill them off. Who knew one day that puzzles would be the bane of dragons.
Game play: 7
The game play is solid. You start off in a stone room with broken down doors everywhere, that leads into other rooms. With these rooms, you are able to increase your static, from better armor, to better spells, to better score multipliers, to more damage. To be able to unlock each door you must run the ongoing dungeon to earn experience to gain levels and to gain gold. While running the dungeon you are given a Bejewel style puzzle game. On the top of the screen you have the character running, He’ll run into monsters, doors, and chest. That you need to match up the squares to progress further into the dungeon. You are given a time limit. You will slowly be pushed backwards to the left edge of the screen. The faster you kill monsters or unlock things the closer you get to the right side of the screen. Once you pass a certain threshold on the screen you will gain a bonus to your score as long as you keep moving ahead. Each Square has an icon that you need to match up to be able to kill monsters or unlock chest or doors. Each icon has special ability to help you progress deeper. The icons you see are, Wood, Boulder, Wand, Sword, backpack, key and shield. Wood and boulder give you materials to use to build the rooms you see at the start. Wand and sword are attacks depending on the monster they can be either be weaker or stronger vs the type you are using. The backpack can give you items to use in your inventory on the right side of the screen. The key is used to open chest and doors, the shield gives you better armor to take hits better.
On the side, you have you’re inventory where you get power ups, From faster moment, to magic attacks, to keys and weapons. They can be very useful. After you die you are able to use the gold and materials you gained from the previous run to build the rooms, or you may hold on to them until next time. The overall object of the game is to get your score to 10,000,000 (Ten million). To be able to escape.
Story: 2
There isn’t really a story going on here. You are a guy who looks like Indiana Jones who has become trapped in this dungeon that is now trying to escape. Having to fight zombies, demons, dragons and such. That’s pretty much it. This game doesn’t really need much of a story to really enjoy it.
Graphics: 6
This game takes on the retro 8-bit style. Like many other indie games that uses 8-bit. They are pretty simple as it is. The mix of colors being used range from grays, to lighter colors like reds and blues. It’s a simple pallet of colors over all. The graphics don’t pop out as anything to flashy to it. they are Kinda of flat graphics. In its own right the graphics are decent.
Music: 5
Like the graphics it takes on an 8-bit sound track. The music is decent sounding but not amazing but yet not horrible either. It does keep in decent pace with the game play. Other than that there isn’t really much else to the music.
Final Though:
Overall I enjoyed this game a lot. It was fun, and challenging. I found the game play being the best part of this game. However this game kinda of lacks any real re playability. It’s a game that is great for a one time play and not touch it for a while. This game doesn’t stand out to other puzzle games. However the unique thing about this game is the RPG element which gives it a nice touch. Having the Bejewel style puzzle being what you use to fight monsters and unlock stuff with does give this game the bit of edge it needs to push it higher than your average puzzle game. With the mix of gaining gold and materials and being able leveling up to unlock more powers to make you stronger does make this game fun.
If you are a puzzle person or someone who simply loves Bejewel like myself you may want to try this game out. If anything this game is cheap so for a few bucks you can’t go wrong with this game.
Final Score: 6

Deponia is one of the best point'n'clicks I have played in a long time. Its puzzles are reminiscent of the old Monkey Island games, and the humour is without a doubt one of the best of the past 10 years. You play the anti-hero Rufus. As the reviews and intro state, Rufus is not a pleasant man. He's annoying, mean, and absolutely self-centered. The game made me wonder what was wrong with the protagonist several times at the start of the game. He sells women into slavery and feeds children to monsters. And, in spite of all this, he grows on you. He's human. He does horrible things but you still want him to succeed in his plans. Rufus is brilliant, and he's utterly fascinating.
Get this game if you want an interesting protagonist. He won't be your immediate hero. He won't be the man you hope to be, or the man you want your daughter to marry. He's definitely not the man you hope to snag in a relationship. But he will be interesting from start to finish. And that's sorely lacking from games nowadays. So, buy this game and support these makers. You'll be laughing from start to finish.

It's a point-and click adventure game from Germany, in the grand tradition of Space Quest and Leisure Suit Larry. The interface is crisp, and the puzzles are generally variations of "talk to this guy, use this thing, combine these objects." That having been said, it's got a weird sense of humor that reminds me of the old school Sierra adventures, complete with a dude with a heavy German accent playing a folk song introduction to each chapter.
WARNING: Some of the humor, especially in the middle and third chapter, can get rather. . . "Dead Baby" ish. The only ones that really upset me in the end are a series of horrible things you end up doing to people in the third game in order to pursue a quest that turns out to have been pointless the entire ttime. (And then there were the baby dolphins. :( ) Plus a few moments of grossout humor here and there, mostly based around the fact that the game is set on a garbage planet with all that entails.
The main character is kind of a jerk who is saved from being an outright antihero simply because there are a few lines that he won't cross. He spends most of his time being a self-centered jerk who mooches off of other people, steals everything that isn't nailed down, and screws people over left and right in pursuit of his own goal and Goal. So in other words, he's an adventure game hero.
Gameplay wise, there are a few puzzles which are completely incomprehensible without a walkthrough or guide. Par for the course for an adventure game, of course, but after playing a few Telltale Games adventures, the older model of "point and click trial and error" gameplay feels a bit dated. One Godsend: the more irritating puzzles include a "skip" option that will allow you to pass the puzzle without completing it, if you get frustrated and just want to go on to the next part of the plot.
One huge pet peeve: "F5 IS QUICK SAVE. F9 IS QUICK LOAD." This is the mantra that most game makers use. This is because it means that there is a minimum chance of accidentally bumping the other button and either saving over your game when you didn't mean to, or quick loading when you didn't want to. Deponia uses "F9 FOR QUICK SAVE, F10 FOR QUICK LOAD." This cost me a bunch of progress at one point when I accidentally bumped the F10 key when I realized I'd gone a while without saving and tried to quick-save.
All in all, I enjoyed it, I was glad I played it. Supposedly there's a New Game Plus mode, and some collectables you can pick up, but I don't think I have the desire to revisit this game any time soon: nothing against it in general, just that linear adventure games tend not to be as fun the second time around.
Pick it up on sale.

It's a simple, fast-paced match 3 game where you make matches based on the event presented to you. i.e. if your character comes to a chest, you match key icons to unlock it and move on. The longer you stand behind an obstacle without clearing it, you are pushed back until you eventually 'lose'.
While playing you can match resource tiles which allow you to upgrade things on your ship, which pretty much just increases your damage, or defense, or something else that will allow you to travel further next time you adventure.
The main problem with the game is that there is an artificial level of difficulty. You adventure for a certain amount of time, then you will inevitably reach a monster much harder than the previous ones which acts as a barrier to your progress until you unlock enough upgrades to move on. In other words, it doesn't really matter how well you play the game, you won't be able to go as far as you 'can'.
Nevertheless I still kept coming to play it just because the main part of the game is very addictive.
This game reminds me of classic Lucas Arts games in a very positive way.

A fun mix of Rhythm with an otherwise mediocre dungeon crawler. In Crypt of the NecroDancer, every action you make must be on beat with a count in the music; and not just walking and attacking. Literally EVERY ACTION. this includes reloading ranged items, using items, eating food, switching holstered weapons, and digging through walls. The game, which otherwise wouldn't be that difficult forces things to move forward, however, as missing a beat means everything else in the dungeon but you moves, and you lose a gold multiplier that increases as you kill enemies and remain in step with the beat. This forces you to think on your feet and react very quickly to some situations, I can't tell you how many daily hardcore dungeon seed runs have ended because I jumped in front of a black skeleton that was either behind a dirt block I dug out, behind a door I opened, or around a corner and I was so focussed on keeping in step, that I jumped right into its attack. It's definately not an easy game, even with a good sense of rhythm. There are a few rogue-like elements to the game, but I hesitate to call this a "rogue-like" When you die, you lose most of your items, but that's about as much punishment as the game gives you. Heck, minecraft does the same thing when you die in normal mode, but we don't call minecraft a rogue-like, do we? Sure you have to start the level over, but when you unlock the next dungeon in the game, you start from floor one of that dungeon, not floor one of the first dungeon. Many other games have done this as well, but those games aren't considered "rogue-like" because you never start from the very begining unless you want to. There's a more rogue-like hardcore mode, that makes you play without any of the permanent upgrades you can buy, but its overshadowed by the "normal" gameplay of continuing from the previous dungeon you left off at. Not to mention I'm not even sure if you can beat any more dungeons other than the first in hardcore mode. I have yet to beat the first dungeon on hardcore, but if it is anything like the "dancepadpad" mode (which spawns less enemies and starts you off with a few spells) to make it hilariously easy in case you're playing on a USB DDR pad (Which seriously, even if you are, this mode is pathetic, play the main mode) you can't play past the first dungeon in that mode. There are only a few bosses of which you will randomly fight one at the end of a dungeon (assuming there is an exception at the end of the final dungeon which I have yet to beat where you fight the necrodancer himself). And how could I forget to mention, custom music is a thing. Needless to say, this is pretty awesome, and it actually works with most songs! There are a few I have found that the beat sensor does not work with (however messing around with the audio and video latency options can fix most of them if you're willing to put a little effort into it, and for the songs this still won't fix, there's a youtube video on how to go into the custom song's data and change the tempo of your uploaded song manually to synchronize with how it should be in game). [and on a sidenote of the custom music, boy am I glad to have gotten the bonus content for electronic superjoy, which included the soundtrack].
Another feature of the game is the inclusion of seperate character classes. As a tip from a player, do not use them. The default character is the best to play the game with. The other two classes you can choose are a bard, which does not have to move to the beat, defeating the purpouse of the game entirely, and simply making it a sub-par, very short dungeon crawler (if you're going to use the bard, just play Cardinal Quest 2 for free on Kongregate, its level design is much better and it has a greater varriation of characters and abilities, but the addition of the whole rhythm-base element to this game still makes it quite a bit more fun than Cardinal Quest). The other class you can play as is a monk, which cannot pick up gold (seriously, it kills him), but gets one free item whenever he visits a shop. Again, this is not a good choice, as there is almost always more than enough gold to get at least one item in every shop, and almost every shop after the first you can completely buy out if you want because there are a LOT of enemies to farm. So in the long run, the Monk's ability limits your movement, as every enemy drops gold when its killed, meaning you can't move on spaces where you killed enemies, and it makes you significantly worse off in terms of equipment too.
A lot of these complaints could be argued against by saying "This game is early access, deal with it" and while that may be true, these flaws exist all the same, and the purpose of reviews are so that you, the potential buyer, will know EXACTLY what you are getting.
When it comes down to it, however, all these complaints are minor, and Crypt of the NecroDancer remains a solid game! (I DID say it was better than Cardnial Quest after all) and while it may be a bit pricey to pay $15 for the game in its current state, I believe it will still be worth the money to most people.
also... playing a dungeon crawler with a freaking DDR pad!!!! What more could you want?!?!?!

Are there bots with limitless chips that make frivolous bets to drain the chips you paid real money for?  I can't say, but there are an awful lot of people named "PlayerXXXXXX," where those x's denote some random number generated by a machine.
What I CAN tell you is that nearly without fail, every time you go all-in the computer will deal itself just the exact cards it needed to win.  Whereas if you should decide to gamble all of a sudden the laws of probability decide to work just fine--don't expect any help from the River card.  This DOES happen in real poker, but it SHOULDN'T happen with you getting the shaft quite so often.  I've noticed that luck runs out right around 70,000 chips.
The spinners are FAKE.  The spinner will slow down on some really big numbers before stopping on a very, very small one.  They will brag about the Jackpot being anywhere from 2 to 1000 times the buy in.  Expect two.  Almost every time.  Never 1000, and anything between 2 and 1000 hardly ever comes up.  I got a 6 once.
The fake spinner issue also extends to the wheel that gives random amounts of chips, just so you don't ragequit every time the game cheats you out of your chips.  Every time, the wheel will dance around some large numbers to get your hopes up before settling on 1500 - 2500, which is chump change in this game's world.  The Jackpot spin is also a fake spinner, except this time it's purple.  It will double your next-to-nothing jackpot, netting you about next-to-nothing.
Just give them $15 for Governor of Poker 2.  Remember when you could just buy a whole game?  Plus, you can wail on the sleep button (reputation means nothing) until you have enough cash to enter a game.  Instead of, you know, waiting 4 hours for the game to give you enough chips to play for ten minutes.
OR
It's a pretty sweet personal poker engine.  Invite your friends to a private table and play nice.

When it comes to Early Access games, it can be hit or miss, most are bare bones and can be left unfinished, but others can be real gems that show the quality and talent indie games are known for, this is one of them, a game that already feels complete and plays very well, but hats off to the developers who wish to improve this game more to the best that it can be.
High Points:  The controls are tight and responsive. The level design is always different, and yet the levels overall are kept rather short and rather straightforward, which is a big plus for these kinds of games. The variety of items and unlockables to get help encourage you to continue playing over and over again. The music, no doubt the highlight of the game, the music is addicting, enjoyable and will get stuck in your head for hours.
Critique: As it stands at the moment, the game is pretty solid, but there is always room for improvment.
1. More variety in items - If there is one thing Binding of Isaac has shown, is that with a large variety of items that all work differently, it helps make every playthrough different, with different items everytime, so it'd be nice to have something new other then rings, boots and such.
2. Floor gimmicks - It'd be interesting if on all floors of other then the boss floor, there was a chance of a gimmick happening that can change the whole experience, like being chased by an invincible enemy, having no map to use, line of sight restricted, or even having a larger level the normal.
3. More traps - I think some more traps might be needed to spice up the gameplay, like spin tiles to mess up the controls, moving traps that follow a set path, and perhaps traps that trigger if you move into their line of sight.
Overall: I feel overall this game is looking really good, and I know when it finally comes out, it'll be a big hit.

Everything you really need to know is above this line.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
My only grievance with this game is where it tries to compete directly with overwatch. It plays entirely different despite both being TF2 clones, and doesn't need to be anything else. Namely, the cosmetic system. Featuring color swaps, emotes, and sprays, it's just trash, a sorry mock-up of OW's shop, and I've completely ignored it for the most part. It's just unnecessary to the game.
The card system, however, (which is the main reason you'll want to open loot chests), is phenomenal. It allows you to customize just what benefits you get from your character and drastically impacts exactly what your abilities do for you. You can make the champion feel completely different just by switching what card loadout you use, and it makes it so easy to personalize a character to do exactly what you need. I really love this system, and it works beautifully.
Almost every character is a shooter of some kind, with no lame-duck last resort weapons. Enemies are also easy to hit, meaning positioning and tactics will determine the fight more than bunny-hopping and twitch-fire FPS skill.
Healers in this game function more like off-tank dps and hit hard as hell, though less reliably than Damage champions, and they can usually heal themselves and stay in the fight to keep hitting. This is a far cry from the dedicated supports of TF2/OW, and with all players getting an auto-heal when out of combat for a while, this kind of dedicated healer isn't necessary (and the same for health pickups, thankfully absent).
Balance wise, I only have an issue with one or perhaps two characters being too powerful, and only a handful of characters seem to be nerfed (I'm looking at you, Lex). The bottom line is, I find myself less frustrated when a specific character kills me; I'm not dying repeatedly to the same character all the time across every match.
If you've made it this far, let me remind you that this game is free. There's no reason not to just try it and figure out for yourself whether it's worth your time.

I bought this game because the premise seemed neat, it looked cute, and the music was enchanting. It was on sale, and I got more than my money's worth.
Where to start? There's a lot of good stuff. I'm not normally a fan of puzzles, but the puzzle mechanics in Mages aren't pushed in your face (Except in the final boss battle, in which it is done BEAUTIFULLY), and they're flexible. Don't have the prerequisite runes for a challenge? If they're behavior runes, maybe you can finagle ones you already have to work for it. Things aren't set in stone, and if you're creative enough, and lucky enough, you can get ahead of the game.
That leads right into runes and spells. Like it says on the tin, you're a Mage. In most games that means you get a few spells that you can customize with a talent or two, making them slightly different. In Mages you have four "behaviours" of spells, each of which determines a lot about the spell - but not nearly everything. Immedi hits things in melee range, right when you use it. Igni creates an orb of its element. Creo creates a full elemental effect. And Ego creates a defensive effect based on its configuration and element.
Runes change how your spells act, and they influence each other as much as your spells. For instance, to start with, Igni creates an immobile, hovering orb of its element (Fire, to start with) that simply sits in place. Not incredibly useful unless you time it right. Combine it with a Homing rune, and you have a mine that seeks out a target when it gets close. Combine those with Move, and you have an enemy-seeking fireball. However, runes have different effects based on the spell they're affecting. For instance, if you combine Ego with a Homing rune, it will pull enemies and objects towards you like a magnet. And then there's combining spells, and...I could go on for a hot minute. Point is, it's fun to see what you can do.
The difficulty scales up pretty quickly, at least for me, which was interesting. It definitely puts pressure on you to stop messing around with funny spells and find ones that work at least reasonably well. Though that isn't to say your "silly" spells aren't useful. Sometimes what you REALLY need is that defunct "bouncing betty" spell you were trying to make work and just left in your spell list.
As well, I've found that there is no one "God spell" or somesuch that will solve EVERY problem. Someone will be immune, or it won't target properly, or it uses too much mana, or something else I can't think of on the spot. Point is, you have to be flexible.
The story is really great. Cute, without being too cheesy or being pointless. I constantly felt as if I had a set goal in mind, even during sidequests. Props.
Probably the only real downside I've found is that the game is SHORT. Not abysmally so, but it's really not long. The story, at least. I've still got a good chunk of game left to explore right now.
It also feels like it might be more intuitive to play it on a controller, but I also feel more comfortable on a keyboard. I don't think it has a real effect on my enjoyment of the game.
I keep thinking that a good way to describe it might be like this: Legend of Zelda, without Link, and Zelda is the hero.
Also: Read the Wanted signs.

Don't get the meager hours I have on steam get to you, I've played the everloving sh*t out of dark crusade since I was like 12 (probs about 8yrs ago ~ 2007) and I can't play any other RTS, nothing compares in my opinion.
It's simple gameplay wise in standard battles (i.e.- destoy all HQs, capture relics/points) but there's depth in each race which can aid in battle and equally be countered by enemies with the right units (e.g.- infiltration units can only be detected by certain enemy units differing between race). Survival with some races at higher difficulty, especially with Imp guard requires utilising the terrain to your advantage, the large units will be mowed down quick by say Necron or Space Marines but in heavy cover they rek everything.
You gain power and resources from generators/slag deposits and from capturing points, building good defenses at these can really turn the tide if you're outnumbered, if you can hide a second HQ it'll give you a good chance at surviving a full onslaught if need be (won't be necessary in single player unless crazy difficulty and high level land. Each race of course has different buildings and path progressions, you upgrade HQs to get more units/capacity, the necrons can upgrade it so it can move which is neato.
When eliminating a race from the game missions get a lot more interesting, for example Chaos marines have a blood purge which will kill all in a certain area every 80s, which will either require fast units to move across quickly to halt the purge allowing vehicles/slow units through. Again this can be counteracted with certain portaling races like the Eldar but I ♥♥♥♥ing hate the Eldar they suck balls. Anyway most elimination missions are challenging, long and fun as hell.
Graphics- I mean it came out like 10yrs ago, I play it on my laptop with everything jacked up (Lenovo flex pro 2) but as long as you have a screen and a potato it should run at 60fps. Saying that the death splatters are pretty gruesome and generally it still looks pretty cool. You can also customise the look of races, which can be handy if you're like me and blind as f*ck, it's pretty easy to miss smaller units when everythings green but make them bright pink with blue trim and they look fabulous.
Sound- Decent, cutscene stuff sounds a bit Matt Damon and the Imperial Guard's commandant voice actor must be in league with Tommy Wiseau but shooty stuff sounds fine, explosions a bit weird but again >2006
Overall: just buy it, the second DoW takes out all the buildy stuff which some like but I hate, so if you're more into just unit tictacs over building 'management' get the second as well but I'd say this is the most bang for your buck RTS you can get, I've played it more than the original DoW

TL;DR: Cute game with a subpar story, some UI issues, but a fun experience at a good length. 7/10
Overall, I liked Mages of Mystralia and thought it was worth the time. I kickstarted it, for your information.
Pros:
- The meat of the game is in the magic creation and the battling. Overall, the battles are pretty good, not great, but by the end of the game you have enough spell capabilities that you can really have some explosive fun. The enemies ramp up in difficulty with a not-too-crazy curve, and it wasn't too hard to keep up, but still felt challenging. The last boss wasn't really "final-boss difficult", but other than that the game's battles presented a good challenge.
- The spellcrafting, while probably not as deep as the creators pretend, is still a lot of fun to build and explore with. I did find that I just relied on four or five powerful spells for most of the game, but it was still fun to create new spells to solve puzzles and earn secrets.
- The art was cute. Not ground-breaking, but cute and it worked for the style of game. The world building was sufficiently interesting and the characters were entertaining enough.
- The game was the perfect length, in my opinion. I always felt forward momentum, and the difficulty curve matched well.
- I enjoyed the constellations puzzles.
Neutrals:
- The story was engaging enough to keep me a *little* interested but it really could have been significantly more interesting. They seem to set up sequels to this game, but the story wasn't nearly deep enough to warrant any sort of multi-part series.
- The items, wands, and side quests were somewhat lacking, but I never felt a huge need to go get more. The game could have used some healing items (I never found any).
Cons:
- The UI lacked a lot of feedback, especially in the spell crafting. Descriptions of what things were (like when selecting elements) was sorely lacking and made the learning curve steeper than it should have been.
- What the hell is there to use money on? I had 999 currency the entire game, it seemed, never finding anything to spend it on.
- The "homing" attribute of spells didn't work as expected like half the time, which really hurt during battle sometimes.
- The camera angles had some issues.
Overall, solid, cutesy, not-overly-long puzzle and action game. Recommended for fans of the genre looking for some mostly-intuitive spellcrafting.

This is probably the best asymmetric RTS/FPS hybrid of all time, but there really aren’t that many of them so that really isn’t huge deal. More importantly, this is probably one of the best games of all time as it contains a mixture of unique gameplay elements that no other games has. It definitely is my favourite game which actually sounds a bit strange to me when I think about it.
I find that strange because I never really enjoyed FPS games a great deal. Prior to NS2 I played mostly strategy titles (RTS and turn based), and I believe what hooked me into this game was the gameplay elements of deep strategy, blended in with teamwork and individual skill. All these aspects of the game are so important that it is really not clear which one of them is more important in this game.
This game is niche title, with an active (albeit small) community where you really shouldn’t have any trouble finding a game. If you are worried that you “missed the boat” I don’t think you have anything to worry about if you are interested in this game. I don’t think it is likely the game will outright “die” as it fills a gameplay niche that is very difficult to get right like NS2 has. For the best experience find a server/community you like, help them seed a their server and you’ll have fun. The game isn’t particularly expensive and even goes down to 5$ at steam sales.
Most people who have an issue with the game don’t really have huge issues with the game itself but with their perceptions of the community and health of the game (see discussions). However, despite these issues the game is still very much supported by the developers and has a dedicated community so their should be no reason why you shouldn’t give the game a shot if you are at all interested in the game. The servers/communities are fairly diverse and I suggest you look into all the different communities (make sure to also look in the arcade tab in the server browser) to find one that suits you before you make any judgements as a whole.
Edit: Anyone claiming this game is full of hackers is full of it. I've ran into maybe 1 or 2 people I was fairly sure were hacking in my >2000 hours of NS2. NS2 is under VAC protection and hacking for this game is rare. Take anyone with <100 hours who claims they've seen a hacker without sufficent proof with a grain of salt. Honestly they likely ran into people who are just likely much better than them, and their egos couldn't take it.
This is a RTS/FPS hybrid so it can be difficult to describe what the gameplay actually feels like in a short summary.
The game can be very fast paced, requiring good twitch reaction skills to be good in traditional combat situations. Thus, it might feel like the game is initially just like any other FPS where for the most part it seems like winning is about out-killing your opponents. However, the goal in the game is actually to economically starve  your opponents (via territory/map control) and to ultimately kill their last command structure. Everything else in the game emerges from that. This means there are other game elements unexpectedly sprinkled in, like stealth elements, tactical fake-outs, secret backdoor rushes, baiting, distractions, and sometimes killing yourself intentionally (to respawn at base or to kill a critical structure). Thus, having a keen strategic mind to spot and exploit opportunity, even if you aren’t a commander, is an asset in this game.
If you want to try commanding it cannot be understated how important the role is, but not in the way you might think. Commanding can be fast paced, like a game of starcraft, but feels different from a traditional RTS as you cannot directly control your core “units”. To win, team cooperation is the most important thing. Each core “unit” has a mind of their own and if you do anything to demoralize them by doing things they don’t understand or don’t commonly see when playing other games this can basically make your time commanding unbearable. To mitigate this, you need communication (to explain what you are trying if someone questions you), and need to show that you have an understanding how the game works (requires watching games/commanders or playing on the field a while).
There is a lot of talk about how hard the game is as relatively high skill veterans make up a large portion of the persistent player base. If you play past the rookie stage you will play against 1 or 2 these guys and I’d imagine it can feel like you can’t do anything against these guys. I’m probably almost one of them at this point, but I do remember a time when I wasn’t, and a key thing to remember is that this game is actually a strategy game and getting kills on your opponents doesn’t matter as much as you might think.
For instance, when I know I can’t out-skill/kill the other team, I instead focus on thinking “what is the most productive thing I can do instead”. In NS2 you don’t need to kill the enemy team’s players to win, so worrying about your KDR is mostly not productive. As an alien, if you can’t win straight up fights realize that you don’t even need to always fight. Get past the enemy lines and hit unprotected resource nodes (you can crawl on walls silently and vents exist for a reason). For new players who find the combat difficult, just being aware of what is happening around the map (flashing red things) can be much more of an asset then being able to obtain a high KDR.
You will get better at the game, in the meantime, try to compensate in other ways. There are some skill limit servers (e.g. Dungeon Gaming <1800 hive) that you could try to seed to minimize your exposure to high skilled players. Finally, I almost feel bad saying this because it is open to abuse, but in the worst case scenario if you don’t feel ready for non-rookie servers and your time is up - Make a family sharing account and play on that to get rookie status again if you need it. Remember, rookie servers are for people learning the game, please don’t abuse it. Overall, after you get the basics from a few rounds on rookie servers and the tutorials I strongly encourage learning the game in depth in non-rookie servers to learn the game faster.

Excellent blend of FPS and non-symmetric RTS game, doing justice to the legendary natural selection 1 for half-life (1). Teamwork is very important and the game succesfully promotes this teamwork, so everyone can do his part and naturally will tend to do so. A failure of teamwork will visibly affect the game and immediately encourage players to cooperate in new strategies. The aliens and marines play very differently and have completely different tech trees and require different strategies. The graphics are amazing for this game's age, and the engine runs incredibly well (in alpha, it had some performance issues which are entirely resolved afaik). Lag is not much of an issue as opposed to for example csgo, the engine handles it very well. The game has quite a steep learning curve, but as the basic unit of each team you can definitely start doing your part and learn by following orders and watching others. Recently some very good tutorials were added also for the commander role. 10,000,000 is a game that took me about five hours to beat.  I spent $1.25 on it a year ago and just finished it.
I bought it expecting something akin to Puzzle Quest.  What I got was a bit different.  Sure, you have the same "match 3 tiles, get an effect" scheme, but the pace is quite frantic.  There's no story at all--you're some guy in a hat who wakes up in a run-down castle, you repair the rooms to the castle in order to power up your gear, and you run the dungeon hoping to get the required 10,000,000 points to win the game.  That's honestly it.
Gameplay's a little different from what you've come to expect from the tired-and-true match-3 formula.  Instead of swapping pieces around, you slide entire rows and columns to make your matches.  Pieces wrap around the other side of the field, and new pieces fall in when you make matches.  Attack monsters by matching swords and wands, give yourself a damage buffer by matching shields, match keys to open chests and locked doors, and match backpacks to give yourself a chance at getting an item to use.  Match wood and stone to give you resources to upgrade and repair the rooms in your home.  Get gold from objectives and chests to upgrade your gear, get EXP from monsters to spend on giving yourself permanent boosts.
The game is also timed, through keeping your little guy from reaching the left side of the screen either by damage taken or taking too long to clear the current obstacle.  Lose, and you're given a report on your run's score as well as the objectives you completed, if any.  The game tracks your progress through ranks and objectives for those ranks.  You have missions like "have an enemy die to poison damage" or "match five panels at once three times in a single run" among others.  Completing these missions gives you wood, stones, gold, and/or EXP, on top of unlocking new missions, of which you can only have three active at a time.  The final mission in each rank is to get a set score, and from there your rank (and difficulty) increase, but so do the score multiplier and the resource multiplier.
It's somewhat of a short game despite the high asking score to win.  I haven't 100%ed the game, but a couple more hours (or more if I do really badly) will see my get the rest of the achievements I missed, and there's not a lot of replay value since you only have one save file and the only thing that can go differently is how much money you put into upgrades.  Everything else is up to how merciful or cruel the game is regarding the board setup, but also how attentive you are with seeing potential matches and not panicking when you come across a boss creature during a particularly-good run.
For negatives, there's maybe a little bit of fake difficulty regarding how the game works with obstacles.  If you make a swords or wands match right before you stop to attack an enemy, the game won't register it.  Same with chests and keys.  You also can't make any matches while there's a chain going on, though that's never screwed me over.  There wasn't very much music, though that's up to the player if that's bad or not.  I didn't mind the pixel art, though I know it's dealbreaker for some people.  It's not terribly engaging, but this isn't a game that I'd sit and play for hours on end anyway.
TL;DR:  I enjoyed 10,000,000.  It's short, it's cheap, and you can probably get a few of hours of enjoyment/frustration out of it.  It's not really easy or hard, but it does require a keen eye and some patience since you will fail repeatedly on your way to the top score.  It's fun enough and it feels good to do really well, just the same as it gets disheartening to keep doing badly.  It's less planning and more quick-thinking action, so if you liked the timed modes of other match-3 games, this might be of some value to you.

Summary: This game is amazing, beautiful, elegant; a definitive example of what a modern action platformer should aspire to. You'd have to be stupid not to buy this game
-----------
Dust has you predictably playing Dust, an amnesiac swordsman who struggles between his present and past personas. He embarks on his journey with a realist talking sword named Ahrah and an idealistic furry fairy, Fidget. The story is the standard hero arc, fighting mobs and defeating bosses to gain the power to defeat a large evil force. The plot is on rails, as a platformer should be. There is precisely one moral choice, between playing a prank on a pompous♥♥♥♥♥or not, and that's the extend of it. While sometimes predictable, the game manages to strike a few heart-strings, and the ending is very satisfying.
The action in Dust is flawless. Attacks and motion are very fluid and enjoyable. Enemies are varied archetypal fantasy mobs. Dust has attacks that will bodyslam enemies into the ground, shoot them into the air, and/or bring them back to earth. On easy or normal difficulties this boils down to button mashing, but you can turn it up to hardcore mode, where many enemies have attacks that take 1/2 or all of your health. At that point, you appreciate the skill based nature of combat. Mastering dodging and blocking are key. Gameplay is of the Metroid-vania type, but with not as much backtracking.
The art is the centerpiece of the game. It's simply amazingly well done, and no amount of praise can adequately express how beautiful the game is. Screenshots are an insult; you simply have to see the game in action. Everything is handled with care and precision, even backgrounds, mobs, and minor NPCs. Music and sound effects are similarly well done, even the voice acting. The only NPCs to not get a voice are the most minor of NPCs. Fidget's voice is of note as being particularly grating, however. Still, I can't say it doesn't fit the character, and I've certainly heard worse.
Oh, and 90% of the game was done by one guy. Like I said in the summary, you'd have to be stupid not to buy this game.

When it comes to Early Access games, it can be hit or miss, most are bare bones and can be left unfinished, but others can be real gems that show the quality and talent indie games are known for, this is one of them, a game that already feels complete and plays very well, but hats off to the developers who wish to improve this game more to the best that it can be.
High Points:  The controls are tight and responsive. The level design is always different, and yet the levels overall are kept rather short and rather straightforward, which is a big plus for these kinds of games. The variety of items and unlockables to get help encourage you to continue playing over and over again. The music, no doubt the highlight of the game, the music is addicting, enjoyable and will get stuck in your head for hours.
Critique: As it stands at the moment, the game is pretty solid, but there is always room for improvment.
1. More variety in items - If there is one thing Binding of Isaac has shown, is that with a large variety of items that all work differently, it helps make every playthrough different, with different items everytime, so it'd be nice to have something new other then rings, boots and such.
2. Floor gimmicks - It'd be interesting if on all floors of other then the boss floor, there was a chance of a gimmick happening that can change the whole experience, like being chased by an invincible enemy, having no map to use, line of sight restricted, or even having a larger level the normal.
3. More traps - I think some more traps might be needed to spice up the gameplay, like spin tiles to mess up the controls, moving traps that follow a set path, and perhaps traps that trigger if you move into their line of sight.
Overall: I feel overall this game is looking really good, and I know when it finally comes out, it'll be a big hit.

Dust's strong presentation masks its disappointing lack of depth across the board.
After several hours playing, I no longer feel like I can keep myself excited about mashing the light attack button any more against waves of mosnters that pose an absolutely minimal threat, even on the hardest difficulty setting. That the voice acting is nauseating, but passable if it weren't for the absolutely dull and at times clichéd dialogue that provides little in terms of urgency or at the very least interest and intrigue. And whilst there's nothing ostensibly wrong with having a plain good vs. bad story-line or even an amnesiaced main hero, having a companion who is seemingly a combination of everything wrong with voiced companion/side-kicks into one and a talking sword that seems to be taking joy in how vague it can be, it all combined just feels very lacking.
The game feels like it could've done with an impartial outsider to just sit there and edit it. Rooms full of monsters to clear go from being standard game objective stuff to a chore, with no real variety from the first ten minutes to four hours in how you engage the lion's share of them. On top of this, when the AI does eventually muster some will to bother to attack you, it can be hard to determine by what you've been attacked by when facing groups as well as some enemy attack animations feeling like they deal damage before it looks like they should do. Whilst there is a satisfactory dash ability, I felt I was at odds with movement every so often when I would be moving/facing in one direction and trying to attack, only for the game to seemingly take control for a second and attack in the opposite direction, much to my continued chagrin. Does the combat improve later on? Quite possibly, but it's a tedium for some time at least.
The game does have a lovely presentation though, clearly being rather polished. It has a great artistic style and the anthropomorphic creatures that inhabit the world are well visaulised, although suffering from the aforementioned dialogue and voice-over issues. Animations are really smooth and movement generally feels consistent, but this feels like a periphery to the core elements of the game that just could not hold up.
Ultimately the feeling I get from the game is that it's just shallow. Some design decisions feel like they were done in spite of things that might make things more enjoyable, for example backtracking is hindered by a need for 'teleportation stones' if you want to return to the world map from a save point in an area, as well as only being able to enter an area from the world map by one of its main entrances. Whilst both might be more in fitting with the lore of the game, it ultimately made me unwilling to really go back into areas and look through them properly when it would've just been nice to have the opportunity to move about with greater freedom. This, overall, I feel epitomises the problems with the game and eventually made me stop playing. A shame!
*Played with a 360 controller.

The story mode itself is okay but underwhelming. I finished it very quickly and didn't realize it was over until I was dumped back at the title screen. It did help that I learned immediately about the ability to continue from the last stage you finished, which diminished the challenge considerably. The story mode is fun, but there's nothing about it that will stick with you. The Tower Mode is a great touch, though. You get to unlock tons of characters for use in all modes, including characters from past games that weren't in the story mode. This gives the game some much-needed extra meat. Especially because they took the time to give each character a distinctive move list.
All in all, not a world beater, but if you come in with the right set of expectations, you might enjoy it. If the trailer didn't do it for you, then you can probably skip it.

It's not a bad game and it actually makes the war feel like a war. If you like RTS's this game needs to be in your collection.  If you are new to RTS's this is a good middle of the road game to wet your feet with. There are better games but this is a good game in its own right.
It's the standard RTS set up, you have a certain number of factions and while they are warring factions they all unilaterally agree that the number of factions on the planet should not be equal to the number of heads on the human body. So fight as one of seven unique (sort of) factions in a bid to elimnate the other 6 from the planet. Pretty standard, but where the game breaks from the mold of Command and Conquer, Warcraft, Starcraft and even it's predecessors in the series is that the campain is not just a linear succession of missions. You are given a map, a place on  and you must selkect which of the neighboring areas on the map you wish to  conquer. I know what you're saying, DUne 2 did this decades ago but there's another twist in this tango.
After you have won(or lost) the engagement your turn ends and each of the other factions does the same, and yes they will be fighting with each other as much as you. But wait it gets better, you see, they can also choose to attack one of your provinces and you must defend them. All these battles take place on RTS style maps  but the fact that you are in a constant battle to gain and hold territory adds a twist to this war that most other RTS's lack. That's not to say it's a 'Gold-Star' game.
There is a finite number of distinct races an RTS can have and that number seems to be about 4. As evidenced by. Warcraft 3. I've yet to see a game successfully manage 5 or more without having them feel like cut and pastes with minor differences. As is this games factions have about 3 playstyles between them and many of the units pretty much equate. There's a healthy selection of units for each and upgrades but you will quickly learn that each race has an optimal army make up and you will never see a reason to deviate from it no matter what you face.
This leads to a rather shallow, if  fun, play experience.
One glaring negative though is the cheating. Now it's a given that RTS games cheat a little. This one cheats a lot and quite brazenly at that. See there is a cap thgat limits certain high power units  that can be deployed like commanders and seige breakers. All well and dandy but what you'll quickly discover is that the Computer gets around this by simply having you up against two or more armies of the opposing faction. Which means in short that you're almost always  going 2v1 at least. Sometimes more. This doubles the amount of high power units the opposing side can and will bring to bear against you, as well as the number of troops they can field. There are also specific factions (Tau) that blatantly break the rules of buiulding placement in their base set up when the pc controlls them. But wait there's more.
I should explain there is a bonus called Forward Base, This pperk is acquired by winning a control of a certain province and it allows you to start any attack mission with certain basic structures already built, For a fee. The problem  is, as far as the PC is concerned. It always has forward base active regardless of whether or not he obtained the bonus. You'll notice this on those defense missions ,  that the pC always has their bases already set up witha  few basic structures. So whether you attack or defend the enemy will always have two pre-built bases.
If you don't mind the cheating however, the game is pretty fun. It's what i would call a spectacle RTS.  The combat and skirmishes are always fun to watch and the reenforcement mechanic means you have to keep a close eye on your units and  thusly keeps the battles quite engaging.
All in all this is a decent RTS. Not as good as the Blizzard RTS's or THe Red Alert games , but a solid RTS in its own right.  Give it and the other expansions a try. So far I can recomend this over Soulstorm, the next game in the series, because, to be honest,  It has a tighter focus and the factions have a more unique feel. There's a reason that, inpite of the gripes I listed , I can  recommend this game. IT's fun, it wiull challenge you and  will provide entertainment.
But in closing I ill say one last thing anbd offer some advice.
"HYPERION PEAKS CAN GET ♥♥♥♥ED OVER A SOGGY MATRESS"
Seriously, just ignore the province.  Unless the tau or eldar have (which is almost never.) this province is an outright middle finger pointed straight at you.. It's not worth it.

Well here it is, the re-return of the Double Dragons? So what is this you ask? It's a quick cash grab game from our beloved retro friends over at Arc System Works and completely messes up the Double Dragon timeline but hey, is it worth your 7 or 8 dollars? Read on.
So apparently Arc decided to change around the Double Dragon timeline a tad so this game falls somewhere after Double Dragon II - The Revenge and sometime before Double Dragon III - The Sacred / Rosetta Stones. According to Arc though, Double Dragon III came BEFORE Double Dragon II (who knew?) regardless of what numbered entry this is in the series, it comes directly after resurrecting Marian in Double Dragon II.
It's your typical Double Dragon drivel, your girlfriend (Marian) gets kidnapped (for whatever reason) and it's time to head out and destroy some street thugs and save her one more time. The problem with this game is that the story doesn't get better as you play through it like almost every other Double Dragon game (especially Double Dragon II). Instead about half way through the entire thing falls apart and the final boss is a bit of a joke and more light hearted comparitively to the dark and gritty Double Dragon II's final encounter.
Well it's a retro title using NES sprites so don't expect much. If you prefered the way Double Dragon II's sprites looked then you'll be pleased because they basically just ripped every enemy out of Double Dragon II and put them in this game. They added a few new characters as well and their sprites just seem completely out of place but what can you do really? The weapons and certain items also stand out a lot and the mixture of using Double Dragon 1 and 2's pixel art together don't really mix well so it loses points for consistency.
You have more than 2 buttons to work with so the battle mechanics aren't nearly as basic or tedious as they were in past installments. In fact every special move can be mapped to a button and you can now combo and juggle enemies in mid air... finally a retro Double Dragon with better battle mechanics.
If you want to know which signature moves returned in this installment, here's the list for the Lee Brothers:
Punch
Front Kick (No longer Back Kick)
Jump (Now 1 button instead of 2)
Jump Kick
Cyclone Spin Kick
Hyper Knee
Hyper Uppercut
Head Butt
Elbow
High Kick
Hair Pull
Throw
It's all there, and it's easier than ever to pull off, as long as you have a controller, you're basically golden. I wouldn't recommend playing this with a keyboard as that was never how Double Dragon was meant to be played. All buttons can be re-mapped however you prefer.
The game isn't as tight as it was in Double Dragon II or III, those games felt a lot slower paced and the hit boxes on the enemies were really big and forgiving. Instead this game feels more like Double Dragon I on the NES, enemy hit boxes are kind of small and your characters feel a bit more floaty. It took me about 2 minutes to get adjusted to the feeling though, once you're used to it, it comes very naturally for any old school veteran.
It has that retro vibe to it and some old school favorite songs show up but over all it's very repetitive and there wasn't much passion put in to it. Honestly I'm kind of disappointed how generic the soundtrack is but the 3 new songs that are in the game aren't bad, they just re-use the hell out of them.... 3 new stage songs (5 total) and there's 12 Missions... so yeah... get's a bit stale too quickly.
There's plenty of content here. There's 12 missions to go through, all of which are roughly the length of an Average Double Dragon II level, the game does get a bit unforgiving in Mission 11 as it's basically an homage to Mission 7 from Double Dragon II (The Trap Room) so be warned you may end up frustrated if you're bad at timing jumps. I for one didn't have much trouble with it, I lost a credit trying to get through it just from cheap pit fall deaths but I had plenty of credits to spare. So long as you're good at the battle mechanics, this part of the game won't phase you if you lose a couple of lives.
There's a new tower mode that allows you to play as every enemy character in the game and traverse a 100 floor tower. Unfortunately I was only able to make it to Floor 65 as of typing this and it's incredibly difficult. You have 1 life to live to make it to the top. On the plus side you unlock every character at around Floor 40 and can play the story mode using them.
There are an enormous amount of achievements in this game and 80% of them require you to beat the entire story mode as every character in the game. There are over 20+ characters to choose from so grab a buddy for some couch co-op and start using some wild character combos!
If you're looking to only play this game once through and unlock all the characters, it has about 4 hours of gameplay total. I would recommend trying to do everything in the game or you're just not getting your money out of it.
It's a great little homage to the series and a love letter to the fans. It feels a bit like an unprofessional fan game and not very well put together at some parts but all the classic stuff is there. You have some conveyor belts, spike traps, pit falls, moving platforms and of course your favorite cast of Double Dragon characters and villains. If it had a tad more polish it could of been considered a mainstream title in the series but ever since Super Double Dragon, the quality just hasn't been the same. It's still worth the 8 dollars though.
Fan favorites like the Mysterious Warrior, Chin Seimei and Ranzou are here as little secret easter eggs as well as a retro version of Jimmy Lee from the orginal Double Dragon NES game. If you're an old school gamer and enjoyed Double Dragon in its early years and know how to handle it's quirks, this game is definitely for you. I was able to crush it on my first playthrough as it just felt like an alternate version of Double Dragon II and I've mastered that game completely.
The only mode that really makes me frustrated is the tower mode but eventually I'll muster the patience to push through it.
It's a great fan game, I wouldn't take it too seriously though, I don't consider this game canon at all but it's fun to relive those old school childhood moments again. If you're someone who wasn't born in the 1980's or early 1990's, you should probably steer clear of this game or you're going to have a bad time.

Simply flawless. It's so very easy to sink hours into this beauty of a game. A charming artstyle combined with a wonderful soundtrack and exhilarating gameplay makes for some of the best gaming hours of your life, at a minute cost.
No two playthroughs are the same, which is a good thing as an entire run of the game will last around 40 or so minutes, should you avoid death. There's no hiding the fact that TBoI is a difficult game, but it's the kind of difficult game that provides enough progression to keep you coming back for more.
Each playthrough is randomly generated. Each "floor" of the game (level) contains an assortment of items, rooms, enemies and bosses, all of which are randomly generated. That's not implying that each run contains new items nobody has ever seen before, more that each run contains item, room, enemy and boss combinations that nobody has ever experienced before.
If you're into difficult rogue-like dungeon-crawling rage-inducing games or perhaps enjoy games that can be described using a lot of hypenated words, TBoI (and its DLC!) is a must-have for you.
Pros:  Randomly generated, exceptional replayability, perfect learning curve.
Cons: -

This is a wonderful game, well crafted and endlessly entertaining. If you want a game that will challenge you and even infuriate a bit, Hotline Miami is for you for sure. The visuals are pleasing in a very unique way. 8-bit pixelated gore litters the screen in a satisfying way every single kill. The one-hit kills being a majority of the game add to the satisfying experience of being a relentless animal-mask clad psychopath, The top-down gameplay is well-executed and utilized efficiently, the environments are as useful as they are complex with plenty of extra weapons littered about, and the enemy AI is some of the most interesting, and even a "look around" feature which allows you to determine the patterns which enemies have established in the (many) attempts it takes to compete a level of the game. The soundtrack shines quite brightly here as well. EDM artists of all genres were selected not only for the "catchiness" of their songs here but clearly as well for the quality of the music they make. However, no piece of art is perfect. The Game tends to chug a bit when it comes to storytelling. It gets somewhat of a pass given that gameplay is what is more heavily emphasized in this game, but it is a mild takeaway from the overall experience; having a mildly underdeveloped story, even if the premise is ultimately interesting. These story issues, as I could point out, are corrected extremely well in the sequel. The other glaring issue is that even with a tutorial stage, Hotline Miami is not noob friendly. It is not a game I would use to get someone into gaming due to the difficulty, hell, that's like using Dark Souls to introduce someone to gaming. But overall, if I were to rate Hotline Miami based on quality it would for sure be 9.9/10. Highly Reccommended!

A surprisingly fun game, 10,000,000 gave me more far more enjoyment than I had expected when I initially purchased it for a few dollars.  Though the game is primarily a Match-Three, every single type that you match provides an effect that drastically alters your current encounter.  Match three (or more for an increased effect) swords, for example, and you'll unleash a physical attack; match three magic wands, you'll cast a magical attack; match three keys, you'll unlock a treasure chest or door, etc.
The game is quite challenging, though each time you run through a dungeon path you'll acquire gold, experience, and items that will aid you in future runs.  Gold can be used to upgrade your equipment (swords, staves, shields, armor, etc.) by choosing a specific trait such as the sharpness of your sword (critical chance) or the material that it is made out of (base damage).  Experience can be used to purchase training upgrades which enhance abilities such as your lockpicking skills and increasing damage against certain enemy types.
All in all, it's a cheap game with a good amount of fun to be had as long as you keep that in mind.

10,000,000? Odd name to say the least, but I'm sure this game will suprise you like it did me. This game is in short a bejeweled spin-off with more action. The way the game work is simple you need to get 10,000,000 score to beat the game and that's the jist of the games core. The game may sound a bit boring with such a simplistic victory condition, but there is more to it than that.
The difference of bejeweled and 10,000,000 is the fact you have a hero at the top of the screen you control. Based on the blocks you break you change the outcome of the heros fate by unlocking doors, killing monsters, or just collecting supplies for when you go back to home to spend them on upgrades.
There are multiple ways to change the flow of the game. Whether it be with Armor upgrades to reduce damage, Sword upgrades to increase the damage and critical chance on your sword breaks, wand upgrades to increase the damage of your spells and increase the RNG of freezes and poison, and even potions to change the multiplier.
I believe that any fan of the puzzle genre should consider picking up this epic and amazing tale of a hero trapped and his only goal is.... 10,000,000

Where to start with Deponia?
Deponia is a very well done Point and Click Adventure game, visually similar to Monkey Island 3 and with a very similar protagonist to boot. Deponia stars Rufus, while he may be bumbling like Guybrush Threepwood he most certainly isn't as noble. His mouth lands him in more trouble than his actions and his treatment of many of his acquaintances (and those he would deem friends) is pretty poor and self centred but deep down he has a heart of gold...deep deep down...just look deeper.
The comedy in Deponia ranges from a little slapstick here to a little silly outrageousness here, puns all around and tons of funny dialogue to keep you smiling as you go with Rufus on his adventure to get to Elysium!
The characters are very varied and Rufus is a little predictable with how he'll interact with each one but as Deponia goes on so does Rufus, he changes and develops (even if only a bit)
The game is fun! The game is puzzling and challenging, or maybe that's just because I'm bad at puzzles. The story is interesting, full of twists and secrets and it even has you sad at times especially towards the end.
The "Complete Journey" bundles all three Deponias into one but it does have it bugs, when transitioning from game to game it will close the application and sometimes with certain cutscenes ending it'll do it again but upon booting it back up it has saved right where it crashed so it's a minor issue. Other than that I've only had a handful of other bugs which weren't game breaking or impeding my ability to complete puzzles and trigger events but should they continue to patch more bugs I'll update this part.
Overall (or a TL:DR) Deponia took me by surprise, I went in expecting mediocrity and was blown away, with its jaunty music, lovable characters, beautifully drawn scenes and a script that'll leave you wondering where it'll go next. Point and Click veterans will love it to bits and newcomers will be quickly drawn in through the tutorial.
Edit: This review was written in 2014 and it is now the 25th of February 2016 and we have just had an announcement for Deponia: Doomsday, Huzzah good things come in....fours?
Edit 2: I am lazy and just got around to finishing it finally in 2017 (August 18th) and that ending was WHAT and now I feel Doomsday needs to answer for a lot of things.

This game is a completely seamless mix of three rather disparate genres--roguelike, puzzle and rhythm game. All three enhance each other well. The rhythm component forces you to think on your toes despite the turn-based nature of the combat (which is really more of a fast-paced puzzle game than anything else, since it's always possible to defeat all foes without a scratch if you make the right moves). And the roguelike nature keeps it fresh, ensuring that the more exotic items and weapons are treats.
The variety of characters, not to mention items and weapons, do a good job adding replay value. Some characters are way more difficult than others on purpose, but that just stretches out the fun longer.
Item balance is among the best I've ever seen in a semi-roguelike--most of the better weapons are mixed blessings, the different rings and helmets are all equally useful in different ways, and item prices for the better items are well-tuned to present tough choices in shops (even if the choice is "is it worth killing the shopkeeper"). You'll get runs with good luck and bad luck, but rarely will you have runs where the whims of the RNG are what made you lose or win--your power level is much more consistent than, say, Isaac or Spelunky. Plus even the best items are useless without skill, and with skill you can win with a basic dagger.
Special modes in the expansion pack add to the longevity, with challenges like "you can't tell what items or enemies are" and "all enemies have randomized AI and stats".
Oh, and it has six ful soundtracks, all of them phenomenal. Not just one, six. And some extremely creative bosses.
Overall, I heartily recommend this game for just about anyone. If you watch the trailer and think that could even potentially be fun for you, I guarantee it will be.

Let me preface this by saying OMD1 is my 3rd favourite game of all time.  It struck a perfect balance between trap and player damage, allowing you to create a great kill box and sit back, a decent one and pick up the slack with player damage, or just kite your way to victory with pure player damage.  Absolute brilliant game & level design.
OMD2 faired less well.  They shifted the focus to players being required to do most of the damage and traps were just there to help out a bit.
OMDU is complete and utter garbage.  Not only did they take the OMD2 model and make it even more about player damage, especially with patch 1.2, they had the absolutely idiotic design choice of forcing players to stick in place for a time before they can attack.  That's right, no kite killing, no chasing down an enemy bashing at it... you have to get out in front of them and stop, wait, and then attack as they run by you yet again.  The player has literally become another stuck in place trap that can be run around.  Add to this the 'free-2-pay-more' greed, a focus on adding needless shrubery to the environment, painfully bad map design for kill boxing/multi-level gaming/pathing or any type of real creativity, no campaign, a crazy number of bugs for a Beta, and recycled audio... this game is the biggest disappointment of recent memory.
Robot Entertainment has alienated a fan today.
