I loved the art, but did not like the character.  I had no issue with her, but I have no affinity for Zia.  I have no issue playing  female.  I just don't care for her.  I have no reason to care about anyone in this story.  The city had one good thing, a reference to Terry Pratchett.  *Salute*
Other than that everything in the world felt telegraphed.  It was too easy - and it had to be because of how linear it is.
The game mechanic is a great step - but incomplete.  I would love to see this grown into a real experience, but for now, there is little more to this than an easy beat-em-up....  with the same areas over and over with more difficult, but not really hard, enemies that scale to your new spells.  Frankly, at that point - this is a one time playthrough that has no pay-off.  Mods will save this, but what is here feels like a game that needs mods, which seems like it is flexible, but actually has less freedom and is somehow more linear than Torchlight.  I keep looking to hope this is just early access.
The spell crafting is neat, but needs more sophistication and maybe some actual context.  It is not *endless* by any means.  No object animation, no combining elements to fuse hybrids...  Also, Regio would be a better name for Actus, and Muto would be a better one for Ego.  Also, what Mage doesn't have conjuration???  The magick is light programming logic with limited effective combinations - to solve puzzles.   The rest is beat em up with magic....  with infinite respawning enemies in areas that are small in size and hedged in.
As for spell crafting - Two Words 2 is ABSOLUTELY MORE FLEXIBLE.
The story is dialed in.  I love Ed Greenwood.  I really enjoyed the world of Faerun for decades.  It does not even fit the atmosphere.  It certainly does not hit like Spellfire, but it has glimmers of it...  The music is lovely, but doesn't shine.  Good background.  As a game, this would likely be a much more fun experience for an inexperienced or casual gamer.

This is an incredible game solely based on its spellcrafting system.
Sure, the writing and pacing might feel a bit drab; the UI isn't the smoothest thing to use; we're sorely missing a minimap/radar function; sometimes the spells don't fly the way you point and you might encounter a few bugs now and then, etc. etc.... None of these distract from the core experience of using magic in varied and creative ways.
I've seen and played a few "customize your own spells" games, and this one simply takes the cake. The spellcrafting system is straightforward and very intuitive to learn. Puzzles strewn around the world are tailored to almost all the runes/effects you're going to find, and the hint system is great to let you know if you've already got the required tools (and somewhere along the path, you might have enough tools in your arsenal to solve them in unexpected ways - and it's going to feel
). The combat leaves enough room for you to win using vastly different setups, though enemies immune to multiple elements might make you feel frustrated at times.
I'm currently around 30%~40% progress, and even if the later parts of the game don't maintain the level of quality as the part I've seen so far, it will still be super fun (there will be more magic to find and more spells to craft - that will never be not fun), and worth every penny of the full price.
The devs seem to have plans to update the game for a while, so I'm looking forward to see the game improve in the near future.

Fabulous game.  Spell creation is really intuitive and fun, and it lets you do a lot of exciting things, like self-multiplying random firing spells that propagate continuously until you run out of magic.  The world is very vibrant and colourful and fun to run around blowing up with magic.  It's very Zelda-esque, with a lot to discover.
The puzzles are all pretty good.  Camera is at fixed angles, so you're never left missing things that you should see.  They take a reasonable amount of thought without ever being frustrating.  I suspect someone who is like, hardcore into puzzle gaming probably won't be that engaged, but otherwise I found them fun to solve.  There's too many "light all the torches in X seconds" puzzles though.
Has some problems, and I really love a lot about this game, so I hate saying that.
The bosses suck.  Just completely suck.  They LOOK awesome, but they're boring, bog-standard latter-day Zelda bosses.  Expose glowing weak point, attack glowing weak point, repeat until dead.  Then there's some that DON'T follow that pattern, but go down like chumps.  So that's pretty disappointing; I've stopped dodging most of the time, as I can usually just stand there and spam my best attacks.
Dungeons and general progression in the game are/is pretty formulaic.  You will require an element from the previous dungeon to progress in the next one, and that's a little disheartening.  I feel it would have benefitted a lot with a more open design that allowed you to build your own solutions to problems, rather than putting solid barriers in your path that say "you must have X element to proceed."  Something like Zelda 1 where you are just in the world and so are all the things you want to do and get but in no specific sequence, would have been perfect.  Or like Zelda 3 where the plot happens in intervals but how and when you get to those intervals is up to you.
My one problem with the puzzles is that a lot of the minor ones (that is, puzzles which don't bar your progression in the game) can be solved without the "correct" solution, but it's never creatively.  That is to say, I've never solved a puzzle I shouldn't have been able to solve by doing some quirky trick with a new spell, but I HAVE solved a lot of puzzles by spamming random bouncing fireballs that proc more random bouncing fireballs.  It's funny the first couple of times, but it's not much of an accomplishment.  Compare this with a Metroid game where I can get an item early by figuring out how to do angled bomb jumps or mockballing or some other clever trick.
So what it boils down to is there's a beautiful set up that lets you be super creative with all this magic... and then the world doesn't really give you an opportunity to excersize that creativity beyond how you choose to annihilate full screens of enemies.  Instead, you progress through a very linear series of dungeons and plot events with very clear solutions reliant on the most basic of your spells.
But in spite of all that, it's a super fun, amazing game, and I highly recommend it.

Overall this game costs too much money for too little content.
Think Dishonored, but twice the price, minimal story, only 3 types of enemies, and overly-simple core mechanics that don't evolve as the game progresses.
Cons:
The enemies don't have any real means of countering your absurd shadow powers, meaning the only real "difficulty" comes from your character being a 1-hitpoint wonder who dies instantly from being hit by an attack or falling into water.
Checkpoints are also oddly spaced, meaning you may have to replay a huge swath of a level over again just because you accidentally teleported yourself into a moat.
Unlike other stealth games like MGS, Hitman, or Assassin's Creed that require you to pick up and carry bodies in order to hide them, Aragami has an unlockable skill early on that straight up erases corpses with his shadow magic, which pretty much makes the whole "guards discovering corpses and going on alert" mechanic totally pointless.
- There is absolutely no way to interact with corpses aside from using this skill, so you can't even do fun stuff like tossing bodies out in the open to lure guards (which would have been awesome if you could mix it with your teleporting powers)
While it is possible to earn "pacifist" medals by ghosting through levels, there's no way to incapacitate guards without killing them, and the storty forces you to kill the bosses you fight, meaning a true pacificst run is outright impossible.
There are ALSO medals for killing every enemy within a level, you get awarded points for doing so, AND the number of people you kill has ZERO impact on the outcome of the story.
- In other words, this game has the atmosphere of one that COULD be pure stealth with optional killing (despite the vengeance-themed story saying otherwise), but always ends up turning into a shadow-powered killfest, except the killfest isn't even that satisfying because the game lacks true combat mechanics and everything just dies in one hit :steamfacepalm:
This game was fun at first, but after 3 hours the "novelty" had worn out, and I quickly realised that if I wanted to go on a teleporting power-fantasy killing spree I could be playing Shadow of Mordor instead.
(which funnily enough, is also $19.99 on Steam)
Pros:
This game DOES have online co-op, a level editor, and mods.
So if you REALLY happen to like the idea of playing a co-op stealth game with a friend and this game happens to be at least 75% off, then MAYBE it might be worth trying it out.
HOWEVER I personally found the core game mechanics far too bland to bother with the online content.- even with the level editor you're still stuck with the same core assets and 3 enemy types (sword dude, archer dude, sword dude with a torch), and any enterntainment derived from Co-op mode would most likely be from watching your teammates screw up, since multiple Aragami's running around would be WAY too OP.
DISCLAIMER: All game prices listed above are from the time that this review was written, and may be subject to change due to steam sales and price drops.

The Binding of Isaac is a very interesting and endearing game that makes great use of its macabre atmosphere and story. The randomly generated levels and power-ups means that no two play throughs will ever be the same. Given the high level of difficulty this is a must given how many times you will be starting over as there are no save points allowed. A single play through can be done fairly quickly though can often lead to the "just one more game" mentality.
The gameplay itself is fairly straightforward top-down shooter though the huge number of power-ups and combinations there of keep things fresh and exciting even after dozens of playthroughs. It can occasionally be frustrating that you won't know what a certain item/power does until you use it. Having a pill and never knowing if it will heal you or kill you can be off putting though it fits within the game's setting and style. Other items or power-ups need to simply be memorized over time or looked up to know which you will want to use or keep.
The enemies faced are interesting to both look at and in their behaviours. This is a fairly decent enemy variety given the size of the game. The best ways to tackle each are learned through mostly trial and error and you will almost certainly come to have favourites as well as ones you dread to see when entering a room. The boss fights encountered at the end of each level are less varied and can become somewhat stale after many playthroughs.
While very challenging The Binding of Isaac never felt cheap. The varaibility in the gameplay and great use of style and delightfully dark atmosphere had me coming back again and again as I tried to save poor Isaac.

So much has already been said about this game so I'll just give some points on why I like it.
- The outrun aesthetic.  This game wears its 80s retro influences on its sleeve and it oozes with style.
- The music.  I love the synthwave genre and there's a lot to love here (ex. Perturbator, Carpenter Brut)
- The pick up and play gameplay.  I'm really busy so it's nice to have an intense and fun session for about 10 or 15 minutes.
- Combos!  In order to get a big combo you have to be both strategic and relentless.  It's really rewarding once you clear a whole floor in one combo.  If you die, getting back into the game is really quick.
- The scoring system.  I personally like trying to get top scores for all of the levels.  For me, this gives the game a lot of replay ability.
- The cryptic story.  A lot of Hotline Miami players may not know this, but some of the story is presented through details in the environment.  Even when the story is presented directly to you, it's not quite clear what's going on.  I really enjoy this style of storytelling.
Maybe you and I have similar taste in games; I don't know.  I hope this helps, and if you pick it up have a good time.

Pure mind games. Every aspect of the game maximizes the amount of trickery, deceit and figuring out the insides of your opponent. Like a fighting game distilled to a core of the battle between 2 minds. The fight is direct, there are no obstacles in-between, no cover to hide, just you and your opponent face to face, the duel taking place inside your heads.
It's best to play this game with a good amount of different people, perfect for tournaments, game nights, LAN parties, local multiplayer gatherings or even board game events! Because the matches are short and interesting to watch, as long as you keep changing the players up, nobody will get bored if they like mind games (if they don't, then again: it's pretty fun to watch close matches). It can both be played casually and competitively, too. There's not that much to learn about the game for it to be competitive, anyone can pick it up really quickly, really, you can invite anyone to play, quickly explain it and 5 minutes later, they beat you (true story). The real competitive part is that of how attentive a player is, you need to concentrate into your opponent's actions to play really well, there's no real skill cap, you just have to be better at it than your opponent. (note that reaction plays a very trivial role here, it's not a reflex game)
A tournament was actually the way I discovered this brilliant game.
This can still effectively be played with one friend over and over again or even singleplayer, too! If you're into this sort of stuff, the AI poses a good challenge and often feels like a real person but nothing beats playing this with your opponent sitting right next to you and hearing them furiously control the sticks and click the buttons while the real fight is in your minds, trying to figure out your opponent and outsmart them, real-time.
Note that the game has no online multiplayer but this is to be expected: it has to be real-time without any latency and, in this game, feeling your enemy right next to you is magical.
Controllers highly recommended, if you have custom controllers (not xbox), it will be hard to setup but it's definitely doable and I hope to soon make a guide on how to do just that.
My only real complaint is that some color themes are not very clear (there is also a random colors theme for some reason) and one of my friends disapproved of the visual style completely.
My other complaint is that I don't have many friends :(
Just be sure that you will like playing mind games with your friends, there isn't much content here and all of it revolves around this "fast paced mind-reading competition".

The Roguelike genre may be expanding very quickly nowdays, but Crypt of the NecroDancer adds exciting new depth on top of an already solid foundation. The core elements of any good Roguelike are strong here, with randomized loot and dungeons and (at least semi) perma-death, but the rhythm-based combat forces you to approach encounters with more strategic thinking rather than less, on top of testing your reaction time.

Botolo takes the basics of fighting game mechanics and strips it down to nearly the pure mind game. At the core, you are attempting to predict when you opponent is going to make a steal. There are interesting meta games that come out of the positioning, and trying to trick your opponent into thinking that you are attempting a steal. This game would work just with those bits, but it also contains a ton of different powers for the different players that change either the positioning game or the way the mind game works (you can do bluffs with some of the powers, or lock down zones with different tools).
Try to play with a friend for your first match, it really comes alive against a human opponent.

Bought this game on impulse, and it was absolutely excellent.
The spellcrafting system is actually interesting and purposeful, with all the spells you can make being functionally different. Most games centered around this sort of thing will still only have a few /functionally/ different spells, with the only real difference being stats, but not this one.
You can make spells loop in on themselves, and add modifying runes like size or time onto various other runes to change their properties. I found myself spellcrafting constantly, not just to have fun and mess around but also to modify my setup for the present situation. By the end of the game, I utterly annihilated the final boss, which felt a bit cheap, but at the same time it was very satisfying seeing how powerful i had become through my creativity, which is kind of the point.
Completed it to 100% in 22~ hours, and am left wanting more. Short and sweet, it was worth the money, and I'm proud to have supported the developers. Okay, i've played nearly 30 hours of this game.
Here is my overall advice - if you REALLY love off-road simulators, buy this on sale. Otherwise, if you are "kind of" interested, the camera angle, limited options and general simplicity of the game might annoy the crap out of you. I'm on the fence, love playing, hate dealing with the camera ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. You'll understand in game why camera is so important, not just for recovery, but for watching the road, making sure you don't go into a ditch, hit a rock or worse case scenario, roll the entire log load.
Below is a short summary
Pros
1 - very realistic terrain deformation
2 - very realistic traction modeling
3 - very realistic physics modeling
4 - realistic 4x4 and diff lock settings
5 - Somewhat active mod community
Cons
1 - CAMERA IS ANNOYING AS♥♥♥♥♥♥
-want to zoom out more while in game? NO.
-want to zoom in more while in the map? NO.
-CAMERA HAS AUTO MOVEMENT WHICH CAN NOT BE DISABLED = ANNOYING
-Camera axis cannot be set - no x-axis or y-axis reversal!
-Camera will set back to default 3rd person EVERY time you select advanced/non advanced
-Camera is focused around some psuedo axis, forget rotate and zoom, there is some weird elliptical motion centered on the middle of the truck that doesn't care whether or not you can see a winch point
2 - 2wd vehicles (BT-130) are basically useless unless you love winches
3 - Confusing log loading. Have to load 3 logs, then position cart, then pack. ZERO instructions in game for this.
4 - Nighttime mode is almost impossible to see. Sure you can see right in front of you, but forget about winching or manuevering or seeing anywhere except straight ahead. I turn off lights for all rescue operations because otherwise you can't see♥♥♥♥♥♥br>5 - No plot or story. Just move logs and you're done
6 - Very limited vehicle choice, like 8 or so in game
7 - Winch has max tension and you will constantly be maxing it out, i.e. you hit "pull" and the winch doesn't move♥♥♥♥♥♥ VERY annoying when you are really stuck and could use a real ♥♥♥♥ing winch.
SO yeah, not a bad game, but not a great game. A simulator with some interesting gameplay but a camera angle that really takes the joy out of the game IMHO.

Having played the other 2 Mafia games I was looking forward to the next installment. So I'm not quite sure why this gets such negative reviews. I'm guessing it's because it didn't quite live up to the hype. This is different than the other games in the Mafia series. Instead of the rise up through the ranks and it all go wrong scenario, this game is about revenge against the Mafia. It's more of a one man crusade than the other games but there are plenty of other successful games that use this formula.
The story is great, the characters are strong, the setting is wonderfully evoked through the open world, cars and music of the 1960's. It even tries to deal with the racism of the period. I particularly liked the documentary style cut scenes.
I would guess the main criticism would be lack of variety of gameplay, the game focuses on destroying rackets and replacing them with your own team. It means a lot of stealth and some straightforward assault. Therein lies another of the game's weak points. The opponent AI is a little simplistic and tactically your approach for the game won't change once you've found your groove. However, that said they do a good job of compensating by varying the environments and opponent strength. In any case, it can all go south quickly if you don't take care.
The lack of variety of gameplay is not bad as some reviews make out as there are all the usual assault, defend, destroy, steal, tail, etc. missions that you would usually see in open world games.
So is it as polished as the other Mafia games? Probably not. Is it a good game? Yes, especially if you're a fan of stealth games. Does it deliver a good story? Certainly.

Hotline Miami is just as fun as it is punishing, that is to say that it's a whole lot of both. It's a top-down fmup (think shmup but extremely brutal) with a pretty heavy tactical element to it that keeps you thinking about how to approach every situation more and more efficiently each time you die--and you'll die an awful lot. Any enemy can kill you or knock you out in one hit, so you'll be trying one idea, failing, and then refining that idea a few times until you have that glorious satisfaction of overcoming all the odds against you. The level design is pretty complex and the enemies are varied enough that the trial-and-error gameplay doesn't become stale. There is almost always a genuine challenge (apart from two absolutely ridiculous boss battles and a pretty cheap stealth segment), making the "trial" in "trial-and-error" something really, really compelling. The AI isn't great at picking up on signs that you're in their midst, but if it was, the game would probably be absolutely impossible. The campaign follows a narrative that isn't very strong, but it's definitely something interesting. It complements the stressful gameplay with some really weird hallucinations that actually make you wonder what the hell is actually going on, and then, even though it's not very complex, it ties up loose ends in a pretty fascinating way. The graphics, despite the really ugly face drawings, are stylish and give off an extremely eighties vibe, though there are no options to turn off some features like screen sway, which will probably end up hurting the game's accessibility. The real aesthetic star is the soundtrack, though. For 2012, it's one of the absolute best game soundtracks, right up there with Vessel. Because of its extreme challenge, Hotline Miami is probably not a game for most people, but it's extremely good at what it does, and despite a few caveats it's one of the best games this year.

It's a Match-3 game, with a simple objective: Get 10,000,000 points. The narrative throws in something about escaping a dungeon, but really that's a lame excuse for the mechanics.
Fortunately, the mechanics are where the game shines. The gameplay reminds me of a more strategic version of Chuzzle, which is pretty high praise. You automatically gain points as your avatar keeps moving through the dungeon, but that doesn't continue for long before an obstacle stops your progress and starts whittling away the time you have remaining on your run.
Your matches are used to overcome obstacles and collect resources in order to boost your score. The resources that you collect can be expended at your home base (like, say, a less complicated version of Rogue Legacy) to provide upgrades and bonuses to plow through obstacles more easily, defend yourself against said obstacles, or on the rare occasion just provide a percentage boost to your overall score.
The graphics are deliberately retro, even excessively so, but it definitely has a unified aesthetic. The music and sounds are sufficient, but I found after about 30 minutes of playing and hearing all the tracks, I enjoyed it more with the music off and a different soundtrack in the background.

10,000,000 essentially takes the core gameplay concept of Chuzzle (dragging whole rows and columns to make  a match) and adds classic RPG elements. It's easy to pick up, and it's not TOO hard to put down. If you like slow-paced contemplative tile-matching that make take you an hour to complete a run, this is gonna be a little much for you.
It is expected that each run will only last a short time (a minute or two in the early stages), because you are working against the clock. Your hero runs through a long dungeon (displayed at the top of the screen) and meets various obstacles. The type of obstacle will determine what type of match will allow you to advance. The hero runs fast enough to regain time, but the screen keeps scrolling slowly while you are working on an obstacle.
Doors and treasure chests require that you match Key tiles. Enemies can be attacked with Sword or Staff tiles. Most enemies will need to be attacked multiple times; they have health bars to let you know how you're doing. You must also endure enemies' attacks, which will reduce your timer (there is no HP, only the timer). Shield tiles can give you damage reduction, and Item tiles can generate useful consumable items for your inventory (one-use weapons and magic spells, keys, food to add time to the clock, etc).
You also match Wood and Stone tiles, which accumulate resources that are used back in your hub area in between dungeon runs. You build item shops which allow you to upgrade the effectiveness of each type of tile matches. You'll accumulate Gold and EXP with each dungeon run. Gold can be spent on your various tiered equpiment upgrades, and EXP can be spent on a variety of one-off permanent bonuses (like decreasing the cost of weapon upgrades, or granting bonus time for long combos).
You'll also be given up to three objectives to try to complete at the start of each run. These range from "match [X number] of Stone tiles over the course of your run" to "defeat an enemy by only using Items"
"Beating" the game requires getting a cumulative 10,000,000 points across all your runs, though you can keep playing after that.
I've played through the game before, and I'm on my second playthrough now that some new content has been added. It's a nice way to kill a few minutes before I go to work, or a few hours when I get home.

I'm not going to be too detailed here. Not yet anyway, as I still want to finish the game.
So let me just start by saying that I love this game, and nearly everything about it. Right from the start I was grabbed by it, not to say I'm a hard mark(I'm probably not) but to say that there is so much that I find captivating about it. The music is the first thing you get to experience and it is anything but lackluster, the puzzles made me stop and think(again, probably not that hard) and the world is beautiful.
I wanted to mention this last because I think it is the most important aspect of this game; the spellcrafting. The spellcrafting is an extraordinary system imo as it allows you to tailor make spells for any situation and encourages exactly that through it's combat and puzzles. It has so much potential as a mechanic and I've ALWAYS played mages before other classes in games for their flashy magic. Let me just say that this did not at all disappoint me.
Now for fairness sake I will say there are a few parts that fell a bit short; the story isn't 100% engaging(to where I am in the game), there isn't any (real) voice acting throughout the game(so for the most part I just did it myself XD), the characters aren't all too memorable, the enemies are a fair bit too predictable.
This kind of gameplay makes me want to love everything about the game but I can't currently say I do, however these are small things in an indie like this and I would LOVE to see an expansion on this solid effort and beautiful piece of art.
Just to end this off I would like to put a more in depth review of the things I loved and didn't but I'll leave that till the end. Either way, for anyone that loves to be creative, watch things blow up, or is just a fan of throwing fire; this game is worth your time.

Great game. Storyline is relatively cliche but fun, while adding in a few elements I thought were reasonably unique. While there is quite a bit of backtracking, the gameplay is solid and some of the puzzles will leave you scratching your head for a few minutes trying to figure out which spells you need to design to optimally complete them. You can suboptimally complete them as well, but it will be more difficult and/or take several attempts. So far it hasn't given me any trouble.
The real strength of this game is the spellcrafting system though. You start out with some basic spells which are fairly generic, and your first few runes start giving you very mundane things. ("Woo, firebolt. Oh, oh wait now it's *homing* firebolt.") Yet, after you get a bit through the game you start being able to combine and chain spells and add different modifiers and contigent triggers that your spells start getting very complex and incredibly fun to experiment with. This really makes the game unique, and aside from Magicka (which still didn't really have fully customizable spells), I can't think of anything that approaches it in that regard.
8.5/10, Short and rough in places, but with unique mechanics. Very enjoyable.

This is a really, really good game. The art style is fantastic, resembling the prettiest SNES game you never played, and the soundtrack by Danny B (of the Binding of Isaac fame) is incredible - as it needs to be, since music is the core of the game. Everything you do in the game, you can only do on the beat: moving, attacking, etc. It might sound like a strange concept, but it's the foundation for an incredibly solid game design.
As a roguelike-like with persistant elements (similar to Rogue Legacy), you start each game in the lobby, where you can spend diamonds to unlock new items or bonuses, and choose which game mode you want to play. Presently, there are four game zones (each consisting of 3 levels and a boss fight), a local co-op mode, a daily challenge similar to Spelunky, and several different options for difficulty modifications, including a hardcore mode, or a "dance pad."
Yep, you heard that right - you can buy and hook up your own DDR style dance mat for this game. A controller or the keyboard works just fine too, though, with four keys (up, down, left, right) being all you need to control the game. Apart from the beat, the gameplay will be familiar to anyone who has played a roguelike dungeon crawler: delve, loot, destroy.
I honestly wasn't expecting to enjoy the game as much as I did, but I have to say - it's incredible. Pick it up if you've ever enjoyed the roguelike genre, and don't worry too much about the "Early Access" state, or the curious core mechanic - once you get used to it, you'll love this game. Bought the game way back when the game was originally announced, and I'm finding that I just dont enjoy the game compared to OMD and OMD2.
Because the team decided to make it a 'free to play' game a lot of the systems that I enjoyed playing with in the originals have been replaced by a un-rewarding grindfest. Even though they're supposedly fixing the drop system, you can't experiment with different builds or traps to see what you like; and even if you have the resources a LOT of the good traps/equipment/etc is random drop from chests only.
I can see a lot of potential in the core mechanics, it's just buried so far underneath the systems designed to 'encourage' players to invest money in the market that it just ruins the game for me.
I bought the founders pack way back, way back when the game was announced and I completely regret it now. The founder's deal gave a bunch of unique skins and offered more gold than the current packs for a lower price. Even with the better deal the game isn't worth it, wish I could get a refund based on the current game.

*** Another Revised Review ***
So, good ol' SPINTIRES.
It has had a lot of up's and downs. Mostly circling around the Dev and the Pub's ' misunderstanding, arguements, much spread tales of hate '.. choose one.
It also suffered the ' time bomb ' for which the community found an answer, then an official fix came later.
NOW if you remove the drama from the outside, and just take the game itself... its a must have for mud fans, fans of tough real life based work in a place that many of us have experienced...
The game is very realistic in attempting to navigate the mud / water hazards. If you ever experienced time in Europe back in the cold war days, these fields and roads ( or what pass for roads ) are sure to bring bitter memories of cold, wet, stuck in the mud nights and days of places like Hohenfeld, Graf, Reforger moments...  You will suffer the same fate of smaller wheeled vehicles trying to navigate along tracks torn up time and time again by heavier vehicles.. you will be stuck.. you will see and hear the mud sucking you deeper in..
But its fun. Especially since unlike the real life days.. you dont have to get out and sink in the mud or water.. ah.. love the sim for the lack of misery from those days!!  HINT: If you do remember tricks from the days of following a line of tanks and APC's in a battered 2 1/2 ton you will do well..
Reasons to play:
Its fun.
Its a great candy for the eye. Watch the mud fly, stick to your truck.. build up on the tires.. knock / fall off on hard tops and run it through water to clean up a bit.
If you ever thought mudding would be fun.
Mods. Mods are amazing. ( STEAM does have a workshop )
Never had a problem tech wise out of it. I missed the actual time bomb myself, I was involved in another game at the time. But no problems before or after that.
Reasons to not play:
The drama. One way or another, if you follow the updates or post of others.. you will hear see about the drama. Everyone has some opinion. But I dont advise to buy or not based on that.
If you cannot imagine being stuck in the mud.. or a load overturned on the side of a mud track and trying to figure out how to recover the load, the wrecked truck and still deliver the logs as amusing..
If you have PTSD related to those frozen nights in Europe when the mud would freeze so hard you had to have an M88 recover you..
** Its a great way to kill time. **
SP and Co Op available.

I used to have this game on disc, I'm so glad I was able to pick it up again, all of these years later. This game is really the meaning of "Traditional RTS", set in the Warhammer 40k Universe. Dark Crusade includes 7 Factions to play as, including the T'au Empire and the Necrons of Kronus. The campaign has been changed entirely, into a risk type of game. The objective is to conquer the map as your selected race. To make booting another race off of the map a bit more exciting, each army (including your own) has a "Stronghold". This is basically the main base of the army, you could even consider it as a boss battle. Now I will move onto a more brief list.
Pros:
- 7 Armies, each can be played in the Campaign. Replayability can last a while.
- Balancing is fairly good, some things might still be considered a bit "OP".
- The pinnacle of the DoW Franchise.
- Multiplayer has still been kept online to this date, about 10 years later!
- Each Army has a different playstyle, rather than just using the same tactic for every army.
- Quite a large learning curve if you are new to the franchise.
- In my opinion, this is still better than it's successor, Dawn of War 2.
- Variety of unique units for each faction.
Cons:
- Multiplayer community is quite small here, though it is still alive.
- This game isn't really a "Pick up and be good" game.
- Some units do have slight pathfinding issues in some cases, like the Necron Monolith.
- There isn't really a playable story. Though there is a background story to the campaign, it's not like Winter Assault or Dawn of War.
Even though it isn't perfect, I would reccommend picking this up any day. The latest Dawn of War 1 game is Soulstorm, however Soulstorm has it's fair share of dis-advantages. I'm just gonna put it this way; Dark Crusade for the Singleplayer and vanilla game, Soulstorm for the mods.

10,000,000 is a fun little casual match three type puzzle game with an RPG theme. In the main part of the screen you have are trying to match 3 or more of a symbol, getting cascades and so on for bonuses. The key twist is that your character needs specific types of matches at certain times - match keys to get through doors or open chests, match swords or staves when you are fighting a monster, and avoid spoiling/using such matches in between while the character is just running along. Meanwhile the other item types you can match give you resources to build up your base, or get bonus items.
You also have special subquests to do while running each dungeon, like getting a 5 match, or using only items to kill a monster, etc. It all adds up to give a bit of a strategic element to the basic match three gameplay, and a bit of a fun metagame building up your characters skills and equipments to get more powerful, fighting more dangerous monsters, and eventually achieve the titular 10,000,000 points to win your freedom.

This is a really, really good game. The art style is fantastic, resembling the prettiest SNES game you never played, and the soundtrack by Danny B (of the Binding of Isaac fame) is incredible - as it needs to be, since music is the core of the game. Everything you do in the game, you can only do on the beat: moving, attacking, etc. It might sound like a strange concept, but it's the foundation for an incredibly solid game design.
As a roguelike-like with persistant elements (similar to Rogue Legacy), you start each game in the lobby, where you can spend diamonds to unlock new items or bonuses, and choose which game mode you want to play. Presently, there are four game zones (each consisting of 3 levels and a boss fight), a local co-op mode, a daily challenge similar to Spelunky, and several different options for difficulty modifications, including a hardcore mode, or a "dance pad."
Yep, you heard that right - you can buy and hook up your own DDR style dance mat for this game. A controller or the keyboard works just fine too, though, with four keys (up, down, left, right) being all you need to control the game. Apart from the beat, the gameplay will be familiar to anyone who has played a roguelike dungeon crawler: delve, loot, destroy.
I honestly wasn't expecting to enjoy the game as much as I did, but I have to say - it's incredible. Pick it up if you've ever enjoyed the roguelike genre, and don't worry too much about the "Early Access" state, or the curious core mechanic - once you get used to it, you'll love this game. This game makes me feel conflicted.
The music is enjoyable, and very fitting. It is, however, forgettable. Good nonetheless.
The story is really boring and typical. Evil king, mages are persecuted, go save the world or something. The game ends on a needless cliffhanger, even though the game already feels a bit short on story content.
Visually, the game is quite nice. It has the typical cel-shaded Unity game look without looking lazy or bad. It actually is kinda nice. The shadows look kind of bad in some spots, but the game look really good in general.
The real point of the game, however, is to craft and cast spells. And this is the part of the game that makes me feel conflicted. There is a fair amount you can do with the spellcrafting system, and that is the part that I love. But the part that I don't like is that there is no real reason to actually come up with creative spells. In a weird way, the game falls flat in terms of both combat and puzzles, but it succeeds in the spellcasting system itself.
So the combat fails for one main reason. The only thing that really matters in combat, besides blocking and dodging, is dealing tons of damage, and there isn't a lot of creative ways to do that. Sure, you can create a rotating image of yourself that shoots out homing projectiles, but why do that when you can create projectiles that shoot out projectiles that shoot out projectiles and so on? Pretty much every combat encounter in the game can be solved by creating these recursive spells that just annihilate everything until you run out of mana. Even the last boss was a joke, with every phase of the fight ending with a single press of the right mouse button. But in a way, the combat was kind of enjoyable. There was something fun about watching my spells destroy everything in the room and lagging out my game. Just seeing how much mayhem I could cause with a single spell was fun in a way. But it leaves me wishing that the spellcasting system was a bit better tuned and that the game found a better way to actually challenge my spellcrafting abilites.
Puzzles kind of have the same problem. Pretty much every puzzle at first was solved by me dashing around and shooting projectiles in quick succession with some exceptions like logic puzzles involving creating statues of yourself and putting them on buttons. But the story puzzles never really challenged me in any meaningful way. I also went out to find all of the spell components to see if those puzzles were any better, but they were solved in mostly the same way, and the teleport component further trivializes the puzzles. In a way, it was kind of fun to solve the puzzles in an unintended way when the game tells me that I may not have the proper components to do so, but I really wish that they would make their puzzles actually require me to be creative.
And that is the main issue I have with the game, and the reason why I can only recommend this game if you are really in love with the idea of creating spells. There is never really any reason to utilize all the different components. In my opinion, the game should have given you all of the elements and most of the components early, and then forced you to actually use these components in a creative way to actually progress through the game. But as is stands, you can beat the game without most of the components (quite easily, in fact), you unlock the elements in the last stretch of the game, and you can kill all the enemies by just creating spells that continue to just create themselves. The game feels like it has done the job of fleshing out the underlying mechanics, but not done the job of actually giving you a reason to use them. So I had fun with this game, but I was left a bit unsatisfied.

So, good ol' SPINTIRES.
It has had a lot of up's and downs. Mostly circling around the Dev and the Pub's ' misunderstanding, arguements, much spread tales of hate '.. choose one.
It also suffered the ' time bomb ' for which the community found an answer, then an official fix came later.
NOW if you remove the drama from the outside, and just take the game itself... its a must have for mud fans, fans of tough real life based work in a place that many of us have experienced...
The game is very realistic in attempting to navigate the mud / water hazards. If you ever experienced time in Europe back in the cold war days, these fields and roads ( or what pass for roads ) are sure to bring bitter memories of cold, wet, stuck in the mud nights and days of places like Hohenfeld, Graf, Reforger moments...  You will suffer the same fate of smaller wheeled vehicles trying to navigate along tracks torn up time and time again by heavier vehicles.. you will be stuck.. you will see and hear the mud sucking you deeper in..
But its fun. Especially since unlike the real life days.. you dont have to get out and sink in the mud or water.. ah.. love the sim for the lack of misery from those days!!  HINT: If you do remember tricks from the days of following a line of tanks and APC's in a battered 2 1/2 ton you will do well..
Reasons to play:
Its fun.
Its a great candy for the eye. Watch the mud fly, stick to your truck.. build up on the tires.. knock / fall off on hard tops and run it through water to clean up a bit.
If you ever thought mudding would be fun.
Mods. Mods are amazing. ( STEAM does have a workshop )
Never had a problem tech wise out of it. I missed the actual time bomb myself, I was involved in another game at the time. But no problems before or after that.
Reasons to not play:
The drama. One way or another, if you follow the updates or post of others.. you will hear see about the drama. Everyone has some opinion. But I dont advise to buy or not based on that.
If you cannot imagine being stuck in the mud.. or a load overturned on the side of a mud track and trying to figure out how to recover the load, the wrecked truck and still deliver the logs as amusing..
If you have PTSD related to those frozen nights in Europe when the mud would freeze so hard you had to have an M88 recover you..
** Its a great way to kill time. **

I have an incredibly extensive and large Steam Network, and have 10+ years on my other account.
During this time its possible I have never reviewed another game.
I played many of the Orc's Must Die series, and we all know how plagued they were with limited multiplayed features, and limited creativity.
I am glad to see they have FINALLY satisfied my need for an RPG.
I will go over the basics for all those that care, and are interested in this game. And I will start with the bad things.
Limited charaters at this point. Its scary to buy any champion because they are probably going to be in the free rotation soon. Most characters already in game feel very basic, and without pizaz.
This game is a MID GRADE MMO. That means if you are looking for anything beyond mid level customization, skins, and basic item unlocks, you should stop.
Character Customization? Easily more extenisve than most MOBA's, especially the free ones, but mid level feeling in the end.
Graphics? Excellent for the Orc's trilogy, mid level detail overall. Regarless= great effects and look.
Sounds? Absolutely hilarious the things you hear and the theme songs they implemented. Mid grade quality and synthisizing.
I think your getting the point.
Now lets continue to the PROS:
This game is absolutely hilarious. I mean the song the guy hums when you load into que makes me lol every time. ANd its not just a chuckle, like i actually start reflexing from my belly.
Many people have stated P2W, and P2P but that is NOT TRUE AT ALLLLLLLLLL. The correct terminology they are looking for is PAY TO PROCEED. If you want to play with your Level 50+ friends first day then sure, drop 50 bucks in the shop, get a whole bunch of chest, and enjoy.
The default farm rate of all items ingame seems legit. I mean its literally fresh open beta (as of cinco de mayo) so I get the feeling the developers want you get ur fair share of items so the game expands.
If you play 1 game a day? Can you proceed? (1 win) Yeah about every weekend I would guess that  you would have enough points to unlock one new trap, champion, guardian or whatever you choose. That seems fair since your not even grinding.
The community is amazing. I have played 20 hours so far, so about 20 games and only ONE game was someone toxic. It was still hilarious because the other players kinda just banded together and played around in the corner of the map.
This game is not a high stress game. You lose very little games while farming xp (thats right BONUS xp) in the survival area and the item drop rate seems very fair if not generous. I havent ventured into the siege mode (5 man vs 5 man) but I assume you would maintain a 50% win ratio there.
Lastly the largest PRO in my opinion is the ability to build your own trap/guardian/potion deck, which is entirely based on your creatitivy and farming capability. Isn't that what an MOBA is about?
In Conclusion:
I tried to answer some basic and broad questions, but I would 100% recommend downloading and playing this game maybe once a day to giggle intently at the loading que tune, and plenty of other hilarious, action packed and creative moments.
I guarantee end game playability will leave you a little bit hungry for more "keys" (infinite survival map unlocks),  advanced trap/attack physics, customization, and diverse champions but remembering to enjoy the little things in life is what I believe Orc's Must Die is all about.
Afterall its only open beta and they are doing a great job so far. Most of the hunger will be solved by periodic released of new champions, maps, traps, etc etc.

First of all, I will open this by saying that I would recommend this game if it is on sale. I think the fact that many people have enjoyed it cannot be ignored, and you are perfectly entitled to enjoy and think positively of it. So why give it a negative review? I did enjoy this game and was glad I played it, but ultimately I could not feel positively about it for a number of reasons.
Overall, the style of gameplay is fun. If you can stomach the ultraviolence, it's really quite satisfying in a bloodthirsty sort of way. It's especially relieving to bludgeon that guard who's killed you 20 times to death with his own weapon. It forces you to think about how you are going to attack. The fact you can only take one hit offers a challenging mechanism where failure is not tolerated for a split second.
The look and feel is fits the era very well. I greatly enjoy top-down games like this one and I think in terms of gameplay it was a wise decision. The attention to detail however is questionable; it's fairly difficult to tell what many things actually are, and sometimes the art style can get in the way of gameplay (lose a knife amongst a pile of bodies and it's sometimes difficult to find it again). The spinning maps, whilst fitting in with the design, are sometimes very unpleasant and gave me motion sickness a few times - there is no option to turn them off. But this is just a small inconvenience. More annoying is how it's impossible to tell whether an object can be shot over or not (a fountain is inpenetratable, but a pile of boxes isn't).
The music is overall quite good. I was surprised by how hyped it is though. It sets the mood well but, after the same track has looped for the 100th time, it begins to do your head in. In the final levels the music is also distorted for what I presume is artistic effect but this fails; it simply turns out irritating. I found myself muting the music a lot. When I did this I could focus much better.
The difficulty curve is generally good at the start. As many point out, it's skilfully created so that you don't realise how far you are progressing until you go back and try an earlier level. This is something many games have tried and failed to implement. There are no hoops to jump through, no instructions left at various stages: only a few elements that get gradually introduced (such as dogs and guns). However, about half way through, this falls apart. The personal advancement you can get from the game levels out, and whilst some levels increase in difficulty as one would expect, others - completely out of place - are bizarrely quite easy. It leads to a very disjointed experience where you might spend half an hour or more on one level and five minutes on the next.
One of my troubles with the game is it cannot make up its mind as to what it wants to be. Is it a simple arcade fighting game? But the combat is too basic to really live up to the title, and the repetition is just too much. Is it a stealth game? I don't think the creators ever intended for it to be one, but if they did, they failed miserably - the AI is simply too crude.  Is it a puzzle game? Then it is irritatingly inconsistent. A puzzle relies on everything being near enough the same when you try it again - when the AI's behaviour seems to rely on a coin flip this does not measure up.
As far as I could decipher, enemies have three states: patrol, alert and attack. You have to be aware of how the AI works to beat a level. The problem here is that the AI is actually quite inconsistent. Often levels will require you to "bait" an enemy to get him to follow you to somewhere that's easy to dispose of him. In theory there is nothing wrong with this, but in practice it's pretty much anyone's guess whether the AI is going to take a few seconds to see you or do a split-second 180-degree spin and instakill you. The game relies on the mechanic that a gun will alert an enemy, but it's completely random as to who will be alerted. Sometimes, it's enemy across the map. Other times, the enemy in the room next door will completely ignore it. When you actually want the AI to come to you and be alerted, this is frustrating. The randomisation is cheap, and means that I rarely found any gratification in victory - only the feeling that the it had gone my way for once.
I found a number of bugs that frustrated me and only compounded my issues. Firstly, the game crashes a lot, at least on my computer. I got an average of about one crash every hour or so. Most of these crashes were to do with doors somehow, and it's no surprise, since doors themselves are a mess. It's easy to exploit the AI by standing in the door and letting it glitch out and swing to and fro; this will slow them down for some reason and make it easier to take them on. Sometimes a door will travel right through an enemy instead of knocking him down, especially if there are multiple ones around. Combat bugs are relatively common; I enjoyed performing a "hug of death" where you stand right in front of an armed enemy. For whatever reason, they will fire but cannot hit you, so you simply wait for them to deplete their ammo. It's an amusing but basic issue that should have been fixed. Dogs will often ending up circling around underneath you for some reason (making them impossible to attack) until they decide to kill you. The way bullets interact with walls is strange and often to kill an enemy coming around a corner you have to make sure your gun is pointed at a wide angle rather than perpendicular, otherwise your bullets will not hit. Hitboxes are sketchy too...
I did finish the game, if only to be able to sufficiently review it, and there were many times when I really had to force myself to continue. There comes a point where you will have attempted a level many, many times and failed. It's 2am, the music is going around and around, you're slumped in your chair and you think to yourself... "why am I actually playing this? What is my motivation to continue?"
The bonuses at the end of the level are something. If you get a high enough score you might get a weapon and/or a mask. Both of these have limited use. The masks are a clever mechanic that add perks - changing how you play. They're fairly interesting but I think the masks were too specific to ever make a massive difference. The weapons are virtually useless; you hardly ever actually get them. Regardless, it's very dispriting to spend an hour finishing a level only to get a glass bottle as a reward.
The second motivator is the story line. The story is... limited. In many games I have been motivated to continue an especially difficult level by wanting to continue the story line. In Hotline Miami, I can't say that any motivation existed. Though the ending is mildly interesting, it's really not fitting for how much time is spent on it, and a fairly big insult.
The only motivator I can think of after that is personal challenge and the score. These are fine, and will be different for everyone, but it's a sign of a half-baked game if these are the only
motivating factor.
Ultimately, my biggest problem with Hotline Miami was boredom. The level design is sameish. The enemies are all the same. The difference between weapons is minimal. The fact you have to play the same level over and over again gets old, quickly. The story line is, up until the end, mostly unengaging. The boss fights are anticlimactic.
You can say that the repetition and difficulty is all part of the fun. You can apply the same principle to nailing jelly to the ceiling. It's a difficult task where you fail a lot of the times, come frustratingly close often, and maybe at one point succeed. That does not mean you feel good about the thankless task of having nailed jelly to the ceiling. You simply feel that you have wasted your time.

TLDR; If you like coop tower defence games with a bit of action, this is game your game. It's like Orcs Must Die (OMD) 1 and 2, only online. the PvP game can be skipped if you like the PvE gameplay from OMD 1 and 2. I recommend the game. The game has a few issues with are mainly the grinding which can be boring.
For those who haven’t played OMD 1 and 2 here’s a short description. It’s an action packed tower defence game where you build traps to defend against orcs. The gameplay is seen in third person where you control a hero. During the game you can shoot and use abilities. The game consists of two game types. PvP that’s kinda plays like a moba (only with OMD twist). In the PvP you build traps and lead armies to the enemies rift. There’s also a PvE coop part where you defend against a certain amount (or after level 80 endless) of waves. Each wave is more difficult than the other. You have to stop getting the orcs to your rift. Your rift only has a certain amount of health.
Why not just give the game a try? It's free! While the game has micro transaction it can be completely forgetting. Only things you have to pay for are the skins. The rest you can farm.
Often the Orcs are heroes will shout some stuff which are pretty funny one-liners. The orcs also sometimes die in the most funny ways. For example eye pop out when walking past fire.
While the graphics aren't something that will make your PC cry and ooze high graphic quality, the graphics look good enough. Coming from OMD 1 and 2 this is a step-up. The graphics look cartoony and fit with the tone of the game. The game isn't even high demanding in terms of hardware requirements.
Almost every week we get a patch that fixes stuff. Almost every month we get new content.
As of writing I played 46 hours so far and I'm level 55. Levelling up happens by levelling your heroes. Each level of your hero gets added up to your account. So if you have played with two heroes that are level 2, you are level 4. If you own a hero you get more XP which levels you up faster. With each level you get, you get rewards in terms of unlocks and loot.
I load a game within 20-30 seconds I would say. In-game you need to wait for other players though.
Each hero brings their own power, traps and gamestyle. There are even heroes that excel at solo-damage, trap building, magic, tanking, etc. There's a hero for each type of player. Each hero can be build each match up to 6 talents maxing at level 12 where you pick your last talent. Each week a new rotation is done to play a hero for free (but get less XP if you don't own the hero).
Each map brings it's own atmosphere, challenges and recommended traps. No map feels the same in terms of tactics. Some maps even give fun things like one map has swimming sharks. Once an orc dies the shark eat the orcs. Over time you revisit a map only this time the challenge goes up by having bigger, badder and more waves.
The traps are the main thing about this game. It's fun to place traps and make various combinations. Just like OMD 1 and 2 you can place traps on ceilings, walls and ground. Natural Selection 2 is a sci-fi, team based, first-person-shooter, in which one member of the team takes on the role of a birds-eye-view “Commander” to build structures, research upgrades, and issue orders based on reconnaissance.
This is a fascinating game design concept and I commend Unknown Worlds for their creativity and artistic talent.  If this was a college design course, they would receive the highest marks, but as a piece of commercial entertainment this game fails miserably because, overall, it is simply not fun.
this game looks great.  The world that they have created here is beautifully realized, interesting to look at and to explore.  The amount of detail and thought that has gone into the ‘lore’ across each map environment and the faction design choices is immense.  Every inch of this game (human/alien models, environment, effects) has high production values.
the RTS/FPS combination is intriguing and the buildings and weapons do much to support this interesting hybrid; remaining true to well-worn game concepts while adding their own interesting spin.  Well executed.
when you first start, you are branded a "rookie" for a certain amount of play time.  Most servers are segregated in some way, either "no rookies" allowed, or "only rookies" allowed.  After your rookie time expires you are kicked out into the main server base.  But since rookies only play with other rookies, you won't know any of the advanced strategies or techniques required to have fun in these servers.  This leads to you getting utterly destroyed by your enemies, and then blamed by your team mates for being the weak link and screamed at/harassed over voice.  Since the games are so fast-paced, there is almost no room for error and therefore no time to learn/teach on these servers.
For "intermediate" players the game is effectively over at this point - it's literally unplayable and their money is lost: the main server base holds no fun, they aren't allowed to join rookie servers, and there is no native functionality to play against bots (you can't start a bot server, you might be able to find one and hope that people don't join or kick you out).
because players are segregated, they never have to learn to live with one another.  Veterans don't learn patience to play with newer players, rookies don't learn appreciation for higher skill gameplay of the vets, and the intermediates are effectively homeless because they aren't welcome in either community.  This leads each group to harbor resentment toward the other two which EVEN FURTHUR decreases the number of servers that allow mixing, and makes the player interaction even worse than usual online.  This is compounded by the fact that the player base is only a few hundred strong anyway.
it's almost an afterthought compared to the first two points, but the mechanics of the game just don't work well.  The alien side has a huge learning curve and takes a ton of skill to play well, but experienced players are all but unstoppable as alien.  On the other side, while humans will win most battles because they are straightforward to play, they are grossly undermatched when fighting an alien player with really any level of skill.  It's as if the devs shot themselves in the foot, and then shot themselves in the other foot and called it even.
in any multiplayer game, it's not just about winning and losing, it's about playing the iconic "good game".  You want to meet a worthy opponent and you want to be challenged right up until the end.  In "good games" you still feel accomplished when you lose because you know that you played well and it was a fair fight.  You will literally almost never have this experience in NS2.
Because of the extensive balance issues (both in the game and the community) winning almost always feels hollow and random, and losing is protracted, painful, and hopeless.
Along the same note, there is no incentive to play as the "Commander" even though having a good commander is essential to winning.  The role is difficult, under-appreciated, and unrewarding.  As a commander you don't get score or unlockables based on your contribution, but you will bear almost all of the blame for any failings of your team.  This leads to a constant shortage of commanders because no one wants to open themselves up to ridicule and potentially get kicked for being bad.
In summation, NS2 is a very pretty, very interesting, waste of money.  You will only be able to enjoy this game for a short period of time before it becomes unplayable.  From reading their blog, the devs are aware of these issues and have tried extensively to fix them (in fact they believe they HAVE fixed them).  Because of this, they are moving on to other projects and will likely not be making any more changes to this game.  For this reason, more than any other, I do not reccomend this game; it is not fun, it is broken, and very soon, it will be dead.

DEFCON borrows some of its lore and most of its appearance from portions of the movie WarGames. The multi player scene is still active, and it is very easy to find open matches with all kinds of different settings. Personally, I prefer playing against the CPU, much like in the movie. The map is fairly accurate, depicting the geopolitical era of the Cold War. Implementing orders to your units can sometimes be confusing and inadequate, but with enough attempts, you become used to the interface, and will be able to do all of the game's strategical requirements. What is most valuable in DEFCON is the replay ability. Certainly, each match has an ending, but the game truly shines when you play it repeatedly; alone or online. Winning is not easy. Several things must go right, and occur at specific moments in order to be successful. Because of these timing issues, sometimes you will win or lose depending on how quickly or how slowly your units execute orders in conjunction with timers. Nuking cities and other strategic locations doesn't exactly feel like you are killing people. There isn't very much tension. It all just feels like you are clicking around on the map and delegating orders. The feeling that lives are actually being lost is not truly present. At the end of each match, you will be shown a small statistics screen with how much of the enemy population you have killed, how many of your population have been killed, and so on. Each match takes between 15 to 20 minutes to complete, and it often feels like each instance ends abruptly without much of a climax or excitement in the confrontations. The entire atmosphere is very cold and impersonal. Setting up a new single player match means you will have to go into the advanced settings every single time in order to change a few options to single player mode. The default (which can't be permanently altered) is set to multi player, broadcasting your match as public. This is quite annoying and should not have been programmed as such. I am certain that there are many DEFCON players that prefer single player mode and this preference should not be hindered by permanently set options from the developers. The longevity of DEFCON is dependent entirely on the player's interest in its short matches, be it single player or multi player. Besides your initial location on the match, it feels like every single match is played almost exactly the same, with very little occurring differently or alternatively. The strategies necessary to play this game are limited and basic, regardless of whether you win or lose. The only major change as you become better at the game is that you will begin winning, but this does not mean each match will be played differently, or go through a different turn of events. As repetitive as it is, there is a small amount of entertainment gained from playing DEFCON for more than three or so matches at a time. The gaming experience quickly becomes dull, repetitive, tiresome, and almost identical to every other match you play. DEFCON is best played in short bursts in order to preserve its replay ability. Seriously lacking in variety, this diversion is suited for fast breaks and brief encounters.

Not too sure what to write here so here's a recipe for Pancakes instead:
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it:
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

What makes a truly great game? Well, in my personal opinion, a great game isn't about showing off the best graphics or having mass appeal. A great game, to me anyway, is a true work of art and that's what I feel this particular one is.
The visuals and soundtrack are two of the things I find to be the most remarkable about Dust: An Elysian Tail. Gazing into the vistas and listening to the BGM almost made me feel like I was playing one of my old all time favorite games ever. Legend of Mana. I felt that every track complimented each scene well and was enjoyable to even just stop and listen to for a moment without being too distracting at the same time.
The movement and combat are fluid and easy to grasp. You rarely ever feel like the game is ever at fault for any mishaps. Combat is very fast paced and stylized like in Devil May Cry. It even has it's own little combo counter for those who like to show off their skills. And while your arsenal of attacks might feel a little limited, watching the protagonist soar back and forth across the screen in a whirlwind of blood and death never seems to get old. Level progression is also well balanced. I never felt like finding the newest upgrade for my equipment ever impacted the difficulty of the game too drastically or was ever essential for advancing in the story.
Speaking of, the story isn't too bad either. The dialogue between the protagonist and the inhabitants of Falana(the in-game world) is humorous and well written, yet there have also been a couple parts that jerked a tear out of me too. As a bonus, throughout the entire game, you'll find lots of little references and easter eggs from other games dotted out through each map, if you're a big gamer of course.  It's also refreshing to play a game that doesn't require you to make some kind of moral decision at every turn for once.
If there were anything at all I'd change about Dust, it would probably be the way the NPCs were animated. I just felt that the animations between the NPCS and protagonist clashed a little bit and while it's not a big detail, it certainly would have added some polish to an already amazing game.
So if you've got some scratch to spare and enjoy games that are more art and less mass appeal, this one is definitely worth picking up.

I was quite drawn to 10,000,000 because of the promise it showed in mixing RPG and puzzle elements. While the game delivered less depth than the concept seemed to allow for, I still got a very fast-paced, addictive, and satisfying puzzler. It was cumbersome using a mouse to play a game that was clearly designed with touch screens in mind, but the gameplay was enjoyable enough at its core to ease that pain most of the time. The music was catchy, and the variety of things to level up provided enough incentive to make it through most of the game. What I most appreciated was the fact that you're unlikely to brute force your way to the 10,000,000 point goal by simply grinding enough to level everything. Success is ultimately the result of strategy, speed, and good fortune, which was refreshing after the way so many other smartphone ports that have made it to this platform just hand victory to the player after a significant enough investment of time and virtual currency. It's unlikely that you'll want to revisit this one after beating it, but the asking price is very reasonable for a game of 10,000,000's overall quality.

Fallout Shelter is a dungeon master type simulation game set in the Fallout universe. It nails the visuals, theme, lore and feel of the Fallout games, fits into the universe. You play as the overseer of an underground fallout shelter managing the dwellers and trying to keep them alive.
The game opens up once you build the Overseer's office, because it lets you send dwellers on missions and fight enemies, explore and loot locations, that gives a needed variety to the game.
I have played it on my Android tablet and that actually fits the gameplay well. Still, controlling would have been better on a PC with a mouse. Very often happened that I only wanted to scroll the view, but I accidentally moved a dweller to another room. Annoying.
The game was designed for mobile devices, it is not for continuous playing, because it has crafting, training and traveling times that can be pretty long on higher levels. I had fun with it for a couple of weeks as a secondary game I would play when I had 10-15 minutes to do a mission or two.
The game is free-to-play with micro transactions, but it is well done, does not actually force you to buy anything. Of course the usual money grabbing tactics apply, like special pets, money and resource packs, speeding up training, crafting and traveling times by a special item, and so on. But everything can be looted in missions or crafted as well,
so you are not forced to buy it, I played without paying any real money.
The basic tutorial is OK, but some game mechanics are not explained at all.
If a dweller dies and is resurrected, he forgets his assignment, and needs to be assigned to his post again,
otherwise he will just aimlessly wonder around the Vault.
Crafting is nice and simple for normal and rare weapons and armor, but crafting legendary items takes a disproportionately long time (making a power armor with trained dwellers took 8 actual days!)
Combat is a bit too simplistic, you basically send your team of dwellers to a room and watch as they kill the enemies
while pumping your injured team members with health packs. More interesting combat would have been better, this makes the game feel repetitive after a while.
I experienced crashes and long loading times on my tablet, but it is not very powerful, so it could be just my hardware. On my PC there were no such issues.
The attributes of the dwellers are trained in specialized training rooms and not at all during normal work or missions. That is a weird design choice. This way it is possible to train super-humans that excel in everything, from fighting to water purification, but have never actually left the Vault or worked a minute.
Despite its faults, I had fun with it. If you like the Fallout setting, give it a try as a second-screen game!

I do not write too many reviews, but I decided to start doing so recently. If nothing else I hope the Developers appreciate the comments and suggestions.
About this game:
~Tells the story of a handful of surviving humans in space, and I do mean SURVIVING because it seems every couple of hours there is another devastating, ship destroying, squad crushing event taking place, usually involving these small zerg-like creatures that never stop advancing... even when I napalm their faces off... if they have faces that is.
~The gameplay is much like any other Squad-based Tactical RPG: Move, Attack, Repeat, but Trese Bros. have definitely achieved a unique feeling with elaborate growth choices for the squad members and a level of violence I personally did not expect from a game with such... simplistic artwork (I'm being nice here, while the artwork and animation are not NEARLY the worst I've seen, this game is no more beautiful than if your doodles in the margin of your science notes came to life and did battle...). The overall feel of the gameplay is how I imagine a well-done Starship Troopers TacRPG to play... absolutely nothing wrong with that, I think most fans of Starship Troopers would agree.
~There is also a high level of detail put into the individual advancement of squad members, which is in my opinion the entire reason this game has any replay value at all, as the story is, while deep, also very boring and repetitive. Don't get me wrong, it's well done... a little too well done in fact... like a charred black filet mignon. It drives it's points home a little too much and too often, and I find myself skipping many scenes even in my first run because I just can't handle the tedious narratives of characters they never gave me a chance to even care about. To sum up, it's great writing but terrible story telling.
To the Developers:
~Change nothing about your gameplay techniques and character advancement, but next time don't worry so much about trying to make me feel something for your characters, especially since the idea of these types of games is that all party members are very expendable and will meet their ends for just about no reason at all. And if you need some artistic assistance, I am in fact a semi-professional video game artist and animator (Full Sail Alum 2003) who prefers to work on small indie projects, hit me up! ;)
To all potential buyers of this game:
~Do it! This game is great honestly and well worth the asking price, and then some really. I'd pay as much as $15 for this game at it's current overall quality. I got it for the steal price of $5 and am feeling a little guilty for it... only a little though... If you are a fan Tactical RPGs you will appreciate nearly every aspect of this cheap little gem!
Thanks Trese Brothers,

Do you like guiding a squad of badasses in giant powered armor through a huge number of tactical scenarios? Purging xeno scum? Executing traitorous alien-worshippers? Smashing ancient killer robots? Then this is the game for you.
Graphics are good quality for what it is, a 2D top-down, turn-based tactical game. Story is told by text boxes up on top of the screen with portraits. Gameplay is pretty straightforward - move your guys, shoot or slash aliens. Buff up your guys with special abilities. Get in good position and set up to prevent aliens from hitting your guys - they're tough but not invulnerable. Also watch your heat level, who knew that running a power armor suit at full tilt while holding down the trigger on your flamethrower might heat you up?
Want BS microtransactions and constant nagging to connect to some online service or watch some ads for "premium currencty"? None of that here. Put your money down and you can play the whole game. Hell, they even threw in an extra mini-campaign for free after release that meshes in with the main game. Kind of sucks that I have to point it out explicitly, but that's the world we live in.
Technically, it's been spit-shined and polished over its 70+ updates. I didn't see a single bug.
Also, one of the few squad-based games which gets perma-death right, kind of like the original X-Com. You can lose squad after squad of dudes, and man, does it sting (I just about broke my keyboard in half when some piece of crap alien crawled out of a hole in the ground and killed my favorite flamethrower guy), but it doesn't prevent you from winning the game.

Step 5) Wait 2 - 12+ Hours
