Step 7) Build/upgrade rooms, upgrade dweller skills, Scrap the trash in your inventory
Step 8) Repeat step 1 - 8
If that sounds appealing and rewarding enough to suck you in then by all means it's a good game but that said it also makes me sad at how this sort of genre and gameplay could have had so much potential if they really put a little more effort into it. Hell add some more enemies/NCP's (Where are the Super Mutants at Bethesda!?) Add interesting quests with speech options and stories that actually equate to something and can we please have more locations than the Red Rocket, The Super Duper Mart and a randomly numbered Vault identical to all the others.
That said I still really like this game for some reason but this could have really been something S.P.E.C.I.A.L (See what I did there) and I guess I'm just a little disappointed with what it turned out to be. Natural Selection 2 is a sci-fi, team based, first-person-shooter, in which one member of the team takes on the role of a birds-eye-view “Commander” to build structures, research upgrades, and issue orders based on reconnaissance.
This is a fascinating game design concept and I commend Unknown Worlds for their creativity and artistic talent.  If this was a college design course, they would receive the highest marks, but as a piece of commercial entertainment this game fails miserably because, overall, it is simply not fun.
this game looks great.  The world that they have created here is beautifully realized, interesting to look at and to explore.  The amount of detail and thought that has gone into the ‘lore’ across each map environment and the faction design choices is immense.  Every inch of this game (human/alien models, environment, effects) has high production values.
the RTS/FPS combination is intriguing and the buildings and weapons do much to support this interesting hybrid; remaining true to well-worn game concepts while adding their own interesting spin.  Well executed.
when you first start, you are branded a "rookie" for a certain amount of play time.  Most servers are segregated in some way, either "no rookies" allowed, or "only rookies" allowed.  After your rookie time expires you are kicked out into the main server base.  But since rookies only play with other rookies, you won't know any of the advanced strategies or techniques required to have fun in these servers.  This leads to you getting utterly destroyed by your enemies, and then blamed by your team mates for being the weak link and screamed at/harassed over voice.  Since the games are so fast-paced, there is almost no room for error and therefore no time to learn/teach on these servers.
For "intermediate" players the game is effectively over at this point - it's literally unplayable and their money is lost: the main server base holds no fun, they aren't allowed to join rookie servers, and there is no native functionality to play against bots (you can't start a bot server, you might be able to find one and hope that people don't join or kick you out).
because players are segregated, they never have to learn to live with one another.  Veterans don't learn patience to play with newer players, rookies don't learn appreciation for higher skill gameplay of the vets, and the intermediates are effectively homeless because they aren't welcome in either community.  This leads each group to harbor resentment toward the other two which EVEN FURTHUR decreases the number of servers that allow mixing, and makes the player interaction even worse than usual online.  This is compounded by the fact that the player base is only a few hundred strong anyway.
it's almost an afterthought compared to the first two points, but the mechanics of the game just don't work well.  The alien side has a huge learning curve and takes a ton of skill to play well, but experienced players are all but unstoppable as alien.  On the other side, while humans will win most battles because they are straightforward to play, they are grossly undermatched when fighting an alien player with really any level of skill.  It's as if the devs shot themselves in the foot, and then shot themselves in the other foot and called it even.
in any multiplayer game, it's not just about winning and losing, it's about playing the iconic "good game".  You want to meet a worthy opponent and you want to be challenged right up until the end.  In "good games" you still feel accomplished when you lose because you know that you played well and it was a fair fight.  You will literally almost never have this experience in NS2.
Because of the extensive balance issues (both in the game and the community) winning almost always feels hollow and random, and losing is protracted, painful, and hopeless.
Along the same note, there is no incentive to play as the "Commander" even though having a good commander is essential to winning.  The role is difficult, under-appreciated, and unrewarding.  As a commander you don't get score or unlockables based on your contribution, but you will bear almost all of the blame for any failings of your team.  This leads to a constant shortage of commanders because no one wants to open themselves up to ridicule and potentially get kicked for being bad.
In summation, NS2 is a very pretty, very interesting, waste of money.  You will only be able to enjoy this game for a short period of time before it becomes unplayable.  From reading their blog, the devs are aware of these issues and have tried extensively to fix them (in fact they believe they HAVE fixed them).  Because of this, they are moving on to other projects and will likely not be making any more changes to this game.  For this reason, more than any other, I do not reccomend this game; it is not fun, it is broken, and very soon, it will be dead.

Here's a zen koan for you: When is a hidden object game not a hidden object game? When it has no hidden object scenes, obviously. Minus those the game should become a point-and-click adventure, and yet there's something quintessentially HOGgy about what you're left with. Namariel Legends is just that, a hidden object game in design, scope, and style, just without the scenes that would qualify it as such. And the adventure you're left with is just as charming, if a little simplistic and illogical at times.
The kingdom of Namariel was humming along just fine until the Iron Lord showed up with his legions of scrappy robots, blasting the castle into submission and dethroning its king. The only child of the royal family gets rather hilariously chucked out a window and saved by a passing dirigible, and then the game fast-forwards about 15 years to your Edward-Norton-looking uncle recounting the story to you, who DEFINITELY isn't the lost kid or anything. A chance encounter with the Iron Lord's tinpot soldiers starts you on a journey to save the whole kingdom from his cold, unfeeling grip.
Mind you, this is going to play out with all the jank and circumstance of a hidden object game. You'll wander off to collect crystals and engineer a pulley system to get a bag out of a tree, and come back to your uncle being dragged away by robots. At one point, a big bad will blow up his own airship just to get rid of you. And you'll spend like an hour doing chores to eventually take down a giant Ferngully-style deforesting machine, only for the grease monkey child pilot to join up with you just because. Things will happen because they have to happen that way, and you'll go along with it because most of the game is just mindless clicking anyway.
Every scene of Namariel Legends is from first-person, looking out over some expanse of cave or workshop or forest. They all have items laying about to nab and use in other nearby areas to get yet more items or, on rare occasions, help people out with some problem like being hungry or stung by bees. Parts of the scenes can be zoomed in on for closer looks, and your pointer icon helpfully changes to indicate whenever you can pick up or focus on something. The puzzles involving these items and environments are extremely simple and only require you to use single items to progress; there's no combining or interacting with items beyond that.
This makes for an extremely thin puzzle aspect to the game, which doesn't pair well with the extremely thin story and virtually non-existent NPC interaction. There are some additional gimmicks like a mindscope that lets you read thoughts, necessary for a few puzzles involving animals, and a flying robot helper who you'll need to knock down ladders and shake loose fruits every few screens. Even with these though, there's not much more going on than just having to remember to use them. That just leaves the few actual puzzles, which at least tend to be more creative than the usual ones you get in hidden object games. There's an interesting keycard puzzle that requires moving links of a chain, recasting broken keys from start to finish, and some mazes with tricks to getting around them (though a few of these are a little longer than they should be).
You'll be doing all of this in a fairly well-realized steampunk world that doesn't go bonkers with gears on top hats or anything like that. The scenes are clear and detailed, and you'll run into some creative machines and creatures as you roam the fanciful lands on the way to the embattled castle. This is hardly a groundbreaking or even challenging title, but it's not trying to be, either. Hidden object games exist to pass the time between more substantial activities, and taking the hidden object scenes out of one just makes it an equally casual point-and-click adventure. If you're looking for something with plenty of clicking through simple scene and puzzles, this will definitely get the job done.

First things first I do reccomend this game, albeit a 20€ price tag for 7 hours of gameplay is a bit anemic. The 7 hours of gameplay are of course assuming you go trough the game reasonably quickly and don't loose a lot of sleep on style points.
The Bad:
The game is just a tiny bit buggy, nothing gamebreaking for the most part but every now and then you will be unable to make a kill or a jump where you feel like you should've had that but the game just didn't want you to succeed.
It is not always immideatly apparent which surfaces you can teleport on and which ones you can't and this can sometimes be annoying when planing out your route.
Whilst the learning curve is far from broken the increase in diffilculty seems a bit weird at times, like it's more tailored to show how the enemy responds to you becoming an ever greater threat, rather than to the skill of the player increasing. Many areas are so dark, and darkness such reliable of an ally, that you barely need to be careful to avoid being spotted. The potential of having an ally by your side to do double takedowns with, or just kunais, which are quick, extremly far ranging kills make the game feel a tad overforgiving at times.
Whilst I don't want to spoil anything everything seems to be building up for a big twist the entire way through, with hints being dropped more frequently than soap in a prison shower, which makes for an eye rolling "oh no, who couldve seen THIS coming" moment at the end.
The good.
Whilst certainly not having AAA polish, the visuals of the game are georgeous, everything just looks REALLY cool, the animations are smooth and really help support your feeling of the "ultimate ninja assasin"
Aragami follows the old school style of tutorials, meaning that when it introduces new types of enemies and hazards, rather than hitting you over the head with a wall of text it let's you observe the danger from a safe distance and generally does enough of a job signalling what you want to avoid that you won't have a lot of "oh that kills you!" moments.
It's an awesome game to play with a friend or your SO though I'm not sure how good the random online matches are. Failure of one doesn't automatically mean failure for the other and if one player dies and the other goes on, the dead one will respawn at the next checkpoint. There are plenty of opportunities for double takedowns, which look and feel REALLY cool and having someone to cover your back is great. Literally my only complaint here is that I'd love some form of 3d markers. Most of the levels don't really lend themselves to giving callouts by position. Here I should note that it's a great and important touch that most of the enemies wear differently coloured outfits, making it a bit easier to call who takes who.
The core gameplay is very fun, though as the game progresses it seems to struggle to keep things interesting.
If you want a fun thing to do with someone together for a weekend or a couple of sessions here or there then this might be a game for you. If you're however looking for a stealth game that you can really dig your teeth into like the hitman series you might just be wasting money.

Aragami seems to be an attempt to translate Mark of the Ninja into a 3D title, with the addition of cooperative play.  On many levels, I'd say it succeeds. It is great fun to walk into an area, use an ability to locate enemies and see their line of sight, and systematically begin dismantling them. Some of the abilities acquired by the ninja are very powerful, such as a brief invisibility skill and your thrown darts. However, uses of these abilities are limited, and may only be replenished by performing a stealth takedown that makes your character a bit more vulnerable than usual, and shrines that are spread across the levels. This creates a nice loop of taking out an inconveniently-placed enemy with an ability, then using the special takedown on an enemy that is easier to deal with to replenish. It's quite satisfying.
The only issues I had with the title were:
1) For both myself and my partner, the game always crashed on shutdown. This didn't hinder our play, but was a bit irritating.
2) Enemies sometimes get stuck in place, glitched into a rock, etc.
3) We were unable to find a use for some of the abilities - things like the shadow wave or decoy.
4) The game would benefit greatly from a map that the player might access. Some of the areas appear very similar and you can wander into a bad situation.
Despite all this, I don't regret the time I spent with the game. If you have a buddy who enjoys stealth titles, give this one a go! Though I wouldn't put it on par with something like Splinter Cell: Conviction (in terms of co-op stealth), it's a quality game.

Many people complain about the crafting system, and I will agree it's a pain point for this game. To get to a new trap or hero or piece of gear you really need to get a huge amount of games done. But the thing that really gets people is that the crafting mats are completely random, so it could take you anywhere from 30-100 games to get to a certain item.
This is largely frustrating because I feel like of you ignore that glaring problem the game is relatively fun, free-to-play and an okay succesor to the OMD franchise. I've had a good few laughs at the character dialogue, some great moments with trap combos and some very satifying wins with their PvP. It's almost enough to make up for the fact that past your first dozen or so hours of play you won't get anything worthwhile to add to your arsenal for a painfully long time.
But this isn't what made me stop playing. What made me stop playing was the game's level difference filter. To explain, if you group up with a friend (in PvE) who is 10-15 levels higher or lower than you you cannot que in the matchmaker and it'll just be the two of you. The level scales with number of players so it's not like the level is impossible. But what this does is that it prevents me (the higher one of my friend group) from doing anything without then making it harder for my friends to catch up. I was literally punished for playing the game if I wanted to play with friends.
Combine this with the painful crafting system, several underpowered traps, slow hero balance and small hero roster my faith in Robot's capability to refine this game into a worthwhile experience (for the amount of time they're trying to squeeze out of you) has been eroded greatly.

Aragamis are shadow ninjas who can manipulate the shadows in their favor. Sounds good? But in reallity it is not. Aragamis gain shadow power in shadows and lose this in lighted areas. They need this power to fuel their basic abilities, which consists of shadow painting and teleport.
With teleport you can only move to shadows and have very limited range. With shadow painting you can create shadows, this also have limited range and also requires shadow power and the power will not refill in these created shadows.
For the reason you only gain shadow power in shadows, many times you will run out of it as you try to progress the game, these times you will search for bits of shadows to try to refill yourself and move forward. If you didn't get enough you will use it up for shadow painting but you will not have enough for teleport. This makes the game very frustrating.
Other than to gain shadow power, the shadows have no purpose. The guards will see you depending on how far you are from them and shadows not change this fact at all.
If we are talking about guards, there are 2 types of it, but in reality there's only 1. We have a guard with a lightsaber that can shoot lightbeams and an archer who basically do the same thing only from a little higher. If the guards see you, or a dead body they will go alert, and somehow they will know your exact location. When this happens 5-6 guards will try to kill you and you have nearly no chance to deal with them cause you have only 1 life and as you try to kill one, the others will kill you during the animation and you can't do anything while you kill, to evade it.
The game is terribly repetative. All you do in every level is get near your objective, shut down the light barrier get the quest item and then exit. You have to do this numerous times under a misson, and in every mission.
The game has 3 difficulties, easy normal and hard.
Easy is not even worth mentioning, you don't need to be affraid, you can run through the map. You can easily run forward to guards to kill them. While you are running the guard may humbly ask you to leave, but thats all.
On the other hand, hard is really unfair. The guards will notice you as you try to sneak up on them, block your attempt to kill, then cut you with a backhand slash.
I didn't play on normal so I cant say anyting about it. Other than the guards the difficulty will not change anything.
In the game you need to collect scrolls to get access to the skills. These scrolls are usually so well hidden you have no chance to find them, unless you unlock the ability to see them, which should be a basic ability. (You need to find 5 scrolls to unlock it)
There are 3 skill trees Aragami tree, Defensive tree and  Aggressive tree. You can unlock every skill, there is no specializing.
Aragami tree has basic skills like hiding dead bodies or see the scrolls. Other than this 2 the abilities in this tree are worthless. There's the shadow killing skill which could be usefull if you wouldn't have to hold down the button as you try to use it. You can only start holding it down, if you're near enough to kill, and you need to stay close to the target or you will fail. In hard difficulty, most of the times while you try to use this ability, the guards will notice and kill you.
Defensive and Agressive skills have only 2 charges and you have to refill these at shrines (Or with shadow killing)
In defensive tree there's invisibility, decoy and the ability to see enemies through walls. Invisibility might be useful, and seeing enemies is a must have, but you wouldn't want to use decoy just to alert the guards.
The aggressive the has the kunai, blind and opening black holes. Kunai is good obviously, but the other 2 is really hard to use.
Even though its possible to play coop, the game do not support it. Basically you play a single player game together with your friend. First when one of you die the other one have to as well, you can't revive him. He will revive if you finish the current objective but that defeats the purpose of playing together.
There is really no reason to play together, there are no situation you can't solve alone, honestly probably you will not play with your friend, but both of you will go on your own way.
I played this game in coop so maybe they are not present in the singleplayer, but there are terrible bugs in this game. Both of us died, restarted from checkpoint, and the guards instantly alerted because of our previous missplay. An another time both of us died, revived then died again. Sometimes the guards go on alert for no reason. And finally its not really a bug, but you cant cross water. You will die even if the water so shallow, its not even reaches your knees.
I don't recommend this game at its full price (20 euro), maybe for 5-7 euro. As for coop gameplay, honestly I don't recommend it.

Artistically, the game is simply gorgeous. The animation in character movement and even fighting animations is very fluid, and it's clear a lot of love was put into making Aragami candy for the eyes. The feudal Japan scenery is nothing less than stunning, and I could honestly play this game over and over just to look at everything and take in all the details.
Gameplay-wise, it's highly enjoyable. Controls are a tad bit different from what I usually see, but it's quick and easy to get used to. The mechanics, both unlockable ones and starting ones, are uniquely creative, adding more ways to get through each map, and more styles you can play. Plus, it's totally badass being able to destroy your enemies by summoning a death dragon from the shadows to swallow them whole.
!!! SPOILERS BELOW !!!
As for the story, I must applaud the writers. They kept us in the dark the entire time, gradually uncovering the secrets and background to Aragami and Yamiko both. We were lead to believe one thing, then another, which greatened the impact of the plot twists revealed at the end. Very well done. Although with the reveal of Aragami actually being Ryo from the Kaiho, and Yamiko and her people being evil, I didn't feel the same sorrow and grief that Aragami did, knowing we'd been tricked into killing our own people. The reveal was so sudden, we went the entire game believing that these people were evil, even had lines from guards depicting them as cruel. There could have been more of an emotional impact from this reveal if Aragami and Yamiko had both escaped their encounter, and the game continued build on our understanding of what the Kaiho truly were, seen their humanity, and gotten to know Sora so we(the players) could form an emotional attachment, then the ending of Aragami and Yamiko killing one another would have been much more heart-breaking. Along with the knowledge of how many Kaiho we'd killed along the way.
Still, this is by far my favorite indie game, and I'm very impressed with what everyone was able to do with what they had.

I haven't played anything like this before and that is why this was such a joy to play through. The graphics are all hand drawn manga, meaning that wherever you happen to be in the world, it's going to be beautiful. And the soundtrack is superb too. I've seen too many reviews that go into insane amounts of detail and spoil the fun of playing the game, so I'll just leave it at that, they are both scoring very high in their respective fields.
The gameplay, unlike some other platformers I've played, focuses more on a seriously stripped down rpg levelling system, special attacks and tactics as you find yourself flying through hordes of enemies with those familiar combos. It really does leave a lot to be desired but I'm still happy with what there is. Their aren't many combos, not many attack options, not many of anything really but it's enough. Anybody who played the real-time fighting systems of the early 00's rpg titles knows what to expect when I say Dust is better in the combat department. Given the simplicity of the game though, I wouldn't have minded a little more depth to the combat.
The final thing to mention is the story and without giving too much away it's actually touching, very interesting at times and entirely surprising at one very important part of the game. Sure the voice acting might not be so strong at times, but it's better than fellow rpg 'Baten Kaitos' and not a million miles away from being great. And while I try and escape the facts at hand, this game is actually very challenging at times, especially when you encounter a certain birdman enemy. You'll be managing skills, choosing which to upgrade with every level up and being stuck like that until you level again. It's tense when things start to unravel and plans don't quite work out as they were planned. Thankfully health items are frequently dropped when you're wearing an item of clothing with luck, so it never gets too frustrating.
8/10 - I wanted just a little more than was given, but for a metroid-vania style game with a courageous plot and plenty of hidden secrets, it's well worth a look. For those still unsure, wait until there's a steam sale, you won't regret it!

Where to begin,
Mages of Mystralia is a puzzle-action game where Zia, a to-be mage, is tasked with going around solving issues as she matures, slowly mastering the four types of magic through runes.
Runes are the basic aspect of the game. They are unlocked through puzzles throughout the world. Unlike most other games, this game incourages strategic combination of runes, which imbue the magic casted with specific properties such as the ability to create a path of ice or homing projectiles. At some point, you gain the ability to chain abilities, which is when the true strategic aspect comes to play.
The art is radiant, pleasing on the eyes and is accompanied with nice cleansing music that soothes the player in a great way.
Not only are the art, music, and concept amazing, but the gameplay is as well. There are TONS of chests and quests to find, and the game encourages backtracking to finish quests or start new ones that hadn't been opened up before. From start to finish, the game was crisp and nothing really felt repetitive. As you played, your skill developed, and every time you hit peak, you got a new rune or ability that opened up to more possibilities for you to uncover. You see the world that you've been visiting change as the story develops and there are so many approaches to doing each and every thing that you do.
TLDR: MoM is a game that has great art, calming music, fantastic gameplay, and makes you think and strategize!

I think this may very well be the best "free-to-play" game on Steam. That doesn't mean the game does not come with the usual quirks associated with micro-transaction (free) games. And maybe I am being a bit biased because I was already a fan of Governor of Poker 2. Both games are very similar to each other. The major difference being that in GoP 3 you can now play online against human opponents. The money isn't real, but that feeling of playing with real people is what makes the game priceless. GoP 2 was single-player only, but it had one advantage over this game. You could buy properties, organize tournaments, and play against boss-characters. I still recommend it if you don't mind playing alone.
Yes GoP 3 does have a micro-transaction system, but it is not an obligation for enjoying yourself. You can buy extra chips and gold, but you can earn them in the game by playing regularly. Chips can be won at tables, and gold can be collected by unlocking in-game achievements. Experience points will also be rewarded and will be automatically used to level-up your character. This creates a good sense of game progression. You can spend gold on cosmetics such as hats, shirts, and buttons. These items are entirely optional but are a fun part of the game.
As you progress in rank more areas will be opened up to you where the stakes are greater and the players are slicker. Later you will compete in tournaments and earn trophies. Texas Hold'em poker is the primary game, but you can also play blackjack against the AI dealer. It's an easy way to get more money, but the dealer seems to cheat just like in a real casino. There are also "Sit & Go" tables where people are not allowed to drop in and out and the winner takes all. The buy-in is higher on those tables, but the payout and experience is worth it. One of the best variations for me, though, is "Spin & Go". It's similar to the other tables but the game spins a prize at the beginning (usually 5k chips or higher). Three players will then play for that prize. It's a fun and easy way to get a lot of chips.
If you are a fan of Texas Hold'em or high-stakes gambling with imaginary money then I recommend any game in the Governor of Poker series. If you prefer to play with real people then GoP 3 is the way to go!

Don't let the early access tag fool you, this game is the real deal.
Crypt of the Necrodancer provides a unique blend of rhythm games (featuring the sick beats of one Danny Baranowsky of Super Meat Boy and Binding of Isaac fame) and old school dungeon crawlers like Nethack and ADOM. Each move you make has to be done in time with the beat of the music. The game finds a balance between the time constraints of a rhythm game and strategy of a dungeon crawler by making every enemy highly patternized, making every room a sort of mini puzzle for you to navigate. These highly patternized enemies also give the game room to be stern, but fair. Dying in one hit is a very realistic possiblity even on the first floor. However, when you lose, you can always attribute why you lost to a mistake you made and learn from the experience.
The visuals are simplistic, with a certain whimsy to them. The art design takes advantage of the game's musical emphasis, with enemies ranging from river dancing gremlins to headbopping dragons, including some clever bosses for whom I won't spoiler the surprise.
And if you aren't a fan of Baranowsky's music, theres good news! This game allows you to import your favorite songs to use as ingame BGM! I admit, I haven't used this feature, so I can't say for sure how well it works, but I have seen online resources for recommended songs, so presumably it works fine.
Lastly, as I said before, don't look down on the game despite its early access status. The core game is largely finished (with only the final zone locked off), and the developers are very involved with the game's community, releasing somewhat frequent content patches and listening closely to fan feedback.
Crypt of the Necrodancer is one of the most innovative and interesting games I've played in a long time. It won me over its amazing audio and visuals, and it can only go up from here. I can heartily recommend this game to anyone.

A good majority of strategy wargames out there focus on the high action or grand spectacle of seeing tanks and troops move in sweeping engagements. Not DEFCON. This takes the pure strategy approach to Mutually Assured Destruction, putting you in the seat of the head of state who gets to sit safely in some bunker while they watch the body count rise in the millions. It's very challenging, but also haunting when you really realize what you're doing exactly.
This is one of those simple games that is simple to get the concept of, but it takes a long time to really get the hang of it. Anyone expecting a grand victory for moderate work is going to be disappointed, as fortunes can change quickly from overwhelmingly good to horrifically bad in one salvo or even one white-hot nuke detonation. There's some initial challenge when you are learning the control interface, but with practice you can quickly issue orders and begin to focus more on strategy.
The best comparison I can come up with is the ages-old game of Chess. It's simple, it lacks flash and thunder, but if you are willing to apply your braincells, you can orchestrate victory for your nation. Whether you feel good for laying waste to millions of civilians or not is a whole other question...

I had my eye on this game for a while and recently bought it during the fall sale. I was not disapointed. The combat is simple to understand but full of options in strategy, their are definitly more than one way to do things. The game rewards you through extra experience and RP (Requisition Points) for finishing the level under a certain amount of rounds, but it does not force you, and the bonus is small enough that it punish you for taking your time, it just gives you an incentive to be efficent. Speaking of RP, the Requisition tree is HUGE!!! It isn't that complicated once you get the hang of it however. I would suggest you only buy things that you need (eg the next level of a skill once one of your templars is at the current max and you want to keep leveling that skill, or something to spend your tech level on). Each of the 8 classes has several diferent paths they can go down skill and tech wise allowing you to create a templar to fit the exact role you want. The fact that you can change a templars skills, attributes and equipment as many times as you want, whenever, wherever (exept for during a mission of course) allows you to experiment and try new things. My final comment about this game is about the people behind it. I had an issue with the game continuously crashing one night, so I left a message on the message board. I went to sleep and woke up the next day to find that they had found my problem and had patched it, all during that night. I have never seen anything like this in any game I have ever played ever. If your thinking about getting this game but are unsure, do it! Wait for a sale if you want, but you will not regret your purchase!

A steampunk adventure puzzle game, not a HOG, Namariel Legends was an unexpected surprise. I picked it up in bundle never having heard of it, and found a gem. On launching the game, the main menu makes it feel like a standard run of the mill HOG (Hidden Object Game), but when you click play, what you get is a strong point and click adventure with lots and lots of puzzles. The art style was excellent, the puzzles challenging, the story interesting enough to keep you playing, and a nice soundtrack.
The only negatives were that the music was repetitive (can be turned off), the plot was typical and predictable (main character is not what they seem and is prophesied to save the world), and in places the story left me asking questions .... why did they want to blow up their own perfectly good airship when you were trapped on it and had nowhere to go?
Having said that, I thought the game was a lot of fun, the bonus content was large and took almost an hour to complete with as much quality and attention to detail as the main story, it's a nice length, not too long, or too short, of about 3-4 hours of gameplay, maybe more if you aren't familiar with the genre and I don't think adventure game or HOG fans would be disappointed if they bought this. Highly recommended!

The story is also a little bit of a let down but if you're just looking for a really unique and solid stealth game, Aragami is where it's at. While the game is kinda short, I've got a solid amount of time on the game and I'm still trying to unlock the skins and finish the modes. It's definitely replayable if you can think of new ways to approach situations and its so satisfying to finally pass through an area that you might have been stuck on, or if you're sneaking up behind someone and demolish them right behind another enemy, hoo boy does it feel like you're a true ninja (despite the fact that you killed them with a dragon made out of literal shadows, but who really cares about reality amiright).
Like I said before, the art style is incredibly cool with an almost comic book feel to it and it makes the scenery so pretty just to look at, really nice for those of you who just want to spam screenshots.
The abilities that you unlock with ingeniously hidden scrolls put a whole bunch of strategy into the game too, which is really nice to switch up the combat from the stock standard sneak and stab. Being able to plant a wormhole on the back of an enemy and watch them mindlessly parade into a group of their friends before you activate it and deal with them all on one fell swoop is so satisfying, and throwing a kunai at an enemy on a cliff edge where their body falls off the edge just before another enemy walks past to notice nothing out of place makes you feel like a criminal mastermind.
All-in-all this game is pretty solid with a few janky bits but its still an incredibly unique and thoroughly entertaining experience for anyone looking for a new take on the stealth genre. Would definitely recommend the purchase.

The game itself I really enjoy - placing traps and watching them decimate minions is great fun. Where I have a real problem is the often (I say often because its not everyone) over critical community with little or no tolerance for new players entering PVP games. Instead of offering advice, games are instead sprinkled with name calling and abuse from other players. And even when advice is offered from players to other people, its often ignored (possibly due to language barriers).
As for the game itself, you can either play in pvp or pve modes. Heros are rotated weekly at the moment with 5 heros available per week free to play. Others can be crafted with stuff dropped in games, or bought from the shop. At 134 hours I've crafted 2 heros with enough saved for a third. To give an idea of the time it takes to progress, I've made around 4-5 traps, 2 bosses, 2 trinkets, 2 traits and several minion types as well as upgrading two traps to level 2 for PVE (upgraded traps dont have anu extra effect in PVP).
In PvP mode, you choose a character, select a role (Pillager, Defender or Attacker) and select your deck (basically your loadout of traps, traits, items, minions and bosses that will be available to you in the game).
Defenders (usually 2): Defend the rift (the zone that enemy minions try to reach) by laying traps and shooting/hitting enemy minions that try to get past you. Maximising combo's and use of barricades to channel minions to kill boxes is important to these players. As a free tip: Do not line the walls/floor with arrows and spikes!
Attackers (usually 2): Escort friendly minions to the enemies rift and decide which minions to deploy in each friendly portal. They gain XP points for being near friendly minions and place glyphs (which also buffs minions) if they are available to the character. Attackers shouldnt normally be placing traps as a matter of course.
Pillager (usually 1): This character roams the battlefield shooting caches/crates (coloured red) and gathering XP from them. They can also help either attacker or defender when needed by ganking another player by surprise or simply killing enemy minions if your defenders need help. They would not normally place traps.
On each map there is also a Boss that can be summoned by one team or the other if they complete the objective for that map. On one map its to kill a beast and cook the steak that is dropped in the middle of the map. On the other its to capture two flags on either side of the map by standing in the zone. Once complete, you place a boss in the minion portal shortly after help him lumber towards the enemy rift.
PVP games last anywhere between 10-35 minutes depending on the skill level of people involved.
In PvE mode, you go alone, with a group of friends or use the matchmaking system to group with some random players. The game is then very similar to the original Orcs Must Die! games with players basically building traps to stop the minions reaching your rift. You all are effectively playing as defending, coordinating kill box design and earning coin to place yet more traps. It's fun, although my preference is more towards PvP at the moment.
As for Pay to Win, I would say this is certainly not:
1. People can buy hero's sure (but there are 5 on rotation and you can craft them
yourself if you want).
2. People can buy chests which grant materials/cards for crafting new stuff like traps. You can make these yourself with enough time and because its fun to play, it doesn't feel grindy. Just level up on some PvE missions, gather the materials and make more stuff.
3. The only thing you can't gather without paying is the customisable skins for characters which are purly aesthetic (as far as I know).

What a sleeper this game is!  Fun, fast paced, LOGICAL, unique puzzles, lots of unusual maze types, well written storyline, and though it is not technically a Hidden Object game (no HO scenes) it plays like one.  It has a find and use inventory and is classified as a Hidden Object game by most game companies.  I really recommend this game.  Plus it is steampunk.  How can anyone go wrong with that?  (Circa 2013)
Storyline: When the Princess of Namariel was one year old the Kingdom was invaded by the Iron Lord.  Her mother while fleeing with her infant daughter gets tripped by the nasty mechnical centipede and the baby flies out the tower window.  The infant instead of falling to her death she is snatched out of the air by a fleeing citizen in his balloon airship.  Fast forward 17 years, and the Iron Lord has found out where the fleeing citizen, the great inventor Davincino (and yes, that sounds just like DaVinci) has been hiding.  Of course the Iron Lord sends his mechanized minions to capture Davincino and our young former princess sets out to rescue her Uncle Davincino.  Several plot twists later, she discovers she is the Princess of Namariel, just exactly who the Iron Lord is, and becomes the savior of her Kingdom.
Gameplay:  As I have said before this plays just like an Hidden Object game with a find and use inventory, and most game companies classify it as a Hidden Object game.  The only thing missing are actual Hidden Object scenes.  The gameplay is very logical and is very fast paced.  The game does make one tongue in cheek comment about not having a screwdiver so something else must be used.  Truly a recognition of HO gamers complaints that if one has a hammer why, oh why can one not just break the window with it instead of having to use convoluted means to open it.  Best example of the games mind set on this subject is when needing a three pronged lever, one gets to use a three pronged fork.    (Thumbs Up)
There is no map, it is not really needed.  The play scope is generally limited to only three or four areas at a time.  Since the game logically progresses in a linear fashion, once an area is complete the player can not go back.  There are 8 chapters in the main game and a bonus chapter which is an after mass epilogue.
Puzzles: For me, I had great time with these puzzles, many I consider to be classics.  Some of these puzzle types (brain teasers, dots, logic) I have not seen in years and are not found in newer games.  This game also uses all types of mazes.  The aquarium is three phase maze puzzle, though not hard, certainly makes one think.
Overall nothing in this game is difficult to figure out but it does take a bit of thinking to solve the problem or puzzle presented.  The in-game achievements are nothing like to ones found in newer games.  There are filled-in characters instead of their silhouette making a scene.  There is a built in strategy guide, and two game modes, casual and expert.  Extras include wallpapers, videos (cut scenes), concept art, music, etc.   One last thing the player gets two helpers: a squirrel cat that loves acorns and a flying round robot named Jim. : )
Highly recommend the game.  It plays in about 6-7 hours depending on how fast the gamer plays.
One last comment the Steam price is less expensive then other game sites.

A true masterpiece of a game. Dust looks great. has amazing soundtracks, badass and smooth looking combat filled with a ton of effects, precise and well made controls, an interesting story and tons of optional content to explore.
Dust itself plays like a highly polished metroidvania game - you make your way through areas, later on you get new moves that allow you to discover optional paths and treasures in areas you have already visited before.
During your explorations, you will meet some civilians that offer you sidequests which reward you with additional items and experience points.
This, ofcourse, makes Dust stronger in a variety of ways. Experience Points are self explanatory, you collect them and get level ups (level cap is 60), each level up rewards you with one skill gem that can be used to upgrade your health, attack, defense or fidget (fidget is your companion and can be treated like a magical stat).
Every skill can be upgraded 15 times, but the game limits you in a way that your highest skill can only be 4 skill levels higher than your lowest one (your defense is on level 1, so you can't upgrade anything else past level 5).
This sounds like a big limitation at first, but it helps alot by keeping the game challenging throughout all areas, otherwise you could just max out fidget and oneshot everything while ignoring all other stats.
In addition to leveling you can also get stronger by finding / crafting / buying new equipment.
Every area has different enemies that drop different items, and every area also has some places where you can buy and sell items. Enemies can also drop material items, those can be used to craft your own gear (if you have the required blueprints which also drop from enemies and from treasure chests).
Equipment slots that you can fill are the following : armor, sword augment, amulet, 2x rings.
Dust only has his sword in terms of physical damage, and if you equip yourself with a sword augment you will increase your physical damage output. the other items can also provide various other bonus attributes - automated health regen, better chance for item drops, more experience gain etc.
The icing on the cake however is the absolutely amazing soundtrack. Rarely do you find a game where the soundtrack adds so much to atmosphere and fun. You enter a new area and listen to the music, and you are just like "damn, that sounds amazing". Even with Dust being an extremely colorful game, the music still manages to provide a dark and mysterious atmosphere when needed, which really makes it a joy to play. example track :
Depending on the difficulty level (4 available) you choose, you will get around 10-15 hours of gametime when going for 100% completion - and trust me, you will go for 100%, since the game manages to make backtracking and exploring a lot of fun.
No matter who you are, i can only recommend Dust to you. It has been the best game i have played for ages (since the release of Final Fantasy 10 i guess) and you will definitely not regret spending money on this masterfully crafted gem of a game, especially if you like metroidvania games with stylish combat and great music.
10/10 would buy again.

I love this game!
I love the simple cartoon art style. The ability-upgrade system is easy and pretty fast once you get going. I love the ninja-like gameplay and hiding in the shadows. Those features are beautifully integrated into the game, and are a necessity to master if you want to progress. Don't expect a deep and interesting story. This game is about its gameplay, not the investment in the characters. I love this game despite the story I couldn't care less about. There are a few things though that hurt this game from being perfect:
1) its really short. I finished the entire thing in maybe about 12 hours of total game time, and that was me being thorough making sure I got all the unlockables and killing all the enemies. Im sure if I was just trying to beat the game, I could do it in under 8 hours. I wish it was longer.
2) The one-hit kills. If you're right at the end of a really long level and just about to move one, an enemy sees you, throws his magical sword shot at you, boom. You're done. There's no blocking it. Dodging it. Or surviving it. This game says you can either choose to be stealth or just go all out with a sword. But you definitely can NOT beat this game with just your sword. Your enemies have swords that can kill you from like 50 feet away, and it only takes one hit. At the very least it should take 2-3 hits to kill you. One hit just ruins combat all together, especially when they can kill you instantly, and the gameplay animation for your character to kill is relatively slow.
3) No real replay value. Because of the way I played the game the first time through (trying to complete everything), once I finished, there is no real reason for me to go back and keep playing. The levels are fun and going back to early easy levels with your spec'd out character is alright. But theres just not much enjoyment in the game the moment its done. Thats why I wish it was longer.
Aside from all this, I did love the game while I was playing it and before I finished. I would recommend it to someone who's never played it before. I just wish they expanded on the game a little more.

10,000,000 is just another matching game, but it is far superior to many of these types of games. For one, there is a story: You are trying to reach a score of 10,000,000 so you can get out of the dungeon/prison environment in which you are in. Simple enough, but this directly affects the gameplay, as at the top of the screen, your character goes through the hallways of the dungeon and has to fight or open doors/chests when you match these tiles. You also match wood and other materials to upgrade things after each quick play-through and armor to protect yourself against your foes.
You must complete achievements as well to get higher levels and more of special crystals, which also help you upgrade things (swords, armor, wands, ect.). It gives a very nice variety when you get bored of things like Candy Crush because of no in-app purchases, no limited number of plays, and an actual objective besides beating all the levels (even though there is no levels). The level itself is randomly generated, so you can play as many times as you want and it will almost always be different.
In all, it is a very unique puzzle game, and although it is suited best to only 1-3 play-throughs at a time, it is fun for the time you play it. If I had to give a rating, I'd say 8 or 8.5 out of 10.

In this game you play role of a mysterious anti hero.
It is set in 1989 Miami and it gives you a goal to kill everyone on the floor.

Enemies are quite different some stand with guns, some patrol rooms with crowbars, and all are ready to slash and shoot and murder the heck out of you.
Every mission is based on a lie, a phone message asking you to kill for false reasons.
You own a apartment with an old tv and a phone, bathroom and a bedroom. You pick up pizzas and VHS tapes and then gain a roommate and the most strange this is that you can't interact with any of them in a significant way.(Thay are all background elements)

Before every mission begins you put on a mask which gives you a quite a lot of different bonuses from looking further to starting with a knife or being not attack by dogs.

Crypt of the NecroDancer is half turn-based dungeon crawler with randomly-generated dungeons. The other half of the game is rhythm: each dungeon floor has a unique music track with a visually emphasized steady beat. Your moves are (ideally) made to that beat. Enemies also move to the beat, so the pace at which things happen is determined by the music. Having a steady rhythm locks the participant into a timeframe in which to act, not unlike speed chess or the rate at which a block lowers in Tetris. By removing the infinite time in which a player could decide which move is most optimal in your traditional turn-based dungeon excursions, the game becomes instead one of relying almost wholly on experience. After a while, experience becomes instinct, leading to creative leaps of strategy made entirely in the moment, in the space between the game’s figurative and literal heartbeats.
You play as Cadence, a headstrong delver who - through an unfortunate combination of a terminal fall and an evil NecroDancer stealing her still-beating heart - must now travel down multiple dungeon floors, fighting monsters and finding useful items. You technically don’t have to move to the beat, but not doing so will cause you to lose a vital multiplier that increases how many coins you earn from defeated monsters. The higher the multiplier, the more likely you can afford powerful weapons and items found in dungeon shops. You know when you’re moving to the beat, because the dungeon floor starts pulsing with light, making it your very own little dungeon rave.
There is very little randomness to the combat in Crypt of the NecroDancer. Everything behaves according to very set rules. You move into a monster to attack it, different weapons change the shape of your attack. If an enemy moves into a square you were trying to move to, you’ll take damage instead. Certain enemies take advantage of your urge to rush in, waiting a beat before moving, or moving in interesting patterns. Monsters have unique little dance animations, their movement sounds become a part of the melody of what’s happening on the screen. These sounds are often a clue to defeating them. As you delve deeper, the music becomes faster, the monster patterns more complex. The game is ingenious, fun in ways indescribable unless you’re there, in the moment, taken by the rhythm and amazed at how well you’re doing.
You can use your own MP3s for the soundtrack, and there’s even a DDR mode for use with a dance pad. The DDR mode makes a game a bit easier so you don’t kill yourself. There’s permanent progression via character upgrades, like a health increase and magic spells, unlocked by collecting diamonds.
The music is being provided by the excellent Danny Baranowsky (Super Meat Boy, Canabalt, Binding of Isaac, Desktop Dungeons).

I am still early on in the game, I think.  It's not bad for a top-down turn-based tactics sci-fi adventure. I am a bit confused by the tag, "Rogue-like" which is one of the tags associated with this game; as I grew up with Nethack, Rogue, et al., which are true rogue-likes.  The battles here are not random generated levels, with random items which I figured would give it more replayability.  I read some posts by the developers explaining the tag rogue-like means the save game system is rogue-like, which means there is only a single persistent save file per campaign.  The save file is not so restrictive though, the developers have it tamed in such a way as you can replay the battle before accepting the save, or quit without saving which allows you to restart and replay from where you last saved. That is the only thing that is somewhat rogue-like --and a forgiving rogue-like, at that-- as far as I can tell.
If you want a turn-based tactics adventure, and care less for an engaging story, then this is recommended. However, if you want both fun gameplay and an engaging story then you may want to shop around some more before settling.

You'd never have considered that rhythm games and dungeon crawling go together, but this game makes it work.
First off: this isn't a very serious dungeon crawler.  Most levels are small-ish and relatively uninteresting, with just a few rooms full of monsters linked together by various corridors.
What makes this work though is that the game is half real time, half turn based.  Based on the music playing for the level, each beat of the music is one turn, and enemies have a fairly mixed movement pattern based on the turns (e.g. one moves towards you every other turn, one moves in 4 directions each turn randomly, etc.).  This means that enemies move whether you move or not, but if you have the rhythm, you can anticipate where they will be and outsmart them.
On the easy levels, this is fairly straightforward.  As enemies progress and become more complicated, you also need to develop more complicated patterns, but what you will actually do depends on the minor variations in the level.  This means that unlike other rhythm games, you can't just memorize a button sequence for a particular song.  Instead, it is constantly changing.
The soundtrack is top notch, and design is pretty good.  There are plenty interesting enemies, weapons, accessories, spells, traps, etc. that make each replay sufficiently different to be fun.
Early Access note:  As of this writing, the game is In EA.  It has 3 zones (12 levels) and 5 characters ready to play, with a planned final zone and another 5 characters.  However, the current maps are plenty playable, plenty fun, and not buggy at all.

Beautiful art, but really a one-note game.
Namariel Legends is a beautiful game artisticly... at least for the most part. The gorgeous hand-painted backgrounds and items are a delight to look at. The CG bits are clumsily done in every way, but they can be forgiven for just how beautiful all of the rest of the art in the game looks. Adventure game designers take note: THIS is a game to emulate in the graphics department.
Unfortunately there's no real story to this game. Really there are only a half dozen 'story' events and none of them really build character or make the world feel alive. The rest of your time is spent on the most tired of Point-and-click adventure game tropes: Rubbing things on other things. Because the art is so beautiful, this often turns into a pixel hunt for items since nothing stands out visually. It's all beautiful... but that also kinda works against it. Yea, there are a few other puzzles but most of them aren't that interesting and serve to bog down the game rather than move it forward.
That's not to say this is all bad. With one or two exceptions, the puzzles are at least logical. Or... rather... they pretty much tell you what to do by reading the text at the top of the screen. The fact that there's a help button and strategy guide built into the game also prevents you from getting stuck. Likewise all of the really difficult puzzles can just be skipped outright, which I had to do on only two occasions. Because these 'cheat' features keep the game moving forward it can serve a an OK introduction to the genre for those who have never experienced a point-and-click adventure game.
I should also make note about the game's soundtrack. Great music... but often poorly used. There are a few tracks that create a very tense atmosphere including one right at the beginning of the game when the high stakes and hair raising action involve... finding oil for an artificial leg. Yea... not exactly the best time for the "hurry up or people will die" track.
Speaking of, the game also tries its best to make for a couple of tense moments... but because it's a point-and-click adventure there's no real possibility that you're in danger. Once you realize this, all of the 'danger' seems really artificial and almost off-putting. Why lock off half of a screen when realistically the 'dangerous' thing can't hurt you? Gameplay/narative segregation at its finest.
Finally there's the lack of followthrough for one of the mechanics I thought would be most interesting: The mind-reading device you get at the beginning of the game. Yea, for being made such a big deal of you really only need to use it three or four times... and even then could probably get on without it for most of the puzzles. It's like they forgot about it half way through development or added it in last-minute. A real shame.
I feel bad giving this a thumbs down. It's obvious that the artists worked their fingers off creating an amazing looking game. It's really just a shame that the game's designers didn't put the same level of skill into their part of the craft. :(
Not bad of a beta to start. Looking forward to more updates!

Namariel Legends may look like a hidden object title, but it is actually a short point ‘n’ click adventure with no hidden object scenes. It has a good story, nice visuals, and a decent amount of casual difficulty puzzles.
Namariel Legends: Iron Lord looks like a hidden object game, feels like a hidden object game, and plays like a hidden object game. The user interface, the point ‘n’ click elements, the casual puzzles, and the gorgeous hand-drawn graphics all point to a modern hidden object title, except for one thing: it doesn’t have hidden object scenes. Not a single one.
The story is as simple as it can get: an evil overlord takes over the fairy tale/steampunk kingdom, and to save said kingdom and its royal couple, you must destroy the overlord’s power source.
Strangely though, it works. Despite the simple setup, it is an exciting and fast-paced adventure from almost start to finish.
The level design is another strong point. It never hinders you, but gives a fair challenge.
If you expected a hidden object title, you may be disappointed, but otherwise Namariel Legends is a fun game for anyone.

And I only cried for twenty minutes.

Когда небо было голубее и трава зеленее, мы играли в классические нынче платформеры. Эта игра перенесла меня туда, и я вспомнил, что меня "цепляло" - всё было интересно и в новизну. Проработанные и красиво нарисованные локации населенные, такой же, проработанной и красивой фауной. И да локации весьма разнообразны: от зелёных лугов с разрушенными остатками былой цивилизации и тёмного подземелья, до заснеженных горных вершин и вулканических земель - всё очень ярко и запоминающееся.
По всем канонам платфомеров присутствуют и секретные локации, на которые попасть не всегда просто и очевидно. Если для некоторых просто необходимо пройти дальше по сюжету и получить новую способность (да тут способности будут выдаваться по мере прохождения сюжета, но об этом дальше), то для других нужно воспользоваться как чьими-то записями или же просто интуицией. Когда Вам в последний раз хотелось пройти игру открыв все секреты и локации? Я уже давненько не помню такого. Именно это отпечаталось у меня в голове после полного прохождения данной игры. Ибо автору удалось облегчить поиск секретов ровно на столько, что бы это оставалось интересным, но не вызывало мучений.
же в игре сделана, по-моему мнению, в угоду возрасту игрока (рейтинг 10+), без наличия рек крови, но вполне интересную на высоких уровнях сложности. Среди обзоров наткнулся на фразу о том, что все бои проходят за одной, изредка двумя кнопками. Странно видеть такие замечания к слешеру, коим по-сути и является этот платформер в боевой части. На самом же деле в игре присутствует парочка комбо, но действительно хотелось бы больше комбинаций т.к. со временем эффектная анимация приедается и становится немного скучно. Скуку помогает разбавить сложность, т.к. протагониста могут положить на лопатки всего несколько ударов, а так же наличие нескольких нетипичных врагов, к которым необходим особый подход.
Так же присутствует и
: система уровней с прокачкой одной из характеристик, которых 4 (на самом деле их 5, но прокачивать можно только 4) и которые не могут разниться между собой не более чем на 4 очка; а также система экипировки персонажа артефактами которые влияют на все 5 характеристик и еще несколько игровых моментов.
Как
игра не так хардкорна, как тот же Mario, Darkwing Duck, но на некоторых местах заставляет изрядно понервничать и сжать контроллер покрепче. Да я сказал контроллер, игра пришла к нам на ПК-платформу прямиком с Xbox360 и изначально была "заточена" под геймпад и в процессе игры ни разу не хотелось пересесть за клавиатуру. Ну да ладно, вернемся к самой игре. Чтобы собрать все секреты необходимо открыть все способности протагониста, поэтому придется возвращаться вновь на локации. Кстати, после зачистки локации, враги появляются вновь стоит только выйти за её границу. Это сложно отнести к явным недостаткам, но создает некоторое неудобство, которое по мере прокачки протагониста будет всё меньше и меньше.
И наконец
. Он имеет как излишнюю пафосность и какой-то детской наигранностью, так интригующую составляющую (сюжет не по книге/фильму/игре, а свой собственный, хотя и имеет в себе парочку-другую штампов) и юмор, который действительно способен вызвать улыбку. Но всё же он сделан , по моему мнению, опять же в угоду возраста игрока.
P.S. Игра проходится за 8-12 часов. Я же столько наиграл банально из-за низкого уровня знания английского - что заставляло меня перманентно держать в оверлее гугл-переводчик (хотелось просто подтянуть уровень английского, а происходящее было вполне интересено, чтобы не отбивать желания понимать происходящее).
P.P.S. Кстати интересный факт, что над игрой работал по-большей части один человек около трёх с половиной лет. Я думаю это и помогло стать игре такой какой она задумывалась...

First off i would like to say that there is alot of times that you will get screwed on a hand, there are also times that it would appear to be rigged against you and i agree it does happen too much to be just 'sods law' or coincedence but providing that you stick to a few rules this is a good little poker game...

2. DO NOT TAKE IT SO SERIOUSLY (it's a colourful cartoon game after all, not pokerstars or WSOP)

4. DO NOT BOTHER WITH BLACKJACK (unless your feeling like you could do with lightening your chip stack)
5. PLAY FOR FUN (if you set up tables with friends at least the chips are just being passed around between you)
6. KEEP CLAIMING YOUR FREE CHIPS WHEN YOU REMEMBER (it all helps and its free)
7. DO NOT BUY CHIPS!!!!! (i've told you once, now blinking pay attention to this advice)
At the end of the day as long as you treat it as it advertises (FREE TO PLAY), don't get worked up by getting done over on a good hand more often than not and just have fun with it, it's quite good.
But if you want a serious and totally fair/even deck poker game then this is not it.

July 23, 2014 with  1 hour of game play. *
10,000,000 is a match 3, where your are in prison and you need to get a score of 10,000,000 to get free.  I hesitate to call it a story, there is a intro bit that informs on the plot and that’s all you get. You have to level up your character and prison to get multipliers to even think you’ll get that score. There is lot of rpg elements like extra objectives, leveling characters, leveling weapons, and leveling up your prison. Also there is some action elements to go along with the match 3 game play.
The rpg aspects are very minimalist. You don’t level your character automatically as you play. You have to fix up the rooms with stone and wood you have accumulated through matching. Then buy your upgrade with the ingame gold or xp. There is extra objectives, such as ‘use an ax against a monster’ or ‘match 70 in one run’ which adds a bit of twist to the otherwise very grindy gameplay.
It could be considered an action side scroller. Your 2d pixel guy runs at the top of the screen, when you get up to something then you have to match three to get past that obstacle.  There is not anyway of saving up the match. If you get a run of drops it could be bad, first it slows you down as you can not match other stuf while it is falling, and it can clear the board of items you might need later. The match 3 is also a full slider style game play, instead of a single slide, flip, or twist style match 3. The control of the slide is iffy at times, forcing you to waste more time to get past the obstacle because you weren't right over the match.
10,000,000 is a fast pace hectic match 3 with action-rpg elements. At $4.99 USD it's not a bad price if you like fast pace slide style match 3.  However if you're on the fence I would definitely wait and pick it up when its a buck or as part of a packaged deal. I would give 10,000,000 a 2 out of 5.
* I’d have more time on the game but I personally dislike slide style match 3. However I am aware that others do.
Also be aware this game is apparently a port of the IOS version.

I rate the game Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War - Dark Crusade 4/5. Good. This is far more than a simple add-on to the largely mediocre Dawn of War. This is an excellent and fairly vast expansion.
In terms of its overall structure, this is probably the best Command and Conquer style "RTS" (Real Time Strategy as they are called, though applying the term "strategy" to this kind of game may be a little bit of a misnomer as most "RTS" games includes relatively little actual strategy but more often merely include certain tactical elements) I have ever played. It's most notable strengths are that it allows you to play as one of many different, unique factions, each faction has its own ending and the global-scale battle map allows the single-player campaign to give you, the player, a great many choices as you attempt to progress through the war.
But this game is not without flaws. Indeed, this game, particularly the single-player campaign, has some fairly serious flaws.
An example of The Good (if not Great):
+The single player campaign map gives you excellent strategic options. Remember the old between-mission battle maps that were found in some of the oldest Command and Conquer games? This mode works a lot like that but instead of letting you select either one battle or another, your options are much more varied. If you capture the sector which has the spaceport your options become even more numerous because then you can attack most places across the globe. Likewise, capturing certain other sectors gives your forces certain other strategic and tactical benefits which make an enormous difference as the campaign progresses. This between-mission global strategic map mode is a truly excellent feature which lets you choose how you want the single-player campaign to progress while showing you your options (or lack thereof) and letting you see how your campaign is progressing. It is a feature I would honestly like to see in every other "RTS" game ever made as it offers unparalleled choice and strategic options well beyond what most other similar such Command and Conquer style "RTS" games ever come close to offering you. The inclusion feature should set the bar higher for every other command and conquer style RTS to follow. For me, this feature (combined with the inclusion of the Tau as a fully playable faction) made the game for me and made me want to keep playing the main campaign through to its conclusion.
The Mediocre:
+/- This game requires you to make heavy use of your lightest infantry units. This severely limits the number of tactical options which ever become available to you while at once causing the body count in each battle to rise dramatically. This makes some sense for certain factions (like the Imperial Guard) but makes less since for other factions. Worse, the Imperial Guard factions still don't have unit sizes which seem to ever be large enough or populous enough while the Space marine units never seem to be durable enough for them to be remotely canonical. The Tau units take casualties far too often as well for them to be canonical. When playing as the Tau or the Eldar the game should penalize you (severely) for taking heavy casualties but it doesn't. All factions require you to heavily rely on infantry before building ANY tanks or other vehicles (making the game all too command and conquer styled for my tastes) and units do not seem to ever level up or gain any experience for being in combat which further decreases this game's tactical depth. Ideally, Imperial guard units should automatically include huge numbers of soldiers and some tanks should be available from the outset. Tau forces should heavily rely on tanks and their APC units from the outset. Necrons should be very, very, very slow (much slower than they are shown to be in this game) but almost indestructible. Space Marines should be much, much more durable but much, much fewer in number. (Remember, in Warhammer 40k, there is said to be fewer space marines than inhabited planets in the galaxy) and they cannot afford to lose the sheer numbers they lose in this game (and neither can the Tau or the Eldar or the Necrons). Since all the factions play so similarly to each other (and none of them truly play like they really should) the tactical options are severely limited as a result and the battles are, as a direct result, much, much more repetitious and uninteresting than they could have been. From what I can tell from reading a few of the Warhammer 40k codexes, what we have here in these Dawn of War games is not really Warhammer 40k, but something with its name that sort of looks like it but doesn't really feel much like it. Still, the world of Warhammer 40k is a big one and so there's some room for my suspension of disbelief. However, this game should also be highly commended for the sheer variety of factions which it attempted to include and everything it did well about each faction (especially their voices and sounds they make when responding to orders). The great many factions and thus the great many campaigns which this game includes greatly adds replay value to this game. My Tau campaign lasted over 30 hours. I'd imagine other campaigns would take just as long as well.
The Bad:
- The singleplayer campaign is blatantly unfair. In the single player campaign, battles wherein you attempt to attack and take over enemy strongholds or main bases all have additional, almost unfair objectives which must be completed. (I found the Necron main-base to be worst because the mission would automatically fail if you failed to get your little commander-unit out alive (and this is not true in any other battle and that particular battle tried hard to make this objective particularly difficult resulting in some frustration.) Now needing to complete extra objectives to take over an enemy base is fine, if the game was fair about it but this game isn't remotely fair about this-EVER. If an enemy attacks YOUR main base then you only have one or two little bases and all the CPU computer enemy has to do to make you lose the ENTIRE game is to destroy those one or two bases. The CPU must complete absolutely no other additional objectives to defeat you. To make matters worse, regardless of which side you play, in terms of number of main-bases you are very nearly always out-matched in every battle, whether you are attacking a main base or not. In the vast majority of battles in the main campaign the enemy has at least 2 main bases when I had just one (and I was playing on EASY difficulty. Indeed, One might think this kind of blatant, in-built unfairness is due to the game's essentially poor AI but this game doesn't seem to have poor AI. The enemy AI actually acted quite well. And, of course, on higher difficulties the AI responds more quickly and acts more aggressively. The AI is at least adequate to provide excellent challenges when all things are equal (though it is of course less creative than a person can potentially be). Honestly, I don't think that the kind of in-built unfairness that I mentioned above needed to exist in this game and it made for a needlessly frustrating experience. After slaying innumerable dragons and demons during what was definitely the best run I ever had, and within inches of recieving the score of ten million, my run was ended by my lack of ability to open a treasure chest. This wasn't the first time, and each time seemed to be more infuriating than the last. This was after hours of trying, and with every upgrade and perk purchased. This was the final nail of the coffin, and if this doesn't convince you of why you should avoid this game, please, continue reading.
****
The game does shine at first, promising variety and throwing you straight into the action, but the game quickly begins to demonstrate an abject amount of laziness. The graphical style is retro, to say the least, but the game is very modern, feeling like a frankenstein of other popular mobile games crushed into one jagged mess. 90% of the sceen is devoted to a very archaic match 3 game where you have to move entire rows instead of individual tiles,  and is where you will be putting your focus, but the top half is where the "action" occurs. Up top is an endless runner directly tied to what you do in the match three. Match up swords, you'll attack the monster. Match up keys, you unlock the chest. However, if you don't address the problem in front of you, you'll be slowly pushed off screen and your game will end. Good in concept, but here's my biggest issue: like every match 3, score is a large component, especially given how the game is literally named after the ideal score. However, to do this, you must compile the best combos and deal with the problem at hand, but you have to do it directly infront of the creature or object. If you matched the correct set a second before you stop in front, be it in anticipation or by accident, it doesn't stack and your move becomes invalid. This is particularly frustrating when you have to match certain sets to move on, only to watch your carefully calculated moves get screwed up by a chance mega combo. Too many runs have been ended that way, and to have treasure chests be a mandatory to unlock is absolute bull. There is absolutely no option to skip anything you encounter, which would've spared the game some frustration, but the game just doesn't care enough. Another mobile trope is the "meet one of the three objectives" thingy that also grinds my gears, as they don't enhance or challenge, but merely infuriate as their increasingly impossible demands completely based on luck (or in my case, rawheaded stubborness) to recieve, solely to unlock a harder difficulty with more objectives.
Note how I said difficulty instead of level. This is because there is only one level in the game: A grey dungeon hallway. A hallway that never ends. Monsters, for the most part, are simply pallet swaps with other monsters, which is uncannily lazy for a game in which even the most complex characters are composed of 20 pixels and are the size of your thumb. The only thing you can change is difficulty, which ramps up quickly and is basically required of the player to grind for hours just to recieve some paltry bonuses to attack just to HAVE THE CHANCE to get by. Quickly you learn that some monsters can only be substantially hurt by magic and others by striking, but the problem, once again, is that you rarely have the right board to fight them. Even during your best games, your best is never good enough, for the board may just vomit out a variety of support tiles that do absolutely nothing to help your awful situation, and then your run ends. Outside of a couple items you might get by chance that are specifically one attack or the other (and even they don't always finish the job), the game never gives you the advantage for long, if ever at all.
Tl;dr: 10,000,000 demands concentration and strategy when it builds itself around luck and reflex. Conflicted even in design, the game never fails to give you the worst possible set up in front of the most dangerous to the most menial tasks, matching frantically until you either lose or move past the obstacle for another few seconds before you're forced to beg again for lady luck to bless you again. Like the trials of Sisyphus, your attempts to push forward will gain you ground, but will very quickly add momentum to your downfall. Unlike our unlucky boulder rolling friend, however, this game is not your punishment for defying the gods, and you can easily skirt this suffering by not buying this game. So don't. Please.

Let's start with good things:

+ Cars handling - not as arcady as in GTA V
