Now to the bad things:
- Horrible optimization - I play on a quite powerful laptop (i7-6700HQ, 12GB of RAM, GeForce GTX 950M) and I can't get stable 30 FPS on minimum settings in Full HD, instead I have 25 FPS in the city and it drops to 20-21 in areas with more foliage. Come on, this laptop runs GTA V on mostly high settings in stable 50-60 FPS and GTA looks better in many aspects.
- Interface is not scaling so I can't reduce resolution to improve FPS a bit because then the interface covers most of the screen.
- Enemies AI - it's terrible - they can't see you aiming at them from 20 meters, if you play slow enough you can kill all of them without firing a single shot for the most of the game, having a silenced weapon makes you feel you are playing with cheats, unless you basically run into them, when they actually start firing they become slightly more dangerous.

- Concrete bushes - come on, game from 2016 and you can't run or drive through soft foliage because they have full collision? If you couldn't animate it properly just make it non-solid, it would look bad but it wouldn't be annoying.
- Glitches - there are lots of them - items floating in the air, weird ragdolls, strange physics behaviour, sometimes you can get stuck so much you have to reload checkpoint.
- Graphics problems - sunsets look pretty bad, sky can act weird sometimes, rain also looks quite bad
- Some stuff that throws 60's feel through the window - interface looks very futuristic, something that is like a mobile phone to instantly call for things, magical intel view that highlights all enemies around, only GPS is kinda acceptable because navigating on a big map manually would be annoying.
Overall: Not a very good game, absolutely not worth 50€, repetitive, unoptimized mess. Have to say that some glitches were quite funny though.

You'd never have considered that rhythm games and dungeon crawling go together, but this game makes it work.
First off: this isn't a very serious dungeon crawler.  Most levels are small-ish and relatively uninteresting, with just a few rooms full of monsters linked together by various corridors.
What makes this work though is that the game is half real time, half turn based.  Based on the music playing for the level, each beat of the music is one turn, and enemies have a fairly mixed movement pattern based on the turns (e.g. one moves towards you every other turn, one moves in 4 directions each turn randomly, etc.).  This means that enemies move whether you move or not, but if you have the rhythm, you can anticipate where they will be and outsmart them.
On the easy levels, this is fairly straightforward.  As enemies progress and become more complicated, you also need to develop more complicated patterns, but what you will actually do depends on the minor variations in the level.  This means that unlike other rhythm games, you can't just memorize a button sequence for a particular song.  Instead, it is constantly changing.
The soundtrack is top notch, and design is pretty good.  There are plenty interesting enemies, weapons, accessories, spells, traps, etc. that make each replay sufficiently different to be fun.
Early Access note:  As of this writing, the game is In EA.  It has 3 zones (12 levels) and 5 characters ready to play, with a planned final zone and another 5 characters.  However, the current maps are plenty playable, plenty fun, and not buggy at all.

DEFCON is perhaps the only game which allows you to commit a global-scale nuclear genocide...and award you for it.
Although simple in design, this is probably one of those rare games which have a "timeless" stamp on them. The slick, elegant graphics that pay homage, or rather, "totally worship" classic films such as Dr. Strangelove and WarGames, serve their purpose in a most appealing way. You may only see one screen in the vanilla game, but it is more than enough for the sheer beauty DEFCON is.
Background music also deserves massive praise - it is simple, minimal, ambient, atmospheric, yet haunting. Haunting is the right word. It is the perfect setting for this game.
Hearing a distant, muffled cry of a woman somewhere in the background while the screen is coldly informing you that you have you just erased millions of lives is an experience no other game offers.
As for the gameplay, the most important thing, after all - do not be fooled by the looks of the game. It is a complex strategy title, a unique one in the bunch, which doesn't fall back behind any of its genre "collegues".
There are many ways to commit nuclear holocaust, many little details and tactical manuveurs to be had - I admit myself that I'm still quite an unskilled player, but seeing the ways I was eradicated of the map and reading several walkthroughs, I can confrim - this game is truly a strategy game.
Only real flaw of the game is its community, or to be precise, the lack of it.
I had to wait for more than half an hour, sometimes, to fine an open spot in a game. Creating your own game can result in even more time spent.
However, there are still players, you just need to be a tad bit lucky.
In the end, I recommend this game - if you're interested in an unique experience, picking this up on a sale day is no wrong doing.

I personally enjoy playing this game. It's a very easy game to get the hang of, and it's honestly very calming to me. It reminds me of when I was a kid and I would ride in the back of the truck at the wood cutting area with my parents.  I'm not sure why it does, but it does. Haha!  But, anyways. The game's graphics are good for the game, and it has improved a considerable amount since it was first released. Granted, I still get a 2 1/2 ton+ 6x6 truck stuck on a two foot twig from time to time, but compared to how it used to be when it first came out, there has been a lot of improvement. The trucks aren't as prone to flipping as they once were(I still flip some if I have a lead foot. Hahaha! XD ) I've always loved the physics in the game. Watching the roads deteriorate as you drive over them a few times can sometimes present a challenge. Also, I know I've accidentally made an etire side of a map inaccessible because I flipped a truck with long and short logs twice because I wasn't paying attention(Remember children, never text while driving. XD ). I suppose one of the things I didn't like at first was that they changed the trucks that spawned in some of the maps, as in, the ones that appear for you to unlock. But, since they now have the option to have different 'beginning garage loadouts' as I call it. It more than makes up for it.
In conclusion, I think the game is a great time, and my friends and I have had glorious amount of fun wile playing this game. Watching your friend roll down the side of a cliff, only to roll yourself for not watching where you are going has caused a massive amounts of laughs. Sometimes, the game can be frustrating, though. Especially when you get stuck in a place where there's nothing to winch to, or no other truck that's able to make it to that spot so you have to get a little overly creative, which can be a hassle. But, if gives you the feel of what a true log transporter would have to deal with in such conditions.
I'd give this game an 9/10. I recommend this game to everyone I know that likes driving games, and for those who just want a game to relax and not have to focus super hard on it.
P.S. Evertime I see a truck with a trailer with logs on it in real life, I joke to myself about how long it took them to get the trailer aligned properly. Hahahaha! XD

While art style, plot and overall atmosphere are quite nice, I have a bone to pick with gameplay.
The whole concept of being a being of the shadows is great and neat, and has not, to my knowledge, been ever taken this far, with most games keeping shadows and invisibility pretty simple (Splinter Cell franchise, or the most recent Thief, for example).
However, my main problem with it is that interacting with shadows simply doesn't work all that well in 3D gameworld. It is easy to find places in Aragami, where mechanics do not work as expected, as in - you see a dark area yet character is not hidden within it.
Even worse are game mechanic conflicts, in which main character can at the same time both be in the shadows (which is properly represented by shifting his color to black) yet be under the effects of nearby light (which is also correctly represented by progressively draining the white pattern of his outfit and turning it to red).
All in all - nice concept, may be interesting to some, but not that great.

There are 2 problems I had with this game, the first being your AI partner, Fidget. Steam do a lot of things that annoy me. One such thing is making me look through a queue of games that I probably won't like and don't want, just to get the stupid free trading cards every time they do a sale. However, in this case they did me a service.
This game was on the list, and as I like turn-based strategy I stuck it on my wishlist. I didn't buy it until about a year later when there was an offer on it but I wish I'd bought it earlier.
Templar Battleforce is a turn based squad game where you control a team of different classes in various missions against an alien menace. There are several things that I like about it:
Firstly, the different classes feel pretty distinct. There are a few that do similar things but even they have subtle perks that make them different. Maybe not as individualised as the classes on the XCOM games but still a nice selection.
Secondly, despite the fact that I am not finished there is a pretty good storyline, which is often missing in games at this pricepoint. There is a whole lore and universe that is fleshed out fairly well during the missions themselves and in a few expository scenes between the main combat.
Speaking of the missions, there are a lot of them. I recently got the achievement for completing 30 missions and I think there are still 10+ to go (excuse me devs if I'm selling this short). It definitely feels like value for money in terms of longevity. Considering that there are several different difficulty levels and an ironman mode there is also some replayability too.
There are other things I like, such as the music, which ramps up the drama well as you progress through a mission. There are times where you are surrounded or struggling to work out how to defend yourself against a wave of "Xeno" and the music definitely adds to the tension.
I am playing through at normal difficulty and that feels like the perfect challenge already. There are times I have had to reset and redo a mission when I make a mistake like leaving a tactical point undefended, or walking into a horde of tough enemies with just a scout to fend for himself. Even when I have to do this it rarely feels like the game is picking on me, and when i refine my tactics a little I can plough through, but it feels like an accomplishment rather than a chore. Once I complete it I will definitely see if I can handle a tougher difficulty.
To add a little balance to an otherwise positive review, some of the mechanics are a little hard to understand at first. It can take a little effort or some looking through discussion boards to work out what is going on. Even with this relatively minor complaint, the developers are still incredibly helpful. Despite the game being out for a long time already, the two queries I have had have been answered by the devs within minutes of me asking them, and looking at other discussions this is not a fluke.
Overall, if you're a fan of turn based games then it is worth paying the full amount. Even if you're not, get it on sale.

A surprisingly rich blend of tactics and strategy.

● The campaign is long and interesting. The missions don’t feel too repetitive, and the short written narration and dialogues sketch a universe with a rich history.
● The game successfully blends tactics (the missions) and strategy (the use of limited resources to build your team between missions).
● The units are diverse and complementary; they can accommodate different playstyles.
● The controls are intuitive.
● The music is evocative and the units well drawn. You can even personalize the look of each unit, which is more than a gimmick when you have several, let’s say, soldiers, but each with its own specialty, and you want to distinguish them easily during play.

● The underlying rules are complex, maybe overly so, and the online guide is sparse. Among other things, I wish there were tables to compare the basic stats of the different units (and, if possible, items).
● It’s a detail, but sometimes the music switches in the middle of a mission, from a “danger” mood to a “victory” mood—for no apparent reason.
● There are a few typos, such as one talent that says it uses 0 AP (Action Point) per weapon, when in fact it uses 2 AP.
● The developers are very responsive. Two years after the game came out, they still answer questions on Steam, still welcome feedback, still fine-tune the game.
● The developers are very dedicated. Over the past two years, they’ve not only updated the game on a regular basis, they’ve also added content: new units, talents, items, even a whole new mini-campaign. For free!

Aragami is a simply straightforward, but still very enjoyable 3rd-person stealth action game. Built by a rather small team of dedicated indy devs, Aragami has a lot of heart that makes  it very difficult to not enjoy. Sometimes the best titles are the simplest ones.
As a stealth action game, it has the standard formula: You play as an assassin, who in this case is a vengeful spirit conjured by a trapped sorceress to exact her vengeance and set her free. An entire army stands between you and your goal, seeing as how you can't fight them all you have to quietly sneak past them and avoid confrontation alltogether. The stealth mechanics are intuitive, as can be expected. Stick to the shadows and avoid the light, in order to encourage this, Aragami himself is a being made of shadows, so when he's in a strong shadow he becomes invisible to distant enemies. This is not, however, a guaranteed free-escape from guards as they can still see you if they are close enough, and depending on your actions the guards may become more alert, so the shadows wont always save you. The guards cone of vision also has some verticality to it, so they can also see you if you are above them on a ledge. So unlike Skyrim, hiding in the slightest shadows won't protect you when your enemy is close, and unlike Dishonored crouching on a slightly elevated platform won't keep you out of your enemies sight.
The main method of movement is the Shadow Leap ability, which allows Aragami to warp to a shadow, bypassing barred gates and climbing up buildings as well as letting you progress through the level. However, the shadows in a level are not always within reach of eachother, which is where the Shadow Essence comes into play: You can paint a surface with shadows that you can warp to with Shadow Leap. Both the leap and the paint abilities are managed by the "Shadow Essence" meter that is cleverly indicated on the back of the player's cloak instead of an obstructive HUD element. The Shadow Essence drains when you warp/create shadows, and using a combination can quickly drain the meter, so careful planning and management is key. But don't fret, the Shadow Essence is refilled gradually when you are in the shadows, but is also rapidly drained away when near a bright light...
The level design and layout is probably some of the best I've seen in a stealth-action game. Each consecutive level gets more and more challenging, with the guards gradually setting up more fires and lanterns to limit the amount of shadows you can use, all the while increasing the manpower they send out to try and stop you. So while enemy distribution rarely deviates from the norm, the level design more than compensates for this, with the few types of guards instead complementing the level rather than overpowering it. Additionally, hidden throughout each level are collectable scrolls which both unlock little pieces of the story accessable in the menu with F1 as well as allowing you to purchase and upgrade other abilities. These powerups can be quite useful, ranging from simply increasing your Shadow Essence regeneration rate to observing enemies through walls to throwing knives to take out pesky guards from range. They're a welcome addition and can even the playing field against the progressively increasing challenge with the levels and guard distribution. But in my first playthrough, I've only used a total of 2 of the 6 powers. So the option is there if you want, but the game is perfectly beatable without them.
Probably one of the best things I've found with Aragami is the few boss battles. These aren't forced encounters that tediously make you exit the gameplay you've come accustomed to, but like the enemy distribution in levels actually complement the gameplay style, acting as a sort of challenge or pop-quiz on everything you've learned while playing. All the bosses are generally aware of your presence (as cleverly implied in a few cutscenes prior) but like their footsoldiers cannot actually see you unless you leave the shadows or get too close to them. The boss battles are very intense, but also fair. They don't pull any punches and require you to be quick on your feet.
If you're looking for more of a challenge, then you can hit up the options menu and change the AI difficulty AS WELL  as disable other aspects. You can remove guard alertness meters on your HUD, as well as remove the slowed-reaction time when you are detected. These options are welcome, considering that the game's guard AI isn't the most refined. It's not terrible, just standard.
The story, I feel, is absolutely terrific. Taking place in feudal Japan, every character actually speaks Japanese (sorry to those who dislike reading, but this is a subtitled game). As well, Aragami treats the Japanese culture with dignity and respect, which earns it a lot of cookie points in my books. When most people typically think of a Japanese game, they either think of some out-of-their-mind craziness or obnoxious anime dating sims. The story is subtle, seemingly straightforward but plays its cards close to the chest. But if someone is attentive they can pick up on subtle hints that clue one in to how the story will really play out. I appreciate a good story as someone who enjoys reading novels, and Aragami has a very solid story. The narrative feels a little forced now and again but for the most part I think it's very engaging.
Also, Aragami boasts a VERY well-made soundtrack. Props to Two-Feathers for composing it, the music is a perfect fit for the game's environment and tone while also being perfectly listenable to.
I do have some cons to go over. The graphics and animations in Aragami are very mediocre. The game has a very minimal HUD presence, which can make a game all the more immersive; but with the sub-par graphics, the robotic animation cycles and HORRIBLE facial animations, you can't really get all that immersed into it.
The Shadow Leap is kind of clunky, mixed with some holes in the level design can make for some frustrating glitches. For a few examples, I teleported near a rock to escape some guards who were getting a little too nosey to find myself clipping through the map and falling down into an underground bunker that you're supposed to reach later in the level. I thought to myself: "Oh! Well this just happened, might as well take advantage of this." That was probably the best example of level clipping, the worst was when I warped behind an enemy to stab them through the heart, I ended up clipping through the wall, falling out of the level and dying. Which was very frustrating since that happened on the FINAL BOSS. I won't give a quote, but let's just say that some foul language was fired off.
Finally, the last con is that the game leans a little on the side of being TOO easy... This might just be me, since my first playthrough was on normal difficulty and I was doing a lethal playthrough, killing all the guards instead of sneaking past them. Taking advantage of the robotically standard AI was pretty simple, maybe it's harder on more intense difficulties (and I know for a fact that a silent ghost playthrough is a lot harder), but except for a few levels and the boss encounters the AI didn't really challenge me as much as I felt it could.
In closing: I highly recommend Aragami. Everything it does right, it really gets right. The level design, the music, the setting and story, gameplay mechanics and overall layout all come together to make a very solid and worthwhile game. It's simplicity is endearing to me, and if you are a fan of stealth games then I would recommend picking up Aragami.

Excellent game. 9.5/10 overall. Despite it's many criticisms for being an Overwatch "knockoff" or "clone" Paladins has great aspects to it. There is an in-match customization feature where you can enhance certain abilities of you character-there are currently 24 champions soon to be 25(all with unique skill sets). The main objective of a basic game is to be the first team to four point. At the start of the match both teams rush to the center to capture a point; after doing so, a payload cart appears and the team that captured the point must push the cart to the other team's base while they defend their base. Capturing the objective is 1 point as is pushing the payload successfully to the opposing team's base. Most of the gameplay is very fast paced and is all over the place making it harder to learn your enemies plan of attack. You can talk with your teammates using chat or giving a simple command code that starts with v. The only feature of the game that is terrible is the matchmaking system. For example, if I wanted to play competitive and I queued up for a match there is no specific design where you will play with or against players that are close to your skill level. If you are a high ranking player, play with noobs, and lose, your champion's rating will fall exponentially. Yet if you play against insanely high ranked players and beat them your champion's rating will go up. It is all up to chance whether you get paired up with good or bad players.

Feminist movements have campaigned and continue to campaign for women's rights, including the right to vote, to hold public office, to work, to earn fair wages or equal pay, to own property, to receive education, to enter contracts, to have equal rights within marriage, and to have maternity leave. incredibly important. Players must constantly clear the shield, pack, wood, and stone icons that are of lesser use during the run in order to seed the board with useful tiles-- especially weapons as monsters can attack the player, costing more precious time. Defeating monsters quickly is both necessary and frustrating as it adds a layer of
to the game: it is possible to happen upon a long string of monsters without the compartively easier chests and doors, effectively dooming a run since the player doesn't have time to manage the board.
Between dungeon runs, the game gives gold, stone, wood, and experience, all of which are used to level-up your strength and defenses. However, none of the upgrades ultimately change the way the game is played, neither increasing the complexity or even effecting the difficulty due to the increasing strength of monsters. Instead, upgrades are a brick wall that serve to force a particular rate of progression upon the player. Players cannot progress into the deeper levels of the dungeon until they grind out enough resources to upgrade their stats. Instead of barring players based upon skill, players are
.
The way the value of tiles changes based upon the scenario presented in the dungeon makes the game decent, but the title ultimately turns out to be more of a
than anything else due to its simple gameplay and leveling system.

Final Fantasy VII is a classic, there's no debating that. With it's first release on the Playstation back in 1997, this release is a repackaged version of the PC port released in 1998.  With cloud saves and achievements, it doesn't really stand out to people who may have already bought the game or have it elsewhere.
Final Fantasy VII uses almost all the assets from the original PC version of the game. Music was re-encoded to OGG Vorbis, but was still based off of fairly ugly MIDI tracks that the PC used. Thankfully they are easy to replace as some poeple have even decided to use remixes of said tracks instead.
Visually the game is very dated. 2D backgrounds, 3D sprites from that era with resolution stretching 2D elements while providing a modicum amount of improvement to the 3D models. While in the field, higher resolutions don't really help, but in battle scenes and in full 3D environments (Chocobo Racing, Submarine Minigame), there is a noticeable improvement.
Controls are a bit awkward as for a 360 controller, the triggers, d-pad, and right stick aren't usable. However, you can get around that either by binding everything to usable controls or using a utility like JoytoKey.
This is a bare-bones re-release, with the hard work for making it work with a modern OS stripped away for most people.
Update: SquareEnix has managed to replace the MIDI quality music with PSX quality tracks. This means the game's music sounds extremely detailed compared to the original PC release.

Hotline Miami is a game that wants you dead with a passion. It will kill you, time and again, be it by crushing blows to the skull or a belly full of lead. It will, without hesitation or remorse, utterly ♥♥♥♥ing brutalize you.
It is also, without a doubt, the most rewarding, interesting, and thoroughly enjoyable game i've played in a really long time. The gameplay is fast. Like, blisteringly freaking fast. You can slash, bash, and gun your way through an obscene number of enemies. You die in a single hit most of the time, and you restart each level from a checkpoint at the beginning of a each larger room you enter. Because of this, the game is lent a sense of urgency, and man, do you have to be urgent in some of the later levels (Or risk becoming best pals with the blunt end of a steel pipe).
This grungy, gritty, very '80s atmosphere is made all the more potent by the soundtrack. By god, the soundtrack. Quick, simple beats and synth chords make up most of the BGM, but man, it's really good stuff. If you're into that, it's certainly a plus. Pretty much everything about this game, from the chilling, semi-improvised bursts of violence to the flashy, achingly saturated colour palette the game sports to the eerie, meta-commentary narrative  just reeks of not necessarily beauty, but a certain style.
And indeed, that's what Hotline Miami is.
Pure, bewitching, and stomach-churningly ultraviolent style.
So, if you've ever thought about redecorating public spaces with an astronomical number of assorted innards, go ahead and pick up Hotline Miami. It's super fast, super gory, and super fun.

For $10 I was a tad skeptical that this game could really take up my time. But when I got into it, the time wasn't spent on playing the game...
It was spent on dissecting every little aspect of gameplay mechanics up until the cultists missions.
I really like dice rolling system, as a whole it's a solid 10/10 for how it "feels" when just jumping into the fray and letting things take their course. Attack an enemy! Hit or miss? Feels slightly more forgiving than say... Xcom. You don't have to understand how it works, it works well either way.
It's very entertaining to anyone who likes options for the sheer fact that there's options. Because there's a LOT of options. And just about any way you want to play it is valid for completing almost every mission.
There's some important information I need to impart however. If you're anything like me, you like to optimize. You like to Min/Max. You can't stand it if you complete the objective just under a perfect score. This is where I feel the game has a terrible flaw, and if the devs are still alive out there, I'd like them to take this to heart.
In order to gain new skills and equipment, you need requisition points. Requisition points are awarded upon completion of each mission you do. However, there is the possibility of earning EXTRA requisition points, and it's very clear from the size of the requisition tree that you're going to need as many points as possible. So, how do you earn the extra points for that sweet sweet "perfect" score? Two ways: Kill as many enemies as possible in as few turns as possible (as the score is based on an average kills per turn) AND complete the mission in general in as few turns as possible. From here, the games compatibility with all of its "possibilities and options" goes down the drain.
Picking anything that is slower and/or safer is immediately going to be less effective in the long run. You absolutely must rush every mission while strategically picking which spots are worth stopping on to potentially snipe some poor xeno who happened to be on your speed path. The best Kills per Turn bonus I've ever gotten was 8%, and that was at 6 kills per turn. The best speed bonus you can earn is a WHOPPING 20%!! And that doesn't just apply to RP, it applies to EXP too! Getting that massive bonus is possible on almost every mission, so going without it just seems like a bad idea.
Now since the goal is to go as fast as possible, this limits which character classes are valid to play with. Obviously scouts seem like the go to pick, but they're so fragile they explode instantly. Sensorkit scans supposedly keep them aware of enemies, but the scans cost as much AP as a shot and a ton of heat too. Combine this with the fact that A:running further causes more heat and B: you can't stop running because you NEED to complete the objective as fast as possible and C: you can't use sensorkits while overheated means you're out in the open just hoping that a xeno doesn't pop out the one dark tile you can't see 5 tiles away from you.
Engineers also have sensor kits, but have far too many responsibilities to free them up, are too expensive to deploy more, and have too many skills needed to properly defend themselves AND go exploring.
Soldiers are pretty go to with rallying charge, but they'll soon suffer heat problems and slow down.
Hydra and Neptune are fancy soldiers with a higher deploy cost, but without the soldiers practicality (Dalan Ortho 4life).
Berserker is like the mix of your captain and paladin... good at melee attacking stuff with various buffs and debuffs but can't heal.
Paladins are a godsend which stop for no one and don't overheat easily (until you need to start healing).
Then there's your captain, who also stops for no one when built as a melee tank. He can speed buff himself and run through maps to do all the objectives for you.
Look, I like what's here, but the game doesn't properly incentivise the use of other classes. I play this on Demanding difficulty. My sole loadout is always Captain, Dalan Ortho, and Paladin. Squad sizes are too small to make use of other classes, and the starting SP is never enough to get more than one expensive unit (which means I end up getting my pally, but never an engineer). Missions have tactical points, but the missions never last long enough for them to matter. You go in with who you have, maybe recruit 1 extra guy if there's an easy tactical point, and it's over. The game suffers from the fact that it only has the campaign (which must be rushed) and no free play.
SOOOOO, here's my suggestions. For the reward system, make bonus objectives gives +5 bonus Exp AND Rp. For the kill system, remove the kills per turn and install a kill threshold system. I'm thinking along the lines of the threshold being hp based? So in a mission, deal 400 hp in damage as the goal, and hp is only added to the counter when the enemy is killed. Got a skittering down to 1 hp? Doesn't count. Kill it, then you get its hp value added to the counter. Going over the target value will earn bonus %, which will hit a cap (I recommend 20%, like your turn completion bonus).
For the start of missions, give out a little more starting SP. Second to this, give an option recall or add troops based on SP cost. Conversely, tweak the costs of troops so that they're cheaper, and the difference in cost isn't literally 50% of a whole unit. For some of the bigger missions you are FORCED to use some crappy soldier or scout you've never used before, but you're unable to swap them out because there's never enough starting SP. If squad sizes were a little bigger, you could decide whether you want 3 cheap units or 2 special ones.
A free play or challenge mode would be nice. I would love to see how different setups fair against waves of enemies that get progressively stronger. Maybe add this mode as a reward for completing your first optional mission in the campaign.
Lastly, auto-block is really powerful, not sure if it's OP though. The stat is basically non-negotiable. Armor is however, in conjuction with deflection. Unfortunately anything with low deflection and high armor defeats the purpose of wearing it since everything will penetrate it, causing half the armor value to be lost. As such the only practical option is to pick high deflection suits with low or moderate armor. Not sure how to balance it for really low deflection values.

I don't usually review games, and when I do, it's because I wanna badmouth it.
(TBH, this here is probably my second review)
I wasn't expecting anything from Mafia III, so maybe that's why I actually enjoyed it.
I barely played the first Mafia game, and never touched the second one, which, when it came out, everyone was saying bad things about it, how it "wasnt a real Mafia game", etc.
But I got this Mafia III for "free", well it was coming with some hardware, whatever. My point : I didn't really want to play it.
But even tho, I decided to give it a shot. And I don't regret it.
For the last decade, I've had troubles finishing games that I had started. Lack of interest, of motivation, of time, or genuine lack of good games? I'm not sure.
But I finished Mafia III in pretty much 44 hours. And it ended with that sweet, familiar... feeling... how to name it... that kind of sadness that comes with ending some game, book, or TV show, in which your poured many hours of your life.
Sure, 44 hours ain't that much, so I guess I've had it worse. But it had been a real long time since I felt this, and I guess I kind of missed it.
Anyway enough about this crap let's get to the actual GAME. WHY do I RECOMMEND it?
Well, if you liked the repetetive aspect of Assassin's Creeds games (secure area, go on tower, eagle vision, leap of faith, repeat), you're not gonna go nuts on this game, because it's here too, way less obnoxious tho.
If you like shooters? I'd say it's pretty efficient in this field too, tho a bit basic. You may even have some fun sneaking around and slicing the baddies' throats.
The IA sort of sucks, but if you don't try to challenge it too hard, you'll still manage to have fun.
But clearly, what impressed me the most in this game, is that it seemed to have been designed to make us feel like a badass killer. Walk around shooting at the bad guys, try to be cool, and you'll feel it : Mafia III can be fun.
Some "targets" felt really AWESOME to murder. Not gonna spoil anyone here, but you'll know what I mean when you get to them. Walking your way through bodyguards up to the boss feels badass.
Sadly there are only very few of these targets that really felt cool to kill. But IMO, they really made the whole game worth it.
TL;DR :
Don't expect too much or you'll be disappointed,
but if you wanna be a badass killer and play a nice yet basic shooter game,
Mafia III 's got some of it for you

The setting is obviously Warhammer-inspired in that you are the last hope of mankind in shining, martial, awesome armor and you fight off the invasion of an evil swarm.
If over-the-top heroics are not your thing (you find Warhammer to ridiculous to follow), the setting here won't be yours.
What surprises me is the campaign, which is incredibly diverse in its goals and how you have to play. If normal tactical turn-based games seem too repetitive to you sometimes, try this one.
The difficulty changes a bit from mission to mission, but I do prefer that over each mission just being straight harder than the last one. It is nice to get a pause sometimes. The overall difficulty does increase, of course.

This game is an odd one, Immagine being in an underground bunker at the times of the cold war. Only instead of the USA and Russia being the ones who are having that cold war they could be any or all out of a preset of North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Russia and Asia. The only thing in front of you is a screen and possibly some high-rated generals. This is your "war room" At your disposal are radar-stations, airbases, nuke-silo's, and quite a few naval vessels. The carriers carry planes, the battleships battle, and the submarines do what submarines do. Best get your war face on, get your combat vessels in the ready, prepare for the inevitable nukes that soon will be flying overhead on this map. Send your battleships to engage other battleships, which in turn also carry nukes so you can guess what happens if they make it to the shore of your terretory. Submarines can do the same but they are below the surface, it is to anyones guess where they might hang out, untill they surface and drop a few nukes up the undefended side of your area. Fighter/Interceptor planes are best used in the sky because they can shoot down incoming bomber-aircraft from your opponent and incoming long-range nukes, unless if they can be shot down themselves. It is a game where you get twofold the points for anything you kill, and lose onefold the points for anything you lose.
This game will no doubt be very interesting upcoming LAN party, it will run on an old laptop of mine and as such will be running this game from the edge of my table, running the "diplomacy" game-type. In that game-type you're allied to everyone in the game, untill anyone decides to leave the alliance ( perhaps start a different one with a different player ? ). Scoring is determined on the amount of survivors left in your area instead of normal "scoring". And like with any game-type it takes 12 minutes to set up your pieces on the board, after that hostile actions are allowed, and after 30 minutes nukes are allowed. Playing this in real-time instead of fast or faster speed as is usually the case on many multiplayer games ( The speed can be changed by the press of a button ) should give the nessesary "why do you break the alliance now ? You know I just started on my pizza !" funtimes :)
In the end though, every game stops when 80% of all assets are destroyed, which can take infinitely long with the diplomacy game-type.
Everybody dies. Well except for Australia, Because Australia is not a zone this game is taking place in. And hence will not be bombed... I guess that Introversion Software has a soft spot for kangaroos.

I have been using Pro Motion since a few years now as my go to tool for making pixelart. So what makes ProMotion different or even better than other tools on the marketplace? The first and foremost point of importance is the developer. I have not witnessed such a level of responsiveness and diligence in customer support as with this developer. The way Cosmigo listens to customer feedback and handles bug reports is unparalleled in my experience.
So for the software itself, what makes is good, what makes it bad. Lets focus on the shorter list first.
It is a Pixelart software. If you are looking for a simple image editing Program that lets you paint with infinite colors, do yourself a favour and use Photoshop. This program allows you to use a maximum palette 256 colors per palette. So you can have different palettes on different layers and even on animation frames, and there is gradual layer transparency. But nonetheless, if you plan on doing digital painting, go look somewhere else. Pro Motion NG is for pixelart only.
Also there are still a few minor issues with how certain file paths are associated with your project and a few issues with tilemapping, but those are getting ironed out already.
Apart from that, you will face a certain learning curve in order to get into what pro motion has to offer, as it does some things very differently from other software packages. But if you want to learn pixel art or just want to get to know the software, this shouldn't be much of an issue.
Apart from that, that is pretty much it for the cons.
The first CON is actually a PRO for pixel artists. I want limited palettes. Also I want good palette creation and management option. And in this regard the software is top notch. Not only does it bring along a number of accurate retro palettes along with tile size limits etc, it also has a ton of options to generate your own palettes. It makes it fun and easy.
Gradients are also a pretty big part of the software. They allow you not only to create dithered and non dithered gradients from arbitrary color selections, they also double as guidelines for some more exotic paint modes.
Pro Motion NG brings along a number of so called paint-modes. Some of those are familiar, but some of them are simply mind blowing and time saving like nothing else. The star of the paint modes is the Multi-Shade paint mode, which basically allows you to shade pixels in shades of a gradient without changing the active color. Hard to explain, but once you try this you will be blown away. Not only that, there is also the option to use auto dithering, which basically lets you set a dither pattern and only paint in this pattern. All pixels outside the pattern will not be touched as long as dithering is active. How awesome is that?
Pro Motion has multiple Layers. Static image layers, which do not change across frames, image layers, which change per frame, and tilemap layers for special tilemap projects. Layer-handling is straightforward and supports opacity, layer based, index based and by alpha channel, which can be painted separately or simultaneously.
The Pattern Drawing feature is really useful for tileable textures. Just set it to on and off you go. It's fast. It's precise and has a number of options (e.G.: setting the displayed grid size) to get you exactly where you want.
Animation is a blast in this software. All the staples are there along with a very nicely customizable onion skin feature. Really great to work with.
Tilemapping is actually really fun. It let's you set and define tiles and really build AND edit tilemapped layouts at the same time. Which saves so much time.
One of the most unusual thing that Pro Motion NG features are brushes. They are not strictly used in the sense like other software uses brushes. Essentially, it allows you to cut any part of the pixelart on screen and store it as brush for every paint mode (stamp, continuous, airbrush, lines, circles, boxes, ... ) So you can use simple brushes for creative painting, but you can store whole parts of graphics (arms, heads etc.) and store them conveniently for later frames or even in between project files in global brush containers. This feature is an immense time-saver. You don't have to scrob back and forth to find what you are looking for, you just look to your brush containers.
I could go on with the feature list, since there is so much more, like text, the use of bitmap fonts, wild symmetry options, frame scrolling, so many convenience options, the really nice UI, the animation preview window you can actually paint in. There is so much going on. If you really are into pixel art, there is no way around at least testing the software. Sure, there is other really good software out there (I also own Aseprite and Pyxel-Edit), but for me at least, this one is the best.

I am using PM for more than 2 years now, and it is by far the most powerful pixel-oriented drawing program I have used (I have started doing pixel-art with Degas Elite and Deluxe Paint on Atari ST/Amiga in the good ol'days ;-))
+ Powerful set of tools, with many helper functions
+ Great color palette management with many functions for sorting, creating color ramps, ...
+ Stencil function to easily protect part of your drawing
+ Anim painting to easily create animation of moving objects
+ Highly customizable (keyboard shortcuts, mouse wheel functions, windows arrangement, full screen mode, ...)
+ Fully integrated support for animation and multi-layers tilemap definition
On the downside, my main complaint would be the small UI elements (but at least you keep most of your screen space for the drawing canvas)
Highly recommended!

This game is both figuratively and literally a work of art. The beautiful music, painstakingly detailed environments, and passionate voice acting blew me away. Then Fidget and all 304% of her adorable-osity sealed the deal. At first the story didn't really spark much interest--being the typical "all powerful mysterious warrior with amnesia traversing the land helping it's people while trying to regain his dark and mysterious memory"-- but as it went on it started to pull me in. It's best described as a cross between Okami and Rayman Origins with a little bit of Kingdom Hearts sprinkled on top. (Pros and cons below.)
Pros:
-Beautifully orchestrated music
-Painfully detailed environments and weather effects
-Very touching and emotionally impacting. Feelings of pain, sorrow, love--concepts of life and death are handled maturely like they should be and conveyed to the player
-Excellent, passionate voice acting
-Exciting and tense moments
Neutral:
-The humor is 50-50. There are some funny jokes. There are some dry jokes.
-Storyline may or may not provide the player with much interest.
-The difficulty fluxuates. Some areas are very easy, some areas suddenly♥♥♥♥♥♥you.
Cons:
-A bit on the short side
-Typical hack'n slash with redundant combat
-VERY few combos to use; especially for a hack n'slash
-Hordes of respawning enemies can be a bit overwhelming and annoying at times
-Boss battles are complete jokes. Normal enemies are more life threatening than the bosses
-Practically no replay value
Conclusion:
-6.5/10. While the gameplay and hack'n slash elements are regretably limited, this game is a work of art. It's a 2D game that has infinitely more heart and soul put into it than most overrated 3D Micheal Bay games out today. It is TRULY a work of art and deserves as much support and recognition as it can get for its BEAUTY instead of gameplay which unfortunately is below par. Of course artistry isn't for everyone. This game is not for everyone. But that doesn't stop it from being truly beautiful.

Aragami is a game that I'll probably never play again. Its saving graces are the excellent controls and co op mode but that won't save it from being shelved indefinitely.
The levels are very repetitive. Dash around, destroy lamps, collect scrolls, try not to be seen. The only variation in design appears in the last 3 levels. It would have been nice to fight more bosses.  By end game with all scrolls collected everyone will have the same maxed out abilities.
Changing the difficulty doesn't change the A.I. behaviour, the A.I. is still super dumb on hard. Changing the difficulty did make one of the early levels impossible due to the distance needed to cover a gap from a pillar to the other side of a canyon. I was hoping that gaining abilities would allow me to traverse the distance on hard, playing through again on hard with all abilities maxed out did not change anything.
The story is generic with no real choice or consequence with terrible 1 to 3 second animated cutscenes that don't elaborate on the story any more than the dialog does. I could see the plot twist coming a mile away, it's a run of the mill betrayal/tragedy. Generic, boring and forgetable.
I did experience some game breaking bugs during my playthrough such as, invincible players, invisible npcs, npc alert status on player respawn, unlimited shadow pool, aragami always crashing on exit and a few others.
Overall the gameplay is solid with reliable controls and performance but the levels and story are very spare in design and originality.

It's true, this game has many repetitive missions. It's true, this game has countless bugs and glitches. But it's also true that it has a very amazing story.
The game starts in the late 1960s, where racist is still everywhere. We play as Lincoln Clay, whose a war veteran but still treated just like any other black guys. The story in this game is very rich, where it tells how corrupt the city is, and how the whites stand tall over blacks. 2K dare to put that element, and honestly, it works. It's amazing how they makes us feel like we are back in the United States in the late 1960s.
The city, New Bordeaux, is perfectly craft, and it's a beautiful city. One side, the city is just a swamp, filled with the rednecks, and the other side is the high-profile Downtown, where tall buildings is everywhere. It's amazing to just roam the city and see every details the team has put in the game.
The soundtrack is really what makes the game feels the 1960s. Personally love the WNBX station, where it's put the rock musics like Rolling Stones.
Well, of course the game is not perfect. The repetitive gameplay is the main reason why people hate this game, and I gotta say, it's true. But, I didn't hate this game. I just didn't say this game is perfect. It's a shame since the game already had an amazing story, great characters, and awesome city.
And a lot amount of bugs and glitches can be found in the game.

As someone who grew up on both music games (DDR, Beatmania, Frequency, Guitar freaks, Guitar hero) AND Action RPG's of various sorts (Baulder's gate, Diablo 1&2, Gauntlet) This game does hit on pretty much all of my nostalgia, right off the bat, so I'm going to try to review this game without my biases intact.
the enemies have super basic AI with generally super-telegraphed attack animations, and yet because of how the game is designed, they can still kick your♥♥♥♥♥  Everything is specifically coordinated and timed. every movement, every swing. you know when they're going to attack and usually where they're going to move to, just on sight.... and it still manages to kill you if you don't take the time to get good and learn the patterns, but is incredibly satisfying to go through without taking damage.
The levels are procedural, and the procedural generation works fine, but there's a problem. stage 1, stage 2, stage 3, boss, menu. stage 1, stage 2, stage 3, boss, menu. There should be a mode for unlimited stages w/o bossesses, or where after you beat a boss, you go to the next area, rather than going through the menus. sure, the items carying over seems overpowered, but as longa s you made some items only drop on specific areas, it could work out quite well. Sadly, the game does not do this, but it's still early access, so here's hoping that the devs read reviews of thier games on here.
the last thing I wanna say is probably the biggest downside. Sure, importing your own music has a fugly text-UI that I, without programing knowledge, feel like I could design something better.... That isn't even a problem. you only deal with it for a few moments, and only if you use custom music. but that isnt' the problem. the problem is with how it reads custom music. There are some bosses which use music that isn't a standard tempo, like the conga boss. there it's 7 beats, and then a pause without a beat, and it restarts. so you can make 7 moves, and then you have to wait. and then 7 moves, and then you wait. if you try to move on that missing beat, you lose your combo and nothing happens. that's fantastic. there's a button you can step on that smoothly changes the tempo of the songs, making you play faster or slower. fan-freaking-tastic.... So what happens if you put in a song with a missing beat? it still counts as a beat. no fun little stutters or rests. What happens if a song has swing? it doesn't pick up on it, and you end up being able to move where there isn't a beat in the song, but can't move on beat. And what happens if you load a song that changes tempo, smoothly or otherwise? the game recognizes the song, says "we can't find the beat", and if it uses that song on a level, it just skips that level.... which means with custom music you can skip right to the boss without any items. this is very very bad.
I understand that the tempo-detection software isn't good enough to interpret rhythms and tempo-changes, I'm a musician, I know what software limitations we have at this point in time... but there IS a way around it, after all, they have songs built in that do exactly those things. I offer a solution to fix it, if the devs read this, then great, it might get implimented. Custom songs, when the game can't detect the tempo, it will give a warning. if it has a variable swing, you can tell the game what that swing is. and add more than just MP3 support. combine MP3 and a midi file that matches the tempo and rhythm of the song. I want to be able to do healing vision from DDR 5th mix. I want to be able to do march of the pigs by Nine inch nails. but right now... you can't. the game can't figure it out, and just bugs out, skiping the stage.
Oh, and there seems to be a maximum tempo. I tried putting in 500BPM speedcore, and the auto-detect said it was 125, which means that double-time was still only 250bpm... I know what you're thinking. "ONLY 250BPM?! ONLY?!"... I like breaking things. admittedly 250 BPM turned out to be great fun to play though.
At this stage in early access, compaired to other early access games, I give it a 9/10 - the only in-dev games i've had more fun with have been Dwarf Fortress, Kerbal Spaceprogram, and Minecraft.
at this stage in early access, compaired to NON-EARLY ACCESSi games, I give it about a 6/10. This little point'n'click adventure is the best proof that games are not to be judged by how they look and sound. This game is horrible and awesome at the same time.
At first sight the graphics look like they've been done by a 10-year old with MS Paint. The music is annoyingly repetitive and can't be turned off (the setting in the configuration doesn't do anything), the font is horrible and just on the border of being unreadable, there is no voiceover (thankfully?) and even the controls are a bit clumsy.
But wait, despite all that, I enjoyed every moment of playing it, because the epic and over-the-top story, the insane and funny things you have to do, the funny dialogs and everything else completely outshine the horribleness. Actually, I'm pretty sure the horribleness was done on purpose because while the drawings are ugly, they are consistent across the whole game and everything is perfectly recognizable, made with a lot of effort to make it look ugly and appealing at the same time. Only a great artist can draw something so beautifully ugly.
Highly recommended with or even without a discount.

Excellent game! Lots of replay value. The controls can feel a bit "delayed" or "clunky" at times. But that caveat is completely overshadowed by the overall gameplay. It's very immersive, and I found the story line to be interesting.
One thing you should be aware of is that there is one "gatekeeper" jumping puzzle that I found more than a little "challenging!" If you dislike jumping-puzzles, as I do, the appearance of this one is pretty shocking and totally out of character with the rest of the game. Fortunately, however, the designers appear to have realized that a certain "frustration threshold" is not good! So, if you can't get past this stupid thing after some number of tries, the next time you start up the game into that spot, the spinning disks will be halted, and the spinning light swords will not exist. Then you can easily jump up past the thing and get by it. GOOD thinking on the part of the devs. I otherwise hate "gatekeeper" things that halt progression.
Of special note is that the designers really got right the way "success" is tallied up. You can play high-chaos or high-stealth, and you are rewarded regarding how successful you are in either approach. For example, if you decide to kill guards, you get (significant) extra score for killing ALL of the guards on the map.
The maps feel very open and expansive, not like you have to approach your objectives in any particular way. And the increasing powers available to you feel, well, powerful! The additional powers as you progress mean that there's enough range of different sorts of capabilities you can employ, that you will be able to fit your particular game-play style.
Multiplayer (co-op) is also really well handled, and you can build characters that complement each other if you play with friends. Once you max out all the powers, you can still adopt play styles that are complimentary. And the maps are the same whether you're playing co-op or single-player. It's not like so many games in which there's one "campaign" for single-player and something completely different for co-op. Those, to me, always seem stilted.
In short, this is a very well-conceived and well-executed game that is extremely immersive as long as you linger in its "shadow world." :-)
You can't go wrong for the $14 I paid, that's for sure.

Hotline Miami is a game that wants you dead with a passion. It will kill you, time and again, be it by crushing blows to the skull or a belly full of lead. It will, without hesitation or remorse, utterly ♥♥♥♥ing brutalize you.
It is also, without a doubt, the most rewarding, interesting, and thoroughly enjoyable game i've played in a really long time. The gameplay is fast. Like, blisteringly freaking fast. You can slash, bash, and gun your way through an obscene number of enemies. You die in a single hit most of the time, and you restart each level from a checkpoint at the beginning of a each larger room you enter. Because of this, the game is lent a sense of urgency, and man, do you have to be urgent in some of the later levels (Or risk becoming best pals with the blunt end of a steel pipe).
This grungy, gritty, very '80s atmosphere is made all the more potent by the soundtrack. By god, the soundtrack. Quick, simple beats and synth chords make up most of the BGM, but man, it's really good stuff. If you're into that, it's certainly a plus. Pretty much everything about this game, from the chilling, semi-improvised bursts of violence to the flashy, achingly saturated colour palette the game sports to the eerie, meta-commentary narrative  just reeks of not necessarily beauty, but a certain style.
And indeed, that's what Hotline Miami is.
Pure, bewitching, and stomach-churningly ultraviolent style.
So, if you've ever thought about redecorating public spaces with an astronomical number of assorted innards, go ahead and pick up Hotline Miami. It's super fast, super gory, and super fun.

This is just an amazing game with an amazing backstory.
Ever thought of how X-Com2 doesn't make sense because a squad of 6 cannot possibly change things on a world scale ? Here, you have templars on battlemechs that FEEL like you're not a puny human. And, you need it. The "smallest" enemy is a 5 meter tall spider that puny humans have to gang up 5 to 1 to beat.
But. You're templars. You've got the firepower.
Another point is that not only the character classes feel different, you also have multiple paths to choose in each classes to further specialize your units. Example, your scout can be so stealthy that no one catches him, or can be a deadly sniper headshotting anything in sight. The "gear" mechanic is also well thought out, as are the stat system (finally not something based on str / dex / con...).
Not only that, but the devs on this are not only still developping content, they also respond to bug reports in a few hours / days at most.
If you're looking for a cross between warhammer 4K & X-com, there it is.

Nearly every moment of my time during the first 30 hours of playthrough was filled with this thought "If I were designing this game, I'd include a game mechanic that did X". Immediately after each of these thoughts "X" happened. I really couldn't be more pleased.  I'll break this down into a categorical deep-dive:
This game has kept me playing for about 100 hours thus far (my hours currently appear inflated due to AFK time. This game has a rich set of rules that govern how combat plays out. At the easiest couple of difficulties, you can survive without knowing the details. However, the well-crafted ruleset (mechanics) lend importance to every single decision you make and nuance layerd upon nuance.
The game has many difficulty levels which not only add immesurable amounts of replay value, but also caters toward those who are masters of strategy as well as the novice more interested in the story, and everything in-between.  I always enjoy myself when playing this game, win or lose.
The music is somewhat simple, while also appropriately bombastic, and anxiety-enducing. (This is particularly the case when I've just realized I'm surrounded, out of range of my turrets and supplies are running low.) It loops in a simple pattern, which I orginally thought would drive me mad, but surprisingly I haven't been bothered by the repetition a single time. Consider that this entire game was made by three brothers and tell me you aren't impressed that at least one of them had enough musical talent to do this.
The graphics on this game are typical of an indie studio. Think around the range of a Sega Genesis game in terms of detail . However, the art is extremely good and sets the stage for the plot and overall ambiance. I'm not a huge fan of GPU-intensive games anyway so I'm pleased enough with the quality here.
I won't spoil the plot here but know that the story builds as you progress in a satisfying way. I never felt a break in the immersion while playing due to a plot foible or poorly written line of text.  The game is consistently good in this department, and actually wasn't predictable to me. One nice thing is this game takes place in a broader ecosystem of games and so I feel I get value out of learning about this portion as it will apply to earlier/later titles.
Ok, so I've mentioned I spent 100+ hours so far? Yeah, that's on two difficulty levels I've played. I am a slower player of this game. There are totally different sets of strategies that would end maps more quickly but I prefer slower, methodical, alien bloodbaths.  I expect to put another
into this game. Why? Let's count the replay-enhancing options:
1. There are many story paths you can take that aren't available in a single playthrough.
2. There is a limited amount of a resource you use to give team-wise specializations (called "RQ" in the game) that means you effectively have *many* mutually exclusive options as you play through an entire game. Trying to get through the game without one branch of skills/items gives you more room to play with other abilities/toys.
3. There are something like 9 difficulty levels. I skipped over Easy as it isn't massively different than Normal and I didn't consider myself enough of a novice to start on Easy. However, the other difficulty levels are distinct enough in their challenges that I intend to play through each at least once. (The higher difficulties will take longer, and some permanently punish failure so they'll take many times more hours to play through.)
4. There is a new game+ mode through which you can continue on the same or a different difficutly with all of your skills/levels/gear that you earned throughout the game but the enemies' levels scale as well. This is the mechanism through which you can get all of the possibly abilities/gear on a single squad. However, I've enjoyed playing with famine more than feast so I haven't even tried this yet.
5. There are new levels occasionally added to the post-campgain section, for free! Think DLC worth 20% of the buying price of your favorite game being released every few months or so, but at no cost to you. Pretty sweet. The set of missions they have out right now are at least as good as the main campaign.
6. There are Steam achivements that might require a special setup to acquire. You could burn some hours hunting these down for sure.
Now, here's really the only weak point of this game. It has some weird bugs every now and then, but I personally have never encountered any that broke my game. (I have been saddened to get a new item only to discover it was bugged such that it took no effect.) However, the asterisk I'm applying here is because the game developers are continually fixing bugs as they are reported (and I mean like within hours of the report) and adding new content, again, for free! This is truly the game that keeps on giving.  Also, if you consider the team size (3) of the developers, this is a rare masterpiece.
In closing I definitely think it is worth the asking price of $50. Wait, it's only

This is a gray area in gaming. I would review this differently if it wasn't free. However, it is free, so I'll review it as such.
This game is one of many CS clones, but an okay one at that. Even if you're a gamer with a bad computer and on a budget (like me) , then this game probably still isn't for you. This review will take you through the pros and cons.
Pros:
The gameplay is very rounded, no overly extreme weapons, no underwhelming weapons.
The point/money system is well-made, as killing gives a certain amount of points, depending on how you do it, letting you upgrade your weapons at the beginning of each spawn.
Cons:
Hitboxes are garbage.
If you are English, you won't know what literally anyone is saying.
There are about 5 hackers per 3 games and all the Devs do about it is label the hackers "Cheaters". No banning, nothing.
Graphics are terrible.
Horrible optimization. (Plenty of options, not enough change)
After all this, I cannot recommend this to you with a clean conscience. This game is about as bad as it gets.

Duck Game is one of those rare titles where you don't want to buy it because it seems too good to be true, but when you do buy it you only regret not buying it sooner.
This game plays and feels a lot like Super Smash Brothers, which is strange because it isn't really anything like that game series. You jump around, pick up items, and you try to kill other players. Most weapons kill instantly, so it's hard for this game to not feel balanced. Whenever an item is in place and does seem overpowered, it typically just makes the game more interesting as the players fight for it.
The levels are okay, but the fact there is the ability to make your own levels, post them on workshop, download other people's workshop, etc. is just amazing. This game ALWAYS feels fresh. The only complaint I have is how difficult it can be to mark levels as crap. My friend will mindlessly download a bunch of maps, but whenever one sucks, we kinda just deal with it because it's too difficult for him to delete. I feel all players should be able to mark each level on the start menu as good or bad in order to avoid these problems. Additionally, if host had such control, they can later go through their selections and realize which ones they don't like and remove them. I also notice that I have to download levels everytime. It's a fast download, but I feel I should have the option to keep every level I play.
There is a single player mode, which is okay, just okay. It's basically an arcade full of mini games and various situational objective based games that's just like the core gameplay that serves as a tutorial for players. It unlocks hats and stuff as well, which is a cool bonus. I kinda wish it had some sort of coop mode for it.
You're able to download stuff from workshop, such as mods, but you're not able to play them online unless other players have it... which I find ridiculous since that's the whole point of workshop.
Though you cannot use it for weapon mods, you can use a bit of an exploit that allows the use of custom hats online. It's not super difficult to do, but I think it's stupid I have to do something of the sort.
There is also various weapons that's a part of the game that cannot be used online. Not mods, actual parts of the game that is singleplayer only. I find this strange for some of these items and weapons are really interesting. When you make a level in level editor, you shouldn't see some items and know they're not online capable.
Despite those problems, the game is still an overwhelmingly yes. The gameplay is quick, fluent, addictive, and ultimately fair depending on level design. Also, there is a button for playing dead; which, like dead bodies, players can pick up the player playing dead and punish them for doing it. This is great for intense gameplay. There is also a button for quacking. It literally does nothing else, you just quack. This game is fun. It's worth full price.

After 20 hours of playtime, I can honestly say I enjoy this game! It may not live up to the high bar set by the first two installments in the franchise, but in my opinion, is still a good game in its own right - but not one without its issues...
Pros:
-Music, Vehicles and Weapons Create an extremely authentic portrayal of the 1960's American South
-Open World Districts are teeming with charm, uniqueness and personality
-Story, may follow well-trodden revenge stereotypes, but Hangar 13 have thrown in some cool twists to the tale
-Lincoln! The way he moves and interacts with other characters make the player feel truly badass and feared
-Doesn't shy away from the atrocities of the time
-VITO
Cons:
-Well-trodden Open World side missions and gameplay mechanics get very repetitive very fast
-Dull, boring colour palette and below-average graphical fidelity for a modern AAA title, even on high
-Lincoln again, while on the surface he is a cool character, he lacks nuance or any real personality
-SHOCKING optimisation, and I mean shocking - at 1080p on High Preset my GTX 1060 cannot run this game without significant stuttering, so I am confined to the locked 30 FPS if I want decent graphics - this really is unacceptable...
So overall, Mafia 3 is fun, but corporate greed is really on show here, and this isn't even an EA game... If you can deal with poor PC performance and repetitiveness, Mafia 3's storyline and setting are one of the most unique of 2016, but otherwise, stay well clear.

A turn-based tactical RPG which is rather plainly an homage to the Warhammer 40k universe. Lead a squad of genetically engineered Templars in the massive powered armor suit against hordes of xenos, heretical human forces, and hyper-advanced machines. Basically, tyranids, Chaos cultists/renegade Imperial Guard, and necrons. A wide variety of classes abound for your Templars to choose from, with new types of armor, weapons, relics, "call-downs", and other bonuses made available to that class and, in some cases, other classes as well.
One of the great parts of the game is that it captures the feel of fielding an individually superior, albeit numerically outmatched, force. You face unending waves of enemies which you will cut apart, burn to a crisp, or blast to pieces in droves. Managing your unit's overwatch as you move to achieve your objectives is reminiscent of the Space Hulk games. Achieving the main objectives, as well as bonuses objectives, awards you with points you can use to recruit more Templars, or upgrade existing Templar class lines. As well, individual Templars level-up over time, giving you stat points to assign, and allowing them to use more/more advanced gear.
Overall, recommended. A fun title for a reasonable price.

As someone who grew up on both music games (DDR, Beatmania, Frequency, Guitar freaks, Guitar hero) AND Action RPG's of various sorts (Baulder's gate, Diablo 1&2, Gauntlet) This game does hit on pretty much all of my nostalgia, right off the bat, so I'm going to try to review this game without my biases intact.
the enemies have super basic AI with generally super-telegraphed attack animations, and yet because of how the game is designed, they can still kick your♥♥♥♥♥  Everything is specifically coordinated and timed. every movement, every swing. you know when they're going to attack and usually where they're going to move to, just on sight.... and it still manages to kill you if you don't take the time to get good and learn the patterns, but is incredibly satisfying to go through without taking damage.
The levels are procedural, and the procedural generation works fine, but there's a problem. stage 1, stage 2, stage 3, boss, menu. stage 1, stage 2, stage 3, boss, menu. There should be a mode for unlimited stages w/o bossesses, or where after you beat a boss, you go to the next area, rather than going through the menus. sure, the items carying over seems overpowered, but as longa s you made some items only drop on specific areas, it could work out quite well. Sadly, the game does not do this, but it's still early access, so here's hoping that the devs read reviews of thier games on here.
the last thing I wanna say is probably the biggest downside. Sure, importing your own music has a fugly text-UI that I, without programing knowledge, feel like I could design something better.... That isn't even a problem. you only deal with it for a few moments, and only if you use custom music. but that isnt' the problem. the problem is with how it reads custom music. There are some bosses which use music that isn't a standard tempo, like the conga boss. there it's 7 beats, and then a pause without a beat, and it restarts. so you can make 7 moves, and then you have to wait. and then 7 moves, and then you wait. if you try to move on that missing beat, you lose your combo and nothing happens. that's fantastic. there's a button you can step on that smoothly changes the tempo of the songs, making you play faster or slower. fan-freaking-tastic.... So what happens if you put in a song with a missing beat? it still counts as a beat. no fun little stutters or rests. What happens if a song has swing? it doesn't pick up on it, and you end up being able to move where there isn't a beat in the song, but can't move on beat. And what happens if you load a song that changes tempo, smoothly or otherwise? the game recognizes the song, says "we can't find the beat", and if it uses that song on a level, it just skips that level.... which means with custom music you can skip right to the boss without any items. this is very very bad.
I understand that the tempo-detection software isn't good enough to interpret rhythms and tempo-changes, I'm a musician, I know what software limitations we have at this point in time... but there IS a way around it, after all, they have songs built in that do exactly those things. I offer a solution to fix it, if the devs read this, then great, it might get implimented. Custom songs, when the game can't detect the tempo, it will give a warning. if it has a variable swing, you can tell the game what that swing is. and add more than just MP3 support. combine MP3 and a midi file that matches the tempo and rhythm of the song. I want to be able to do healing vision from DDR 5th mix. I want to be able to do march of the pigs by Nine inch nails. but right now... you can't. the game can't figure it out, and just bugs out, skiping the stage.
Oh, and there seems to be a maximum tempo. I tried putting in 500BPM speedcore, and the auto-detect said it was 125, which means that double-time was still only 250bpm... I know what you're thinking. "ONLY 250BPM?! ONLY?!"... I like breaking things. admittedly 250 BPM turned out to be great fun to play though.

This game has been clearly written by people like me, who grew up playing adventure games. The humour is great, the puzzles keep you entertained and you get sucked right in. However, there are some fundamental interface issues that I'm really surprised they didn't pick up on.
The single click to move between actions quickly became frustrating, changing to walk mode to get to the door, changing to use to use the door, then changing back to walk mode to walk to the next door etc. got quickly irritating. Double click to walk when in any action mode would have saved so much time. Or, adding keyboard shortcuts to each mode as many other adventure games do. Even the simple things like "i" to open inventory would have been useful.
This meant that every process was slow, even when you knew exactly what to do. And it was painful when you ended up in a try everything with everything scenario.
The other problem is that of saving. There is no autosave feature, nor is there any warning if you try and quit without saving. Two quite obvious things, the latter especially important if there isn't the former. Assuming I would be able to reload and continue, I quit after my first 1 hour session and found my self having to start all over again the next time I opened up the game. On no less than 2 occasions after that, the game crashed and I found myself redoing entire sections because I hadn't saved regularly enough.
Finally, there are no options for the resolution and it kept running an incorrect resolution. This wouldn't be so bad, if the performance wasn't also terrible. It's hardly graphically taxing - is smooth scrolling across a room really too much to ask for?
If those issues haven't put you off, then I would still recommend the game, but it pretty much ruined it for me. Developers I hope you're listening.
