Metal Dead is a 2D point and click adventure that follows metalheads Malcom and his best friend Ronnie through the mayhem of a zombie apocalypse. Driving along the zombie infested highway in a rust bucket of a car, Ronnie reveals to Malcom that he's driving them directly to where he believes the outbreak began. Malcom isn't exactly thrilled over the idea, and he grabs the wheel and ends up crashing the car; inadvertently killing Ronnie in the process, who then turns in to a zombie. Stricken with grief, Malcom severs Ronnie's head and carries it with him for the remainder of the game. The story then dives into a spiral of hilarity, filled with cultural references to both metal and horror.
The art direction of this game is absolutely fantastic, though some may argue that it resembles free flash games that you can find on places like Newgrounds. It's a simple, overly-cartoonish style for sure, but it adds to the vibe that Metal Dead doesn't exactly take itself seriously. There's also plenty of blood, entrails, zombies, and violence to go around, further enunciating the dark humor of the title. The chiptune soundtrack is also worth talking about, because the songs are extremely catchy and I'll admit, I even headbanged a little bit to the track at the very beginning.
Though it's not necessarily unpredictable by any means, the story is fun to indugle yourself in. No matter the simplicity of the base plot or premise, the dialogue is what's really captivating as it provides chuckles and even good laughs throughout the 4 hour length of Metal Dead. Each character has a thriving personality of their own, and you really have no idea what may happen to them next. The puzzles aren't very hard to figure out, and even though this is a point and click adventure game, it feels more like an interactive story instead at times.
Without a doubt, Metal Dead is a must play title for horror fans, and especially metalheads. The cartoony graphics, kickass soundtrack, and morbidly hilarious story/dialogue are well worth experiencing at least once. Sadly, there's not a lot of replay factor here, all of the achievements can be unlocked on one playthrough and there's no bonus content. The ride lasts roughly 4 hours, so enjoy it while it lasts! Well worth it for the low price of $5.49 CAD.

Pray for Diamonds is an indie film about a witch and a wizard who live in a trailer house by a country road and are trying to correctly perform a ritual that will give them... diamonds. And they try to sacrifice three random people to a face inside of a briefcase in order to do so.
Oh, but Double Uppercut! It's artsy! It's pretentious! You like artsy and pretentious things, because you yourself are artsy and pretentious.
I appreciate the flattery, but it will get you nowhere.
See, Pray for Diamonds advertises itself as "laudable", and that struck me as an odd way to describe your film. Anything can be lauded. I could laud Transformers: Dark of the Moon right now if I really wanted to (or if I hadn't recently eating, so I wouldn't vomit while making the attempt). You could laud a f***ing deer you spotted out in the woods, for Chr***'s sake!
It's shot by who I'd guess is a group of 20-something college students (like me), but the difference between them and me is that I'm better. Why? Because I said I am.
But seriously, I've seen art films that don't make sense. A few good examples of some art films I really like are Eraserhead, The Neon Demon, and the recent Nocturnal Animals (if you haven't seen it yet, you absolutely must). I like these artsy films because they actually are ART. They're shot fantastically, well acted (well... all except Neon Demon kind of), and have something to say. What is Pray for Diamonds trying to say? That you should become a witch and make tons of money by sacrificing people?

Despite it's age, NS2 looks very nice and runs beautifully, which wasn't always the case. The game is definitely the most stable it has ever been, in terms of performance.
Despite showing some age, and having a pretty ancient netcode which results in many "round the corner" type deaths, NS2 is still a very enjoyable experience and a great game to fill up a night or two.
However, the community has problems. First off, the game is dead. NS2 will host an average of 250 players daily, if it's lucky. This means you'll be playing the same people, which can be a good or bad thing depending on how good you are at the game, and your standing with everyone. Be friendly and try not to alienate anyone because of this, as you'll probably only have 2-3 servers at most to choose from. If you get banned from them, or make people hate you, you will literally be screwed out of playing this game ever again.
If you are looking to pick this game up to play with friends, I sadly recomended that you reconsider. Once you and your friends reach level 5, and you are no longer able to play on the few 'Rookie Servers', you'll be pingeonholed into one of the two servers remaining - where everyone votes for "skill based teams" that will result in you being placed on the opposite teams than your friends.
You'll go from having fun playing with your buddies on the team you want to play on - to having the game constantly dictate itself to you with it's constant restrictions and lack of care for your playstyle. You like playing aliens? Chances are you'll be forced marines more often that not and you'll have to sit through rounds of drudgery just to play what you wanted in the first place. By then, you won't even care.

Dark Crusade is an improvement on the mechanics of Dawn of War and adds new factions, units, and a world map-based conquest mode as the campaign in the game.  For those of us who enjoyed standard scenarios and multiplayer this is entirely an improvement.  Unfortunately, for those of us who were more caught up in the story-based campaigns where a story unfolded before you as you played, that feature no longer exists.
The world map does offer a few advantages that I will admit are enjoyable.  First off, you feel more like a true commander as opposed to a company leader in the prior Dawn of War iterations.  You decided on where and when battles will take place and often those decisions are based on which provinces offer the most requisition (currency) and benefits for your units.  The enemy also acts with the same goals and will actively invade your territory if it sees fit, bringing the battle to you.
The unfortunate part to this, in addition to the loss of a well developed story from earlier campaigns, most of your battles end up being frantic zerg fights where you churn out your units and upgrades as fast as possible and slam them into the enemy until they are dead.  Obviously, the old strategies do apply, and the classic rock-paper-scissors aspects of the units remain, but I myself always felt more caught up accomplishing objectives and advancing the story.
It was a toss up for me, as you may have guessed after reading the above, but I have decided that I'm going to recommend this game since it will satisfy previous DoW players who enjoyed the basic scenarios even if the heavily story-based campaign is gone.

If you're a fan of sci-fi in style of WH40K, with a desire for a top-down squad based RPG version of the space hulk board game, then you've potentially found what you're looking for.
Features:
- You dictate which troop type & skills your squad will gain access to. e.g. Scout, Engineer, heavy weapon specialist (Machine gun, flamethrower), melee specialist.
- Penalty free re-assignment of skill points (can't change a character's class though) between battles.
- mission's can have 2+ possible paths e.g. wait for enemy to attack a place of importance (colony) or deep strike into the enemy base camp.
- some missions allow reinforcements to arrive and new recruits to join your team.
- only small parts of the map are revealed on deployment, such as entry point, exit point and some enemy spawn points in selected missions. This helps add an element of suspense.
- bonuses for: completing mission within turn target, how many foe have been killed, carrying out secret secondary objective (collect object(s) hidden on map - that you may not have been told about).
important game mechanics to be aware of are:
HEAT: Every action generates heat, and you can only dissipate some of that heat each turn. Doing nothing means you loose more heat than if you only move around or fire your gun. This is important as a full heat guage means you take damage until you let your mech cool down.
NO UNDO MOVE: you can cancel a characters move whilst they are part way through moving, but you can't undo an accidental move. So you need to be aware of who you've selected when you click move. I've accidentally moved the wrong person before, and had the crucial squad member head away from the objective.
The mechanics are table top based (d10, d100), so some of the descriptions for the game mechanics can be too technical if all you want to know is does this stat boost my damage for my gun/sword/grenade and by how much.

Either way, the game is looking great, players new to this game will quickly get punished by the games relentless dedication to movement/rythm based fighting, often meaning that anyone who jumps in unprepared will end up dying a lot.
What does this say about the game? Maybe for the common, run of the mill gamer it might mean frustrating and unpreventable deaths. But to the dedicated gamer, those who use tutorials or at least have played a rythm game of some kind can grasp that everything requires key timing and a suprisingly large amount of strategy.
Do I reccomend this game? Yes. As of this moment its £10.99 ($17.94, €13.85), if you have the money, I fully reccomend buying and trying this game to anyone who is interested in it. More importantly I reccomend it as a backing to this genre of gaming as it is not often you see Rythm based games being produced. I know right now that more and more companies are making music based rythm games, but there needs to be a larger supply of them. With the people who made this game I do hope they make more like this as this genre is genrally underated, undersold and the variety of game titles is just too small.

This game is a good TRPG, but for me is ruined by a single game mechanic. Overheating.
Basically, whenever in combat you move, attack, use abilities or run in flames (duh), you build up Heat in your mechanized armor. Which would be fine as a mechanic if it was balanced correctly.
If a character's Heat reaches the top of its armor's tolerance, it will go in Overheating, in this status, a character won't be able to use certain skills, will have penalties to combat features, and will take damage over time based on how much Overheat there is.
Point is, Heat takes quite a lot of time to dissipate, and to make it dissipate, you have to make your soldiers do nothing at all, or barely anything, for many turns, this while enemies are rightly swarming at you from all sides.
If you don't care and just run for it and let your characters oveheat, they will lose more and more health each turn, and before or later, since missions a bit further in the game are pretty long, will die not because of enemy damage, but because of Overheating! While if they have to cool down and sit doing nothing for some turns, the enemies will tear them apart most likely.
This single mechanic, in my humble opinion, totally kills the combat, which is the large part of this title's entire gameplay. I really like the setting, the style, and the management mechanics, but after i failed my campaign just because of Overheating decimating my teams, and making me lose veteran soldiers i carefully built, i can't stand this anymore.
You may or may not agree in this opinion, i won't say i am right, it's just what i experienced.

I'm not really good at writing these types of reviews but I felt the current mixed rating this game has is, in my opinion, undeserving. So I'm hoping that this review might help people look past the current rating.
So what is Orcs Must Die!: Unchained? It's a MOBA combined with turret defense type gameplay (or trap defense in this case). In most MOBAs (say DOTA 2) minions spawn from 3 lanes from a barracks type structure and head towards a main structure in the enemy's base to attack and destroy between them are Heros (players) and turrets.
In OMD: U it's slightly different. For starters theres only 2 lanes and the minions spawn from portals. Which must then travel from their portal from your base in to the enemy's rift. There's nothing for them to destroy once there, they simply must get in to the rift to score points. Once the enemy has lost all of their points your team wins. The minions must overcome traps (laid out by the enemy team heros) and guardians (which is a big dude in armor with powerful aoe attacks) which stand in front of gates.
Now heres the cool thing: you are free to customise what gets sent down the lane! There are 3 slots for front, middle and back positions. You can send everything from orcs which are numerous but not very tough and only worth 1 point each to giants which are big, tough but slow and I believe worth like 3-5 point each. You can also get dwarfs that cast protective shields or crossbow infantry that perforate heros and guardians from a distance. To get different minions to need to unlock thier cards which are crafted from materirals you get as you play the game or from chests (which can be bought with real money).
Your can also unlock different traps in this way and traits which are minor boosts to your hero. From bonus starting gold to slight increase in health or mana.
But thats for a 5v5 match Siege mode. If you're not feeling competitive theres a Survival co-op mode where you and up to 4 other people must endure several waves of minions.
Most people will complain about micro-transactions and whatnot but well thats how a free to game works I'm afraid. Do they expect that the poeple who work on this game work completely for free? Not to mention they are completely optional. Maybe if people focused more on the actual FUN of the game instead of grind this game might get more favourable reviews but I don't really want to get more in to that. If that's their opinion then so be it.
In short this game is really fun and even though it's in beta it's very well polished. And well it's completely free if you wish to at least try it out.

Dark Crusade is an improvement on the mechanics of Dawn of War and adds new factions, units, and a world map-based conquest mode as the campaign in the game.  For those of us who enjoyed standard scenarios and multiplayer this is entirely an improvement.  Unfortunately, for those of us who were more caught up in the story-based campaigns where a story unfolded before you as you played, that feature no longer exists.
The world map does offer a few advantages that I will admit are enjoyable.  First off, you feel more like a true commander as opposed to a company leader in the prior Dawn of War iterations.  You decided on where and when battles will take place and often those decisions are based on which provinces offer the most requisition (currency) and benefits for your units.  The enemy also acts with the same goals and will actively invade your territory if it sees fit, bringing the battle to you.
The unfortunate part to this, in addition to the loss of a well developed story from earlier campaigns, most of your battles end up being frantic zerg fights where you churn out your units and upgrades as fast as possible and slam them into the enemy until they are dead.  Obviously, the old strategies do apply, and the classic rock-paper-scissors aspects of the units remain, but I myself always felt more caught up accomplishing objectives and advancing the story.
It was a toss up for me, as you may have guessed after reading the above, but I have decided that I'm going to recommend this game since it will satisfy previous DoW players who enjoyed the basic scenarios even if the heavily story-based campaign is gone.

I just stumbled upon this diamond (see what I did there? A lame joke, that is...) and did not know what to think about it at first, but having some credit on my Steam wallet led me to buy it. In the following few paragraphs, I shall summarise what exactly I think about it.
First impression: Well... what is this? Looks like a proper movie about... well, something. Let's watch the trailer.
After reading the Steam page: It's only available in Italian (which is a blatant lie, no one speaks in this movie and the credits are English)... Whatever, worst case could be that I don't like it and got some simple amusement from it.
After imagining what it could be: Well, I like this dark mystery theme and the way the characters seem to work out.
Watching the prologue: The music is really great, hope the actors step up their acting when it comes to the action though.
After a few minutes more: What the...?! I LIKE THIS. I won't spoil anything, but I was kind of impressed at this point.
Quite some time into the film: Okay, I am REALLY intrigued and want to know how the storyline develops.
The last ~8 minutes: Having my eyes fixed to the screen and ignoring my phone I held in my hand due to being so involved with what was going on, that I did not even care.
FINAL VERDICT:
This experimental short film is an absolute gem and I cannot begin to recommend it highly enough. Especially for the price, this is far better entertainment than you get from some random movie in the cinema! The music used ranges from indie / experimental to opera music, and at least I really enjoyed how the music synergized with the screenplay.
If you enjoy kind of weird, but amazing movies that make you think and involved with what is going on, this is definitely for you. And if you normally are not, just watch it anyways - it's not expensive for what you get and unless you are extremely sensitive to fake blood and (very rarely directly displayed) mild gore, you will have an awesome time.

I stumbled upon this game one night searching through the endless stream of mediocre that is the indie genre; and frankly I have been of this opinion since being one of the ignorant fools that bought No Man Sky ('nuff said -_-). But after playing 11 hours of Aragami, I can safely say its an outstanding indie game. The controls were very easy to adapt to giving the player more time to focus on maneuvering through the game, which requires alot of strategy and is suprisingly challenging. The story had a solid and very engaging plot. In terms of artistic quality, Aragami blended brushstrokes within a "Wind Waker"-esque design. The art style not only made the game very easy on the eyes but also enhanced the contrast of shaded areas in game (a VERY important aspect in maneuverability through levels). Lince Works, the developers of the game, took all this and implemented a SOLID co-op mode which I  was simple, efficient, and seamless in functionality.
But what really suprised me about this game was the music. The soundtrack was quite simply epic. Composed by Twin Feathers and using actual instruments, Aragami's music did its job by enhancing the quality of the gameplay. Unlike some game soundtracks, that make you want to toss your headphones across the room after fifteen minutes, Twin Feathers composed immersive music that coincided well with the plot twists and boss fights in the game.
Overall, I would say Aragami is a hidden gem that raises the bar and redeems the indie genre :)

3D Mark of the Ninja; 3rd Person Dishonored; the Japan-set stealth ninja game that Ubisoft could be making: all labels that could apply to Aragami.
-Gameplay:
Aragami at its core is a very basic and simple third-person stealth game. There is plenty of room for both lethal and non-lethal runs, and the game manages to achieve the balance where juggling between the two on the fly is also enjoyable. Regarding combat, there is no reliable way to engage the enemies in face-to-face combat: either you assassinate them unawares, or not at all. AI is extremely simplistic, but aggressive enough that if you are not careful nudging between their lines of sight, you WILL feel the pain. The handful of boss fights are a little gimmicky and suffer from Deus Ex: Human Revolution syndrome a little bit, but at least one involves approaching an archer, ducking and blinking between cover as you make your way up. It was tense and used the core mechanics for a climactic moment, so I had a good time, for what it's worth.
The core mechanic bares its own discussion. You blink around at whatever your camera points at just like, well, Blink from Dishonored. We all know that Blink made Dishonored an extremely easy game to complete, so I must emphasize that developer Lince Works managed to find some very clever work-arounds by restricting the blink mechanic to shadows: if there are no shadows around within your reach, you aren't going to wizz over everyone's heads. Fortunately, you are given the ability to create your own personal shadow in front of you that drains your resources and shrinks quickly: this also forces you to think carefully about where you are blinking to, and when. Overall, I am thoroughly impressed with their implementation of this mechanic and the levels they designed around it.
-Story
Nothing to see here. The "twist" is immediately obvious to anyone even a little familiar with Japanese mythology. It's not that the story is bad, just very simple and no-frills. Some cutscenes look fantastic and are worth a view at least once.
-Presentation/Visual Design
Very, very impressive. A cel-shaded design that immediately evokes the darker areas of Okami and the Wind Waker is used to great effect here. Character models overall are overly simplistic and same-y, although The two central characters look great. Animations run the range from clunky, robotic, and amateurish to fluid and highly entertaining, with most of the assassinations on the latter side of the spectrum. While I would prefer the whole game to be up to those standards, at least the developers understood that they needed to nail the ninja's movements if nothing else.
-Sound
Emotion and tone are effectively carried out with pseudo-Japanese voice acting, not unlike Midna or Fi from the Legend of Zelda franchise, and dialogue quick enough to keep the game moving along briskly. Two Feathers deserves recognition for the soundtrack, as it is very well executed. It's the style you would expect from a game like this: traditional Japanese instruments with an emphasis on flutes and strings during ambient moments, and heavy drumbeats when you are spotted and on the run. Overall no complaints at all on the audio design.
-Co-op
Ok, so this is basically the reason I bought the game and enjoyed it enough to write a review. The game allows two players to quickly pair up and jump into any level you've unlocked and have at it. Romping through the game start to finish blind with a buddy on voicechat was an unbelievably good time. The game by no means is exclusively balanced for it, and it DOES give players a bit of an advantage on the easier difficulties, but if you have the friend and the inclination, co-op is a hell of a good time.
-TL;DR:
Aragami is the casual party game for stealth enthusiasts, and the gateway drug for anyone overwhelmed by the intricacies of "full" stealth games. If you want to play a game that lets you play as a ninja who sneaks around and doesn't pull off DMC combos (although that is fine too), then do yourself a favor.

It took me way longer than I'd like to admit to decide whether or not I should give this a "Yes" or "No" to the question "Do you recommend this game?". But ultimately I've decided to give this a positive review for a few reasons:
First: The developers are adding free content updates, which goes to show that they care about the game and peoples overall opinion of it, and that they're trying to make it better. These free updates includes more outfits, car customization, races etc. Which may not be a lot but sometimes great things comes in small packages, something to snack on while we wait for the bigger (hopefully) story expansions to release.
Second: Even though the game has only been out for about 3 months they've still had the game for a quite generous price during sales, a bigger percentage than a whole lot of even older AAA games has.
As someone who pre-ordered the game I may give you the advice that the game, in my books, is worth picking up during sale, and perhaps not for it's full price.
The real kick in the balls is the repetitiv gameplay, to progress in the story you essentially have to take over more territories by causing your enemy as much damage as possible, to do so you will have to do such things as going to a factory to destroy their moonshine shipments, make your way to a warehouse/club/factory or such and kill everyone including the person who runs the place etc. After you've caused enough trouble eventually the owner of the territorie will take action and reveal himself and then you go to him and take out him and his men, that's what you basically have to to over, and over, and over again.
In all honesty though, if you look past the somewhat boring process you have to go through to unlock new parts of the story, the story itself is really good and interesting. It's your typical "I got backstabbed by someone I trusted who killed my friends and family" story they got going on, even though it's been done a thousand times it still feels really satisfying to kill your enemies knowing what they've done.
A lot of people are complaining about the driving, but in my opinion Mafia III does have a really nice driving system, and making a real drift turn in full speed without crashing at all is beyond satisfying.
The graphics may not have set a new standard but they do look nice, the lights during night, the rain, the sun shining through windows, those small things really do go hand in hand with the open world.
The open world recreation of New Orleans in 1968 is beautifully crafted, however the city does feel somewhat dead due to lack of activities and things to do, aswell as a small setback of NPC's roaming the streets.
The NPC's are really lacking least to say, you can literally walk up to an old woman, pull out a rifle and shoot a bullet right infront of her feet and her reaction will be "Well, I'm going home!" as she then proceeds to walk away in a calm maner as if she has been slightly offended. They also do have the habit of randomly spawning right infront of you out of the blue at times aswell, 1968 sure was more magical compared to today.
There are of course a handful of more pros and cons about the game, but overall it's a fun game to fool around with for a few hours, as of this review I have about 10 hours of playtime and I don't feel like the spark has died yet, even with the repetitiv gameplay. But as stated this is one of those "Buy during sale" kind of games, to put it in another perspective: Mafia III is like McDonalds, it's disgusting but you still like it, but you're not really sure why, but you do.

Match-3 meets procedurally generated, forbiddingly difficult dungeon delving.
If you like spending hours matching 3 while bobbing your head to a kickin' tune, you will probably enjoy the core mechanic that this game gets you to grind for a good handful of hours to get all its unlockables and have a good chance of actually achieving the objective.
There's a lot of character here, from your little faceless protagonist's enthusiasm when he flip-jumps out of bed every morning to go dungeoneering to the array of monsters you face, although I have to admit I was slightly happier with them when I thought the "goblin cannon squad" was actually a diseased cat coughing some kind of deadly hairball at me.
You won't spend long with this game, but what time you spend will be spent doing more or less the same thing. Don't buy it if you don't already like match-3 puzzlers at least a little bit.
You will definitely be frustrated by bad luck when you just can't get enough swords, keys, or staves at the right moments, or realize you were desperately looking for a match when you could have just used the handy standby you had in your pocket and forgot about. However, if you're up for a little frustration in the search of fun and you like puzzles and old-fashioned Nethack-style dungeons, this is the game for you. I bought it at full price and had a lot of fun with it. It was a little like Super Hexagon in its ability to keep me playing for hours just trying to get that one run that does well enough.
If you're still not sure, go check out a YouTube video for some game footage. There's no plot to spoil, so you can still enjoy the game for yourself after watching someone else play it a bit, and that will probably tell you whether you want to try it or not.

Rhythm games and roguelike games are both fairly small niches, and you wouldn't think they would go together well.
But apparently they do!
They go together as well as chocolate and peanut butter. Butter crackers and salmon spread. Uncooked fish and soy sauce.
This is a fantastically fun game. It is rather brutally difficult (just like roguelikes), and the music is head-noddingly addictive (just like rhythm games). It is a beautifully weird marriage made in a version of heaven I had never even imagined.
It's early access, so it's too early for a full review, but I love every minute I spend playing this. The only mild flaw I could ever say is that the music gets a little repetitive, as it's a roguelike, so you will be playing levels over and over and over (you can use your own music though).
If you have anything better than a hatred of roguelikes and rhythm games, you owe it to yourself to check this out. This game is a perfect example of why indie games are, in a small way, the saviors of the gaming industry. This game is weird, bizarre, unbelievably fun, and a game a AAA studio wouldn't even listen to the first sentence of the pitch for.
Also, that trader has some seriously operatic pipes!

I had 3 surprises while playing this game:
1.) I could stomach it! The violence is all very pixel-ated and overdone, so it didn't feel real to me.
2.) The ambiance in this game was top notch. The whole game reminded me of the movie Drive. The music was top notch. The twisting fonts and buildings really served to highlight how deranged your character was. There were twin-peaks-esque conversations with people wearing animal masks, who may or may not be figments of your fractured psyche. The whole intro may take place in hell? They did a great job here.
3.) All that said, I doubt I'll play this game again. It's a twin-stick shooter at it's root with one-hit kills and fast restarts. That really isn't something I enjoy, and I no longer have the time to replay a level 30 times.

Their titles are so thorough and rich that they stand out even on PC. On mobile, nothing can even hope to compare with the depth that they offer.

Especially if you're the sort of person who enjoys sinking hours upon hours into a game. I can't recommend this game, depending on the kind of player you are.
This isn't really a 'tower defense' game. It's more like 'tower OFFENSE.'
What I mean is that the game modes are basically made so that matches are as short as possible. There's a very clear meta in the game in terms of what towers are best, which sends are the most difficult to defend against (and when to send them), etc. What this amounts to is that almost every game plays out exactly the same. All of the people who have good winrate percentages play like they are the same person. You might as well just be playing an AI that does everything it can to screw you over.
Sure, there is a defensive mode, but hardly anyone ever plays it, and even that mode is kinda made so that you 'late game' matches are a rarity. You are also limited to 3 towers in that mode as well.
They also just recently patched the game with some tower rebalancing, and it's made everything even worse than before.
The quality of the game isn't bad at all... my only gripe with it is that I am a tower defense player who likes to put a lot of thought into tower selection and placement against endless waves of sends. Unfortunately, in this game the meta is so winningly powerful that you basically have to play WITH and AGAINST that meta in order to stand a chance, otherwise you *will* lose fairly quickly due to people all doing the exact same crap. Try doing your own thing and using some imagination and you'll get decimated by an early zebra heart rush. (Which, once again, everyone does.)
I can't complain much since the game was free (I even purchased the club pack for it) but after about 2,000 matches or so, I just can't recommend it for lovers of tower defense games. If you are the type of player who merely wants to win no matter what, and don't mind sticking to a meta and doing the same stuff everyone else does, you'd probably think this is a great game. Unfortunately, you are forced to play a certain way.

I rarely write reviews. I dont seem to have the flair needed to keep the pace up and end up compressing what should be full-bodied paragraphs into one huge patty. For this game though, I will make some effort as this is most certainly worthy of it.
CotND is one indie game awash hundreds of a sea of "Faux 8-bit" titles trying to hit a retro niche. This game has a lifeboat though, a huge rubber dingy! It captured my imagination with a soundtrack from the ultra talented Danny Baranowski, who has worked on such titles as Super Meat Boy and The Binding of Issac. Here he has pulled out all the stops and shown such creative flair and diversity, this is his Opus Magnum for sure.
Why am I gushing over the music first and foremost, surely that shouldn't be the first thing I should talk about? Well, actually yes! CotND is a Rhythm Based dungeon crawler. You play as Cadence, a hot blooded, rash young lady who is searching for her missing father amonst the Crypt. You must move through the various levels in tune to the music, battling the various nasties who reside in the Crypt. The enemies all have set patterns and like you they move to the beat of the tune. This is where the depth of the game comes into play:
Learn the individual patterns of each enemy and learn to predict their next move, take a good look around, see if you can use the enviroment to protect you. Perhaps you would care to use an item you've found, a bomb maybe? Or a freeze movement spell! Do you want to risk charging that ultra fast minotaur using your memory of his pattern alone or should you beat a hasty retreat until you've purchased a weapon with a longer range from the shop keeper? I know im doing what I said I wouldn't, compressing many paragraphs into one but there are so many well structured reviews on the store page should you wish for an in-depth analysis.
I am a tough man to please. Im 28 now and have grown up with SNES, PS1 +2 and anything in-between. I've witnessed the rise of indie games and the inevitable over-saturation of the genre. I support them and have enjoyed quite a few. With such a (typically) small team, it is fun and engaging to be a part of someone's world and watch it grow.
I was rather hesitant at first to opt in to another Early Access game on Steam as recent examples have been very dissapointing. One game in particular....which rhymes with "Jarhound" has been a disaster and from a overly-ambitious team without the programming skills or project management needed has rather tarnished the name of Indie development. I wont go into the full story and this is not the place to go deeper, but I wanted to say it to show the Juxtaposition between it and CotND. I am glad I took the risk, in this instance it has paid off well.
Frequent updates, a developer who encourages an open forum regarding it's progression, a fresh idea and a convenient pick up and go gameplay style leads me to cite this as one of the best steam games i've purchased (out of a damn library of 274!)
Im excited to follow it and so should you be. For me at least, it has saved the reputation of Indie games.

It's a neat base-management mobile game come to Steam. Not much else to it.
First and foremost, if you're planning on playing this fullscreen, you might want to look elsewhere. This game is incredibly slow-paced. Play it windowed, off to the side, while you watch YouTube videos or the news or wait for a real game to install. It is a MOBILE GAME, and plays as such.
You build your very own Vault, and micromanage the residents within. You construct rooms, send brave souls out into the wasteland to scavenge for materials, fight fires, manage your three main resource pools, fight off raider attacks... For a mobile game, let alone a free mobile game, it's quite something.
It's obviously marketed to Fallout fans, but I don't think there's any reason a newcomer to the franchise would be scared off.
I really like it. I've actually got about 40 hours in it before Steam picked it up and haven't paid a cent. You can buy speed-up items if you're a small impatient child with unsupervised access to your mom's credit card, but otherwise it's just not worth it.
It's free, and surprisingly comprehensive for a mobile game. Give it a shot.

I highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys tower defense elements in a fun and cooperative MOBA environment.
There are two different modes to this game, one pve oriented and one pvp. The pvp is a lot of fun and engaging. Teamwork is definitely required to win and having to place traps and create a killbox in a pvp game is a lot of fun. Traps add a lot to the MOBA environment. Obviously there are your many damage traps, but there are also ones like a speed pad that gives you a burst of speed, mana wells, damage power ups, all sorts of different things that encourage you to think tactfully if you want to win. There also seems to be a lack of a meta and I have had good success with many different types of traps and heroes played in many different roles.
I have only played a little of the pve in this game because the pvp mode is just way more fun. But it isn't as trap heavy as the previous games and put more importance on creating killboxes so you can increase your money gain and killing things yourself rather than letting the traps do all the work. Overall still pretty fun, just hard to pull myself away from that pvp mode.
The downsides are things you would expect from a newer game, longer queue times once your mmr gets up there (10 minutes on average) and the matchmaking can be a little weird at times. All of which could probably be solved by having a larger player base, which will inevitably get larger since the open beta just started recently.

Defcon simply put is perhaps the most brutal yet elegant strategy game you will ever play. While the game only supports 1 map, little gamemodes and very little unit choice, this opens a whole new realm of micromanagement/strategy where games can be won in a matter seconds.
I could go for a whole page critically examining the intricate depths of Defcon strategy and how intense but fantastic it is, but honestly I find the mood of Defcon speaks for itself......
"The Defcon counter slowly counts down to DEFCON 2, as you manoeuvre your subs to deliver a fatal first strike to Asia. The slow hum of a massive turbine and background radio remind you of a massive nuclear bunker, where deep underground you are determining how many people die from your orders. The slow strings of a cello pass the time, as you anxiously wait for DEFCON 1.......3.........2...........1........the massive letters of DEFCON 1 flash across the screen along with a high pitched siren.
Suddenly you spring into action clicking on your subs, activating your dormant SLBM's methodically targetting the major cities across the Asian continent. A quiet piano beings to play but you don't realise it when your too busy concentrating. As you finish the last of your targets another warning signal blares and a small nuclear signal flashes on top of your sub. The SLBM's slowly fire up, then gracefully turn towards their targets. Satisfied you take a break and nervously watch the SLBM's fall down as a now louder piano plays sombre, dark notes......flash......Tokyo hit....4 million dead.....success your first SLBM hits the target dead on, soon after the entire coast of Asia is alight with bright flashes and messages.....Beijing hit.....Honk Kong hit......8 million dead.....6 million dead.
As the last of the SLBM eradicate the last survivors you glance at the scoreboard, excellent you are leading by 50 points. Content you move over to your Pacific fleet to co-ordinate your bombers to deliver another fatal attack on Asia and as you again click on further targets with deadly precission you hear the faint coughs of a woman along with the humming of the loud turbines. Horrified you realise how clean and elegant the deaths you have been presented with. A flash, a confirmation and a number killed. Reality brings you back as you further witness the extermination of the rest of Asia, the whole continent  glows brightly as ALBM's rain upon the cities illuminating the world map.
Despairingly you imagine yourself deep underground, ordering the death of an entire population by a simple click and you don't even see their deaths. Only a small flash and a number killed.
This is a really good tactical game, I greatly recommend this for people that like to play tactical shooter and RTS

The following review was copied straight from my review at
, because I'm too lazy to write a new one.
I’m a huge sucker for the movie WarGames. So when I found out about the game DEFCON, I naturally couldn’t resist. Finally I could play the “WarGame”.
How wrong I was.
Being a gamer, I naturally was like “eh, tutorials, I don’t need those.” However, this is one of those games where you do need those without them telling you. And boy is that tutorial lengthy. So, 6 chapters and 30 minutes later I was thrown into the 7th chapter: use what you’ve learned to defeat this extremely-easy AI. Oh wait, did we say easy? We meant hard. as. ♥♥♥♥. Oh, and I still really didn’t grasp the game.
Well, that was demoralizing.
Thing is, officially DEFCON is a multiplayer game. It’s possible to play against the AI, but that’s even harder than in the tutorial. When you keep in mind that one can’t complete the tutorial because the AI is too hard, you get really depressing ideas about what the AI in the actual game is like.
But it’s a multiplayer game right? So why not just face other players? Yeah, about that… There aren’t any other players, really. You’re going to need a friend to play, if they’re willing to play this♥♥♥♥♥♥at all.
Thing is, the game was “inspired by the infamous 1983 movie WarGames.” So, naturally, I had big expectations. I knew that I probably wasn’t going to play against Joshua, but still. When you make a game inspired by a movie about computer from the MS-DOS era, at least make the graphics resemble that era. Don’t make elaborate maps with perfect borders – make them liney and polygonal. Don’t make elaborate icons – make sure that the game looks like it could run on MS-DOS.
So what are you supposed to do? Well, the game starts off at DEFCON 5. It’s time to build a military defense system. Place missile silos, create fleets, create military airports, place radars. You know – a defense system.
Many actions don’t unlock until you hit a certain DEFCON level. For example, you can’t dispatch planes until DEFCON 3, and nukes can of course only be launched at DEFCON 1.
Now this is the point where you expect hell to be unleashed. Nope, that’ll take a while. You can use missiles to explode nukes in the air (because the radioactive material totally won’t fall on your territory if that happens above land), but it takes a while for those nukes to come. You can try to strike first – but if you’re Europe and your enemy is North America then you’re screwed because you’ll need nuclear submarines, and once those get above the surface they get destroyed because they’re suddenly visible.
It’s also really not clear what the goal of the game is. My best guess is “destroy the enemy’s cities” – but that’s damn near impossible because I needed all my nukes to destroy New York (I had like 40 nukes). So what then? “Destroy the enemy’s defense systems”? That might be possible. I’d rather just know instead of having to guess though.
I feel incredibly let down by this game. It’s just not fun. There’s also some kind of alliance feature for when you play with 3 or 4 players, but I didn’t get to test it out because I didn’t grasp the game and only have one friend to play it with (and he uses the demo).
Know what I miss most? The command prompt. That stuff was awesome about the movie. It would’ve allowed for some great references as well. A missed opportunity.
So, all in all, this game is a huge letdown. It fails to deliver what looks like a fun game, and falls short on many aspects. Too bad, guys, too bad.

Short version for the impatient:
If you like stealth games, particularly atmospheric ones, Aragami is a solid purchase. Fantastic OST, beautiful art and the core gameplay is very satisfying. The only real downsides are the rather gentle difficulty curve, which some veterans of the genre might find too easy, and a rather predictable story which should've been a little more subtle.
Longer version:
Presentation-wise, Aragami hits all nails straight on the head. The HUD is kept at an absolute bare minimum, the relevant information you need for sucessful stealth all clearly visible on the protagonist himself. Visibility is indicated by your color palette, going from bright and highly noticeable in light, to low profile black and white while reamining in the shadows. Your ressources, Shadow Essence and the Charges for your abilities, are also clearly indicated by Aragami's cloak. The symbols on it will empty as you use your Essence, and fill back up again if you recharge it. All of this combined makes for an extremely immersive experience, further improved by a fantastic soundtrack and well designed Maps.
While the missions are not quite as sprawly as those in classic like Thief 2, they are big and still offer plenty of variation when it comes to your approach to stealth. The game rewards both the "Ghost" and the "Killer" playstyles. I was somewhat dissapointed that the game didnt support any sort of terror tactics, such as in Mark of the Ninja, since in my opinion, the game would have lent itself greatly to it.
Then we have the difficulty and progression, both a strong and a weakpoint. On one hand, the skill tree noticeable changes the game up and makes you stronger as the game progresses. A couple missions in, you will have access to a very mighty arsenal of tools for both sneaking by completely undetected, or slowly killing a small state's worth of guards.
On the other hand, the enemies never really pick up the pace, and mostly stay their standard, scrubby selves troughout the entire game. There is a certain point where your toolbox will simply outclass anything the game throws at you. And even if you self impose restrictions, such as not using the skills, the guard's AI suffers from the age old "probably just rats" syndrome. It's very easy to dispose of most peeps by luring them in a direction, teleporting behind them and then repeat the process until the map is empty. And even if you do goof it up, Aragami can cover ludicrous distances with just a few mouseclicks.
The problem here is not actually you being overpowered, but the fact that the games challenge does not grow along with you. What it would have needed is a greater variation of enemies and more suspicion mechanics. Enemies do not notice blood puddles, dissapearing buddies and generally need a LOT of very obvious mistakes on your part to actually become alerted. They are also completely unable to get reinforcements and the game very rarely throws a curve ball at you. I was really looking for some more punishment coming my way, but the game ultimately failed to deliver for the most part.
Where I want to give the game credit, is in the Boss fights. Usually Boss Encounters in stealth games tend to feel either out of place, or are implemented in such a way that they are just frustrating intermissions. Aragami, in my opinion at least, does them right, with making them feel intense while still making them feel fitting with the rest of the experience.
Finally, the story. While it's presented nicely, it's predictable as fu*k. Which creates a rather big seperation between the protagonist acting very clueless, while the player will have figured out the relevant parts halfway into the game. it's not awful, don't get me wrong. I've seen predictable stories that shot themselves withing 5 minutes of starting. But the game could've done with more subtetly.
Also, just to have it covered: The game does offer COOP, altough, where the game is sort of too easy in Singleplayer, it becomes a cakewalk once you have two magic shadowninjas stalking the playground. It's still fun mind you, and a good way to kill a couple hours, just by being able to execute some rad looking combinations. And as some people will agree, ocasionally feeling like YOU are the big badass murderman is a great experience too.
To wrap this up: Aragami is worth buying, even if it's just to support a DEV who obviously cared about what he put out, and wanted to put out a quality product. And the game, on a fundamental level, is a great one. Recent updates also added new difficulty settings in response to people finding the game too easy, and also added some skins to the game. While it doesnt fix the difficulty curve completely,  it's a push in the right direction and added even more cred to Aragamis Developer.
Personally, I look forward to hopefully seeing more like this in the future. Particularly if we get a sequel that ups the Ante.

Frustrating RPG Puzzle Freedom Simulator, which while wrecks your very soul into a slobbering pathetic of lifeless drool (and will leave you contemplating your very being) offers one of the most (strangely) rewarding completions ever.
It's a simple game that on the surface should be completed within a matter of minutes - the goal is simple: Achieve 10,000,000 points in 1 one and you're free to leave. If you die your score is reset. Yet, it's not that simple. Not only do you face a string of increasingly difficult monsters on your run to freedom, you also have to overcome your own inability to match 3 or more tiles together.
So simple.
Yet so freaking difficult.
And thus addicition is born.
The feeling you can beat this game, with the secretly scoffing bellows of laughter from whatever twisted mind designed this game spur you on to play it. There's not much more to say than that.
It would probably be best enjoyed as an iOS/Android game, certainly one where you could pick and play in small time windows, rather than long drawn out PC sessions (and a quick look shows that it is available for less than £2 most of the time).
If you like puzzle games, and games that tease you with their simplicity (yet burn you with their difficulty) than this game is for you. If, however, you cannot stand iOS/Android apps, and despise their existance on Steam... avoid it.

I wanted this game to be good, but it's just too flawed.  I bought it on sale and still requested a refund.  In less than two hours, I encountered two level-breaking bugs.  One forced me to act out half the level over again to prompt a waypoint to appear, and I couldn't progress without it.  The other would have forced me to restart the entire chapter, and there was nothing I could do to fix it.  Enemy movement frequently bugs, with guards getting stuck on each other.  This game also has WAY more performance issues than it should, likely as a result of being made in Unity.
A less technical issue is just the actions of Aragami himself.  As fun and fluid as blinking around is, it's the best part of the game.  Kills are sluggish and repetitive, movement is slow outside of blinking, and Aragami just doesn't feel as mobile and fluid as a ninja made of shadows should be.  In Dishonored (a game that heavily influenced this one with the blinking mechanics), you are highly mobile, quick, fluid assassin badass who can also teleport around.  By contrast, Aragami feels like it's a hair's breadth from a VR game where your movement is entirely based on teleporting around.
I got this game on sale, and as much as I wanted to enjoy it, it just doesn't succeed.  I can't recommend it.

With such an odd name, you would expect an odd game to go along with it, and you'd be correct. The game mixes RPG elements into a match-3 game that requires quick reflexes.
Your character awakens in a dungeon and the only way to escape is to enter a dungeon and survive until your score gets to 10,000,000. But you cannot do this right away as your score multiplier is too low, so you need to complete mini-challenges to unlock harder dungeons with higher multipliers so you can reach your goal.
Along the way you earn gold, experience, and wood which you use to upgrade your weapons, learn new skills, and upgrade the individual stores you purchase these things from. You get a real sense of progression from all this as you do progressively get stronger as you progress.
The game itself involves your character running across the top of the screen, and you needed to react by completing the matches. If there's a monster, you need to match swords and staves to do damage; locked doors and chests require you to match keys to open them; match other blocks to get resources to upgrade equipment. The game is simple, yet very addicting. The game itself features 8-bit retro graphics and a soundtrack that is very catchy. For the price, the game is absolutely worth it.

10000000 is a game that mixes the match-3 genre with an RPG angle. Now, it's not as enjoyable as the Puzzle Quest games but the game is not a complete trainwreck either. Despite the horrible controls (or morel like 'control' - it's mouse only and 'slide'-based, naturally intended for a smartphone device), it can serve you a bit of fun for a couple of hours. However, if you're out to get all of the achievements then you might be in for a long and painful grind. This is due to the very annoying RNG.
All the negativity aside, let's get more into how the game works. You start out with a simple character, trapped in a place with barred up doors. You want to break free from this prison, but to do so, you must get a 10 000 000 score. Simple, right? Well, not really. Your toon is weak and in order to become stronger and advance then you need to gather supplies and gold. How do you do that? Well, that's where the core of the game comes in! You will need to arm yourself and venture into the dungeons!
At first, you'll see the familiar match 3 board and you'll start to match tiles as you would in any type of game like this. Soon you will notice that you're not only meant to match them, you're meant to match certain tiles at certain times. Your toon will encounter foes with different abilities and weaknesses, knowing when to match the sword or the staff tiles might save you a lot of trouble here! There are also locks on chests and doors that you need to open by matching keys. Sometimes you will gain an item or a consumable by opening chests, but also if you match the chests on the tile board. These you can use to help you progress in the dungeons. Then there are the wood and stones that you need to upgrade the different shops.
I had a lot of fun with the game in the beginning, especially when it felt like you made progress. Each new rank you unlock is a higher difficulty, and with each ranks there are several challenges to complete that grants you various bonuses. However, when you've reached the highest rank and completed all of the bonuses then the game kind of loses its potential. It takes a lot of luck and patience to even reach a score of 10 million, in any rank. I managed to 100% the game after nearly 13 hours of playtime. I've read about people who still hasn't been able to even after 30 hours, so keep this in mind if you're looking for an easy game to get perfect.
Despite all the flaws and lack of fun end game I enjoyed it when I didn't feel too stressed out. The further you get, the quicker you need to be to match the tiles. You need to be able to notice when the border of your board turns red (encounters/events) or green (when your toon is mainly walking) and adapt to this in the best way possible. It takes time getting used to how the game functions, especially when it comes to matching the tiles by sliding the columns and rows. It can be extremely frustrating at times and I wish the developer had thought about this when porting the game to PC. It's already a challenging game and believe me, being defeated just because you weren't able to align the tiles perfectly due to whatever or any reason is just flat out aggrivating.
I can recommend it if you like casual games that are a bit of a challenge. 10000000 is a challenge, both physically and mentally. In a good or bad way? Well, a bit of both to be honest.

To start off, Mafia III is a solid, good game. I had bad impressions of it from reviews I have read and I was even regretting that I purchased it a little in the opening parts of the game. I kept comparing it to Mafia II and thought it did everything wrong. However, as I kept on going, I found a really solid game. It's not as technically impressive as GTA5. It's not as cinematically impressive as Mafia II. It is a good game in my opinion, though. I would reccomend people Mafia II over Mafia III, but they both are also offering different experiences. They both have quality writing and memorable characters. I assume due to complaints of linearity Hangar 13 tried a more tried and true modern sandbox experience and some parts of that were good and some parts were bad. I do think people should buy this game, however. The writing, gameplay, and story are good enough to warrant a purchase.
The Good:
+Solid Shooting and Driving, shallow, but solid
+Brutal Kills are a lot of fun
+Actually useful favors you can call in from your lieutenants
+Character models look great
+Lighting is pretty good
+The story, while stretched, is well told
+Memorable characters
+Great voice acting
+Decent, while more unrealistic compared to Mafia 2, enemy AI
+Good variety of weapons, cars
+Servicable stealth system
+Decent to great animation for characters, deaths, attacks, etc.
+Fun set piece missions for special character assassinations
The Bad
-Dated visuals
-Somewhat shallow gameplay
-The sounds of guns and vehicles aren't as good as Mafia 2
-The story gets too spread out because the open world nature
-Two weapon only limit (Personal Nitpick)
-Some glitches remain (none game breaking)
-Crashed once in 21 hours of play (So not terrible)
-Repetition of levels (Especially ones where lieutenants/capos return to)
-City not as interesting as Empire Bay, not enough to personally do not related to criminal activities.
-Vehicle modification, even with the update, isn't as good as Mafia 2
TL;DR
Mafia III is a good game, and I reccomend it. I bought it and the season pass in a steam sale and I felt I got every cent out of it. It's lacking in areas that its predecessor, Mafia II, was better in, but it's still worth your money.

Crypt of the NecroDancer is a fantastic entry into the Roguelike genre, so let's break it down.
The primary draw of the game is the great music and how it is worked into the mechanics. In order to succeed you must move and attack to the beat of the song assigned for the floor. This is both simple and wickedly difficult to keep up, but the better you manage the more gold coins you earn due to a multiplier effect.
Stats in most roguelikes depend heavily on luck in finding items or leveling up, but in CotND you can definitely succeed with just the basic starter gear. The reason why is because the game doesn't rely on huge health pools and in fact most monsters can be killed in a single hit and the only monster you MUST kill is the boss on the final floor. Playing conservatively is a very viable tactic because there are many ways to advance to the next floor and there is no leveling up that requires killing monsters.
Each dungeon, at least for the moment, is three dane-a-thons of fun and a final boss. So game sessions are short and failure does not leave that typical bitter taste.
There's a light quirky sense of humor, especially when the shopkeeper starts belting out tunes with the music. Colors are bright and all the monsters get a little dance-y jig which makes things pretty playful. If you're doing well you also get magical disco lighting all over the dungeon, huzzah!
This is the Roguelike for people who like music and a shorter, more meaningful play session. The game itself isn't super long, but the random elements and multiple character types will keep you as busy as you would like.
Final Score: A-

There are two different modes to this game, one pve oriented and one pvp. The pvp is a lot of fun and engaging. Teamwork is definitely required to win and having to place traps and create a killbox in a pvp game is a lot of fun. Traps add a lot to the MOBA environment. Obviously there are your many damage traps, but there are also ones like a speed pad that gives you a burst of speed, mana wells, damage power ups, all sorts of different things that encourage you to think tactfully if you want to win. There also seems to be a lack of a meta and I have had good success with many different types of traps and heroes played in many different roles.
I have only played a little of the pve in this game because the pvp mode is just way more fun. But it isn't as trap heavy as the previous games and put more importance on creating killboxes so you can increase your money gain and killing things yourself rather than letting the traps do all the work. Overall still pretty fun, just hard to pull myself away from that pvp mode.
The downsides are things you would expect from a newer game, longer queue times once your mmr gets up there (10 minutes on average) and the matchmaking can be a little weird at times. All of which could probably be solved by having a larger player base, which will inevitably get larger since the open beta just started recently.

Developed by Humble Hearts, Dust: An Elysian Tail centers around a character with amnesia, who has been chosen by a legendary sword to be its wielder.  And so, Dust is tasked to right the wrongs of the world and eventually discover his past through his journey.
Design – I’m going to mention the most obvious thing first: Dust: An Elysian Tail is pretty.   Very pretty.  It says in the trailer itself that everything is hand-drawn.  Not even in the early days of gaming did you find this kind of work and really hearkens back to playing a Disney Animation.   The colors are vibrant and the designs, although simplistic, offer variety and give each character a unique image.
Gameplay – The action and animation was very smooth.  The combos were powerful, but never so much that there was no challenge.  There were plenty of spots where I was clearly in over my head and I had to back out, train up a few levels and get some new armor crafted before I dared venture into the area again.
I greatly appreciated the introduction of a Blacksmith, especially when she handed over a device that allowed her to instantly craft objects and give them to me without having to adventure to her forge in Mount Doom and then back.
You have a sidekick and although her attack doesn’t look particularly powerful, I generally started the fight with it to give me an edge and it was probably the move that saved the day when it came to the final boss.
One particular element in Dust that will make you grit your teeth are the vine jumping puzzles.  As with many standard Fantasy games, there are skills that you learn down the road, so I was elated when I finally learned the skill Vine-climbing.   Right from the start, I had issues with the Vine skill.  This game is a 2D Side-scroller and the directions for jumping were very 2D themselves.  You could jump strait up or straight left or right, depending on what direction you needed to go.   I was trying to hop out of my first Vine-puzzle, but the vine wall didn’t go up high enough.  I kept hitting the very edge of the platform I needed to get to.  I must have attempted this a dozen times.  I’m still not entirely sure how I managed to finally get out, but that was not the last Vine-climb to make me pull my hair.
Story – The story has rock solid writing and plot, however it is a very standard Fantasy story.  Old clichés are the base of the story.  This does nothing to take away from the story, but it also does almost nothing new for it.  Almost.  There are scenes where the characters step out of the clichés to give them a life of their own and make them even more empathetic and unique.
About the only thing that bothered me about the story is that occasionally the story would break the 4th wall, in a way.  The game never directly addresses the player, but it does directly address the fact that it’s a game and you need “to save your progress” and “press this button.”  I don’t like this particular style of writing.  The game just ends up taking me out of the story whenever this happens, because it almost interrupts the synergy of immersion that people like to get when they’re looking for entertainment.
If you enjoy Fantasy at all, you will enjoy this story, but keep your expectations in check.
Side-kick – Why, oh why, are side-kicks generally annoying?   They also often come complete with an annoying voice.  Fidget is no exception.  Her voice is highly annoying and there are even scenes where she’s even made fun of for being a loudmouth.   However, she is at least useful and doesn’t treat Dust like a simpleton
There are definitely times when she really brings a lighter touch to a scene where the mood is dark and heavy.  I actually got to the point where I started to enjoy her presence, so while her voice is annoying, she at least retains her presence as a character instead of just a tool.
Overall – Dust: An Elysian Tail is a very solid and good game.  The graphics are rich, the animation is smooth, the voice-acting is excellent, the gameplay is great fun, and the story is compelling.
Highly recommended.

Do you like stealth playthroughs of games?
Do you like puzzle games?
Well here's both.
This isn't like Assassin's Creed, where you can survive a fight if it breaks out but it's really in your best interest not to. You are punished for being caught. And that's why I love it. Everything gears itself towards remaining undetected, to the point where half the time you won't even want to kill the sentry because you're afraid someone else may stumble accross the body when you're on the complete other side of the map and alert EVERYONE INSTANTLY, even after you've determined no one else goes down that path.
While there is a story, it's poorly executed and practically nonexistent. If you need a good story for a game, this isn't for you. I get much more of an arcade vibe from it, in that there are independent levels, a scoring system, and it's all about the gameplay itself.
Specific elements I really appreciate:
- Their detection of you is very well done
- Lures become necessary, but it's extremely easy for them to backfire if more than one person happens to hear it
- While you can learn new abilities, the god curve present in games like Shadow of Mordor, Dishonored, and Assassin's Creed is nonexistent
- The score system is fun and reinforces the idea that the whole point of the game is that it's a level by level stealth game and the goal is to be as stealthy and deadly as possible

Probably my disappointment of the year being such a huge Mafia fan. Played the first game like crazy when I was younger and really enjoyed the second one despite it's flaws. The ONLY reason to play the game is the story and even that doesn't outweigh the flaws in this unfinished messed.
Pros:
-Great story like with the previous two games.
-Amazing setting. Love the look and feel of the 60's, even if it looks pretty awful in some places in this game.
-The soundtrack is fantastic. Some seriously amazing artists in this game that fit the time period perfect.
-Game can look very beautiful in some areas.
Cons:
-Bland combat. Cover shooter with no depth whatsoever.
-Driving is nothing special and not very enjoyable.
-Mission structure is horrendous. You'll play the same missions over and over again.
-Relates to the last point. But repetitive missions kill this game.
-Pretty buggy although I didn't have problems as bad as others did.
-Game looks awful in some places (Skybox).
Avoid this game. Although the story is great and there is some fun to be had, it isn't worth the price and the great story isn't worth suffering through the repetition of the missions. MUD.
LOTS. OF. MUD.
An interesting and conteplative although not very leisurely drive through the countryside of Siberia, in which you are tasked with collecting logs, but the real object seems to be finding creatively desperate measures to avoid becoming mired in, or retrieve vehicles from being stuck in The Mud.
Did I mention that there is Mud?
Not for impatient people; some areas will require creating a strategy to repair, provide fuel for, and retrieve various trucks which serve different specialized purposes. There will be frustrating moments, as you spend lots of time extracting yourself from Mud.
The truck models and rendering are great. The physics and visual effects are also good, especially the deformable terrain (Mud) and destructible small trees, which allows you to feel like you are actually affecting real objects.
The current number of maps is small, and once you conquer the rough spots on one map, you will be eager to move to the next, and all of the available maps are soon completed. Hopefullty there will me more in the future.
Lots of fun, with Mud.

The off-roading genre has been my favorite genre since I started gaming way back in the 90s. Games like Test Drive Off Road, 1nsane, Screamer 4x4, and Cabela's 4x4 Off Road Adventure series - those are what I started with and I had a lot of fun. They all did a lot of things right but left a lot to be desired. Even the later games like Rigs of Rods or BeamNG Drive don't do off road gameplay very well because it's not their main focus. Spintires on the other hand is one of the first off roading games that actually plays like you expect it and want it to. The trucks feel heavy and powerful but aren't unstoppable which keeps the gameplay interesting. You can winch vehicles, tow trailers, operate cranes, haul logs and with the addition of the workshop you can download a ton of new community made vehicles which keeps things fresh. The mud and water physics are the best I've ever seen in a game, the graphics look fantastic and the coop mode means you can complete campaigns with your friends. I'd highly recommend this game to anyone with the slightest interest in the off roading genre.

I haven't played this game in a while, but out of all the games i miss and consider under-rated when i consider playing a game of something after playing a lot of something else, i miss and want to return to this one the most.
The balance has always generally been good, with subtle variations in the aliens being strong early game due to their manouverability and the marines strong late game due to their firepower, i've still found the game very satisfying and playable. Those subtle variations said, the game has never been more balanced and i consider those issues largely addressed as well as they can be.
I enjoyed this game for the short period that i played it in pre-release (not that i can tell i ever had the cool, unique skin you're rewarded for doing so ever being properly equipped when chosen). But one thing to be aware of is there is a relatively high skill ceiling that makes the game quite competitive due to the fact it's very fast pace, quite punishing of mistakes made and rewards fast reaction times and accuracy (the latter one there being a slightly more important skillset for marines).
Playing marines is certainly a lot more easier than playing the aliens, probably largely due to the familiar gameplay. This does result in the marine team filling up faster than the alien one. You might find yourself having played a lot of games as the alien and wanting to swap, but find it difficult to find a slot on the marine team.
Not a whole lot i can really say about the tactical aspect of the game. I do enjoy commanding both teams, though it can be a pain finding a good one when you want to be a player. The alien commander is a little easier on account of being to operate almost indepentently of the players since the structures tend to build themselves if only slowly, whilst the marine commander absolutely relies on his marines for this.
Use of personal requisition is more difficult as marines as an alien player can perform well with even the basic tier 1 class and can happily sit ontop of a pool of requisition waiting to be used. Whilst the marines will want to invest in consumables and upgrades throughout the game meaning if they die they likely wont have that pool of resources to immediately replace their loadout. Some consolation does come in the form of being able to re-acquire your weapon from the map within a certain time period, but that does also come with the potential for being ambushed.
TL;DR It's balanced, it's fun, it's different if not a tad competitive compared to its peer shooter titles.

The result is a think fast game which will get you hooked on the beat. You'll dance through a room and eliminate all inside and you'll feel great for doing it~

A note to those who started playing from the time it was initially introduced - the new functions really make the game a lot harder and the odds of getting rare characters are a lot less than the earlier versions - my iphone record has 3-4 rare characters and so far i have NONE at all in my current STEAM record - so be warned!
Also, one of the fun bits is to do quests for all sorts of things for your vault - i really encourage you to check out the daily, weekly quests and especially those near holiday seasons - halloween 2017 was a real blast as i received the ghost sheet and skeleton attires which i get to keep even after the event!
All in all, it is addictive, yet fun - highly recommend it to anyone who loves to manage things!

A true RPG classic finally available on Steam. Final Fantasy VII may be a tad overhyped in its impact to the RPG genre but the vast majority of its praises are fully justified. - While this game runs at 60FPS, most animations in this game were not optimized for that framerate.

The off-roading genre has been my favorite genre since I started gaming way back in the 90s. Games like Test Drive Off Road, 1nsane, Screamer 4x4, and Cabela's 4x4 Off Road Adventure series - those are what I started with and I had a lot of fun. They all did a lot of things right but left a lot to be desired. Even the later games like Rigs of Rods or BeamNG Drive don't do off road gameplay very well because it's not their main focus.
