Fallout Shelter (FS) developed by Bethesda Game Studios and released on Jul 31, 2016 for PC platform. According to Metacritic
, it has:

Is this title a worthy additional to the Fallout series? Not everyone will agree to this. Few I knew threw this into the shredder machine

While I may be disappointed to hear these words, I've to respect people's opinions.
FS is the first mobile game developed by Bethesda Game Studios. Unfortunately for me, my mobile phone was unable to run this game. So when it became available on Steam, I grabbed it immediately & suit up my vault spandex and gears!
What is Fallout Shellter (FS) about?
FS is a rpg + simulation game where you take control of the few survivors in this horrible land and manage them/the vault's survivability activities. You're the vault boss. You decide who gets to wear what/do what/and who gets to have "happy" hour. *ahem*
Base building is simple and straightforward. The prerequisite to unlock a new building is to reach a certain amount of survivors in your vault.
Apart from the common basic rooms that keeps your vault/people alive (power,food,water) you get to build training rooms, 2 form of medic rooms, a weapon & armor crafting room, a theme customization room and finally a hair saloon@character customization.
You can send your survivors on a variety of quests, most of them are fetching types. You will also get a quiz quests. Pick the right answers and you don't need to kill anyone. Pick the wrong answer.. well, lets just say it's a pew pew pew session.
To aid you in this wasteland, you have a robot that helps to defend the vault and also assist you to pick up resources. You also have pets that comes with some form of bonus (weapon damage/damage resistance/more $ or junk pick up and etc). The rest is micro-management.
Controls, Visuals & Sounds:
Nothing fancy. It's mainly on mouse.
Visually, It's 2D, cartoonish looking. I am assuming the main target audience are young kids. Despite the art being children-friendly, there is a GREAT DEAL of
on everything. Hats, hair, clothing's, weapons, pets, rooms, enemies, objects, animations. Every visual element has been crafted, colored with great deal of effort. Surprisingly, FS is not dark at all. Its pretty and is colorful. This becomes visibly apparent once you are able to craft armor/clothing/theme room. Imagine a room with 6 survivor don in a White cleric like hats and robes. or room with 6 red swim-wears. xD literally its like a mini vault of cos-players..with guns.
The enemies that in this mad land: Human raiders, creature/monsters; death claws and rad roach/scorpion, moles and ghouls. Each faction has been carefully designed. Some of them will have abilities - especially mini boss/boss fights. The only saving grace which us players have is: 1) Critical Hits 2)Medic/Rad packs 3) Perseverance and if all fails 4) craft a BIGGER gun.
As for the sound, every animation will have feedback sounds. It's simple and sharp. The audio keeps the mood of the game flowing. Good work to the visual & audio team.
Game Mechanics:
There is the base building, the combat, the exploration, crafting, customization, keeping-the-vault-survivor-happy thingy, leveling system, training-stats system. There's a bunch of mechanics in this product. Everything is working as intended - I've not experienced any crash or bugs. Of the surface, people may think this product was designed for kids but if you actually gave it a try, pretty much after a couple of hours, people will realize that there's actually a lot of things going on & incorporated into this product.
One of the things that will keep many players busy is keeping vault survivors happy & leveling up their stats.
The vault survivors can die. The only way to bring back a dead vault survivor is to revive them by spending credits. Credits rule, baby! Credits play a major role especially base building. Some of these upgrades are freaking expansive.
Now comes the premium-in-game currency: nuka cola bottles. These colas don't over-write the credits role instead they compliment them. cola's lessens crafting time, sending and calling survivor backs from quest immediately. It also can be used to speed up crafting and base building. a lot.
Having a ton of credits is like having a sports car. Having colas on the hand, is like having a nitro.
While FS is a free 2 play game, it does have in-game purchases. This is FS's business model. I am not against them because I know, this is a business after all. What I am rather concerened is the legendary dweller. Just how many boxes do i need to open to get 1 ?
My personal thoughts:
FS is a great game. So many elements has been incorporated into this product to keep players engage. It is fresh and interesting.
Now, hold on. After 30+ hours into the game. I am having second thoughts. Things are becoming a routine/grind! To make it a mess, if you have above 150 dwellers, you are going to click A LOT. Scrolling the vault becomes a pain when you have a big vault. Identifying dwellers, dragging them around becomes a mess. The spy-like person that comes and goes becomes irrelevant once you have a big vault. You sacrifice your own vault dweller to the wasteland to maintain sanity in your vault management. Rad Scorpion keeps invading your vault and things turn into a big freaking mess. Death left and right, insufficient resources, productivity is low because the entire vault is unhappy -RIPS HAIR ARGHHHH-
So here's 2 scenario:
1) the game experience does take a dip once everything becomes a routine. When a catastrophic event hits your vault and you stop coming back/When you find yourself repeating the same action over and over again - and you quit. That's the end of its shelf life.
2) However despite all the misery & setback that you've faced and you keep coming back to FS. You know, you either got a special connection with FS/you are person on a mission! That's the 2 major difference in terms of gaming experience.
My Summary:
Despite it's children-friendly visuals, FS was developed for the mass. Not just for the kids. Yes, it may have been ported over from mobile but there were no bugs for me. Some aspect of the UI could be improved. For me, I would love to see:
FS left a very strong impression in the first 30 hours. After that it was just routine to keep everything in check and made sure my dwellers were happy. It became a chore. The quests and vault incidents/attacks break up that chore. Achievement was what kept me going.
*Click & drag myself into the drums room*  It disappoints me but this has to be done. *drums roll*
So, on the scale of 0 - 10, my personal rating for Fallout Shelter is a minced death claw served in rad sauce, worth 6/10.
As Exquisite this product may be, with long duration of repeated tasks and a lacking objective/a closure to the vault experience, it feels meaningless. It requires so many clicks to perform an action - when a tweak in the UI would save PC gamer all the hassle.
So much to share but I've hit the word limit.
*Walks out into the wasteland in my vault spandex* Adios Amigos. Peace.

One of those games that is both well programmed and well made to make nuclear war just another giddy joyride.
The game focuses on a world during the late 70's and early 80's, where nuclear war is taking place, and up to 6 nations can declare into it, the nations include The European union (and several other nations not currently in the EU) The USSR, (A and some parts of Kazakhstan) Asia (Not Ocenia, Australia, or Mongolia) Lain America (Not including Cuba) Africa, and North America including Canada and the United States.
In order to win, you must get more points than your foes, you get points by killing each millions of people with your ICBMs, there are multiple modes, but I'm covering the stock mode.
The game starts at Defcon 5, you can place Radar on your territory, Nuclear Silos (Which will shoot down enemy bombers and fighters as well as launch ICBM) and finally, military air bases that can launch Bombers with nuclear capacity, and fighters.
Also during Defcon 5, you can place ships, either battleships, which focus on fighting directly at sea, Subs, which can scan the area and launch nuclear missiles (However said launch will let the rest of the players see them) and Carries, that can't fight, but can use depth charges to take out said Subs, and can also launch bombers and fighter jets. (Each jet also has some small amount of radar to let you see enemy silos and Radar)
You can only place units until Defcon 3, when battle becomes more intense, and you are allowed to send jets into enemy territory to scan for military bases and whatnot.
After getting to Defcon 1, Nuclear weapons are permitted, and can be launched by Bomber, Silo (Which will prevent the Silo from protecting against incoming jet, bomber, or ICBM.)
After you or them launch, the entire game flashes with the warning that one of the players dared to go launch nuclear missiles, and silos (Or Subs) That are launching them will be revealed to the world, and nuclear missiles will launch, but will only be seen if it's under a general radar of a team..
A nuclear missile will destroy Radar in one hit, and air bases in two, and silos in three, also destroying half of that building's current housed warfare. (Be it be bombers/fighters or ICBMs)
A missile, hitting a city, will kill half it's living population, which is usually a a couple million each hit, depending on where you strike.
Despite a majority of the community is gone, the game is still here, unlike TF2, which is aimed at multiplayer play, this can be played with well programmed AI, of which aren't generic, and actually are quite hard at times.
The achieves, however, can't actually be attained form fighting bots, so you have to play online to actually get them, but due to a dwindling community, it's quite hard to find those players, so try to get friends to play if you want to competition against an actual person.

This game is essentially a wave-shooter, something I have never particuarly enjoyed, but after playing four hours I can safely say this is some of the most fun I've had in a long time. I initially described this as "Dynasty Warriors with guns and bugs", which is hugely reductive, but will give you a sense of what this game is like. The missions are linear, sending you from point to point, either defending an area, destroying spawn points, or fighting a boss, all of which are essentially the same mechanic of 'point and shoot'. Imagine Gears of War without the cover mechanic, plus Dynasty Warriors drops and hordes.
But to compare this game to typical 'wave-shooters' would be a great disservice. The graphics look great, the voice acting is beleivable and entertaining, the swarms of enemies are extremely dynamic in their movement and serve to never let there be a boring moment. Unfortunatley what this game
do is give you too much of a good thing. Waves last a long time, and defending a single spot for 5-10 minutes can begin to feel tedious, especially when you've been playing for a few hours. You want to love it, you want more, but the few truely cool moments can often get swarmed from having to mow down hundreds of drones (pun intended). This is compounded by the ludicrously slow growth rate - levelling up from rank 1 to rank 2 took 4-5 missions, the XP requirement for the next nevel was doubled, AND each of the four classes level up indipendently, for which I see some serious grinding required in the future.
All that said; the visuals are great, the sense of scale and tone are spot-on
, and I am looking forward to playing more!

I initially grabbed this game and its cousin, HoS (a fantasy title by the same publisher/developer and using the same engine), because they reminded me of top-down half-board game, half-roleplaying game modules from my youth, such as TSR's
and
, which came with glossy full-color maps and flat cardboard playing pieces representing characters, monsters and other things. And additionally because in the case of
, I was also reminded of its obvious
inspiration.
Those first impressions seem to have been on target, as after many hours of playtime in both titles, whether by design or by accident, they still evoke that comparison for me — except the "playing pieces" are well-animated and the game master comes with the software.
Unlike its fantasy-themed cousin, the several campaigns that come packaged with
are written in the same genre as WH40K: grim, dark, military science-fiction. So be forewarned, it lacks its cousin's commendably intimate character development and interpersonal drama. On the bright side, you'll find a lot more wonderful science-fiction influences bubbling beneath its surface than just those of WH40K; fans of BattleTech, Dune, and even Battlestar Galactica might be pleased as well.
Whatever HoS has that
doesn't, TB successfully makes up for it with fully customizable characters and gear load-outs, much bigger squad caps, and a whole lot of "into the breach!" battle-brother romanticizing that's not always quite up to par with
Gabriel Angelos and his ilk, but serves the purpose anyhow. And the genre's exciting, stress-inducing, 'surrounded on all sides' glory is here in full spades.

Inbetween:

This is not ment for classes, who are inflexible themselfs, as two-handed axe, flamethrower and sniper cant replace one another for obvious reasons. No, as a squad they are inflexible. This game is one of those that suprises you by how fun it actually is. On the cover it looks like just another match three game, but once you actually get into action you'll notice it's just so hectic that it's super fun and addictive. And then you notice that  you can actually upgrade your character. To do this you must combine some specific blocks like wood. The upgrades generally provide you more time. So in the beginning a round might take just 15 seconds, but once you're upgraded to the max you'll be in the dungeons for minutes.
There's actuallyl not that much grinding if you know what you're doing. Just use the right potions and you'll get an extra amount of wood and stone. Complete the required objectives and you get more skill points. The game never gets frustratingly hard, nor is it too easy. It's just more down to luck of which blocks the game gives you. But once you learn to manage the field properly, even that shouldn't be a big problem.
But in the end, the game is just a match 3 game, so if you don't like them, this might not be for you. Although I'm one of those people who doesn't like them, and this was just a blast from the beginning to the end.

A fantastic little game and I wish I could give it a more meaningful rating than just a little thumbs up.
For a rough idea what it is, just think WH40k Space Hulk but without the license.
Gameplay is good and challenging (see below for one little nitpicky caveat), lotsa classes for your Templars, a ton of weapons and possible loadouts and skills and whatnot to choose from, all with a meaningful impact when it comes to how you approach your objectives.
More than a handful of difficulty settings will make sure you get it exactly the way you want it.
Plenty of bang for the buck when it comes to comparing price to content.
Graphics are a bit dated/simple but they work perfectly fine and you will repeatedly have a stupid smile on your face when things go together just right.
Some of the sounds are unfortunately rather grating (Xenos spawning in is... horrid to put it mildly) and there is one song in the background that makes me mute the music whenever it's on, but otherwise, again, it works and fits.
One little caveat about the mission design, sometimes there's a rather irritating disconnect between the objective at hand (exterminate all Xenos outside of the city comes to mind) and the fact that the Xenos spawn in endlessly until you touch the extraction zone and they magically poof away to nothing. I get why it's done this way, don't get me wrong, but it still doesn't feel right. But this is an extremly nitpicky thing to bring up and isn't an issue in the absolutely and utter majority of the time.

This game feels like it's a fan campaign for Nerubians from Warcraft 3. Nerubians are also a spider like race that are controlled by a larger conciousness. The story in this game is fairly confusing. The opening cinematic talks about humans leaving earth due to an asteroid and going to a new planet, then goes oh theres bugs on this planet and never talks about the humans ever again. The only mention is one level where the ship or part of it is found.
This game seems to copy Warcraft 3's item drop system. Theres 7 different types of items that enhance attack, defense, dodge, etc but you can put it on any unit unlike in Warcraft 3. There are no hero units in the hive but there is the queen and the avatar which I guess are heavy hitters? I just don't understand why even the basic units can equip items. Items play an integral part of upgrading your units or unlocking new units if you 'scrap' the item. This not apparently being explained or I must have missed the text box until discovering it sometime on the third mission.
There isn't much to the game in terms of maps, everything is underground lakes, islands, and legends of hidden temples. The base building is very basic with there being the main hive, a barracks, a worker drop-off/upgrade center, and a defensive structure. The drop-off building doesn't seem to be that useful for drop-off because you get the two resources right when the workers mine them. The defensive building is less than useful as it's not strong enough to take an enemy out on it's own and most times enemies just walk right past it. I've put them into groups of threes and they are still pretty useless.
Every map is essentially the same gameplay wise. Build 5-6 workers, get your resources up, get a nice little ball of soldiers, then sweep then across the map. Repeat 20 times.
Pros:
Exploring the map is sometimes fun
Cons:
Confusing story, opening cinematic has nothing to do with the game for the most part.
Game lacks a lot of content compared to most RTS
Four buildings, 2 1/2 are uctually useful.
Unneeded item drop system
Same map type across the entire game
Two resources, very limited per map.
Repetitive gameplay
Do you get one Hour of gameplay per $6 paid?: Yes
Ease of 100%: Easy.
(100% Being all achievements, Unlocks, Upgrades, Ect.)

The touch of creativity is here, but it feels like a kickstarter that did not get its full amount. There are slots that are never used and it just feels like so much more was planned.
It definetly ends hoping for a sequel of sort, and I am curious to see where it leads if they do get one.
The one major flaw of this game is its lack of replayability. With Starcraft or warhammer, you can play the game off story and as different races. Overall, I support this game and hope they produce some more games. This game has a lot of heart despite its limitations and It won me over.

There's an RTS element, with a commander, who focuses on giving commands (although with human players, they're more like requests than commands, as the players don't have to obey them), placing buildings, researching tech, and managing resources.
The players meanwhile play it like an FPS. I prefer playing as a marine because it's fun to shoot down aliens. Although you really have to watch your shots, as it's really easy to miss, and you burn through ammo quick. Fallout Shelter is your usual idle mobile game with a bit of simulation and some clicking. Made by Bethesda and Behaviour Entertainment, released first in 2015 on iOS and other mobile, updated significantly since then, arrived to PC in 2016 and to Steam in 2017.
Technically, it does have occasional glitch fixed by restarting game, such as when I couldn't remove elevator. And people say that they had their saves wiped out due to error or crash many hours later. So uncool.
And eh, idle games are idle games. As far as I care, they are soulless. Well, though this game has a bit of soul, in artstyle. It's really neat in-universe-cartoon thing. Quite nice, mhm. None the less, the one who wins at these games is not the player who fully maxes it out after 100 hours. Nope, that one loses. The player who wins is the one who checks it out and goes away once it gets shallow.
None the less, I tried. The normal play. There is your base building and basic recource management. Wait long time to get smthing. Can rush, with percentage that it can go wrong. The only microtransactions are either boxes of random stuff that you can get as loot anyway and ability to arrive to quests immeditly, doesn't matter much. Usually you can leave the game for a while unless you sent dwellers out exploring, then it goes against whole idle thing with them possibly dieing out of injury while you aren't paying attention.
I mean, it's not Pay-2-Win but it's still an idle game which is completely shameful on PC.
It's actually funny how game was different combat systems in shelter and quests. In shelter animation matter zero, everybody's health is just getting slowly sapped by presence of NPCs with their stats and only Endurance stat matters for health. Quest kinda does it more with aiming, attacks, critical hits minigames at rare times. But eh, still shallow.
And yea, it's idle. I played normal vault for a while and stopped very quickly after realizing at how easy it will be. So I tried survival instead. And boy, instead of proper challenge I got cheese-land of cheesy tactics. It's hard but in merely annoying way, not the way that makes you think or tests you.
Here are some examples of these pro tactics that are based off real life:
Nothing bad ever happens if you don't pay attention to things. In survival mode you will be bombared with incidents every few minutes which will be sapping away health of your dwellers so in nutshell you want to do stuff and leave ASAP. Leave workers to live happily and restore health, for we all know that presence of exploitative class brings only unhappyness and bad luck.
Just like in real life the best way to handle conflicts is just run away and ignore it. Right? So if you ever get incidents, in order not to get health of dwellers sapped away, you just have to move them away from whatever or whoever is invading you. If it's internal then it will spread to horizontal and vertical rooms and then end. Which also brings the only non-cheesy tactics of how to build base, aha. And if it's from outside then they just go through each row back and forth to the bottom and then go away. Just send dwellers to rooms where they already passed. It doesn't even matter if they have to go through fire on the way, it only takes away health if they are assigned to same room. Raiders also sap away recources while in shelter but in early game it's quicker to just let them run through than confort, thus takes less recources.
Did you know that pregnant women are the best workers? While they can't fight back or do quests or explore, their AI is set to always run from incidents, practically making them completely invincible. And you wait forever about bringing babies out of their bellies. What an utopia.
It also seems that if you have too much population then their odor will spread all over the wastelands, bringing bigger threat in. As a result you will have to stop at certain population and then wait patiently as you grab the needed loot. Send people on quests and exploration to gain better equipment before getting bigger. Idling. Don't upgrade to level 3 rooms early either, makes bigger internal incidents there.
Overall, I quickly realized that in order to progress in Survival I will have to wait for days to get better equipment and once I got into the fairly stable movement in the game I figured that this mobile idle game can't provide any more proper enjoyment and left the game.

"Greetings.  Shall we play a Game?"
If you like a great strategy game, you should look into DEFCON.  Reminiscient of the popular nuclear deterrence movie, WarGames, DEFCON really pulls you into a world where you're on the brink of nuclear holocaust.  The whole of the game operates on real-time, and every second counts when placing your units.  As the tide of war edges closer to DEFCON 1, you need to really be vigilant on where and when your opponent will strike.  And one of the ways they can strike is by nuclear attack sub, which is really the proverbial knife at your throat.  Another way for them would be to send a squadron of nuclear-armed bombers into the heart of your territory.  But if you are capable of countering the enemy, you may stand a chance of surviving the looming apocalypse.  All in all, a great game for a superior strategist, or for people who just want to blow sh*t up and end the world to feel better.  9.5/10

10,000,000 is a jaunty little puzzle/RPG game that is easy to play and addictively enjoyable. The plot is simple, you wake up in a dungeon cell and as the title of the game implies, you escape the dungeon for good when you score 10 million points in a single run. The game plays like bejeweled in that the player shuffles tiles on a grid by dragging a row or column in order to make 3 symbols match. Successful matches yields attacks, magic, keys, items, gold and materials that you can use to improve your cell, converting it into a base of operations which provides better gear, perks and special potions. The gameplay is easily accessable and there is a method to process of running dungeons that might feel hectic and challenging but never really feels frustrating. An average dungeon run takes only a few minutes but you can run the dungeon as many times as you like before returning to your base. The graphics are simple and have a Commodore 64 quality to them and the chiptune music is nicely composed.
10,000,000 is simple, fun, and addictive. Easy to pick up and play, yet challenging when you want it to be. The price is very reasonable and the game is not graphically heavy so you can play it on an older machine. I really enjoyed this game and I think you might too.

If there were a thumbs-sideways on Steam, that's what I'd give The Hive.
Let's start with the bad - this game feels like the development team bit off way more than they could chew. The pacing is a bit sluggish, the UI is kind of primitive, and there are a very small number of units available to you, described in a way that suggests there were a lot more planned (you've got a barracks "for light infantry" but literally no other building for producing military units). There are also a very limited set of enemies to face, there's basically no soundtrack, and let's not forget the graphics remind me of Age of Mythology or, if we want to be very generous, Warcraft 3 - it's not ugly, in fact the units are visually well-designed all things considered, it just looks like an RTS from the early 2000s. There are also flying units that don't actually move differently to anyone else - I'm guessing they didn't have the bandwidth to build out distinct pathfinding and combat logic for flying units. All of this makes me think the developers had grand ambitions and ended up having to cut corners, which kind of sucks for everyone.
There are a few things that are just genuinely bad, though: the dialog writing and voice acting. For a story-based RTS, they've actually got a pretty interesting high concept and some neat ideas (there's no clear good and evil for the most part, there's a neat sci-fi backdrop, there are a lot of weird races and ancient history, the ecology implied is kinda nuts), but every time a character starts talking it just feels stilted and awkward. The story did little to help me care about my faction or any of their characters. Units in combat also don't have much weight - impacts don't register strongly visually or aurally, so things feel a bit floaty.
That said, I do think this is an interesting game worth considering if you're into RTS games. Aside from the interesting story concepts mentioned above, there are a few things here I really appreciated. Some were small AI innovations - if you tell your army to attack-move somewhere, your healers will automatically move along and start healing any units they can instead of running at the enemy, which is nice. Others were balance things - resources are pretty scarce in this game, as befits something set entirely in a cave, and a bit part of the challenge is using the few resources available to you wisely, which is a big part of what an RTS is all about.
There are also some enemies with complex boss-style attacks, and while the UI is primitive and the pacing is off, they're well-telegraphed and force you to consider what units to apply and how to move them around to keep them alive. One of the most interesting dynamics is the fact that loot and equipment you find for your units can also be broken down into DNA, which is needed for research - so do you keep a persistent item that can buff any one unit throughout the campaign, or do you melt it down into points for persistent research that unlocks new units or boosts all units? It's an underdeveloped system, but it was an interesting trade-off to have to think about, and one I've never seen before.
So, long story short, we have here an interesting but flawed game. Why am I saying recommend? Well, I think that if the developers have the chance to develop the (heavily implied) sequel, and if they learned good project management lessons from this game, they could actually be onto something really special. There's potential here, and I can appreciate potential in a game even if the execution isn't great, to some extent. So if you're open to something with a lot of rough edges, maybe give The Hive a try, and you'll find something kinda interesting.

I always enjoy picking the “exotic” option when it comes to RTS’ playable races. Starcraft was my first real time strategy title and I had the privilege to play in on PC, around the time it launched and took the gaming world by surprise. What was there not to like? Players had three distinct factions with clearly defined strengths & weaknesses and they could finally leave behind, the dreary conflicts between Americans vs Soviets (Red Alert) or Orcs vs Humans (Warcraft). Starcraft had it all and revolutionized the genre with its narrative as well. Of course I preferred the Zerg. What was I supposed to find interesting about the “vanilla” Terrans or the pretentious Protoss?
So I stuck with the “space bugs” in most LAN battles and those were the days. RTS as a genre, become my favorite along with Open Worlds. The Hive isn’t in any way revolutionary, but it’s a competent 3D RTS which could have benefitted from more unit and level diversity. Even as it stands now, it’s a promising Steam debut for developer, Skydome Entertainment. Controlling giant insects instead of robots/tanks/humans, is one of the strategy genre’s advantages when compared to action or adventure, for example.
The story isn’t as developed as I would have liked but it’s enough to get you going. Humans fled the cataclysm on a certain planet, insects came rolling in and settled since they can survive in climates that make other life forms a bit…uncomfortable. I presume players represent the “hive mind” in this title and it is up to them, to ensure the survival of the species and subsequent acquisition of new territories for the Hive to prosper.
Against your relentless efforts to colonize new land, a race of mystic lizardmen and walking skeletons shall attempt to stop you in your tracks. You can’t blame the dev for at least trying to be original. I bet you would have complained more if the insects you’re controlling would have fought against space marines or cyborg elves. I’ll take skeletal bipedal lizards any day of the week over RTS  tropes and clichés. So kudos to Skydome for trying something different. The narrative is weak, but the gameplay is pretty self-sufficient and I almost turned a blind eye to the lack of noteworthy characters or even a plotline.
The Hive is another Unity Engine title. Not many strategy games are powered by Unity, yet I couldn’t find technical flaws to The Hive. It runs smoothly in my monitor’s native resolution and on constant 60 frames per second. It looks more than decent for a 3D indie game developed by a team which had no previous experience and an undoubtedly smaller budget than what the “fat cats” of the genre have to contend with. More related to gameplay than graphics, I still found some small design mistakes in the form of a rigid control scheme (few options as it is + no macro support) and no manual saving.
That is really weird, especially when considering the large maps and potential for battles which can cripple the level economy and prevent players from mustering another large horde if their previous one got massacred. In other words, if you fail within a certain level, you have no option to load a previous save file and apply a different stategy to an upcoming battle. You either restart the level or rage quit. I’m sure you’ll pick the former option, right? Real time strategy is as much about learning from your mistakes, as it is about pure tactics mixed with a healthy dose of patience. Blitz chess may be fun to spectate, but I’m not really in favor of it or the “zerg/tank rush” tactics.
Voice acting AND a nice soundtrack. If It sounds as if I’m surprised, I really am. In a most positive way, too. Sound effects lack diversity, but you can always find a small flaw here and there. It won’t deter me from appreciating the overall sound quality. Silent eye candy is never desirable.
You might be tempted to think that The Hive may follow the classical RTS formula, yet the base building aspect has been streamlined enough, for players to just focus on the frontline. It’s true that there are even fewer structure types than units, yet considering the foes you shall face, I’d say that you’re adequately equipped. The Hive produces pure melee infantry, along with ranged and support options. It doesn’t take a strategic genius to figure out that it always pays off to keep the enemy “busy” with a frontal attack followed by flanking maneuvers with your acid-squirting troops and the occasional hive queen kept behind the lines along with specialized medical insects. The queen can even produce low-tier units that can become meat shields for your more rare (and expensive) servants.
Keep in mind that the resources across the levels, are limited and you can’t afford many failed assaults and casualties. Attack only once you have created an advanced army following the tactics above and in sufficient numbers to even overwhelm those lizards and other various monsters. Another nice touch to The Hive, comes in the form of RPG elements related to unit customization and inventory enhancement. Some enemies drop loot or you may find treasure chests hidden across the maps. You then have the option to either dissolve the items into DNA (a special resource required for skill upgrades and access to high-tier infantry) or assign them to certain troops.
As I mentioned previously, the levels feel large enough and offer you the chance to develop a base and army before attacking or securing a new location (depends on the mission objectives), yet they are only 10 and won’t offer much of a challenge for those accustomed to the sharp mind of a fellow strategy fan. No gaming AI has yet to defeat me when faced with equal opportunity and means of conducting digital warfare. Giving the AI unfair amounts of in-game funds or larger healthbars will never be the same as playing against another human.
That being said, I was never a big fan of multiplayer yet I can acknowledge some of its benefits. The Hive seems to have aimed for the other extreme in terms of replay value. It has a story and a well diversified gameplay, yet it feels severely limited in its potential by the inclusion of too few levels and no AI/human skirmish support. This is becoming a basic feature for the RTS genre and I hope that the game I reviewed today, will include skirmish mode in a future update.
As of this writing, I won’t blame you if The Hive might seem overpriced to you. That’s still no reason to avoid purchasing it during a Steam Sale and I strongly encourage you to do so. Real time strategy remains one of PC gaming’s finest exclusive genres and indie developers which exhibit the courage and creativity to attempt new RTS perspectives, deserve our support, one way or another.

Dust... Ah, Dust...
I could go on about the great writing and the beutiful world, but one is already apparent and the other would keep us here for hours, so I'll just talk about the gameplay.
At it's core, Dust is actualy a simple game. there's your standard combo, and a couple branching moves including a launch, for bringing your fights to the sky, and a grab move, both of which are inisiated during your standard combo. In other words, your entire moveset is unlocked straight off, and is suprisingly small.
So does this mean the game gets boreing fast? I suppose that depends on your own mentality. If your looking for a game with clear advancment such as unlockable skill trees, classes, and such, this is not for you. This game will get stale fast.
If your looking for a game about mastery, this is the game for you. Just because Dust's moveset is small does not make it easy to master.
You will spend hours upon hours honeing your ability to chain dust's various attacks together, with each passing minuet becoming more fluid and building up larger combos. You'll start learning when to group enemys up and when to pick out the straggelers. You'll learn which moves flow into the next. You'll learn about dodge-canceling. You'll learn about how to effectivly use the dust storm. You'll learn when to use Fidget's magic, untill eventualy you'll be wracking up 1000+ combos without batting an eye.
Dust is, at it's core, a game about mastery. Thats all there really is to be said.

Terrible name aside, this is a semi-decent time-waster in the classic "match 3" puzzle genre. The twist in this one is that the matching mechanic works in conjunction with the actions your character takes at the top of the screen. The character's goal is to keep moving to the right, clearing obstacles such as monsters, treasure chests and locked doors. In order to clear those obstacles, you need to match specific types of tiles (swords to kill monsters, keys to open chests, etc). Getting hit or not matching tiles causes you to slow down and creep towards the left side of the screen. If you get pushed all the way back, the run is over. After each run, you return to a dungeon where upgrades can be purchased using the resources collected during the run (wood, stone, gold and experience). And that's pretty much all there is to it. Basically, you just keep running through the dungeon and buying upgrades when you die. Reaching certain score milestones causes you to rank up, which allows you to achieve higher scores and travel further into the dungeon. The ultimate goal is to score the titular 10,000,000 points and escape. On the technical front, the graphics are extremely simple, done in a low-res pixel style. It works for what it is, but the visuals are really nothing to write home about. I did really like the music, though. It's pretty catchy and very NES-esque.
In summary, if you are a fan of "match 3" games and don't mind spending a few hours on the mindless grind it takes to complete (I would estimate around 5-6 hours or so), then by all means, give this a shot. However, I really must reiterate that the gameplay is the very definition of a grind - the whole experience from start to finish is extremely repetitive. If you have a short attention span or really don't like doing the same thing over and over for hours, do NOT buy this game. Additionally, I have to say I also think the price is a little too high. For some reason, it's double what it costs on iOS, which doesn't make a whole lot of sense. I'm not saying it's a rip-off, but this might be one of those cases where you may want to wait and see if it goes on sale at some point.

For everyone who’s allergic to reading, here’s the TL;DR version:
If you like turn-based tactics game in which you can customize your units according to your preferred playstyle, this is the game for you. The game features over 50 levels in which you fight various alien and human enemies, leading to a playtime of about 30-35h for your first playthrough.
Your Templars level up, get better and learn additional abilities which – if used correctly – will bring you victory. New equipment and additional classes are unlocked via a research tree. The difficulty settings allow beginners as well as pros a challenging but enjoyable time with the game.
Buy it, it’s absolutely worth the 10 bucks.
Some more details now:
In the grim future of Templar Battleforce the remaining humans go on what gets called the great Exodus after the Great Galactic War to settle new planets far away from their devastated home.
You’re controlling a group of Templars, members of a martial order, who pilot giant battle suits and are sworn to protect the human colonists. You’re bigger and stronger than any normal human and basically the only one who has a proper chance in fighting the threats the vast galaxy has to offer.
Granted, the presentation is a little bit dry: Lots of completely unvoiced dialogues, no shiny CGI cutscenes and relatively unimpressive graphics. If you’re willing to read you will soon see, however, the devs put a lot of effort into the lore of the game (you can also jump straight from battle to battle of course).
The story is motivating enough though to keep you playing and the slight Warhammer 40k vibe going on also is pretty cool.
The core of the game of course is the fighting. You send your heavily armed Templars on space ships, through cities or into a seemingly empty desert. Each soldier has a certain movement allowance, measured in tiles of which the levels are made of. The action points are used for attacking as well as using buffs, building defensive turrets and more. The game therefore is turn-based, requiring you to end your turn if you used up all points and let the enemy act – similar to for example XCOM.
The mission types vary: Sometimes you have to quickly push to a certain objective, for example to destroy a xeno lair, another time you have to capture and hold points on the map or wait for support. Usually you are on the offensive and should therefore avoid getting entangled in prolonged fights. Captured tactical points produce supply points which allow you to call in more members of your squad or buy ordnance like medi kits.
Your squad consists of various specialists, always lead by your captain. You got the soldier who combines good accuracy and range with a variety of buffs and the extremely useful overwatch ability to control zones. Scouts are great long-rang-combat units and can be developed in either a scout or a sniper direction.
Then there’re engineers, the only ones who can capture points and erect turrets. The Hydra equipped with a deadly flamethrower and the ability to set whole areas ablaze. The Paladin, a melee warrior with a lot of useful buffs and healing abilities. The Berserker as the high damage melee unit and the Neptune, a heavy weapon specialist – a little bit like the big brother of the soldier.
The interface is unobtrusive and shows the range for movement, shooting and buffs of all your units; you can also get detailed info about the enemy types you’re facing. Enemy variety meanwhile is decent, the majority of your playtime you will fight the Terrox xeno which look like your standard alien species and come in different versions: from small crawlers over ranged units to some really brutal late-game elites. Occasionally you find yourself opposed by some human adversaries and then, finally, you will face the Narvidians. A hive-mind race which was the cause for the already mentioned great galactic war.
If one of your soldiers reaches a new level, you will be able to spend points on various attributes which either increase your health points, your chance to hit with a particular kind of weapon, your chance to get critical hits or your defence in case an enemy gets the chance to attack you. Not all attributes are similarly important to every class of course and some classes have special ones like the scout’s stealth or the Paladin’s medic attribute.
You will also be able to spend points on your Templars’ abilities, improving them or unlocking completely new talents. Generally, it’s worth thinking about which role you want each of your units to play and put their level-up points accordingly. You can easily recruit two soldiers and make one into a heavy hitter who likes to get close and personal while your other guy focusses on overwatch and defensive buffs.
Finally, there’s the equipment screen where you can give your happy soldiers new guns, a new shield or an improved armour. More advanced weapons don’t always deal more damage, there’re also ones which trade damage for higher accuracy or some additional elemental damage. Some armour may be really tough but slows you down etc.
To get new equipment and to unlock new talents, you have to use some requisition points in what basically is something like a research tree. You won’t be able to unlock everything so you have to carefully choose. In which direction do you want to focus your captain? Pure melee or with a sidearm? Does your soldier need grenades? Do you want to unlock the Neptune class or rather put more points into the Berserker? And doesn’t the Paladin desperately need a new weapon?
Loading times are extremely fast, the game runs stable and there basically aren’t any bugs – performance overall is great.
While I like the art style and atmosphere of the game, you can see by looking at some screenshots or videos the graphic isn’t exactly what you would call beautiful. If you don’t really care that much about shiny graphics anyway as long as the game’s great that’s not a concern ofc.
As mentioned before, none of the dialogues are voiced; the sound effects are mediocre and the soundtrack, while fitting, gets old pretty fast. I turned off all sounds for the game and just listened to some music while playing.
If you like these kind of turn-based games and the futuristic scenario there isn’t really any reason not to buy this (maybe you even played Space Hulk in the past). It works so incredibly well, all classes and abilities feel useful and the mechanics are easy to get into. Building up your own squad of super soldiers which you can name, customize and level-up in any way you want feels great.
Visually it’s not the most impressive and the story and its presentation won’t knock your socks off but the game itself just feels so satisfying.
The devs are very active, regularly checking the forums and fixing any bugs people encounter; they even add new content to the game and generally have an open ear for the community – exemplary!
One playthrough will probably take you between 30 and 35 hours, depending on your skill. Due to the way the requisition tree is designed the game has a lot of replay value for everyone who wants to go at it again using different strategies or previously not unlocked classes. Trying a higher difficulty level may also be an incentive; for players like me who are only…ehm…passable at these kind of games easy or normal are still enjoyable without being frustrating while pros can jump directly to the higher ones. Another thing to do after finishing the game is replaying the game with your veteran squad: The game offers a new game plus mode where you keep your experienced Templars, your equipment and your research level and play through the whole campaign again, if desired on a different difficulty level.

TL;DR Traditional comedy/horror point & click, with a great sense of humour and decent puzzles. If you don't mind a bit of cartoonish gore and some crude jokes in your adventure games, it should provide you around 3 hours of solid fun.
Metal Dead first came out at 2011, as the very low budget brain child of the two aussie developers behind Walk Thru Walls Studios. Despite its very basic art style, the low-fi music, the lack of voice acting, the short playtime and some minor (non game-breaking) bugs here and there, it completely embraces its crazy humour and oddball set of characters and ends up managing to both charm and entertain.
Immediately after your unlikely duo of metalhead heroes manage to crash their car right in front of what appears to be Zombie Central, everything turns from weird to weirder; including your protagonist Malcolm ending up with one of the funniest hint delivery systems in gaming history stuffed right into his pocket. (Feel free to use it now and then even if you aren't stuck, it offers some very amusing moments). Any more story details will, I feel, take away from your enjoyment, but suffice to say that the writing is quite polished. The dialogues are successful in delivering both jokes and a sense of character, and the insane plot ends up holding your interest despite (or because of) its absurdity. There are some unexpected twists and turns to enjoy, plus an oddball cast of engaging folks to save - or escort to their inevitable comedic demise. And while much of the humour could qualify as crude or gross, it somehow still manages to hit the mark more often than not.  As for the puzzles, they are all inventory based and mostly logical. I was happy to see that they tended to be backed up by dialogue and built neatly into the story instead of distracting from it. The difficulty isn't very high, but some of them are clever nonetheless.
There is something to be said about developers that succeed in making something this fun out of such a low budget, but you should still come to this game understanding that corners were (mostly gracefully) cut. The low-fi metal music has some nice moments, but I was more impressed with the clever use of sound effects that help emphasise the right points in the plot, either for shock value or for comedic effects. Similarly, the cartoonish art style may have character but is nonetheless very basic and doesn't scale well in larger monitors. However the animation saves it and deserves praise for its fluidity.
So Metal Dead is a fun little game, provided it finds the right audience that will appreciate its wacky sense of humor. I enjoyed replaying it, and I'm looking forward to
, which is expected to stomp into our lives sometime in the next year or so.

Templar Battleforce may be one of the best turn based tactical games I've ever played. I say that in comparison to Xcom (Old and New), Xenonauts, and both of the UFO series. What it simplifies in the meta game it makes up for in templar build options, map design, and the tech tree.
While the graphics aren't on par with some AAA titles, the art is functional and clear. The only major visual complaint I have is that at times ledges can be hard to distinguish from passable terrain.
Templar loadouts opt for a system of max equip points rather than requiring the player to maintain an economy in the meta game. New gear is unlocked via a tech tree with many branching paths, requiring you to focus on a strategy rather than be a jack of all trades. All classes feel useful, though you may find a handful really shining with your play style.
Combat is tense, as your templars can dish out high damage, but are almost always outnumbered. The game tends to focus on forward momentum, and rewards a mobile playstyle, as enemy spawns are infinite. The enemy spawning may be off putting for some, as it can at times be unpredictable, but it maintains the claustrophobia and tension from beggining to end. One must cover their 6 and keep their eyes on every avenue. Scale-able difficulty allows you to customize the challenge of the experience you want, from casual to Ironman deathslog.
All in all, a great purchase for anybody in the market for a turn based tactical game. The developer is extremely active (and still updating), and will likely respond quickly if you have more questions in the community discussion forum.

I wish this rating system was more complex. Personally, I liked the game, but I would only recommend it for die-hard graphic adventure fans who are also partial to horror comedy. (In this case, I totally fit the target demographic.)
: Fun, engaging zombie comedy plot -- it plays like the b@stard child of Shaun of the Dead and Maniac Mansion. The story wisely puts characters ahead of gimmicks -- it does not require familiarity with *specific* aspects of zombie lore or heavy metal culture to enjoy. The big reveal in the end made the gameplay feel worth it.
: The gameplay is almost never time-sensitive and doesn't quite capture the dread and tension of an ongoing zombie apocalypse. The puzzles lack challenge for veteran adventure gamers. Minimal replay value once you've finished it.

The game is a mix of a First Person Shooter and RTS (of sorts), but in a good way. The teams consist of a single commander on both sides that will build structures whilst also, taking advatage of his top down perspective, trying to instruct and organize his Ground Troops. Of course the playstyle is diffrent depending on which team for the marine commander needs the Ground Troops to build the structures he placed whilsed the alien commander doesn't need his Ground Troops to do so. The objective is to take out all of the opposing team's Command Stations (Marine) or Hives (Alien).
Because there is only a single commander per team you will likely be spending a large majority of yoru time being  apart of your team's Ground Troops.

-As the Marine Ground Troops you will have to communicate with your team to build structures set down by your commander and try to not be killed by the Aliens by trying to engage them at a distance.
-As the Alien Ground Troops you will try to slow and prevent Marine progression and explansion by destroying Marine Structures and killing them yourself. The Marines have Machine guns that are very effective at killing Aliens at range, and as the Alien you do not have range a large majority of the time. This leads to creative ways to try and get to them, from Crawling into the vents to try and flank them to crawling on the walls to ambush them.
*Keep in Mind that the things I just described are the very basics of both sides and the game has much more to it.
Something really nice about the game I would like to note is that there are rookie servers that only new players can join where you can only play with other players that are also realitivly new to the game. So you will never really have this pressure in these servers. Yet when you start feeling comfotable enough to start playing on normal servers you will find many servers will have vey organized teams that create amazing games! It's a very nice system having freindly rookie servers and amazingly organized normal servers.
The only issue I have with this game is trying to practice with commander. When I started becoming proficient with playing commander (online) I was locked out of the rookie servers. Normally this would be a good thing as the game deemed me with enough expirience to start playing on normal servers. Now in these servers you play with a large amount of veteran players, and this left me very little room to practice playing commander. Of course I'm not saying it's impossible to play commander because every once in a while you with find a team with no commander that is very supportive of you being a new commander and will help you do so. But most of the time on the normal severs I was contemplating either: "A. Taking command and being inexperienced and slower and more than likely lose the game for our team because of this." or "B. Letting someone else take command that is faster and more expirienced whilst  be part of the Ground forces where I have the most experience in playing."
Either Way I find this game to be overall fantastic and a lot of fun to play. I would recomend this game to anyone who enjoys playing with orginized teams to create amazing strategies and extensive engagments.

New Review!!! Yay! -------------------------------
Greetings Everyone!  I want to start by saying I was given a copy of this by the developer to provide critique and amend my review if I so chose.  I will state that my thoughts have changed about the game to some degree some for the better others for the worse.  I plan to submit a list of some improvements that I feel could be made to the game if they are wanted.  I am not one to think that my opinion is somehow valuable but I do try to be honest and true to my opinions as they are.
How do I walk:  The controls have been improved, though I do take issue to the choices of hotkeys used, there is still no hotkeys for the buildings and many other items.  This is unfortunately not a large issue because you have access to only a handful of combat units (7 in total I believe) with only a few active abilities between them.
To tell a story:  I still enjoy the setting, but after playing the game from beginning to end (something I did not originally do) the story fell really flat.  I’m not even sure what the point was.  I could sum up the story in a single sentence but even then it wasn’t really interesting.  If it were up to me the entire campaign would be condensed into 2-4 missions and simply be the first chapter of a much bigger story.  This may be the plan but each mission just feels like a generic dungeon crawl with RTS mechanics.  Like a game I just reviewed I am left with the ideal that this setting is fresh and interesting but told from a boring perspective.  The pacing left much to be desired and I found myself dazing off watching TV or reading something as the game really didn't push me to the next plot.
Did I do good:  I love the concept of playing something non-human, just like in Grey Goo but the units still don’t feel unique, they all feel like some offshoot of the same 4 legged insect, with as broad appearances that insects have in real life there is no need for this.  I’d really love to see some color added to the game, the scenes still feel a bit flat, why the Rhino can’t be a bright color to convey taunting or the hunter and legionnaires have some unmistakable cosmetic differences.  I see some inspiration from the HomeWorld series here as many of the units are too ‘real’ and functional but need some ‘umph’ to make them stand out.
Overall, I still do not feel this game is worth the $20 in the current condition.  BUT! I do think that it should be supported; the developer cares a lot about this game, is constantly interacting with the community, creating new patches and seems to have a passionate direction for this game.  I say that we can spend our money on more entertaining games yes, but the value we provide to support this game is by no means a waste.  With that if you want to see the next generations of indie games take off we need to support the creators.

An interesting concept in story but fall flat in presentation but I’m getting ahead of myself.  Let’s start with the controls, the hallmark of any good RTS, because that is what this game really is, an RTS with (albeit interested) poorly conveyed narrative.
The controls for the most part are okay, disappointing, but okay.  The issue is that there have been so many great RTS’s that have established essential components that are painfully missing from this game.  I constantly found myself trying to use normal shortcuts, features or quality of life improvements that are just plainly missing.  The interface only makes this worse, as the HUD feels unfinished and lacked icons that left an impression.  I can only hope in the designer’s goal to make the HUD feel ancient that they merely lost sight.
The graphics continue a feeling of incomplete, like a college project or a game still focusing on the mechanics and not the graphics.  Ultimately it feels more at home in the early C&C days not in the age of Age of Goo, StarCraft and Dawn of War.  If this was early access it would be a lot more understandable but only just.  The story continues this incomplete feel.
This is my largest concern, the story and RPG mechanics.  Both found wanting, the story focuses on the mysterious nature leaving a painfully dull campaign that feels more like a dungeon crawl with unlimited resources.  The RPG mechanics are just leveling mechanics of throwaway units with gear that just didn’t seem all that needed.  Again, everything is left feeling unfinished.
I hope this game is completed, I love the idea of an RTS RPG (Dawn of War is an amazing example), leveling heroic units while equipping them along side an army in a well tuned and inspirational story of an alien species rising from below.  Until then, I’m afraid I’ll just have to keep waiting…

1. What's new and groundbreaking? Nothing. What's fun? Everything. What's a ripoff? MAYBE some of the aesthetic items from the in-game store, but they don't change the game at all.
2. Remember the days of Blockbuster? Pay five dollars and you can try a game for one week. If you don't like it, you're out five dollars and you have to give it back anyway. Well for 20% of that ($1) you can try this game, and believe me when I say it's worth trying. If you don't want to spend that dollar, just sell some of the trading cards you picked up from other games.
3. If you get only four hours of fun out of this game, it's a victory. That's $.25 per hour of fun. To get that same value from a AAA title you need to have 240 hours of fun. Be honest, did you play CoD: Ghosts for 240 hours and enjoy it the whole time?

After playing a mere 4 hours of the game since I bought it yesterday, I feel like I can safely write a review.
-Played the demo ages ago and got bored, plus it performed badly.
-Slightly expensive.
-Seemed very 1-ended, very linear.
-Thought I would bore of it in mere minutes.
-I had some money and couldn't decide what to do with it.
-My brother really wanted me to get it.
-I have a GTX960 for a GPU, and while some other games stutter, this game gives a CONSTANT 60 FPS on absolute HIGHEST settings.  The graphics in this game are
nice looking!
-The developers have done an amazing job with the physics of the trucks; I love the "heavy" feeling of the vehicles.  Each truck handles differently than each other, and each one has its own challenges to overcome!
-Every single part on the vehicles seems to be animated, from the suspension to the chains and hooks.
-Immense customization for each vehicle, you can make a whole fleet of loggers, tankers and rescue trucks!
-A nice array of maps to choose from, with the ability to  choose starting vehicles.  Each map is extremely well made!
-The developers have made literally EVERYTHING on the map interactive; from the deformable terrain (you will hate mud after you finish playing for a while), to rocks, trees, and bushes!
-A nice career feel to the game, with you having to first go ahead and scout to remove cloaking from the map, as well as find paths to fuel stations and lumberyard/objectives.
-Trucks burn fuel at different levels depending on each model, and whether dif lock and AWD are enabled.
-Controls are very easy to set up, and are simplistic from the beginning.
-The game really requires you to think about the route you are taking, in order to not cause damage to your truck or load.
-An excellent group of devs as well as a phenomenal community of modders!
-The ONLY complaint I have that would make the game better would be an interior camera.  The camera options as of now leave a lot to be desired, and make it very difficult to see at some points.
All-in-all, the pros of this game FAR outweigh the cons, and there is absolutely NO reason not to buy this game!  I would not hesitate to buy it again, even if it was 10-15 dollars more expensive (which I honestly think they could get away with).

I picked Templar Battleforce up whilst it was on sale for a tiny amount (I think either £2 or £3) and I thoroughly recommend it, it's a great game!
-GAMEPLAY-
The best way I can describe this game is to say it is a simpler version of XCOM (in a good way). There's no base-building, it is simply mission after mission of your squad of troops against the enemy. From my experience of it so far you are normally massively outnumbered by the enemy on each mission, but to make up for this each unit in your squad is far stronger than the enemy. You'd expect 1 of your units to face off on its own against 4-8 of the enemy at once and usually come out victorious (depending on the unit's class). There are a range of mission types, such as survive x number of turns, reach a certain point, capture parts of a map, escort civilians etc.
-RPG-
The RPG element of the game is awesome, and you really can specialise each unit how you want as you spend ability and stat points. For example, I have one Soldier (long range unit) in my team who specialises in the overwatch ability, so that he can guard captured bases by himself. Each victory earns you Research Points which can go into unlocking new classes, or unlocking new features for existing classes - each class has several different specialities (e.g. your Captain can specialise in close combat, support, ranged fire, or as a grenade specialist).
-STORYLINE-
I've been playing this game for just over 13 hours at the time of writing and I'm already hooked. I won't give anything away but I will say although it's not the most advanced storyline, it's good enough to keep you interested. I also like the fact that there's permadeath for your characters - I am already massively attached to each and every one of my characters and refuse to let any die for that reason.
-IMPROVEMENTS-
At the start of most missions your team (usually 5 or 6, although this amount might increase later in the game) is pre-selected from your roster for you. You start the mission with a currency called 'SP' which can be used to immediately swap one unwanted member of your team out for one of your preferred members, but I think a massive improvement would be to just let the user pick their own team at the start of every mission. I understand for some missions you need a specific class such as an Engineer which is fine, but the user perhaps should be able to pick the rest of the team themselves after the mandatory ones.
As I've made clear though, I love this game already and this last point is just a suggested improvement to what is otherwise a fantastic game.
TL;DR - Pick this up if you want a simpler version of XCOM with awesome combat missions and good RPG progression.

DEFCON is all about the most hypothesized and alluded to cause of the end of the world in popular culture: nuclear war. You are cast in the role of a high-ranking general from a mega-nation (like the European Union or the African Union) that has the ultimate goal of not dying as much as everyone else when the nukes start flying. What an original concept! There's no resources to collect or money to spend, just your bombs and their bombs, and nuclear annihilation. No surprise the subtitle of the game is "Everybody Dies". For having such a simple game design it's surprising how challenging and entertaining DEFCON can be. During the entire game you are situated in front of a world map that looks purposefully like something USSPACECOM might use during a nuclear war--with appropriately picked displays and sounds--even machine noises running in the background. You can also write on the map if you have battle plans and see fallout from detonations. It really makes you feel like you're locked down in a sophisticated military bunker somewhere, intently watching the monitor, waiting for the inevitable as you give the order to launch mass destruction.
DEFCON follows DEFCON which is actually a five-phase/level state of alert system used by the United States to describe its level of preparedness for military situations. In-game the phases begin consecutively after a countdown of allotted time that you can choose to speed up or slow down. During each level you are restricted to undertaking certain actions. These restrictions are lifted as you progress through the different phases. For instance, in DEFCON 5 you are only allowed to strategically place radar, air force, missile, and naval assets. In DEFCON 3 you are allowed to have conventional naval and airborne combat. And in the final phase, DEFCON 1, you are permitted to start the nuclear holocaust from missile silos, nuclear submarines, and bombers. The ultimate goal is to have the highest population kill count (which sounds horrible). The action can escalate quickly and it is truly a sight to behold when you witness missile launches all over the world, creating webs of color, and watch the dashed tracers of missiles as they slowly seek out their targets. The audio and soundtrack do a wonderful job of setting the atmosphere, spine-tingling, especially after you just destroyed a population center, see the bright explosion with the tallied dead, and the faint cry of a women in the background. DEFCON usually turns into a game of chicken to see who blinks first. That's because when you decide to launch your nuclear payload and by what degree can make all the difference in the world, no pun intended. This psychological warfare can intensify if you have the full number of players and nobody is an ally or they're multiple alliances.
I recommend DEFCON and for the price, the soundtrack as well. DEFCON is an easy game to pick up but difficult to master. Finding online players will be a challenge but you can always actively seek out people to play with via the forums or other resources, buy the game for some of your friends, or just play the AI. Either way I still would give it a try.

So Metal Dead is initially a pretty cool looking game for fans of metal, a standard zombie apocalypse title set apart by its metal-loving protagonists so much so that the very title is a play on "metalhead". Unfortunately however it doesn't really live up to this promise either as a game or as a humorous take on the genre and subculture. The game itself is only a few hours long which for the price is about right, but during those three or so hours it doesn't really do much. Your character simply progresses from room to room picking up items and collecting elevator access cards from other characters in a rather dull manner with uninteresting and sometimes annoying controls, making for a rather drab playing experience. This could easily be at least partially salvaged by the story, aesthetic or humour the game clearly aims for but it doesn't really nail this either. Jokes are very surface level and basic but lacking the raw punch to actually produce real laughs. It has a couple of mild smirk-worthy moments, but nothing inspiring anything more and a couple of comments made by characters are somewhat questionable. Dialogue isn't exactly invigorating, characters are stereotypical without actually making jabs at those too much, and most disappointingly of all the comical look at metal itself it seems to suggest is nothing to write home about. Once in a while the two main characters will refer to something as "brutal" in a Metalocalypse-esque fashion and South Park-ish usage of metal to drive away enemies is central to the climax (in fairness the root explanation of the zombie apocalypse is more creative than many, if a little random), but anything beyond that which would resonate with members of that subculture is painfully lacking, and an ending comment by one character on how using image to define yourself and your deeds is no worse than being mindless undead just comes across as tacked on, ill thought out and a little preachy with absolutely nothing coming prior to set up or question the issue. Ultimately it's not an awful way to spend a small handful of hours especially for the price but where there was potential to make something unique, entertaining and memorable there's a merely serviceable game with underwritten jokes and subtext and a whiff of missed opportunity.

Metal Dead is a regular adventure game with enough demented elements that makes you wonder if you're playing a spoof, and in a way, you are. The game is filled with hilarious dialog (well, it's funny once) as two metal heads who somehow found yourselves in the middle of zombie apocalypse, your travel companion, Ronnie, met an untimely end... but not quite. As you encounter zany characters, from mad scientist to drill sargeant and much more, all with hilarious dialog options, and you can interact with objects by touching, looking... and tasting, you'll get even more hilarious reactions.
The graphics are low-fi, not low as voxel or deliberate sprite-y, but it's 2D, and very 2D.
Once you're in the game, the game runs the standard gamut of "talk to character, figure out what he wants, which is probably elsewhere, held by somebody, who wants something else, and so on." So the game is basically traveling back and forth, figure out what is available, how to get what you wanted (either a trade or distract and steal), and so on. Obviously, the items you encounter along the way, and the zany characters (some of whom chose to ignore the zombie apocalypse around them)  leads to even more hilarious situations and dialog.
In other words, the fun of the game is in finding all the dialog gems by doing things not quite right, rather than speed through the game picking the right solution at every turn.
So if you like adventure games, relatively simple puzzles (no forced "solve this puzzle box to advance" here) and hilarious dialog (at least to me), this is your game.

I really enjoyed this game. It was a gift to me from my BF and him and I played it Co-Op together online, it definetely reminded me of Tenchu games, but I must say the things that stood out most to me about the game were the artstyle and the simple yet deep storyline. Which you have to take the time to read scrolls to fully grasp as you progress through the game because not everything is pointed out to you. I would give this game a 10/10 personally and this is why. I played the game on a horrible toaster. many times during the game I was running it at as low as 6fps, and I STILL enjoyed the game because it was just that much fun for me. I have fond memories of Tenchu growing up playing as Ayame who was a source of inspiration for what a ninja was to me from an early age. And so to me this game sort of hit home in a special way and took me back there, although it has no Ayame.
The graphics are really good, the gameplay flows smoothly and I had no lag issues (outside of what my toaster provided me with, which is not the games fault.) The mechanics all work fine for a stealth game, traveling through the maps with my BF I found sometimes we would literally just take our own paths through an entire map and end up meeting back at the end somehow....which is actually really cool to me because it meant there were many ways to beat a stage. We could kill everyone, or kill noone at all..and still succeed.
Finding all the scrolls on the maps was rather fun and interesting challenges as some of them are well hidden, so the scavenger hunt alongside keeping track of enemies locations and stealth killing them was fun. The characters seem underdeveloped but again if you read the scrolls themselves there is actually alot of lore most seem to miss out on that develops them further and might even connect you to one or two of them. Over all I loved the story itself it was a highlight for me towards the end especially I related in my own ways.
The downsides I found were that it is not that well optimised for PC it seems, but again..I cannot accurately give you much feedback here since my toaster..is..likely better off used making pop tarts. The other downsides were that there were some frustratingly irritating points in the game where there were bugs. But I easily overlooked it for how good the rest of the game itself is. I recommend playing through using Co-Op.
Honestly to me this is a simple game with simple mechanics that was simple fun, but had a surprisingly good story even if some parts were predictable.. It's worth the buy. I'd pay full price for it if I had to buy it knowing what it is.

Did i enjoy Aragami? Hell yeah. The stealth mechanics are solid, it's always clear whether you are in the shadows or bright light allowing for sneaking about to be simple but still challenging due to the placement of shadows later in the game. The guards are well placed with interesting dialogue providing some background info for the story and allowing moments of nail-biting terror of whether you can teleport out of sight of a guard in time, especially on pacifist runs. High replayability due to the option of play styles. You can sneak through undetectedm, leaving no bodies or blood behind you or you can butcher the population of a small city. The lack of a mid-range reward however is annoying, it's all or nothing when it comes to rewards for kills in a level. The guards walking paths can go wrong sometimes and cause them to turn sharply when walking in a straight line, get stuck on boxes or sometimes simply stand still and swivel.The art style of the game is lovely with amazing views from vantage points from which to plan a route through the level. The kill everyone approach for some levels requires certain upgrades to be achievable and the tutoialisation is apalling for this game. It doesn't tell you how to spend skill points on upgrades or how to use some abilities. the cape on Aragami's back (showing your power gauge) has a habit of wrapping round itself leaving you with no idea about how many ability uses or shadow essence you have left, leaving you high and dry for teleporting and shadow making sometimes.The various character skins are a nice addition adding extra rewards for certain playstyles for yet more replayability.
Pros:
Solid stealth mechanics
Interesting dialogue and story
Fun upgrades that never make you feel overpowered
Various challenge modes for different play styles
Cons:
Short game, about 7-10 hours for an easy mode playthrough to 100%
Frustrating detection rates on higher difficulties
Poor quality boss fights, basically the Mr Freeze boss from Arkham City with annoying minions
Unclear goals with non-updating mission hints
Aragami is a game that tries is hardest to be fun, mysterious and challenging and succeeds almost every time. If the issues i mentioned are cleaned up then it would definitely be one of my top games of the year. A good 9/10.

Even after 16 years since it's original release, Final Fantasy VII is, without a doubt, one of the absolute best RPGs in existence. It's characters, story, and gameplay are some of the finest the JRPG market has ever had. This is a game that anyone should play through at least once. This port of the classic is definently worth purchasing for both veterans of FFVII and first-timers alike. Cloud saving is a very nifty feature that allows you to play your saves on multiple computers, although there are occasionaly network issues with it. The character booster will be a great tool for those who want to observe the story rather than focus on hours of grinding. The textures have been polished up nicely, and the FMVs look a lot smoother than before. Overall, this is a gaming experience worth having, and this is the perfect version for those who wish to try it for the first time. My only recommendation: Make sure you have a controller, as the standard keyboard controls are a bit wonky.
