I bought this game long ago, but I never got around to play it. Tried it for a bit but it didn't reallycatch my attention. Two days ago I was looking for something to play, and to my suprise I noticed they are still updating this game!

I'm probably still in quite early game, so the game seems very lengthy. I started on second hardest right away (Since it has permadeath for squad members) and it's giving me a great challenge. There's a lot of strategy involved on how you play out your fights.
There's a good tutorial on how the game works, but it took a while to find the inner workings of the combat system. The dice system it uses for attack and defense is pretty cool, although it's almost impossible to guess how much % higher to hit you will get when you add 1 standard dice to your attack, it all depends on who you attack and how many dice you already have. Not a problem in itself, but it makes deciding between say +3damage or +1 accuracy item quite difficult.
Anyway, the game is definitely worth the cheap price. There's a lot of game to be played, and since they've supported it for so long, it feels very polished and balanced.

vets know we rip offs when we see it. But its not bad here, just sounds and Zergling-ish skins.
When you start the game you meet you advisor whose voice is rather questioning, is it a bug or a slow talker with a weird voice. I listened to it the first time through the game, but skipped after that because it wasn't so great.
Now the slow march to finish and repetitive nature of missions is problem. In a RTS game there is always some incentive to try and rush through a mission with some measure of strategy. In my case all I needed to do was turtle up and max out my army to be able to handle everything.
. So strategy is out the window.
Inventory sorting needs work. A quick fix to this would have been adding an auto-sort. Also, the fact you can't place items from one bag into another isn't great.
Hotkeys for building should have been implemented before the game was released. RTS games do require this.
Camera controls are undefensibly terrible. For me I just rotated my camera to face north and left it there,
.
Puzzles are not puzzles, its basically like using the Claws in Skyrim, then rotating the dials to complete a picture. Not puzzly in my opinion.
There are too few different types of enemies with all the same weaknesses. If you have a high attack power you win since almost every enemy has about the same attack power and defense power.
. Stat differences would be welcome.
. In most cases right-clicking on the map makes the units move immediately but there are times when the units just sit there (idle)  for a second or two (sometimes even while in battle) then decide to run. Bad because theres a chance you could lost your squad or important units.
DNA is kind of unique, there are systems like this in other games but none (in my experience) that continues between missions. Basically its research points acquired through disassembly of your unwanted items. Its awesome, but you'll have so much more than you need by Act 7. Not a deal breaker though and still a positive.
The story is what can make a game great, this is getting there. While the story can be slow and the ending leaves you wondering why there wasn't more Acts introduced, its decent and can definitely be expanded in future updates.

The bullet physics are weird. From what I've read they use 'rays' instead of actual 'bullets' which breaks down to "if you're retical was over them when you fired then it will register a hit on their end". Unfortunately it leads to some issues with latency and hit registration ie. I shot him but it didn't register. This leads to some unfortunate gameplay issues as the alien team is almost entirely based on jumping around to avoid getting shot. So when you're trying to shoot aliens that are already hard to hit because they're jumping/flying around and your bullets aren't registering when they should it leads to some frustration. Also latency issues exist with bullet registration in terms of the gun firing faster than the bullets can register, which makes it seem like a temporary immunity after being hit, but it's actually just the latency not being able to keep up with the faulty hit registration system. From what I've seen the maximum "accuracy" that can be achieved is in the range of 30% and this is from watching people who play using 'questionable means'. Also the game has triggerbots available for it, which is not cool.
And the community is a bunch of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s.
**edit**
Almost forgot to mention that there's only like 3 servers on the North American west coast and if they're not full, they're empty. From what I've seen most of the east coast servers (also not that many) autokick people with 'high latency' ie. >100. Which is totally understandable given the latency issues with hit registration.
Apparently there was an update at some point which removed access to the European servers for North Americans and visa versa.

There hasn't been a game like this one before, or at least not to my knowledge. There are plenty of games in which the player displays their ability to comprehend music and beat, and there are a fair number of games where the player explores a dungeon, travelling deeper and deeper, growing in strength as their enemies become tougher and tougher, where any misstep will result in a "game over" screen and the option to start over from square one. I don't think mixing these kinds of games has ever been done before, and I'm in love with the result!
Crypt of the Necrodancer isn't just a groovy music game, nor is it just a dungeon-crawling roguelike - it's both. It's a very demanding game, as it requires quick thinking and decision-making, and throughout the whole experience you will absolutely want to groove in place, getting as deep into those juicy tunes as you can. Play it with a keyboard or a dance mat; you'll have extreme fun no matter which way you play.

Ahh Mafia 3 where do i begin...
First thing you see is quite lovely visuals and HUGE improvement to driving over old games. Intro mission is quite good fun (i was annoyed by the "ducking" interruptions tho)
Sadly the good fun ends after finishing intro as it becomes same old story with go there kill/interrogate/sabotage this/that types of missions (im not against it considering the point of this game is taking over the city instead of getting into the family story type which offsets a lot of people who love Mafia series)
I could write a long review with time i played already but ill shorten it down to CONS and PROS:
CONS:
No real garrage leaving you with 7 vannila cars in it that you can modify thanks to one of latest updates (Family kick back DLC adds 4 more vehicles to your "garage" 3 of them are avaible as soon as you get your "garrage" while last one needs some unlocking to do).
You are locked to 2 weapons on your loadout, primary and secondary not to mention ammo cap just blows without upgrades (machine guns got 4 clips in total and they, sniper rifles got 20 total and ect with no upgrades) some of the weapons are even same just different model and minor changes on stats (ooh lets take 9mm submachine gun and add silencer and count it as a different weapon of higher rank as well, same with some of the pistols)
Cops are just more messed up than GTA V. You kill one 7 cars just rush you in mere 5 seconds overwhelming you and "popping a cap up your butt" and they keep spawning new ones after you kill one instantly(its like zombie games where you make too much sound and got whole horde on your back in mere fraction of a second and they never stop comming) not to mention their damage is increased taking out whole healthbar in mere 1-2 shots with a frigin pistol.. also you can still drive over red lights with no consequences next to cop car....
Taking any physical damage like hitting a wall while driving fast or taking some fall damage will damage you BODY ARMOR not your HITPOINTS which is plain stupid as it sounds.
Some of reppetitive missions are as reppetitive as broken rubics cube (you cap out income yet and after some time it says you can do mission that you did to increase income again, go to waypoint just to find nothing spawned in there making it imposible to do again)
Wiretapping specific points on map gives you: Locations of enemies over walls (aka xray vission), marking up every collectible on minimap, and ofc marking up things like med aid kits and weapon lockers over walls as well.
As i mentioned problem with weapon ammo capacity without upgrades (that you need to unlock on specific conditions)
there are upgrades to following as well: Health, weapon accuracy, ammo cap, cars (thx to latest update).
No real clothing shops as youre locked to multiple preset costumes that you cant even modify.
Some of missions cinematics just ignore outfit youre wearing and shows preset one.
Bushes are made of stainless steel
PROS:
Great new driving system compared to other games in series (better than GTA V in my opinion)
60's with whole racism thing going on, "whites only" cafes, hill billies and their pickups painted with confederate flags.
Some great cars from the era that are based on:
*Ferrari 246
*1965-1970 Buick Electra
*1968 Lincoln Continental
*1969 Buick Gran Sport
*1968 Chevrolet Corvette
thats few of my favourites
Great classics on the radio like:
Rolling Stones - Paint it Black, The Animals - House of the Rising Sun, Johnny Cash - Ring of Fire, Canned Heat - On the Road Again, to name a few.
Great atmosphere be it in city of far off in bayou
Story might not be as detailed and deep as last 2 mafia games yet this brings a gust of fresh air not only giving us a story how we took over whole city and created our own family, but lots of choises who gets what, who gets left out, who lives and who dies which is something new and lots of fans will be angry about because they loved the linear storytelling with no choises first 2 games had.
As many problems the game has it seems devs are slowly adding new features that game lacks, they might not add every feature we lack from other Mafia game series, and not fix every problem game has at this point...
But i would still recommend trying this out (grab it on sale), the atmosphere is what really this game is about..
But this is just my humble opinion. (If something changes over the rest of my gameplay i will edit this review)

Even after 16 years since it's original release, Final Fantasy VII is, without a doubt, one of the absolute best RPGs in existence. It's characters, story, and gameplay are some of the finest the JRPG market has ever had. This is a game that anyone should play through at least once. This port of the classic is definently worth purchasing for both veterans of FFVII and first-timers alike. Cloud saving is a very nifty feature that allows you to play your saves on multiple computers, although there are occasionaly network issues with it. The character booster will be a great tool for those who want to observe the story rather than focus on hours of grinding. The textures have been polished up nicely, and the FMVs look a lot smoother than before. Overall, this is a gaming experience worth having, and this is the perfect version for those who wish to try it for the first time. My only recommendation: Make sure you have a controller, as the standard keyboard controls are a bit wonky.

This is a turn-based squad tactics game.  There is an Andoid App with the same base rules, but the PC version has been extended with more missions, equipment and skills to choose from.
It plays like the old Space Crusade tabletop game, in a similar universe. That means your opponents are aliens (mostly melee-based) and sometimes their loyal followers (with guns).
Your templars gain levels and aquire new skills, and they can be respec'ed to try other builds. Classes range from melee and scouts to grunts and heavy weapon troopers, and your commander.
The game has several difficulty levels, and the AI can be pretty tough to beat in some scenarios.
Graphics are on the basic side, the sound, too. But it's fun and it's turn-based.
So if you're looking for a board game clone, check out the Android App and give the PC version a try if you liked it.

Ah Metal Dead, what a fun little time waster with a good ending to lead up to a sequel.
There isn't a terrible lot to be said about it though, it's a solid puzzle point-'n'-click game where you and a certain friend go through trying to solve the mystery of the end of the world. I can't reveal spoilers obviously, but it's worth 5 bucks to sit down and just try and play it.
It has a certain charm to it in the way that it's drawn and it both can be fun to just look at and can be seen as rather bland. In some instances, the characters look great for how simple the crayon-simple designs are, others not so much like the head security guard. Just something about him seemed off in design.
The puzzles are good but seem random with some of their answers and solutions however I was able to figure them out eventually. It strikes me really as a game you'd give to your kids if it didn't have some adult themes. But I do look forward to an eventual sequel.
Overall Review? It's a simple couple hours of clean, harmless fun with corny jokes and silly characters with an okayish ending. The game looks alright and it didn't bug out at all and I tried everything I could think of. Overall, solid.

I have a deep and abiding hatred for this game. It could have been so good but...
- Most of your combos are either useless or wind up hurting you later.
- The alchemy "upgrades" are largely useless.
- The multiplier system ensures that you'll have to grind for hours to win.
- The achievements have you continue grinding even after beating the game.
The core mechanics are good, the music is catchy, but these numerous flaws just bring the game down. If only you could "bank" your bonuses so that they aren't wasted so much, that would be a good first step. As it stands, this is a short diversion and nothing more.

- combat rules are very transparent (almost like playing a board game)
- a heat system (in addition to health), meaning that you can't go all-guns-blazing all the time
- if you allow your enemies to impose their terms on the fight, you will suffer, even on easy difficulty
- you can redesign your characters mid-game, if you want to try a different skill set
- different difficulty levels do their job (for me).  Easy is easy, hard gets hard
- there's even a storyline to connect the different scenarios, and some rudimentary NPC interaction
CONs:
- from my observation, not all enemies always exhaust their moves, even when it would be advantageous to do so (I'm assuming here that enemies should always try to attack as much as possible - they have no reason to hold back)
Now, this is not JA2 or even X-Com.  There is no hunting-gathering of new equipment, no manufacture of equipment or items and the progression of scenarios is for the most part linear.
Overall, two thumbs up.

A very solid, "Maybe not Warhammer" game. The fluff isn't bad, but the mechanics are much more original and compelling, in my opinion. There are several major types of enemies (xenos and otherwise) that each feel different and possess different strengths and weaknesses.
The progression is interesting, and the missions are well-balanced to my findings so far - the only real flaw I'm finding is that with the Mission Completion reward system, you are strongly encouraged to stack movespeed buffs as much as you can, overheating your team constantly and not relying on skills that require you not to be overheated. This allows you to generally outrange and overwatch-spam your enemies to death as they chase you, or to simply outpace them, complete the mission in 60%-80% of the 'par' number of turns, and get a huge bonus to your XP/RP unlocks.
Also, to give you a perhaps slightly better idea of how things work than the trailers do...
That massive tree with "Unlock 1000+ unique talents and gear" is a general unlock tree for your full force. The Berserker, Paladin, Neptune, and Hydra trees unlock both a new class and gear shared with other classes, which encourages you to branch out into them based on what you plan to do with your squad. For instance, some of the best Heat capacity gear for the Engineer is on the Hydra tree.
Progression along the tech tree, of sorts, allows you to raise the level of skills and equip gear to a Templar who has sufficient level. When they level, they also gain stat points to distribute to Attributes and to Skills; each of them provides a small bonus to either a dice pool (like accuracy) or percentile (like crit chance). The choices you make for unlocks are permanent; choices for assigned gear and abilities are able to be reset and reassigned freely between missions. This means, for instance, you can have a low-level Scout specced in Quickness and Stealth for light weapons, debuffing attacks, and scouting, then as its levels increase you can swap to Strength and Tactics plus the Headshot skill for dealing massive critical damage while still being able to hit. The only thing that has any limitations on use are "Relics," pieces of gear that can only be used by one Templar at a time, some of which are amazing and some of which are "eh."
The combat system is worth reading a Steam guide on - it's not explained much unless you dig deep, but it's a system that can be loosely described as 'easy to learn, hard to master.' Part of this is that you can't be sure what sort of dice pools you're facing on the enemies, so you can't be certain of when you have 'enough' accuracy to hit reliably and can move on to other stats, as you don't receive any bonus for overshooting an enemy's defense pool that I know of.
In short, as long as you're comfortable with the faults I'm mentioned and you like Turn-Based Tactics, this game is definitely worth a buy; if you're hesitant but like the genre, it's worth a buy on sale. I've put quite a few hours into it and expect to put many more in to try out different playstyles.

What is 10,000,000?  It sounds like the beginning to a terrible essay but I've had friends constantly ask me while I play.
Enjoy Bejeweled but are terribly bored of rolling in riches and crushed gem shards?  Puzzle Quest quests just not instantly gratifying enough?  Well welcome to 10,000,000!
You are an explorer trapped in a dungeon and you must fight your way through hordes of monsters and dragons.  STORY.  Not really, that's pretty much all you get.  You match tiles to use magic or melee attacks.  Match keys to open chests and doors.  Oh, but that's not all.  You need to match lumber and stone to gather resources for your home base.  Home base, well that's where you get all beefed up for your next expedition.
But what happens when you finally reach 10,000,000 points?
Farther you get in the dungeon, the more points you get along with experience and other such wonders to help you in future journeys.
It's a nice time killer when you are waiting for friends for other such online gaming shenanigans or just when you really don't want to think and maintain some level of sanity.

It's buggy, laggy, and has graphics in the vein of Half-Life.
It also has guns, vehicles and lots of dinosaurs to point them at.
ORION keeps things simple and doesn't stray too far from it's core of dino-slaughter. It's similar to Killing Floor, where you start out with just a pistol and work your way up each game to better weapons and abilities. There's a level system, like in KF as well, granting you permenant bonuses the more you play each class.
It has a decent selection of weapons and upgrades, as well as three classes with unique abilities and two unique weapons each. Killing earns you money, which you use to buy these items.
Vehicles are a weak point, with pretty much all of them armed with the same minigun(s), with the occasional rockets. Vehicle design is largely unattractive, and most feel pretty clunky. There are some exceptions, namely the flying vehicles, and the hover bike which is pretty fun.
Classes are assault, support, and recon, with their own unique abilities, jetpack, healing gun, and cloak, respectively. These are the major differences between the classes, along with some base health/armor differences, so you can largely play whichever you prefer and ignore the others. Jetpack and cloak are probably the most useful, as typically you don't have much time to swap to your healing gun during a wave, and both can completely remove you from danger.
Overall, it's not much of a game. It's simple, repetitive, and has some playability issues. But it's got multiplayer, both coop and PvP, solo play if you prefer, and is largely entertaining when you just want to kill some time or want a more relaxed gaming experience. When it's on sale for a dollar, it's hard to say it's not worth it. If you only got a half hour of entertainment from it, you'd still have a fantastic money to entertainment ratio, and who knows, maybe the developer will improve the AI and vehicles over time. Not much of a risk for a dollar.

The Hive is a story-driven fantasy game that combines RPG elements and blends them with real-time strategy. Players take control of the Insectoid Hive mind.
After a very solid presentation that details the background to the game you begin with a single worker and an objective. The first objective is to build a hive. The objective system is the primary game mechanic that leverages the storyline and the gameplay. Each time you complete an objective you are presented with a new challenge. Rinse and repeat.
In order to complete a number of these objectives resource management comes into play. You must hunt or dig for resources – food and minerals. It is these that enable you to develop your armies and your villages.
Without a shadow of a doubt the highlight of the game is in its presentation. This includes the graphical and audible presentation as well as the narration.
I thoroughly enjoyed the opening cutscene to the game. I thought it served extremely well as an introduction to the game and it inspired me to want to play through the game. This led in well to an overall graphics and audio display that is of an exceptionally high quality for an indie studio. It is one of the best presented indie games that I have had the pleasure of playing.
The screenshots and gameplay footage featured within the trailers serve as an accurate reflection of the artistic approach to the game. They have not been doctored to make them look better than the actual quality you will see within the game.
The narration and the overall storyline are top notch. This kept my motivation levels high to grind through the game even as the actual gameplay itself was disappointing. It invested me into the game to the degree that I was certain that I wanted to continue playing the game when any drop in quality may have seen me quit entirely. Therefore, I absolutely give kudos to the writers as well as the artist and sound engineers.
The game falls short of the mark when it comes to being a deep RTS. Although the game has all of the mechanics and tools that an RTS has it generally lacks depth and polish. This, in my opinion, is because the game attempts to be everything and when that encompasses a number of genres that’s almost impossible to achieve. Had the developers spent a little more time attempting to specialize the game in a strategic direction it would have resulted in a vastly improved title.
Another criticism that I have of the game is that there always appears to be one best way to accomplishing a certain task. There is a distinct lack of variability and this reduces the replayability of the game. Therefore, I find this to be more than a little disappointing considering the game bills itself as a game having ‘many different endings and possibilities’ with players being able to ‘create their own unique route, strategy, and story.’
A final criticism is that the AI of the computer is poorly designed. Whenever the computer is successful it feels as though it is a result of the player’s own stupidity and sheer dumb luck rather than being a hard fought contest. Once you do figure out that one best way to any given solution players will utilize the same strategies again and again throughout the course of the game.
The Hive has 40 Steam achievements as well as a set of trading cards. Given the nature of the game this is about as Steamified as what we could possibly ask for.
If the developers were able to produce the same quality in the gameplay as they did in the presentation, we would be looking at an indie game of the year contender. The Hive is not a poor game but it’s just not a great game. It lacks the overall polish and depth in the gameplay department to be a truly special game. However, we must bear in mind that this is the first game developed and published by Skydome Entertainment. I genuinely believe that they would have learned so many lessons through the creation and development process of this game that it should hold them in good stead in the future. Consequently, they are a game studio to keep a close eye on. The potential is there if they are able to put those lessons into action in their next game. The Hive is a good beginning.
I recommend The Hive for the high quality of work in the presentation of the game.

There hasn't been a game like this one before, or at least not to my knowledge. There are plenty of games in which the player displays their ability to comprehend music and beat, and there are a fair number of games where the player explores a dungeon, travelling deeper and deeper, growing in strength as their enemies become tougher and tougher, where any misstep will result in a "game over" screen and the option to start over from square one. I don't think mixing these kinds of games has ever been done before, and I'm in love with the result!
Crypt of the Necrodancer isn't just a groovy music game, nor is it just a dungeon-crawling roguelike - it's both. It's a very demanding game, as it requires quick thinking and decision-making, and throughout the whole experience you will absolutely want to groove in place, getting as deep into those juicy tunes as you can. Play it with a keyboard or a dance mat; you'll have extreme fun no matter which way you play.
I have nothing but praise for this game, and it isn't even finished yet. Even when I began playing in advance of the early access hitting steam, I never once felt like my money was misplaced. Even if this game were never finished, it'd still be worth every penny I spent on it.

This game is the most realistic offroad truck simulator I could find. It is hard to review this game properly. On one hand, it is immensely realistic and therefore it is fun to play. On the other hand, there is not much gameplay. The only 'mission' is to haul lumber from one end of the map to the other. But: because this is realistic and because roads contain lots of deep mud, you can play for 6 hours to haul three loads of lumber.
Trucks are worked out very well. Some trucks are really useless (like the rear-wheel-drive B130), some are great (like the C255) and some are just awesome because of the brute force approach (like the D537). And there is the small and remarkably agile B-66.
The greatest problem of this game is the lack of steering wheel support. Why do I play simulation games on the PC? Yes, because of the steering wheel. I missed opportunity if you ask me. OK, keyboard controls work fine, but camera movement is awkward and actually really bad sometimes.
For this lack of real challenges, I think this game is too expensive. Nevertheless, I do recommend this game because of the great realism. The realism brings the fun, but only if you are patient enough.

I had previously written a review in which I did not recommend Aragami, primarily because of the boss encounters. With the most recent update I am pleased to say that the developer has addressed every grievance I had, and as such I felt it important to be equally vocal in my recommendation.
Aragami is the closest thing to Tenchu since... well, since Tenchu. This is not to say that it is a clone, but rather an homage. It clearly has its own formula and mythos. A true stealther, toe-to-toe confrontation is not an option. Taking a single hit = death. What's more, in the scoring of each level there is an achievement not only for eliminating all threats, but also an equal achievement for killing no enemies whatsoever. I particularly enjoy this deviation from the norm.
If you're looking for Ninja Gaiden, wrong place. If you're looking for something like Tenchu but even more focused on stealth, look no further. Highly recommended.

8/10 fo me. It's a great time capsule for virtual tourists. Just get in the car, listen to the great music and drive through beautiful city. The graphics are awesome! Characters models, cars, environments are great. Main missions interiors are specially treated with lots of details and care. The lighting in the game is also very nice. Orange light hitting the environments is stunning. The animations of the NPCs are also something to admire to. The music selection is one of the best soundtrack in GTA-style game (along with the Mafia 2, LA Noire). At first I didn't like the main character but it makes perfectly sense in presented story and it couldn't be otherwise. The moments in the story are incredible good. Very memorable and fresh.
Ok so is there any negatives? Sure.. It's an open world so you can encounter some bugs. I have seen some minor ones like 5 bugs with the NPCs, 1 with the car, several with the lighting but nothing too big.. No ground breaking stuff. Overall I'm pleased with the performance (keep in mind it was played on GTX card). As for the gameplay... the game will be forcing you to repeat the same tasks quite heavily. On the plus side the gameplay mechanics are really well done. So the shoothing, driving are very pleasing and I didn't mind doing it a lot.
Once again this is a great game with some grinding chore elemnts but story is well worth it!

Ok, now that you're reading more than the first line, I can go into more detail. If you like squad-based, strategy games, this game is, and I don't say this lightly, amazing for the price. Regular updates (so far), give you a reason to come back after you've completed it and the size/depth of the requisition trees (basically what kind of gear is available to each type of troop) means that you're encouraged to keep playing to explore new builds.
Yes, it's not as polished or nice-looking as some of its rivals, but I think a true fan of this kind of strategy doesn't care. The mechnical depth more than makes up for it in my opinion. The addition of the 'heat' mechanic makes for some interesting trade-offs at higher difficulties (my poor scouts always end the mission close to exploding from heat) and the armor/block/defense system allows for many different builds. The story has the classic "grim dark" slant to it and it borrows a fair bit from other fantasy, but I still found it reasonably engaging.
TLDR; Worth every penny if you like squad/turn-based strategy. Look forward to more from these developers.

Let me just say that I only BARELY recommend this game, and that you would really do yourself a service getting this game while it's on sale or something.
Main premise:
The point of this game is to reach a score of 10,000,000. This is done by playing a Chuzzle-esque tile match game wherein the tiles you match has an outcome on a dungeon battle. If you by example matches 3 tiles of a sword the guy attacks, 3 keys and you can open chests and doors, 3 wood or stone and you get resources to upgrade later in the game. The game include upgrades, shops, potions, bosses, and a suprisingly big number of valuables (experience, wood, stone, points, and money).
Graphics/Sound:
The game originated on phones and tablets and you can definitely tell that by a lot of factors. First of all the graphics are in a very heavy and sometimes grating 8-bit style and the sounds and music are entirely in chiptunes. The chiptunes are not bad by any means, but they're put on a short loop and they can get rather repetitive and annoying. It's not a game that needs to be great looking or sound amazing. It does its job, with average success.
Gameplay:
This is a grinding puzzle game. The main point is to get as far as possible and then retry again and again, until you can buy more upgrades and get a little further into the game until you reach the target score. This is a slow moving process. There really isn't much progress in terms of mechanics. All mechanics of the game is presented in the first 30-45 minutes and then the question is if you actually want to continue doing the same thing for a few hours.
The main problem here, is that the game does a very poor job at spacing apart and adding game mechanics as you go along so everything feels fresh. This makes the game stagnate pretty quickly, and you get bored by it easily. You can only play this game in short bursts.
This game has two parts to it; the action-puzzle part, and the management/upgrade/RPG-ish part. The first part, is mostly pretty well executed. The tiles do what they do, and you can most of the time tell that a bad run was mostly because that you didn't do well. The game can be a bit unfair in the distribution of different tiles, giving you 3 key tiles in total, when you really need it, but other than that, the nature of the game makes it difficult enough to be challenging, but forgiving enough to not be frustrated.
The problems with the game originates from the second part, which is poorly executed. It has the growing of character RPG elements. You know, you start out as a weakling, but then you become stronger and stronger the more you play. Except that this game makes you not feel like progressing at all. It's hard to describe, but I got the same feeling out of playing Defiance. Despite constantly leveling up and progressing to the next level, and fighting tougher enemies and buying more upgrades and improving your various weaponry, it doesn't really feel like you're making a difference. Well, maybe a little, but 2 hours in the game, you don't feel that your character has gotten that much stronger since last. I speculate, that this is because that the core game (the tile game) does not become easier or harder, only the outcome becomes greater.
This, together with repetitious gameplay, makes the game stale after longer amounts of play.
Story:
This game does not really have a story, and for a game like this, it's fine without.
Replayability/Concept:
I really like the concept, and I feel that with a bit more tweaking and tuning this game could have been a lot more fun and a lot more addictive, which it isn't now, because of the repetitive nature of the game. There is also a bit of originality by this concept, mixing two genres together only really done well in PuzzleQuest.
Other than achievements, there is no real reason to start over and try again.
Length and fun factor:
To be honest, I haven't beaten it yet, but judging by where I am at right now, I estimate a total play time of 3-6 hours.
I find the core game (the tile puzzle game) to be very entertaining. It's hectic and it's stimulating, however it's hard finding joy in having to do this, let's be honest here, primitive game over and over again just to feel a bit of evolution and progress.
Final Thoughts and judgement:
If you are a big puzzle fan, especially of things like Chuzzle, PuzzleQuest, Bejeweled or even Candy Crush, and looking for a simple tile game with even simpler RPG elements over it, then this is recommendable. The puzzle aspect is fun, and if you're into that, the RPG part will not totally ruin it for you. For anyone else this is hard to recommend. For what it's worth I have found entertainment in this game, but some of the core aspects are flawed.
If you like puzzle games and you see this on a sale it couldn't hurt to get this (and therefore earning my thumbs up). There are just much better alternatives.

Surprisingly good tactic game (that, incedently, has nothing at all to do with Warhammer, as I originally thought). It scratched the same itch as the old Incubation: Time Is Running Out: a small squad of powerful soldiers against a endless flow of mindless, relatively weak enemies.
However, it's NOT a spiritual successor to Incubation we all are waiting for :) Templat Battleforce is somewhat simplier than Incubation, because of sameness of enemies: no need to attack from behind or only attack doing enemy's turn with Overwatch. Levels are less like puzzles where you have to get everything right to pass through, because turns limit is not hard (you get bonus for completing a level under turns limit, but you do not lose if you fail to do so).
On the other hand, many elements will be familiar to anyone who played Incubation: overheating and equipment points which limit how much things a soldier can carry, for example.
Unlike Incubation, soliders don't disappear here if they died during the mission, which makes it less painful to lose one. However, there are also no quicksave/quickload option during the battle (unless you revert to manual save-scumming, which I did at the very end of campaign), which makes longer levels a pain to replay.
Overall, I definitely recommend this game if you like tactic games, and especially if you liked Incubation.
I must also mention that this game is a surprising example of a well-made mobile port. Yes, everything is bigger-than-it-needs-to-be on PC screen, and there are some problems with mouse controls (mostly, scrolling; why was it impossible to implement hold-and-pan in battle, I can't righly imagine). But it doesn't cause much pain, and what's more important, the gameplay is NOT dumbed-down for mobiles (I guess the game is not a big hit in that market, however...).

10,000,000 is one of those rare games that tries to mix RPGs, autorunners, and puzzles.
It's one of the many that completely fails to be any good at all 3.
First, the RPG elements are clunky. They explain it once, but then give you little to no way to actually improve. You'll always fight monsters the same way with the same spells. And considering the barebones graphics, music, and the looming end, it adds virtually nothing to the gameplay other than an annoying distraction and an indicator of what you now need to match.
Secondly, the autorunning nature feels more like an arbitrary way to make it difficult without ever having to change anything on the field or in the game. A vague "end" keeps chasing you. When it reaches you or passes you or some other vague idea of "you reach it" that seems to change from game to game, you lose. Except you can keep matching for a few seconds.
And then there's the puzzle elements. They're, at best, clumsy. The game will not simply suggest a certain chain, it all but enforces it. See a skeleton? Get those staff and sword blocks. None of those? Fine, I GUESS get some resources. Oh there's a sword. Ignore that double/chained set, just get that sword or the looming end will get you! But that's not the worst of it. Oh no. The WORST of it, my friends, is that when you scroll it around the screen...it makes no difference if there are 3 blocks. They must be blocks that were initially placed in a way to complete a chain. If you scroll it around and there's 4 swords and you need four swords? Sorry, only the wood resource that had a 3 piece chain will count. Nothing else. This seems like a drastic oversight. Even the likes of Tetris Attack on the SNES would let you change blocks with no outcome, thus allowing a deeper gameplay. This offers no depth in that sense. It has to be already on screen, already apparent, and already set up.
All of this combines to create a tedious but inoffensive puzzle experience. But what makes it truly heinous is how many times you repeat a level to complete challenges to get resources to unlock do-Hold on, champ! You flawlessly performed all those tasks, but you need 500 wood and 500 stone for the next door! You only have 300 wood and 120 stones! Nope, get back to the time sink.
All in all, I cannot recommend 10,000,000. It is a clunky, rushed, and overall ugly game that seems to hope to garner more love off the Atari-era graphics than any actual quality or effort.

If what you're looking for is a poor man's Warhammer game, my friend, this is a destitute man's Warhammer game.
It's a rip-off of the IP from top to bottom, from the names of units to the tone of the dialogue.
But that's not even that big of a deal - if the Warhammer folks don't wanna sue, that's their business.
However, the slow (and dull) cut scenes, the tedious as Hell tutorial, and the constant random spawn of enemy units from the floor all around is just bad. It's bad and a lot of the levels are the result of bad game design.
You get these "protect the X" missions and the only thing difficult about them is whether or not an enemy randomly spawns near them - and whether or not it is ranged or melee. A ranged enemy unit can shoot past your front line and just take out whatever you're protecting. Mission over. Start over.
Oh, and there's no saving. So you can't protect yourself against ridiculous random spawns.
Which is really lovely because the tactical combat is (unederstandably) slow, but when combined with the slow dialogue and cut scenes, you're an hour or more into a level when a random spawn one-shots a mission objective and now you must start over completely.
I admire these kids (I assume they are kids, because I don't think any self-respecting adult would rip-off IP so blatantly and not be aware of the very basic concept of a save) for their work, but they have a long way to go.
It's a title you can safely buy on sale - a dollar or so won't hurt you - but you *will* lose an hour or two of your life to the design choices, so be aware.

You are Malcolm, a typically untypical metalhead. He loves beer, cones, blast beats and his best friend Ronnie (Beavis + Butthead + a beard), but he is into death metal more than death period. With the undead apocalypse well underway, we find him sitting in Ronnie's car as they drive into the night - my bad, the Eternal Foreboding Grimdark - until an unfortunate accident strands them at the foot of a building towards which all the zombies seem to be converging, and threatens to separate them for good. Fear not! Science will help them reunite, and they will forge the kind of bond you can only experience with someone when you have spent a lot of time near their soiled underwear.
Just don't call Ronnie a punk lest he bites you where it counts.
I was surprised to find a very traditional point'n'click experience in Metal Dead. I'm not sure what I expected from a cursory glance; some kind of retro indie shooter/platformer? This is straightforward, old-school adventurin'. My playtime reaches almost 6 hours and that barely includes any time for backtracking and aimless wandering, because I'm that good - and mostly because the puzzles are deceptively well-designed and the flow is logical all the way to the end, even when the environment opens up.
In a way I'm sorry I didn't have to resort to the hint system, which is highly original and fun in its implementation.
It wasn't 6 solid hours of play though, as I'm so metal that I went to cook dinner IN THE MIDDLE OF A DAMN ZOMBIE INVASION. A meat dinner, of course! I'm not a hippie! (although we should all become vegan unless we want to be turned into zombies someday)
Metal Dead is a solid game, with no padding or inventory overload - I believe the only item I had left at the end was a badass red guitar. I see another reviewer say he completed it in 90 minutes and is now going for a speedrun; which seems very feasible but I'm sorry to say it's playing this wrong, like run'n'gunning your way through Dishonored. You're here for the script: the narrative is pleasantly goofy and over-the-top (should I say brutal?) and almost every item interaction is dignified with its own silly line.
If like me you find the ending sad, get to the Walk Thru Walls Studio website and quench your manly tears while you watch the trailer for sequel Metal Dead: Encore!
tl;dr - if you're a metalhead, Metal Dead was made for you. If you're not - what are you then, a punk? What are you doing in this mosh pit? Go listen to Gouge's song
. That is all.

I did not know what to expect. A Hardcore Rythm based Roguelike? So I watched the trailer and got hooked. Then I got it and I am absolutely amazed.
the basic priciple is like a turn based roguelike - when you move the enemies move according to their pattern. You crawl through randomly generated floors, try to find a boss monster, kill it and find the exit to the next floor. But what sets this apart is the rythm component. Because you can only move on a beat of the background music. And every beat makes the enemies move as well.
The Pixel art, albeit simple looks amazing. the Music gets you pumped and theres allways something new to discover.
the Gameplay and Action itself is tight. As in, you could take it slow, but if you so much as miss a beat, your multiplicator gets reset. Which means less gold and probably less equipment in turn, so you have to keep the rythm, move every beat and make quick decisions. And if the song runs out, the floor is over.

the music, Kick♥♥♥♥♥ The way it should be for any rythm based game. But if you dont like it, you can use your own library to fill the floors with life.
the geme itself keeps you frustrated enough to make you wanna try again, because every enemy behaves in a certain way and you can train combat against them pretty early on - so if you die its because you got careless.
oh, and the shopkeepers voice is divine. Get the Soundtrach edition if you can.

Dark Crusade sets you in the over-the-top-ridiculousness that is Dawn of War. The Campaign is narrated by one of the most coolest narrators I've ever listened to. I'd look up his name for this review, but it's 5am.
As you begin and end your campaign your adventers will be narrated in an epic voice, and you can immerse yourself into the world of Dawn of War. The cutscenes are whimsical and magical in a way I can't describe, like with the Orks, and the Necrons, the game presents itself with a certain type of charm that I can't forget. Dawn of War 2 didn't give me the same kind of character and gameplay that this game delivers. Dawn of War - Dark Crusade brings you on an epic adventure, to an epic Campaign. The game's narrator makes your actions feel truly noble, brutal, or just downright awesome. The gameplay can't be compared to something like starcraft or command&conquer, it is a truly unique way of presenting RTS with requisition and relic resources. It's simple, makes some sense, and effective.
The gameplay itself centers it's focus on your units and their various personalities. Like with the Imperial Officers shooting their own soldiers to gain morale, or the awesome Necrons and their units. The game's Campaign is just fantastic and epic, with a charisma that is almost on par with the Disney movies, but for gamers who love Dawn of War. Dawn of War-Dark Crusade, a game I can't forget.

When I first got this game, I decided to mark it as recommended. It did seem fun, and I was blinded by the hype. I will say, now, that it
a fun game if you want to kill a ton of people in scenic 1968 New Orleans, but it is no Mafia game. A Mafia game has an intricate story and fantastic gameplay. This has.. neither. The story is pretty bland until the very end, and everything is black and white. The missions are worse. They're repetitive to no end. After you've played for a couple hours, you'll have noticed that for each district you take, there are three types of missions:
1. Break into warehouse, kill everyone, steal vehicle
2. Break into warehouse, kill everyone, interrogate man
3. Break into warehouse, kill everyone, destroy the marked crates
These missions are the vast majority of the game. Aside from these, there are side quests which you can do for your underbosses. These include:
1. Break into warehouse, kill everyone, steal vehicle
2. Find vehicle, steal vehicle
3. Break into warehouse, kill everyone, kill someone else

Yes, the art is a matter of taste in it's Avatar-like western manga-style and if you truely cannot handle this or anthropomorphic characters, you either have to get over it or deny yourself one of the single best action platform brawler RPGs for PC.

I was in a mood for strategy and blowing things up one day. I found this game while I was cruising through my queue and pretty much bought it impulsively. How'd that turn out? Surprisingly well. While I haven't gotten too far into the game yet, it did provide me with some inspiration to start a Let's Play of something that wasn't a dating sim. (And the dating sim Let's Play didn't even begin that long ago either.)
The thing about this game that may either attract or repel you is that it is heavily reliant on dice rolls.
With each attack, dodge, and parry, many dice get rolled under the hood. This part of the system relies on comparing successes, similar to how contested rolls work in Classic World of Darkness games. Certain dice are more likely to score successes, which are called Strong Dice. The other dice are Standard Dice.
Blocks, deflections, and critical hits function on a percentile system, where rolling under a certain number blocks damage, automatically deducts half of your armor from the damage incoming (in the case of deflection), or causes a critical hit.
Damage, however, functions pretty differently than what you'd expect. While I could explain it, it can be pretty complicated mathematically, but the short version is that the attacker has an equal chance to roll any particular number in a given damage range (26-50, for example) and the target has a few factors that reduce damage, some of which function similarly to how one generates damage rolls.
I got this game not too long after it came out of Early Access. I went into this blindly, although I had the urge to play some kind of strategy game that wasn't the ones I had been playng for years (various hacks for Shining Force games, Vandal Hearts 1 and 2, a couple others) and wanted to do something involving a sci-fi setting. After looking up some games, Templar Battleforce caught my attention as it was on sale at the time and it had generally positive reviews. So I got it.
It took me a while to get used to the mechanics of moving around, the order of operations during a turn (AP usage also uses MP, but not vice versa), the concept of heat (well, it makes sense to me at least), and trying (and failing a lot of the time) to master the art of stealth. After learning all of that, the game works pretty solidly. There are times where I do dumb things (I was recording a second video of an Ironman playthrough, but derped for a moment and closed one of my templars in airlock doors and killed him
), but for some of my riskiest actions, I do well. And it's rewarding when that happens.
Upsides of this game include many diffculty settings to play on (my playthrough is on Normal, the next to easiest setting, although I've been going through a save that's on Brutal, which is three steps above Normal, and there's three more difficulties after Brutal), a pretty good variety of classes to use for the composition of your squad (I'm finding myself tending towards the use of
, who burns every last alien, alien lover, and alien monstrosity they see
... Oh, sorry, 40k flashbacks), and some interesting lore.
Downsides of this game include the lack of mod support (which, while the developers are working on it, may be a long shot at getting it to happen), some of the classes perhap feeling underwhelming for a good while until you progress far enough into the game (I'm looking at you,
), and RNG-sus occasionally laughing in your face and smacking you with massive damage and critical misses (just misses that happen when you need that one hit to either kill the alien or alien lover or to stop them in their tracks
... not the 40k spasms again).
I'm nearing what I think is the end of the game, before New Game+. A good number of updates have arrived since the last time I touched this review (as of this writing, Update #62 just came out), and I think I should cover some of those.
A few new enemy types have been introduced. While I have yet to go back through levels with humans and seeing the new human enemy types, I've dealt with a good chunk of new aliens of the type that I wrote of previously. I'm just now coming across the Narvidian menace, so my experience with them is limited enough for me to not really know the difference unless another type of Narvidian is introduced. With that said, the new types are nice to see.
Along with new enemy types, we've also gained new options for our Templars. Engineers can use equipment specialized for burninating the countryside
(ah, sorry, old Internet things) such as flame turrets and flamer pistols. Hydras can use the special flame tank armor that engineers can use to further increase their fire damage. Berserks can now dual-wield axes to decimate foes (running around with axes that bypass a lot of armor is nice offensively, but not the best defensively). Paladins can use big two-handed shock hammers, which I've found quite fun for smiting a lot of foes.
Neptunes... well, they've been improved in that the Overwatch abilities between Soldiers and Neptunes now differ, and that their weapons tend to have higher armor piercing capability. With that said, they're still a little behind, but they'll be caught up at some point after the enemy updates are done.
In addition to modifying the units, some map changes have been done too. I have yet to see the new versions of the maps that were affected (or at least, that I notice), but it's good to know. Also, UI changes have been made to make things more convenient.
Overall, I give this game a 9/10 for fans of the genre. It's pretty well-assembled, and updates to the game are free and plentiful. Enemies are just as plentiful as the sand. Also, there's Space Hulk vibes somewhere. Vae Victus!

Developers clearly put a lot of heart into this game.
Lets start with the least remarkable part (in my opinion): graphics are functional and not much more, they're expressive anyway. This way, at least you don't need a big computer to run the game).  The story exudes atmosphere, it's basic but well told and the ambiance is well-supported by the graphics. (it will remind you quite a lot of another well-known game universe, though, you see what I mean)...
Everything is well-polished. The user interface is very usable, there are convenient keyboard shortcuts for everything that you'll need to use often and they come handy in most situations, saving time with the trivial things so you can focus on the heart of the game: the turn-by-turn tactic, and the composition, leveling and specialization of a force that will suit your play style.  And there are often several ways to tackle most problems, depending on the composition of your force and your favorite ways to deal with those problems.
There is a HUGE skill tree, it will take a lot of runs through the game to explore it all. There are many stats/skills/talents/classes that can be combined to produce nearly endless different results. Pick your favorite, make it work (it will take some adjustments here and there), and win the game with it. Rince and repeat.
The "normal" difficulty is a bit on the easy side. You're never really threatened by xenos in this difficulty. People who're used to tactic games should use "demanding" or more difficulty.

Enjoyed the game, and got exactly what I asked for. Upon checking the store page I thought -- "This looks like a funny, tounge-in-cheek, point/click zombie adventure game." -- and that's what it is. Neither mind-numbingly hard nor vapidly easy (actually quite 'goldilocks just-right' in the difficulty department), the game doesn't revolutionized the genre or anything but it DOES tell a fun and interesting story, and for something so low-frills actually has some interesting characters. I didn't expect much, but my expectations were well exceeded. Only took me a couple of sessions to finish it, but I have no regrets -- I've been burned on steam before by games promising retro-thrills and substance over style -- this is not one of those games. It stands well on it's strengths and delivers on it's promises. It was fun, interesting, and a good "candy" play -- a puzzle game for a relaxed sunday where you won't need a walkthrough, just a little focus and dedication to get the job done. I wish more games like this would get made - value titles that are like the free-fare on newgrounds, but cranked a little further, a little longer, and a little better. No regrets. Would play the sequel! <3

Okay i know your thinking, "This game looks like a something rip straight out of newgrounds"
And yes, Graphically it looks rough. (Runs pretty rough too)
But that's also what makes this game stand out from the many point and click adventure available.
Why, You may (Or may not) ask? Well well aren't we a curious one:)
Let me explain.
It's quite simple really, It's a 90's adventure game, Made today.
(Well not today but you get my point)
Everything from, How it looks, How it sound.(Synth music at it's fineist:) How it acts, How it feels, (How it runs)
The game is as old fashioned, As it looks. And that's why it's such a good game.
The writing is generally funny, And really well writen.
The characters especially malcolm and rodney, Are a generally likable bunch.
(A few horror stereotype as well)
The game's puzzle are logical, And doesn't fill your inventory full of useless items.
(Which is nice.)
The game leads you in the right direction without being patronising. (Which is a feat in it's self:)
It last's about four, Five hours.
And their's not much backtracking.
So you won't be going back to Previous areas clicking on everything to find your way forward.
(Well not much anyway:)
So quick summary. If you love, And i do mean LOVE ye olde adventure games.
I could not recommend this enough.
If you don't, This game REALLY won't convince you.
But if your interested in, Giving the point and click adventure a go.
I can not think of a better (Or cheaper) game then this:)

Fast paced, sadistic, cruel and unforgiving is this game.  And it's AMAZING!!  Played this first on my friend's computer and I've loved it so much I had to get it for myself.
Pros:
The gameplay is insanely fast, killing, running and even dying and respawning all happens with a blink of an eye.
If you like harsh and cruel games, this has that.
The music is amazing!  That combined with the gameplay do a good job at keeping your spirit high and blood rushed even after failing.
A lot of replayability with new weaponry and masks which grant new abilities.
If you like difficulty, then you'll enjoy this.
Levels are complex enough to make you think, even get a little mad every now and then.  But never enough to smash the keyboard.
Cons:
Pretty much no ability to change controls, specifically the mouse sensativity.  As the crosshairs move away from the character they move slower, so learning to keep them right by you all the time, and dying from not being able to move the mouse fast enough is a serious problem when starting the game.  Died more than a few times from this, very very aggravating.
The game is very unforgiving, I like it a lot, but many people don't.  You will have times where the very last enemy in a massive complex is the one to kill you only to restart completly.  If you don't handle difficulty well, then this will be rage-inducing.
The game lacks in story, in attempt to keep things ambigious and secret, it also comes off as just being lazy.  But I'm not really here for the story.
Honestly this game is a nice little gem, and it's worth the full cost and a steal on any sale.

And it's like, how much more niche can you get?  The answer is none.  None more niche.
Seriously though, this is a pretty fun roguelike.  It gives me the same vibe as One Way Heroics, even though their gameplay is fundamentally opposed: They both add an element of tension that isn't present in normal roguelikes.  In the case of Crypt of the NecroDancer it's a very frantic tension, which makes it hard to play for long stretches at a time but I'm really enjoying it when I do play.  Ideal coffee break game, each run is nice and short.
Replayability is similar to Spelunky: It's very challenging as you play through it, but I'm not sure how much I will feel like replaying it once I'm finally through.  Various things to unlock along the way though.  Playing with the different weapon types is a lot of fun, it feels more visceral than most roguelikes and that's very satisfying.
The music is addictive.  There's a mode that lets you play it with a dance pad, too, and I'm really looking forwards to that--will update this review when my new dance pads (with official Crypt of the NecroDancer art from
arrive in a month.

Here is what it comes down to: I honestly think people are being unfair in their reviews.

I have tried so many F2P games on steam, and never been hooked as much as I have with this game. You can hop on a off mutiple times a day, complete your daily quest, and just leave it for a couple day and come back. Matchmaking is a work of art, I never have to wait more than 20 seconds for a game. The community (so far) is welcoming, chatty and helpful.
IMO, this is the best F2P game of 2016 so far... please try it and don't let negative reviews drive you away.

The story is pretty decent, even though the big twist is not a twist since it's been known before the game came out. The setting is beautiful, and the soundtrack is just what you should expect from a game set in the 60's. The frame cap has been removed and the game looks great, a lot of bugs have been fixed, and it has been getting a few free DLC here and there such as the outfits and racing updates.
Would I recommend this game for $60? No. $40? Only if you really want it. $20 - $30 would be a good price for this game. Wait for steam summer sales.

This is a decent turn-based strategy game.  Stylistically it's a mix of WH40K and Incubation, with powered armor and an endless stream of bugs coming to get you.
The game biggest fault is what some would consider a feature: it loves to throw numbers at you.  One of the very first screens you see is the difficulty screen, which offers 7 different levels, expressing each as a collection of levels and percentages.  If something attacks you, the computer will consider your dodge, block, parry, armor strength, deflection, and "damage soak" when determining if and how badly you're hit.  And there's flames, plasma, and bio-poison too.
Consider the character screen: one of the 7 sections on the character sheet reads: "Melee Defense = 16 strong + 9 standard :: Weapon/Shield Parry (4s) + Warrior (12s) + Armor Evade (0) + Evasion (8) + Parry Bonus(1)".
All of these mechanics make the game muddled and uncertain, not deeper.  It's explained in the "library", but why bury the player in numbers when it just boils down to "more is better"?
The UI is generally clean, though there are some questionable choices.  For example, you can respec your soldiers at any time, by resetting them to base stats.  It would have been easier to work with "+" and "-" buttons instead of "+" and "reset".  The equipment screens have you choose between "what you can equip now" and "what you could equip someday", which makes it awkward to compare what you have with what's available if you spend "requisition points".  (Should flip between "equip now" and everything, with the "available someday" in a different color scheme.)
The graphics are decent, though sometimes it's hard to tell which squares are open, which are walls, and which are obstacles that can be fired over but not moved through.
The separation of "movement points" and "action points" is an interesting idea.  By encouraging move-then-shoot, you have to think a bit more about how far to move.
The AoE damage is a bit dodgy, as it's not always clear which cells will be affected by attacks at certain angles.  Some sort of attack overlay would have been useful.
Despite its shortcomings I had fun playing it, so I'm giving it a thumbs-up.

10/10 highly recommend this game.

This game is a sweet mix of character persistance and squad tactics.
Unlike a lot of other tactics games, this one lets you respec your characters whenever, and has no scarcity of items, not considering unique relics. This works due to character's item level, which restricts the total quality of items a character can use. and the requisition tree. The requisition tree works like a tech tree that you branch throughout the campaign, and it determines what classes you have, what items you have, what skills are available, and the max trainable skill levels. I really enjoy repsecing my characters to try out different tactics and builds. Additionally, the gameplay works in such a way that you are rewarded for splitting up your squad into smaller groups to explore. For some reason, I love this, and it's something you are usually heavily penalized for doing in other squad tactic games. Also, the levels are large, and kind of remind me of story tactic games rather than one-of team deathmatch style tactic games.

The first time I played this game, I said to myself, "What the hell is that music?".  The main soundtrack of the game is a heavy metal low-fidelity music that sounded like crap.  But don't press the exit button just yet.  Wait until you click on the characters and read their dialogues.  It will really crack you up.
The game's primary saving grace were the characters in this game because they were so funny and witty.  There are no sounds when they speak though,  it is only text-based.  There are tons of jokes here with a lot of pop culture and movie references.
Another wrong impression I made about the game was that, I thought it would be another generic zombie game, but this is definitely not.  It gives us a unique twist on how the zombie plague occured.  It was not viral but something else.  Got you interested yet?
I'm very proud of indiegame developers who hit the mark when it comes to game development.  Kudos to you Walk Thru Walls Studios.
The main character that you play is a true die hard heavy metal music fan.  But for a metal head slacker, he is quite a smart aleck and knows a lot of scientific sheet and stuff.
The game is a typical point and click adventure game.  You get your usual dose of of puzzles to solve with a "CLEVER" hint system when you get stuck and don't know what to do.  Your ultimate objective is to escape the building you are trapped-in and to survive the zombie horde trying to enter the premises.  The game has a great and surprising ending, you'll see.
In conclusion, the graphics are adequate and unique, the sound is terrible and low quality, the gameplay is a lot of fun and the story is unlike anything else.  I recommend this game.  You won't regret it.
Note:  I nominated this game for "The I thought This Game Was Cool Before it Won An Award" during the Autumn Sale 2016

This has got to be one of the most boring and most disjointed games I have never had the pleasure to play.
This game has recently had a name change, for the second time, because for some reason these developers change the ♥♥♥♥ing name of their game whenever they release a "big update". This game was and still is a buggy pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥since launch and despite these "big updates" the bugs remain. First time they changed the name, they didn't fix anything... They just added a microtransaction store. Because they changed the name it caused a lot of bugs with Steam and it brought the game back on the front page of the Steam store and it did NOT deserve it. And now they did the same♥♥♥♥♥♥but it didn't seem to break the Steam Store like last time; No, all this update added was some hats, controller support (which by the way made it so that it only shows the Xbox controller buttons in the main menu, well done guys), and some game modes. I didn't even bother to play any of the other game modes after seeing how godawful their MAIN gamemode is.
So what actually is Orion Dino Beatdown/Horde/Prelude you ask? Well, it's a horde mode game involving dinosaurs. A fairly simple concept: there are waves, there are enemies, you kill enemies, progress through the waves and so it goes on. But the presentation and gameplay are so horrible that it doesn't work right (which is probably why they added the other game modes to make up for the garbage that they have created).
Presentation: This game looks hideous, even for an Unreal Engine 3 game, and it runs terribly dispite how bad it looks. I had to lower all the settings down to get a decent framerate and the game definitely does not look good enough to justify it. And it appears that they added a disgusting cell shaded look that just seems completely out of place recently, weird black outlines on some places. Besides graphics, the animations are atrocious and the modeling on the guns look pathetic, the sound design is just bad, many of the guns feel weak as a result of having poor animations and sound quality. ♥♥♥♥ing magnums should not sound like BB guns. The dinosaurs look alright, decent enough modeling and sound design... Until they attack you with their adorable little nibbling animations, making them look completely unthreatening. Yeah, this game doesn't look good at all.
But ok, graphics aren't important, gameplay is what matters in a game, right? Of course, only one problem, THIS GAME IS HORRIBLE! The gameplay is so bland and generic, it has nothing original about it, it only takes game mechanics from other games, and the mechanics that it takes it doesn't do as well as where they were originally taken from. I mentioned before how the guns feel weak, and they really do. Nothing has any of the OOMPH you would otherwise see in  a competent FPS. This game's gunplay is almost as bad as Borderlands', and the guns themselves are completely uninteresting. There's very little variety in the enemies and it gets boring to fight the same dinosaurs REALLY FAST. So the gameplay is also a failure here.
So it looks bad, sounds bad and plays bad. Is there any point in getting this game? Absolutely not. It's not even so bad that it's funny, it's just awful, it isn't even worth the $1. If you want to play a good horde mode game, I highly suggest Killing Floor, it does everything right where Orion does wrong. I decided to write this review now because it seems like the developers are trying to squeeze out every little bit that they can from this game and it's just depressing to see. It feels like they really tried their best here but this just doesn't work. Guys, this game is not good, you have to move on, from here you have two choices: You either realise that game development isn't your thing, or you improve upon what you did here and take note of your mistakes. Either way, let go of this game and focus on stuff you really want to do, rather than just change the game's name multiple times and milk the ever living♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it.

There is some overabundance of gore and disgusting scenes, but Metal Dead is a solid voiceless indie point ‘n’ click title that thankfully doesn’t take itself even the least bit serious.
If you are the kind of person who likes horror comedies which are full of guts and blood (and faecal matter), but don’t take themselves seriously, then you will like Metal Dead.
As a low-budget game it doesn’t have any voice acting, and the animation is quite crude. It focuses on the story instead, which is a standard zombie survival scenario, where you and a bunch of other people are trapped in a building (this time a hospital) and try to escape before the undead overrun you.
Many indie adventure games tend to have problems with puzzles that are either way too obvious or just insanely overcomplicated. Although Metal Dead has parts which need some luck or trial and error (which is a little awkward thanks to the not too user friendly interface), it’s almost impossible to get hopelessly stuck.
In essence, it may be like a Flash game with a price tag attached to it, but it’s enjoyable and fairly long for that price.

Very rarely do I "want" to like a game more than I do this one. The style's fun, matching games in general are addictive, and I really do want to keep progressing. But the balance feels wrong and much more often than not the game really frustrates someone just looking for a good time. It's a matching game but if you're not matching the blocks you're supposed to be matching to defeat a monster or unlock a chest or whatever the game is throwing at you, then you die. And you die pretty quickly at that. You can go from full health on a great run to dead in just a few seconds if you haven't matched the tiles that you need. Most of the time you can't find the blocks you need at any given moment, without having cleared other tiles first. The game simply has one block type too many obstructing combo flow. Two of the seven block types have no function in the dungeon crawl except to impede your progress, at any given enemy encounter only two of the blocks might be useful to you. With less than half of the screen being useful and enemies eating your time you'll frequently die in less time it takes to read this review.
It wouldn't be so bad if it gave you more time to plan combo chains. Or maybe you could stockpile matched blocks so that items like keys would stay in your invetory for unlocking doors and chests. Instead you can only match blocks at the moment you need them with previous matches disappearing uselessly. Mind you, it has to be at the very moment you need them, if you make the match too fast before the character runs up to the encounter, it also doesn't count wasting valuable blocks.
If you somehow ended up becoming a master genius at the game, or if you've grinded enough hours to buy enough perks, it could be great. But the early stages are just no fun and only succeeded in frustrating me. After a while I lose interest in mastery. The game just feels too unfair.

This game earns an "A" for being a clever blend of genres, but a "D" by poorly balancing them it makes the game repetitive, unrewarding, and leaving the player wanting for more.
It is a really great concept and fun to play at first. If it was play tested to adjust the poor "grinding" curves, it could be an addictive smash hit.
Problems and improvements:
1. Resorces... The game has a great concept with harvesting materials to unlock new "shops" to upgrade your character, but wood/stone become obsolete as soon as these shops are all open (which can be done in the first couple hours of game play). Even worse are "Experience Points", which are only spendable at one store. You quickly buy all these upgrades in the first couple hours of gameplay, leaving you a lot of game play earning useless points with nothing to spend them on. Gold is the last to go. After you spend gold upgrading everything to its max, you find that you can't upgrade any farther, and you're still only in the first half of the game.
- To fix this, the game needs more options for upgrades with a better price curve to make sure there is always something more to buy or upgrade. The game should be complete or close to completion before you run out of upgrade options in any rpg.
2. Effectiveness... Upgrades, even when all are purchased in the first half of the game, do not do enough to make your character feel more powerful or effective. Grinding for upgrades is hard enough, but these upgrades should make even the worst player more effective at the game.
Items, if used too early, will be wasted (The same goes for matches that are lined up too early). This is counter-intuitive, since every second counts. When approaching an enemy or chest, it would be great if your continuing multi-combo or clicked item was aimed at them instead of simply lost. Also, while just 4 keys in a row will take care of 2 locks, 4, 5, or more staff/sword tiles do little more than 3 against enemies.
3. The Clock... The clock is also your health bar, which is fine and the shield idea makes it work well enough. However, there is far too much working against the clock and not enough helping it. You only gain a small amount of time back after defeating an enemy or unlocking a door/chest (or matching wood/stone with an upgrade), there is a lot that wastes time like combos, which continue to fire off leaving you helpless to act until they are done. These combos, while sometimes helpful, usually just eat time and give little back outside score (which is really only helpful in reaching the overall 10,000,000 to beat the game. Keep in mind, score is NOT cumulative, and is only there to let you know how close you are to getting to the end of the game). Chain combos and 4+ matches should offer a small time bonus as well.
4. Luck factor. I have no problem with the Critical hit probability, but the luck of having the right combination of tiles in anything close to the right order to get what you need to match up in time is very random. I've had great runs where I've just had great luck, and blaze through every obstacle, and I've had luck where I lose on the first enemy due to this.
5. Gear... There are unlockable potions you an use to trade one thing for another (i.e. 20% of wood/stone earned becomes gold but you earn 0 wood/stone ). These can be turned on and off. The rest of the gear, although upgradable, has no options like many RPGs do. It would be nice if you could buy upgrades for gear, but also swap them out for different effects (i.e. a staff that uses Freeze when it crits, or armor that has a lower effects against close range enemies but blocks ranged attacks, etc.).
6. Curve... It could use a difficulty setting. Even if that meant just adjusting time limit, damage effects, etc.
Not just that, the overall "Grinding" takes the fun out of the game.
Final Verdict:
- It's not worth $5. I got my copy on sale for $1 and had cash in my steam wallet from selling trading cards, so... it was basically "free". I wouldn't suggest it for retail price.
- If it had the above adjustments made, It would be worth the $5, maybe even $10.
- While it has great roots, and is technically a finished game, it really lacks the polish to make it feel like more than a "free to play" you'd find on NewGrounds.

And it's like, how much more niche can you get?  The answer is none.  None more niche.
