Players are bullet spongey, but nearly any gun can kill with a head shot. the knife has an odd range, so it's possible to feel like you were stabbed from 10 feet away. Worse off, many servers are "ruined" by hackers who can instant kill the entire team from safety or glitch outside the map. I put ruined in quotes, because Warmode is already bad, so it's impossible to care, especially when I can jump to another server. If you're decent at shooters, you can learn the "feel and mechanics" of the gunplay and get to the point where you dominate the leaderboard. Warmode is terrible, and it is so janky that it ends up funny and somewhat enjoyable (only if because it's a game I'm kinda good at, not that I should be proud of that). I've spent many hours cracking up at the nonsense of people running around with knives, or people apparently having no idea that I'm shooting at them.

As a geek one of my favorite movies is WarGames where a hacker breaks into a military computer and starts playing a game of global thermal nuclear war with a advanced AI computer that the computer later trys to make real.
Well DEFCON is that game.
The game was a really simple premise pick a side at the start and progress through the defcon levels setting up for when defcon 1 is reached and nuclear fallout begins.
Defcon 5 is were players start setting up radar, bases, silos, airfields, and the naval fleet. Defcon 4 the radar starts to work. At Defcon 3 players can't build anymore but by then they should be trying to explore a little with the navy and find out the best places to attack when Defcon 1 is reached and players can finally deploy nukes. Single player Defcon gets really old fast but playing multiplayer can be really fun as players can make alliances with friends and attack their enemies together or turn on one another in the midst of conflict.
Multiplayer also has some great alternatives to play like Office mode where the game is played in real time so it can take 6+ hours to finish and also if the player need to hide the game from the boss they just need to press Esc and the game is minimized and a word document is opened. Speed mode is what is sounds like as the game can finish in under 30 minutes and Diplomacy mode is where all players are on the same team and can see everything until one breaks off and attacks.
Graphics are minimal but really stylish in bringing a real life WarGame game.
Sound is really simple and subtle that is makes you feel like the player isn't really playing game but playing real nuclear war.
Overall the game is really good and can be found for under $20 some places so it's also a great buy.

Pros:
Music
Detailed open world, with nice little touch like garbage piles, the bayou, sewer system, etc
Nice cars from the 1960-70s
Compelling Story
New strategic gameplay
Cons:
Repetitive gameplay mechanics
Plot-advancing mechanics that destroys gameplay suspense
AI glitch
Quest glitch
Numerous other physics bugs, I often restart my game because of missing objectives (e.g. suspended-in-the-air heist boat, unobtainable fuses/posters/magazines)
Open world public services that are just beyond logic
Cops that just police gun usage
Too many cutscenes ruin gameplay continuity
The game simply started right, with very compelling story that drives you further, putting you in Lincoln Clay's place. But like most of franchise title, the mechanics went for dumbing down, while the story improves.
Gameplay mechanics:
Planning to get away after a hit mission on hostile mobster? Don't bother, cutscene right back to your safehouse will save you all the tense. Driving back to your headquarters after a mission? Nope, instant cutscenes will take you back. Worrying about cops after a furious gunfights? Don't, because the cops are insanely incompetent. Running over red lights? Walking cops do nothing. Injure a pedestrian? Nothing. This New Bordeaux is consequent-less.
Driving mechanics:
Gone are the speed control, which allows you to just roam freely without attracting too much attention, enjoying the radio playlists and listening to bits of interesting mood from that era. Lincoln's default and only driving mode is full throttle mashing and 11 longest skid marks leaving contest. Thankfully, the residents and authorities of new Bordeaux are fine with it. Then, the traffic AI is also annoying as hell at junctions and intersections. Mafia II improves a lot from Mafia I, but Mafia III is probably the worst.
Shoot-out mechanics:
The game has always been a 3rd person shooter, and this one feels the most natural, yet it is too easy. Any FPS veterans shouldn't bother starting with the medium difficulty.
All in all, this is a beautiful game that is marred with too many annoying problems. It seems like too much focus was given to its content. You can now explore many of the buildings in the open world, its back alleys, even goes inside it, or just stroll around the sidewalks of the beautifully modelled house that is just like the real-life French Quarters. This kind of openess doesn't exist back in the previous 2 Mafia games. Less effort was given to test play this game, because the game difficulty is for 3-10 years old, despite featuring Mature content. And also the persisting annoying AI and glitches. I bought this game at a discount, so yes. I'm not sure about the full price just for looking around the crime-ridden New Orleans' virtual counterpart.

The lesson to be learnt from Natural Selection 2 is that good Management is essential.
Especially for a multiplayer only game.
One cannot create a wonderfull, near flawless game then leave it or mismanaged it and expect no fallout.
Although Unknown Worlds Entertainment are very talented and hard working creators they are poor managers.
It is true that Natural Selection 2 is a very unique game with unique problems, but since the launch of this game up until now and also predictably in the future this game was and is being mismanaged and as such has been ruined to the point of no return.
Players have been leaving from the start because of the game changing too much in the wrong direction more and more.
The players leaving was just met with ignorance and intolerance towards their reasons for leaving and so the game and its community which can be treated as one and the same for a multiplayer only game became unstable with very large skill gaps in players since the bulk of the players left.
The community also turned hostile as members fought aggressively over changes that were made to please only one group of players the "professional bracket" which was and still is the smallest and the least important.
This is because proffessionals only play if you pay them.
You have to hand over a very large cash prize at a reliable rate if you want to encourage enough competitive play that will draw in attention which you then can sell. This is a large and complex business model which is why large companies can simply afford to do it.
The larger "casual bracket" was discarded as the unimportant bracket since the professional scene was and is UWE's goal.
Ironically the more important bracket was and still is the "casual bracket" because, more people have more money. This game is not free. The more players you have the more money you will have.
You only have to look at this game's history of decline to know that your time and money is better spent elsewhere.
Most of the players have left and servers have been shut down.
UWE is not concerned as their efforts and resources are fully directed at Subnautica since it is doing very well.

All in all, I think Orcs Must Die! Unchained is a great game!
Short Review:
Has a nice concept, and a well enough execution. Obviously still needs more polish and balancing, but it is still in the Beta stage. It still has a feel of the previous game while bringing a new playing experience. It requires strategy and thinking. The new characters also add more to the game, and are relatively balanced. NOT OMD 3.
7/10, definitely recommended.
Long Review:
I know it gets a lot of hate, and I completely understand why. People were expecting an Orcs Must Die! 3, and this is what they got. If that's  what you are looking for, you won't find it here. It is definitely not an Orcs Must Die! 3. But it was NEVER meant to be an OMD 3. Robot Entertainment wanted to bring something new to the table instead of another recreation of the fantastic previous games. Not saying an OMD 3 wouldn't be awesome, but let's be honest, it was bound to get old.
So instead, they made this. A game that was supposed to have a feel of the previous games while bringing something completely new and different. And in my opinion, they did it well! OMDU definitely still fits in the OMD franchise, with the trademark mobs and traps. But it also integrates an entirely new mechanic; a PVP gamemode. A lot of people have problems with the PVP mode. So I'm going to try my best to explain why I think that the problems really aren't that bad.
A lot complain about the pay to win aspect. But come on, let's be real; it is a free to play MOBA game, and the devs have to eat too. So they have to make tempting deals in the game that cost real money. But here's the thing: it's not that bad. It really isn't. It doesn't disturb the fun of the game by much. So far I haven't encountered any game breakingly over powered opponents. Of course there was that time when I got repeatedly chain killed, and that time my team lost in the first five minutes. But that doesn't happen often at all. As long as you play well (unlike me), and have a team that aren't complete trolls, you'll do fine. You will find players that are better than you, but come on, you don't have to be the best player in town right? It is after all an online game, and there will always be that guy that gets 10.000 kills in ten seconds or something like that.
And then there is the grindy aspect and how long it takes to level characters, traps, make upgrades, etc. Again, it is a MOBA. It is meant to be a game that is played for an indefinite amount of time. The previous games can be finished in a week or even much less (three days or so). As a result, the game provides you with various traps and quick progress. Imagine if that happened to this game. You play for three days, and you get all the cool traps and the powerful weapons. The new players would be decimated and have no chance. Then you'd enter a game against a guy who's been playing for a month. He snaps his fingers and he wins the game instantly. The long and slow leveling is necessary for a more balanced experience. It stops the game from getting boring too quickly. As you have no levels to complete, your motivation is to get better things an upgrades. If you get them so soon, what would be your motivation to keep playing?
The last problem I am going to address is how the traps aren't as effective as before. This aspect is to be expected, and while slightly unfortunate, is crucial to the balance of the game. In the previous games, the traps are really effective because there is only one idiot blundering about with his crossbow and blunderbuss, and God knows he needs all the help he can get. In OMDU, there are five idiots blundering about. If your traps just kill everything, both teams won't make progress. And it will be boring for you because there will be no challenge. You'll just be sitting ducks watching orcs pop and explode. The traps need to be nerfed so that you actually have to get in there and do something about the onslaught of orcs. That being said, traps are still very helpful and still very satisfying. In fact, it is almost guaranteed you cannot win without a decent setup of traps.
And yes, this is admittedly a lot different than the previous games. I'm not gonna sugar coat it. It was suprising and shocking, and certainly not the sequel I anticipated. But while it is not an exact replica of OMD, it is still a good game. I will not condemn a good game and not recommend it simply because it does not fulfill my personal expectations, because I don't like the company who made it, or because it doesn't replicate previous games from its franchise entirely. And a point I have to make, is that Siege (PvP) is only ONE of the gamemodes. You can also play the more classic Survival (PvE) mode, where you just fight against orcs. Personally though I like PvP better because it is more difficult as you have to counter another team's strategy instead of simply butchering countless hordes of orcs.
This game is challenging, and it requires strategy. The new set of characters also bring a nice change of pace. Of course, this game still requires more polishing, development, and balancing. But again, it is still in Beta, so I don't judge some of the lacking aspects too harshly.
Of course, this one hour essay will not be as good as experience. So really, I urge you to get it. Play and see if it is to your liking. If you don't like it, just uninstall it. It IS free. RECOMMENDED.

The Hive is a fun strategy game where you control The Hive and your Insectoid units and destroy the opposition you will face. I will add a TL;DR at the end.
You start off with a single worker and must build a Hive (your primary building) which allows you to construct more workers, a hive queen and eventually a medic. You will need to gather food to allow you to build more units. You must then construct a barracks to get your first fighting units; one melee, and one ranged. The melee unit comes in a pack of 6 while the ranged comes in a pack of 4. Resources are what allow you to build these building however food is vital. The game is nice but the camera controls seems off to me. The RPG aspect that the developer has added is fun but still unrefined along with the DNA aspect as we are never formally introduced with the features as of yet. On Act 4 the difficulty curve is immense right now and It is hard to beat as your enemies clearly outnumber you and are quick to strike in force. However, from what I know the developer is planning to add a turret type building and I can see the potential for this game.
The graphics are nice and I do like how the Hive and the units are designed and displayed. I do wish that the enemies exact attack or amount of health would be displayed if possible. The scenery is nice to look at and the music is well-done.

Aragami is a stealth game in which you play as Aragami (the title is a real brain-twister, I know...), a vengeful spirit summoned by a mysterious white-haired lady called Yamiko to carry out her revenge against the Light Adepts for slaughtering the entire population of the shadow people, of which she was part. Now you are given the tools to use the shadow essence to find the talismans that are keeping the seal on the Shadow Empress, so she can be free again and thus fulfill Yakimo's thrist for vengeance. Whether you also proceed to meticously murder every single Light Adept you find in your path or let them be, is up to you.
This game reflects an approach on stealth mechanics like I haven't seen since Mark of the Ninja, and it takes it to an extreme. All enemies die in one hit regarless of how you attack them, but so do you. Remember when games like Dark Souls boasted about how even the weakest enemies, even by themselves, can kill you (and then it didn't turned quite to be like that)? This is the same logic with a one-hit-kill-everything buff applied to everyone. If you get spotted and you can't scape, it comes down to whoever is quicker on the draw. IF you you face a single guard, that is. Any more and you are royally screwed.
The gameplay itself comes down to you being presented with a "room", of sorts (or several sets of rooms connected with each other), filled with guards and you'll have to traverse it. If you are killing your enemies, you must find a way to isolate and execute the guards without the others noticing, and if you are playing a ghost run, good luck never getting spotted. Some hours in and several collectibles later, you'll get to upgrade your skills and get new tools to ease the almost aggravating amount of enemies in some levels, but those skills are usually limited in uses and it more often than not it'll come down to going close and personal with a Ninjato to the throat.
I've heard this game being described as "a simpler Dishonored" (you have a short distance blink skill by default, and all abilities are mana-based), "HITMAN without the social stealth" (the way the camera and the controls work are very reminiscent of that game) and "the spiritual succesor of Mark of the Ninja (the game makes a great deal of dark and illuminated areas, which effectively have a crucial impact in how you hide from you enemies). And I couldn't agree more with this claims. I enjoyed every single one of those games, and I certainly loved my time with Aragami.
+ A stealth game that drills you into your head the message "DO NOT GET CAUGHT". The enemies are brutal when alerted. Much less so if they are unaware of your presence, so keep that advantage!
+ Unlike other games in the genre, going for a genocide run of a pacifist one does not get you different endings, with the "lethal is bad" stigma. Actually, the game rewards you for commiting to one or the other play styles with medals at the end of each level (the Yurei medal for never getting spotted, the Kami medal for not killing anyone, and the Oni medal for killing EVERYONE).
+ The cell-shaded graphics are lovely. And so is the soundtrak. I'll probably never forget "Spirit of Vegeance".
+ The story, while seems secundary at the beggining, starts picking up the pace in the middle game and reaches a very satisfactory ending which wraps it up nicely. Have you ever felt like a story ends in a way that makes sequels impossible because everything has being tied up to the point that there is no need to continue? It's one of those endings.
+ Cleverly designed boss fights. How do you implement a boss fight in a stealth game, you say? By removing your upper hand: they know where you are, and they are coming for you!
- Incredibly basic enemy AI. The guards are not hard because they are clever or umpredictable, it's because there is a ton of them and they can swarm you. The fact that you die in one hit does not help one bit.
- Some segments can be very frustrating for certain play styles. In some levels, the guards are all clumped toguether and that makes it near impossible to kill them without being cought red handed. In others, the patrol routes and their positioning cover up large amounts of terrain, making it very hard to ghost your way through without stepping into someone's field of view.
- The game is surprisingly stingy with checkpoints. Have fun dealing with that one.
- By far, my biggest complain is that the game is way too short. I only clocked in at ten hours for my first playthrough because I kept getting stuck in some levels. I think that the term for this kind of situations is "short but gold", which certainly applies. I heard rumors of a story DLC that took place before the actual game's story, and a level editor, being developed as I write this, but until then I must keep this point negative.
This game gets a 8.5 out of 10, though. I'll probably go back to it to do actual focused playthroughs rather than just stumble my way through it. And if that extra content is added, you'll see me here again on day one.

I have played all the OMD games.
I have played the beta of this game (it was awful). It was trying to be League of Legends and DotA, from the character designs to the client UI. They even had a MOBA mode - Siege Mode - and the game was split in its design because half of the skills and upgrades were only useful in Siege Mode and the other half were only useful in the regular game.
Then the developer contacted me and was like "would you consider updating your review?" after they had a nasty divorce with their publisher.
So here is this update.
Don't play this garbage. It's still an extreme grind, wildly unbalanced, actively punishes experimentation, and requires both online access and multiplayer. The positive, redeeming qualities are the quality of online connections are way better than OMD2 (which is setting a very, very low bar) and that there's a lot of new characters with their own abilities.
Good luck ever unlocking or upgrading everything, and be aware that once you purchase a trap or upgrade, there's no refunding it, so there's no room to experiment with different trap combinations.
If you want single-player OMD, then OMD2 is still the best game out there.
If you want multi-player OMD, the endless grind is your only option.

Absolutely phenomenal turn based combat game. Templar Battleforce is a love letter to games like Space Hulk and the early days of X-COM.
You play as a group of superhuman, genetically enhanced warriors who are protecting a newly colonized section of a vast interstellar empire. Imbued with the ancestoral memories of your templar ancestors, it is your duty to beat back the unreleting hordes (and they really are hordes) of Xenos scum looking to make a meal of you.
Gameplay consists of top-down, turn based combat. You command a small squad of templars in a manner very similar to the original X-COM. Unlike your crysalid-bait rookies, (and more like Space Hulk) your templars have tremendously powerful skills and infinite ammo. The downside is that both abilities and weapons generate heat, as does movement, forcing you to pick which targets to kill, but to decide when as well. Overwatching a bridge swarming with xenos may provide excellent fire support, but the resulting weaponsfire may also overheat your critically toatsy templar.
Also like Space Hulk, you are always completely and totally outnumbered in Templars Battleforce. Enemy reinforcements are infinite, and many battles are fighting advances or retreats against mounting waves of foes. This makes for some surprisingly intense combat, and will definitely give your grey matter a workout. Do you split your forces into two advancing teams to get to the objectives faster? Do you leave one behind at the beacon to wait for your own reinforcements? Do you hold at the beacon until you are at full strength and hope it is sufficient to beat back the mass of xenos that have arrived?
The game also rewards quick mission times with greater experience, giving incentive to take risks. However, your troops are persistent, as is death. Don't spend your Templars unwisely.
TLDR:
If you're a fan of Space Hulk, X-Com, or Turn-based Strategy, you can't go wrong with Templars Battleforce.

Overall score
2/5
"Just one step below good"
PROs
+ Simple mechanics;
+ Extended RPG development of units.
CONs
+ Bland looks and terrible music;
+ Shallow and repetitive tactics;
+ Lots of choices (RPG development) don't pay off;
+ History uncompelling.
Graphics and Audio 1/5
The looks of this game are quite unimpressive overall. There is not a distinctive look, design, or quality to make it stand out, so most definitely graphics is not a selling point on this.
Pretty much the same applies to musics and audio. Being a strategy game, the musics cannot be repetitive or even annoying, as it is often the case for this game. I ended up turning off the music and playing my own, and after several missions, ended up also turning off the effects.
History and Setting 2/5
The history of the game got me interested at first and the concept of a "small battleforce" against endless waves of enemies is one that I personally like, but later on in the game the story really became quite dull, with unimpressive turn of events, and tremendously lacking character development.
The theme is very much alike to Warhammer 40K, portraing the fight of "stronger humans" (Space Marines?) against "swarming aliens" (Tyranids?). The analogy is striking also in the looks and selection of armors and weapons.
RPG and Skill development 3/5
The skill development and weapons selection is impressive to say the least, lots of choices in very many different directions allow for plenty of strategy customization, and since the very type of units that can be deployed have to be unlocked, it has a direct impact on the degree of adaptability to the different missions.
This point would be 5/5, however it is offset by many bland choices available in the tech tree, equipment listing and skill selecvtion, that really are not useful at all, and by few extremely powerful skills (overwatch?).
In the end, of many choices theoretically possible, only a handful are actually useful. Stats, on top of it, are definitely straightforward and do not offer any additional depth at all.
Tactical depth 2/5
This one point got me struggling for a while, and is the reason I kept on playing to decide it it was "just good enough" or "just not good enough". In the end the redundancy of the mission overall feel pushed toward the latter. Although missions seem varied at first, it really boils down to this:
-enemies behind us! only way possible is forward!;
-quick, do this and that while you run toward the big green EXIT signal;
-only kill enemies that stand in your way;
-KEEP RUNNING;
Since in many missions the margins for error are very narrow, this tactic ends up being most of the times a puzzle where you just have to know ho to solve the level, get that right through trial and error, go on with next iteration.
Conclusion
The game has the potential for improvement, but right now does not deliver.
Needs more polishing in terms of story.
Needs a sleeker tech tree, with still many choices and directions, but less useless branches.
Needs "satisfactory" missions where one sets the pace of the battle. Currently, the aliens always decide the pace, and you keep up (puny human).

This one adds some new qualities to the Dawn of War style of RTS. The campaign is structured in a more non-linear way, allowing you to choose what areas you attack, whether you want to defend an area yourself or let the computer figure out what happens. It's like they spliced in elements of Risk, while maintaining the base building and combat mechanics you've come to expect from Dawn of War.
One thing to note is that you should save often, because if you screw up a mission you'll lose your turn. Also, when attacking an area build the best base and defenses you can because if that area comes under attack by an enemy you automatically start off with all your structures.
This would have been nice to know at the start, as I've pretty much screwed myself over and have to wait a few turns to build resources. Prepare for a little less forgiving experience, and a little more strategy in your attacks. Anyway, it's still Dawn of War and that means it's good.

With over a hundred hours playing Spintires, I felt it was finally time to review this game.
When I first saw this game a couple months ago, I thought how fun could driving trucks through forests and mud be? (Not that fun).
After giving this game a try I am really impressed. What initially convinced me to buy this game were the graphics. The scenery alone is nice to look at. I really was in awe just looking at the trees, grass, rocks and bodies of water I was plowing through.  Upon playing and witnessing the change in the days, sometimes overcast, sometimes bright and sunny, I was hooked. There are also atmosphere sounds, like woodpeckers as the sun rises early in the morning and crickets and owls in the evening and over night. The vehicles all have great sounds.
When starting a new map, most of the area is cloaked in dakness with only your starting point visible. So with only a map and a compass you are expected to find routes to the fuel stations, garages and lumber yards. These maps can be played again and again and eventhough I haven't tried it yet, there are lots of vehicles users have created that can be modded into the game. Hummers, Fords, Porsches jacked up on super swamper tires!
My only complaint with Spintires is the camera controls are sometimes awkward. I may have to winch one of my over turned trucks and sometimes trees, hills or even the rescueing truck can obscure the view.
Well worth the money and I also enjoy going on Youtube to watch other peoples adventures and misfortunes playing Spintires.

I don't usually review games, but I feel a strong need to do so for Mafia II, as I feel so sad to see all these negative reviews...
I love the Mafia series, but Mafia is not a game for all - it never has been, due to its focus on storytelling and historical aspects of the scene they take place in. When Mafia II came out, most people saw it as a disappointment, just like in the case of Mafia III now.
Mafia the City of Lost Heaven was one of my all-time favourite games. Mafia II felt very different, but it did still keep the "Mafia game" feel. Similarly, Mafia III feels very different from Mafia II, but it does keep that feel, which is what I wanted.
Yes, the game was poorly optimised for PC in the beginning, but after the recent patches it became incredibly smooth (steady 60 fps at high settings for me).
As for the game being "repetitive", I honestly haven't been feeling that at all. Getting to know the people who rule the city really motivates you to find them and take them out! I haven't felt a game motivate me this much to do what I am told to do in ages. This game really exposes the horror of a racist, fundamentally psychopathic society of the 1960s, which feels disturbingly similar to present day America...

Ahhh. NS2. The perfect combination of RTS and FPS. I have spent hours doing pretty much everything possible in this game, sans competative play. From shooting aliens to chomping marine scum, I have had the pleasure of playing NS2 for a while, through its low phase of small player count, and into what is now a fine time to purchase the game, as people are once again active and the servers are finally occupied. NS2 to a stranger hosts a team of marines, who play a standard (from a control standpoint) FPS game with a birds eye RTS commander, and a team of aliens with their own RTS commander. Both teams struggle to earn resources, both for the commander to place structures and assistance to players (tech, medpacks, etc), and for the players who need to buy weapons and stronger aliens. As the marine experience is more standard, and is not the most unique and in need of description part of this game, I will describe only the aliens in more depth to save you time reading this. The free one (the skulk) walks on walls, the others include a flying bat like creature with poison bites and spikes, a blade handed creature who can "teleport" short distances, a tubby hippo with healspray, and a giant gorilla rhino thing. The learning curve is steep for marines, steeper for aliens, and the steepest for commanders, but once past it, the game opens up into a unique, unforgettable experience.
Here is what NS2 is to me though:
-Crawling through an airvent as a marine and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ yourself when a cloaked skulk bites you and you spray and pray like nothing else.
-Running away as a gorge from a marine that is pelting your behind and begging your teammates to save you.
-That one guy who buys a flamethrower and everyone judges.
-Beginners learning how to play as a higher alien lifeforms and thinking they are immortal (spoilers, they are not).
-That marine who gets his exosuit for the first time, then screams "I NEED WELDS" when he loses 15 HP.
-Commanders who care about their teams and strive to win, yet lose respectfully (most of the time).
-A community that makes the stereotypical FPS community weep in jealousy...so many people who aren't pointlessly disrespectful and irritating.
-Rookies (and people in general most of the time) who listen to advice, play hard and have fun. No matter what.
In short, I 100% recommend this to anyone who enjoys strategy, FPS, and gaming with people who are mature (most of the time), intelligent team players, especially if in need of a unique twist or change of pace.
I have come back here to say a few things that one should know about this game and what they should expect:
-This game is about resources and should be treated as a strategy game. Although yes the FPS aspect is incredible and for the alien team unforgettable, but you will only win matches by keeping a close eye on enemy resources and tech. Do not be pursuaded into thinking otherwise.
-There will be players better than you until you have experience. These players require strategy to work around, and sometimes it will be frustrating. Some players are simply god like but again, there are balance features and ways to work around one very high skilled enemy.
-Communication is invaluable. You do not need a mic to play this game, but being able to hear other people's communication is crucial to hear tactics and create and excecute plans. Not to say that in all matches there is perfect teamwork, but if you pitch in and communicate with your team you will ALWAYS make a difference even if you don't think so.
-Find a community, or even better, make one. Natural selection 2 is a team game, and the best way to use that to its best potential is to be a part of a community of regulars who all work together on a server(s). Knowing other players makes teamwork easier and you have the added bonus of knowing your opponents better. Balance also becomes more easy as regulars will generally be able to detect any possible errors in skill balance. Even a server full of rookies that are regulars can grow as players and enjoy such a beautiful game.
-Finally, please be constructive. Avoid pushing players down, and instead tell them how to improve for next time. If a person is being a pain, ignore them or if needed mute them (from the scoreboard) so you can continue to work with other construcive players. In general people are nice, but there will always be a rotten one in the bunch that will try to ruin your day. I promise that they are not as common as they may seem, and can be worked around if you put just a small bit of effort in.

DEFCON is probably my favorite concept game. The gameplay is simple but it has tons of replayability and is especially fun with a big group of friends.

First off, if you like stealth games like Dishonored, pick this up, especially if it's on sale, you won't regret it. This game had a few kinks that irritated me to no end, but when the credits rolled I was really happy I played it.
The gameplay is the real reason to play this game. It's a good mix between slow paced planning and stealthing, as well as being able to move fast if you really need to. The game his hard and punishing, while only saving at checkpoints (so no save scumming) but is one of those games that (almost) allways follows it's own rules, so everything seems fair.
The story is abismal. It's boring, and genaric, and the "Twist" should be obvious to anybody who hasn't undergone a labotomy in the recent months. The worst part is that it's let down by the 3D animation. The game switches between 2D flashbacks with mirrors edge style animation and mo-capped 3D. The 2D is great and they should have just used that, but the 3D is awkward and has that unclean mo-cap feel to it like RWBY, where everybodys feet kind of float across the ground, and the motions are overexagerated to a fault. Mo-cap is hard, I know, I've done it! But if you are not going to spend big money to do it, and invest the time in cleanup afterwards, it tends to hurt more than it helps.
That said, the story gets actually VERY good in the last 5 minutes or so, and the animation quality and cinimatic quality does as well, which is a shame because the last level excluding the final boss almost made me quit. It's not just hard, it starts to break it's own rules. There is basically a sniper that can see you at all times (in a stealth game) and you can see their lazer sight always following you, where if you step out of cover for a second theres a seemingly RANDOM chance you are instakilled.
The final boss is pretty good though. The tone is spot on and I was getting a real "Duel of the fates" vibe. It was too easy though and ended in under a minute :(

A darker, grittier version of the wacky budget game Earth Defense Force. While it is certainly the most visually impressive installment in the EDF series, it also feels the most hollow. As far as I'm concerned (and I'm sure many EDF fans will agree with me) much of the charm the series possesses comes from the over-the-top, colorful and corny action and dialouge which is completely lacking this time around.
Don't get me wrong, the massive hordes of insects to shoot are still there and the gameplay has hardly changed at all, but it still doesn't "feel" like an EDF game to me. The drab colors and serious overtones make it seem like this game was a blatant attempt to cash in on the often too serious and "dramatic" American war movie tier trope seen in games like Call of Duty and the like.
All things considered it is a decent little timewaster if you're just looking for that mindless shooting itch to scratch and for ten bucks you could definitely do worse.
My advice though, if you're looking for the definitive EDF experience that you may have heard others gush about, get EDF 4.1 and ONLY jump to this one if you've exhausted yourself on that and are looking for a bit more.

Real-time Strategy game + focus on Story and Puzzle elements + crab creatures!
This is the first and only RTS I ever played that features puzzle gameplay as a main feature. But does it work?
Disclaimer: Before you read further, even though I gave this game "thumbs up", I am only 50/50 on this one right now. My assessment is about whether it is worth your money or not, in Early Access. Keep that in mind.
For $20 you currently gain access to the Hive race (crab/crustacean creatures) with 3 buildings and few soldiers (about 4 types in total + workers). They can only be played in campaign (currently only 3 missions) with moderate enemy variety. I don't think this is currently worth $20 UNLESS you like the concept of [RTS + Puzzle game] combination and you want to support the developers as they add more content.
On the plus side, the developers are very passionate and dedicated about their work, and they respond to the players relatively well. If they maintain this level of commitment, The Hive has good potential. The are adding new features and content on a monthly basis. If you buy the game, you can see a TIMER that indicates exactly when the next update will be.
Graphics: The Hive race reminds me of the Zerg but more like sea creatures than insects. The environment looks cute and grabs your attention with lots of details. Enemy monster design is very creative. I haven't seen anything like them in other games. The interface is very basic, but they are planning to add more tooltips and improvements with player feedback.
Sound: Music is repetitive, but the ambiant sounds are perfect for the environment. The voices that your fighters make are just ADORABLE! Overall, the sound is solid for early access.
Gameplay:
Besides the standard (and very basic) RTS elements like building your base with workers, gathering resource and training fighters, you can also collect treasures (resources) and quest items (for puzzles) by clicking on them directly. Just like point-and-click games, you gotta zoom in and pay attention to details. Objects that "sparkle" indicate that you can interact with them.
Puzzle solving is fun, but they need to add some random variables so that the solutions are different for the same puzzle in every playthrough. Otherwise, there will be little replayability and you will feel less motivated to play through it again (unless they add Multiplayer or Skirmish mode)
Your workers can dig through the rubble in some areas to uncover minerals, but these locations are rare right now... and not very rewarding. They might contain hidden treasures with future patches.
There are some odd bugs and/or poor coding (such as your soldiers attacking themselves if you right click on them while they are selected OR units clipping through terrain and, rarely, getting stuck). But I am confident that they will be fixed soon.
Early Access rating: 6/10

This review is current as of Alpha 0.5 "The Wasteland," and contains potential spoilers.
This is a fairly standard RTS with a unique story that will be interesting to see unfold as the Early Access alpha progresses. I have posted some screenshots of curiosities in play that may represent known or unknown bugs.
For the prospective player, I would suggest considering this game if you if you like your RTS with lots of story. If you're looking for constant explosions and AAA graphics interlaced with hyper-masculine robo-marines, I think you know where to go. This is an indie title in development, not a finished game, and not THAT sort of game to begin with.
For the player/developer, like me, this is a great game for several reasons, not the least of which actually is the state that it's currently in. We can see that the game engine works fine, it may be Unity based on a number of observable factors but there are other things it *could* be, and as each act is released we see the gameplay mature.
For the developer of this game, I do have some notes.
Story - The introductory movie actually strongly implies that we are playing the humans, which was confusing, and then we are not playing the humans, and then three levels into the game there are human-like things but they don't seem to be the humans. The levels we move through appear to be sunlit but there is reference to "the surface," and there are trees and such, which again imply that we are not in catacombs or underground, but are on a surface of some kind. This is confusing. While story in RTS is usually very linear, it would be nice to see player agency used to some degree. We appear to be playing the villains of the story, and the Insectoid Advisor character, having voice acting that comes out similar to a cartoon villain, frequently commands you to kill things that could have been talked to. Also, from the science fiction beginnings of the 'ark in space' we are immediately then fighting undead and summoning golems and performing rituals to contact the underworld. Some preparation for that would have been nice. It makes this a Fantasy game, or a Science Fantasy game, rather than a Science Fiction game.
Art Assets and Theme - The Hive we are controlling is frequently referred to as 'insectoid' but it appears to be more like crustaceans and snails. Particularly the Hive Queen who has a beautiful shell. These features are not typical of insects or hive creatures, but of animals we are familiar with for being individual, though small and often found repellant. Obviously it's far too late in development to change the art assets themselves, but some explanation and description of the animals hierarchy, their anatomy, how they work as a hive, these things would be interesting and would add a lot to the game. The strength of this game is all in the name, people come here for the bugs, it's good that they're beautiful, I think they should be diverse as they have been made so far, and I think they should probably be linked at a psychic or magical level (whatever fits your mythology better) and differ from what we have previously understood as insects or hive creatures. This should probably get some discussion in game, but perhaps not directly as instruction. The hive might absorb a new creature type (consider the highly successful mechanic from Endless Legend in having secondary kingdoms provide new units) and get a chance to have the advisor discuss how "These two species are both compatible with our hive psyche, but we lack the strength to absorb both of them! Choose one, and destroy the other!" And then you pick, say, whether you take over the lizard people from the first couple levels as scouts or the mega-turtles as heavies. The assets change to match your color scheme and after a couple levels have tentacles or bug armor and their name has changed. They've gone from "lizard thrall" to "Lizardoid Scout" without any ceremony.
Terrain - I like the terrain for the most part, but it could really benefit from normal maps and shadows. If the game is in Unity, consider the Relief Terrain Pack and Advanced Foliage Shader assets. It might be a bit of a job integrating them into your project, but I think you would find at least some use of the shaders beneficial. The terrain stands out as less animated and lower quality than your other art assets. I'd recommend introducing wind and weather. If the game is intended to be underground, that needs to come across in the terrain. You've clearly got a good grasp of particles and smoke, use those skills to do shafts of light reaching down, dust sifting through huge caverns, that kind of thing. It shouldn't be so sunny if it's underground.
RTS Mechanics - The Hive has a squad cap apparently equal to 1 + (11x(The Number of Hives you build), but each unit type has a hidden cap as well. I discovered this by accident when I built a second hive in the second mission in order put a healing station next to the ritual so my army would not face any attrition during the time attack sequence. After building the second main base building, I had a squad cap of 23, but I could really only build to about 15 units including 5 or 6 workers. This number of workers made resource gathering easy, and they are combat capable. In the third act adding the Medic brought the total squad cap to 16, even though building a second main base building brought it to 23 again. I have some screen shots on my profile documenting this. Also, perhaps before the enemies get any smarter or numerous, we need an "attack move" command, really a staple of the modern RTS, in which units are commanded to move and attack anything in their pathway.
Gameplay - The biggest area for improvement for this game is the way it feels. The Hive really feels very much unlike a hive. The units build and fight pretty much like any other army in any other basic RTS I've played. The game is in the early stages of development, and the story is really what shines here, but I think there is huge potential here that is being overlooked.
Make the Hive into a hive.
It may sound impossible to go back and change these fundamentals. If it is, sorry for saying negative things and providing solutions you can't use. However, I'm going to suggest these things because, as a developer myself, I can see a way that these solutions could be made a reality and how they could really make this title pop.
A unit should be a swarm of units, rather than a group of 3 to 5. The Queen should be the first unit out, and should be able to start producing drones. Rather than specific commands and individual orders, worker drones should be given targets, and since they should be particles under Boid logic rather than individual units, they should be commanded from the Queen unit or a fundamental menu. So, you can still have the workers build buildings and fish fish pools and kill turtles, but there should be a whole lot more of them doing it at once. Then the Queen builds the hive and moves into it, gaining an upgrade to Squad cap and uses it as a protective measure. The same really goes for the other unit types, though honestly, they should be promoted up from worker drones. The drones should always be doing something, and they should be crawling around all over everything. There needs to be tons of them.
The reason I think this is doable is that, for example if the game is in Unity which I develop in, it's a change in game mechanics which is mostly a secondary scripting issue, and it's a change from using prefabs of individual assets to using prefabs of particle emitters which emit particles that are prefabs of those assets. The particle density would actually be controlled by the capacity of the machine the game was running on. So your squad cap is 12 *swarms* each of which is automatically created as blank drones that just run around, and those swarms might be dozens of bugs.
I think it would be fantastic.

Early Access review for Alpha 0.04.
I decided to pick up this Early Access game as it was on offer, although it is still in very early development. I'm very glad that I did.
I'm a fan of older real time strategy games, like Age of Empires. I've found a lot of the more modern RTS games concentrate more on combat. This game looks like it's shaping up to be more like an adventure/RTS game, with possible role play elements.
Despite being in early development, the team have created a beautiful and fascinating game world and have a great concept. The game levels are full of detail and really show the potential that this alien Eden has. It also has an interesting back story, although that hasn't been explored fully yet. How do the Human colonists in the game intro fit into the tale of the emerging Hive? What happened to the ancients who built the ruins in the caverns below the surface.
The game concept and setting make this RTS game stand out. I'm very keen to see this game develop. Although there is a lot of work still to do, the developers have made an excellent and promising start. Definitely an RTS/adventure game to keep your eye on, or support in early access. With what is available to play so far, The Hive looks like it will be an interesting, relaxing and enjoyable RTS/adventure title, rather than a frenzied 'Zerg-Rush' style battle game. That really appeals to me.
+ Original game concept with the emerging insect hive, and much potential for the story.
+ Beautifully realised game levels and settings so far. The games concept artists have done an amazing job.
+ A mix of older style RTS gameplay, like Age of Empires, and newer RTS innovations, such as building squads instead of individual units.
- Still very early in development. Very stable game, seems well put together, but has limited content at time of writing.
If you like to support promising early access titles which promise something different, I'd encourage you to give this game a careful look.
If you're not so sure about paying for a title which is still in fairly early stages of development, I'd say keep your eye on this game. It has Cult Classic written all over it, at the very least. If it lives up to it's early promise, The Hive could easily end up being something very special.

If you're looking at the screenshots and thinking it looks pretty, wait til you get into the game itself. The work of an independent developer and animator, Dust excels in its utterly beautiful scenery and animation. Much hard work has gone into how it looks, and it plays just as well - it's a side-scrolling platformer with lots of beat-'em-up elements (or slice-'em-up, you play as the amnesiac warrior Dust, with an amazing sword!) and a great story set in a fantasy land. And for all its beauty, the game manages to inject some tear-jerking moments with its massive array of characters and missions. Interspersed are some comedic moments with your companion, Fidget, who has some hilarious, witty dialogue. It's best to play this game with a controller due to the relatively simple controls and combos. Battles are a real challenge; you'll soon be up against hoardes of enemies and will need to chain together sword and magical attacks to survive. And to keep you playing, there are dozens of sidequests and secrets to unlock.
Pros:
-Beautiful graphics and animation
-Witty dialogue
-Long, interesting story
-Easy-to-master combos and simple controls
-Lots of items that affect your stats
Cons:
-Enemies do startling amounts of damage
-Checkpoint save system with occasionally long gaps between them
-Health topups soon get expensive
Conclusion: easy to get into, challenging to master, hard to put down. Worth whatever the asking price is, this is a brilliant game!

I have not played a game so well rounded and fun in such a long time.  I tried TF2 and a ton of random shooters and squad based games, but Paladins is seriously fun and has kept me wanting to play.  Even when it feels like you are losing, it's still super fun.  The champions have enough variety and different abilities to keep it interesting, nothing feels repetitive or "the same" between any of them.
You can create different builds using the card system to make your characters play way differently, and save your builds to load up depending on the map, team composition, and enemy composition.  For example, Ruckus (a front line tanky champion) can be built to have high mobility (normally he's relatively slow), or you can build him to be a super tank with sheilds that load quicker and cover more area etc.
Being able to plan loadouts for your champions is really great, (you create your loadouts outside of matches, so you can take the time to think them through).  The items you buy in the matches with points you earn from playing/killing are well balanced and allow further versatility for your champion.  (Heals too strong on enemy? Buy cauterize to reduce effectiveness of enemy heals when you shoot them).
It's still beta, but there are no serious issues.  At first, certain champions will seem impossible to counter (Fan favorites include Torvald, Evie, Ruckus) - but once you figure out their weaknesses you can feel the balance shifting as you get better at playing.  (Sure, Fernando has a huge sheild that people can stand behind, but he cant attack while using it - and your flankers can get behind him to snipe away anyone standing behind it)
The teamwork involved in winning really comes into the limelight when you reach competitive games (requires 12 champions at level 4 or higher to enter competitive) - And the limit of 2 in a party maximum to queue for competitive means you won't be fighting a 5 man premade uber-stomp group as a solo que.
If you want something that is honest fun, check this out.  You won't regret it.

Zombies in media have gotten stale after a boom of popularity in the past 8 years, but its to Metal Deads credit that none of the situations the game throws at you seem anything but. Making it larger does not change the game resolution but just streches the pixels to be blurry and a complete mess.
Sound wise the music is decent though repetitive, I think the only thing that kept me playing was I could enjoy the music; it's just the rest of the game is a frustrating mess.
Don't expect the story to make any kind of sense. This was written by someone on drugs and it shows from beginning to end. I wouldn't care if the gameplay was more enjoyable; but in trying to justify why you would force yourself through another level it helps to have a compelling story. This doesn't, so you are just doing it to prove you can push through frustration.
And than there's the gameplay. A lot could be forgiven if the gameplay was tight, smooth and fun. But the controls are poorly thought out, and the in game actions don't always do what you want them to.
Trying to throw a knife at someone? Nah, it picks up a random weapon nearby because it's the same button. Trying to shoot someone? Better hope they are at far enough distance away because the bullets don't come out of the gun they spawn a space in front of you so it's possible to miss at near pointblank range because the bullets spawned BEHIND the person you were shooting at.
And don't try to make sense of the what you can or can't shoot over or through. Oh this couch? No you can't shoot through this couch, it acts like a wall. But that couch? Oh yea that couch (that looks the same on the other side of the room), that one you could shoot over... too bad the enemy knew that and you didn't because now you're dead.
During the first few levels I really thought I was going to enjoy the game. Though it's dressed up as a shooter it plays more like a puzzle game. You have to move from room to room killing and since the enemy can kill instantly you have to plot your way through like a puzzle.
Unfortunately between the blurry textures and the poor control setup the entire thing turns into an excercise in frustration on the larger levels as enemies rush you or shoot at you from distances and angles you can't predict. And even when you know what you want to do the game doesn't always bother to respond with that action. Throw in some randomness just to up the frustration and you can't even reliably plot your course ahead of time.
Why does a finishing move sometimes kill with one hit and othertimes you have to sit there and pound the guys head into the floor for a while? Too late you're dead.
Maybe if there were more savepoints or the levels stayed small you could push through some of the mess. But the problem really starts to glare at you as the levels get longer and longer and suddenly you can only really plan for the first portion of the map and than rely on luck to have everything else fall in place and not get screwed over by a random wandering guard as you are trying to finish a silent kill that decided to take longer than usual so there you are still smashing some guys head in instead of ducking behind a wall for cover.
And don't even get me started on the stupid gun designs or the inability for the game to pick up ammo (you have to switch guns, good luck mid fight)

I got this game on a whim during it's 0.99 cent sale. At the time, I was suffering from a very painful toothache, which was almost dehibilitating. I wanted something I could do that didn't require focus, so I figured I'd try this game. Two things of note; one, my estimate for not requiring focus was completely off-base. Two, I played it from install to near completion in one 5 hour sitting. My toothache was an afterthought. I have no more praiseworthy sentence than that.
The concept is simple; it's a match-3 game. Even worse, it's my least favorite kind of match-3 game; a move has to end with 3 or more matching. Nothing akin to, say, Tetris Attack, where you could meticulously plot out an amazing chain, one block move at a time. So why would I recommend this game, even when the first two paragraphs of this review are faintly condemning it?
Because it's amazing, that's why. It takes cue from other match-3 games with the simple but addictive gameplay, and then adds it's own finess to the mix. You're exploring a dungeon, and your actions are based on matching tiles. Clear 3 Key tiles to open a lock on a treasure chest, match 3 Sword tiles to swing a sword at an enemy, you get the idea. Run the dungeon as long as you can, slaying enemies, collecting loot, and get as far as you can. Strive for that 10,000,000-point mark.
What makes this work so well is it's so frantic. At any given time, you're matching in the grid, while watching your inventory of special, one-shot items, while at the same time plotting for the next encounter. Fighting a dragon? Forget those keys, those wood, you need lots and lots of attacks. At a chest? Those swords do you no good, you're waisting them as only keys will open the locks. The most stressful moments for me were the time between encounters; "I have a five-chain of attacks lined up, I hope it's not a chest or door next..."
The game rewards you for each attempt, too. Clearing wood tiles and stone tiles give you those in currency form, you collect gold and EXP from felled monsters and opened chests, and you can refurbish and upgrade your impromptu-home with facilities. Not got enough 'umph' behind your swings? Upgrade your sword at the smithy.
It's a repetitive cycle to be sure, but there's no greater joy than building up a horde of gold from your failed runs, pumping up your sword's destructive might, and then laying waste to enemy after enemy with your newfound strength. However, the cycle doesn't continue forever, and once you hit max, that's it. The game will get no easier from there, and all that's left is you and your 10m goal.
It's certainly not without it's own flaws though. Early on, the runs are frantic and short. Very, very short. Even in the tutorial run, you won't completely grasp what's going on or even how to plan things out because it's ALREADY OVER. It takes running after running to finally get a feel for the game, and then it goes out of it's way to make you attempt sometimes rediculous maneuvers to advance. These goals include simple things (get a certain score, get a certain amount of EXP), to difficult without planning things (defeat a ranged mob in less than 5 seconds) to downright infuriating (use a scroll to get a triple clear in one shot, seriously? No amount of planning will get you that). These shortcomings I don't nessicarily say are the game's fault, rather, the intencely random nature of this brand of match-3 makes them far harder than need be.
When all is said and done, it's welcoming enough for beginners (given some time to adjust), and has enough depth and breadth for hardcore gamers to get a good kick out of it. At 0.99 cents, this was a steal of a game. The full-fledged pricetag of 4.99 is still low for the enjoyment you'll get out of this game. Expect to clock in at least 5 hours of good, solid gameplay before completing, and based on how much the random number god loves (or hates) you, another 3 hours until 100% completion. Even then, it's just fun to do a quick dungeon tromp to burn some time and some dragons.

Your mission is to ultimately score 10,000,000 points to free yourself from the dungeon, but you have to purchase a bunch of upgrades using gold and experience points before you will be able to achieve that goal. Upgrades are available for your sword, staff, armor, and shield. Plus you can buy additional training attributes through earned experience points. Then there are the potions which have both positive and negative effects that you must weigh to determine whether to activate them or not.
The gameplay consists of frantically matching gems to attack or unlock doors and chests in an effort to keep your character from hitting the left edge of the screen. Your character continues running to the right as long as you match the right gems to vanquish your enemies or open doors and chests.
There is no polish on this game whatsoever. The concept is nice, but the game itself is pretty cheesy. However, for a buck, is does provide reasonable entertainment value.

Game itself is a good, dev is a failure.
This game has had several dramas / controversies between the developer and publisher. It's "good" at the moment, but new features might never come and current features might break any given moment.

This game is just sliding tiles. It tries to seem like more with the RPG elements but that is little more than a skin. The game rewards you for making as many matches as possible, as fast as possible, regardless of what is happening in the top section. Sure, you have to match the right tiles to proceed past each obstacle, but that happens naturally through frantic matching. If you try to play the board strategically you'll find things simply don't happen fast enough and you'll fail the level because time is always ticking down and you HP usually is too. The whole experience feels like it was designed by a gambling cartel trying to get me addicted to slots.
The upgrade system was compelling at first but quite quickly became a chore and no longer enhances the experience after a few hours. There is a little strategic freedom in how you spend your resources on upgrades and perks but it really doesn't affect gameplay, it just shifts difficulty from one element to another. There is also an arbitrary wait while upgrades are occurring in which you can't do anything but watch the progress bar. This wait increases with each upgrade for no reason. It isn't long but it is completely unnecessary. The investment type perks are pointless because they effectively just adjust how much grinding is necessary and players won't know how much grinding they want to do until they've missed the opportunity for the investment to be economically viable. I honestly think they game would be better served by automating or removing the entire upgrade system and just implementing a few sliders so players can adjust how good they have to be at tile matching to not lose.
The only thing which is still interesting after a few hours is the challenges. There are at most 3 challenges active at any time and new challenges aren't made available until space is made for them by completing an existing challenge. They are things like 'Kill an armored monster with only staves' and 'Open a chest within 5 seconds'. Challenges provide a reason to adjust strategy which helps stop the game becoming stale, however I'm fairly frequently stuck on (a) challenge(s) and the game stops being fun at all. Completing an overly difficult challenge is a relief, not a reward, because a combination of grinding and luck is what gets me there. An option to skip challenges would fix this but might reduce the worth of the challenge system.
To put it simply, if you're expecting anything more from the game than a pretty good tile matching time-waster you might be disappointed. I think there is potential in the format but a lot more weight needs to be given to the RPG elements for me to enjoy this as a hybrid puzzle RPG and not just a puzzle game with a guy running at the top of the screen.

In Fallout: Shelter, you are a Vault Overseer. You must ensure that your dwellers are happy, you have to make sure everything is full - make sure you don't run out of power, food or water - and you must ensure that your shelter is safe for your dwellers to live in.
As a fan of the Fallout series on Xbox, I saw this on Steam and thought that I would grab it and see what it was like. I was expecting something a lot more like the original gaming series, maybe walking through the vault itself. It's not like that at all. It's very much a one dimensional game, with just the layout of your vault in front of you. However, there's a lot that can actually be done in this game and it exceeded the expectations when they dropped upon seeing it when I first opened the game.
This game isn't at all what I thought it would be like. It's a lot of strategy and being ahead of the curve, a lot of being mindful of resources and having to know when to send dwellers out, when to rush things, when to build things. There's a lot that needs to be considered at the same time. It's a little hard on this aspect, but it's actually really fun. I'm having a blast with it, and the achievements definitely make it worthwhile to play, if you're an achievement hunter. This isn't what I thought it would be, but it's a lot funner that I originally expected.
It's definitely a bit of fun and it's free to play on Steam, which is a total bonus! This is totally a play to pass time game, but it's fun for sure, in my opinion.

*** This review contains spoilers ***
I got a 75% coupon for this game, the description and media material looked promising, and since I´m a strategy/rpg/scifi fan, why not.
First, an option dialog opens and lets you choose a resolution and window-mode as an option.
This seems to be the only way for it, since the in-game "Option" option doesn´t work so far (can´t click it). Besides that you have options for "continue", "new game", "load game" (you can´t save games atm, so nothing to load), "credits" and "exit". Continuing a game, you can choose the first and second map (a third to be expected soon), it also says "Page 1 of 5".
There is a countdown timer until the next big release is scheduled.
Starting a new game, the intro sets you in Earth´s +100ish years future. One day meteors literally start falling out of the sky. This comes as a total suprise to its inhabitants. (If you plan on becoming an astronomist, don´t, there obviously is no market for it in the future.)
Humanity then goes on to build one (1) spaceship.
After three years of meteor rain, the ship is launched just as earth is destroyed, and mankind boldly goes where no one has gone before.
After some time of travel a planet is discovered. The planet seems to be inhabited by monsters, living in a harsh environment. Oh, and there are underground ruins.
Despite being a nice intro, it has nothing to do with the actual gameplay. Like, at all.
After an intro showing earth´s destruction and humanity escaping into space, you would think that you actually play a human civilisation, right?
WRONG!
you will play bug-like aliens, who have to kill lizard-like aliens to satisfy fire demons.
True, the title says "Hive", but still. Well, maybe it´s just me.
You start your civilisation with one worker, being able to build 3 buildings: Hive, Barracks, and Worker Den (storage building).
You can build Workers (building and ressource gathering), Legionnaires (light melee), Hunters (light range), Hive Queen (heavy melee).
On the first mission, you have to build up your base, an army, an then venture out to kill some mobs and some more mobs. You´re finished after killing the boss, which a fire demon tells you to do.
On the second mission (which I´m currently playing), you have additionally a puzzle to solve.
This is an early access review, so I will not bother to list any con´s or complain about missing content until the game is actually released. From the actual content it seems to be more like a pre-alpha, but still, by far not the worst early access I´ve seen.
On the positive side, the game sets the ground for a lot of nice things and has lots of potential. Despite being labeled as adventure/indie/strategy it is more a strategy/scifi/rpg.
Could be compared with Age of Empires. You can collect ressources, at the moment food and ressource, and have a population cap. You can build different units in different buildings. I´d like more buildings, units, hopefully research.
The fact that your units have the slots for items (Weapon, Shield, Helmet, Armor, 2 Rings), even though you can´t build items yet, gives me great hope for the final release. Units have attack and defense values, and the ability to level, even though you don´t see any xp values so far. Looking forward to this.
The fact that you´re playing alien bugs on a different planet is just awesome, right?
I´d like to see more races, maybe some humans mentioned in the intro could venture out into the game.
Besides your UI on the bottom you also have a minimap. The view can be rotated 360° horizontally and about 30° vertically (meaning almost birds-view to almost overseeing the entire map). The game has decent graphic and atmospheric voice acting.
I personally am really hoping for a crossover between Age of Empires and Heroes of Might and Magic. Also, multiplayer would be appreciated.
If you happen to come across this game and like the genre, but don´t want to buy an early access game, it´s at least worth putting on your watchlist.

I hear a lot of this game being compared to Dishonored. While its primary mode of transportation is a teleport that is similar to the blink ability from Dishonored, that's pretty much where the similarities end. This has a much simpler stealth and combat mechanic, there isn't much fighting back if you get caught.
With that being said, this is one of my favorite releases this year. It has its issues, but its one of the best stealth games I have ever played. It does a great job of making stealth feel necessary instead of just an option. There's a simple progression system that gives you some further options as you make it through the game. The coop option makes the game that much better, letting you experience the game with a friend, requiring you to communicate and strategize to make it through each level. Lastly, the boss battles are unique and require some thought rather than just brute force.
This is very high on my list of games I have played recently. I would recommend this to anybody who enjoys a stealth experience.

Disclaimer~ I have played this more on the PS3 version of game
I've heard so many negative things about this game. This is odd, because the reviews are very positive on the Steam page. The negativity seems to be very similar to what Duke Nukem Forever struggled with. Players that remember the previous titles wanted a specific experience the new one didn't deliver on. Like Duke Nukem Forever, this game isn't actually that bad as long you judge it for itself rather than the others.
I have not played the previous title of Earth Defense Force. I can only say that my experience with this title was simply positive. Do I think this is the best thing since gravy? No. I will say this was a better Starship Troopers game than the actual Starship Troopers game.
The gameplay is okay. It's not too slow, it feels like it's actiony enough for it to be arguably be considered fast paced. While it is fun at first, I will say that the weapons you start with get very dull after awhile. All the enemies you fight, they have a lot of health. This causes you to resent yourself for choosing any of the fully automatic weapons later in the game. The solution is to have slower rate of fire weapons or missile based weapons.
It gets more tedious, however, when you start unlocking the good weapons that hit the targets for you by heat seeking them. You could literally aim at the sky and the missiles will figure out the rest for you. This basically means that you don't even have to play the game anymore to play the game.
This is sad, because I feel it could be very gun to combat against enemies with a variety of firepower instead of feeling I have to use specific type of weapons. I cannot help but feel a simple solution would be to just make each weapon have different strengths and weaknesses rather than just saying "these are the best weapons, you unlock them later."
The player can also pick classes of soldier, which is an interesting touch. There is one with a jetpack, another that's compensating speed for other perks, etc. You can pick based on your playstyle. Downside when playing online? The fastest player gets all the kills and all the tanks sorta just show up late to the party, thus you can argue you're being punished for picking the armor class soldier. Though, not as punishing as being the one guy that picks a cannon based weapon while the other players spam rockets into the sky and hits everything in the area.
The enemy diversity isn't drastically huge, it's pretty limited. It isn't so small that you will get bored right away, but it does tarnish replay value. That's the same with the actual missions, they're all the same. The game just doesn't feel interesting as far as goals or purpose. You sorta just play to kill.
Online has some expected choices, such as survival. It's okay, it's not super enjoyable because of the weapons once again as earlier mentioned. The main attraction is just coop for the main game, the "story" I guess we'll call it.
Overall, it's a positive experience. It's an okay game, kinda like how some B-Movies are an okay movie. You might not play that movie a whole lot, you'll watch it every time and again. This game? I beaten it on PS3 for single player and never touched it since. I have a hard time wanting to play it on PC. I do think $10 is worth it, but maybe even wait for a sale.

I don't get the negativity for this game.  It seems like people generally think this was a bad entry into the franchise, but I haven't seen the problems.
The game is about 20 minutes of new and unique content, interspersed with immense amounts of grind.  You get more powerful weapons with credits and random drops.  You need more powerful weapons and higher levels as missions proceed, because the difficulty curve is wildly inconsistent and enemies become bullet sponges very quickly.  Thus, to proceed you get to the point where you grind early levels for the credits and random drops required to progress.  To my understanding that is the series formula.
The AI is terrible, and often suicidally runs into combat.  The enemies aren't challenging, but they tend to attack in the middle of reloading animations and double the time they take.  The achievements are...frustrating time sinks.  I think the worst part of this game is that you have to grind through it an immense amount of times, because the separate classes all require experience building and the purchase of new weapons to make them viable.
All of this said, the game is good stupid fun.  Grab a couple of friends, spend an afternoon grinding, and completely forget about the game two days later.  It costs less than some movie tickets, doesn't aspire to being something high concept or avant garde, and revels in stupidity (if you beat the last level on the highest difficulty you'll know exactly what I mean.
All in all it's a good game.  Not great, deeply flawed, buggy for a long time (the radar function was enabled my default for the longest time, removing the need for the support unit's special ability), but satisfyingly shallow and fun.  Maybe 4.1 will be better, but I can't really say I'm unhappy about this game.

Excellent game if you like squad based tactics.  I picked this game up on sale, and it has been well worth it so far.   For an indie 2d game, it is very polished and well supported.  The gameplay offers a lot of good choices for customizing nearly everything in your squadron. The missions so far have had enough map, enemy and mission based variety to keep it interesting. The lore and story line give you a sense of purpose and keep you wanting to see what's next, and if that's not your thing, they have a handy skip button for the RP.
The choices you make in building your squad is probably the strongest feature.  I really have liked the idea of heat to keep you from overusing certain moves and gear customizations that can augment that.The ability to respec unit abilities also is handy if you need to adjust to beat a mission you are failing to complete.
If I had one complaint, it's the design of the requisition tree.  It's too much like confusing 4x games, and I feel a more streamlined design would make it a lot easier to understand.
All in all, I highly reccommend this game.
