Templar Battleforce is a top-down, turn-based strategy title evoking memories of Laser Squad (forerunner of the original UFO: Enemy Unknown).
The game is essentially a linked series of missions interspersed with squad and tech management, plus a smidge of storytelling.  The units under your control, the eponymous Templars, are not entirely dissimilar to WH40k Space Marines, being humans piloting suits of battle armour that augment their abilities.  The twist here is that rather than having a concept like 'gene-seed', a Templar's memories and experiences are passed down through their bloodline across generations.
Anyway, enough of the fluff.  The meat of the game - the tactical battles is competently done; movement and combat is handled via a variation of the time-honoured action point system and works intuitively.  Most missions seem to have a turn goal - completion of the objective within this will bestow extra experience, and this mechanic - coupled with a large sprinkling of risk/reward secondary objectives and tactical points to capture -  can lead to some nail-biting mission climaxes.
There are excellent customisation options available for your Templars in between missions too, an RPG-lite skill and talent progression system for them to work through and  a very detailed tech tree which you unlock parts of by using the 'resource points' tallied up at the end of each battle.  Contained within the tech tree (which in terms of presentation reminds me of Sword of the Stars 1) are many weapons (some unique), abilites and miscellaneous items all of which allow for many varied takes on a Templar squad's makeup.
Graphically the game is serviceable and has improved with recent patches.  The audio is functional but nothing to write home about.  If I had one niggle it would simply be the relatively minor suggestion that the game lacks a little polish - there are points at which grammatical/spelling errors crop up in some of the story text for example and while I freely acknowledge that these are far from game-breaking, they do nonetheless pull me out of my 'zone' in the game and bring me back to reality with a bump.
All things considered (including the fantastic support Trese brothers continue to lavish on the game) I would heartilty recommend this title to anyone who enjoys turn-based squad level combat.  It's probably the closest we'll ever get to a genuine turn-based WH40k game, yet it does have its own distinct and well-developed lore.  Blend this with some brilliant research and management options then ask yourself - what more could you want for the price?

Earth Defense Force: Insect Armageddon is a semi-reboot of the series and is the only game in the series not made by the original developers Sandlot. It takes place around the same time of EDF 2017 and is set in the city of New Detroit. Upon starting the game you can either choose to play the game by yourself or create a new online game for people to join. If you decide to go it alone you will be accompanied by two AI bots named Kid and Cyrus who are not entirely useless but nowhere near as helpful as real players. You can then choose from one of four classes to play as. The Trooper who is your jack of all trades with no real special talents, the Tactical who can lay down turrets and mines, the Battle who is essentially a walking tank with the biggest and most destructive weapons and finally the Jet who can zoom around in a jetpack.
Each class has a different set of weapons exclusive to them and with the addition of being able to change your armor to a few different colors it helps making each class feel unique. So far the game is looking awesome and you eagerly jump into mission 1. The first thing you will likely notice is that this game looks much better than the previous entries and every enemy has been resigned to fit this new, gritty theme it's going for. Personally I actually prefer this art direction compared to the previous entries and it makes it all the more of a shame when you actually start playing it. You see they decided to add RPG mechanics by gathering experience and leveling up your character but the problem lies in that you'll start off completely rubbish.
Your gun barely does any damage, the clip for each weapon is insanely small meaning that you'll be reloading 80% of the time since this is a game about fighting hordes of enemies and probably worst of all is how the Jet class starts off. You know how he has a jetpack? Well yeah, starting off you can very likely jump higher in real life than that thing lifts him off the ground which is just sad to look at and turns him into a glorified roller-skater. 7 hours of playing nearly exclusively as this class and his jetpack is noticeably better after leveling a few times but don't expect to be able to reach most of the surrounding rooftops for a vantage point.
One of the selling points of the game is that it features 300 guns. Well that too is messed up by this completely unnecessary leveling system since whenever you pick up a gun crate from the battlefield they are inexplicably unable to be used until you reach a certain level. Not only does that take the fun out of collecting loot since it takes so long to level up but it also means you will be forced to stick with your rubbish weaponry due to bad game design. Another thing that is really strange is that every weapon of a category looks exactly the same. As an example the first rocket launcher looks the same as the latest rocket launcher you just picked up, the latest assault rifle does too and every other gun has a single weapon model for its entire category. This makes the feel of finally leveling up and being able to use a new gun all the more disappointing.
Using explosives in the midst of battle is still as satisfying as ever since every building is completely destructible and by the end of a mission most of the city will be in ruins due to fierce fighting. Unfortunately these new and improved graphics do come at a great cost. There are red “invisible walls” everywhere and you will quickly notice how small the area you can actually play in are. The game tries to hide this fact by drastically changing how missions are designed. While most of the mission from the previous games set you in a huge environment and tasked you with simply surviving the onslaught, this game is chock filled with way-points you must head to. Go to a certain area and switch a beacon or something equally mundane, fight a horde, then go switch another beacon and rinse and repeat until the game finishes.
This gets old fast and since there are only 15 missions in this game, each of them last quite some time further making the repetition noticeable. The worst part of it all is that this game switched from the cheesy, plain dumb dialogue of the rest of the series and instead went the dull, serious route. I found the dialogue plain unbearable and most every word you hear out of someone’s mouth will be a random string of words like “Bravo Zulu Lightning over” or “Affirmative, Oscar Bravo Lightning Strike”. I guess they were trying to make it sound cool and edgy but it just sounds like a bunch of things kids would say when they take a match of CS:GO far too seriously.
Moving back to the topic of compromises caused by the improved graphics, the amount of enemies that can be on the screen at any one time has been greatly reduced. To give the illusion of facing a horde of enemies they now spawn right around you by crawling out of the ground. This could have been cool if it was used a few times but that is how most of your encounters play out. You go to a way point, receive a string of random words from the mission handler and then enemies predictably pop out of nowhere instantly surrounding you time and time again. Gone are the days when you see hundreds of ants marching to your location as you desperately pick off as many as you can before they reach you. Yes the previous games had graphics right out of the original Xbox but this is a prime case in where graphics are not everything.
Ant hills make a return and still spawn in infinite number of enemies until destroyed. Yes, they messed that up too as you are likely imagining. No longer can you destroy the hill with your rocket launcher that is capable of destroying several skyscrapers with a single blast, now you must walk up right next to the hill and plant a tiny charge on the outside. The worst part of this is that it takes several seconds to set it up and a single hit causes you to start all over again. This was clearly designed to “enhance” coop by forcing your friends to cover you but with how fast most weapons run out of ammo, it's likely they simply won't be able to in many cases. Friendly fire is always on and you will take damage if you mindlessly run in front of a friend that is firing his gun. Your AI companions if playing solo are pretty good at not shooting you but seem to constantly try to get themselves killed when you are firing.
If you are downed they can revive you and you will be back at full health. Once you finish the campaign you will have the option to turn off the AI bots in future playthroughs. You will also unlock a “campaign remix” mode that randomizes the enemies encountered. Not really a mode that makes much of a difference to the missions. You also have survival mode where you can play with up to 6 other players and fight until you all drop. In survival you can only play as the Trooper class, gain no experience and none of your guns from campaign can be used. One thing I must praise this game for is that vehicles are now finally helpful and no longer have controls designed by someone that has never played a video game. It is pretty fun to ride in tanks, mechs or just get into anti-air turrets. There are quite a few new awesome looking enemies added as well. At the end of the day I get the feeling that Insect Armageddon wasn't even originally supposed to be an EDF game due to how badly they messed up the basic features this series is known for. It may be fun for a bit if you plan on playing with some friends but I just cannot recommend it.

At the current point in time I do not recommend this game for varios reasons.
A) The game involves extreme grinding. There are a dozen crafting materials and getting traps requires a significant amount of grinding. Unlike the previous games, one can not simply pick a trap one likes and upgrade it over time to maximize its performance. One has to farm the particular crafting items over and over again using the same 5 simple and annoying traps to finally be able to craft this trap in the first place.
B) There is little variation in the players' loadout because it takes ages to unlock a single new trap. Whereas it was possible to reset the loadout in previous games it is not possible any longer. Thus, one has to spend additional time in the game doing the exact same thing with the exact same traps to achieve a marginal level of trap variation.
C) The free-to-play business model is frustrating. I'd rather pay money for the game to have an even battlefield in multiplayer. Currently people paying for the game have a significant advantage as they can skip a significant part of the grinding process and easily destroy people who spend an equal amount of time on the game simply because they were able to afford better items at lower levels (e.g. items granting brief invincibility).
All-in-all, while Robot did a lot of work to improve the game and to re-invent parts of it by adding a MOBA style multiplayer mode - I feel that there is little appeal to OMD players. The game feels like it is designed for a new customer group such as SMITE players and did not fulfill my expectations.

Well well well, where to start with this game?
Awhile back I heard about 10,000,000 and I was looking forward to getting my hands on it to play, after I got it, I spent 2 or 3 hours playing it nonstop, soon after my play session ended I relised I felt really weird,  so I tryed to stand up, and I felt so disorentated dizzy to almost the point where I felt intoxicated, I couldnt understand it.
That aside, the time spent playing 10,000,000 has had its frustraitons, but it was very fun, what ever it may be, getting huge combos going, to the silly hints, everything about it brings such a retro feel, the music and audio compliments the game.
In a nutshell, the top side scroller looking area of the screen is a cleverly disguised timer and health bar. Your character runs through a dungeon, and all of his actions are controlled by the blocks you match. Need to unlock a door or a chest? Match some keys. A monster blocking your path? Physical attacks are executed by matching swords while magical attacks fire off by matching staves. Standing still by not matching causes the timer to tick down, pushing your character to the left, and getting hit by monsters also pushes you to the left. The damage aspect can be mitigated by matching shields, which are absorbed instead of pushing your character. Fall off the side of the screen and it's game over.
To supplement these mechanics are a set of shockingly deep loot, item, upgrade, and experience systems. Monsters can drop loot, and you can also get loot by matching backpack tiles or unlocking chests. Loot can either be gold to buy upgrades or actual usable items. A few items you'll come across are a red orb that'll damage whatever monster is in front of you, a key to instantly unlock a chest or doorway blocking your path, scrolls to spawn more tiles of a certain type on the board, and much more.
Every time you start up your game and get ready to explore, your character lierally Jumps out of bed and is ready to rock, I first noticed the score and the goal, which reminded me of one of those Awful motivation posters that were en vogue in the 90's and acts like one too.
You really need to think about the games mechanics, because 10000000 doesn't tell you much beyond the qwerky loading hits, and leave you on your own to explore, I find that this works perfecly with short playt sessions, and adds a sense of discovery that I found fun.
If you have one of your 10,000,000 runs that lasts more than a minute or two you are doing considerably well, it gives you a chance to catch your breath and break down what you learned during your last attempt to reach your goal of 10,000,000.
This is a game with a protestant work, and you have to Aceept failure as part of the Journey, and try your best to do a little better every time.
I have really enjoyed my time so far playing 10,000,000 and I hope everyone else can have some fun with it too.

Natural Selection never got the love it deserved in my opinion. The marine team is essentially what I've always wanted FPS games to be like in the multiplayer section. A commander has a birds-eye view and can order marines specifically [Giving you, as the player, side objectives that help the team]. In most games I would complain about the ability to full auto and have such small spread, but you NEED it, as the aliens have a lot of finesse. This is truly a team game, where a high kill count and low death score isn't as important as securing strategic locations and getting resource nodes for your commander.
As Alien, it's a bit tricky. It's very easy to understand, but hard to master. This game often plays as a horror game, as good alien players often will ambush and surprise marine teams, making it hard to steady your aim. Onos has to be the most fun [In my opinion] to play, and let's even a noob who's willing to save up resources try out this behemoth of a xenomorph.
Trust me, you won't regret at least trying this game.

I hear a lot of this game being compared to Dishonored. While its primary mode of transportation is a teleport that is similar to the blink ability from Dishonored, that's pretty much where the similarities end. This has a much simpler stealth and combat mechanic, there isn't much fighting back if you get caught.
With that being said, this is one of my favorite releases this year. It has its issues, but its one of the best stealth games I have ever played. It does a great job of making stealth feel necessary instead of just an option. There's a simple progression system that gives you some further options as you make it through the game. The coop option makes the game that much better, letting you experience the game with a friend, requiring you to communicate and strategize to make it through each level. Lastly, the boss battles are unique and require some thought rather than just brute force.
This is very high on my list of games I have played recently. I would recommend this to anybody who enjoys a stealth experience.

This game is all about patterns. Each type of enemy moves to the beat in a specific way, and you need to learn these patterns to effectively defeat them.
The simplistic controls are what really drive this game home. You only use four buttons to perform all of the moves in the game - up, down, left, and right, to be precise. The game's control scheme is so simple, in fact, that you can play it with a USB-enabled dance pad, like the kind used for DDR-esque games. Personally I have not tried this, though I definitely want to!
Even though this game is in alpha, it is still jam-packed with features to entertain you for hours of playtime. I highly recommend this game.

But if on the fence, I'd have to say wait until there is a little more meat to the game to decide whether or not you want to get it. I'll keep and eye on it and change my reccomend option when/if the game gets to the point where it's worth buying for the average person. The Hive has gorgeous graphics from level designing to concept art, the intro cinematic reminds me of homeworld 2 cinematic which is really well done. The graphics are similar to Starcraft 2 but more detailed.

While The Hive is in Early Access it has provided a good strategic game and I expect great things from it!

A nice little indie adventure made with Adventure Game Studio, which is a pretty old and creaky engine by today's standards, but also has a proven track record of being able to perform miracles (like Time Gentlemen, Please!) in capable hands. Succeeding with AGS demands a lot from the writing department, and this is where Metal Dead shines.
The story follows the exploits of two metalheads in the middle of an zombie outbreak, and is just about as anarchistic that can be imagined from the premise. The game does not skimp on the gore, but it's all presented with a deftly light and funny touch and endearingly crude graphics. In fact, the game's sense of humor is its strongest asset: The dialogue and writing is generally quite funny and pokes a lot of fun at various pop and alternative culture phenomenons.
The puzzles are surprisingly logical as well, which does mean the game is a bit on the easy side. I don't really see that as a negative thing, however - It keeps the narrative moving and the jokes incoming, and Metal Dead is above all entertaining throughout its duration. It's not quite as laugh-out-loud funny as the Ben & Dan games, but worth experiencing nevertheless. Rough on the outside, but beats a lot of the generic adventure bulk put out by actual publishers with ease.

Nearly 50 hours into the game, I've been taking my time, true, but that's how I like it, I pick up every last penny I see.  I don't like it that the cars and guns you order turn up so fast without any explanation. The shooting controls from a moving car, ( in drive by mode ), are really stupid and awkward to use. If we had a record mode, (let's call it instructor mode), you could have had an AI employee sitting on the forklift with you till you've fully loaded the truck or off-loaded the truck into a warehouse..
It would have been nice to see some mini games like this within this M3 game and GTA5 / Online.  Some of the building interiors don't make sense, like most shops don't have a kitchinette / sink for coffee / tea making and a loo to use - if you run the shop but don't live above it for instance.

Most of the missions need patience, if you take the stealthy whistle and whack route to killing all your foes. It's just about picking you moments correctly, once you get the hang of it, the game is really too easy to play even in hard mode and that's why it gets really boring doing stealh kills all the time.
I just don't understand why they made it so easy to play. I often get bored with the game and just try to shoot it out and make a bit of noise to break the monotony of silent kills in every mission.
Much has been said and complained about - regarding the level of gore and violence in the game, you can turn it off as I understand, but I haven't, it really becomes boring since there are only so many ways you can surprise a guy and stab him in the face, neck, head, or torso.. I found myself sitting patiently drinking coffee with my cup in my left hand and controller in the right. Its just a press of 'B' button and the cutscene takes over.. Yawn...
That cut-scene taking over is just like the crap Mafia 2 did in certain places and I bet someone on the devs team are clones of the LA Noire devs too, since LA Noire did that too, remember that in LA Noire you could not park up at the scene of a crime as you arrived,- because as you drive up tot he location, the cutscene takes / snatches the game off you and thows you kicking and screaming into the detective role mission.. It is rally annoyeing..
Any developers that think we buy games to have our controller snatched off us, and think we won't strike out like I am doing now is mistaken.  This M3 game is spoiled by those cutscenes that interfere with our gameplay.. 10,000,000. An RPGish, Bejeweled-like game. Well... ok...
While the game does have an interesting concept it annoyingly relies on luck and what tiles the game decides to generate more than anything else, much like Bejeweled or similar puzzle games. If a monster is in your path, you'll have to quickly match sword or staff tiles to do damage. A locked chest requires matching key tiles. And as tiles are random, one might find oneself stuck, matching any tiles at all, hoping to match enough of what is needed before time is up.
At the start of the game, be prepared to lose, quite often, until enough materials are gathered to unlock upgrades. While initially the upgrades that can be purchased come in handy and allow one to make quick work of monsters, the upgrades have a max level which in my opinion is too low. Especially during the latter ranks, and especially when fighting bosses. Even completely maxed out requires, more often than not, way too many tile matches and wastes way too much time. However, there are items to find thru out the dungeon run which can help somewhat. Scrolls that will change wood or stone tiles to keys, swords, or staves. Various weapons and orbs to hurl at monsters. Skeleton keys to easily unlock chests or locks. And food items that will give you a time boost. With that said, the weapons, orbs and skeleton keys must be used rather precisely; if used a split second too early when arriving upon a chest or monster the item does nothing and disappears. The same can be said for tiles too. It would have been nice if there was some leeway as making sure the dungeon runner is close enough to an obstacle before using items can waste valuable time, even if just a split second.
And possibly the biggest time waster in the game, combos. Match some tiles, more fall down and they match. Combo! They are sometimes handy like during a boss fight. Except when the tiles continue to fall and continue to match it becomes a potential death trap. Yes, I've lost more than once awaiting tiles to stop falling and matching others because during this time nothing else can be done. And if the reason I lost wasn't because I ran out of time, it was shortly after because the combo completely used up tiles that would have came in handy just a few seconds later.
Replay value? Prepare to spend several hours upgrading everything before even attempting a run for 10,000,000. But after one does achieve freedom by getting to a score of 10,000,000, the only reason I can think of to come back to this game would be to try for a higher personal score (no Steam leaderboards), or to earn all achievements. Personally, once I complete all the achievements I doubt I will ever play this again.
Is 10,000,000 fun? Sure, it can be. Would I recommend it? Hmm. Not at the full price of $4.99. I picked it up on sale for less than a dollar. At that price it was worth it. While I don't really want to vote thumbs down, I'm going to have to since Steam has no neutral option.

Governor of Poker 3 is one of the best poker games I have played in a long time. Despite the micro-transactions, it is still worth the value of 'free'. If you are a good enough player, you can avoid micro-transactions and still win. The chat system keeps communication fun and friendly with pre-set chat options and faces. Your character can be customised with hats, shirts and pins (all for the gold currency, which is hard to get unless you pay for it).
The game also allows you to play blackjack for your chips. This means that (if you're feeling lucky), you can up your stack before you enter a game. Be warned! This could also put the game out of your reach with the minimum buy-in.
The game has multiple styles of poker including standard in game cash-games, sit and go's (you pay a set amount of money for entry, 5 players. 2nd comes out even, the winner gets a lot more), push or folds (small buy in with big blinds) and the big win (buy-in goes to the community pot and then you play. At the end of the time period, money is given out depending on your position on the big win chip leaderboard). They are all fantastic modes.
The one thing I would say is that a glitch made me lose all of my money. THIS WAS UNDER A SET OF UNIQUE CIRCUMSTANCES AND IS HIGHLY UNLIKELY TO HAPPEN TO YOU. I have also enjoyed climbing back to the top in the most terrifying way possible.
This is certainly a game to buy!

Anyone who enjoys XCOM, Final Fantasy Tactics, Disgaea, Space Hulk or any other turn-based tactical games should buy and play the hell out of Templar Battleforce. Assemble a crew of badass dudes in badass 'mechs with awesome diverse weapons, equipment, stats, skills and talents. Missions are fast-paced and hectic and never feel unfair even when you're playing with permadeath. Endless enemies force you to work quickly while accumulating Heat punishes you for pushing too fast. Art and sound are simple but handsome, the game loads and plays extremely fast without bugs or crashes. Delve into the lore and dialogue options and you'll find an obvious labor of love, establishing a very cool universe even if it's not always explained well. The creators are constantly updating and improving the game well after release and stay active with their community. It's too bad Templar Battleforce hasn't gotten more press. It is a fabulous little strategy game. A true Steam gem.

This game takes one part Warhammer 40K and one part X-COM and mixes them well. Do not let the dated graphics put you off. The game has a depth to it that you would not expect if you judge it by its looks alone.
While not evenly polished, the game is quite enjoyable. On normal difficulty, the game will challenge you without becoming overly frustrating. There are a couple of levels that add speical objectives that are difficult to achieve either due to time constraints or due to the sheer amount of enemies that come after you. Others, such as the final battle, put your units in situations that make it very difficult to keep them from being overrun and torn apart before you can get backup to them.
All of the unit types are useful in combat, which is something that other games do not do well. Your engineers can hold their own, the scouts are death dealing glass cannons that can save your units from ambushes through their ability to scan around corners, and the hand-to-hand units deal and absorb damage with a flare that put a smile on my face. The later units tend to be a little too similar to their predecessors, and tend to have weaknesses that offset their heightened powers to the point that you are better off investing in boosting the older unit types rather than spend precious research points on the newer units.
While it might seem that I am being harsh in my review, it is because there were so few flaws in the game that they stand out like proud nails on an otherwise unblemished floor. I give this game my full recommendation, if you like either Warhammer 40K or X-COM. If you like both, I think you are in for an unexpected treat.

Clearly inspired by the classic move Wargames, Defcon puts you in charge of the nuclear arsenal of a bloc of countries during the countdown to nuclear war. It's coming and there's nothing you can do to stop it. The whole game is played out on a world map that resembles a NORAD command display. There are no fancy 3D graphics, just clean vector lines. It's pretty chilling, especially considering that the folks who would have to do this in reality would be looking at something quite similar.
There are many, many strategic decisions to be made over the course of one game. You have to manage your naval and air forces intelligently, and plan where and when you will launch from your silos.
It plays slowly and deliberately and requires some patience, but is worth it in the end.

After so many years, some clever bugger had the smart idea of combining metal slug, worms armageddon and super smash bros and then made possibly one of the most brilliant multiplayer games ever.
Up to four players spawn as Ducks on a map with weapons and you all move very fast. All ducks die in one hit, and have to avoid dying while trying to kill the other ducks. Normally this all lasts 20 seconds tops, if not more, before moving onto the next map and different weapons. There's 50 maps and 50 weapons to play with.
Utterly genius concept for a game where everything is simplified as much as possible yet very fun. A truly defining example of a game you can pick up and play, getting the entire concept down in a matter of seconds and discovering new weapons all on the way. Even then, there's a lot of depth in the game when it comes down to it, finding out new things all the time, new ways to thwart enemy ducks. Stab 'em, zap 'em, burn 'em, toss 'em off an edge', blast them into smithereens. And so much more...
Openly making it moddable is a generous option if you ever get bored of the standard stuff. It adds brand new levels, new weapons to your arsenal. You can also make your own hats if you want which is a huge added bonus. You'd be amazed at what ideas the small yet innovative modding community came up with, and it can only be hoped that, if ever there was a sequel, a lot of the especially great ideas (A highly rated mod for a bunch of new, flashy grenades for example) are added in the next time around.
If there was anything that needed fixing about this game it would possibly be the fact that there isn't any real punishment for ducks quitting so you end up with that happening a lot of the time, but I guess that's to be expected. Also maybe some sort of matchmaking system instead of pairing up with random players. A system which frequently ends up pitting absolute god-tier players that clocked in a thousand hours in game to someone who's just, well, played a couple of hours and are brand new.
Despite that, it's an overall fantastic and amazing game that's soon to be updated over the summer along with a release for the PS4. Here's hoping it gets a lot more recognition. Woo.
(And there is also a dedicated button on your controller of choice soley for quacking, naturally.)

People need to stop comparing this game to Overwatch. If you actually took the time to play the game and try to find the similiarities, you'd see that it's actually fairly difficult to do. The only thing that the two games share in common are the base game-modes, which you could say the same for Overwatch and TF2. Paladins is almost nothing like Overwatch, and an easy example of the differences I can give is-- Healing in Overwatch revolves around one or two players' jobs to manually make sure their team is at full health or they can get health packs themselves. Paladins has healers but that isn't their job, their job is to deal damage just like every other character in the game, and healing in this is primarily focussed around getting out of combat quickly and essentially " retreating ", as you regenerate HP from inactivity from combat.

It's angry. It's violent. And damn, does it feel good.
Wondering why a game was made illegal to own in Australia just days after it was announced? Check out this game. This game is why.
You take on the role of what would appear to be a serial killer who gets phone calls vaguely telling him where to go every day. You go there, kill everything and everyone, and eventually go home for some top ramen and to sleep.
The music is great, compliments the game fantastically. It's constantly pushing you forward, into the carnage, rather than simply accompanying it. It's almost like you want to keep fighting, and killing, as fast as possible so as to not let the music down.
The gameplay itself is brutally unforgiving, but not impossible. The names of the game are Speed and Brutality. The enemies all drop just as easily as you do, and you'll never forget it. You'll replay a couple of stages a dozen or more times, until you really are a homocidal psychopath, but when you finally break that final skull, you will feel such a wave of vindication and relief that the MONSTERS who took up like TWENTY MINUTES OF YOUR GAME TIME are FINALLY GONE that it will have all been worth it.
The story is... confusing. You'll never really know what's going on, and that's the point. Every bit of the story is engineered to be piecemeal, as though you're watching a movie with all the opening scenes and dialogue cut out with drunk goggles on. Figuring out what the hell is going on is a game in and of itself, and you're best off spending that time after you've beaten the game. Until then, just treat it as mindless carnage. You're better off not trying to solve the puzzle until you have all the pieces.
Overall? Great game. A tad short for the full asking price, but if you can pick it up on sale, you have no excuse not to. This is one of those games EVERYONE should play through, or at least know about.

Ah, Hotline Miami.
It's a top-down shooter with lots of gore, lots of action, lots of badass music, and lots of confusing plot. But that's okay.
You're a guy (who is named Jacket by the fans and eventually by everyone) who lives in an alternate 1989 Miami who suddenly starts to get phone calls and a rooster mask. Totally not weird at all.
So, you obey the voices, and end up going on a slaughter spree that costs 307 Russian mobsters their lives. (I got the kill count from the Hotline Miami wiki, by the way.)
Along the way, you rescue some hooker who then becomes your girlfriend, you lucky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, an old friend of yours with a nice beard gives you free movies, pizzas, and drinks, and you find three people with animal masks; Richard, Don Juan, and Rasmus.
Richard's a cryptic sonuva♥♥♥♥♥, Don Juan is actually nice to you sometimes, but Rasmus hates you. That's okay, because I don't like Rasmus either.
Richard asks you four questions, makes three predictions, and then eventually tells you that none of your actions matter because you're a bloody idiot. At least he sticks with you until the end.
Some assclown named Richter eventually shows up but I'm not spoiling anymore. Play for yourself.
Combat. Whew, this part's the best. You've got a pretty big variety of weapons to use, but not all guns are found on some levels. For example, you probably won't find the Silenced Pistol until the chapter Deadline. However, if you get crazy good scores on levels, you'll unlock more and more weapons, from hammers, to Skorpion SMGs, to beer cans that you can throw at people.
You die incredibly fast in Hotline Miami. But so do your enemies. One stray bullet from an Uzi can mean certain death, so rushing into rooms with an assault rifle really isn't a good idea. Guns make lots of noise, too. Melee weapons are much, much quieter.
You'll have to use guns sometimes, though. Just manage your ammo, but you may want to use the Peter mask if you love guns but don't want to have the entire map flocking to you.
There are boss fights every few chapters, and of course there's one at the end of Jacket's storyline.
Surprise, surprise, though, you get to play as Biker, who's actually the first boss fight in Jacket's story. Neither Biker nor Jacket die, by the way.
Biker just so happens to be in the same masked maniac boat as Jacket, and was trying to find the source of the phone calls. There are actually two endings to Biker's story but there will be no spoilers of that here.

It's really disappointing to see all these negative reviews for the game. It's a match 3 puzzle game (but instead of swapping two tiles, you move an entire row or column to match, so it'll take a bit to get used to), but instead of leaving it at that adds in some RPG and combat elements to keep things interesting. In short, you make runs to escape a dungeon (which happens at 10,000,000 points - spoilers!) by matching tiles; sword and staff tiles do damage to enemies you run into, key tiles open locked chests and doors, backpack tiles give items that aid you along the way, and wood/stone are resources you use to upgrade rooms in the initial area you start in. At the end of the day it's still a match 3 puzzle game, so if you're not into that this probably won't do anything to change your mind, but the system of progression it uses to keep things interesting is great. Relatively short, I guess, considering it has a definitive end, but you can keep playing after the end for more upgrades/higher scores. It kept me entertained long after completion on iOS and the PC version will likely do the same.

I was optimistic and really wanted to like this game and go against the masses, but the bottom line is this game has a huge world, recreates a re-imagined New Orleans very well, but suffers because of low frame rates and horrible controllability.
First, about the frame rate. I am running a system with an Intel core i-7, 32Gb RAM, and dual NVidia gtx-760's in SLI surround. Frame rate averages low 30's and gets down into the teens. As you can imagine, it is a jerky visual experience very likley to cause headaches or siezures. Unfortunatey, the graphics settings aren't very configurable and you cannot turn off ambient occlusion, antialiasing, etc. but can only select between low/medium/high. The frame rates I emntioned here were with everything on "low". Needs the ability to turn off features that have a huge impact on performance. Great little indie adventure, with remarkably well-designed puzzles that actually make sense and a goofy sense of humor that - despite all the gore - has a lot of charm. Most of the characters are well rounded and likeable, but the main character in particular is a fairly rare thing in graphic adventures: a relatable protagonist who doesn't come off as a complete sociopath!
There's also an incredible amount of attention to detail. Most possible interactions have individual responses, many of them funny, and I loved the way the game keeps expanding and changing its office building setting. Highly recommended if you like this sort of thing.

Author's Note: Don't judge this review by the time I've spent on the PC version of this game. I bought it on the PC when it first came out, knowing that it probably wouldn't run on my PC, I was right. So, I decided to get it for the Xbox One. I won't really be able to cover any PC glitches or anything of that nature, but I can give you my opinion on the game. So, here we go.
After playing Mafia II, I had high hopes for this game. I heard that the story was great and that the soundtrack was amazing. Sadly though, it didn't meet my hopes.
The game is set in 1968, in the fictional city in Louisiana called "New Bordeaux" (Which is basically New Orleans). You play as Lincoln Clay, a man who just got back from the war in Vietnam. All's well in his life until tragedy strikes and Lincoln is out for revenge. Now, I do admit that the story is pretty darn good! It's probably the best thing going for it. If you've played the previous game, you'll also recognize some people.  The new characters are also interesting.
After the story, though, things start to get a little average. If you couldn't tell already, this game is a third person shooter, just like the rest of the series. There are a multitude of guns in your arsenal, available to purchase in-game. There's pistols, snipers, shotguns, automatic guns, and more. The shooting in this game isn't anything new, if you've played any third person shooter, you've probably played this one too.
Being that this is an open world game, there is also driving. Now, the cars in this game look pretty sweet, but the driving isn't anything new either. Once again, if you've played an open world game with cars, you've probably played this one too. The one plus with the driving is the radio. The soundtrack has some great hits from the era and do make driving worth it!
Here's where it drops more...the missions. If you've ever read a review on this game, you probably already know this. The missions are all basically the same. You either kill someone or you destroy something...yep. When I first started, I was excited about the missions. I do admit that they're pretty fun, but they get old FAST. It came to the point where I was so lazy that I just got the sniper, drove to a vantage point, parked the car, got out, sniped the target, and drove off. You can stealth-kill targets, which can be fun, but it just gets mundane. Mission after mission of the same thing. Back in Mafia 2, missions felt more unique. Sure, you had your shoot-outs, but there were some great missions! Now, there are some unique missions, but most of your time will be spent doing the same interrogation animation 12 times, killing one fool several times, or smashing up something.
One of the goals of the game is to take over the map, and that is done by completing missions. When this is done, you can assign pieces to your three lieutenants and it's done by holding a meeting. Giving pieces of land and completing missions for any of your lieutenants can give you access to new stuff, such as weapons. Doing the missions though means more of the same stuff. Overall, I thought this system was fairly cool, but it still makes you do the same old missions.

Another thing to note is the graphics. The in-game graphics are pretty good, but sometimes seem a little lack luster. The cut scene graphics though are extremely well done and the whole thing feels like a documentary you'd find on the History Channel. Also, when you're not killing targets or busting up places, there's also collectables to be had, different cars, and clothes to buy. Other than the missions, though, there's not much to do.
In the end, Mafia 3 turned out to be a decent game, due to its story, music, and amazing cut scene graphics. Mafia 3 doesn't do a good job in terms of being the next installment to Mafia 2. If you're looking to buy this, I'd say wait for it to go down to $20, at the very most. $15 dollars would be more ideal though and if you're truly looking for that mafia experience, stick with the first two games.

So, these are my thoughts on this game. I will not go into the gameplay or -mechanics in detail, other reviewers already did that extensively. I bought this game a while ago after noticing it in my steam queue and browsing the reviews (esp. vintoks' and Arkelis' recommendations I found very appealing). Played it for a bit and dropped it for XCOM2. Now I am back at it and that alone should tell you something.
+ It's been said before, this is the game Space Hulk wanted to be and failed at.
+ The game is very accessible, I consider myself to be a filthy casual when it comes to squad tactics games and I knew my way around pretty quickly without reading a manual. The tutorial is excellent in that regard and tooltips are really helpful. All the powers/actions are adequately explained and those explanations are easily accessible from all the relevant screens.
+ The game mechanics allow for a very good scaling of the difficulty level. I have only played on normal yet (which isn't too much of a challenge even for me *yet*) but I took a peek at other difficulties and the heat distribution of your armor alone requires more planning on your part on the higher ones.
+ I enjoyed the tactical challenges and diverse missions I have encountered so far and I don't miss the hilariously aggravating RNG of XCOM 2 for one second.
+ Customization of your troopers helps identifying and becoming invested with them, as far as you can get invested in something without a personality (your Captain is the sole exception there, as he actually talks) ;).
+ The ability to - at any point between missions - completely and freely respec any character is brilliant and invites you to experiment without having to start a new character. This is (for me) a serious long term enjoyment factor.
+ Same goes for the diverse equipment options you can unlock for your Templars.
+ Various troop specializations give you a wide variety of tactical options (once you unlock the relevant classes in the requisition tree).
+ The story is nice, if not very surprising or unexpected, especially when you are a 40k aficionado like me.
+ The devs. If you read - for example - the negative reviews, you might have noticed, that each one has a calm, objective comment, addressing key gripes of the reviewer where those where recognizable. Frankly I have yet to see something like that anywhere else on Steam (didn’t do ALL the research here tho, so do not make that into a gospel, please). At the same time there is still tweaking and improving of the game going on, months after the official release. And I am not only talking bugfixes, but also new skins and general improvements lesser people would hide behind a DLC.
Things I didn't like with the game(play) itself, as opposed to outside appearances (see The Ugly). I am struggling with this a bit, since I pretty obviously enjoyed the game so far. Also I haven't finished it yet, but I wanted to get a positive review out as small games really can use those. So I might come back later and add to this here, but for now, this is what I got. As of now, none of them are anything major, just small annoyances:
- While there are secondary objectives to a mission, I haven't yet found a way to actually discover what they are without stumbling across them accidentally on the map. This clashes with the bonus you get for completing a mission in as little time as possible. That may be intentional, but I'd like the opportunity to decide beforehand if my squad should rather try for secondary objectives or speed. As it stands I don't even positively KNOW if there are secondary objectives at all most of the time (mostly there are, I think, but there seems to be no way to know beforehand) and this leads to a tendency to do a mission twice, once to chart the map and once to actually progress the campaign. Again, this might be intentional, but me no likey.
- There are opportunities to pick up loot from containers during a mission. You can recognize those by the coloring of their adjacent fields. This I discovered accidentally, it would have been nice to get a hint towards this in the tutorial. Also it seems there is a limit on how often this works during one mission, because I had times when I had already picked something up and then further containers I came across didn't give me anything (again a little annoying, because of wasted turns to get there). This too would be nice if it was mentioned somewhere, I haven't found a hint in that regard yet.
- Sometimes the dialogue options between the missions don't make it sufficiently clear that picking them will start a certain mission and close off other options.
- If you are looking for eyecandy, this might not be the game for you. The devs did good (and upgraded it noticeably a short while ago), but it can't hold to current standards. And why should it? It is an Indie game, catering to your tactical needs, graphics are a secondary means to that end at best.
- The soundtrack, yeah same. It is ok, but we are pampered by AAA games in that respect. I personally turned it off after a while and have something playing in the background (I hear all the cool kids do that these days anyway).
- No voiced narrative or characters. It's all reading here. That is no problem for me but it bears mentioning.
- The action, hmm. Action and round based strategy? Yes possible (see XCOM(2)), but imo more of the eyecandy category.

Plot summary:
You start the zombie apocalypse outside a high rise hospital with zombies all around.
You need to get inside, explore, gather items, meet people, help everyone survive (or at least yourself).
Game is mostly played on the floors of the hospita via elevator.
Must find security cards to access various floors in hospital.
The good:
Fun game, fairly linear script (so you can't blow things by doing them in the wrong order).
Funny lines, enjoyably offensive lines, homage to famous movie quotes throughout.
Items have specific uses; game won't let you use them wrong.
Once you complete all the activities on a floor, game will sublty suggest you go elsewhere.
Relaxed game, no time pressure except for final scene (see blow under BAD 3).
Enjoyable puzzle-ish solving experience.
With heavy metal and zombies.
The bad:
Only three negatives that I can think of, and they shouldn't keep you from giving this a try.
1) It's a 22 story hostipal, but you only have game activities on about half those floors.
2) Game's too short--just as you get the hang of finding/using items, it's almost over!
3) Really the only negative I wish they'd done differently is the final/boss room.  Prior to this room, the entire game is a relaxed, laid back style.  No time pressure.  No "hurry up, more here or die!" type things.  Then, suddenly, for the very last room with the final boss, it's "hurry up or die!"  Was just an unwelcome, rushed end to a quirky, relaxing game.

Templar Battleforce is a polished indie turn-based squad tactics game with base building and RPG elements, set in the Trese Brothers' original Star Traders universe. It's a great game by a great developer. The Trese Brothers, long-time veterans of tabletop tactics games, got their start developing games for smartphones.  They have since produced numerous games exploring multiple genres in a short handful of years. Templar Battleforce represents a return to their stated mission: the creation of high-quality, multi-platform RPGs and Strategy games, supported by strong community involvement and a commitment to lifelong game updates.  All of their games fulfill this vision in some manner, but Templar Battleforce checks every box.  Furthermore, in creating Templar Battleforce, the Trese Brothers have used the lessons learned over their first few years as a fledgling studio to re-envision and re-invent the spirit of one of their earliest games- Templar Assault. It's a great feeling to play a game that is an indie dev's dream made real.
Before I discuss gameplay I'd like to address a common criticism of both the Star Traders universe and the Steel universe (Trese Brothers' fantasy setting).  The Trese Brothers have time and again explicitly recognized the Warhammer and WH40K settings as major inspirations for their work.  They also acknowledge many other sources of inspiration for their original settings.  Are the Trese Brothers' settings derivative? Yes. Does that make their settings rip-offs? No.  Point me if you can to a fantasy or spce opera setting in a game that is
derivative, because I've never seen it.
The Trese Brothers settings combine common tropes in original and compelling ways, building an internally consistent universe on the foundation of inspiration.  Yes, some devs cut & paste together bits and pieces from popular settings.  The result is a lazy pastiche of improbable bedfellows, without depth or heart.  The Trese Brothers are clearly heavily invested in their settings, and as a result the world-building is unique, coherent, and immersive.
Gameplay is divided into two primary components: missions and combat, and HQ activities.  The game features features a branching storyline that is tense and dramatic without being overbearing.  You will encounter story dialogue during most missions, but it rarely lasts longer than a handful of sentences.  The combat is top-down and grid-based.  Each Templar has a set number of Action Points (AP) and Movement Points (MP) derived from their base attributes.  The bottom of the screen displays an action hotbar, portrait, and HP and Heat bars for the selected Templar. Actions use AP and generate Heat. If MP is available acting will consume that as well, so it's often prudent to move everyone first and then go back have each one act.  If the Heat meter fills the Templar will not be able to use hotbar abilities. If it overfills they will take damage. Luckily, taking no action dramatically cools the armor.  Cover, line of sight, smart ability use, and overwatch are key elements of success.  The math feels polished, precise, fair, and detailed.  Many maps contain multiple main and secondary objectives; you will rarely play a "Kill All Enemies" mission.
Between missions you manage your squad at the HQ screen. It looks like a base-building interface but there's actually very little of that.  Instead, this is where you choose how to level each character, hire new characters, and requisition new items and abilities.  It's a class-based paradigm, with each class having access to unique skill trees and equipment.  Each level attribute and skill points are distributed manually, allowing for enormous flexibility and diversity.
Perhaps my favorite piece of the HQ experience is the requisition tree.  You earn RP by completing objectives, which you can then spend on an astounding array of global unlocks. Many of the unlocks are class-specific, and the skill-tree paradigm means getting the unlock you want first requires unlocking everything below it.  This is where the game requires careful consideration of your own gameplay style- you can't just unlock everything, you have to choose.  Of course this aspect also adds to the games replay value.
If you've enjoyed other Trese Brothers games, you will definitely enjoy this one.  And as always the Trese Brothers offer the game attentive and continuous support.  I don't know of any other studio as endlessly committed to improving every product they release.  If you are new to Trese Brothers games, Templar Battleforce is a great place to start your journey.
I recommend this game for all fans of turn-based squad tactics or of space opera RPGs.  I also recommend this game to almost anyone else, because it both imminently accessible and thoughtfully compelling.

Earth Defense Force: Insect Armageddon (Alternative Title: "Kill Aliens With Bloom: The Game") is a game where you shoot giant bugs and some alien ships. If you’re familiar with the other games in the series, like 2017 and 2025, be aware this is a different game due to not being developed by Japan.
Overall, the game is nice. While best played with friends, the game does allow for AI teammates that will try their best to revive you when you go down, as well as supplying supporting fire. Dialogue in the game is humorous, in a silly sort of way. Guns are somewhat unique, although on a much smaller scale than other EDF games. (You ever shoot a rocket launcher and find out it splits into a bunch of swirly plasma missiles that crash down and bombard the area?) The feel of each class is enjoyable, and I don’t feel completely useless if my class’s specialty fails (looking at you, 2025). Each class has their own thing they do, and they stand out from each other. Except... maybe Trooper. That's the normal jack-of-all-trades class. No specialty, just "flexibility" to choose from any weapon class to use. Bless your soul if you choose to play Trooper.
Cons. Campaign is short. I suppose this is meant to be remedied by the Campaign Remix mode, and three difficulty levels, but I know some people tend to drop games once the campaign is finished. Not to mention that repeating missions can get very boring. As far as I’m aware, absolutely nobody plays Survival mode. Story is weak. It doesn’t even get resolved, even with the alternate ending. It's assumed you're just here to shoot bugs and aliens, and doesn't give you much more. This game is kind of old and not incredibly popular, online multiplayer will probably be a little empty. I can’t say I checked. If you want to keep playing after beating the campaign, maybe you think Inferno difficulty will be a fun challenge, understand you will be in for a real grind. Achievement hunting? Haha. You’re in for a long ride.
If those things don’t really seem that awful, well, give it a spin. The game was fun enough for me to play it on two systems.

A fun game to pick up and play for a few hours at a time. This shooter places you into a very well scripted b-movie vibe millitary shooter.(Playtime does not reflect my substantial offline time commitment)
Obviously you fight giant bugs and robot bugs in the streets of New Detroit with either two generic NPC soliders who don't really get a chance to show you much of thier personality except through the generic chatter they exchange during missions. Or you can replace the NPC's with online players (a much more helpful prospect, the NPCs are tragically underprepared for air combat). While the game advances or the waves of survival continue the types and abilities in enemies introdces new ways the enemy tries to bring the battle to you. The enemy types range from simplistic, to ludicrous health walls, or in the case of most flying enemies extremely challenging targets unless you are carrying the right weapons.
Luckily the game gives you a massive list of weapons to choose from as you play through and unlock more weapons with interesting differences like specific weapon spreads, tracking, DOT and explosion radius. These all may sound like basic shooter fare, but when coupled with the class abilities for each armor (which each have thier own weapon classes used and level up seperately) makes the experience drastically different for each armor. Wether you fly around with the jetpack, taking carefully aimed sniper shots (or rain death with a rocket launcher) from far above the battlefield, or use the tactical armor to drop turrets to add another gun while blasting with your weapon of choice, or play with the largest weapon selection with the solider or use the heavy to deliver maximum firepower to the enemy.
Unfortunately after beating the main campaign, the story remains totally static, difficulty increases simply give enemies more health, even in the Game + mode the only difference is that enemy types are changed so advanced enemies show up earlier than normal. This makes going back into the story (the only way to advance armor level since survival uses a set level core trooper armor) something of a chore, but with a few friends playing for fun it becomes more enjoyable. Survival is a fun distraction, but without any advancement beyond a number of waves it can become stale once you stop trying out new weapons (especially since you can't unlock new weapons or amor levels in survival) and maps.
All in All: I really like this game on principal, my first playthrough solo was a huge blast, but I regretably didn't get as much out of subsequent returns to the battlefields of New Detroit. Initial Playthrough: 9/10 (only the prolongued sequences of me trying to shoot down aircraft with a shotgun or gernade launcher prevented the ten). Subsequent Playthrough: 6/10 Man.... it just feels grindy once I change to a new armor... and the NPC playstyle only compounds this issue.
Final score: 8/10

Orcs-must-die is a fast-paced beatemup-survival type towerdefence game where nearly endless waves of monsters rush at you at once, each trying to reach the mcguffin you are defending with your life, forcing you to rely on your quick-thinking, fast reflexes, and powerful weapons, traps, and spells to defeat them.
Orcs-must-die is placing a new barricade directly behind a barricade that's seconds away from being destroyed and placing twice as many traps to defend it mid-round. it's placing three paladins down in a row in the middle of the hallway while four archers and two dwarves cover them from the platform above. Orcs-must-die is rapidly spam-clicking your bladestaff for a hithithithithithithithit on twenty enemies at once before swapping to your blunderbus or acid bombs to take out the flying units above you. Orcs must die is carefully picking the spells, weapons, traps, and guardians you want at your side, and upgrading them in a way that suits you best and makes them do the job you need them to do.
In this? Orcs must die 2 had over twenty different levels, each with the warmage, sorceress, and archmage talking to and bantering off one another the whole time, giving the world a feeling of immersion and interest! It's angry. It's violent. And damn, does it feel good.
Wondering why a game was made illegal to own in Australia just days after it was announced? Check out this game. This game is why.
You take on the role of what would appear to be a serial killer who gets phone calls vaguely telling him where to go every day. You go there, kill everything and everyone, and eventually go home for some top ramen and to sleep.
The music is great, compliments the game fantastically. It's constantly pushing you forward, into the carnage, rather than simply accompanying it. It's almost like you want to keep fighting, and killing, as fast as possible so as to not let the music down.
The gameplay itself is brutally unforgiving, but not impossible. The names of the game are Speed and Brutality. The enemies all drop just as easily as you do, and you'll never forget it. You'll replay a couple of stages a dozen or more times, until you really are a homocidal psychopath, but when you finally break that final skull, you will feel such a wave of vindication and relief that the MONSTERS who took up like TWENTY MINUTES OF YOUR GAME TIME are FINALLY GONE that it will have all been worth it.
The story is... confusing. You'll never really know what's going on, and that's the point. Every bit of the story is engineered to be piecemeal, as though you're watching a movie with all the opening scenes and dialogue cut out with drunk goggles on. Figuring out what the hell is going on is a game in and of itself, and you're best off spending that time after you've beaten the game. Until then, just treat it as mindless carnage. You're better off not trying to solve the puzzle until you have all the pieces.
Overall? Great game. A tad short for the full asking price, but if you can pick it up on sale, you have no excuse not to. This is one of those games EVERYONE should play through, or at least know about.

Not dubbed Orcs Must Die 3, and for good reason: It isn't.
It's slower, much more restrictive, less dynamic, and despite its obviously high production values, it lacks the essential feel and character of its predecessors. Basic minions (or creeps) are small and nigh faceless 'bullet sponges,' you can only place traps in blue areas, there's a limit to how many traps you can field, and you gather resources to craft basic items and upgrades. Or you could do what Robot Entertainment would rather you do and pay for the upgrades, heroes, and skins with real money in their cash shop.
This game may mean the end of the Orcs Must Die franchise as it has been known, as an authentic sequel would take away from what its developers are trying to do here: get rich quick or go broke in this modern MOBA gold rush.
Fans of classic OMD need not apply. You won't find much of what you loved in the originals under this game's hood except for the conspicuously familiar coat of paint that clashes jarringly with its unfulfilling gameplay.
Play OMD 2 instead, enjoy it, and long for the 4 player cooperative winner this game could have been.

Ah, Hotline Miami.
It's a top-down shooter with lots of gore, lots of action, lots of badass music, and lots of confusing plot. But that's okay.
You're a guy (who is named Jacket by the fans and eventually by everyone) who lives in an alternate 1989 Miami who suddenly starts to get phone calls and a rooster mask. Totally not weird at all.
So, you obey the voices, and end up going on a slaughter spree that costs 307 Russian mobsters their lives. (I got the kill count from the Hotline Miami wiki, by the way.)
Along the way, you rescue some hooker who then becomes your girlfriend, you lucky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, an old friend of yours with a nice beard gives you free movies, pizzas, and drinks, and you find three people with animal masks; Richard, Don Juan, and Rasmus.
Richard's a cryptic sonuva♥♥♥♥♥, Don Juan is actually nice to you sometimes, but Rasmus hates you. That's okay, because I don't like Rasmus either.
Richard asks you four questions, makes three predictions, and then eventually tells you that none of your actions matter because you're a bloody idiot. At least he sticks with you until the end.
Some assclown named Richter eventually shows up but I'm not spoiling anymore. Play for yourself.
Combat. Whew, this part's the best. You've got a pretty big variety of weapons to use, but not all guns are found on some levels. For example, you probably won't find the Silenced Pistol until the chapter Deadline. However, if you get crazy good scores on levels, you'll unlock more and more weapons, from hammers, to Skorpion SMGs, to beer cans that you can throw at people.
You die incredibly fast in Hotline Miami. But so do your enemies. One stray bullet from an Uzi can mean certain death, so rushing into rooms with an assault rifle really isn't a good idea. Guns make lots of noise, too. Melee weapons are much, much quieter.
You'll have to use guns sometimes, though. Just manage your ammo, but you may want to use the Peter mask if you love guns but don't want to have the entire map flocking to you.
There are boss fights every few chapters, and of course there's one at the end of Jacket's storyline.
Surprise, surprise, though, you get to play as Biker, who's actually the first boss fight in Jacket's story. Neither Biker nor Jacket die, by the way.
Biker just so happens to be in the same masked maniac boat as Jacket, and was trying to find the source of the phone calls. There are actually two endings to Biker's story but there will be no spoilers of that here.

Mafia III is an exercise in tedium.
The first couple of hours are decent, then the story grinds to a halt as the player is tasked with taking over different rackets and districts of the city. This makes up the large majority of the game, and involves you driving between repetitive, filler-tier activities that take less time to complete than it does to drive over to them.
It's a shame, because the handful of properly-designed missions that are in the game are fairly decent. The combat is pretty slick, the enemies have good hit reactions to gunfire, and the gunfights can be quite fast-paced with the mouse and keyboard controls. Most of the gunfights in the game will last about thirty seconds to a minute though, considering the repetitive racket-takeover missions make up most of the time.
The game has a fair number of bugs, too. A few times I'd have to restart missions from a checkpoint because it bugged out and I couldn't progress. If you shoot and kill an enemy near a railing, they'll play an animation where they fall over the railing, but they'd often freeze at the point where the canned animation was supposed to transition to ragdoll physics, so they'd end up suspended in mid-air. If you have police chasing you and you call in the favour to get rid of the cops, they'll literally disappear right in front of you.
The optimisation is an issue, also. In my experience, they actually fixed the game up and had it running quite well through post-launch patches, but with the latest update (the one that introduces racing and car customisation), they seem to have reverted all of these optimisations and the game runs like crap again. You can't roll-back to previous builds through Steam either, so the only way to play the game with good performance now is to download a cracked version of the last build, which is absolutely ridiculous.
Overall, on the plus side - the game has a nice soundtrack and world; decent characters and acting; and good combat. On the other hand, there are only a few good missions hidden amongst 30 - 40 hours of absolute tedium; there are bugs; and the latest build screwed up the performance.
Would only recommend this if you can get it super cheap, and you're willing to accept the risk of possibly slipping in to a coma from mind-numbingly boring missions.

Dark Crusade was, in my opinion, the best game of the Dawn of War series. It gave players more freedom than the previous two games with its multiple factions, while not suffering from the recycled concepts and poor storyline/voice acting of Soulstorm. The RISK style dynamic is one that I have found inherently fascinating, and one that I hope that Total War: Warhammer will exploit in the future. My personal highlight of the game, and probably the series overall, were the stronghold assaults. With entertaining storylines and objectives that make it feel very much like a special mission in the tabletop game, I found them to be a refreshing and rewarding experience. My one gripe is what seems to have been faction favouritism amongst the production team. Multiplayer combat is made less enjoyable when people play as the Eldar, and make their webway gate invisible, warping it all over the map, and forcing you to adopt time-consuming  strategies to beat. Overall, however, the game rates among my personal favourite RTSs.

Well... This game is literally crazy, I've had it for awhile now and haven't really played a whole lot of it, but of what I have it just is really different from most games that are out there.
Basic premise is.. from the title, DEFCON stands for DEFense readiness CONdition, a military concept for alert readiness for the Armed Forces.
As such, this tasks you with playing on a realistic representation of a global worldmap in a region of the world and places you in the position of basically that countries nuclear armed arsenal.
And then.. game plays out as if the world is going through the real-life DEFCON countdown which ranges from 5 the lowest state or nominal/normal, all the way down to 1 which means Nuclear War is about to ruin your day. It gets crazy at that point, with nukes passing by each other in the sky waving to each other as they are about to warm-up a couple million people. Yes, crazy but for some reason also fun in a morbid way.

It's a littley funny, because there is this option to change speed of AI turn to high and it turns off animations. I do think the game has potential, so if you are not sure, remember you can try and ask for refund if you don't like it (which I'm going to do now).

Paladins has healers but that isn't their job, their job is to deal damage just like every other character in the game, and healing in this is primarily focussed around getting out of combat quickly and essentially " retreating ", as you regenerate HP from inactivity from combat.

Well i have been trying to think of a review for this game for a long while. I have even been encouraged to do one by the developers and i genuinely think they take criticism on the nose and act on it. They're good developers, i like them. Though as a disclaimer i use to like the BoE (Battle of Empire) devs too until they screwed up so....Take that with a grain of salt i guess.
Anyway on with the review.
For starters i'll look at it's aesthetic and how nice it looks, mostly because that's what i see first on the store page. And it can be very, very misleading sometimes, for better or worse. So how does the game look? it looks like a top down 2D strategy game (as you can probably guess). When actually playing the game it looks pretty good, it looks how it does on the store page and even has a few nice little details here and there, it looks nice for what it is. If i had a complaint it would be that i think they could go even further with the details but we're talking tiny, usually not noticable things here, it looks fine as it is.
I couldn't really think of anywhere else to put this so it'll tie the graphics and gameplay segments together. It looks like Warhammer 40K and XCOM had a baby. It shares the gameplay of XCOM (with a top down 2D view) and even the perma death (at normal difficulty and above only, i think). The Warhammer 40K part comes in just from the lore and its general look. This, keep in mind, is not a rip off of either game and it only looks like it was inspired from it. The gameplay itself is your standard squad based turn based strategy game in the same vein as XCOM. Most of it actually feels a lot like the XCOM except with some functional differences. There isn't any cover (sadly) but there are tiles that boost your defense or your weapon range. There is melee combat as well which opens up a few new possibilities. The level design is pretty good as well, layouts are good, squad loadouts and levelling up is also pretty nice, it lets you play how you want for the most part.
Audio is fantastic, i love the soundtrack for the game, the weapons sound a little weak (in my opinion) but other than the plasma rifle's its ok for the most part. Not a lot to say here as its all ok at least and fantastic at best.
Bugs, glitches and optimisation. I haven't noticed any bugs, i don't think i've even seen reports about them or any wide spread problems on systems. The optimisation is pretty good. It shouldn't be hard to get a game like this optimised due to how little it actually uses of my system but hey, worth mentioning.
Extra comments or thing's i think should be said: the game is pretty awesome, i finished it in around 20 hours. Will add any more edits or thoughts as time goes on and i play it more.

Templar Battleforce is a game where you guide your
Templar Knights  through a campaign figthing against
xenos,
cultists, and... Yes, this is indeed like playing a squad-based Warhammer 40k tactics rpg.
Your Templars are very much like the Space Marines of the Warhammer universe: the enjoyment of slaughter, the willingness to die, and the massive suits of power armor. However, unlike Space Marines, they can be women too. And that's about the only difference.
The story is mediocre, centering around colonizing a new system and fighting off xenos and cultists, but provides a few intersting moments. It is a squad-based tactics rpg though, so story is put on a backburner to the combat, which is... alright.
Combat is by far the better part of the game. Multiple classes, most of which actually do use different tactics and even feel different. The Soldier/Neptune and Berseker/Paladin basically play the same except that Paladins can heal. Scouts move fast and hit with snipers, Engineers can fortify and build turrets, soldiers overwatch, hydras can create lakes of fire to limit enemy movement. All this makes choosing who you use and how you use them an actual challenge, especially in the missions with tight corridors.
Unfortunately, that really is all there is to say about this game. It's an enjoyable play of squad tactics and provides quite a bit of fun. On the harder difficulties, your squad members die permanently, but you can recruit replacements any time, so that makes it pretty pointless. If you enjoy tactics games, this is worth a playthrough, though probably pick it up on sale rather than full price.

Shadows on the Vatican Act II: Wrath 2015 is sequel to the point-and-click 3d fully voiced adventure Act 1 of the Shadows on the Vatican series. This game while almost as short if not shorter than the first game, is rage inducing. I never know an adventure game can be this frustrating. If you scroll through all the recent negative reviews you will see the phrase "trial and error" quite a lot, and they are correct to use that phrase to describe this game. This game, while looking a bit prettier than the first game, is insufferable. For example there is a scene where you need to tie some kind of knot by looking at the pictures to tie it correctly, first you see 3 pictures of the start of three different kinds of knot, you pick one, and then you are shown 3 more pictures to choose from, and then you pick one of them again, and then the game tells you you are wrong, and then you are back to the first set of three pictures to choose, and this whole thing you have to choose correctly for 4 times, so it is basically 3 x 3 x 3 x 3 that is almost 81 clicking, you will not have to click exactly 81 times because when you are wrong at the second or the third set you will go back to the first but it is just as maddening, and every click waste you 1 to 3 seconds.
