This game was interesting, i've been looking for a game like Tenchu for years now and this caught my eye. but ultimately i believe it is not worth the money (£14.99 when i bought it) due to a number of reasons:
Firstly let me point out where this game went well
[Pros]
-Amazing art style: The game looks beautiful and i believe it will age very well.
-Mechanically interesting: The Shadow mechanic which is used to maneuver and stay hidden, while also gaining power is done perfectly in my opinion.
-Sound and Music: Very good audio cues and traditional japanese music make a nice environment.
On the other hand, the negatives i feel make this game not worth the price
[Cons]
-Short: This game is short, when i mean short, im saying i 100%ed this game in 10 hours, completed every achievement as well as every optional mission complete objective for all 13 missions. My fastest time to complete a level was 7 minutes and i feel that this is a disgustingly weak part of the game.
-Repetitive: This game can be completed simply by either teleporting in a straight line to the next objective (and when i say straight line i mean STRAIGHT), waiting 5 seconds for a guard to move from an orb that blocks the next location. Hitting that orb and moving to the next area. If you are trying to kill every enemy in the missions, its simply teleport behind them, kill, rinse and repeat. Or leading them into a room around the corner, kill, repeat.
-Extremely Easy Difficulty: Every enemy in this game either suffers from cataracts or a severe case of short sight. As long as you stay crouched and teleport around with the use of the shadows, you can be 10 feet infront of any enemy on a bright sunny day. If they do spot you, its simply a quick teleport away and recover. Because of this, the developers put an excessive amount of enemies in an area that just adds to the time of progressing through the level. Once you have unlocked the upgrade to your Bird, you can locate all scrolls in the game, ultimately destroying any level of exploration or fun regarding secrets.
-Lack Luster Boss missions: It just involves the same mechanic of teleporting behind them for a stealth kill just repeated 3 times with a slight alteration of an aeriel kill on the second hit. The final boss is no different but i believe it is 5 times instead.
-Uninteresting Story: the story was generally uninteresting and a bit rushed in my opinion, i believe this is partly due to the shortness of the game and how vague the plot is through out, besides at the end where the plot just begins to open up and i feel that the game could have alot more depth... But it ends. The character development was terrible, what felt like simply throwing characters existences in to give some reason as to why you even exist in the first place. The origins of the Aragami were a good idea to begin with but wasn't correctly followed through.
-2nd to last mission: This mission takes what ive just said about difficulty and doesn't make it harder, it makes it frustrating. Being sniped continously while trying to kill everyone in the map is the most hair pullingly rage inducing thing i've experienced in this game. 85% of my deaths in my 10 hour run were in the last 40 minutes it took me to complete this game under those conditions. IT ISN'T FUN as a mechanic, I see where the developers were going, but i don't believe it fits with the theme by having an aimbotting archer continually rain sweet justice down on the Stealth Assassin that hasn't been spotted or killed anyone since the first mission began. To say, it ruined my immersion.
[IN CONCLUSION]
The game is fun and very pretty, I definitely enjoyed myself but it shouldn't be classed as a full game. If you came here expecting something difficult and gritty, you are only met with hand holding, mediocre challenges and repetition. The story needed a revision and for the price that is requested I wouldn't buy this again if i knew everything i know now.

Imagine if Worms Armageddon was made in 1991, was real-time, and used ducks as their mascot species.
This is an incredibly fun couch-multiplayer game with so much charm, my attack went down sharply (eyyy, unnecessary Pokemon puns... I'm here all week). The weapons are varied, unique, and each have some kind of disadvantage. The pre-made maps are well constructed and feel different from one to another. There is just a button for quacking and a ton of weird hats and masks you could wear.
This is a game where you could practice all day and all night, but still get beaten by someone who only played this game once. More times than not, the winner of a round is the person who didn't participate in the battle.
There's even a map maker, an instant-include in any amazing multiplayer game. Timesplitters had it; Halo 3+ had it; Duck Game has it.
Duck Game may be one of the only retro indie games that goes for a Sega Genesis vibe. The soundtrack and effects sound like they came straight out of Kid Chameleon (excluding the gun sound effects). Far too few retro indie game use that dank guitar sound.
Generally, this game is worth every penny. $12-14 is well worth the night(s) of fun you and your friends will have with this. Even if you have no friends, the singleplayer's pretty decent (although, it's mostly training for multiplayer).

Wrath continues the political thriller that was set up in the first episode of this four-part point ‘n’ click series. While the episode tries to tell us more about its cast of characters, it also came at the cost of the plot not really moving too much from where we left off.
Episodic adventure games can be a little risky to buy, but in the case of Shadows on the Vatican, we can always say that the premise is good enough to invest in the series.
The story’s second Act, Wrath, starts right off where Greed ended: a female assassin called Sylvia literally drops into the life of our ex-priest protagonist, James, so they can—reluctantly—join forces against their unknown foes.
While the store description really tries to sell Sylvia as the new lead, in reality she is only in a secondary support role. The game still mostly follows the investigation of James, as he slowly discovers that maybe the financial crime he is trying to get the bottom of leads deeper than to the bowels of the Roman Mafia.
How deep? We only learn a little bit, since the plot is a lot thinner this time around, putting more focus on smaller point ‘n’ click puzzle segments and the cast. I have to admit, it was nice to know a little bit more about the characters, but I hope that the story will finally start to pick up in the third quarter; because as of now, we are still just setting up the promise of a thriller without most of the actual thriller itself.

Wondering why a game was made illegal to own in Australia just days after it was announced? Check out this game. This game is why.
You take on the role of what would appear to be a serial killer who gets phone calls vaguely telling him where to go every day. You go there, kill everything and everyone, and eventually go home for some top ramen and to sleep.
The music is great, compliments the game fantastically. It's constantly pushing you forward, into the carnage, rather than simply accompanying it. It's almost like you want to keep fighting, and killing, as fast as possible so as to not let the music down.
The gameplay itself is brutally unforgiving, but not impossible. The names of the game are Speed and Brutality. The enemies all drop just as easily as you do, and you'll never forget it. You'll replay a couple of stages a dozen or more times, until you really are a homocidal psychopath, but when you finally break that final skull, you will feel such a wave of vindication and relief that the MONSTERS who took up like TWENTY MINUTES OF YOUR GAME TIME are FINALLY GONE that it will have all been worth it.
The story is... confusing. You'll never really know what's going on, and that's the point. Every bit of the story is engineered to be piecemeal, as though you're watching a movie with all the opening scenes and dialogue cut out with drunk goggles on. Figuring out what the hell is going on is a game in and of itself, and you're best off spending that time after you've beaten the game. Until then, just treat it as mindless carnage. You're better off not trying to solve the puzzle until you have all the pieces.
Overall? Great game. A tad short for the full asking price, but if you can pick it up on sale, you have no excuse not to. This is one of those games EVERYONE should play through, or at least know about.

Ah, Hotline Miami.
It's a top-down shooter with lots of gore, lots of action, lots of badass music, and lots of confusing plot. But that's okay.
You're a guy (who is named Jacket by the fans and eventually by everyone) who lives in an alternate 1989 Miami who suddenly starts to get phone calls and a rooster mask. Totally not weird at all.
So, you obey the voices, and end up going on a slaughter spree that costs 307 Russian mobsters their lives. (I got the kill count from the Hotline Miami wiki, by the way.)
Along the way, you rescue some hooker who then becomes your girlfriend, you lucky ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, an old friend of yours with a nice beard gives you free movies, pizzas, and drinks, and you find three people with animal masks; Richard, Don Juan, and Rasmus.
Richard's a cryptic sonuva♥♥♥♥♥, Don Juan is actually nice to you sometimes, but Rasmus hates you. That's okay, because I don't like Rasmus either.
Richard asks you four questions, makes three predictions, and then eventually tells you that none of your actions matter because you're a bloody idiot. At least he sticks with you until the end.
Some assclown named Richter eventually shows up but I'm not spoiling anymore. Play for yourself.
Combat. Whew, this part's the best. You've got a pretty big variety of weapons to use, but not all guns are found on some levels. For example, you probably won't find the Silenced Pistol until the chapter Deadline. However, if you get crazy good scores on levels, you'll unlock more and more weapons, from hammers, to Skorpion SMGs, to beer cans that you can throw at people.
You die incredibly fast in Hotline Miami. But so do your enemies. One stray bullet from an Uzi can mean certain death, so rushing into rooms with an assault rifle really isn't a good idea. Guns make lots of noise, too. Melee weapons are much, much quieter.
You'll have to use guns sometimes, though. Just manage your ammo, but you may want to use the Peter mask if you love guns but don't want to have the entire map flocking to you.
There are boss fights every few chapters, and of course there's one at the end of Jacket's storyline.
Surprise, surprise, though, you get to play as Biker, who's actually the first boss fight in Jacket's story. Neither Biker nor Jacket die, by the way.
Biker just so happens to be in the same masked maniac boat as Jacket, and was trying to find the source of the phone calls. There are actually two endings to Biker's story but there will be no spoilers of that here.

NecroDancer is a great rhythm-based Rogue-like where you take turns to the beat of the music.  Miss a beat, everything around you takes a turn anyway. The main challenge is balancing keeping the beat up with putting yourself in a good position to deal with whatever comes at you.  You need either quick decision-making or good muscle memory from repeated plays to deal with complex situations.
Unreservedly recommend it once the game is completed.  $15 for early access is alright, but you'll probably have to be interested in the concept beforehand to feel fully happy about your $15.

Tl:dr; Many games like to try and wear the "easy to learn, hard to master" hat. Crypt of the NecroDancer is one of the titles that wears that hat like a ♥♥♥♥in' champ.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is a rythm game. No wait; it's a roguelike. No wait; it's both. It's a procedurally-generated labyrinth in which your actions come in pace with the music. It's an absolutely superlative example of the best Early Access has to offer; oodles of content that's already more than playable, and promising to only get better as time goes on.
You play as Cadence, a novice gravedigger (I think; it's not really important) who makes one shovel cut in the wrong place too many. Now your still-beating heart has been stolen. Turns out this isn't as fatal as you'd expect, and it even means you can't die permanently, but it HAS made you a Slave to the Rythm(TM). Can you make it through the NecroDancer's lair in order to kill him and reclaim your heart? Or will you be a slave to the rythm for all eternity?
Everything in the NecroDancer's crypts moves and acts to the beat of the music. You can use your own MP3s for this, but the included soundtrack from Danny Baranowsky is so awesome you won't need to. Mastering the beat of the music is the key to victory in this game.
Remember when I said Crypt rocks the "easy to learn, hard to master" hat like a boss? This is why. Moving with the beat is one of those things which is very easy to wrap your head around, but mastering the beat is a whole other story. It's a simple concept executed flawlessly, made all the more satisfying by the fact that it makes you angry in the exact right way - with yourself. Harm comes because YOU screwed up. Failure becomes because YOU screwed up. At no point does the game throw anything at you that you can't deal with - or at least, can't learn to deal with it. We can all name dozens of games that are plain broken, where often failure comes because either the game did a whoopsie in its pants or because the random number generator decided it hates your face. Crypt doesn't do that. There's only one thing Crypt will get you angry with; yourself. And that makes it so very compelling. When you fail, you want to do better. You want to get back in there and get further - to wipe away the shame of your earlier failure. Before you know it, you're hooked.
Speaking of which... I need to find a new vein so I can get another hit of this delicious juju.

Its the best multiplayer strategy fps hybrid game on the market. It is also the only fps game that can truly call itself a strategic mutliplayer FPS game, no other fps game comes even close. The game is all, and I mean 100% all, about skill, strategy, and on your feet tactical decision making.
The game has a steep learning curve, but there are rookie only servers and tons of guides and tutorials so you will not be overwhelmed unless you intentionally try to not learn. In order to play, you have to be able to hear other's voice commands, and you are missing half the game if you yourself do not have a microphone, it really is that strategic and cooperative focused. The game also does assymetrical warfare in a great way, and it stays feeling fresh and fun for hundreds of hours.
The community can be hit or miss, largely dependant on the specific servers and the moderators. The majority are great, some cater to specific players (ie competitive), and a small number are toxic trash.
If you ever want strategy in your FPS or action in your RTS this is the only game for you.
BUT. If we are being honest here. The game is dead. The game is still being updated and supported, but there are ot enough concurrent players to ensure that there are even always servers up and people to play with, and at peak players you will only get to choose between maybe a dozen different servers if you are lucky. If the cost of this game is not a factor for you (ie cheap sale or something), or if you think that this sounds like an amazing game for you then I suggest that you do pick up the game and try it out.
Overall, time has come and passed and this game, as amazing as it is, should be relegated to the dustbin of "games that were" as we look to the future. Not that I want the game to be removed of course, I and many others still enjoy it and will hold on as long as we can.

I try to be an optimist in my life as much as possible. I don’t find it enjoyable to be a pessimist and be cynical about everything. That’s why I’m going to try and look at Mafia III as a glass-half-full kind of game. The good parts of Mafia are really tremendous but the bad parts are equally as frustrating.
Mafia III follows the, dare I say it, “underrated” Mafia II released in 2010. Mafia II followed the story of Vito Scaletta as he rose through the ranks of the mob and told a really compelling and gripping story. The narrative was tight with great characters but had one nearly universal criticism; the gameplay. Mafia II was an open world game that didn’t need to be open world. There were prolonged amounts of having to drive from point A to B with no real reason to do so. You couldn’t interact with the rest of the world and there was nothing else to see, so it was literally just a waste of time. Unfortunately, Mafia III follows this same path.
Mafia III takes place in fictional Louisiana in 1968, with the biracial, Vietnam vet Lincoln Clay in the lead role. That’s a lot to digest right there; late 60’s, racism, the Vietnam War. Mafia III puts a whole heck of a lot on its plate and attempts to finish it all. I would say that the devs at Hangar 13 do quite a deft job of navigating the themes and issues of the time while taking them head on without beating you over the head with it or coming off as offensive. Their depiction of racism during this time is done in a believable way. Yes, there is a gratuitous amount of racial slurs thrown around, but as the disclaimer at the beginning of the game says, it’s done to be accurate to the times and not to diminish or shy away from what people went through.
The characterization in Mafia III is really great, giving you characters you can empathize with as well as ones that you loathe. They give Lincoln Clay an interesting backstory and mostly make great use of it in a revenge story that doesn’t feel cliché.
Mafia III’s story provides a great foundation yet it’s the game’s design that really shows its cracks. Now I know that game design is a tough job and I don’t want to come across like an armchair quarterback but the mission designer really dropped the ball here. With the exception of a handful, the majority of the mission structures in Mafia are exactly the same. You need to weaken a Racket so you go to [insert building here] and either kill or interrogate the boss at that site as well as destroy any contraband and take any money that’s there. While there are permutations and different settings, that’s effectively what the game is. I think it goes without saying that it can get a tad bit monotonous. Thankfully, the gunplay and the stealth are good enough that you can mix up and vary your play style to keep things from getting stale. I was specifically impressed by how viable of an option the stealth was, which is almost unheard of in a GTA-style open world game. There were numerous missions where I ghosted the whole place and didn’t fire a single shot.
The other design choice that left me scratching my head was no fast travel. It’s 2016, what the hell. Now I’m not necessarily for games being easier, I know some people appreciate hard games, but what I have little to no tolerance for is a game that wastes my time. The developers here seemingly left out fast travel for no other reason than to pad the game’s length. Much like Mafia II, there’s no reason for me to stop anywhere while I’m driving to a destination. My eyes nearly got stuck the amount of times I rolled them back as the game wanted me to go from one side of the map to the other. That’s simply insulting to me as a consumer. I will say though that the driving is damn fun. Perhaps the best open world driving I’ve experienced. So while I may have complaints with the lack of fast travel, having to drive everywhere didn’t really wear on me until the very end because the car handling was so sublime.
Mafia III was a game that I was hoping would be in my GOTY discussion. Sadly, it’s not there and it’s not even particularly close. But that does not mean that it’s a bad game. The narrative and the characters that are presented are top notch and are what kept me coming back and driving (literally) through the so-so gameplay to reach its finale. I recommend people play Mafia III because, without sounding trite, it’s a bold and brave move for a AAA game to have a black protagonist and deal with the themes and issues that it does. But with that recommendation comes a caveat; know what you’re getting into. If you think that the nature of the mission structure will not bother you, then there is a ton of fun to be had here. Is it worth $60? Absolutely not, but if you can get it around $20 then I think there’s enough there to satisfy. I wouldn’t have played it for 23 hours had I not enjoyed it.

In my mind this is the best expansion in the Warhammer 40,000 Dawn of War franchise. Dawn of War vanilla was good, yes, but its only drawback was the short single player campaign.
Dark Crusade's single player campaign is designed like a Risk map, where you get a province on a planet and have to wrest control of the planet from the other 6 races (Space Marines, Chaos, Orks, Eldar, Imperial Guard, Tau and Necrons). In each province you have to buiold a base and then destroy the other faction's base. The more provinces you take, the more perks you get for your army (production bonuses, armor for your commander, veteran squads to boost your amry, etc.). It lacks a bit in story, but taking a enemy fortress allows for some narrative.
Again, it is in the multiplayer or skirmish games where this game shines (don't take my word for it based on the amount of hours I played - I already bought the Dawn of War box set and played the crap out of it - for the Emperor!)

How do I give a clear picture as to how good this game is?
Before installing this game I never really cared much for Warhammer 40,000.  Assumed that it was an overratted series the internet hype way to much.  Merely bought this because it was on sale for a cheap price and so far the reviews are saying the game is good.
After installing and spending three hours of this game: HOLY ♥♥♥♥ING♥♥♥♥♥♥  WHY DIDN'T I GET INTO THIS SERIES BACK IN HIGH SCHOOL!?!  NOW I WANT PUNCH PAST ME IN THE FACE FOR SAYING ONLY NECKBEARDS CAN ENJOY SUCH A GLORIOUS SERIES AS WARHAMMER 40K!!!!
Now for the actually  review:
- As an expansion to the Dawn of War game, Dark Crusade live up to title of being the best of the four games.
- The gameplay is easy to understand but a challenge to get a hang of as difficulty varies based on what army you are going up against.
- The graphics aged well for a sixth generation game, especially when running on a lower processing machine not built for gaming.
- The sounds are great whether it is the epic music the plays in the background or the ham infested voice acting of the characters in the games (mostly the latter, a game this over the top must have Brian Blessed level of ham).
- The community for the game is friendly and would love to do a match or two (fair warning, you may wanna buy the previous two games of Dawn of War to be able to play all the armies).
- The campaign is awesome and open ended for its Risk-style of settings and RPG-esque rewards it gives out for successful battles.
- Customization is awesome as you can color your army in any way you want.
- And lets not forget the mods!  If you are not getting any satisfaction from this game whether it is gameplay not akin to the original tabletop or a race you want to play isn't in the game, there is a mod that improves the game.
So in short if you are a fan of the tabletop game, this is a pretty good representation of the game it is based on and a must have.  If not, not only is it a good standalone game but also one that would make you a fan of the series real fast.

Lo and behold one day we got our grubby hands on EDF 2017. we both together spent at least 300 hours on the game. we never beat it on inferno. that being said, I was excited for this game to come out. after quite a few hours of play, i have come up with two reviews. first one is for long time EDF players, second is for newcomers to the franchise, behold the reviews underneath.
Newcomer review
Pros:
-giant bugs to shoot and kill
-many different unique weapons, including some useless unique ones
-four classes each with their own unique weapos. perks, and skills
-robots
-not your average shooter
-funny comentary
-good replay value

Cons
-gameplay may be repetative especially if you use the same weapons over and over

-cant use all weapons with all classes
-short story
Long time EDF players
Pros
-nostalgia
-new enemies
-new maps
Cons
Okay, before i get into cons, these are for those who specifically want that old nostalgic feel. there will be a lot
-classes. you cant use all weapons with all classes and it loses that feeling of you being just a soldier amongst the ranks
-weapons arent that unique compared to 2017. no assult rifles that have 999 rounds, about as accurate as a political campaign and deals massive damage. no more 100m blast radius rockets. etc.
-hectors dont flinch. i used to spray them just to keep the bullets away, now all you can do is run
-wasps. f*cking wasps. all they do is fly so fast they give you a headache and they have lots of health.
-ant hills dont die after shooting them. you have to plant bombs. bloody annoying when you have 150 ants around you squirting acid and your plant gets reset.
-vehicles are garbage, but even worse than 2017 garbage
-explosions hurt you. no more running into the center of the explosion to pick up the weapons crate
-what a terrible campaign. so short, story is terrible, and levels arent unique. no underground, no beach, just city maps.
overall, great game for newcomers to the series. if you play the game you will LOVE it, but then will wonder just how much better the others can be. if you have an xbox, i recommend you pick up 2017 immediately.

If you haven't played Binding of Isaac yet, I don't know what's wrong with you. It grows on you. It grows like a fungus, starting out as a dark smudge on your mind that frustrates you as you die, over and over again, before even reaching "the end." Later, when you reach the boss, you will find you've been infected, the smudge has become a wart, and the end you thought you sought is farther than you knew. The wart takes roots in your mind, you find that it will not be removed, and it festers and takes over your being as you confront what you originally thought were Isaac's demons, but turn out to be the darkest minions within your own psyche.
Deep within this game are statements about child abuse, religious fundamentalism, neglect, narcisstic parents, and childhood pain and suffering. But this game balances art with entertainment better than many indie titles - the themes will haunt you, but the gameplay will keep you addicted.
I started out by suggesting there was something wrong with you if you hadn't play this. Truthfully, you may be alright. You may be better off never playing this... but then you're missing out on something special. Dark, but special.

NecroDancer is a great rhythm-based Rogue-like where you take turns to the beat of the music.  Miss a beat, everything around you takes a turn anyway. You need either quick decision-making or good muscle memory from repeated plays to deal with complex situations.
Unreservedly recommend it once the game is completed.  $15 for early access is alright, but you'll probably have to be interested in the concept beforehand to feel fully happy about your $15.

Tl:dr; Many games like to try and wear the "easy to learn, hard to master" hat. Crypt of the NecroDancer is one of the titles that wears that hat like a ♥♥♥♥in' champ.
Crypt of the NecroDancer is a rythm game. No wait; it's a roguelike. No wait; it's both. It's a procedurally-generated labyrinth in which your actions come in pace with the music. It's an absolutely superlative example of the best Early Access has to offer; oodles of content that's already more than playable, and promising to only get better as time goes on.
You play as Cadence, a novice gravedigger (I think; it's not really important) who makes one shovel cut in the wrong place too many. Now your still-beating heart has been stolen. Turns out this isn't as fatal as you'd expect, and it even means you can't die permanently, but it HAS made you a Slave to the Rythm(TM). Can you make it through the NecroDancer's lair in order to kill him and reclaim your heart? Or will you be a slave to the rythm for all eternity?
Everything in the NecroDancer's crypts moves and acts to the beat of the music. You can use your own MP3s for this, but the included soundtrack from Danny Baranowsky is so awesome you won't need to. Mastering the beat of the music is the key to victory in this game.
Remember when I said Crypt rocks the "easy to learn, hard to master" hat like a boss? This is why. Moving with the beat is one of those things which is very easy to wrap your head around, but mastering the beat is a whole other story. It's a simple concept executed flawlessly, made all the more satisfying by the fact that it makes you angry in the exact right way - with yourself. Harm comes because YOU screwed up. Failure becomes because YOU screwed up. At no point does the game throw anything at you that you can't deal with - or at least, can't learn to deal with it. We can all name dozens of games that are plain broken, where often failure comes because either the game did a whoopsie in its pants or because the random number generator decided it hates your face. Crypt doesn't do that. There's only one thing Crypt will get you angry with; yourself. And that makes it so very compelling. When you fail, you want to do better. You want to get back in there and get further - to wipe away the shame of your earlier failure. Before you know it, you're hooked.
Speaking of which... I need to find a new vein so I can get another hit of this delicious juju.

Natural Selection 2 hit a draught in the gaming industry, the market was overflooded with yearly titles and streamlined content. Along came a stand alone sequel to one of the greatest mods to Half-Life 1.
It launched with an editor. This was a HUGE deal at the time. You didn't have the option of the free UE4 Engine,  and all of the major titles on the market were booming the DLC deal.
Player retention hasn't been good in Natural Selection 2, but the game deserve so much more play than it does. One of the reasons is that it's an old school titel, with roots in the mindset of the hl1 times. Getting good as either marine or alien takes time and practice, also a fair bit of knowledge, and on top of that you have the commander aspect which is basicly an RTS game with real players (some may act like AI's).
Not many players has the patience of old times, where people would defrag in a mod for Quake3, for weeks, only to outrick their opponents movement wise the in their matches.
TLDR:
- Getting gud is hard. (like in the old days)
- The game is awesome and have one of the best communities of all time, who are all happy to help / teach new players.
- Active forum / steam community.
- All it really needs is more players.

Counter-Strike meets Starcraft.
Natural Selection is the single most thrilling, most competitive first person shooter I have ever played since the release of its Half-Life 1 mod in the mid 2000s. Sure, Battlefield delivers large-scale modern warfare in life-like graphics and SFX, but it fails nonetheless (like any other FPS I could think of) to implement half incredible teamplay potential that Natural Selection does!
Basically, you have a team of marines on one side of the map and an alien Hive on the other. The alien Hive is where the eggs spawn, and the aliens will aim to optimally build three or more Hives to unlock all their upgrades and reach full strength. It's up to the marines to eliminate the aliens before the situation spins out of control.
The game goes by controlling the map's resource nodes (scattered evenly between the 8-12 rooms that make up each map) in order to unlock higher weapons/lifeforms and upgrades faster, and ultimately kill all the enemy's command structures (the alien Hive or marine Command Center). And what makes it so full of heat is how quickly a single move could change the tide of battle! Both teams have structures made for quick commuting: teleporters for marines and underground tunnels for aliens. If used correctly, your entire team could be in the enemy base in less than 20 seconds.
Normally, the marines have to set up and DEFEND teleporters at Hive entrance chokepoints to suffocate the aliens by constantly teleporting in and damaging the Hive while preventing the aliens from scattering all over the map. The aliens on the other hand are better at sneak attacks; eliminating lonely marine resource nodes and setting up "sneaky tunnels."
When the aliens successfully lay a tunnel to the marine base undetected, their whole team could be in the marine base in less than 15 seconds! And then it's up to the marine commander to trigger the Distress Beacon to teleport all marines back in time or else the base would be overrun. But even when the base is defended successfully, the aliens will usually utilize this mass relocation of the marines to eliminate their structures somewhere else on the map!
The aliens also have the choice whether to destroy the marine structures in each room or to aim for the power node, which, once broken, conceals the room in pitch black darkness and disables all marine structures in it. Up until the red emergency lights come online, the only thing any rines in the room can see is whatever crosses the thin strip of flashlight that they have.

Short summary this game is a brilliant squad turn-based RPG. One of the best ones in my opinion.
You have a RP system, earned for completing deployments. These are used to unlock new classes and upgraded weapons/armour/talents across a massive talent tree. There are 8 classes total including the captain.
All templars earn xp, which is used to upgrade stats. They also earn points to apply to talents. A nice and interesting feature is they earn 'wargear' points. The higher this is the better the gear they can equip.
Loadouts can be changed at any time, none of the weapons/armour/gear cost anything, once they are unlocked you have them.
There is a nice variety of enemies trying to separate your limbs and the levels, even though turn based are really tense.
There is too many features to list them all here, from the tact points, reinforcements and the excellent overwatch system.
You get attached to your customised templars and beg for miracles when one is getting swarmed.
The campaign is long, I don't feel like I've even scratched the surface of it. It is full of choices, go this way? Help these people? The game/story is well written and it's an interesting universe the devs have created. The art is actually quite nice, and  you can zoom in close during battles. The sound is well done and it really adds to the atmosphere.
The devs are really active, really supporting their games and easy to communicate with.
Honestly I couldn't recommend this game higher, it's a bargain at it's price.
The game has complex systems at work in the background but it is really easy to understand and learn.
Do youself a favour and pick this one up, it's an overlooked gem for sure.

I love this game.
This easily compares to the experience of the SNES Front Mission game. The writing is beautiful space-knight chivalry and politics, and works well into the scenario design. There are many levels of difficulty, no doubt there's one that's right for most any player.
The interface design can be a little overbearing with the visual bluntness of it, however it's very intuitive.
This is a game with somewhat complicated mechanics going on in the statistics, and it also fully explains all of them. Contrasting this with many other games that leave the players in the dark about finer points for the sake of appearing simple, this game spells out all its rules for the player in the help area.
The tactical play is solid. Templars have battle armor that generates heat with every move and action, and dissipates every turn. They take damage from overheating and lose access to some abilities, so this is literally a set of rules where "every move counts".
There may be a nuance or two that leave something to be desired for some people. The permadeath is relatively gentle and squishy - new recruits are free and infinite outside of battle, come at a percentage of captain level (depending on difficulty setting), and can be respec'd and redesigned freely - so you never really "lose" a soldier, just some negligible amounts of experience(perhaps less negligible on harder settings). The soldiers in your roster are just ready-to-deploy sets of specs and loadouts so you don't have to use the random stuff on new recruits in battle(though that'd be an interesting alternate way to play).
One might also say that some of the 8 soldier classes are too similar. Three of them are just gunners - gunners that are mostly offensive, gunners that are strictly offensive and use flame attacks(though the fire trails can be defensive), and gunners that emphasize overwatch, grenades and buffs. Many of the classes have limited gear options and the choice isn't about how you build that class, just using it or not (gee, do I want my guy that generates a lot of heat to have gear granting greater max heat? yeah probably). Other classes have a big variety of useful abilities and it pays to have two of them that are specialized differently, so it feels like some of the classes got the short end of the design effort.
Despite this I do NOT think the tactical decision making in the game leaves anything to be desired, the choices all impact the game. I find myself agonizing over the simplest stat growth choices.
Anyway, this game has far exceeded expectations, and I've played my share of XCom, FFT, and etc. I think it will please anyone who doesn't have strong preferences about the nuances of the genre, and rather is open to the design choices of individual games. This game's choices work really well for it, in my opinion.

I have owned this game for three and a half years and it's come a long way.
First of all, this is exactly what it looks like: A hybrid FPS/RTS game of two unequal factions, Aliens (Kharaa) and Marines (TSF).
The Marines have the classic long range weapons, grenades, big♥♥♥♥♥Exo suits and some kind of sonic artillery.
The aliens on the other hand are mostly fast moving units that do most of their damage in melee range. There are five lifeforms and each of them has several abilities.
Where does the RTS come in? Every team has one player that is the commander, and views the map from above just like a RTS game. There are ressources to be captured and defended, buildings to be built and upgrades to be researched, which help your team in the fight. A good commander will tell the team what to do, where to push, which areas to hold etc. Both commanders have abilities that benefit the team in the fight, for example the marine commander can throw medpacks or ammo anywhere on the map, while the alien commander can disturb marine vision, or make the aliens attack faster for a short time.
The game has built in voice for the very essential communication with your team. As this game started itself as a Half Life mod, it has strong built in mod support, and several highly customized mods that can be played. There is constanly new content pushed in form of skins (to support the developer) and maps from the community.
The visuals are really awesome. When the aliens take over a room they infest it with their green stuff, turn off the power so instead there is emergency light, and their buildings look somewhat squirmy and alienesque. Attacking such a room as a marine with flamethrowers, rail guns, and all the awesome techy stuff while coordinating with your team over voicechat is a deeply engaging experience and something truely unique in gaming today.
Now, where are the problems of this game? Originally it was designed for 6v6. One of each team being the commander means there are a measly 5v5 players in a siege situation like described above, which in reality aren't even happening that much. Most of the time there are teams of 1, 2 or 3 moving around the map and having short encounters, where you have to have very high FPS skills to not get stomped constantly. You will find not much fun on these servers, if you don't posess these skills. But luckily the developer has already made a move to allow bigger servers, so officially there are 12v12 server supported, while the performance is even good enough to have modded servers of 21v21. This is where the true epic cluster♥♥♥♥y battles happen. It is still very important to know about the games deep mechanics, but a single poor player doesn't have a strong impact on these servers, and can learn and enjoy the game in a much more forgiving manner. Nevertheless I deeply recommend everyone to spend some time on the smaller servers and actively ask for help, so he may learn the mechanics of the game and decide for himself whether he wants to stick with the pros or go to a more casual higher population server.
There a very friendly community, that will gladly assist new players with the first steps. Additionally to vanilla servers they have servers for several awesome modifications running, and also all working community maps.

Having played Heroes of Steel (previous game by the same developers) I'm going to make a comparison. TBF is much more focused and mostly you aren't going to roam freely around the maps, but it's not a bad thing, since it makes the gaming experience more compact and probably more enjoyable for the average gamer. (In reality you can explore the maps as you wish, but it's dangerous because xenos are costantly spawning and there's a turn limit for XP bonus, if you're trying to obtain it).
Tactical combat and character development are excellent as in HoS, while the tech tree adds a layer of complexity, that makes up for the more linear structure of the game. Feeling of progression is also faster, and so the general pace of the game.
I can't decide which one I like more, it really depends if you prefer a fantasy or a sci-fi setting, and I like them both.
Pros:
+ better graphics and sounds than in HoS
+ more focused mission-based gameplay helps keeping a good pace
+ missions are not repetitive, objectives are varied and you need different approaches
+ more character types, with lots of possibilities for talent/gear customization
+ extensive tech tree that makes talent choice much less obvious than in HoS
(Very minor) Cons:
- as in HoS, music is mainly made of loops; there are some brilliant tunes among the lot, but also some that you'd wish to skip (but you can't, unless you exit the mission and reload)  (you can check my Extended Soundtrack mod if you wish, look for it in the Steam forum)
- unlike in HoS, the story isn't a very important part of the game, even if it shares the setting and the world lore of other games by the same developer (the Star Traders series).
- a bit shorter than HoS
Overall the game is great, and you should play it if you like turn based combat. Don't expect XCOM (I mean the old one), here there's a story that enfolds, and missions are pre-scripted. It's very rare that I keep playing a game after I've finished it once, and it happened with this one.
I also have to say that some of the few negative reviews insist on the fact that it's a mobile port or that it has a mobile feel, and have put really little time in actually playing the game. I've never played a game on a mobile device so I can't judge, all I know is that if you focus on the game's qualities you shouldn't really care if it's a port or not.

This game is alot of fun, but is really just a port of the mobile game. The gameplay is fun and addictive, there is micro DLC, which annoys me a bit, matchmaking is non-existant, and if you try to quit, it pulls an Infinite Warfare and stops responding.
Trash port, but still fun.

Wow, where do I start? I love this game.
After playing through "Dishonored" and getting stuck on a brutal mission in "Metal Gear Solid V", I needed a new stealth game. And then the magic happened: I visited the shop tho look for stealth games when the first recommended game that popped up was "Aragami". I decided to buy it without doing much research, because I had seen it before on some "top 10 games coming out in 2015/2016" video on youtube.
And boy do I NOT regret it.
You play as the "Aragami", a spirit summoned by a woman in need of help. She has been captured, and is beeing hold hostage, so you sneak and stab your way through all the levels to save her. That is all I'll tell you about the story.
The Gameplay is simple. Keyword beeing "simple", most people mistake "simple" for "easy". The first thing you will notice is, that the controlls and stealth mechanics are.... simple. You can walk and run for fast movements, and crouch for silence and cover. You are hard to see in the shadows, a little easier to spot in areas light up by the moonlight, and very easy to see on bright lit surfaces, like... next to a torch or a campfire. You unlock abilitys which will spice this up.
A big + in my book, is the co-op. Stealth games that allow co-op are rather rare. Tho the playerbase is pretty much non existant, or everyone play's private matches/singleplayer, so don't expect to be able to join some random game whenever you feel like. I've been playing with a friend who decided to quit midway because his computer can't run the game well on later levels, after that I got lucky once and actually found a random player. Both experiences where realy fun and satesfieing.
TL DR:
It's simple, it's fun, it has co-op. I highly recommend this indie game gem.

This game has the potential to do what Battleborn could not. it looks like it will take everything i loved about Battleborn and the few things i liked about overwatch and put them into one game.
That is, to make a first person hero class shooter with MOBA elements (a first person MOBA if you will).
The good:
The characters are interesting and familiar yet different enough to warrant their existance. The game modes are extremely team oriented.
It takes a more classic MOBA as far as selecting one character and using that one character through the entire game approach as opposed to Overwatch's on the fly character changes. (good for those who dont like the on the fly reactionary style of Overwatch)
EXTREMELY team oriented, no teamwork = no win
The bad:
matchmaking, like in Overwatch and Battleborn alike, Solo play is a deathwish, and 9 times out of 10 you either stomp or get stomped. bottom line, group play is almost a MUST.
Lack of game modes (currently). I understand this is only Beta, but id like to see game mode(s) involving creeps and a that classic moba style slowcrawl to the enemy base via destroying towers on your way there. in my opinion this kind of style worked very well in battleborn, and could definitely work well here.
Cannot change card loadouts.  okay, so you can put together loadouts unique to each character (up to 7 i believe)  that can be used for different situations and allow you to specialize each character in different ways. the problem is, while im okay with using just one character the entire game, id like to at least change the card loadouts, bring that ONE thing from overwatch just to a lesser extent so that you may adapt the character itself to the situation.
Overall, I highly reccommend this game to anyone who was/is a fan of battleborn, and if you like overwatch, its familiar enough that you could give it a try and have fun. And i truly think that if this game comes out of Beta with a solid Free-to-play model, instead of being sold outright, this game can contend with Overwatch, and if given enough depth can breath new life into the MOBA genre of game.
of course take my criticisms with a grain of salt, this is only beta after all.

A tactics game done right.
Here's the game in a nutshell: you lead a squad of totally not Space Marine Terminators in repurposed industrial suits who fight endless swarms of totally not tyranids aboard spaceships.
Your templars can level up, use different gear, be customised, etc - you know the drill.
The game mechanics are a cross between space hulk (action points, swarms of deadly melee aliens coming from everywhere, overwatch) and generic tactics game features (use of stealth, different classes, melee is actually viable).
New gear and skills are unlocked through big huge requisition tree.
Graphics is... okay, I'd say and music is scarce. There is a plot, but it's not important. All you need to know is that YOU GUIDE VALOROUS BATTLE-BROTHERS IN A NEVERENDING CRUSADE OF PURGATION AGAINST VILE XENO SCUM FOR THE GLORY OF THE MANKIND. And almost all of these totally not WH40K terms are said by your squad leader at some moments.
All of this might give you an impression that the game is a bland low-budget space hulk clone.
And you will be very wrong, because it is AWESOME hardcore tactics with deep gameplay, which only draws some inspiration from aforementioned space hulk. And did I say that the game is hard? I mean really hard, as in "your squad can be wiped on normal during tutorial" hard.
Also,the devs are super cool, they fix bugs quickly, add new content and implement features requested by community.
Verdict: go buy the game, its cheap and awesome, or Teh Emprah will smite you.

Having played Earth Defense Force: 2015 on the XBox 360, I had high hopes for the subsequent iteration. While Earth Defense Force: Insect Armageddon doesn't quite capture the magic of its predcessor, it's still an enjoyable sequel that should be considered by any fans of the franchise or newly interested gamers.
The staples of the series are all there--giant bugs, giant spaceships, and an endless supply of bullets and bombs, The game places more emphasis on a progression system that upends the simplicity of the previous game. Instead of killing bugs to get armor and weapons, you have to earn the weapons THEN upgrade the specific clase enough to unlock the weapon.
The familiar chaos of the series is still as campy as ever. Every building is destructible if enough rockets are thrown at it. Bugs fly in every direction.
Despite my issues with the class system, it makes the game more interesting in co-op.
Overall, it's a good game and any curious should pick it up during a sale.
